en: Oṃ, salutation to Śrī Gaṇeśa;
Oṃ, salutation to the Śrī Gurus. Peace. [This is] the preliminary prologue, the lotus-handed one.

Elsewhere, there are matters concerning the recitation of auspicious verses (*svastivācana*) and so forth, which are useful for all rites of pacification (*sarvaśāntikarma*) that have been extracted [from various sources].
Among those, first is the prayer to the venerable Guru (*śrīguruprārthanā*) and so forth:
"The Guru is Brahmā; the Guru is Viṣṇu; the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara."
The Guru is the Supreme Brahman manifest; salutation to that venerable Guru.
Therein, first is the invocation of the deities and so forth:
"I bow to that elephant-faced one, by saluting whom Vāgīśa and the others, being well-disposed, shall have their every purpose accomplished at the commencement of all undertakings."
I salute the great preceptor Subrahmaṇya, who shines like the moon, the king of the twice-born and a treasury of arts, for the attainment of my desires.

The thief who plunders the vast expanse of pride, envy, and the like; who crushes the embankment of the mountain-like mass of sins that fill the belly of every vice; who destroys the fistful of delusion held by those of dull intellect regarding the fruit of the knowledge of reality; and who pierces the threefold suffering—may he [protect you].
May he who tames even the untamed, the doer of good, the son of Śaṅkara, protect you with compassion.
Brahmā has four faces, Hari has two arms,
Śambhu has no eyes, and the Lord Bādarāyaṇa has no plow.
Kaśyapa, Bharadvāja, Vaśiṣṭha, Gautama,
Jamadagni, and Vasiṣṭha— these seven are indeed the great ṛṣis.
Manu and others were the authors of the Smṛtis who awakened [the knowledge of] action and Brahman;
Āpastamba and other sages were all solely devoted to Dharma.
These compassionate ones, who are always grateful and worthy of veneration by the twice-born,
have been brought here by us for our own great welfare.
May thousands of salutations be offered to that father, the omniscient embodiment, by whom this body was manifested for the sake of the seeker, acting as the venerable Guru.
Salutations to that Blessed Goddess, by whose power all the deities have attained an increase of their respective strengths, yet who herself remains devoid of such power.
In this work of printing, for the sake of pleasing the assembly of virtuous Brahmins,
may this effort be fruitful through their blessings.
The Lord, perceiving both virtues and faults, accepts the former with his head while he restrains the latter in his throat. He who grasps the moon and the poison is indeed the Supreme Lord.
For the wise, the learned, who are adorned with virtues, are being requested:
may they show their compassionate regard with respect for this collection of texts.
Salutations to the venerable gurus.
The ritual procedure for the recitation of auspicious benedictions (*svastivācana*) from the introductory section of the *Śānti-kamalākara*.
Om, Hari!
For the pacification of all obstacles, one should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who wears white garments, who is moon-colored, who has four arms, and whose face is serene.
That alone is the auspicious moment, that alone is the fortunate day; that alone is the strength of the stars, and that alone is the strength of the moon.
That alone is the power of knowledge, and that alone is the power of destiny—O Lord of Lakṣmī, I remember Your pair of feet.
May it be auspicious for a moment; may it be well-established!
The gods generated divine Speech, which cattle of every form speak.
May she, yielding us vigor with her lowing, come to us like a cow that is well-milked.

May it be auspicious for a moment; may it be well-established. May there be auspiciousness unto the glorious Śrīnivāsa, the Lord of Veṅkaṭa, whose limbs are wondrously beautiful and who bestows desired objects.
Wherever the Lord of Yogins, Kṛṣṇa, is, and wherever Pārtha, the wielder of the bow, is, there will surely be prosperity, victory, well-being, and steadfastness; this is my conviction.
I constantly go for refuge to that unborn Lord Hari, by whose remembrance a person becomes a vessel for all auspiciousness.
For those in whose hearts dwells the Blessed Lord Hari, the abode of all auspiciousness, there is no inauspiciousness at any time or in any undertaking whatsoever.
They have gained their wealth, they have achieved victory; how could there be defeat for those in whose hearts Janārdana, dark as a blue lotus, resides?
Again and again, I bow to Śrī Rāma, the remover of calamities, the bestower of all prosperity, and the delight of the world.
O auspiciousness of all that is auspicious, O Śivā, O accomplisher of all goals,
O refuge, O Goddess of the three eyes, O Nārāyaṇī, salutations to you!
Salutations to Śrī Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa; salutations to Śrī Arundhatī and Vasiṣṭha; salutations to Śrī Umā and Maheśvara; salutations to Śrī Sītā and Rāma;
salutations to Śrī Vāṇī and Hiraṇyagarbha; salutations to Śrī Mātā and Pitṛ.

Salutations to Śrī Śacī and Purandara; salutations to the venerable Ācāryas; salutations to the venerable Gurus; salutations to all Brāhmaṇas and great men. May there be prosperity! Om. Tat Sat. Aum. Let these spirits and piśācas who burden the earth rise up;
without opposition from them, I shall commence the work of Brahmā.

Having restrained the breaths: *Oṃ bhūḥ, Oṃ bhuvaḥ, Oṃ suvaḥ, Oṃ mahaḥ, Oṃ janaḥ, Oṃ tapaḥ, Oṃ satyaṃ, Oṃ tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt, Oṃ āpo jyotī raso amṛtaṃ brahma bhūrbhuvassuvaḥ oṃ.*
For the purpose of destroying all the misfortunes acquired by me, and for the sake of pleasing the venerable Supreme Lord, [I offer this] directed toward the venerable Supreme Lord.

On this auspicious and beautiful moment, today, in the second *parārtha* of the current Brahmā, in the Śvetavarāha Kalpa, in the Vaivasvata Manvantara, in the first quarter of the Kali Yuga, in Jambūdvīpa, in Bharatavarṣa, in the region of Bharatakhaṇḍa, in the southern direction from Meru, in the middle region between the Kṛṣṇā and Godāvarī rivers, in a beautiful house, in the presence of all the deities, Brāhmaṇas, Hari, and Hara, in this present year of the Vyāhārīka lunar calendar... in the [specific] year... in the [specific] solstice... [and so forth].

In the year ... , in the month ... , in the fortnight ... , on the lunar day ... , in the auspicious constellation, auspicious yoga, and auspicious karaṇa—on this auspicious lunar day characterized by such specific qualities—the illustrious one of the ... gotra, named ..., [performs this] for the sake of the illustrious one of the ... gotra, named ... .

For the destruction of all my accumulated sins, for the sake of pleasing Śrī Parameśvara, and for the sake of purification, prosperity, peace, and spiritual advancement as an integral part of the rite I intend to begin, I shall first perform the *svastivācana* and *puṇyāhavācana* together with the great men; and at the outset of that, for the sake of completing it without obstacles.
Oṃ! We invoke you, the Lord of the hosts, the sage among sages, the most highly praised, the supreme ruler of sacred prayers, O Brahmaṇaspati; hear us with your aids and sit upon your seat.

I invoke, establish, and worship Śrī Mahāgaṇapati, who is peaceful, accompanied by his limbs, weapons, vehicle, and powers, together with his wife, sons, and retinue, and who is of gracious countenance.
Oṃ, O Anunīti, bestow upon us again sight, again breath, and here, enjoyment.
May we long behold the rising sun; being gracious toward my family, grant us well-being.

Oṃ. The vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed nectar; the waters are nectar. Thus, one invokes the vital breaths back to their respective places. "Be firm! Be a granter of boons! Be well-pleased! Make your seat firm!
One should meditate upon Viṣṇu, who wears white garments, who is moon-colored, four-armed, and has a gracious countenance, for the sake of the pacification of all obstacles.

Having performed the sixteen-fold worship (ṣoḍaśopacāra-pūjā) according to one’s wealth, according to the extent of the ritual, and according to the available space— beginning with "I meditate upon [the Lord]" (śrī mahāgaṇādhipataye namaḥ dhyāyāmi) and so forth—
one should recite: "Sumukha, Ekadanta, Kapila, Gajakarṇaka, Lambodara, Vikaṭa, Vighnarāja, and Gaṇādhipa."
Dhūmaketu, Gaṇādhyakṣa, Phālacandra, Gajānana, Vakratuṇḍa, Śūrpakarṇa, Heraṃba, and Skandapūrvaja.
Whoever should recite or even hear these sixteen names at the commencement of learning, at a wedding, at entering [a new home], or likewise at departing;
In battle and in all undertakings, no obstacle shall arise for him.
Homage to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati! I offer this golden, divine mantra-flower; I offer self-prostration, circumambulation, and salutation.
O curved-tusked one of massive body, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns;
O God, grant me freedom from obstacles at all times in all my undertakings.
O Gaṇādhipa, O Lord, whatever has been worshipped by me— whether deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in devotion— may that become complete for you.

Through this worship with the sixteen services, beginning with the invocation of meditation (*dhyānāvāhana*), may the Blessed One, the Great Lord of Ganas (*Mahāgaṇādhipati*), who is the soul of all, be well-pleased, well-satisfied, and become the bestower of boons. May there be no obstacle in the auspicious rite to follow. I receive the grace of Śrī Mahāgaṇapati upon my head.
The worship of Śrī Vighneśvara is completed.
Oṃ tatsat. Oṃ! Hear this my call, O Varuṇa; be gracious to me today. Seeking your protection, I approach you with a prayer, praising you and seeking refuge in you.
O Varuṇa, as the sacrificer offering the oblation, may you be without anger; do not steal away our common life-span.
Oṃ bhūḥ, I invoke Varuṇa; Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I invoke Varuṇa; Oṃ suvaḥ, I invoke Varuṇa.

Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ! O Varuṇa, I invoke you; O Varuṇa, I offer this worship consisting of the sixteen services, beginning with invocation, meditation, and so forth. Through this worship of Varuṇa, may Varuṇa be pleased.
May Lord Hari— the beginningless one, the master of masters, who exists as the essence of all— be present at all times, in all places, and in all undertakings for the increase of my auspiciousness.

With the *pavitra* in hand and having performed the regulation of breath (*prāṇāyāma*), [he says]: "On this day, in this lunar date (*tithi*), for the sake of increasing the prosperity of ourselves and our families, and for the attainment of all auspiciousness, I shall perform a rite of pacification (*śāntikarma*). Within that rite of pacification, for the sake of accomplishing the bestowal of the most excellent and supreme auspicious fruits for those among the nine planets—beginning with Āditya—who are situated in favorable positions..."

Aiming for the nine planetary deities beginning with Āditya, and for the sake of pleasing the nine planetary deities beginning with Āditya, I shall perform the rite known as Navagraha-makha. At the outset of this, for the sake of purification, prosperity, and auspiciousness, I shall perform the *puṇyāhavācana* along with the great assembly. Oṃ! May it be an auspicious day; may there be long life. May the waters be auspicious. May there be goodwill. May there be well-being and freedom from calamity. Oṃ! Worship, worship ye, O Priyamedhas, worship!
Let the sons also worship, and worship boldly like a fortress.
Oṃ! Her whose door is fragrance, who is invincible, eternally nourishing, and bestowing prosperity;
the sovereign of all beings—her, Śrī, I invoke here.
May the fragrances protect you; may there be auspiciousness.
Oṃ, let these flowering dūrvā grasses ascend toward this supreme goal;
these are the lakes, the lotuses, and the abodes of the ocean.

May the unbroken grains protect you; may there be long life. May the flowers protect you; may there be auspiciousness. May the betel leaves protect you; may there be sovereignty. May the sacrificial fees protect you; may there be much to give. May there be your own spiritual welfare. May Prajāpati be pleased. May there be peace. Having made the syllable *Om*, which is the beginning of all Vedic sacrifices, rituals, and undertakings of action so that they proceed auspiciously and beautifully, I shall, with your permission, cause the declaration of the holy day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) to be recited. Let it be recited.
Oṃ! May we hear with our ears what is auspicious, O Gods; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious, while our limbs remain firm.
With steady members and praising bodies, may we attain that lifespan ordained by the Gods.
Oṃ! May the giver of wealth grant us the wealth of the swift one; may the giver of wealth grant the beloved wealth of the noble man.
May the giver of wealth grant us a hero-filled dwelling; may the giver of wealth grant us long life.
Savitar from behind, Savitar from the front, Savitar from above, Savitar from below—may Savitar impel us toward every success;
may he grant us long life.
Being born, he becomes ever new; as the banner of the days, he goes at the head of the dawns.
He ordains the portion for the gods; for his arrival, the moon-streaked one bestows long life.
May the waters moisten me for life, for long-livedness, and for splendor.
Oṃ! You, whom I, a mortal, calling upon you with a yearning heart, invoke repeatedly;
O Agni, source of all that is born, bestow glory upon us, and through our progeny may we attain immortality.
O Agni Jātavedas, for this well-performed deed, create a pleasant and comfortable world for us;
may we attain wealth consisting of horses, sons, heroic offspring, and cattle, and may there be well-being for us.
I sprinkle you with the Yajus for the sake of progeny, long life, and wealth.

Taking the southern pitcher, he pours a little water into the eastern pitcher [saying]: "May there be long life! May you attend to us! We are attentive. May you be gracious; we are pleased. May there be peace! May there be prosperity! May there be longevity! May there be health! May there be well-being and auspiciousness in our work! May there be success in our work! May there be success in having sons! May there be success in the Vedas! May there be success in the Śāstras!"

May there be abundance of wealth and grain. May there be the attainment of desired objects. In the northeast, outside the area, may there be the removal of misfortune. Thus, one should sprinkle water in the northeast region between the two jars. May whatever sin exists there be averted. May whatever is auspicious come to pass. May all the planets—Venus, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Saturn, Rāhu, Ketu, and the Moon, with the Sun as their leader—be pleased. May the lunar days (*tithis*), the *karaṇas*, the *muhūrtas*, the birth asterism (*janmanakṣatra*), and the deities of the directions be pleased.

"In the south-western direction, may the terrible things be pacified; may evils be pacified; may calamities be pacified. Thus one should sprinkle water. In the first jar: "May auspicious things increase; may the seasons be auspicious; may the medicinal herbs be auspicious; may the trees be auspicious; may day and night be auspicious. In the north, may there be no obstacle to auspicious deeds; may there be ever-increasing great prosperity; may ever-more auspicious actions be accomplished."

May the Viśvedevas, with Agni at their head, be pleased. May the Mothers, with Maheśvarī at their head, be pleased. May the hosts of Maruts, with Indra at their head, be pleased. May the hosts of Ṛṣis, with Vasiṣṭha at their head, be pleased. May all the gods, with Śrī Viṣṇu at their head, be pleased. May all the planets, with Āditya at their head, be pleased. May the Ṛṣis, the Chaṇḍāṃśas, the Teachers, the Vedas, the Sacrifices, and the Dakṣiṇās be pleased. May Brahman and the Brāhmaṇas be pleased.

May Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara be pleased; may Śraddhā and Medhā be pleased; may the blessed Nāgāyana be pleased; may the blessed Parjanya be pleased; may the blessed Lord Mahāsena be pleased; may the blessed Pitāmahas be pleased. May these blessings be true. May the auspicious times be proclaimed. Thus one should sprinkle. Oṃ, like a singer of the Sāmans, O bird, you sing; like a son of Brahmā, you recite at the libations.
Like a vigorous bull lowing toward a cow in heat, O Śakuni, announce auspiciousness to us from every side; O Śakuni, announce merit to us from all directions.
Speak auspiciously, O Śakuni; speak what is good. Sitting silently, consider our well-wishing thought.
When you fly up and cry out like a karkarī lute, may we, possessing brave sons, establish great speech in this dwelling.
He sacrifices with the *yājyā* verse; the *yājyā* is the sacrifice itself. Fortune is auspicious; he thus brings about auspicious fortune and consecrates auspicious fortune.

"Oṃ, that which is the auspicious constellation, let him perform [the rite] before the dawn. Indeed, when the sun rises, the constellation disappears. At whatever time the sun has gone there, where one might see the last [star], at that time he should perform whatever he intends to do; he performs it on an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*).

Oṃ. Whatever constellation it may be, one should perform [the rite] before dawn; for when the sun rises, the constellation has already passed. One should perform whatever task one intends to do at that point where the sun has gone as far as the last [star] can still be seen; thus one performs it on an auspicious day.

Oṃ. These indeed are the lunar mansions of Yama; they are the very same as the lunar mansions of the gods. One should perform whatever rite he intends to do under them; thus he performs it on an auspicious day.

Thus [one should say] "Salutation" four times. Then, one should say three times: "Oṃ, may you declare it an auspicious day; Oṃ, an auspicious day! [And: "Oṃ, for the sake of well-being, let us invoke Vāyu and Soma; Svasti is the lord of the world's course."
May Bṛhaspati with his entire host be for our well-being; may the Ādityas be for our well-being.

The Ādityas rise with well-being; they depart on the path of well-being. For the sake of well-being they rise; for the sake of well-being they know; for the sake of well-being they rise; for the sake of well-being they go forth.

Oṃ! Tārkṣya is the bringer of well-being, the one with unharmed limbs, the great wonder, the one who possesses the power of the gods; he is the slayer of Asuras, the mighty friend in battles, like a great vessel for glory, as if crossing over waters.
I, with palms joined in reverence, seek refuge in Aṅhomuc, Āṅgirasa, Saṃgaya, Svastyātreya, and Tārkṣya of the mind; may there be well-being for us, and may fearlessness prevail in times of distress.
May Indra of far-reaching fame grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being;
may Tārkṣya, whose wheel-rims are unhurt, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati bestow well-being upon us.

"Oṃ! May the eight gods, the Vasus, who are worthy of Soma, and the four goddesses, the ageless Śraviṣṭhās—may they protect the sacrifice from the far distance, bestowing the year-long, immortal, and auspicious well-being. Thus, praying for prosperity, [he says]: "May you, sirs, pronounce auspiciousness for me and my family, granting long life! May there be long life and auspiciousness! Thus three times. "Oṃ! May you, sirs, pronounce auspiciousness! Oṃ! Auspiciousness! Thus three times.

"Oṃ! May we attain prosperity; may we win the hymn through sacrifice; may our prayer reach you both. Come hither! The fame, the cooked honey within the cows—the portion of beings—has fulfilled the desire of the Aśvins. Thinking, "May I attain all prosperity," he indeed encompassed him from the front with vigor (*tejas*), in the middle with the meters, and before his injury with the *gāyatrī* verses. Having encompassed him on all sides with the twelve-day rite, he attained all prosperity. He who knows thus attains all prosperity.

Oṃ! May we prosper through our offerings and through homage. May Mitra the god be our friend; may there be for us the attainment of friendship. Worshipping the Anurādhas with oblations, may we live a hundred autumns with all our heroes.

Oṃ! Threefold indeed is the prosperity of the gods; three are the meters, three are the pressings, and these worlds are three. By means of prosperity and power, he thus establishes himself in these worlds.

Simultaneously grasping the southern and northern pitchers with his left and right hands, [he says] over the eastern pitcher: "May there be well-being, may there be the prosperity of an auspicious day; may a full hundred years of life be attained... may there be the increase of the lineage; may there be peace, nourishment, and contentment. Again, may there be welfare for cows and Brahmins. May all perfections be attained; may the Lord Vāstoṣpati be pleased—may you all say this! If they respond, "May the Lord Vāstoṣpati be pleased," [the rite is concluded].

Oṃ! O Maruts, you whose vows are pure, I offer these pure oblations to you who are pure. I impel the pure one toward the pure ones, the pure one who dwells in the midst of the pure. Through the Eternal Law (ṛta), they have come as those who perform true deeds; born pure, they are pure and purifying. Agni, whose vow is most pure, is the pure inspired singer (vipra) and the pure monkey (kapi); pure and unoffered, he shines brightly.
Oṃ! O Agni, your pure, bright, and radiant flames rise up; your rays are like the stars of heaven.
Oṃ! Come now, let us praise Indra, the pure one, with a pure *sāman*;
may the pure, swelling, and blessing-bestowing one be exhilarated by pure hymns.
O Indra, come pure with your pure aids;
being pure, bestow wealth upon us. Being pure, drink the Soma offered by us.
O Indra, as one who is pure, you bring wealth; as one who is pure, you grant treasures to the donor.
Pure, you strike down the Vṛtras; pure, you strive to win the prize.

Oṃ! The immortal benefit for the Brāhmaṇa is that by which the gods always purify themselves with the filter. May the Pāvamānī verses purify me with that thousand-streamed [filter]. The filter belonging to Prajāpati is golden and has a hundred rays; through it, we who know the Veda purify the purified Veda. May Indra purify me with good guidance, Soma with truth, and Varuṇa with harmony. May King Yama purify me with his crushing powers, and Jātavedas purify me with the strengthening [power].
Thus, one should sprinkle oneself with the water from the eastern jar:
"May the deities of the eastern direction and the officiating priests purify me!
May the months and the ancestors purify me in the southern direction!"
In the western direction, may the houses and cattle purify themselves;
in the northern direction, may the waters, the plants, and the lords of the forest purify themselves;
in the upward direction, may the lord of the sacrifice purify himself.
Thus one should purify the directions.

To these Brahmins of various lineages (*gotra*) and various names, who are the embodiments of the nine planets beginning with Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, Umā-Maheśvara, and Āditya, and who have performed the recitation of the *puṇyāha* and the chanting of mantras—[to them] I offer this mental *svasti-vācana*, the chanting of mantras, and a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of a limited amount of gold; [this is] *svāhā*. It is not mine.

Oṃ, O Lord of the Dwelling, acknowledge us! Be our own home, free from disease for us. When we come to you with great desire, be pleased; grant well-being to our bipeds and well-being to our quadrupeds. O Lord of the Dwelling, may we always partake of your auspicious, golden, and path-providing protection. Grant us excellent security in our use [of your abode]. Do you all protect us always with blessings. O Lord of the Dwelling, these [beings] of every form enter you; as a friend, be very kind to us as we prosper—grant us fortune and splendor.

Oṃ! May we ascend Tārkṣya, the auspicious one, whose rim is unbroken, the great wonder, the wind among the gods, the slayer of Asuras, the friend of Indra, the subduer of the arrogant, and the possessor of lofty glory—just as one boards a ship. I take refuge with my mind in Aṃhomuc, Māṅgalya, Saṃgaya, Svastyatreya, and Dārkṣya. With hands joined in reverence, I seek the Protector; may there be well-being for us and fearlessness in times of distress. Auspiciousness! Good fortune!

Peaceful is the earth, auspicious is the mid-air; O Goddess Heaven, may there be no fear for us. Auspicious be the quarters, the intermediate directions, and the upward directions; may the waters protect us from every side. Peace, peace, peace everywhere—Hari, Om Tat Sat. Thus ends the Puṇyāhavācana ceremony. Not the Graha-makha.

Having sipped water (ācamya), seated upon *darbha* grass, holding *darbha* blades, with *pavitra* grass in his hands, and together with his wife, he performs breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and makes the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). Having obtained permission from the assembly (*pariṣad*), and having performed the *kṛcchra* penance, at the time of the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) for the ritual about to be commenced—whatever planets [or influences] are causing misfortune...

For the sake of attaining perfection, for the purpose of increasing longevity by warding off untimely death, and for the propitiation of the nine planetary deities beginning with Āditya, I shall perform the sacrifice known as Navagraha-makha; having performed its preliminary rites, such as the delineation of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and everything up to the spreading of the sacred grass (paristaraṇa), one should perform the worship of the planets in the northeast direction.

In the center is a circular mandala for Āditya; in the northeast, a bow-shaped one for Budha; in the north, a long quadrangular one for Bṛhaspati; in the southeast, a triangle for Śukra; in the west, a bow-shaped one for Śanaiścara; in the southwest, a winnowing-basket-shaped one for Rāhu; and in the northwest, a banner-shaped one for Ketu.

For Āditya, fuel-sticks of *arka* wood; for Soma, *pālāśa*; for Aṅgāraka, *khādira*; for Budha, *apāmārga*; for Bṛhaspati, *aśvattha*; for Śukra, *audumbara*; for Śanaiścara, *śamī*; for Rāhu, *dūrvā*; and for Ketu, *kuśa* grass.

For the Sun (Sūrya): regarding the mantra beginning with "Ā kṛṣṇena," Hiraṇyastūpa is the seer (ṛṣi), Savitṛ is the deity (devatā), Triṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ). With reference to the deity Sūrya-graha, for the purpose of pleasing [him], and for the sake of accomplishing the grace of the deity Sūrya-graha, this is the application (viniyoga) in the worship of Sūrya-graha together with his presiding deities (adhidevatā) and counter-presiding deities (pratyadhidevatā). The placement upon the hands; the placement upon the heart and other limbs.
With *akṛṣṇena*, salutation to the thumbs; with *aṅguṣṭhābhyām*, salutation to the heart; with *rajasā*, salutation to the index fingers; with *tarjanībhyām*, salutation to the head, *svāhā*;
with *niveśayan*, salutation to the middle fingers; with *madhyamābhyām*, salutation to the tuft, *vauṣaṭ*.
To the immortal and the mortal, to the two Amānikas, salutation to the armor, *huṃ*.
With the golden chariot of Savitṛ, to the little fingers, salutation to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*.
The god approaches, beholding the earth, to the palms and backs of the hands, salutation to the weapon, *phaṭ*.

Thus is the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*), the placement on the heart and other limbs (*hṛdayādinyāsa*), and the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) with the mantra *bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ oṃ*.
The Meditation (*dhyāna*):

In the center of the altar, upon a charming lotus, is the Sun-god seated in his chariot within the pericarp. His body has the brilliance of molten gold, he possesses seven horses and seven reins, and has seven arms. Born in the noble lineage of Kāśyapa, endowed with manifold virtues, and born of the wife named Kālī, he faces the east, holding a lotus in his hand. Seated upon a lotus, with lotus-like hands, two-armed, possessing the luster of a lotus, drawn by seven steeds, the Sun-god, the protector of the world and wearer of a crown—may that Lord bestow grace upon me.
With his golden chariot, Savitṛ, the god, comes beholding all beings, moving through the dark space, establishing both the immortal and the mortal.
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! O Sūryagraha, come here! O Sūryagraha, you who are red in color, wearing red garlands and garments, and possessing a red parasol and banner...

Adorned with chariot banners and the like, mounted upon a divine chariot, circumambulating Mount Meru, facing the east, seated upon a lotus, two-armed, possessing seven horses and seven reins, sovereign of the Kaliṅga country, of the Kāśyapa lineage, born on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha in the Prabhava year under the Viśākhā asterism, lord of the zodiac sign of Leo, joined with a Sunday, wearing a crown, seated upon a branch, accompanied by his wife, sons, and retinue, within the circle of the planets— [Visualize him thus.]
Upon this wheat grain, I invoke, establish, and worship the Sun during an eclipse.
The presiding deity (adhidevatā):

"We choose Agni as the messenger, the invoker (hotṛ), the all-knowing, the one of excellent wisdom for this sacrifice. I invoke Agni to the south of the Sun planet, together with his limbs, weapons, and vehicle, accompanied by his Śakti, wife, sons, and retinue.
*Pratyadhivata*:

To Rudra, the wise one, the most bountiful, the most powerful—we shall speak what is most auspicious to his heart. [Regarding] the presiding deity (*pratyadhidaivata*) of the solar eclipse, Rudra, together with his limbs (*sāṅga*), weapons (*sāyudha*), and vehicle (*savāhana*), accompanied by his consort, sons, and retinue—I invoke Rudra from the north of the solar eclipse; I establish him; I worship him.

For the Moon: regarding the mantra "caṃdra graham u āpyāyasva," Gautama is the seer (ṛṣi), Soma is the deity (devatā), and Gāyatrī is the meter (chanda). Its application (viniyoga) is for the propitiation of the Moon planet, for the sake of attaining the grace of the Moon planet together with its presiding deity (adhidevatā).
[This is followed by] the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa) and the ritual placement on the heart and other limbs (hṛdayādinyāsa).
Oṃ āpyāyasva; salutation to the two thumbs, salutation to the heart.
Sametu te; salutation to the two index fingers, svāhā to the head.
Viśvataḥ; salutation to the two middle fingers, vauṣaṭ to the tuft of hair.
To Somavṛṣṇiya, to the two index fingers, salutation; to the armor, *huṃ*;
to Bhavāvāja, to the two little fingers, salutation; to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*;
to Saṃgatha, to the palms and backs of the hands, salutation; to the weapon, *ṣaṭ*.
Thus is the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*), the placement on the heart and other limbs (*hṛdayādinyāsa*), and the binding of the directions with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ.
The visualization (*dhyāna*):

In the south-eastern quarter, born of the lineage of Atri, the son of the ten horses (the Sun), born in the region of Yamunā, facing west upon a square pedestal, bearing a mace in his limb, and possessing the nature of the Himalayas—may that god, clad in white garments, with a white body, wearing a crown, possessing white luster, holding a staff, and having two arms, whose feet are like the nectar-essence of the moon and who wears a diadem, bestow blessings upon me.

The mantra: *āpyāyasva sametu te viśvataḥ soma vṛṣṇyam | bhava vājasya saṃgathe* || *oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ*. O Moon, come here! [I invoke] the Moon: white in color, with white fragrance, wearing white flowers, white garlands, and white garments; adorned with a white parasol, banner, chariot, flag, and so forth; mounted upon a divine chariot; circumambulating the peacock; drawn by ten horses as his vehicle; facing westward; and having two arms.

I invoke and install for worship, and pay homage to the Lord Moon (Candragraha), who holds a staff, is the ruler of the Yamunā region, belongs to the Ātreya *gotra*, was born on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika in the Nandana year under the Kṛttikā asterism, is the lord of the sign of Cancer, wears a crown, is joined with the moon-month (*indumāsa*), is seated comfortably, is accompanied by his wife, sons, and retinue, and has entered the planetary mandala; in this ritual context, in the south-eastern direction of the solar eclipse within a square mandala upon a mound of rice and grain.
The presiding deity (*adhidevatā*):...
In the waters, O Soma, you have proclaimed all healing medicines;
and Agni, who brings welfare to all, and the waters, which possess all healing powers.

I invoke, establish, and worship the deities presiding over the lunar eclipse— Apaḥ, along with their limbs, weapons, and vehicles, accompanied by Śakti, Pati, Putra, and their retinues— to the south of the lunar eclipse.
The individual presiding deity: Gaurī has lowed, fashioning the waters; she who is one-footed, two-footed, and three-footed;
she who has become eight-footed and nine-footed; she of a thousand syllables in the highest heaven.

To the north of the lunar eclipse, I invoke, establish, and worship Gaurī—the secondary presiding deity (pratyadhidevatā) of the lunar eclipse—along with her limbs, weapons, and vehicle, accompanied by her Śakti, sons, husband, and retinue.

For Aṅgāraka: "Oṃ kuje grahama agniyūrdhe" is the mantra. Virūpa is the seer (ṛṣi). The planet deity Aṅgāraka is the divinity (devatā). Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ). The application (viniyoga) is for the propitiation of the planet Aṅgāraka, together with his presiding deity (adhidevatā) and counter-deity (pratyadhidevatā), for the sake of attaining success.
The Karanyāsa—the assignment [of mantras] to the heart and other limbs:
"Agni is the head," with the two thumbs, *namaḥ* to the heart;
"the summit of heaven," with the two index fingers, *vauṣaṭ* to the tuft (*śikhā*).
To these two ring fingers, *namaḥ* to the armor (*kavaca*), *huṃ*.
To the little fingers, *namaḥ* to the three eyes (*netratraya*), *vauṣaṭ*.
To the palms and backs of the hands, *namaḥ* to the weapon (*astra*), *phaṭ*.
Thus is the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*), the ritual placement on the heart and other limbs (*hṛdayādinyāsa*), and the binding of the directions with "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ.
The visualization (*dhyāna*):
[The deity] holds a mace in his right hand, carries a trident, grants boons, faces the south, and is intensely red.
Where is this region of Avanti? Born in that Bharadvāja lineage, he resides in Sthāṇvīśvara.
May the son of the Earth— red as a hibiscus, red-bodied, wearing a diadem, four-armed, riding upon a ram,
wielding a mace, a discus, and a trident— always be my peaceful granter of boons.
The mantra:
Oṃ. Agni, the upward-tending one, the summit of heaven, the lord of this earth—he quickens the seeds of the waters.

Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ! O Planet Aṅgāraka, come hither! O Planet Aṅgāraka, come hither! [I invoke] Planet Aṅgāraka, who is red in color, wearing red flowers, red garlands, and red garments; adorned with a red parasol, banner, chariot, and flags; mounted upon a divine chariot; circumambulating Mount Meru; having a ram as his vehicle; and facing the south.

Four-armed, bearing a mace, a trident, and a spear; lord of the Avanti country; of the Bhāradvāja lineage; born under the constellation Pūrva-phalgunī on the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada in the Akṣaya year; lord of the zodiac signs Aries and Scorpio; invoked by Bhauma-nāsara; wearing a crown; seated comfortably together with his wife, son, and retinue; entered into this planetary mandala in the southern quarter of the Sun planet.
Upon a triangular-shaped mandala made of one āḍhaka of grain, I invoke, establish, and worship the planet Aṅgāraka.
Adhidevatā: Oṃ, O Earth, be pleasant, free from thorns, and a place of rest for us;
grant us wide-spreading protection.

I invoke, establish, and worship the Earth, the presiding deity of the planet Aṅgāraka, together with her limbs, weapons, and vehicle, accompanied by her husband, power, sons, and retinue; I invoke the Earth from the right side of the planet Aṅgāraka.
The presiding deity—Oṃ: We invoke the two lords of the field with a beneficial hymn;
having nourished our cattle and horses, may they grant us all prosperity so that we may behold them.

I invoke, establish, and worship Kṣetrapālaka, together with his limbs, weapons, and vehicle, accompanied by his Śakti, wife, and sons, as the secondary presiding deity (pratyadhidevatā) of the planet Aṅgāraka, to the north of the planet Aṅgāraka.

Regarding Budha—the mantra "O Budha planet, awaken" (udbudhyasva): Madhu Canda is the seer (ṛṣi), the planet Budha is the deity (devatā), and Triṣṭubh is the meter (chaṃdaḥ). Its application (viniyoga) is for the propitiation of the planet Budha, for the sake of the accomplishment of the planet Budha together with the presiding deity (adhidevatā) and the counter-presiding deity (pratyadhidevatā) of the sacrificer.
Mantra:
*kapanyāsa* (finger placement); *hṛdayādinyāsa* (placement on the heart and other parts): "O Fire, awaken! *Namaḥ* to both thumbs; *namaḥ* to the heart."
Having awakened him, [one should touch him] with the two index fingers: *namaḥ śirase svāhā*.
With the two middle fingers: *iṣṭāpūrte saṃsṛjethām namaḥ śikhāyai vauṣaṭ*.
And with the two ring fingers: *ayaṃ ca namaḥ kavacāya huṃ*.

"Furthermore, making the father young again... *kaniṣṭhakābhyāṃ namaḥ*. To the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*. 'Thou art the thread stretched out by the weaver'... *karatalakarapṛṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*. To the weapon, *phaṭ*.

Thus is the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*). The ritual placement on the heart and other limbs (*hṛdayādinyāsa*). The binding of the directions (*digbandha*) with the mantra: *bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaroṃ*."
Dhyāna:
Facing north, born in Magadha, seated upon a lion, belonging to the Ātreya gotra, stationed within a circle of arrows;
holding a sword, shield, thigh-bone, and mace, he is yellowish-white, bestowing boons, and situated in the northeast quarter.
Clad in yellow garments, with a golden body, wearing a crown, four-armed, holding a staff and being gentle,
bearing a shield and a sword, having beautiful thighs, mounted upon a lion, the boon-granting Budha (Mercury) is thus described.
Oṃ! Awaken, O Agni; be watchful for me. Unite us with what is desirable and what is well-performed. Make our father young again; let him extend this thread of life once more.
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! O planet Budha, come here!

The planet Budha is yellow in color, with yellow fragrance, yellow flowers, and wearing yellow garlands and garments; he is adorned with a yellow parasol, banner, chariot, and flags; he is mounted upon a divine chariot, circumambulating Mount Meru, and has a lion as his vehicle; facing north, he is the sovereign of the Magadha country, four-armed, holding a sword and a shield; he belongs to the Ātreyasa Gotra and was born on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha in the Saumya year under the constellation Uttaraphalgunī.

I invoke, establish, and worship the planet Mercury (Budha), the lord of the signs Virgo and Gemini, associated with Wednesday, wearing a crown, seated comfortably, accompanied by his wife and sons, who has entered the circle of planets in this ritual, in the eastern direction of the solar mandala, within a bow-shaped diagram, upon a heap of mung beans. Adhidevatā—
Oṃ. Viṣṇu strode across this; in three places he planted his step.
The whole world is encompassed by his measure.
I invoke, establish, and worship Viṣṇu, the presiding deity of the planet Mercury, together with his limbs, weapons, and vehicle, accompanied by his Śakti, wife, sons, and retinue.
The Counter-Presiding Deity (Pratyadhidevatā):
Oṃ, the Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet.
Having encompassed the earth on all sides, he stands transcending it by the measure of ten fingers.

To the south of the planet Budha, I invoke, install, and worship the presiding deity Nārāyaṇa, together with his limbs, weapons, and vehicle, accompanied by his Śakti, wife, sons, and retinue. I invoke, install, and worship Viṣṇu for the sake of the planet Budha.
The presiding deity:
Oṃ, the Puruṣa has a thousand heads; he has a thousand eyes and a thousand feet. Having pervaded the earth on all sides, he transcended it by ten fingers' breadth.

To the presiding deity of the planet Budha, Nārāyaṇa, together with his consort, weapons, and vehicle, accompanied by his Śakti, wife, sons, and retinue—to the north of the planet Budha, I invoke Nārāyaṇa, I install him, and I worship him.
[For] Bṛhaspati—the planet Guru.

Regarding the mantra *bṛhaspate atiyadarya*: Gṛtsamada is the seer (*ṛṣi*); the planet Bṛhaspati is the deity (*devatā*); the Jagatī is the meter (*chandaḥ*). For the sake of attaining the grace of the planet Bṛhaspati, together with his presiding deity (*adhidevatā*) and counter-deity (*pratyadhidevatā*), this is the application (*viniyoga*) in the worship of the planet Bṛhaspati.
The ritual placement (nyāsa) of the limbs—the placement of the heart and other parts:
"O Bṛhaspati, that which exceeds the worthy" (Ṛgveda 4.50.1)—to the two thumbs, *namaḥ*; to the heart, *namaḥ*.
"Shining, he has shone forth" (Ṛgveda 4.50.2)—to the two index fingers, *namaḥ*; to the head, *svāhā*.
To the middle fingers, *namaḥ* to the *kratumat* [mantra] for the *śikhā*, *vauṣaṭ*.
To the ring fingers, *namaḥ* to the *yad dīdayac chavasā* [mantra] for the *kavaca*, *huṃ*.
To the little fingers, *namaḥ* to the *ṛcaprajāta* [mantra] for the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*.
"Bestow wonderful wealth! Salutation to the palms and backs of the hands; *astra* to the weapon, *phaṭ*.

Thus is the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*). Then follows the ritual placement on the heart and other limbs (*hṛdayādinyāsa*), and the binding of the directions with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ."
Dhyāna:
On a gentle, very long, and square pedestal, Aṅgiras faces east by nature;
holding a staff, a rosary, and a water-vessel, this lord of the gods, bestowing boons, resides in the land known as Sindhu.
Clad in golden garments, with a golden body, wearing a crown, four-armed, the preceptor of the gods, and serene;
nevertheless, holding a staff and a water-pot, as well as a rosary, may he be the granter of boons to me.
O Bṛhaspati, that which surpasses the enemy, which is worthy of honor, and which shines with splendor—may it extend among our people.
Whatever radiant power you have manifested, bestow upon us that wonderful wealth.

Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ! O Planet Bṛhaspati, come here! O Planet Bṛhaspati, you who are golden-hued, adorned with golden flowers, a golden umbrella, a banner, a chariot, flags, and so forth; mounted upon a divine chariot, circumambulating Mount Meru, facing the east, and seated upon a lotus throne.

I invoke, establish, and worship the planet Jupiter (Bṛhaspati) upon the chickpeas within this long rectangular mandala in the northern direction of the solar mandala in this ritual arena— Jupiter who has four arms, who holds a staff and a rosary, who is the sovereign of the land of Sindhudvīpa, who belongs to the Āṅgīrasa lineage, who was born on the twelfth lunar day of the Saumya year under the Dhaniṣṭhā asterism, who is the lord of the signs of Sagittarius and Pisces, who appeared on a Thursday, who wears a crown, who brings happiness, and who is accompanied by his wife, sons, and retinue as he enters the circle of the planets.
Adhidevatā: Oṃ. Brahmán, the first-born, from the east, has shone forth with great splendor;
he, through his creative power, has revealed the highest forms of this world, the source of both the existent and the non-existent.

To the south of the planet Bṛhaspati, I invoke, establish, and worship Brahmā—the presiding deity (adhidevatā) of the planet Bṛhaspati—along with his limbs (Aṅgas), weapons (Āyudhas), vehicle (Vāhana), and accompanied by his Śakti, wife, sons, and retinue.
Pratyadhidevatā: Oṃ, we invoke Indra from all sides for the sake of the people.
May it be exclusively ours.

To the north of the planet Bṛhaspati, I invoke, establish, and worship Indra, the presiding deity (pratyadhidevatā), together with his limbs, weapons, and vehicle, accompanied by his Śakti, wife, sons, and retinue.

Regarding Śukra: "O Śukra, [accept] this other [oblation] of Aditi"—this is the mantra. Bharadvāja is the seer (ṛṣi). The planet Śukra is the deity (devatā). Triṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ). It is for the purpose of attaining success through the grace of the planet Śukra, together with his presiding deity (adhidevatā) and counter-deity (pratyadhidevatā), in the worship of the planet Śukra. This is the application (viniyoga).
The ritual placement (nyāsa) on the limbs—the placement on the heart and so forth:
"śukraṃ te anyat" [is recited] with the two thumbs, "namaḥ hṛdayāya namaḥ";
"yajataṃ te anyat" [is recited] with the two index fingers, "namaḥ śirase svāhā."
Homage to the two days of diverse forms, to the middle fingers, *vauṣaṭ* to the crest;
you are like the sky, homage to the ring fingers, *huṃ* to the armor;
O self-sustaining one, you protect against all serpents and illusions, homage to the little fingers, *vaiṣaṭ* to the three eyes.
O Pūṣan, may auspicious gain come to you here. Homage to the palms and backs of the hands; *phaṭ* to the weapon.
The visualization (*dhyāna*):
In the east is the region of Bhojakaṭa belonging to Bhṛgu; there resides the son of Bhṛgu (Śukra), whose natural disposition faces the east.
Accompanied by the five [faces], mounted upon a chariot, he holds a staff, a rosary, a boon-granting gesture, and a water-vessel.
Clad in white garments, with a white body, wearing a crown, four-armed, the preceptor of the Daityas, and serene;
holding a staff, a water-pot, and likewise a rosary—may he, the granter of boons, be gracious to me.
The mantra:
Oṃ! One of your forms is bright, the other is worshipful; you possess two distinct colors, O Day-maker, throughout the two days.
You protect all magical powers, O Self-dependent one; may your gift here, O Pūṣan, be auspicious.
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! O planet Venus, come here!
The planet Venus is white in color, with white fragrance, white flowers, and wearing white garlands and garments; it is adorned with a white parasol, banner, chariot, flags, and so forth.

Mounted upon a divine chariot, circumambulating Mount Meru, facing the east, seated in the lotus posture, four-armed, bearing a staff, a rosary, matted hair, and bark garments, the sovereign of the Kāmboja country, of the Bhārgava lineage, born on the tenth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa under the Puṣya asterism, lord of the signs of Libra and Taurus, associated with Friday, accompanied by his wife, sons, and retinue, entered into this judicial proceeding within the circle of the planets.
In the eastern portion of the sun's [mandala], upon a five-cornered mandala made of *rājamāṣa* beans, I invoke, establish, and worship the planet Venus (*śukra*).
Its presiding deity: Oṃ, I praise Indrāṇī, the wife of a noble husband, among women of great renown.
For her husband shall not die from old age nor by any other cause.
I invoke, establish, and worship the deity Indrāṇī, together with her limbs, weapons, and vehicle, accompanied by her husband, Śakti, sons, and retinue, to the south of the planet Venus.
The presiding deity—Oṃ! O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, drink this Soma here, just as you drank it at Śaryāta’s sacrifice.
Under your guidance and in your protection, O Hero, the wise ones perform excellent sacrifices and do not come to ruin.

To the presiding deity of the planet Śukra, Indra accompanied by the Maruts, together with his limbs, weapons, vehicle, and surrounded by his consort, son, and retinue: from the north of the planet Śukra, I invoke, I install, and I worship Indra accompanied by the Maruts.
For Saturn (Śanaiścara):
the deity is the planet Saturn; the mantra is "śam agniḥ agnibhiḥ"; the meter is Uṣṇik.

The presiding deity (adhidevatā) and the counter-presiding deity (pratyadhidevatā) are together Śanaiścara and Graha Vṛṣadaṃśa; the application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of accomplishing the ritual installation of the planet Śanaiścara.
The ritual placement on the fingers (karanyāsa)—that is, the ritual placement on the heart and other limbs—is as follows:
*śam agniḥ* to both thumbs, *namaḥ* to the heart.
May Agni perform the consecration; salutation with the two index fingers, *svāhā* to the head.
May Sūrya praise [him]; *vauṣaṭ* to the tuft of hair with the two middle fingers.
May Vāta [praise him]; salutation with the two ring fingers, *vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes.
Touching [the body] with the palms and backs of the hands, [recite] "Astrāya Phaṭ.

Thus is the *karanyāsa* (placement on the hands), followed by the *hṛdayādinyāsa* (placement on the heart and other limbs). Then, perform the *digbandha* (binding of the directions) with "Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ Om.
The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
The son of Kaśyapa, who has a bow as his seat, a vulture for his vehicle, and is deep blue in color, faces westward;
he holds a trident and a bow, is the bestower of boons, and is the progenitor of the Saurāṣṭra region. He is the planet Saturn (Saurī).

May the son of the Sun— possessing a blue luster and a blue body, wearing a crown, seated upon a vulture, bearing a bow and armed with a weapon, four-armed and serene, yet moving with slow gait— grant me my boon.
The mantra:
Oṃ! May Agni make us auspicious with his fires; may the Sun shine warmly upon us. May the Wind blow auspiciously, warding off misfortune and calamities.
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! O planet Śanaiścara, come here!

The planet Śanaiścara is blue in color, adorned with blue flowers, wearing blue garlands and garments, and beautified by a blue parasol, banner, chariot, flag, and so forth; he is mounted upon a divine chariot, circumambulating Mount Meru, seated upon a bow-throne, facing westward, and possessing a vulture as his vehicle.

I invoke, establish, and worship the planet Śanaiścara in this ritual context, situated to the west of the Sun within the planetary mandala, upon sesame seeds in a bow-shaped mandala: four-armed, bearing a trident as his weapon, sovereign of the Saurāṣṭra region, of the Kāśyapa gotra, born under the Rohiṇī asterism on the ninth lunar day of the Vikārin year, presiding over the signs of Capricorn and Aquarius, appearing on a Saturday, wearing a crown, seated comfortably, accompanied by his wife, sons, and retinue, and entered into the circle of planets.
Adhidevatā: Oṃ! For Yama press the Soma; for Yama offer the oblation.
To Yama goes the sacrifice, with Agni as its well-prepared messenger.
I invoke, establish, and worship Yama, the presiding deity of the planet Śanaiścara and others, together with his limbs, weapons, and vehicle, accompanied by his Śakti, wife, sons, and retinue.
Pratyadhidevatā: Oṃ Prajāpati! None other than you has encompassed all these created beings.
Whatever desire we have as we offer this sacrifice to you, may we, through your grace, become masters of riches.

I invoke, establish, and worship Prajāpati, the presiding deity of the planet Śanaiścara, together with his limbs, his weapon, and his vehicle, accompanied by his Śakti, wife, and sons, from the north of the planet Śanaiścara. I invoke, establish, and worship Prajāpati.

For Rāhu: the seer (ṛṣi) is Vāmadeva; the deity (devatā) is the planet Rāhu; the meter (chandaḥ) is Gāyatrī. This is the application (viniyoga) for the acquisition of wealth from the planet Rāhu, for the sake of attaining the grace of the planet Rāhu together with its presiding deity (adhidevatā) and counter-deity (pratyadhidevatā), using the mantra beginning with "kayā naś citra."
The ritual placement (nyāsa) of the limbs—the placement of the heart and other parts:
"By what [means] for us..."—salutation with the two thumbs to the heart;
"May it be wonderful..."—salutation with the two index fingers to the head (svāhā).
With the verse *ūtī*, salutation to the middle fingers; *vauṣaṭ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*). With the verse *sakhā*, salutation to the ring fingers; *huṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*).
With the verse *kayā śaciṣṭhayā*, salutation to the little fingers; *vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes (*netratraya*).
With the palms and backs of the hands joined: *namaḥ astrāya phaṭ*.

Thus is the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*). The ritual placement on the heart and other limbs (*hṛdayādinyāsa*) follows. The sealing of the directions (*digbandha*) is performed with: *bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ oṃ*. The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
Paiṭhīnasa is born in the land of Barbara; he always sits upon a winnowing basket and rides a lion.
He has a seat in the south, belongs to the southwest, and is of the sign of Sagittarius. He is the bestower of boons, and his weapons are a trident, a shield, and a sword.
Clad in blue garments, with a blue body, wearing a crown, with a formidable and terrifying face, bearing a sword and a trident,
four-armed and holding a shield— may Rāhu, seated upon the king of lions and bestowing boons, be pleased with me.
The mantra:
Oṃ, with what aid will the wonderful, ever-prospering friend come to us as a messenger?
With what most powerful assistance? Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ.
O Rāhu, come here!

Rahu, the planet, blue in color, with a blue fragrance, wearing blue garlands and garments, adorned with a blue parasol, banner, chariot, and flags; mounted upon a divine chariot, circumambulating Mount Meru in a counter-clockwise direction; seated upon a lion-throne facing the southwest (Nairṛti), resting on a winnowing-basket seat (śūrpa-āsana); four-armed, with a formidable countenance, holding a sword and a shield in his hands; belonging to the Paiṭhīnasa lineage, the sovereign of the Barbara country, wearing a crown, seated comfortably, accompanied by his wife, sons, and retinue.

Having entered this planetary mandala, in this context, I invoke, establish, and worship the planet Rāhu upon the *māṣa* beans within a winnowing-basket-shaped mandala in the south-western direction of the solar eclipse. Adhidevatā:
Oṃ, the spotted bull has come forth again toward his mother from whom he was born.
And going toward the father, [he] impels the swift ones.

I invoke and establish for worship the presiding deity of the planet Rāhu, together with her limbs, weapons, and vehicle, accompanied by her husband, power, sons, and retinue; I invoke and establish the Cow (Gau) to the south of the planet Rāhu, and I worship her.
The counter-deity:
Oṃ, let there be salutation to the serpents, those which are upon the earth.
Homage to those serpents who are in the intermediate space and those who are in heaven.

I invoke, establish, and worship Rāhugraha, together with his subsidiary deity (pratyadhidevatā) Sarpa, along with his limbs (aṅgas), weapons (āyudhas), vehicle (vāhana), Śakti, wife, sons, and retinue, to the north of Rāhugraha. For Ketu:

[The mantra] beginning with "ketuṃ kṛṇvan..."—Madhuśchandas is the seer (ṛṣi); the Ketu-gaṇa is the deity (devatā); Gāyatrī is the meter (chaṃdaḥ). This is the application (viniyoga) for the propitiation of the Ketu-gaṇa, for the sake of attaining the grace of Ketu-graha together with his presiding and subsidiary deities.
The ritual placement (nyāsa) of the limbs—the placement of the heart and so forth:
"Making [him] a banner," with the two thumbs, *namaḥ* to the heart;
"to the one without a banner," with the two index fingers, *namaḥ* to the head, *svāhā*.
To the two middle fingers, *namaḥ* to the *peśomaryas*; to the *śikhā*, *vauṣaṭ*.
To the two ring fingers, *namaḥ* to the *apeśane anāvikā*; to the *kavaca*, *huṃ*.
To the two little fingers, *namaḥ* to the *samuṣadbhis*; to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*.

*ajāyathāḥ karatalakarapṛṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ astrāya phaṭ*. Thus is the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*). The ritual placement on the heart and other limbs (*hṛdayādinyāsa*) follows. The binding of the directions (*digbandha*) is performed with *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ*. The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
Dhvajāsana is born in the Jaivami lineage; he possesses diverse complexions in the Antarveda regions.
Ketu has Yāmyāsana as his seat, resides in the direction of Vāyu, and has eight sons: Prakhadga, Carmā, Asi, and others.

May that peaceful host of attendants always protect me— the smoky-colored one with two arms, bestower of boons, holding a mace, seated upon a vulture, with a distorted face, his limbs adorned with a crown and armlets.
The mantra:
Oṃ, making light for those without light, creating form for those without form, O mortal men,
you were born together with the worlds.
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! O Ketu, come here!

[One should visualize] Ketu as having a multitude of forms, possessing various colors, various scents, various flowers, and wearing various garlands and garments; adorned with various umbrellas, banners, chariots, flags, and so forth; mounted upon a divine chariot; circumambulating Mount Meru; seated upon a throne marked by a banner; facing the south; four-armed; the lord of the regions such as Antarvedī; seated upon a lion-throne; and entered into the circle of planets in the north-western direction of the Sun in this sacrificial context.
In the banner-shaped maṇḍala, upon the washed *kuluttha* beans, I invoke, establish, and worship the host of banners (*ketu-gaṇa*).
The presiding deity: Oṃ, O Citra, make him famous; make him most famous in his sovereignty, the bestower of vigor.
Bestow upon the singer, O radiant one, with your radiant rays, splendor, abundant wealth, and great heroic power.

I invoke, establish, and worship Citragupta, the presiding deity of the Ketu group, together with his limbs, weapons, and vehicle, accompanied by his wife Śakti, his sons, and his retinue, to the south of the Ketu group.
Subordinate Deity:
Oṃ, Brahmā is the leader of the gods, the poet among sages, the seer among the learned, and the bull among wild beasts.
Like a hawk among vultures, like an axe among the forests, Soma has shone forth as he passes through the filter.

To the north of the group of Ketus, I invoke, establish, and worship Brahmā—the presiding deity of the group of Ketus—along with his limbs, weapons, nine vehicles, and accompanied by his Śakti, wife, sons, and retinue.

*Jātavedase sunavāma somaṃ arātīyato nidahāti vedaḥ | sa naḥ parṣadati durgāṇi viśvā nāveva sindhuṃ duritātyagniḥ ||* (Rig Veda 1.99.1) We shall press the Soma for Jātavedas; may he burn away those who act as enemies. May he carry us across all difficulties, and like a boat across a river, may Agni lead us beyond all misfortunes.

I invoke Durgā; I establish her; I worship her. Oṃ! We invoke Gaṇapati, the leader of the hosts, the sage among sages, the most highly praised, the supreme king of sacred prayers (brahmaṇas), O Lord of Prayer (Brahmaṇaspati)! May he hear us with his protections; may he sit upon his seat.
With the Lord of the Field as our ally, we conquer;
having nourished cattle and horses, he grants us rest so that we may behold him.

I invoke, establish, and worship Kṣetrapālaka. May the Lord of Beings, the giver of well-being, the slayer of Vṛtra, the subduer of enemies, the self-controlled one, the sovereign bull, our leader, the giver of well-being and the granter of fearlessness, protect us.
I invoke Abhayankara; I establish him; I worship him.
May Indra be for us alone, from every side, for our great people. May he be ours exclusively.
I invoke, establish, and worship Indra, the guardian of the world.
We choose Agni as the messenger, the invoker who possesses all knowledge, the one of excellent wisdom for this sacrifice.
I invoke Agni, the guardian of the world; I establish him; I worship him.
Press the Soma for Yama; offer the oblation to Yama.
To Yama goes the sacrifice, with Agni as its well-prepared messenger.
I invoke, establish, and worship Yama, the guardian of the world.
May Nirṛti, the destroyer of those who are high and low, slay him along with his thirst for dominion.
I invoke, establish, and worship Nirṛti, the world-protector;
accept this water-offering.
I invoke Varuṇa, the guardian of the world; I establish him; I worship him.
O Vāyu, O Forest Lord, O Tvaṣṭṛ, O Son-in-law of Jamadagni, O Wondrous One, we choose our protections from you.
I invoke, establish, and worship Vāyu, the world-protector.
May Soma grant us a milch-cow; may Soma grant a swift horse; may Soma grant a heroic son who is capable in action.
The dwelling of the householder, the path to the field, and friendship—these belong to him who offers oblations to her, so that he may hear the renown of his father.
I invoke, I establish, and I worship Kubera, the guardian of the world. We call upon that Īśāna, the lord of all that moves and stands, who quickens the intellect, for our protection.
May Pūṣan be present for the prosperity of us who are wise, guarding us as an undeceivable protector for our well-being.

I invoke, I establish, and I worship Īśāna, the guardian of the world. "Standing erect for our protection, like a god who is not a protector; we call upon Savitṛ, the bestower of strength, with our uplifted arms and with those who offer praise."
I invoke the Supreme Person; I establish him; I worship him.
O Earth, be pleasant, free from thorns, and devoid of brambles; grant us wide-reaching protection.
I invoke the Earth; I establish her; I worship her.
O Lord of the Dwelling, acknowledge us! Be our own home, free from disease.
Accept this our great offering; grant well-being to our four-footed creatures.
I invoke the Vāstupuruṣa; I establish him; I worship him.

He is the path of the gods, the Brahman among poets, the seer among the wise, the buffalo among wild beasts, the hawk among vultures, the falcon among birds; Soma, the purifier, has flowed across with a roar.
I invoke, establish, and worship Brahmā.
May the goddess Sarasvatī, rich in strength through her hymns, protect us as the guardian of inspired thoughts.
I invoke Sarasvatī; I establish her; I worship her.
Viṣṇu strode across this [universe]; he established his foot in three places.
His step is encompassed in the cave.
I invoke Viṣṇu; I establish him; I worship him.

"Where the wise, purifying themselves with the *saktu* and the *udavita*, have made their speech dwell, there the friends recognize their friendships; upon their auspicious speech, prosperity is established."
O Lakṣmī, I invoke you, I establish you, I worship you.
O most bountiful Rudra, for the sake of one who is wise and active,
may we speak what is most auspicious to the heart.
O Rudra, I invoke you, I establish you, and I worship you.
Gaurī has lowed, fashioning herself with the waters; she is one-footed, two-footed, and three-footed;
she has become eight-footed and nine-footed, possessing a thousand syllables in the highest heaven.
I invoke Gaurī; I establish her; I worship her.
She who is praised, who is joined with the Child, furthering the radiance of Truth, shall encompass all that is dear; she has established the eternal seed from of old.
Thus they behold the light of day, for that which is beyond shines forth as the day.
This Dawn, never before risen, rises dear to the gods, well-born and bringing great glory.
I invoke the deity Aśvinī, I establish her, I worship her.
O Indra, from whatever we fear, grant us freedom from fear.
O Maghavan, grant us that aid for our protection; slay our enemies and those who oppose us.
"I invoke Abhayaṅkara; I establish him; I worship him.
This is the northern recitation (*auttarīya-pāṭha*).
"You are Suparṇa, the Garuḍa; the Trivṛt is your head, the Gāyatra your eye, the Stoma..."
The self is its axle; the *sūrya* and *sudevyā* verses are its two wings, the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* chants;
the *yajñāyajñiya* is its tail; the meters are its limbs; and the sacrificial hearths are its hooves.
This is the name of the Yajus-mantra: "You are the fair-winged Garuḍa; go to heaven, go to the light of the sun."
I invoke Garuḍa; I establish him; I worship him.
With the bow may we conquer; with the bow may we overcome the fierce ones in battle.
The bow frustrates the desire of the enemy; with the bow may I conquer all the quarters.
I invoke Dhanvantari; I establish him; I worship him.
O Lord of Life, release him from consumption and from severe pulmonary consumption.
If the Grāhi has seized him, then may Indra and Agni release him from her.
O Indra and Agni, I summon you; I establish you; I worship you.
Grant us wealth that is well-joined, secure, and brought together; may Varuṇa, who is inclined toward peace, bestow it upon us.
Then let the enemies, fearing in their hearts, flee away, utterly defeated.
I invoke Śatruha, I establish him, and I worship him.
May our enemies flee far away, terrified! O Indra and Agni, O Kṛtānta, O Dviśākha, may the gods favor this sacrifice of ours. May there be safety for us from behind and from before!
Viśākhā is the sovereign mistress of the constellations; Indra and Agni, the guardians of the world, are most excellent.
I invoke the Viśākhā constellation, I establish it, and I worship it. Salutations to the deities of the nine planets, beginning with Āditya, who reside in the pavilion.
Salutations to the eight guardians of the directions, Indra and the others.
Salutations to the deities Durgā, Gaṇapati, Kṣetrapāla, Abhayaṃkara, Vāstupuruṣa, and the rest.
I offer the sixteen-fold worship, beginning with meditation and invocation, along with the water-offering.
Salutations to Sūrya, Soma, Maṅgala, and Budha;
salutations to Guru, Śukra, Śani, Rāhu, and Ketu.
I offer this prayer.
Through this worship, may the deities residing in the pavilion be well-pleased, well-satisfied, and become granters of boons. Thus ends the propitiation of the nine planets.
Now, [the rite of] Mṛtyuñjaya.

Of this great mantra, the Śrī Tryambaka Stotra: the Ṛṣi is Vaniṣṭha, the son of Maitrāvaruṇa; the metre is Anuṣṭubh; the deity is the illustrious Tryambaka Rudra, the Conqueror of Death (Mṛtyuñjaya); the seed-syllable and power are the two Praṇavas (Oṃ) representing the God and Goddess. Here, having performed the purification of the hands with the root mantra and having placed the Praṇava upon the palms of both hands, one should place the four quarters of the mantra beginning with the Vyāhṛtis upon the fingers of the hands, starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger. Then, having performed the pervasive assignment (vyāpaka-nyāsa) with the entire mantra, one should begin the assignment of the limbs upon the body (dehāṅga-nyāsa).
Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ—salutation to the two thumbs;
triyambakaṃ yajāmahe—salutation to the two index fingers; sugandhiṃ puṣṭivardhanam—salutation to the two middle fingers.
"Like a cucumber from its stalk"—salutation with the two ring fingers; "May we be liberated from death, not from immortality"—salutation with the two little fingers;
*Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, the three-eyed one (*tryambakam*).
"May I be released from death, may I be joined with immortality"—with "Salutation to Tryambaka," [he places it] on the palms and backs of the hands; with "Salutation to the head," on the head;
with "Salutation to the fragrant one," on the forehead.
"May it increase prosperity"—*namaḥ* on the face;
"the gourd"—*namaḥ* on the heart; "as if"—*namaḥ* on both [shoulders].
With "baṃdhana" [one should touch] the waist;
with "mṛtyoḥ," the two thighs; with "mikṣiye," the two knees;
with "meti," the two shanks; and with "amṛtāt," the two feet.
Having thus performed the placement of the limbs upon the body, one should begin the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).
Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, the three-eyed one, who holds a trident in his hand; svāhā—this is for the heart.
Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Rudra of immeasurable forms; protect this life; svāhā—this is for the head.
Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, the blue-throated one, whose matted hair is adorned with the moon; svāhā—this is for the crest-lock (śikhā).
Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, the Destroyer of the Three Cities; Hrāṃ Hrīṃ—armor!
Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, the Three-eyed One, whose form is the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharva Vedas—eyes!
Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, Rudra, the triad of fires, who blazes and burns intensely!
"Protect, protect! O Aghora-weapon, phaṭ! Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, oṃ!"—thus is the binding of the directions.
Dhānya:

Then, seated upon a lotus posture bound above a lunar disc, moon-colored, bearing a digit of the moon that overflows with nectar; his two lower hands forming the *yoga-mudrā* and holding a rosary, and his two upper hands holding a golden vase filled with flowing nectar; possessing three eyes—moon, sun, and fire—with a tied-up mass of tawny matted hair, and wearing a sacred thread of serpents.

Having meditated upon Śrī Rudra—adorned with serpent ornaments, wearing a tiger-skin garment, compassionate toward his devotees, and smeared with ashes—and having worshipped him according to the previously mentioned method with a mind full of affection, one should go for refuge.

"O Three-eyed One, O Mahādeva, protect me who have come to you for refuge! I am afflicted by birth, death, old age, and disease, and bound by the fetters of karma. O Savior, my life-breaths are centered in you; I am always your disciple, O Mṛḍa! Having thus addressed the Lord of Gods, one should mutter the *tryambaka* mantra.
Having made this prayer and performed the fivefold worship beginning with "Lam," one should recite the mantra.
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar om—thus is the binding of the directions.
We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the nourisher, the bestower of wealth. May I be liberated from death, as a cucumber from its stalk, but not from immortality.
Drive away untimely death and hunger; drive away the curse.
Now, O Agni, bring hither the increase of wealth together with our beloved ones.
To these thousand deaths, svāhā!
May all my death be destroyed; may my life increase.
Acyuta, Kalpavṛkṣa, and Ananta; Kāmadhenu and Govinda—these three names have been proclaimed. Salutations to Acyuta. Salutations to Ananta. Salutations to Govinda.

*Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaroṃ*—thus is the binding of the directions (*digbandha*). Having performed the release of the directions (*dignimoka*) beginning with *aṃguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ*, one should perform the rites up to the fivefold worship (*pañcapūjā*). Thus ends the procedure for Vṛṣoṃjaya. Now follows the ritual procedure for the nine planets (*navagraha*).

Yājñavalkya: One who desires prosperity, or one who desires peace, or one who desires rain, long life, or nourishment, as well as one performing malevolent rites, should perform the sacrifice to the planets (grahayajña).
The Sun, Soma, the son of Mahī (Mars), Bṛhaspati (Jupiter) who is the son of Soma,
Śukra (Venus), Śanaiścara (Saturn), Rāhu, and Ketu— these are remembered as the planets.
The sacrificial vessels (agrahas) should be made respectively from copper, crystal, red sandalwood, gold, silver, iron, lead, and bell-metal.
They should be drawn with their own respective colors, either on cloth or within mandalas using fragrant pigments;
garments and flowers should be offered according to their respective colors.
Fragrances, offerings, and incense of guggulu should be presented;
and oblations (carus) accompanied by mantras must be performed for each respective deity.
The verses beginning with "asatya," "imam devāḥ," "agnirmūrdhā divaḥ kakut," and "udbudhyasva" are proclaimed according to their respective numbers.
"Bṛhaspate ati yat aryaḥ," "atha u annāt parisrutaḥ," "śam no devīḥ," "tathā kāṇḍāt," and "ketuṃ kṛṇvan"— these [mantras] likewise.
Arka, palāśa, khadira, apāmārga, and pippala;
udumbara, śamī, dūrvā, and kuśa are the sacrificial fuels (samidh) in their respective order.
For each [deity], one hundred and eight oblations, or twenty-eight,
should be offered with honey and clarified butter, or mixed with curd or milk.
Curds with rice as the sacrificial oblation, meat, and various kinds of cooked food.
One should give food free from impurity, meat, and various kinds of grain.
In this manner, a wise householder should provide food to the Brahmins in due order,
according to his capacity or as it may be available, honoring them in accordance with the prescribed rites.
A cow, a conch shell, a reed-mat, gold, a garment, a horse, a black cow, and a goat for the Ārya— these are traditionally prescribed as the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) in their respective order.
Whoever has seen whomsoever at what time, let him worship that person with effort;
for Brahmā has granted this boon to them: "When you have been worshipped, you shall worship [others]."

In the *Vijñāneśvara*, it is stated that these nine planets, beginning with the Sun, are to be worshipped; however, he says "but" (*kiṃtu*) regarding this point: "From copper, etc. This means that the images of the Sun and the others should be fashioned from copper and other materials as desired; if those are unavailable, they should be drawn on cloth according to their respective colors. Alternatively, they may be drawn within mandalas using red sandalwood paste and so forth, according to their respective colors. As for specific details such as having two arms, these should be observed as described in the *Matsya Purāṇa*. For example: "Seated upon a lotus, holding a lotus in his hand, possessing a luster like the interior of a lotus, stationed in a chariot drawn by seven horses—such should the Sun (Taviṣ) always be [depicted] with two arms."
Śaśin should be depicted as white, wearing white garments, possessing ten horses, and adorned with white ornaments;
he has two arms, holds a mace in his hand, and grants boons.
Wearing red garlands and garments, bearing a spear, a trident, and a mace,
the son of the Earth (Mars) should have four arms, ride upon a ram, and grant boons.
Wearing yellow garlands and garments, possessing the luster of the Karṇikāra flower,
with sword and shield in his hands, seated upon a lion, the wise Budha bestows boons.
The preceptors of the gods and the Daityas should be depicted as yellow and white, four-armed,
holding staffs and granting boons, and equipped with rosaries and water-pots.
The son of the Sun (Saturn) should always be depicted as having the luster of sapphire, bearing a trident, bestowing boons, mounted upon a vulture,
and holding an arrow and a bow.
With a formidable face, bearing a sword, shield, and trident, and granting boons,
Rāhu is praised here as being seated upon a dark-blue lion-throne.
All the banners are smoke-colored, two-armed, wielding clubs, and having deformed faces;
they are eternally seated upon vultures and are bestowers of excellent lands.
All the planets, who bring about the welfare of the world, should be fashioned with crowns;
all of them should be raised to a height of one hundred and eight times their own respective limbs.
The location for their installation is also stated in that very same place:
"One should know the Sun to be in the center, and the Red One (Rudra) to the south."
One should know the Guru to be in the north, and the wise one (the disciple) in the northeast.
One should know Bhārgava in the east, Soma in the south-east,
Śanaiścara in the west, and Rāhu in the south-west.
One should place the banner in the northwestern direction with white rice grains.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the nine planets.
Now, the opening of the fire:
Hariḥ Oṃ.
Now, the domestic rites (*gārhya-karmāṇi*), such as those beginning with the *ācāra*, are taken up. Facing east, seated upon *darbha* grass, holding *darbha* or *dūrvā* grass,
with *pavitra* blades in hand, together with his wife, and having restrained his breaths, [he should state] the place and the time.
Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), saying, "Having proclaimed such-and-such a rite,
I shall perform it," one should smear a pure place with white rice-powder and prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring a span (prādeśa),
either square or circular.
Having prepared [the site] and having scraped it with two blades of *darbha* grass—
one oriented eastward from west to east, beginning from the south,
and one oriented northward from south to north, beginning from the west.

Having sprinkled water from the vessel facing downward and set it aside, he pours out the remainder of the sprinkling water. He places another vessel of water to the east or to the north, so that there may be sufficient for the ritual strewing (*paristaraṇa*).
Having established the fire with the mantra "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," he sprinkles the remaining water around it.
Having poured out water toward the northeast and having brought other water, he should place it outside the sacrificial grass-strewing, either toward the east or the north.
Having poured unbroken rice and water into the two vessels for the fire and the *vapā*, and having kindled the fire, [he recites]:
"Oṃ! Four are his horns, three are his feet, two are his heads, seven are his hands; the bull has entered the mortals."
Bound in three ways, the bull, the roaring one, the great god has entered into mortals.
I meditate upon Agni, who has seven hands, four horns, seven tongues, and two heads;
he has three feet, a serene face, sits comfortably, and possesses a pure smile.
He bears Svāhā on his right side and likewise Svadhā on the left;
with his right hands he holds a spear, food, a *sruk* ladle, and a *srava* spoon,
while with his left hands he holds a lance, a fan, and a vessel of clarified butter.

One should meditate upon the Fire-god in this manner: mounted upon a ram, with matted hair, bull-colored, great-bodied, possessing a smoke-bannered flag, red-eyed, seven-flamed, the granter of all desires, and seated facing oneself.
This very God extends across all directions; He was born first within the womb of the universe.
Being born and yet to be born, He stands facing every direction, His face turned toward all things.
O Fire, facing eastward, become my face; become well-faced; become well-pleased; become the giver of boons.
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. We meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he impel our intellects.
Having swept around the fire clockwise with his hand moistened with water, and having adorned it.
Salutation to Agni; salutation to Hutavaha; salutation to Hutāśin; salutation to Kṛṣṇavartman; salutation to Devamukha; salutation to Saptajihva; salutation to Vaiśvānara; salutation to Jātavedas.

He strews darbha grass around the fire with its tips pointing eastward and northward; he places the southern blades over the northern ones and the northern ones under the southern ones. Having strewn darbha grass to the north of the fire with its tips pointing eastward, he sets out the vessels in pairs: the *darvī* spoon, the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*), the *prokṣaṇī* sprinkling-vessel, and another *darvī*. He prepares two strainers (*vitra*) made of darbha grass, each a span (*prādeśa*) long, with uncut tips and containing an inner core. He cuts them using a piece of black wood as a backer, not with his fingernails. Having touched water, he wipes them with water.

Taking the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, pouring water into it, and grasping it with the thumbs and little fingers of both hands so that its spout points north, he purifies it three times by moving it eastward, consecrates it with a mantra, and places the vessels with their openings facing upward.
