With the mantra "namo rudrebhyaḥ," one should offer oblations of gold-encrusted thorns and mustard seeds at midday every day; or alternatively, by performing this for each night, the gods, piśācas, and others within the kingdom fall away, and those belonging to the sky-faring women (khecarī), women, or yātudhānas are reduced to ashes. Now, these are the pacifications (śāntis): With the mantra "imāṃ rudrāya," when cattle are afflicted, one should kindle a fire in the middle of the cow-pen and offer ten thousand oblations of fuel-sticks of *vaikaṅkata* wood. For the pacification of livestock and other animals, the "Great Pacification" (mahāśānti) is performed with double that number.

Then, having worshipped the deity by performing the placement of mantras (*nyāsa*) upon the deity and so forth according to the previously mentioned procedure, and having appointed a Brāhmaṇa who knows the Rudra-hymns as his preceptor (*ācārya*), he should approach a self-manifested (*svayambhū*) Liṅga. There too, having performed worship according to this very same procedure, having bathed it with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and having performed an oblation of clarified butter (*ājyahoma*) with the first section (*anuvāka*), he should fully honor the deity and perform the recitation (*japa*) of the eleven sections beginning with "Obeisance to you, O Rudra, the wielder of the bow" (*namaste rudra manyave*). While causing a continuous stream [of water] to flow, at the conclusion of that recitation, he should recite one by one each of the eleven sections beginning with "O Agni and Viṣṇu, rejoice" (*agnāviṣṇū jarasva*).

Again, one should bathe the deity with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), worship him thoroughly, and offer an oblation (*naivedya*) consisting of various foods and snacks. Then, having worshipped four full jars filled with the five nectars, joined with the five sprouts (*pañcapallava*) and the five gems (*pañcaratna*), and adorned with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), perfumes, incense, and so forth; and having wrapped them in white cloth, one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) while meditating on and reciting the peace mantra: "May the wind be auspicious to us" (*śaṃ no vātaḥ pavatām*). Peace shall prevail, and thereafter, one becomes restored to health.

One should give a pair of white garments, a cow, and gold to the preceptor, and feed the Brahmins; thus there is peace, according to Śaunaka. With the mantra "mā no mahāntam," one should offer ten thousand oblations of *aśvattha* wood. When this is done, there is peace for oneself, as well as for children, women, and the elderly. [Reciting] "namo bhavāya" and "namo jyeṣṭhāya," one should consecrate ashes with these two mantras and provide protection for those seized by the Kumāra-grahas and other such spirits.

At night, one should tie a lock of hair; then there is no fear from Kumāra or other planetary spirits (*graha*). With the mantra "O most bountiful, O most auspicious," one should mentally recite it during great danger, fear of thieves, fear of fire, or when life is at stake; one returns in safety. With the mantra "This [oblation] to Rudra," one should offer gold and sprouts of *dūrvā* grass a hundred thousand times. In the event of a severe fever, one who has lost their vitality becomes long-lived.

One should offer ten thousand oblations of barley, wheat, *gavīdhuka* grain, and wild sesame seeds, mixed with curd, honey, and ghee, reciting the four verses beginning with "namaste pūruṣantapa" one verse at a time. By doing so for eleven or twelve nights, one pacifies Vāyu. A complete protection should be performed with the hymn beginning with "ādyavoca dadhivaktā. Having consecrated mustard seeds seven times, one should scatter them in the four directions; thus protection is established in the ten directions. For those who travel, peace is attained.

With a mustard seed, one is liberated from Brahma-rākṣasas, bhūtas, piśācas, and the like. Having consecrated a protective amulet (*pratisara*) one thousand times with the Ṛgvedic verse beginning "yatā rudra śivā tanūḥ," and having tied eleven knots upon it, one should fasten it on the hands of children and pregnant women. Thus, children and pregnant women shall thrive happily, and there shall be the eradication of yakṣas and rākṣasas.

Regarding the term "thousands": one should worship the deity with red garments, a red turban, red garlands, and red unguents. In a cremation ground, under a solitary tree, on a riverbank, or at a crossroads in the forest, one should grind cotton-seed and rice, anoint it with great oil, and prepare an image—even of a Yakṣa, Rākṣasa, or other being, including an enemy—using barley flour. Having consecrated it eleven times with mantras and smeared the image with pungent oil, one should place it on the southern part of the ground and [strike it] with a single arrow for each [mantra].

One should not cause the vital breaths to fluctuate within the seats of life. This [mantra] destroys an enemy who has arrived suddenly or who pervades all the worlds. With the mantra "Namo rudrebhyaḥ," at midday, the divine beings (*devayoni*), along with the *piśācas*, fall away; for women who move through the air (*khecarī*) or for the *yātudhānas*, it results in their being reduced to ashes. Now, these are the pacificatory rites (*śānti*). With the mantra "Imāṃ rudrāya," in the event of an affliction among cattle, one should kindle a fire in the middle of the cow-pen and offer ten thousand oblations of *vaikaṅkata* wood.

Peace is attained for cattle. For as many [cattle] as there are that have been harmed, one should perform the rite of pacification (śānti) in exactly this manner. With the mantra "namaste rudramanyava," when cattle are afflicted, one should kindle a fire in the middle of the cow-pen and offer ten thousand oblations of *vaikaṅkata* wood. For the pacification of livestock and other animals, the great pacification (*mahāśānti*) is performed with double the number.

Now, one who desires the destruction of an enemy should perform the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) and so forth according to the previously mentioned procedure, offer red rice as a sacrificial oblation (*bali*) to the guardians of the directions, and perform the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) with the mantra "Stuhi Śrutam. Having performed the eleven-fold recitation (*rudraikādaśinī*) eleven times, he should then recite "Stuhi Śrutam" a thousand times daily for seven nights; by this, the destruction of the enemy occurs. Furthermore, one who desires to produce a magical spell (*kṛtyā*) should worship the deity dressed in red garments, wearing a red turban, and adorned with red garlands and unguents.

In a cremation ground courtyard, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of red splinters, each a span in length and soaked in great quantities of oil, while reciting: "Arise, O red-limbed one, red-eyed one, red-haired one! Look upon that maiden! One should satisfy her with a skull-bowl filled to the brim with blood. Otherwise, she will surely harm the practitioner; for when she is summoned and constrained, she speaks thus: "I shall torment you! Speak, so that it may be known what I am to destroy in this world!"

Likewise, there is the application [of these rites] to each individual body in a village, a city, or a house. Having consumed *śāka* (potherbs) for twelve nights and fasted, one should offer the limbs to the sisters; this is prescribed as an alternative to the *tulāpuruṣa*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other penances when one is deficient in food. Upon receiving [the materials], having sipped water (*ācamya*), and being established in the constant self-identification (*nityābhimāna*), one should otherwise recite [the mantras]. Having consecrated the weapon with the six verses beginning with "pramuñcadhanvana," enemies encountered in battle are rendered powerless.

They stand facing [the enemy]. One should offer ten thousand *darbha* thorns as oblations. A Kṣatriya or similar person will become greatly hostile toward the enemy. A Kṣatriya [should offer] one-third [of the number], a Vaiśya one-sixth, and a Śūdra one-fourth; thus they declare that the rite remains unimpeded. With the mantra "O Vīgirida, O Vilohita," one should offer sesame seeds into the mouth of a sleeping dog many times over. All enemies, their minds shattered and turned away, will flee. With the sections beginning "Salutation to Hiraṇyabāhu," [one should offer] pungent substances...

One should offer mustard seeds into the fire for those who have been slandered or are suspected by the king; this causes the wheel [of authority] to be overturned. By uttering the syllable *phaṭ*, one should hang a garland over the head of the deity and a rope beneath it, smear blood and flesh upon it with *trikaṭuka* (the three pungents), and having drawn lines with the finger of the deity’s hand while recollecting the name of the enemy, one should perform the recitation (*japa*). This drives away the enemy along with his entire army and host. In this manner, one may drive away an entire village in a single day.

One should exhaust a Kṣatriya in half a day, a Vaiśya in one-third of a day, and a Śūdra in one-fourth of a day; thus they declare that the ritual act remains unimpeded. All of this was spoken by Śaunaka in the Hemādri. Now, that which is stated in the Merutantra is as follows: "Then one should perform the Raudrī stream; its procedure is also described: with the two chapters beginning with 'Obeisance to you, O Rudra, Agni, Viṣṇu'..."

This is declared to be the "Āvartana," which bestows the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā. Whatever man performs the ablution of Āvartana every day, his sin born of humans and his sin born of gods shall be destroyed. If that [sin] were to be from a previous birth, it is diminished by the performance of the Sandhyā-vandana. A single recitation of this [hymn] and of the next Anuvāka [is required]. Thus: "Bhavāya te namaḥ," "agnāviṣṇū," and "tadhaikakam. This is known as the "Rudrī," which cuts away the sins of Rudra.

Whoever performs the consecration of the Liṅga every day with this [mantra], the sins committed throughout their life are destroyed within a single year. The *Laghu-rudra* is proclaimed to consist of eleven *Rudrī* verses; by those who have sprinkled the Liṅga with this, they behold the Sun-god. The *Mahā-rudra* is proclaimed to consist of eleven times that [number of] verses; it bestows wealth upon the poor and destroys even the greatest of sins. A *Homa* performed with this yields the fruit of a *Soma-yāga*.

This [rite] is considered to be for those who are otherwise ineligible; it is regarded as a substitute for the Kṛcchra penance. Among the eleven Mahārudras, this is proclaimed as the Ratirudra. Since it removes even the most heinous sins, there is no other atonement once it has been seen.
Thus, the procedure declared in the Merutantra was not obtained.
The Namaka— now begins the Mahārudrādhyāya together with the ritual procedure for its application of the respective mantras: *Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed Lord Rudra*.
Oṃ, salutations to you, O Rudra, for your wrath, and also for your bow;
let there be salutation to you, and salutation to your bowstring and to your two arms.

Now we shall describe the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) and so forth for this mantra. Having performed the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights and reciting [the mantra] eleven thousand times continuously for the prescribed number of days, one becomes one who has completed the *puraścaraṇa*. Thereafter, one should perform circumambulation and prostration with this [mantra]. Then, by reciting it eleven thousand times in the presence of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, all sins without exception are destroyed. Furthermore, by reciting it one hundred thousand times, the sins committed over seven lifetimes are destroyed.

Having placed the fire in the very presence of that image of the Giver (Dātṛ) and having caused clarified butter and milk-rice (*pāyasa*) to be cooked, one should offer it into one's own fire; thus one beholds the God directly. Having constructed a sacrificial pit (*agnikuṇḍa*) measuring one *aratni* on all sides in that very place, one should offer a hundred thousand oblations at a time with the clarified butter of Kapila cows into one's own fire; one thereby attains the status of a leader of the Gaṇas (*gāṇapatya*). Now, the worship of kings by means of this image will be described: a king should have a Brahmin who has perfected the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) perform worship of the Liṅga. The method for that will now be explained.

Having prepared a fire-pit to the south of the *liṅga* and having established the consecrated fire (*mathitāgni*), one should offer oblations eight thousand times each with clarified butter, *dūrvā* grass, pure rice, and *śamī* wood fuel, as in the daily ritual. One should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times in the presence of the deity. One should perform eight thousand circumambulations while the deity is being honored. One should perform the *tāṇḍava* dance in the presence of the deity. Prostrations and salutations should also be performed eight thousand times. By these rites, the Blessed Lord becomes exceedingly well-pleased.
Meditation:
One should meditate upon the Great Lord, the youth with a body for battle, who has drawn back his bow and is fixing a blazing goddess as an arrow upon the radiant bow,
who is dressed in magnificent attire, and who is accompanied by ten thousand goddesses.
Oṃ! May this arrow become most auspicious, and may your bow become auspicious. O Rudra, with that auspicious flight of yours, drive away our enemies.

Having recited this mantra for twelve days while subsisting on *caru* (sacrificial porridge), one becomes fit for its application once the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) has been completed. Then, one should offer eleven thousand oblations of a paste made from half-portioned rice, sesame seeds, barley-gruel (*yāvaka*), and *āmalaka* fruits; thereby, one becomes possessed of abundant food. For the purpose of warding off famine, a king should cause one hundred thousand oblations to be offered into his own fire with *caru* mixed with sesame seeds and jaggery; consequently, a state of plenty (*subhikṣa*) arises within his kingdom.
Meditation—
one should meditate upon the God who is seated upon his chariot together with the Goddess, blazing with splendor;
holding arrows and bows with hands adorned with ornaments, possessing a heroic form, and being praised by the gods and others.
Oṃ! O Rudra, that auspicious form of yours which is fierce and appears as evil—look upon us with that most peaceful form, O Mountain-Dweller, and grant us peace.

The *puraścaraṇa* for the *Adāsya-mantra*: By reciting it three nights while subsisting on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), one has performed the *puraścaraṇa*. Then, one should perform a rite of pacification (*śānti*) for the cattle. Having prepared a fire-pit (*agnikuṇḍa*) measuring one cubit on all sides in the middle of a cow-pen, and once the fire is kindled, one should offer ten thousand oblations of fuel-sticks (*samidh*) made of *vikaṅkata* and *apāmārga*, smeared with curd, honey, and clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Now, we shall describe another rite of pacification for the cattle using this very [mantra]. Having had Brahmins consecrate water in a jar, scented it with all kinds of perfumes and the like, and having recited the mantra one hundred thousand times, one should sprinkle the cows; thus the pacification of the cattle is accomplished.

I meditate upon the Lord of creatures, the Sovereign, whose face is smiling, who is adorned with the moon as his crest-jewel, who bears the Gaṅgā, who has the Daughter of the Mountain as his companion,
who possesses three eyes, and who is decorated with ashes and serpents.
Oṃ! O Agni, you carry the arrow in your hand to shoot;
make it auspicious for those who follow the vows of Agni, and do not harm the person or the world.
O Śivā, you speak with a voice from the mountain;
may you cause all our diseases and consumption to vanish, and may we become well-disposed.

The preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for these two consists of twenty-one days of continuous recitation (*japa*). Once the preliminary practice has been completed, one should perform the warding off of untimely death (*akālamaraṇa-pratighāta*) with these two. A king should have a perfected Brahmin perform this; then untimely death shall not occur in his kingdom. For twenty-one days, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations (*lakṣa-homa*) of sesame, rice, wheat, and barley, smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. In that kingdom, there will be no fear of untimely death.
Within nine days, dangers from enemies perish; within eighteen days, it pacifies all untimely death in the entire world.

One should meditate upon the Enemy of Tripura, mounted upon his celestial chariot drawn by tawny horses, shining with a body suited for battle, laughing as he treats the three arrogant cities like blades of grass, desiring to consume the Daityas with the bow and arrows of the Lord of Mountains.
Oṃ! Today Dadhivaktṛ has spoken; he is the foremost divine physician.
May he crush all serpents and all sorcerers.

Now follows the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary preparatory rite) for this mantra: Having performed half a *kṛcchra* penance, thereafter for five days, eating only a meal of barley-gruel (*yavacarū*) at the root of a *śaika* tree, standing continuously during the day without contradicting one's essential duties, one becomes one who has completed the *puraścaraṇa*. Then, that king should cause protection to be performed. For the sake of all protection, an offering of eight thousand oblations (*homa*) should be made daily into a fire kindled by friction, using white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*), rice, and *dūrvā* grass mixed together and sprinkled with clarified butter (*ājya*).

Specifically, on the Trayodaśī (thirteenth) lunar day, there is a homa of ten thousand oblations. On that same occasion, a homa of eight thousand oblations consisting of sesame, jaggery, barley, and milk-mixture (*caru*) should be performed. The king shall become long-lived. At all times, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). And the sacrificial fee is of three kinds, according to the distinction of superior, middling, and inferior. Ten thousand gold *niṣkas* is the superior fee; five thousand is the middling; three thousand is the inferior. Alternatively, three hundred is the superior.

Two hundred [gold pieces] is the middling; one hundred *niṣkas* is the lowest. In whatever rite the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is prescribed as a constituent part of the ritual, one should first give the primary fee and afterwards the fee that is a constituent part of the rite. Thus, at all times, one should give the fee. Alternatively: sixty-four is the highest; three hundred is the middling; twenty-four is the lowest. In rites involving many performers, the highest fee should be given to each person; in a rite with a single performer, it goes to that one alone. Moreover, they cite this example:

"A sacrifice with very meager sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) brings misfortune to the patron. For kings and those equal to them, the highest fees should be given; for others, the middle and so forth. "If one has the means, one should not, out of delusion, fail to perform the ritual in its full detail; for one whose mind is overcome by greed does not obtain the fruit thereof. In a rite performed by ten persons, the fee is three hundred; for the teacher (ācārya), it is double. The teacher should be regarded as the Blessed Lord himself. In all cases, the sacrificial fee should be given according to this rule.

There, one should place the mantra-vessel upon the fire. To the east of the fire, one should establish the mantra-vessel; the vessel may be made of gold or silver. Having invoked the deity there into the fire, the *homa* (fire sacrifice) should be performed in its presence. At the conclusion of the *homa*, one should sprinkle the king with the water from the vessel. By the constant service of the Guru alone, the king becomes protected from *rakṣasas*. Furthermore, by consecrating cotton seeds, salt, and white mustard seeds eleven times with this very [mantra], if one travels toward any direction while carrying them, that direction is avoided [by obstacles]; one should go in any other direction.

One should fly toward the auspicious directions. Then, reciting [the mantra], one should go upward; one is liberated from tigers, thieves, *brahmarākṣasas*, *yakṣas*, *bhūtas*, and so forth. By this very [mantra], another method for destroying disease will now be explained: having consecrated mustard seeds seven times with the mantra and bound them upon the crest-lock (*śikhā*) of a patient, one should establish them there; health shall ensue. By performing it likewise with white mustard seeds, one is liberated from the *kumāragrahas* and other such afflictions.

Having consecrated a *nāgara* fruit with mantras, boiled it in milk, and offered eight thousand or eight hundred oblations into one's own fire, one should drink the remainder; thus, diseases of the fetus are destroyed.
As for meditation:

one should meditate upon the three-eyed God, whose crown is adorned with the moon, who has the enemy of Kāla (Śiva) as his crest-jewel, who wears a serpent as a sacred thread, and who resembles a blazing fire.
Oṃ! Homage to him who is copper-colored, ruddy, tawny, and most auspicious;
and to those Rudras who are stationed here around us in all directions—thousands of them—we implore their favor.
He approaches like a serpent, blue-necked and deep red.
The cowherds have seen him; indeed, the keepers of the cattle have seen him.
All beings have seen him; may he, being seen, be gracious to us.

Having performed one *kṛcchra* penance as a preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for both [mantras], one should recite them continuously for sixteen days. When there is no rain during these two months, rain must be brought about. Until the end of the *Ārdrā* asterism, on the day of *Ārdrā*, one should feed five accomplished Brahmins with offerings. To them, one should give turbans, garments, ear-rings, neck-ornaments, bracelets, and so forth. One hundred thousand oblations of the prepared sacrificial materials—sesame, rice, and barley smeared with curd, honey, and ghee—should be offered.

One should perform the oblation (*juhuyāt*). In the same manner as before, one of those five should mutter the mantra over the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) soaked in milk, while four of them should offer the oblations. Having been initiated for eleven days, on the final day, one should worship each [deity] with eight thousand offerings of the most excellent red substances (*raktatamarasa*). Having muttered the mantra once at the time of the ritual action, while touching and looking at the unharvested crop, if one acts otherwise, there would be a penance (*prāyaścitti*); until the completion [of the rite], protection of the fire must be maintained. On the day of conclusion, the Blessed Lord Āditya releases a great rain.

One should offer ten thousand oblations of *vetasa* flowers; Savitṛ grants a boon. One should worship the rising and setting sun with these two [mantras], standing in water reaching up to the neck; while reciting these two [mantras] over water filling both hands, one should pour it toward the sun. Having performed this eight thousand times every day for nine days, Savitṛ then grants the fulfillment of the mind’s desire for a year. One should offer twenty-one thousand oblations of *japā* flowers that have been moistened with my saliva;
by the grace of Savitṛ, one obtains the memory of past births and is born into a family of the four Vedas.
Meditation: One should contemplate [the deity] situated within the mandala, golden-hued, with a radiant body and a pure smile,
possessing a form like that of the fierce-rayed sun, and attended by thousands of sages.
Oṃ, homage be to the blue-necked one, the thousand-eyed, the bountiful;
and furthermore, to those other beings, to them I have paid homage.
Now follows the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite) for this mantra: one should recite it continuously for fifteen days while subsisting on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*).

In the presence of Śiva, having prepared a fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring one *aratni* on all sides in a western-facing chamber, one should offer a thousand oblations daily with *arka* flowers in a fire produced by friction, beginning from the new moon day and continuing for ten days, while offering clarified butter (*ghṛta*) as a nourishment to the Deity. Having observed the initiation (*dīkṣā*) for five days, one should receive [the mantra] in a place of enjoyment, on a riverbank, or in a cow-pen.

In the temple, one should invoke the deity above [the image], or elsewhere into the *kumbha* (vessel). Then, having established the fire in the western part, one should offer eleven thousand, or half of that (five thousand), or eight hundred oblations of *śamī* fuel-sticks, *śamī* leaves, and items smeared with curd, honey, and clarified butter (*dadhi-madhu-ghṛta*) for twelve days. One should place red lotus flowers (*tāmarasa-puṣpa*) around it; in their absence, leaves may be used. Having performed this, on the final day, one should feed eight thousand, or half of that (four thousand), or eight hundred Brahmins. One should especially perform the formal renunciation (*tyāga*) of the materials offered.
Having worshipped the eleven forms of Rudra and having offered some object to them, the preceptor [should perform the rite] to the south in the presence of the deity.

Having fed [the officiant] with honeyed food, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Even a sacrificial fee is like a field for sown seed. Measurement is also stated: eight hundred *daṇḍas* make a *nārartni*. For the sake of the earring (*kuṇḍala*), one *niṣka* of gold per day should be given; having fashioned the earring from that, it should be presented. A bronze vessel is likewise for the single fire-ritual (*ekāgnipeya*). Thus, by performing this rite desiring a son, one becomes possessed of a son through the power of Śambhu. As long as the sacrificial fee and the land [are maintained], the lineage remains unbroken.
Success is achieved within a year. This fruit extends over seven lifetimes; therefore, one should perform it without interruption.
Meditation:
One should meditate upon Śiva, seated upon a lion-throne together with Umā, his body possessing a cool radiance like the light of the moon and an arrow.
Oṃ! Release the string from both ends of your bow;
O Blessed One, let the arrows that are in your hand fly away.
O thousand-eyed one, wielder of the hundred arrows,
having drawn your bow to your ear and sharpened the tips of your shafts, become gracious and well-disposed toward us.
The bow has been unstrung, Kapardana is healed, and Viśalya has returned with his speech restored.
His arrows have not been exhausted; his quiver remains full.

Regarding these three ṛcs, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is as follows: having performed the *kṛcchra* penance and purified oneself, one should recite them for nine days; then they become effective. At the time of battle, having consecrated the weapons of the king with these [verses], one should offer a thousand oblations of *kuśa* grass and thorns; the enemies brought into battle are thus defeated.
Meditation:
One should meditate upon the Lord, whose head is ablaze with the brilliance of ten million rising suns,
who is adorned with terrifying serpents, and who wields two kinds of weapons.

The second [meditation] is on Rudra, the controller of the gods, who carries a trident and a *khaṭvāṅga* staff, is encircled by a garland of flames, and bestows fearlessness upon his devotees. Thus [it is said].
Oṃ! Your missile, O most bountiful one, has become a bow for you;
with that, protect us on every side from disease and from misfortune.
Homage be to you, the giver of life, the one who has stretched [the bow], the bold one;
and to both your arms, and to your bow, homage!
May the bowstring release its arrow from both ends; may it strike him from every side.
And place this arrow below him in this quiver.
Thus ends the first section.

One should perform the preliminary ritual (*puraścaraṇa*) for these verses as previously described for the three [mantras]. Furthermore, at the time of battle, one should pour oil sufficient for eleven thousand lamps into a large vat, invoke the deity there along with the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), and having worshipped them, touch the oil and recite [the mantra] eight thousand times every day for seven days. Having lit eleven thousand lamps with that consecrated oil while the enemy's kingdom is nearby, the commander-in-chief should go before the king.

Upon seeing the flame of a lamp, an enemy army does not stand its ground; by the power of these [mantras], the enemies of the gods are destroyed. Furthermore, by means of these very [mantras], Brahmins who have attained mastery over spells (*mantra-siddha*) and assume the guise of perfected beings (*siddha*) are capable of performing malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) against an enemy in the city of the foe. Whatever the king employs, once it has been touched or seen by them, they shall mutter, "Let there be malevolent magic," after having heard it from his mouth, making it unfit for touch or sight.

At the end of the mantra, or even at any other part that constitutes a limb of the city, they should dig [the ground] after it has been consecrated a thousand times. That city shall perish from the wrath of Śambhu within three years due to disease. To the preceptor who causes this to be done, a gift equal to a kingdom should be given. In all cases, it succeeds through the power of the mantra; one should perform the rite with a mind fixed on its efficacy.

One should constantly meditate upon the Great Father of the worlds, the wielder of the Pināka bow, whose pair of lotus-feet are reddened by the pollen of the flower-garlands on the heads of the gods who bow before him, and who is accompanied by Bhavānī.
Oṃ, salutations to the golden-armed one, the commander of armies, and the lord of the quarters; salutations, salutations!
To the trees with green hair, the lord of cattle; salutations, salutations!
To the one with white hair, the radiant one, the lord of paths; salutations, salutations!
Homage, homage to Babhluśa, the piercer, the lord of foods;
homage, homage to Harikeśa, the one girt with the sacred thread, the lord of prosperities;
homage, homage to Bhava’s weapon, the lord of the worlds.
Homage, homage to Rudra, the archer, the lord of fields; homage, homage to him who is born, the slayer, the lord of forests;
homage, homage to him whose arrows are red, the lord of trees.
Homage, homage to the one who possesses ministers, the master of the flanks; homage, homage to the one who creates a protective covering for the earth, the master of medicinal herbs;
homage, homage to the one with a loud voice who causes the foot soldiers to cry out, the master of the infantry.
Salutation to the one who has brought all weapons under his control, the lord of living beings.
Thus ends the second section.

The preliminary observance (*puraścaraṇa*) for this *anuvāka* is as follows: having performed an *ārtha-kṛcchra* penance, one should eat only *caru* (sacrificial porridge) eight thousand times. Furthermore, one should perform eleven circumambulations of the temple of Caṇḍī at every twilight. Upon the completion of the recitation (*japa*), having propitiated the deity and fed eleven Brahmins in His presence, one becomes one who has completed the *puraścaraṇa*. By means of that, [the results] previously mentioned for kings shall be attained.

One who desires the destruction of enemies should offer ten thousand oblations of red mustard seeds smeared with oil, while reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times; by this rite, the enemies perish. Having anointed the image of a deity with mustard seeds smeared with oil, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times while uttering the names of the enemies. Within eleven nights, a great fever shall arise among those enemy kings, and by that very means, they shall be destroyed.
When the battle was imminent, having placed a deep red cloth upon the deity and having purified himself, he [should say] with the thumb of his right hand: "Go forth!"

Reciting this at the end of each section (anuvāka), one should mutter it eight thousand times for five days; then he shall not fall from his position as king of enemies. One desiring to bring others under control should offer ten thousand oblations of palāśa, aśvattha, vikaṅkata, and apāmārga wood, smeared with honey and ghee. By this, he brings the four castes under subjection in due order. One desiring a kingdom should offer ten thousand oblations of kumuda, saugandhika, and utpala lotuses mixed with honey; the glory of sovereignty will attend him.

If one desires prosperity (*śrī*), one should offer ten thousand lotuses; one becomes prosperous. If one desires intelligence (*medhā*), one should offer ten thousand *palāśa* flowers smeared with the ghee of a tawny cow (*kapilājya*); one becomes intelligent. One who desires to conquer enemies should perform eleven thousand recitations (*japa*); the enemies are conquered. Every day, for as long as one lives, one should perform one hundred and eight or twenty-eight circumambulations and prostrations. Having become happy in this world, at the end one attains Kailāsa.
Meditation:
One should meditate upon Hara, whose every limb is adorned with pearls, who wears the moon and the Gaṅgā,
and who is seated at the foot of the wish-fulfilling tree together with Umā.
Oṃ, salutation to the one who endures all; salutation, salutation to the lord of those who are free from disease and those who cause no disease.

Homage, homage to Kakubha, the bearer of the quiver, the lord of thieves! Homage, homage to the bearer of the quiver, the wearer of the arrow-case, the lord of robbers! Homage, homage to the deceiver, the over-deceiver, the lord of plunderers!

Homage, homage to him who is fond of ornaments, who dwells in the forests, the lord of the forest-dwellers! Homage, homage to those with fangs, who roam at night, the lord of the beasts of prey! Homage, homage to him who wears a turban, who wanders the mountains, the lord of the Kuluñcas!

Homage, homage to those who possess arrows and those who carry bows; homage, homage to those who are stringing them and those who are fixing the arrows; homage, homage to those who are drawing them back and those who are releasing them.
Homage, homage to those who are eating and to those who are not; homage, homage to those who are sitting and to those who are lying down;
homage, homage to those who are sleeping and to those who are waking.
Homage, homage to those who stand and to those who run;
homage, homage to the assemblies and to the lords of the assemblies;
homage, homage to the horses and to the horse-riders.
Thus ends the third section.

Now follows the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for this section (*anuvāka*). Having performed the *kṛcchra* penance, one becomes one who has completed the preliminary practice by reciting it five thousand times. When there are epidemics in a country, the king should cause a rite of pacification (*śānti*) to be performed. Eleven accomplished Brahmins should perform the recitation (*japa*) in a temple of the Lord (*Īśvara*). Five [Brahmins] should perform the recitation; five should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*). One Brahmin should offer an oblation of sesame and rice (*tilaudana*) with each prostration (*namaskāra*). There should be one hundred thousand recitations. When this is done, the epidemic and other calamities in the country perish.

In the event of disease among vehicles, by performing eleven thousand oblations (*homa*) with cakes mixed with sesame paste in the measure of an *āhuti*, the general ailments of the vehicles are destroyed. In the case of other diseases, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *apāmārga* grains mixed with rice and clarified butter (*ājya*) into the mouth of the vehicle. Of these...

The disease is destroyed. In the case of a primary disease of the king, one should offer a hundred thousand oblations in the temple of Śambhu with pure rice grains sprinkled with ghee. In the case of a disease among the ministers as well, one should offer eight thousand oblations each with *dūrvā* and *pāmārga* grasses; their disease will be destroyed, and the king shall be freed from his affliction. Twenty-one accomplished Brahmins—of whom one is the presiding priest (*brahmā*)—should prepare a fire-pit of the king's dimensions on all sides. Having established the churned fire therein, they should perform the oblation, forming pairs.

The materials for the oblation (homa) are rice, sesame, *śyāmāka* grain, *nīvāra* millet, *pāmārga*, *dūrvā* grass, lotus filaments, clarified butter (*dadhi-ājya*), and all products of the cow mixed with clarified butter (*gavya-ājya*). To the south-west of that fire-pit (*agni-kuṇḍa*), one should touch a water-filled vessel and recite the *Brahma-mantra*. The oblations (*āhuti*) should also be offered continuously until the end of seven *nāḍikās*. Thus, the homa begins on the new moon day and concludes at the end of that new moon day. Furthermore, if a king's illness is severe, the homa shall be performed from sunrise until sunset. The fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the *nāḍikā*-homa is half a *niṣka* per person each day.

In the case of a daytime *homa*, it is double that amount; for the preceptor (*ācārya*), it is double that again. Sprinkling with water infused with *kalā* [herbs] should be performed over objects used by the king. When this is done, the illness of the king is destroyed. Furthermore, it is said: for the sake of destroying the king's illness, eight thousand oblations should be offered daily with white rice grains mixed with royal sesame seeds, accompanied by the recitation of the *anuvāka*. By this, the king becomes eternally free from disease and attains long life.

When other people are afflicted by disease, one should offer eight thousand oblations of sesame, rice, and barley soaked in ghee and honey, reciting this Anuvāka with each salutation; their illness will perish. By means of this Anuvāka, malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) are performed. A king desiring to cause a multitude of diseases in the kingdom of another should perform a hundred-thousand-fold homa (*lakṣahoma*) using the names [of the enemies] and black sesame seeds, saying: "I perform a malevolent rite against the enemy's kingdom, phaṭ svāhā!"

In this way, by means of a *homa* of flesh, the enemy's kingdom and its subjects wither away. Alternatively, one should perform a hundred thousand *homas* using fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of the *ekaṅkata* tree ground with blood and urine; by this, a great fever arises in the enemy. One should perform a hundred thousand recitations (*japa*) upon touching or even merely looking at water and other objects that are to be enjoyed by the people of the excellent kingdom; whoever is connected to that [place] perishes within a year. One should offer a hundred thousand oblations into the fire of the cremation ground using fuel-sticks of *varka*.

By that, the city of the enemy king perishes from disease; it becomes a forest of *arka* trees. By this very [rite], having stood facing south in the abode of Cāmuṇḍā, one should offer eleven thousand oblations of cooked black gram and sesame seeds. By this very [rite], the subjects of the enemy kingdom are afflicted by smallpox and are liberated from it. At the western gate of the temple of Śambhu, having remembered the God...

At the end of the mantra, recollecting [the target], one should say "prajvalajjvālā. By this, the enemy of the king becomes possessed by epilepsy (*apasmāra*). Recollecting the king who has fallen into all calamities, by performing a hundred thousand oblations (*homa*) with offerings of the size of a single *āhuti* made from the flour of pure rice, royal consumption (*rājayakṣman*) arises; by that very same [rite], it is destroyed.
Now, regarding the meditation:
She was endowed with the beauty of form, like an embodied forest deity;
her fullness was comparable to the *śoka*, *puṃnāga*, and young mango trees.
Adorned with a crest of twenty-five stars,
his face was like the stainless, full orb of the autumnal moon;
he wore matted locks bound at the end and was clothed in soft deerskin.
Adorned with garlands fashioned from both right and left [sides],
with a mass of kadamba flowers from the rain-clouds hanging down to his navel,
he was worthy of being gazed upon even by enemies, as he was beautiful to behold all the way down to his shanks.
His wife was beautiful in all her limbs, adorned with forest ornaments;
she was a flawless embodiment of the splendor of wild things, like a polished mirror.
Having placed a bow and a single, spotless arrow in her hand, [he said:]
With his left arm,
he held a second remaining fragrant cluster of flowers; having smelled it with his hand,
he was being fanned very gently by a branch with fresh sprouts.
Surrounded by children and charming dogs,
and with proud hounds running ahead,
that lord of the city of Kirāta, possessed of great splendor, proceeded toward the refuge of the worlds.
Oṃ, obeisance to the non-diseased ones and to those who pierce; obeisance, obeisance to you! Obeisance to the fierce hosts and to those who strike down; obeisance, obeisance to you!
Obeisance to the swift ones and to the lords of the swift; obeisance, obeisance to you!
Homage, homage to the hosts and to the lords of the hosts! Homage, homage to the troops and to the lords of the troops!
Homage, homage to those of diverse forms and those of universal forms!

Homage, homage to the great ones and to the small ones! Homage, homage to those who prosper and to those who do not prosper! Homage, homage to those who prosper! Homage, homage to the lords of those who prosper!
Homage, homage!
Homage, homage to the army commanders and to the generals; homage, homage to the warriors and to the charioteers;
homage, homage to the carpenters and to the smiths.
Homage, homage to the potters and to the smiths; homage, homage to the *puñjiṣṭhas* and to the *niṣādhas*;
homage, homage to the makers of arrows and to the makers of bows.
Homage, homage to the hunters and to the dogs; homage, homage to the dogs and to the masters of the dogs. Anuvāka.

The *anuvāka* of the *Adhāsya* section is the *puraścaraṇa*. Having performed a twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance or half of that, one should recite [the mantra] nine thousand times. Then, in a temple of Śiva, one should perform circumambulations eight thousand times; as long as the circumambulations continue, one should recite [the mantra] without interruption. In this way, one becomes one who has completed the *puraścaraṇa*. Here, specific days and so forth need not be observed; it should be performed whenever one feels inclined. A mortal afflicted by consumption (*rājayakṣman*) should perform a propitiatory rite (*śānti*) after having chosen a perfected twice-born (*siddha-dvija*).

Then, the chosen Brahmin, acting as the officiant, should prepare a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) one cubit in depth in a portion of that house; having constructed an altar (*vedi*) in front of it, he should place there a new jar filled with water and wound with thread. Having invoked the deity with this *anuvāka* and worshipped him with perfumes and other offerings—offering sandalwood paste, camphor, flowers, lotuses, incense, the ten-ingredient incense beginning with *uśīra*, and a lamp fed with clarified butter—and having propitiated the Self through the single *māra* [mantra], he should perform the initiation for eleven days.

On the day of commencement, having performed the rites up to the *mantrapuṣpa*, one should offer oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) eleven times for each *anuvāka* accompanied by a prostration (*namaskāra*), and then recite [the mantra] twenty-one thousand times in its presence. From that point until the conclusion, the fire must be carefully maintained.

After that, on the following day, having performed the daily obligatory rites (*nityakārya*), one should perform the *homa* eleven times with sesame, parched grain (*lāja*), *dūrvā*, rice (*vrīhi*), barley (*yava*), and parched grain mixed with honey and ghee (*madhusikta*), using the *anuvāka*. In this manner, for three days, one should offer oblations every day with honey and ghee. Then, on the second day—the seventh and eighth [days from the start]—one performs the *homa* with *aśvattha* and *apāmārga* wood as before. Thereafter, for one day, beginning at sunrise until sunset, one should recite the *anuvāka* continuously, provided it does not conflict with necessary daily duties. Then, on the ninth day, there is a *homa* with honey and ghee.

On the tenth day, one should recite from sunrise until sunset. Then, on the day of completion, one should worship the Deity with many lotus flowers—eight thousand in number—offering a prostration for each. Thereafter, having worshipped Gaurī, one should cause the Brahmins to say, "May there be the release from the bond. At the time of giving the gift, one should give eight thousand [coins], or half of that, or twenty-five *niṣkas*. Thus, there is a separate gift for the *oṃkāra*. The ritual fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should be given: one *niṣka* every day, and furthermore, as the final fee for all, a cow should be given.

Having thus completed [the ritual], one should dismiss the deity. This procedure applies to the builder of a temple or similar structure. Then, one should bathe and sprinkle him with the water from the jar. By this, consumption (rājayakṣmā) is destroyed. Through the grace of Śambhu, one becomes long-lived. With this very hymn (anuvāka), the pacification of consumption is prescribed. One should offer nine thousand oblations of honey and clarified butter into one's own fire while reciting the salutations.

One should offer oblations; delusion perishes. For other ailments such as leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) and the like, one should recite the *anuvāka* one hundred thousand times; diseases perish. In cases of fever (*jvara*) and *sannipāta*, a capable Brāhmaṇa, standing in water reaching up to his navel in a flowing stream, should cast eight thousand red lotuses while reciting the mantra for each prostration (*namaskāra*). With the remainder, the worship of Bhṛṅgirīṭi must be performed. When this is done, the great fever perishes.

Previously, the eradication of pulmonary consumption (*rājayakṣman*) by this means was mentioned. Because of the gravity of the matter, only a learned Brāhmaṇa may act as the preceptor (*guru*); otherwise, quarrels will arise.
Therefore, no omission should be made.
Then comes the meditation:
one should meditate upon Hara, who has all his limbs smeared with ashes, adorned with a circle of matted locks, three-eyed, mounted upon the bull, and accompanied by the Lord of the Gaṇas.

Thus ends the fourth Anuvāka. Maṇḍala: Oṃ, salutations to Bhava and to Rudra; salutations to Śarva and to Paśupati; salutations to the blue-necked one and to the white-throated one, and to the one with a hundred bows.

Salutations to the one with matted hair and to the one with disheveled hair; salutations to the thousand-eyed and to the one with a hundred bows. Salutations to Giriśa and to Śipiviṣṭa; salutations to the most bountiful and to the wielder of arrows.
Salutations to the short and to the dwarf; salutations to the great.
And salutation to the eldest, to the aged, and to the fully grown.
Homage to the foremost and to the one who goes first; homage to the swift and to the rapid; homage to the fleet and to the quick;
homage to the one of the waves and to the one of the waters; homage to the one of the stream and to the one of the island.
Homage to the eldest and to the youngest;
homage to the first-born and to the later-born; homage to the one who is growing and to the one who is full-grown;
homage to the last-born and to the lowest-born; homage to both.
Homage to Saryāya and to Yāmya, homage to Kṣemya;
homage to Urvarīya and to Khalya, homage to Ślokya and to Vasānya;
homage to Vanya and to Kakṣya, homage to Śrava and to Pratiśrava.
Homage to Aśuṣeṇa and to Suradhāvan;
homage to Śūra and to Vibhindu; homage to Varmin and to Varūthin;
homage to Bilmin and to Kavacin; homage to Śruta and to Śrutasena.

The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for these two *anuvākas* is as follows: one should subsist on sacrificial porridge (*caru*) for three nights and then recite [the mantras] continuously for eleven days; thus, the preliminary rite is accomplished. Thereafter, the ritual application (*karman*) is described: with white lotuses, one should offer them upon the *liṅga* eleven times every day for a month, making obeisance at each offering. Thus, royal prosperity increases. One should feed eleven Brahmins and offer a gift to the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti along with his entire retinue.

On the king’s birthday, one should offer twenty-one thousand oblations of *samidh* fuel-sticks smeared with clarified butter into either the royal fire or a fire produced by friction; likewise, eleven thousand oblations of *dūrvā* grass. When this is performed, the victory and longevity of the king increase. For the sake of victory, one should recite these two [mantras] one hundred thousand times.

When these two armies are drawn up for battle, one should offer oblations eleven times with the cooked food, side-dishes, and meal from the king’s kitchen, along with curd, honey, and ghee, while reciting the *pratinamaskāra* [mantras]. Having offered the remainder as a *bali* on the ground and taking water in his hand, he should sprinkle it toward the enemy army; that army will perish before long. With these same two [mantras], having offered oblations into the fire with pure rice grains sprinkled with clarified butter (*ājya*), one should sprinkle the remainder toward the enemy; he will perish. With these same two [mantras], having touched all the weapons of the king and [recited them] a thousand times—

One should consecrate them; their splendor increases. With these very two, one should throw this [substance] into the enemy's ranks; that army becomes destroyed for a long time. With these very two, the paralyzing of the enemy army is taught. One should offer oblations of *arka* fuel-sticks toward the sun a hundred thousand times while performing prostrations; [this results in] the paralyzing of the enemy army.

"Karomi svāhā. When this is performed, the enemy army becomes paralyzed. With these very [mantras], one should consecrate all food items for a king; they become nectar (*amṛta*). Desiring the withering of an enemy army, one should perform the following with these very [mantras]: one should offer a hundred thousand oblations (*juhuyāt*) of the meat of the deer, wild boar, rabbit, *paṃjala*, *kalavaṃka*, and antelope, mixed with the ashes of a *śūdra* woman who has crossed a river, into the fire, offering one oblation for each substance.

One should offer even with cakes (apūpa) a mere oblation in the measure of one hundred thousand, reciting at each salutation: "I cause the drying up of the subjects of the enemy kingdom, svāhā! When this is done, the subjects of the enemy kingdom wither away. Regarding their sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā)—gold, silver, cows, land, garments, and so forth—it is prescribed specifically for kings. For others, it is stated as follows:

For those who are venerable and childless, one should offer twenty-one thousand oblations of *udumbara* wood sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee into their own fire while reciting these two [mantras]. This is the "Homage" rite. One should recite them eight thousand times and consecrate Mahādeva with these very same [mantras] for the sake of anointment (*abhiṣeka*). This lasts for a period of seven *nāḍikās*. For a woman and a man who employ even *dūrvā* grass thirty-eight or forty-four times, a son is born;
he becomes a sharer of his own portion and is born as a devotee of Śiva. On his hands, there shall be the mark of a trident.

Having cooked ghee and milk-rice with these two [mantras], one should offer eight thousand oblations. Then, in another birth, he will be born as a Brāhmaṇa. Having consecrated a thread with these two [mantras], one should tie it on the hand of a pregnant woman; thus, there shall be no loss of the fetus. With these two [mantras], one should cause protection to be made from ashes for those seized by *kumāragraha* and other spirits. At night, one should also tie a lock of hair [with them]; then the fear of *kumāragraha* does not occur.
For meditation:
one should contemplate [the deity] whose hand holds a golden mountain like a water-pot, whose face is that of a deer,
who holds a bow and arrow in his hands, is mounted upon a chariot, and possesses the body of both man and woman.
Thus ends the sixth Anuvāka.
To me! Oṃ, salutations to the one with the drum and to the one with the kettledrum;
salutations to the bold and to the one who touches; salutations to the messenger and to the one sent forth; salutations to the one with the quiver and to the one skilled with the arrow.

Salutations to the Sharp One and to the one armed with a spear; salutations to the one with excellent weapons and to the one who possesses good weapons. Salutations to the one with a beautiful bow, to the one who follows the tracks, to the one on the path, and salutations to the one of the marshy ground, to the one of the canal, and to the one of the flowing stream.
Salutations to the one who dwells in lakes, to the one who dwells in rivers, and to the one who dwells in ponds.
Homage to the one who is in the metal and to the one who is in the wood; homage to the one who is in the rain-cloud and to the one who is in the rain.

Homage to the one who is in the cloud and to the one who is in the lightning; homage to the one who is in the heat and to the one who is in the scorching heat. Homage to the one who is in the wind and to the one who is in the storm.
Homage to Vāstavya and to Vastupā!

The *puraścaraṇa* for this *anuvāka* is as follows: having observed a single fast, one should recite it eight hundred times; thus, the *puraścaraṇa* is accomplished. One desiring to bring the four castes under control should offer oblations of wood from the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *vaṭa*, and *plakṣa* trees, soaked in honey, ghee, and water from the ocean. One becomes endowed with intelligence [by this]. One desiring nourishment (*puṣṭi*) should offer nine thousand oblations of cakes. One desiring health should offer five thousand oblations of fuel-sticks made of *khadira* wood, soaked in curd, honey, and ghee.

One desiring food should offer mango sprouts smeared with curd, honey, and ghee ten million times. One desiring beauty should offer mango sprouts smeared with curd, honey, and ghee ten million times. One desiring sovereignty should dig a fire-pit in the wilderness measuring one's own height, and there, into a fire produced by friction, offer five thousand white lotuses smeared with curd and other substances. Śrī herself will appear before him; by her grace, his lineage shall endure as long as the earth exists.

One who desires cotton cloth should offer ten thousand oblations of cotton seeds recited over by me; by this, cotton cloths are obtained. One who desires a cow should circumambulate a herd of cows ten thousand times while reciting this Anuvāka; he obtains a cow. One who desires a son should offer ten thousand oblations of Palāśa wood sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee;
he obtains a son who perpetuates his lineage. One who desires long life should offer ten thousand oblations of Dūrvā grass smeared with ghee every year; he becomes a hundred-year-lived man.

One who desires knowledge should offer one hundred thousand oblations of fuel-sticks (*samidh*) anointed with clarified butter; he becomes a master of all branches of knowledge. One who desires sovereignty should offer five hundred thousand oblations of *saugandhika* flowers anointed with honey; he is born as a sovereign emperor (*samrāj*). Now, the means for liberation is described: having first performed the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance, one should recite this chapter (*anuvāka*) twenty-one thousand times; thereafter, [one should perform] five thousand circumambulations and breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*).

Thereafter, having performed [the preliminary rites], one should offer three hundred thousand oblations of *palāśa* and *aśvattha* fuel-sticks smeared with honey and clarified butter into one's own fire in the presence of Śambhu. Then, by the grace of Śambhu, one becomes liberated; moreover, others born in that family shall endure as long as this earth exists.
I meditate upon the God who bestows fearlessness, who dances with long, matted locks,
who possesses a pure smile, and who is draped in a tiger skin.
To me! Oṃ, salutations to Soma and to Rudra, to him who has a staff in his hand and to the ruddy one;
salutations to Śarva and to Paśupati; salutations to the fierce one and to the one who is the earth;
salutations to him who is near and to him who is far away; salutations to the slayer and to him who will slay; salutations...

Salutations to the one with tawny hair who dwells in the trees; salutations to Tāra and to Śambhu; salutations to Mayobhava and to Śaṅkara; salutations to Mayaskara and to Śiva; salutations to the Auspicious One and to the More-Auspicious One.

Homage to the one who belongs to the heretics and to the one who belongs to the clans; homage to the one who is on the far shore and to the one who is on this shore; homage to the one who carries across and to the one who brings forth; homage to the one who cannot be crossed and to the one who is to be praised; homage to the one who possesses young grass and to the one who possesses fruit.
Having paid homage and having caused [the water] to flow forth.
Homage to him who is on the desert path and to him who is on the traveled road;

homage to him who is on the mountain ridge and to him who is in the dwelling place; homage to him who has matted hair and to him who is naked; homage to him who is in the cow-pen and to him who is in the house.
Homage to him who is on the couch and to him who is in the house; homage to him who is on the bank and to him who dwells in the abyss;
homage to him who is in the water and to him who is in the mud;
homage to him who is in the dry land and to him who is in the greenery.
Homage to Lopya and to Lapyā!

Homage to the broad one and to the spear-like one; homage to the leafy one and to the one who rests upon leaves; homage to the one who approaches and to the one who does not strike back; homage to the one who cleaves from behind and to the one who cleaves from the front.

We shall now describe the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rites) and other procedures for this *Adāsa-mantra*. Having first performed two *kṛcchra* penances, one should recite [the mantra] five hundred times; thus, the *puraścaraṇa* is accomplished. This is declared to be for kings. When a king desires universal sovereignty (*sāmrājya*), he should perform what is about to be described. The season is spring (*vasanta*); the place is a mountain, a temple of Śiva, or a forest. There, either at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) or in the presence of the deity, having had the Brāhmaṇas pronounce the success of the undertaking and having honored them, the commencement takes place.

The commencement [of the rite] should take place on either the *ārdrā* nakṣatra or the new moon day. One should select Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the mantras; or else, the *ācārya* may effect the immediate accomplishment of the ritual. By "ācārya" is meant one who is accomplished in the ritual manual (*kalpa*); whatever he says comes to pass exactly so. In that regard, "immediate accomplishment" is explained as follows: the Brāhmaṇas, having become purified by that *ācārya* and received the mantra, should recite it continuously for fifteen days. Thereafter, they become fit for the ritual. Thus...

Upon success, the fire-oblation (*homa*) must be performed. For every prostration, an oblation (*āhuti*) should be offered. The materials for the oblation consist of *tila*, rice, barley, and so forth, mixed with clarified butter (*ājya*). The times for the oblation are now described: starting from sunrise until sunset, one should perform it continuously for thirty-one days; thus should the twice-born act. To those who perform the oblation, upper garments and other items should be given as a vessel; to the preceptor (*ācārya*), earrings and the like should also be given. A vessel of clarified butter should always remain suspended above the sacrificial fire, dripping in a fine stream; this ritual practice should continue in this manner until it is completed. Furthermore, for the duration of that time, eight thousand meals must be provided daily for the deity.

One should feed that many Brahmins every day, and on the final day, twice as many as usual. One must understand that the Preceptor (Ācārya) is indeed the Lord himself. To the Preceptor, the most excellent gifts should be given. To each of the officiating priests (Ṛtviks), one hundred Niṣkas or half of that amount should be given as a sacrificial fee (Dakṣiṇā); to the Preceptor, twice that amount. In that Śiva-worship, the fragrance should be mixed with camphor; the flowers should be lotuses; and the incense should be camphor.

Guggulu is mixed [with the offering]. The lamp is made of cow-ghee. As for the food offering (naivedya), it has been described. In this manner, the propitiation of Rudra should be performed every year. Through such propitiation, a king shall become a sovereign emperor (samrāṭ). Those kings who are slain by forms of Rudra in the midst of the ocean are born here on earth as universal emperors. A mark of the Pināka bow appears upon his hands; by that mark, he is to be recognized as one who has performed the propitiation of Rudra.

It should be understood that any other king in whose hands this [text] rests or who holds it in his lap is also a worshiper of Rudra. In this manner, the worship of Rudra must be performed every year by eleven Brahmins. Regarding this very point, more is said: a king desiring the destruction of his enemies has this [rite] performed by an exceedingly capable Brahmin.

Having fashioned the enemy king into the form of a great *khadira* tree, one should invoke the deity into a water-filled jar in some secluded place. Taking fire into its presence, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations with *śamī* fuel-sticks that are thorny and smeared with blood; cat’s blood is especially recommended for this. Then, one should pierce every limb of that form with iron spikes.

Having caused [the image] to be dug up, the king should place his own foot upon it. At the time of placing it, the preceptor should recite mantras. Then the king should feed a hundred Brāhmaṇas and thereafter dismiss the deity. When this is done, the opposing king will be destroyed within three years. Furthermore, having fashioned that divine form together with its chain, one performs the fire-sacrifice (*homa*) as before. Thereafter, after some time, the king shall become bound by the chain and fall from his royal glory. Another method shall also be stated.

In the city of the enemy king, royal officers disguised in artificial attire, together with Brahmins and Siddhas, shall enter and, having consecrated four thousand wooden stakes (roha-śaṅkus) with mantras, they should secretly plant them at crossroads, at shrines (caityas), at temples (devāyatanas), and at the gates of the royal assembly hall and the palace. Then, they should scatter consecrated ashes everywhere and also scatter quicksilver (jāva). When this is done, that city remains destroyed for three years.

In this regard, trees such as the *khadira* and *badarī* grow there. Then, those of deformed appearance, performing penance in the waters of the reservoirs of enemy kings up to the depth of their necks, facing the sun, should recite [the mantra] eight hundred times every day for eight hundred days. When this is done, those who drink that water—such as mounts and others—perish like those bitten by a venomous snake. Those wise ones performing this should do so in secret; for if it were witnessed openly, fear of the king would arise immediately. Therefore, it must be performed strictly in secret. For those who act thus, the reward shall be the attainment of the kingdom.
Then comes meditation:

one should meditate upon the Lord of Beings, who holds the Pināka bow in his hand, whose splendor is like ten thousand rising suns, who is adorned with serpents, who has matted hair, and who bears Death (Kāla) around his neck.
Oṃ! Homage to you, O Karikas, the hearts of the gods; homage to the Vikṣiṇakas, homage to the Vicinvatkas, homage to the Āmīvatkas!

Now follows the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for this mantra: having performed the *parāka* penance, one should recite it forty thousand times; thus the preliminary practice is completed. For the purpose of purifying the mantra, one should recite it eight thousand times in the presence of the Guru; thereafter, one becomes fit for ritual action. By means of this mantra, nothing whatsoever is difficult to accomplish. Through the power of the mantra, everything is brought under one's control. By means of this, the rites for specific desires (*kāmyakarman*) are described.

In the presence of the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti, one should offer a hundred thousand oblations of *bālā* grass, sesame seeds, and rice into the fire of the self (*ātmāgni*) or the fire produced by friction (*mathikāgni*). Gold will emerge. One should offer ten thousand oblations of *apāmārga*, bamboo seeds, and barley smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. A thousand pieces of gold will emerge.

One who desires a maiden should fashion an image of her desired maiden out of *guggulu* resin; having obtained it, one should recite [the mantra] five thousand times, then cut it up and offer it as an oblation six thousand times. One obtains a beloved maiden adorned with all ornaments. One should offer an oblation of a hundred thousand *padma*, *utpala*, and *kumuda* lotuses; the royal fortune (*rājyalakṣmī*) becomes manifest to him. One should offer an oblation of a hundred thousand fruits and sprouts soaked in milk; *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and so forth, become visible and then vanish.

Having prepared a fire-pit in a great wilderness and kindled the fire therein, one should offer ten thousand *bilva* fruits as oblations. One should offer five thousand handfuls of *bilva* leaves smeared with clarified butter. Gold in the shape of a *bilva* fruit will be produced; it shall be a mass of touchable wealth. By offering one hundred thousand white lotuses smeared with cow’s ghee upon the deity, one becomes the lord of the entire earth.

One should perform oblations; a son who is a sovereign ruler (sārvabhauma) will be born. By offering fuel-sticks of *śamī* wood, one obtains a son devoted to Śiva. Having placed the powder of white *cchāra* fruit in a silver vessel and stirred it with cow’s ghee (*kāpila-sarpiḥ*), [one should offer] ten thousand [oblations].

Having performed the deliberation, one should practice it; one becomes a poet oneself. One should offer ten thousand oblations of *udumbara* wood fuel sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; one becomes highly proficient. Desiring the speed of thought (*manojava*), one should perform a vigil; even the preliminary recitation (*puraścaraṇa*) becomes especially effective. Having performed the year-long *kṛcchra* penance and purified oneself, one should then recite [the mantra] for eighteen days while subsisting on the roots and fruits of the *rukāśa* plant.

Then, at the conclusion of that, one should give five *niṣkas* of gold to the preceptor for the sake of the mantra’s mastery. Afterwards, one should perform the *japa* fifty thousand times in the presence of the preceptor and in the presence of the deity. Thereupon, Rudra, the Lord of Umā, becomes manifest before one's very eyes. By his grace, one becomes as swift as thought (*manojavī*). Whatever region one intends to go toward, one should remember the preceptor and repeat the mantra one hundred and eight times; one will then travel to that region. Thus, the method for attaining the speed of thought has been described.

Next, the method for becoming invisible is described. Here too, as before, at the time of making oneself invisible, one should grind red sandalwood and the milk of a tawny cow together, place that powder upon an *aśvattha* leaf, and recite the mantra eight thousand times while touching it. Then, having smeared oneself with that, touched the deity, and recollected [the deity], one should perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). Thereafter, one becomes invisible to anyone.

Having consecrated red sandalwood powder with ten thousand recitations of the mantra, one should form it into pills bound with thread. By wearing one on one's forehead every day upon entering the royal palace, the king and his officials will become submissive. If one wishes to cause anyone to perish, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times while standing on one leg in the presence of the Lord, preceded by the utterance of that person's name; they will perish within a year.
If one recites it eight hundred times daily in the presence of the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti, there shall be no fear from royal officials.
Meditation:
One should remember Śiva as a blazing mass of light, pervading the entire universe, with hands and feet on all sides, and eyes, heads, and faces everywhere.
Oṃ! O Drāpin, Lord of the Thread, O Daridra, Blue-and-Red One!
Do not take away the flesh or the blood of these men or these cattle; let nothing whatsoever of theirs be lost.

The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for an ineffective mantra is as follows: having observed a fast for one day, one should recite it ten thousand times; thus the preliminary rite is accomplished. One should offer ten thousand oblations of tawny cow's ghee during the *Ārdrā* asterism; thus one becomes wealthy.

In the case of a fever caused by the combination of all three humors (*sannipāta-jvara*), one should offer five thousand oblations of the tips of *urvā* grass; he shall be freed from that fever and become long-lived. Desiring liberation from malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), one should offer ten thousand oblations of *vikaṅkata* wood; for him, no fear from malevolent magics shall exist. One should offer ten thousand oblations of *udumbara* wood and sesame seeds; for him, no fear from malevolent magics shall exist.

Having kindled a fire in the midst of a village or city, one should offer ten thousand oblations there of sesame seeds and flour mixed with ghee. One should present an offering upon the leaves of the *aśvattha* tree. At the outset, one should also offer eight thousand oblations. Then Rudra, in the form of Bhairava, becomes visible to oneself along with the *bhūtas*. Having seen him, if one is unsteady, one becomes insane; however, for one who remains steady, great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*) arises. In times of distress, one should remember that form, and liberation from calamities occurs.
Then the visualization of the meditative absorption (dhyāna):
She has anklets reaching to her ankles, embraces a staff, and her tresses are disheveled;
she holds a trident, her ears are adorned with jasmine blossoms, she bears a tilaka mark, and her anklets jingle softly.
The Lord of Mṛḍānī, whose face is made white by the rays from his glorious and stainless rows of teeth,
and whose body is adorned with the attire of Bhairava, is to be meditated upon.
Oṃ! O Rudra, that auspicious form of yours which is auspicious for all days, which is a healing medicine, and which is the auspicious medicine of Rudra—with that, may you be gracious to us.

Now follows the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite) for this mantra: having performed eight hundred *prāṇāyāmas*, one should recite [the mantra] five thousand times. Thus the *puraścaraṇa* is accomplished. By this alone, protection must be provided for the fetus; nothing else. When the fetus has become manifest, one should perform the protection in the third month. By a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Rudra-mantra, upon that [fetus's] growth, having adorned himself according to his means and having bowed to Śambhu as if he were the fetus itself, [he should perform the rite]. When the fetus is well-formed...

The unrighteous should not be looked upon; rather, whatever is pleasing should be done at that very moment. In a secluded spot within the king’s palace, having accepted two *arvāgāmī* [plants], adorned them with the syllables *dvaja* and so forth, and having scattered pure *prastha* measures of rice over them with the two mantras, one should construct a fire-pit (*agni-kuṇḍa*) and an altar (*vedikā*). Upon the altar, on top of a common water-pot (*ghaṭa*), one should invoke Śambhu with the great mantra using a golden flower, and then place the water-jars (*kalaśa*) there with the two *arvāgāmī* mantras.

Having placed therein [vessels] joined together, wound with thread, containing gold within, accompanied by shallow bowls, filled with water from a river flowing to the ocean, and covered with fine cloth and rags; having placed in the center of that one jar filled with water, and in another—counting the days starting from the first day of the month—having filled it with gold and the nine gems, and having cast three *nīraghaṭa* [measures] into it, and having wrapped them securely in very costly garments; [one should perform] the worship of the Deity with the application of fragrant unguents.

Having worshipped Śrīkaṇṭha with offerings beginning with a red lotus flower, incense of *śītā*, and a lamp filled with ghee mixed with all perfumes and camphor, up until the final limit; and having recited the *upasthāna* mantra in his presence, one should then perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the *paṭasaṃskāra* mantra. As for the oblation materials, one should offer sesame seeds, the tips of *dūrvā* grass, lac, *tulasī*, *uśīra*, curd, honey, and clarified butter combined together. Then follows the worship of the sacrificial food (*havir-pūjā*). The sacrificial food consists of cooked rice measuring one *prastha*; with that, one should perform the oblation in the fire.

One should offer oblations with that mantra; then one should present perfumes, garments, and camphor, or whatever else is desired, for that indeed constitutes the service to the two gurus. Thus, at evening, the teacher should perform the twilight worship and recite the prayers. In that regard, the procedure for the daily rites involves wearing two garments: an undergarment and an upper robe. Such is the preliminary worship. One should always feed those who are learned in the Vedas and possess self-restraint. For one following this ritual, the capacity for these acts is specifically at night.

When this is done, the offspring will be long-lived; miscarriage will not occur. Everything other than the [use of] perfumes is according to the instruction. The offering should be made at the place of the *homa*. Women and *śūdras* should not enter; nor should heretics (*pākhaṇḍa*) and the like, because the mantra is Vedic. On the final day, there is a ritual bath. One should give that [fee] to the preceptor in the form of a staff. Then, one should perform the worship of the Gaṇas for the sake of the child’s protection from the planets. Thus, that offspring becomes long-lived. Furthermore, another matter is stated here as an incidental discussion regarding the girl. [The text continues: ...the girl... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a technical manual on ritual procedures (*tantra*), specifically concerning rites for ensuring the longevity of offspring and avoiding miscarriage. The translation reflects the archaic and technical register of the original.)

Therefore, one's offspring becomes long-lived. Furthermore, as this topic arises, other matters are stated: one seeking a daughter obtains a daughter by offering *alāja* grains soaked in clarified butter (*ghṛta*). A wise man should destroy misfortune (*alakṣmī*) through oblations of fuel-sticks of *apāmārga*. To destroy all taints, he should offer oblations of sesame seeds. By offering oblations of wood from the *akhadira* tree, he brings Brahmins and others under his control. Having wrapped them respectively with white, red, blue, and yellow threads, the practitioner obtains all desires by offering a hundred thousand oblations of clarified butter.

One who desires clothing should offer oblations with flowers such as the white water-lily (*kumuda*). Alternatively, by offering a flower of a particular color, one shall obtain clothing of that same color. One desiring rain should, in a pure place smeared with cow-dung, draw a mandala there using red pigment. In front of the mandala, one should cause a new pitcher to be placed; it should be properly encircled with thread and filled with scented water. [Therein] one should invoke...

Then, the wise man should offer milk there one hundred and eight times. Meditating on the Sun with a one-pointed mind, he should recite the mantra one thousand times. He should perform this for seven days, or even twelve days. Thereupon, the Blessed One, being pleased, causes a great rain to fall. Desiring a son, having fasted for a day and night and remaining pure in his vows, he should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with ghee one hundred and eight oblations. Then, [he should approach] his wife, who has bathed after her menses, is dressed in clean garments, and is adorned.

The wise man should feed the remainder of the food quickly, reciting one hundred and eight times; he should also feed Brahmins and perform a rite for well-being (*svastivācana*) in his own home. Thereafter, he obtains a son who is radiant and free from disease. This applies likewise upon seeing a meteor, upon seeing a bad dream, when afflicted by the evils caused by malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), or when overwhelmed by misfortune (*alakṣmī*); during a conflict, an ill omen, or when fear has arisen; as well as during affliction by the planets, by possession by spirits (*bhūtāveśa*), and in other such mental agonies or when beset by various defects.

Having prepared the previously described mandala, one should likewise prepare a new pitcher filled with scented water and endowed with all auspicious items, including cardamom, cloves, nutmeg, neem, and jasmine fruits. Having invoked the deity into the pitcher, one should worship there and perform oblations (homa). After consecrating [the water] one thousand and eight times with this mantra for oneself or for another, O God, one should perform the ablution; thereby, one is liberated from all defects.

Whoever recites this mantra daily, a thousand times, after bathing in the morning, their prosperity, health, and splendor shall increase at all times. Whoever recites it ten thousand times every day for a year while subsisting on a diet of milk, their health, prosperity, and splendor shall likewise increase forever.
