One who performs this with an incomparable perfection, endowed with qualities such as *aṇimā* (atomicity) and the rest, whose mind is fixed hereon, who is devoted to that alone, who is permeated by the state of that [deity], and who recites the mantra as prescribed—he becomes a sage (*muni*).
For meditation—
one should contemplate Śiva in the form of Skanda, resembling molten gold, holding a spear in his hand, six-faced, and mounted upon a peacock vehicle.

Om! Obeisance to me. Om! To this fierce Rudra, the one with matted hair, the lord of heroes who dwells among men, we offer our prayer. May he grant peace to our bipeds and quadrupeds; may there be all-round prosperity in this village, free from disease. O gracious Rudra, be favorable to us; we shall worship you, the lord of heroes, with reverence. Whatever blessings Manu, our father, invoked through sacrifice, may we attain those under your guidance, O Rudra.

Regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for the two [mantras] beginning with *adā*: having performed the *kṛcchra* penance, one should recite [the mantra] nine thousand times. Thus, the preliminary rite is accomplished. On the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), having established the fire in a place frequented by quadrupeds, one should offer oblations of the essence of curd (*dadhisāra*) to the extent of ten thousand (*ayuta*). One should offer oblations of the essence of curd to the extent of ten thousand. There will be prosperity for cows and other livestock. For the very same purpose of pacifying royal mounts, having touched water and performed the recitation ten thousand times while it is still damp, one should sprinkle the stable for the mounts with that consecrated water.

There is peace for vehicles. Having mixed a small amount of this [substance] with water, one should apply it to the vehicles. For the peace of animals, one should offer ten thousand oblations of *dūrvā* grass; there will be peace for them.
One should meditate upon Soma, who sits upon a divine lion-throne, being praised by great seers,
with a serene countenance, and bearing the essence of Soma.

O Rudra, do not harm our mind, nor our great spirit, nor our small child, nor our growing youth, nor our grown man; do not harm our father, nor our mother, nor our dear bodies. O Rudra, do not injure us. oṃ manoma̭haṃta mutamāno arbhakaṃ māna ukṣaṃtamutamāna ukṣitaṃ | mānonadhīḥ pitaraṃ motamātaraṃ priyāmāna stanuvo rudrarīriṣaḥ || ||

The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for the Adhanya-mantra: having observed three fasts, one should recite [the mantra] five thousand times; thus the preliminary rite is accomplished. By this, one’s own birth-star (*janmarkṣa*) becomes auspicious. One should offer ten thousand oblations of barley and sesame seeds that have not been husked; one should offer ten thousand oblations of *aśvattha* wood fuel; one should offer ten thousand oblations with curd, honey, and clarified butter. Every year, during the month of Ārdrā, one should offer ten thousand oblations. When this is performed, there is peace for oneself, one’s wife, children, and the elderly.

For this purpose of pacification as well, one should perform ten thousand recitations (*japa*); specifically, the king should cause a fire-oblation (*homa*) to be performed with this mantra every month during the *Kānti* and *Ārdrā* constellations. By that, the king's inner apartments and so forth shall also flourish.
Meditation:
One should meditate upon the Lord who has the crescent moon as his crown, whose body is like the rising sun,
who has the form of Nandīśvara, and who is surrounded by the lords of the Gaṇas.
Oṃ! Do not harm us in our offspring, nor in our life-span, nor in our cattle, nor in our horses.
O Rudra, do not strike down our heroic sons in your wrath; we seek to worship you with our salutation.

First, regarding the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this mantra: having performed the *kṛcchra* penance, one should consecrate a thousand *kapila* cows with the mantra using a vessel made of *udumbara* wood; then, having offered eight thousand oblations into one's own fire with that [milk], and having offered oblations with the *mahāvyāhṛtis*, one should consume the remainder [of the milk] in the amount of a hundred [mouthfuls] and fast for three nights. Thereafter, subsisting on *caru* porridge, one should recite the mantra fifty thousand times. One should give five *niṣkas* as a gift. As for the daily rite, the king, having offered oblations into his own fire, should offer ten thousand oblations of sesame seeds mixed exclusively with clarified butter.

Eight Brahmins, holding eight swords and taking eight hundred portions of ashes consecrated with mantras, should perform the protection of the king by placing them around him in the eight directions. This too must be performed constantly. By this very method, another is stated: one should offer ten thousand oblations of white lotuses smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. This should be performed by eleven Brahmins who have mastered the mantras and are either forms of the eleven Rudras or are themselves immediately perfected (*sadyasiddha*). Now, the immediate perfection (*sadyasiddhi*) is described.

Having received the mantra from the preceptor, one should fast for three nights and recite it continuously; thus, one becomes immediately successful. One should offer oblations ten thousand times daily, as prescribed for each specific rite, according to the requirements of that particular action. By this, the king becomes long-lived.

Having consecrated eight thousand or eight hundred water-filled jars made of gold, silver, or copper with this [mantra], having worshipped them with perfumes and other offerings, and having wrapped them in new cloths, the preceptor—having performed other auspicious rites—should bathe the king on the day of his birth using as many jars as there are. When this is done, the king becomes untainted by physical defects, sins, and the like.

Or, for the sake of the king’s prosperity, one should have a single Brahmin perform the recitation (*japa*) eight thousand times daily as a regular practice. Every month, under an auspicious lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), one should perform a propitiatory rite (*śānti*) in the stables for mounts and weapons, in armories, and at jewel-mines. One should offer ten thousand oblations of *aśvattha* and *apāmārga* twigs smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. Even the lifespan of those whose life has expired increases. In gambling and legal disputes, one should recite this mantra.

One becomes unconquerable. Having fasted for three nights, one should recite [the mantra] continuously. Then, eating sacrificial porridge (*caru*), one should offer ten thousand oblations of *bīra* fruits smeared with honey; one obtains a thousand pieces of gold. [The same applies to] *kumuda* flowers.

One should offer ten thousand oblations of [fuel sticks] smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; one obtains a maiden. By this same [rite], for one year, eating only *rubhā* (wild rice) and subsisting on *kapilā* ghee, one should constantly offer eight thousand or eight hundred oblations while reciting the mantra; one is liberated from all mortal sins (*mahāpātakas*). Having consecrated sandalwood powder with this [mantra], one should apply it to the forehead; all [beings] will become submissive.

One should offer eight thousand oblations with *apāmārga* fuel-sticks on one's birthday; this conquers untimely death (*apamṛtyu*). One desiring rain should worship the Sun with ten thousand *japā* flowers on a Sunday, wearing a red turban, garment, and ointment; then the Blessed Sun-god will release a great rain. One traveling a long distance should take ten pebbles, consecrate them eight thousand times with the mantra, and cast them in the ten directions before departing; thus, for as long as the journey lasts, he remains safe.
One who desires that his undertakings be free from obstacles should recite the mantra ten thousand times and then commence his work.

One should proceed with the mantra through effortless action. If one desires a son, one should offer a hundred thousand oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*); one obtains a son who will perpetuate the lineage. Furthermore, whomever one wishes to conquer, having fashioned an image of that person out of sand and standing upon its head, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times; one becomes victorious everywhere. Everything else also comes to pass by means of this. Due to the power of the mantra, it bears fruit only for those who have attained direct realization (*siddha*) of the deity; for others, it is a vain exertion. Thus says the mantra-scripture.
Regarding meditation:

one should always contemplate there the eternal Rudra, who has divided his body into eleven parts, who shines like pure crystal, who is a treasury of splendor, who holds the trident, and who wears a crescent moon upon his head.
Oṃ! O you who strike down the enemy, who slay the cattle-thieves, and who destroy the rākṣasas; let there be well-being for us, for this man who dwells among heroes.
Protect us, speak for us as a god, and grant us shelter, O you who are praised by the twice-born.

Now follows the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary preparatory rite). Having fasted for three nights, one should recite [the mantra] continuously throughout those nights. Thus one becomes one who has completed the *puraścaraṇa*. They say that this is intended only for those desiring long life, and not for others. For it is stated in the Śruti: "A man is said to have a lifespan of a hundred years. This being so, the application of this mantra is taught for the purpose of increasing the lifespan of those who die prematurely due to the burden of karma or causes for the exhaustion of life in this or another birth.

Every day, he should offer eight thousand or eight hundred oblations of clarified butter into his own fire. He should offer eight thousand oblations of *dūrvā* grass smeared with curds, honey, and ghee. He should always recite [the mantra] eight thousand times on the lunar mansion of his own birth, and especially so during the *ārdrā* asterism. At each *ārdrā*, he should offer ten thousand oblations of *dūrvā*, *apāmārga*, and *śamī* wood, as well as sesame seeds, each smeared with curds, honey, and ghee. During the night, he should recite it up to five thousand times; for that same duration, he should perform circumambulations.

On his birthday, a king should offer ten thousand oblations individually with *durvā* grass, *padma* lotuses, *mārga* flowers, and so forth; the king shall become long-lived. For those who are unable [to perform this], there is the *srotasi-homa* (stream-offering). For those who are utterly unable, there is only recitation (*japa*). One should offer ten thousand oblations of pure rice grains smeared with honey and clarified butter; his lifespan increases. With this mantra, one should worship the Deity above with ten thousand *arka* flowers; his prosperity increases.

One who subsists on raw rice and meat, sleeps on the ground, observes celibacy, and eats only forest-grown salt-free food, should recite the mantra a thousand times before the deity for the sake of the Lord; such a person becomes one with a lifespan of a hundred years for seven births. For one who is unable [to observe these], it is recommended that he bring food as an offering.
One should meditate upon the God who bestows joy, who is present in the proximity of the Goddess,
who is as radiant as blazing fire, and who resembles molten gold.

Oṃ! Praise him who dwells in the depth of hearing, the youthful one, like a terrible beast, the fierce striker. O Rudra, being praised, be gracious to the singer; let your armies lay down their weapons against another than us.

Now follows its preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*). Having fasted for one night, one should recite [the mantra] continuously for three nights; thus, the preliminary rite is accomplished. One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of fuel-sticks of *vaikaṅkata* wood, smeared with poison and oil, into a fire from a cremation ground; the enemies perish. Having uttered the name of the enemy, one should recite ten thousand times while holding ashes in one's hands in the presence of the deity; a great fever shall afflict that enemy. One should offer oblations mixed with white mustard seeds; the enemy develops smallpox and dies from it. [One may likewise act] upon the house, field, and so forth of the enemy.
Having recited this mantra ten thousand times, one should cause a pit to be dug there; therein, one should have hair, bones, gravel, and so forth excavated. Its destruction occurs swiftly.

One should meditate upon the fearless corpse, praised by the hosts of gods, who dwells in the sky, is terrifying, possesses a head ablaze with a fire as radiant as ten million rising suns, and is the source of all splendor.
Some say that the form of Śambhu must be invoked.
Oṃ! May the weapon of Rudra avoid us; may the ill-will of the impetuous one, who is full of sin, pass us by.
Spare those who bestow wealth upon us; O Bountiful One, be gracious to our children and descendants.

Now follows the *puraścaraṇa* for this mantra: having performed the *kṛcchra* penance, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times every day for nine days. Thus, the *puraścaraṇa* is accomplished. This should be performed specifically by those desiring sons, and it should be done in secret. One should offer ten thousand oblations at the western door of a temple of Śiva, using fuel-sticks of *khadira* or other trees grown in a forest fire, smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. One obtains a son equal to Śiva.

For the propitiation of the deity, the commencement [of the rite] should take place on the day of the new moon when the moon is in the constellation Aśvinī, or on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, either at one's own home or in a cow-pen. On the preceding day, the husband and wife should partake of *caru* (sacrificial porridge). One should install water-filled jars wrapped with threads, corresponding to each syllable of the mantra; having placed a larger jar in their center, one should invoke the Lord Soma into it: "May the Blessed One come from Kailāsa."

Having thus invoked [the deity] and worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should then, starting from the central pitcher as before, place one syllable at the beginning of each mantra upon every pitcher. Then, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) nine thousand times. Next, having offered eight thousand oblations of *śyāmāka* grains smeared with honey and clarified butter into the fire designated for the purpose, and having likewise offered that same number of oblations with clarified butter, one should then take the first pitcher and bathe [the deity], while meditating upon the Blessed One in the form of those respective syllables.

Having established these two upon a single seat and bathed them with water from a water-pot, one should feed eight thousand, or eight hundred, or at least one hundred Brahmins. There, having given garments, rice, and other provisions to the preceptor and having fed him, one should give five or three *niṣkas* as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) at the conclusion; indeed, the sacrificial fee of such a nature must not be even slightly less than this. Having given thus, the husband and wife should eat; in this way, a most auspicious and long-lived son is born to them.

Now, another method for those incapable of the previously mentioned ritual action is described. One who is incapable should recite this mantra. At the western gate of the temple, one should perform circumambulation for a full day and night—from sunrise until sunset, and from sunset until sunrise. In that regard, if an obstacle arises and the rite is interrupted, it is not a fault for those who are truly incapable. However, one who is capable but considers himself incapable and fails to perform the rite perishes. Therefore, a preceptor engaged in the *puraścaraṇa* should perform it with vigilance.

He shall describe the favor for those who are powerless, desirous of progeny, and without recourse: one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times daily, beginning from the north-eastern root of the *aśvattha* tree as if it were a constant rite; likewise, one should recite eight thousand times every day in each of the four directions around the *aśvattha*. Having thus completed this, one should feed as many Brahmins as possible who are endowed with initiation. It is said that for the sake of the deity, one will obtain a son who continues the lineage. The visualization (*dhyāna*) is as follows:
[one should meditate on the deity] whose body is covered by an elephant hide and who blazes with shimmering weapons.
One should meditate upon the God who destroys all sins and pierces the elephant [of Māra]. Thus [it is said].
Oṃ! O most bountiful one, O most auspicious one, be auspicious and well-disposed toward us.
Having placed your weapon upon the highest tree, wearing a skin and carrying the Pināka bow,
come hither.

The preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for one who has not yet performed it is as follows: one should recite [the mantra] fifteen thousand times for one night; this constitutes the preliminary practice. In the event of loss of wealth, danger to life, terrible suffering, or fear of thieves and the like, one should offer five thousand oblations of pure clarified butter (*ājya*); from these, one is liberated.
One should meditate upon the Lord who is the abode of auspiciousness, a youth exceedingly beautiful,
appearing in the form of a forest-dweller, the wielder of the Pināka bow, as he approaches.
Maṃ. Oṃ! O Disperser, O Blood-red One, homage be to you, O Blessed One!
May those thousand weapons of yours fall away from us like chaff.

Now follows its preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*). For three nights, eating only *caṇaka* (chickpeas), one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times. At the conclusion of that, while performing ten thousand circumambulations, one should recite it. Thus, the preliminary rite is accomplished. By this, in a great assembly of people, one should offer [oblations] smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, which produce a complete destruction.

One should offer ten thousand oblations of *samidh* fuel-sticks; one will not experience fear. Desiring to conquer all, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of *apāmārga* fuel-sticks smeared with the ghee of a tawny cow (*kapilā*). By this very means, wild boars and other such creatures become submissive. Desiring to conquer even animals, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of *bilva* fuel-sticks smeared with curds, honey, and ghee. By this very means, wild boars and other such creatures become submissive.

If one desires to conquer a horizontal [enemy], one should offer a hundred thousand oblations of *bilva* fuel-sticks smeared with curds, honey, and clarified butter. If one desires to conquer water, having established the fire within the water, one should offer a hundred thousand oblations of *kāpila* milk; then both [the enemy and the water] are overcome. In this same way, whatever else one may desire to conquer, having uttered the name of that specific object, one should offer a hundred thousand oblations of *kāpila* ghee; one conquers all of that.
Then follows the meditation:
one should meditate upon Him who has a serene face, who is gentle, who is adorned with the ornaments of marriage, who is accompanied by Umā, and who is praised by hosts of gods.
Oṃ! Thousands upon thousands are the weapons in your arms;
O Blessed One, as their master, turn their points away from us.

The *puraścaraṇa* for this mantra is now described: having performed half of a *kṛcchra* penance, one should recite it fifteen thousand times; thus the *puraścaraṇa* is accomplished. With this mantra, one should perform the pacification of calamities caused by kings for men. One should offer ten thousand oblations of rice, barley, and sesame seeds soaked in clarified butter, using fuel-sticks of *śālmalī* and *vaikaṅkata*; thus the calamities are pacified. In the presence of the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti, one should recite it one hundred thousand times. For the purpose of slaying a chief person, [one should fashion] a linga from the clay of an anthill.

Having performed [the rite] with this mantra, one should sprinkle [the person] as long as the practice has been carried out. Then, taking that clay and casting it into a pond, one should offer ten thousand oblations of purified rice grains smeared with ghee into one's own fire on its bank; his death will be pacified. For one traveling through a great wilderness, having consecrated eight thousand particles of ash with the mantra and having smeared the entire body with it, one should go; for him, no fear whatsoever shall arise.

On the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should offer an oblation (*bali*) at a cremation ground with the flesh of a *vāḍāla* (water-dog) while reciting: "I offer this oblation to the *rākṣasas*. Thereafter, no fear shall arise from them. For those afflicted by the wrath of Mahīśāstu, one should perform eight thousand oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) in the presence of Suvarṇamahāśāstu. One should also offer an oblation with the flesh of a cock. In that case, one should give new garments and gold as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the homa.

One-third of a *niṣka*, or one-hundredth part of a *vāra*, should be given as a fee. For others who have been afflicted by divine calamities, one should offer eight thousand oblations of clarified butter with this mantra; thus, the divine afflictions will perish.
Then follows the meditation:
"One should meditate upon the God who removes all sins, adorned with all ornaments,
bearing all weapons, and the Great Lord of all worlds."
Oṃ! There are thousands upon thousands of Rudras upon the earth;
I unstring their bows at a distance of a thousand yojanas.
O Bhavas, you who dwell in this great ocean of the intermediate space (antarikṣa)!
The blue-necked, white-throated, and black-eared ones who dwell there, moving about in exhaustion—
the Rudras with blue necks, white throats, and so forth, have taken refuge there.

We shall now describe the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) and so forth for these four mantras: having performed the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance for the sake of purifying the body, [one should recite] five thousand [times].

One should recite [the mantra]. Then, having completed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), one should perform the rite of sorcery (*abhicārika-karma*) with those mantras. A king should have the *homa* performed by Brahmins born in his own country. One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of *śālmalī*, *sāla*, cane, bamboo, and reeds, which have been wound around a scale-pan and smeared with rabbit blood. Furthermore, having fashioned an image of the enemy out of smooth, fine flour, and having infused it with life-breaths, one should cut it into pieces in sequence and offer eight thousand oblations.

By these applications, enemies are destroyed. One who counteracts sorcery with these very mantras should offer five thousand oblations of *dūrvā* grass smeared with curds, honey, and ghee. Thus, the faults of sorcery against a king are destroyed for the one who causes it to be performed.
Then comes the meditation:
one should meditate upon [the deity] whose face is formidable with fangs, whose hair is ablaze,
who bears a three-pointed lamp, and who is adorned with serpents.
Oṃ! Those who dwell in the trees, tawny, blue-necked, and crimson;
those who are the lords of beings, hairless and with matted locks;
those who pierce through the food and the vessels as people drink—[to them, svāhā].
For these three, as before, all [the rites] such as the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) and so forth [are to be performed].
To me! Oṃ! Those who guard the paths, the increasers of wealth, who are free from conflict.
Those who frequent sacred fords, carrying quivers and bearing swords.

The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for these two is as follows: having performed the *kṛcchra* penance, one should recite [the mantra] five thousand times; thus one becomes one who has completed the preliminary rite. On the day of entering a woman during her fertile period (*ṛtu*), one should offer eight thousand oblations into one's own fire with the milk of a tawny cow (*kāpila*) mixed with clarified butter. Thereafter, one may approach a woman during her fertile period. In that case, a wise son who continues the lineage is born. For the purpose of visiting a great sacred site (*mahātīrtha*), one should offer ten thousand oblations into one's own fire with pure rice grains sprinkled with clarified butter. One should then proceed to the sacred site without casting [any seed].
Having bathed and returned, he honors his own sacred fire and releases his vow of silence, thereby attaining the fruit of the holy ford for its intended purpose.
The meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and so forth are as previously described.
Oṃ! We bow down to the bows of those Rudras who, as many and even more numerous, dwell throughout the quarters;
we humble their bows with a thousandfold sacrifice.
All [the rites] such as the *puraścaraṇa* and so forth are to be understood as being the same as before.

Oṃ! Salutations to the Rudras who are on earth, those who are in the intermediate space, and those who are in heaven; whose food is wind and rain, whose arrows are these—salutations to them. Ten are toward the east, ten to the south, ten to the west, ten to the north, and ten upward. Salutations to them; may they be gracious to us. Him whom we hate and him who hates us—I place him within their jaws.

Now follows the *puraścaraṇa* for this mantra: having been initiated for twenty-one days, one should not consume any other substance for five times five days; everything must be raw (*āma*). For the first five days, milk; the second, fruit; the third, curd; the fourth, again fruit; and one day of fasting. Thus, during these four periods totaling twenty-one days, remaining always on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), one should constantly recite the mantra. Then, for five days, one should remain standing in water reaching only to the neck.

One should recite [the mantra] for one day and a half according to the prescribed rule. One should give ten *niṣkas* of gold to the preceptor (*ācārya*). Having performed service equal to that [amount] for those who listen, one becomes one who has completed the *puraścaraṇa*. Then, as in the daily practice, one should offer oblations of clarified butter eight thousand or eight hundred times into one's own fire (*svāgni*) with this [mantra]. One should recite it with undivided mind for as long as one lives. Thereafter, the ritual to be performed by means of this is stated.

Thus, on the new moon day following the aforementioned accomplishment, one should offer eight thousand oblations into one’s own fire with monkey-fat and clarified butter. Having offered them, one should smear one's hair and offer one hundred and eight more oblations. Then, the worship is performed according to the procedure prescribed for the *Atharvaśiras*. Thereupon, a magical apparition (*kṛtyā*) arises, red-limbed, with red hair and red eyes. Having previously placed four jars filled with blood, one should satisfy that apparition with them; otherwise, it will destroy oneself.

By means of that [oblation], one destroys everything; by means of that, one should accomplish all sorcery (*abhicāra*). One should offer ten thousand oblations with this clarified butter (*ājya*); knowledge of time arises, and ultimately, every measure of it indeed arises. One should offer ten thousand oblations with the milk of a tawny cow (*kāpila*); one becomes a rememberer of past births (*jātismara*).
He spoke of the fruit:
"By the grace of Rudra, everything has been heard exactly as it is. O King, the gift of eleven times eleven [elephants] was then mentioned; next is the gift of five *gokarṇikas*."

Likewise, the gift of Śambhu, which bestows sovereignty over the entire earth; the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa); the consecration for a split crest (śikhā) and the restoration of what is broken; the gift of the eleven Rudras, the worship of Soma and Vāsuki; the meritorious rite for remembering past births (jātismara-kriyā); and likewise the gift of the lineage (kuladāna)—all these have been described in their entirety, along with whatever else is appropriate for kings. Furthermore, you shall speak of the destruction of the house by means of the Rudra-mantra, the ritual for overcoming untimely death (apamṛtyu-jaya), especially for kings, accompanied by mantras and instructions.
"Time and place—indeed, all this has been stated by Śambhu as being accomplished by this very [means]. Thus [it is said].
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the mantras beginning with Rudra as declared in the Merutantra; may there be auspiciousness.
Thus concludes the Namaka, known as the Śrī Rudrapraśna, within the Agnikāṇḍa of the Yajurvedabhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhāskarācārya.
The [section] together with the mantras and the rules for the ritual application is completed.
May there be auspiciousness— now follow the Camaka mantras useful for the consecration of Śrī Rudra.

Oṃ! May Agni and Viṣṇu, in harmony, and the Aṅgirases, increase you both. Come hither with splendors and with strengths. May vigor be mine; may the Vasus be mine; may the offering be mine; may the pursuit be mine; may devotion be mine; may will be mine; may tone be mine; may fame be mine; may hearing be mine; may light be mine; may heaven be mine; may out-breath be mine; may in-breath be mine; may diffused breath be mine; may prosperity be mine; may thought be mine; may perception be mine; may speech be mine; may mind be mine; may sight be mine; may hearing be mine; may skill be mine; may strength be mine; may vital force be mine; may endurance be mine; may life-span be mine.

Old age is mine, my self is mine, my body is mine, my protection is mine, my armor is mine, my limbs are mine, my stations are mine, my joints are mine, and my physical forms are mine. My vital breaths are mine, my bodies are mine; eighteen in total.

The month of Jyeṣṭha is mine; overlordship is mine; fury is mine; wrath is mine; heat is mine; glow is mine; conquest is mine; greatness is mine; breadth is mine; expansion is mine; height is mine; length is mine; what has grown is mine; growth is mine; truth is mine; faith is mine; the world is mine; wealth is mine; control is mine; brilliance is mine; play is mine; joy is mine; what has been born is mine; what is to be born is mine; the well-spoken hymn is mine; the well-done deed is mine; what has been found is mine; what is to be found is mine; the past is mine; and the future is mine.

May there be for me good fortune and a good path; may there be for me the Buddha and awakening; may there be for me what is prepared and the act of preparation; may there be for me intelligence and excellent intelligence. This is the fourteen-fold Jagaccandhi. || 1 ||

May peace be mine; may joy be mine; may what is dear be mine; may my desire be fulfilled; may my longing be fulfilled; may mental well-being be mine; may prosperity be mine; may glory be mine; may fame be mine; may fortune be mine; may wealth be mine; may the controller be mine; may the sustainer be mine; may security be mine; may steadfastness be mine; may the universe be mine; may greatness be mine; may consciousness be mine; may knowledge be mine; may goodness be mine; may procreation be mine; may the plough be mine; may rest be mine; may cosmic order be mine; may mindfulness be mine; may freedom from disease be mine; may the sinew be mine; may life be mine; may long life be mine; may remembrance be mine.

"May there be fear for me, may there be a good path for me, may there be rest for me, may there be birth for me, may there be immortality for me; may there be fear for me, may there be a good path for me, may there be rest for me, may there be birth for me, may there be a fair day for me. Thus [ends the section on] "All Rest" and the eight [verses].

May strength be mine; may truth be mine; may milk be mine; may sap be mine; may clarified butter be mine; may honey be mine; may the marrow be mine; may the essence be mine; may agriculture be mine; may rain be mine; may victory be mine; may the power of uprooting be mine; may wealth be mine; may riches be mine; may prosperity be mine; may nourishment be mine; may pervasiveness be mine; may sovereignty be mine; may abundance be mine; may more be mine; may fullness be mine; may fullerness be mine; may inexhaustibility be mine; may barley be mine; may hungerlessness be mine; may rice be mine; may barley be mine; may beans be mine; may sesame be mine; may mung beans be mine; may chickpeas be mine.

Wheat for me, and *manu* grains for me, millet for me, and *eṇuva* beans for me; wheat for me, *manu* grains for me, millet for me, *eṇuva* beans for me; *śyāmāka* millet for me, and wild rice for me. The fourteen [grains], including the *masūra* lentils, are pervasive.

Stone is mine, clay is mine, the hills are mine, the mountains are mine, sand is mine, the trees are mine, gold is mine, tin is mine, lead is mine, zinc is mine, iron is mine; fire is mine, water is mine, creepers are mine, herbs are mine, black [iron] is mine.

May my ripening in the dark fortnight and my ripening in the light fortnight, may my domestic animals and my wild animals, prosper through sacrifice. May my wealth and my acquisition of wealth, may my possession and my prosperity, may my riches and my dwelling, may my action and my power, may my refreshment and my joy, may my path and my goal be attained. The dark-ripening [portion] and forty-eight.

Agni is mine and Indra is mine; Soma is mine and Indra is mine; Savitṛ is mine and Indra is mine; Sarasvatī is mine and Indra is mine; Pūṣan is mine and Indra is mine; Bṛhaspati is mine and Indra is mine; Mitra is mine and Indra is mine; Varuṇa is mine and Indra is mine.

Tvaṣṭṛ and Indra for me; Dhātṛ and Indra for me; Viṣṇu and Indra for me; the two Aśvins and Indra for me; the Maruts and Indra for me; all the gods and Indra for me; the earth and Indra for me; the atmosphere and Indra for me; the sky and Indra for me; the quarters and Indra for me; the zenith and Indra for me; Prajāpati and Indra for me. Tvaṣṭṛ and the sky and Indra for me—this is the twenty-first.

The *agṃśu* cup is mine, the *raśmi* cup is mine, the *iḍābhyaḥ* cup is mine, the *iḍāpati* cup is mine; the *upāṃśu* cup is mine, the *antaryāma* cup is mine; the *aindravāyava* cup is mine, the *maitrāvaruṇa* cup is mine; the *āśvina* cup is mine, the *pratiprasthāna* cup is mine; the *śukra* cup is mine, the *manthin* cup is mine; the *āgrayaṇa* cup is mine, the *vaiśvadeva* cup is mine; the *dhruva* cup is mine, the *vaiśvānara* cup is mine; the *marutvatīya* cups are mine, the *māhendra* cup is mine; the *āditya* cup is mine, the *nānā-vitra* cup is mine; the *sārasvata* cup is mine, the *pauṣṇa* cup is mine, the *pātnīvata* cup is mine, and the *hāriyojana* cup is mine. Thus.
The seasonal libations, the thirty-fourfold stoma, the under-layer, the sacrificial grass, and the altar.

My fire-hearths and my offering-spoons and my cups and my pressing-stones and my sacrificial posts and my sounding-holes and my two pressing-boards and my wooden trough and my Soma-vessels for Vāyu and my filter-holder and my mixing-vessel and my Āgnīdhra-shed and my oblation-holder and my houses and my assembly-hall and my sacrificial cakes and my cooked offerings and my *ṛk*-verses and my sun and my breath and my horse and my wealth and my earth and my Aditi and my Diti and my sky and my all-encompassing fingers and the quarters—[may these prosper] through sacrifice.

May my Ṛg-veda prosper; may my Sāman prosper; may my Stoma prosper; may my Yajus prosper; may my consecration (*dīkṣā*) prosper; may my austerity (*tapas*) prosper; may my season (*ṛtu*) prosper; may my vow (*vrata*) prosper; may [the two] through the rain of day and night prosper; may the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* [Sāmans] prosper through the sacrifice. Thus. This concludes the eighteen verses on consecration.

May my embryos prosper; may my calves prosper; may the one-year-old male and female prosper; may the two-year-old male and female prosper; may the three-year-old male and female prosper; may the four-year-old male and female prosper; may the five-year-old male and female prosper; may the calf of the third year and its mother prosper; may the calf of the fourth year and its mother prosper; may the calf of the fifth year and its mother prosper; may the bull prosper; may the cow prosper; may the stud-bull prosper; may the barren cow prosper; may the draught-ox prosper; may the milch-cow prosper. May life be perfected through sacrifice; may the out-breath be perfected through sacrifice; may the in-breath be perfected through sacrifice; may the diffused breath be perfected through sacrifice; may the eye [be perfected] through sacrifice.

May the ear be perfected by the sacrifice; may the mind be perfected by the sacrifice; may the eye be perfected by the sacrifice; may the self be perfected by the sacrifice; may the sacrifice itself be perfected by the sacrifice. Thus ends the section on the Bull and the forty-four [verses].

One cup is mine, three cups are mine, five cups are mine, seven cups are mine, eleven cups are mine, thirteen cups are mine, fifteen cups are mine, seventeen cups are mine, nineteen cups are mine, twenty-one cups are mine, twenty-three cups are mine, twenty-five cups are mine, twenty-seven cups are mine, twenty-nine cups are mine, thirty-one cups are mine, thirty-three cups are mine, forty cups are mine, forty-two cups are mine, forty-four cups are mine, forty-six cups are mine, forty-eight cups are mine, fifty cups are mine, fifty-two cups are mine, fifty-four cups are mine, fifty-six cups are mine, fifty-eight cups are mine.
Thus end the Camaka mantras employed in the Śrī Rudra Abhiṣeka.
Salutations to the illustrious Mahāgaṇādhipati; this is the Peaceful Lotus-Mine (Śāntikamalākara).
The propitiatory rites (śāntis) are now declared in their proper sequence by Kamalākara, the son of Śrīmad Rāmakṛṣṇa, who is himself the son of Nārāyaṇa.
By thus worshipping Gaṇeśa and the planets according to the prescribed rule,
one obtains the fruit of all actions and attains unsurpassed prosperity.
Thus, because Yājñavalkya stated that [this rite] is an auxiliary to all ritual acts, the propitiation of Vināyaka (Vināyakaśānti) is prescribed.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states who the qualified performer is:
Vināyaka was appointed by Rudra and likewise by Brahmā for the purpose of pacifying obstacles to ritual action and for the lordship over the Gaṇas.
O Lord, please explain the characteristics of one who is possessed by him:
he enters half of his own dreams and sees shaven-headed ascetics.
He dons saffron-colored robes and mounts carnivorous beasts;
he stands together with outcastes, donkeys, and camels. Even while walking, he considers himself followed by others.
In the future as well, O Karavīra, you shall remain with your limbs thus moistened and adorned by this misfortune.
Having thus explained the dreams, Yājñavalkya spoke further regarding their effects:
"One who possesses a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) and has bathed after a vow (*vaphala-snāta*) sinks down without apparent cause;
being afflicted by that, a prince does not obtain the kingdom."
A maiden [seeks] a husband, and a woman [seeks] offspring and a womb.

A woman does not conceive a fetus, and a pregnant woman does not give birth to offspring; nor does one attain the goal of life while living. Likewise, a teacher does not obtain discipleship, nor does a learned scholar (śrotriya) obtain study; a merchant does not obtain profit, and a farmer likewise does not obtain success from his cultivation.
His ceremonial bath should be performed according to the prescribed rites on an auspicious day.
Since he who was initiated by him is indeed qualified [for the rite],
and since he may even be a Śūdra, he too possesses the qualification.

"By Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who desire success, you, O Gajānana, are to be well-worshipped for the sake of accomplishing all rites free from obstacles"—thus from the Liṅga Purāṇa. For this very reason, in the Mahārṇava: "If the sacrificer is a Śūdra, [the rite] should be performed by the twice-born..."

"One should engage [them]," so it has been said. Thus, women also possess the authority [to perform these rites]. For this very reason, Bṛhat-Parāśara stated regarding the eligibility of women: "The rite performed by those whose husbands have died is rendered fruitless; likewise, everything performed by women is fruitless. By this, the state of being "approached" (*upasṛṣṭatva*) is declared as the basis for women's eligibility. Here too, although it is said, "A maiden, not yet having a husband," and so forth—even though it says "on auspicious [days]"—it specifies: "On an auspicious day joined with Hasta, Puṣya, Svāti, Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), or Vaiṣṇava (Śravaṇa)."

"Under the asterism [Puṣya], at the auspicious moment (muhūrta) Maitra, or when Brahmā is the presiding deity"—thus are the specific asterisms mentioned in the *Viṣṇudharma* for the pacification of Vināyaka. Furthermore, the specific astrological conjunctions (*yoga*) mentioned in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* should also be understood: "O Hero, O King, on the fourth day of the bright fortnight, under the asterism of Puṣya, and on the day of Jupiter (Dhiṣaṇa), that very asterism is favorable for him."

For the sake of the subsidiary rites of marriage and other ceremonies, and for the destruction of obstacles, one should perform the rite under any asterism—such as Devakṣatra, Kṛttikā, and so forth—up to Viśākhā, as prescribed in the Śruti: "Whatever merit [lies] in the asterism. This is because of the statement: "One performs [the rite] on an auspicious day (puṇyāha) itself. Bṛhat-Parāśara also says: "On the fourth lunar day of the bright fortnight, or likewise during the northern solstice, one should perform the Vināyaka-śānti for the sake of merit and for the accomplishment of all goals. The absence of the Vṛddhi-śrāddha is optional.

Yājñavalkya states: "With the head anointed with a paste of *go-rasa* (cow’s urine) and mustard seeds mixed with clarified butter (*ājya*), and likewise smeared all over with all medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadha*) and all fragrant substances (*sarvagandha*), while seated upon an auspicious throne (*bhadrāsana*), the auspicious twice-born ones should pronounce the benediction (*svasti*). Regarding the paste for anointing and the list of all medicinal herbs: *mura*, *māṃsī*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, *śaileya*, the two types of *javī*, *saṭī*, *campaka*, and *mustā*—this is remembered as the group of *sarvauṣadhi*. Thus it is stated in the *Mahārṇava*."

"Meṣaśṛṅgī, māṃsī, the two types of haridrā, murā, śaileya, candana, vacā, campaka, and mustā—these are remembered as the ten *sarvauṣadhīs*. Thus, these should be accepted according to the *Chandoga-pariśiṣṭa*. In that very context, based on common usage (*rūḍhi*), "murā" is well-known among the Mahārāṣṭras as "moharī"; "śaileya" is "śilājatu"; and these are called the "all-fragrances" (*sarvagandhāḥ*). Furthermore, in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*, cited in the *Hemādri* and *Madanaratna*: "Camphor, sandalwood, *darpa* (bālaka), and saffron in equal parts..."

"Everything-fragrance" (*sarvagandha*) is thus declared to be beloved by all the gods. However, in the *Madanaratna*, "everything-fragrances" are said to consist of sandalwood, saffron, agallochum, camphor, musk, and nutmeg; the source of that [definition] should be investigated. One should cast earth from a horse-stable, an elephant-stable, a confluence, a lake, and a cow-pen, as well as yellow pigment (*rocanā*), fragrant substances, and *guggulu* resin into water. Even when brought from water, [the materials] should be placed in four pitchers of a single color taken from a lake. "Fragrant substances" (*gandhān*) refers to everything-fragrances (*sarvagandhān*).

Regarding this, the specific details are stated: one should take four jars from the four springs, and having taken them, one should place therein all medicinal herbs, all fragrances, gold, rice, barley, bdellium (*guggulu*), earth, and molehills. The word "one should pour" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Furthermore, the auspicious throne (*bhadra-āsana*) should then be placed upon the hide of a bull; and this [throne] is to be placed first.

Some say that because the application was stated previously, the altar (vedī) should be made two cubits or four cubits long and one span high; however, that is to be reconsidered, as there is no measurement for the altar provided. Even in the ritual manual (karaṇa), two cubits are prescribed. In that [other] case, the consecration (abhiṣeka) follows the fire-oblation (homa) and should be performed to the north or the east; here, however, the fire-oblation follows the consecration.

Therefore, the fire-offering (homa) should be performed first, and the auspicious seat (bhadrāsana) afterwards—according to Kātyāyana’s statement that "rites [begin] from the east or the north"—the bathing throne should be to the north, and the fire-offering to its south; this latter arrangement is to be rejected by those who follow the tradition of the "fools" (mūrkhāḥ) who establish [the rites] toward the south. Here, having drawn a svastika in the center, one should spread upon it a red bull-hide with the neck facing east and the hair facing north; thereupon, having prepared the auspicious seat consisting of a śrīparṇī-wood throne with a white cloth on top, [one should place items] in its four directions starting from the east.

Having established the four Karaśas and worshipped Varuṇa within them, one should invoke Gaṇeśa and Śāṃbika upon their two images on a red cloth placed on the altar-pedestal (vedyāpīṭha) in the north-eastern direction, using their respective Gāyatrīs. Other deities are also mentioned for the western side: having worshipped Vyomakeśa, Pārvatī, and Bhāmaja, as well as Kṛṣṇa’s father Tāta, Arka, Māra, and likewise Sita; Dhiṣaṇa, Kledaputra, Koṇa, Lakṣma, and Bharata; Vidhuntuda, Bāhuleya, and the bearer of Nandaka.

Śiva is he whose hair is the sky; Gaṇeśa is born of Bhīma; Bhauma is Āro; Śukra is Sita; Skanda is the son of Bahulā; Viṣṇu is the bearer of the Nandaka sword. The seers have made the thousand-eyed, hundred-streamed [water] purifying. With that, I consecrate you; may the purifying (Pāvamānī) verses flow for you. May King Varuṇa grant you fortune; may Sūrya and Bṛhaspati grant you fortune; may Indra and Vāyu grant you fortune; and may the Seven Seers know [and grant] you fortune. Whatever ill fortune is in your hair, at your parting, or upon your head—[may it be removed].

"May the waters on the forehead, the ears, and the eyes destroy that [evil], O givers of strength!"—with each individual mantra, three jars [are offered], and with all three together, one jar; thus "fourfold" is according to the *Caulādarśana*, as stated by Vijñāneśvara. According to Satyaparārka, one jar is offered with each of the three mantras. For one who has bathed, one should offer mustard oil from a vessel made of *udumbara* wood into the fire using a *sruva* ladle, while holding *kuśa* grass in the left hand over the head, reciting: "Mitaśca, Saṃmitaśca, as well as Śālakaṭaṅkaṭau."

Having offered oil into the fire with the names beginning with "Mita" and ending with "Kūṣmāṇḍo rājaputraḥ svāhā," and having likewise offered the *caru* oblation into the fire with those same names upon the head of the sacrificer, one should offer the *bali* to the ten guardians of the directions, beginning with Indra, using the remnants of that [oblation] along with their names. Thus it is stated in the *Vijñāneśvara* and the *Mahārṇava*. However, Aparārka states: "Having offered oil with the previously mentioned names, the offering of the *kṛtādi-bali* should be performed with those very [names], but there is no *caru*-oblation because of the absence of [specific] names. Bṛhat-Parāśara also says: "One should offer the *bali* with the names, accompanied by the word 'namas'."

"With those [names] beginning with 'Mita'—thus it is said—one should offer the bali-oblation at a crossroads, having spread *kāśa* grass everywhere upon a winnowing basket, along with both prepared and unprepared rice, as well as fruits and boiled rice."

Having cooked fish, as well as meat—whether prepared or unprepared, raw or roasted—and flour-based preparations (lipiṣṭa), some say "māṃsa" refers to meat; rice mixed with that, and cooked meat of this extent; various fragrant flowers, and the three kinds of liquor: the three being *gauḍī*, *mādhvī*, and *paiṣṭī*. This applies to Śūdras. For Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, the *paiṣṭī* is forbidden; however, for a Brāhmaṇa, all three must be avoided. As for the *mahārṇava* [liquor], there is no authoritative basis for its inclusion here.

And because of the statement regarding the four castes—"In the Kali age, the horse-sacrifice and the chariot-sacrifice are to be avoided by the twice-born"—this prohibition does not include the taking of *surā* (liquor) even in the *sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice; this is established by the [text] beginning with "the inclusion of that. Furthermore, it is obtained from the passage beginning with "the exclusion of the *harītakī*."

However, because a general prohibition has as its sole purpose the mere cessation [of an action] and thus does not depend on specific details, there is no restriction [to certain items]; whereas a specific prohibition applies only where there is an excess of fault. Thus he says: "Therefore, in the absence of that [prohibition], milk should be taken by Śūdras and the twice-born. This is because Āpastamba states: "In the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, the milk-vessels are to be used by them. And the learned authorities, such as the *Mahārṇava*, state that this [milk] should be mixed with *naivedya* (food offered to the deity): "Root-vegetables, *pūrikā* cakes, *apūpa* cakes, *staṃdha*, *vaḍeraka*, and garlands [are permitted]."

Curds with rice (*dadhyanna*), milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and flour-cakes with jaggery and water—[regarding these], the *Mahārṇava* states they are "well-known"; Madanaratna and Vijñāneśvara state they are "preparations of flour made in those shapes"; *apūpa* is a wheat product cooked in oil; Aparārka states: "Guḍeraka-srajas are Śūdra-apūpas"; [these are] circular, four-cornered, or long preparations of flour.

"Artificial garlands are called *pauṇḍarīka*," according to the *Mahārṇava* and the *Madanaratna*. "Medaka" means flour mixed with molasses, according to Aparārka. "Laḍḍuka" is mentioned by Bṛhat-Parāśara in the *Madanaratna*. *Kulmāṣas* (fermented grains) and fruits are to be added; the mantras for the offerings will be stated in the ritual application (*prayoga*). Having brought all these together and placed them on the ground, then, having placed his head upon a winnowing basket—that is, on the sacrificial altar—he should then worship Ambikā, the mother of Vināyaka, after offering an *arghya* of dūrvā grass, mustard seeds, and flowers.

Having offered a full handful of water as an *arghya* oblation to Vināyaka and Ambikā, the meaning is that one should stand before them [with this prayer]: "O Blessed One, grant me beauty; grant me fame; grant me fortune. Grant me sons; grant me wealth; and grant me all my desires."

Regarding the worship of Vināyaka, Vijñāneśvara states that there is a constant modification [of the mantra] as "O Bhagavat" (Lord). However, since this is a rule common to all [rites], it must be considered how it applies when the original model (*prakṛti*) is absent. For this very reason, it is said: "O Ambikā. Then: "Wearing white garments and anointed with white unguents, one should feed Brāhmaṇas and give a pair of garments even to the Guru. Having thus worshipped Vināyaka and the planets according to the injunctions, one obtains the fruit of one's actions and attains unsurpassed prosperity."

The sacrificial fee, the consecration garment, and the garment that the preceptor should give—[the rule] "he gives a garment for himself to the preceptor" is stated by Baijavāpa in the *Madanaratna*. Now, there is a specific detail in the *Bodhāyana-sūtra*:

Thus ends the *Vināyaka-śānti*. Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure (*kalpa*) for Vināyaka. On the fourth or fifth day of the bright fortnight of every month, or on occasions such as the rising of the sun, one who desires purity, wisdom, or cattle should offer an oblation (*bali*) to Vināyaka. Having eaten only once the previous day and performed the ceremonial sipping of water (*ācamana*), the sacrificer, facing the gods, having performed the rites beginning with the invocation of the fire (*agnimukha*), faces southward and invokes the deity with an elephant’s face: "O Lord of Obstacles (*Vighneśvara*), come! O Obstacle! Having thus paid homage, he prays: "May you be free from obstacles for us."

Then, with the mantra "bhavodbhava," she offers water for the arghya on dūrvā grass and unbroken grains (akṣata) while focusing her mind; [she offers] these waters which are most auspicious, pure, the purest, sanctifying, the most sanctifying, immortal, having the taste of nectar, primordial, worthy of arghya, worthy of honor, worthy of consecration, worthy of being sipped, and worthy of being used for sprinkling.

"May the Blessed Vināyaka and Ambikā be accepted," he says; then, having worshipped in silence with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, he stands in attendance, saying: "Homage to the Lord of Beings, homage to the Lord of the World, homage to the Lord of Creatures. Then he offers three oblations to Vināyaka: "To Vināyaka, the Lord of Beings, homage! To Vināyaka, svāhā! From the Jaya [mantra] onwards, until the bestowing of the boon by the cow of plenty, he scatters for him as an offering: a cake, sweetmeats, barley-meal, and milk-rice, for Vighna.

Svāhā! Thus [to] Vivāyaka, to Vīra, to Śūra, to Ugra, to Bhīma, to Hastimukha, to Varada, and to the attendants of the Vighnas—svāhā! Then one should offer an oblation to the spirits with the words: "To those spirits who roam here... Then, one binds a five-threaded bracelet upon the hand, saying: "O Vināyaka of mighty arms, by your command, let this obstacle [be removed]."

Having said, "May all my desires be accomplished; I bind this *kaṅkama*," and having circumambulated the fire clockwise, bowed, and offered salutations, he dismisses Vināyaka with the verse: "O Lord of the Gaṇas, if great enjoyment has been obtained by me through what was performed, arise with your attendants, O virtuous one; protect me, O auspicious one, be gracious! He then prepares the dismissal offering of curds, honey, milk, and ghee.

Now, the ritual procedure (*prayoga*): On an auspicious day as previously mentioned, the performer, having recalled the place and time, should make a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), saying: "For the sake of pacifying obstacles to learning (*vidyāyaka-upasarga*) and for the attainment of prosperity (*lakṣmī*), I shall perform the *Vināyaka-śānti*. Having performed the worship of Gaṇeśa, the recitation of the *Puṇyāha*, and the *Vṛddhi-śrāddha*, and having chosen an *Ācārya*, he should select four officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) according to the opinion of Parāśara, or eight.

Regarding those, the *Madanaratna* states that there are four "proclaimers of auspiciousness" (*svastivācaka*): "Now, the preceptor, having drawn a *svastika* in five colors or white in the center of the eight [directions], and having spread upon it the hide of a bull (*māṇḍuha*) with its neck facing east and its hair upwards, he should place there a seat made of *śrīparṇī* wood. Covering that with a white cloth and drawing four *svastikas* in the four directions, he should [seat] four men of a single caste there, starting from the east, with their knees touching the ground according to the verse beginning with 'The earth and heaven' (*mahī dyauḥ*)."

Having placed jars upon a heap of grain, and having poured into them water from a lake, water from a river confluence, or fresh rainwater, one should throw earth into them with the mantra: "O Earth, destroy this sin—the evil deed committed by me—by Kṛṣṇa, the hundred-armed, who raised up the excellent boar. Then, one should add fragrant substances such as sandalwood, agallochum, saffron, musk, and camphor, along with *gorocana*, *guggulu*, and *guggula*, while reciting the mantra beginning with "gaṃdhadvārām."
Oṃ! I invoke here Śrī, the Goddess of all beings, who has the fragrance as her door, who is difficult to behold, who is eternally nourishing, and who bestows prosperity.

Having cast five sprouts [into the vessel] with the verse, "Like a horse... (RV 10.40.10): "O Aśvadeva, you have made a dwelling for yourself like a leaf; indeed, it has been prepared for the sake of cattle, since you, O men, shall win it."
"Having adorned [her] with a garland of sandalwood," and "those which are fruitful"— the word *phalinī* means fruit.
Those plants which bear fruit and those which are fruitless, those which blossom and those which are flowerless—
impelled by Bṛhaspati, may they release this man from his skin-disease.
"Thou art of a pleasing form," [with these words] he threw gold [into the fire], saying: "O Savitṛ, thou grantest wealth to the giver; do thou bestow upon us a wonderful and abundant portion."
Having cast the oblation with the mantra "Of golden form," [he recites]:
"Oṃ! Of golden form, of golden appearance, may he protect us from food.
Golden-colored, having sat down from his golden womb."
O giver of gold, grant [it]; homage to you!
"Enveloped with a beautiful garment"—having thus wrapped [the bride] with a cloth:
"Oṃ! Clothed in a beautiful garment and well-enveloped, he comes forth;
becoming more excellent as he is born, him the wise poets [behold]."
They raise it up, tasting it with their minds as they worship.
Having placed the full vessel with the mantra "pūrṇād arvi," one should say: "Oṃ, may the full ladle fly away; may it return well-filled.
Bring us fortune, bring us food and strength, O Śatakratu!"
Having placed [the mantra] four times in each of the directions for every jar, recite the "Devadāna" at the mouth of the jar.
Viṣṇu is at the mouth of the jar, Rudra is at the neck, and the Vasus reside there;
Brahmā is situated at the base, and the hosts of Mothers are remembered as being in the middle.
All the oceans are likewise contained within the belly of the jar.

During the churning of the great ocean in the dialogue between the gods and the dānavas, the poison that arose was held by Viṣṇu himself in his mouth. O Ocean, all holy places (tīrthas) reside within you; all the gods are established in you.
Abiding in you, all beings are established; in you, the vital breaths (prāṇas) are established.
You yourself are Śiva, you are Viṣṇu, and you are Prajāpati.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Viśvedevas, along with the ancestors (pitaras), [are you].
Since the granting of the fruits of desire resides even in your very sound, O Lotus-born One,
I desire to perform acts such as its expansion;
therefore, O God, grant me your presence and be gracious in every way.
Then, four officiating priests (ṛtvij) in the four directions, having invoked Varuṇa with the mantra "tvanno agne," [should proceed].
Oṃ! O Agni, you who know, may you ward off the wrath of the god Varuṇa from us;
as the most excellent sacrificer, the best bearer of oblations, and the most radiant one, release us from all hateful enmities.

Having performed worship with the sixteen services, they should recite the *Anobhadra* hymn and the peace-chants (*śānti*) found in their own Vedic branch, beginning with "May the wind blow auspiciously for us" (*śanno vātaḥ pavatām*).
Oṃ! May our auspicious intentions proceed toward all goals; may they be unimpeded and victorious. May the power of the gods be ever-present for our protection.

May the protection of the gods come near us day by day; may the benevolence of the gods be easy for us to attain, O upright people. May the gift of the gods turn toward us; we have approached the friendship of the gods. May the gods prolong our lives so that we may live. They have declared this ancient wisdom: may the great Bhaga, Mitra, Aditi, Dakṣa, Aśvins, Aryaman, Varuṇa, Soma, and the auspicious Sarasvatī grant us well-being. May the wind blow healing medicine upon us that brings joy; may Mother Earth [grant it].
Through that [soma], heaven [was established]; through that, the pressing-stones that press the soma, which are sources of bliss; through that, O Aśvins, hear this our most desirable prayer.

Oṃ! May the wind blow auspiciously for us, may Mātariśvan purify us; may the sun shine auspiciously upon us. May the day be a source of peace for us, and may the night be established as a source of peace. May the dawn spread peace over us, and may the Āditya rise for our peace. Be gracious, most auspicious, and most merciful to us, O Sarasvatī. O Mother, do not look down upon us from the sky. You are the dwelling-place of Iḍā; may you be a dwelling-place of abundance for me. May I be possessed of a good dwelling, and may he who hates us and whom we hate be without a dwelling.

Carrying medicine with the wind that blows from the open space, you, O all-healing one, go as the messenger of the gods. These two winds, O Vāta, blow from afar across the ocean: may one blow strength to me, and may the other blow away whatever is harmful. Whatever has been placed here as a store for the mindful one in this house, O Vāta, grant that to us so that we may live; grant that medicine to us. Bring that great medicine to us, O Vāta; let it blow health and well-being upon us, and may it not harm our breath or our life-force.

You are the support of Indra; I take refuge in you, with the horse as my companion. With that which is mine, I take refuge in *bhūḥ*, I take refuge in *bhuvaḥ*, I take refuge in *suvaḥ*, I take refuge in *bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ*. I take refuge in Vāyu, I take refuge in the afflicted deity, I take refuge in the stone and the sacrificial animal. I take refuge in the Brahman-treasury of Prajāpati; I take refuge in the Brahman, *oṃ* I take refuge.

The atmosphere is my wide, vast, and lofty space; the fires, the mountains, and the wind have gone forth. With well-being, with auspiciousness, with safety, and with well-being, may my vital breaths be secure. O out-breath and in-breath, do not fall away from death; O out-breath and in-breath, do not abandon me. May food be in me, may offspring be in me; may Agni bestow radiance upon me. May food be in me, may offspring be in me; may Indra bestow sensory power upon me. May food be in me.

May Sūrya bestow offspring upon me; may he grant me radiance through the days and nights. O Aśvins, protect us with unharmed blessings throughout the days and nights. This we pray for: that Mitra, Varuṇa, the great Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven may favor us. By what [splendor], O wondrous one...

He has become the messenger, the ever-encircling friend. By what most powerful manifestation? Who among the true exhilarations is the most bountiful to you, so that he may find joy in the draught? He breaks even the firm things asunder; he is the protector of his friends and the patron of those who sing his praises. May you be ours with a hundred aids. The birds of beautiful wings, the Priyamedha seers, approached Indra with their prayers. Unveil the darkness, open wide the light for us, like one who releases those bound in a pit! May the divine waters be auspicious for our aid and for our drinking; may they flow toward us for our well-being and prosperity.

I implore the Waters, the sovereigns of the noble and the rulers of the people, for healing medicine. May the Waters and the Plants be friendly to us; may they be unfriendly to him who hates us and whom we hate. O Waters, you are the source of bliss; grant us strength for great delight and for our vision. You drive away the sharpest darkness; like mothers, you bring nourishment to him whose dwelling you quicken with your favor. O Waters, give us life.

The earth is pacified; may it, pacified by Agni and pacified by its Lord, pacify my grief. The atmosphere is pacified; may it, pacified by Vāyu and pacified by its Lord, pacify my grief. The sky is pacified; may it, pacified by Āditya and pacified by its Lord, pacify my grief.

May the earth be peace, may the atmosphere be peace, may the sky be peace, may the quarters be peace, may the intermediate directions be peace, may fire be peace, may wind be peace, may the sun be peace, may the moon be peace, may the stars be peace, may the waters be peace, may the herbs be peace, may the trees be peace, may the cow be peace, may the goat be peace, may the horse be peace, may man be peace, may the sacred word (*brahman*) be peace, may the Brahmin be peace; may there indeed be peace, may there be peace; may peace be mine. May there be peace!

With that peace, with all-encompassing peace, I bring peace for me, for bipeds, and for quadrupeds; may there be peace for me, may there be peace! May Fortune, Modesty, Fortitude, Austerity, Intelligence, Stability, Faith, Truth, and Dharma—these, as I arise, arise after me; may Fortune, Modesty, Fortitude, Austerity, Intelligence, Stability, Faith, Truth, and Dharma—these attend me as I come. May Fortune, Modesty, Fortitude, Austerity, Intelligence, Stability, Faith, Truth, and Dharma—these have favored me.

With the life-span of Uda, with the excellence of my own life, with the sap of the herbs, with the vigor of Parjanya, I have risen up following the immortals. And may that razor, ordained by the gods, shine forth in the east—pure and bright. May we see for a hundred autumns; may we live for a hundred autumns; may we rejoice for a hundred autumns; may we delight for a hundred autumns; may we be prosperous for a hundred autumns; may we hear for a hundred autumns; may we speak for a hundred autumns; may we remain unconquered for a hundred autumns, and may we enjoy the sight of the sun. He who has emerged from the great ocean.

May the wise, red-eyed Sun, the bull, purify me with his mind as he moves twice around the churning of the waters. You are the drop of the *brahman*; you stand at the impulse of the *brahman*; you are the receptacle of the *brahman*. By this *brahman* this earth is supported; by this great *brahman* the atmosphere and the sky are held up. This earth, together with the gods, is supported by it. What I know, that I shall maintain; may the Veda not slip away from me.

I gaze upon the intellect; may it enter me for the securing of all that has been and all that is to be. May I attain a full span of life—may I attain a full span of life! O Lord of the Bay Steeds, may you swell with these songs whatever in us is deficient; growing strong, O Giver of Wealth, when you break open the cow-stalls for the sake of your praisers, may we be sharers in abundant food. May our prayer be proclaimed to you as great. Oṃ. Peace, peace, peace.

Then the preceptor, having prepared a sacrificial altar (*sthaṇḍila*) to the east of the auspicious seat for the purpose of the fire-oblation, shall worship Vināyaka and Ambikā upon a pedestal on a one-cubit-high platform to the northeast of that, with images adorned by cloths and other offerings; the mantras for this are as follows.
We know that Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon Vakratuṇḍa;
may that Daṃṣṭrin inspire us. Thus [is the mantra] for Vināyaka.
Oṃ, may we know Subhagā; may we meditate upon Kālī and Mālinī;
may Gaurī inspire us.
In this manner, one should invoke Ambikā into the golden image.
Around that, as space permitted, they placed images either individually or in clusters.

Having invoked Vyoman (the Sky), Vyomakeśa (Śiva), Pārvatī, Bhīma, Vanudeva, Ārka (the Sun), Maṅgala (Mars), Bṛhaspati (Jupiter), Budha (Mercury), Śanaiścara (Saturn), Candra (the Moon), Rāhu, Bāhuleya (Ketu), and Viṣṇu—these being Indra and the other guardians of the quarters—and having worshipped them with offerings such as wine and food according to the prescribed rites, one should [establish] the fire upon the sacrificial mound to the east of the auspicious seat according to the procedure taught for domestic rites.

Having performed the consecration (*pratiṣṭhāpya*), one should add the supplementary oblations (*anvādadhyāt*). Some perform this as a *grahamakhā* sacrifice; others perform it as a *navagrahamakhā*, for the ritual procedure (*tantra*) there is the same.

There, to the north of Vināyaka, one should perform the invocation of the planets (*grahavāhana*). In that *anvādhāna* (preliminary ritual), having omitted the *cakṣuṣya* [offering], one should offer the principal oblations to the planets with fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and sacrificial porridge (*caru*). Having offered one oblation of porridge each to Mita, Saṃmita, Śāla, Kaṭa, Kūṣmāṇḍa, and Rājaputra; and having offered one oblation of porridge each to Vyomakeśādhīna and the others; and having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering with the remainder, one should cook the sacrificial porridge. Having placed it upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), one should [anoint] all limbs with a paste of white mustard seeds mixed with cow’s urine, as previously described.

"The preceptor should cause the sacrificer, whose head is anointed with all types of medicinal herbs and all fragrances, to sit upon an auspicious seat while reciting the Vedic sounds and auspicious mantras"—so state Vijñāneśvara, Mahārṇava, and others. Bṛhat-Parāśara also says: "Having seated him, one should anoint him. This is stated in the *Majjanaratna*. Thereafter, the sacrificer, together with four Brahmins previously chosen, should perform the *svastivācana* (invocation of well-being).

Then, the lustration (*nīrājana*) should be performed with women who have sons and are well-dressed; it is the custom that the patron (*yajamāna*) should give them garments and bodices. Thereafter, the preceptor (*ācārya*), taking the water-pot situated in the eastern direction, should sprinkle the patron with the mantra: "Thousand-eyed, hundred-streamed, purified by the sages—with that I sprinkle you; may they purify me from sin."

Oṃ! May the purifying verses (Pāvamānya) purify me with the purifier belonging to Prajāpati, that golden bridge extending through a hundred heavens; by means of that, may we purify the Brahman, purified by the arising of the knower of Brahman.
May Indra, through his guidance, purify us along with the powers.
May Soma purify me with well-being, Varuṇa with friendship, and King Yama with his crushing powers;
may Jātavedas purify me, and may he purify me with the strengthening [power].
"May King Varuṇa grant fortune; may Sūrya and Bṛhaspati grant fortune;
may Indra and Vāyu grant fortune; and may the Seven Ṛṣis know [and grant] fortune. Thus it is said.

With the southern pitcher. Then, taking the northern pitcher, one should perform the consecration with the three mantras beginning with "Sahasrākṣam. In the Aparākarma rite, however, the consecration is performed with each pitcher individually using those three [mantras]. Then, one should perform the consecration with all four pitchers combined, according to the teaching of Bṛhat-Parāśara: "This indeed is the purifying bath remembered by the sages as 'Sahasrākṣa'; may these Pāvamānī verses purify you with that [water] flowing in a thousand streams. [Then follow the mantras] beginning with "Śakrādi..."

May the guardians of the ten directions, Brahmā, Īśa, Keśava, and the others, as well as the waters, destroy misfortune and grant peace at all times. May the waters be friendly to us; may they be unfriendly to him who hates us and whom we hate. May the oceans, mountains, rivers, and the sages who observe their vows—all these together—destroy misfortune and grant peace.

May that which resides always—in the feet, ankles, thighs, shanks, face, hips, belly, and navel; in the breasts, thighs, arms, fingertips, neck, shoulders, and joints; and in the nose, forehead, ears, eyebrows, and the ends of the hair—destroy misfortune and grant peace at all times.

Then the preceptor, facing east and standing behind the sacrificer, places *kuśa* grass upon the sacrificer’s head with his left hand; having taken mustard oil there with a ladle (*sruva*) made of *udumbara* wood, he offers six oblations: "Oṃ *mitāya* svāhā—[the sacrificer says] 'Idam mitāya'; likewise the subsequent offerings: "Oṃ *saṃmitāya*, Oṃ *śālāya*, Oṃ *kaṭaṃkaṭāya*, Oṃ *kūṣmāṇḍāya*, Oṃ *rājaputrāya*. Thus he should offer the six oblations.

In the opinion of Aparārka, there are four oblations: one each for Śālakaṭaṅkaṭa and Eka-kuśmāṇḍa, and one for the Rājaputra. Furthermore, the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa* of the Atharva-Veda Kauśika school also states this: "Then, having performed the placing of fuel (*idhmādhāna*) and so forth in the fire, and having offered the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) into the fire with the six previously mentioned mantras, and having offered one oblation to Vyomakeśa and the others, [one should perform] the *sviṣṭakṛt* and subsequent rites up to the end of the expiatory oblations (*prāyaścittahoma*). Then, in the directions starting from the east, one should offer the remainder of the *caru* as a *bali* to the ten world-protectors beginning with Indra, using their respective name-mantras."

Having bathed with pure water and wearing washed garments, the patron (yajamāna), together with his preceptor (ācārya), shall worship Vināyaka and Ambikā with the previously mentioned *gāyatrīs* using the sixteen types of offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*). He should offer cooked rice mixed with unhusked rice, sesame seeds, and *tila*; various kinds of fish, both cooked and raw; and liquor (*surā*). In the absence of these, he should place milk mixed with rock salt in three vessels, along with cooked and raw meat, radishes, cakes (*apūpa*), *pūrikā*, *koṇḍeraka*, garlands, curd-rice, milk-porridge (*pāyasa*), flour mixed with jaggery, sweetmeats (*modaka*), *laḍḍuka*, and various fragrant flowers.

Having placed the variegated fruits in a single vessel or winnowing basket, one should offer them as an *upahāra* (offering) to Vināyaka with the previously mentioned mantra, saying, "I present this offering to Vināyaka. Having given the offering to both Vināyaka and Ambikā, and having filled the hollowed palms (*añjali*) with water mixed with flowers, sandalwood paste, incense, and mustard seeds, one should offer the *arghya* (water of respect) to each individually with the two previously mentioned mantras. Then, having offered handfuls of *dūrvā* grass, mustard seeds, and flowers with those same two mantras, one should place one's head upon the ground.
O Blessed One, grant me beauty; O Blessed One, grant me fame; grant me fortune. Grant me sons, grant me wealth, and grant me every desire.
Thus [one addresses] Vināyaka:
"O Goddess, grant me beauty, grant me fame, bestow upon me fortune;
grant me sons, grant me wealth, and grant me all my desires."
Auśija Vaiśya, Kautsa Radhītara, Śaṭha Kaukīvāṃdana, Upārjāyani, Ambarīṣa Marṣaṇa,
Bṛhadukṣa, Śiśira, Darbhapiṅga, and Bhadraṇa.

Thus one should worship Ambikā. Bṛhat-Parāśara states another mantra: "O Ambikā, grant me good fortune, beauty, fortune, fame, prosperity, sons, desires, and likewise valor—grant these to me. O Mother of Gaṇeśa, O Bālā, whatever I desire, grant that to me by your singular name; O Gaurī, grant me boons. According to the *Madanaratna*, the offering of the *arghya* (water libation), the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*), and the *bali* offering at the crossroads should be performed after this. Then, the preceptor, having spread *kuśa* grass upon a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*)—whether prepared or unprepared—[proceeds with the rite].

Having placed the sacrificial offering (dyupahāra) there on the ground, having sprinkled water upon the four-footed [spot], and having spread *kuśa* grass there, one should worship the deities mentioned in the mantra. Having placed a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) there, one should present the oblation (*bali*). The mantras are: "May these gods accept the oblation: the Ādityas, the Vasus, likewise the Maruts, the two Aśvins, the Rudras, the Suvarṇas, the Pannagas, the Grahas, the Asuras, the Yātudhānas, the Piśācas, the Mātṛs, and the Uragas."

Śākinīs, Yakṣas, Bhairavas, Yoginīs, Pūtanas, Śivās, Jṛmbhakas, Siddhas, Gandharvas, those who possess various sciences, and mountain-dwellers; the guardians of the directions, the protectors of the worlds, and those who are Vighnas and Vināyakas; the great sages beginning with Brahmā, who bring peace to the worlds—may they cause no obstacle, may they not harm me, and may my adversaries perish. May the spirits and ghosts be gentle, satisfied, and bringers of happiness. Then the sacrificer, having returned home, having washed his hands and sipped water (ācamana), and having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti)—

Having worshipped the preceptor (ācārya) and given him a pair of garments and gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and having given abundant fees according to his capacity to the officiating priests (ṛtvij) and others; having performed the subsequent worship of Vināyaka and Ambikā and dismissed them; having given [the fee] to the preceptor, worshipped the fire, applied the sacred ash (vibhūti), and dismissed the fire; and having fed the Brahmins, one should perform the dedication of the ritual act to the Lord of Karma (Karmeśvara).

Thus ends the *Vināyaka-śānti* from the *Śāntiratna*, composed by Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa—the son of Rāmakṛṣṇa Bhaṭṭa, who was the son of the scholar Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa. In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* as cited in the *Hemādri*: "On the fourth lunar day, having caused a beautiful golden elephant weighing more than one *pala* to be fashioned, one should place it upon a heap of a *droṇa* of sesame seeds mixed with *kuśa* grass. Having worshipped it with garments and flowers and offered food oblations (*naivedya*), one should then give it to a Brāhmaṇa, saying: 'May Gaṇeśa be pleased. In all undertakings, no obstacle shall arise for him."

Hemādri states that through this *vināyaka-śānti*, the obstacle is removed; otherwise, one becomes intoxicated with pride for seven births. Furthermore, he maintains that this rite should be performed in the months of Caitra, Śrāvaṇa, or Kārttika.

Now, regarding the *gṛhayajña* (domestic sacrifice) for the pacification of the planets (*graha-śānti*): because it is the subject at hand, it is called the "domestic sacrifice. Skanda and Yājñavalkya state: "One desiring prosperity, one desiring peace, or even one performing malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), [should perform it] on the fourth lunar day (*caturthī*). It may be performed alone, as the *ayutahoma*, the *lakṣahoma*, or the *koṭihoma*. Of these, the first was taught by Yājñavalkya and others. In the *Mātsya Purāṇa*, three types are mentioned: "The *grahayaṣṭi* is declared to be threefold, as taught in the Purāṇas and the Śrutis. The first is the *ayutahoma*; after that, the *lakṣahoma*."

The third category is the *homa* (fire sacrifice), which bestows the fruits of all desires. It is of two kinds: occasional (*naimittika*) and optional (*kāmya*). Its location is in that very same place.
