A wise person should cause a pavilion to be constructed to the north-east of the planetary deity’s site, or on the ground of the temple of Rudra; it should be square and sloping toward the north. One should construct it according to the rules with ten or eight cubits [in size]. Four doors should be made for it by the discerning ones. [This is stated] in the *Mantramuktāvalī*.
It should have four corners and four doors, measuring eight cubits or ten, or twenty-four cubits; it should not be less than that.

The intermediate and superior [sizes] follow in sequence. Alternatively, they may be two, four, six, eight, ten, twelve, fourteen, sixteen, eighteen, twenty, twenty-two, twenty-four, twenty-six, and up to twenty-eight cubits; thus it has been stated by certain wise men. It is the same in the Agni Purāṇa. However, this pavilion (maṇṭapa) is for optional (kāmya) rites, occasional (naimittika) rites, and so forth. For the daily (nitya) and occasional rites, it is excluded; "all of this [is the pavilion] here" according to the Śāradātilaka. The method for the circular pavilion (kuṇḍala-maṇṭapa) should be known from my father’s *Pramodadīpikā* and from my own *Dānakamalākara*. [It is also mentioned] in the Skanda Purāṇa.

In the sacrifice to the nine planets (navagrahamakha), the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be one cubit in measure and perfectly square. Its base should be one cubit deep, its opening (yoni) should be equal [to the base], and it should be provided with a girdle (mekhalā). The girdle should have a width of four finger-breadths (catur-aṅgula) and be raised to the same height. A pit that is deficient in measurement and so forth is said to bring fear to the practitioner. Regarding the *yoni*, the *Matsya Purāṇa* states: "The *yoni* should be two spans (vita-sti) in length, six or seven finger-breadths in width, elevated in the middle like the back of a tortoise, and at the sides, it should be one finger-breadth high. Everywhere above the girdle, it should resemble the petal of a half-blown lotus."

"In the absence of a pit (kuṇḍa), there should be an altar (sthaṇḍila). One should perform the daily and occasional fire-oblations (homa) on the altar," according to the *Śāradātilaka*. "One should resort to such a pit or an altar," according to the *Skanda Purāṇa*. To the northeast of that [pit] is the altar-platform (vedī). It may be triangular or quadrangular, measuring one span (vitasti) in height. A rampart (vapra) two finger-breadths high is declared to be the first; above that, there should be two ramparts joined with a height of one finger-breadth each.

The width for all [the altars] therein is stated by the wise to be two finger-breadths (*dvyaṅgula*). In the sacrifice to the nine planets (*navagraha-makha*), four auspicious officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should be appointed; or else, having worshipped even a single one according to the rules together with the Brahman priest. In the *Skanda Purāṇa* within the *Madanaratna*: "In the sacrifice to the nine planets, four Brahmins who are exponents of the Vedas [should be used]; or else, for the sake of pacification (*śānti*), only two are prescribed by the Śruti. In the case of ten thousand oblations (*ayuta-homa*), however, one should not engage in excessive elaboration. On the prepared altar, the *Sarvatobhadra* [mandala] should be constructed.

"The *sarvatobhadra* mandala is known as common to all [deities]," according to the *Śāradātilaka*. In the *Mātsya Purāṇa*: "On an auspicious day declared by a Brahmin, having performed the recitation by Brahmins (*brāhmaṇavācana*) and the bringing of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*), one should invoke the gods upon the altar (*vedi*). All [the deities], including the presiding and subordinate deities (*pratyadhidevatā*), face the Sun. Regarding the images, Yājñavalkya says: "The planets may be made from copper, crystal, red sandalwood, gold, silver, colored cloth, iron, lead, bell-metal, or wood, according to one's desire."

Or they may be painted on cloth in their respective colors, or with fragrant pigments within a mandala. In the *Matsya Purāṇa*: The Sun (Ravi) should always be depicted as having two arms, seated upon a lotus, holding a lotus in his hand, possessing a luster like that of a lotus petal, having seven horses, and being equipped with seven reins. The Moon (Śaśin) should be made white, wearing white garments and white ornaments, having ten horses, holding a mace in his hand, and bestowing boons. The Son of the Earth (Bhauma/Maṅgala) should have four arms, wear red garlands and garments, hold a spear, a trident, and a mace, ride upon a ram, and be a bestower of boons.

Wearing yellow garlands and garments, with a luster like that of the *karṇikāra* flower, holding a sword, shield, and mace in his hands, the wise Budha (Mercury) stands granting boons. Likewise, the preceptors of the gods and the Daityas (Jupiter and Venus) should be made yellow and white respectively, four-armed, holding staffs, granting boons, and carrying rosaries and water-pots (*kamaṇḍalu*). The son of the Sun (Saturn) should always be depicted with the brilliance of a sapphire (*indranīla*), bearing a trident, granting boons, and having a vulture as his vehicle; he holds an arrow and a bow. Karālavaktra (Rāhu) has a terrifying face, carries a sword, shield, and trident, and grants boons.

And Rāhu is praised here as being seated upon a blue lion-throne. They are all smoke-colored, two-armed, wielding maces, and having distorted faces; they are mounted on vultures, according to the Skanda Purāṇa. One who performs a propitiatory rite (śānti) for the planets without knowing their birthplaces, clans, fires, colors, positions, and faces, by him the planets are disregarded. The Sun was born in Kaliṅga, and the Moon at the Yamunā. Mars was born in Avantī, and Mercury in Magadha.

The Guru (Jupiter) was born in the land of Sindh, Śukra (Venus) in Bhojakaṭa, Śanaiścara (Saturn) in Saurāṣṭra, Rāhu in Vairāṭināpura, and Ketu in Antarvedī; these are the birthplaces of the planets. Āditya (the Sun) belongs to the Kāśyapa gotra, and Candramas (the Moon) to the Ātreya. Bhauma (Mars) is Bhāradvāja, while the son of Soma (Mercury) is Ātreya. Guru (Jupiter) is of the Aṅgiras gotra, and Śukra (Venus) is indeed Bhārgava. Śani (Saturn) is Kāśyapa, and Rāhu is Paiṭhīnasi.

Ketava and the Jaiminiyas are the fire of the planets; that which is without interval [is the fire of the constellations]. The Sun is named Kapila; Soma is called Paṅgala. Dhūmaketu is said to be the fire of the wind (Vāyu); Budha is known as the fire of digestion (Jāṭharāgni). Guru is indeed named Śibi; Śukra becomes Haṭaka. Śanaiścara is of great splendor; the sacrificial fire of Rāhu and Ketu is Hutāśana. The Sun and Aṅgāraka (Mars) are red; Śukra and Nirākara are white. The son of Soma (Mercury) and Guru—both of these are remembered as being of the nature of fire.

One should know Kṛṣṇa as Śanaiścara (Saturn), Rāhu, and the various Ketus. According to Gobhila, however, the castes are stated as follows: "The two Brāhmaṇas are Bhārgava (Venus) and Ācārya (Jupiter); the two Kṣatriyas are Arka (the Sun) and Lohita (Mars); the two Vaiśyas are Soma (the Moon) and Budha (Mercury); and one should designate the remaining [planets] as Śūdras. In the Skanda Purāṇa, their positions are described: "One should know the Bhāskara (Sun) in the center; the Śaśin (Moon) in the south-east; one should know the Lohita (Mars) in the south; Budha (Mercury) in the north-east; Guru (Jupiter) in the north; and Bhārgava (Venus) in the east."

One should place Saturn in the west and Rāhu in the southwest. One should establish the Ketus in the northwest using white rice grains, or they may be fashioned from colored powders or metals such as gold. Venus and the Sun are to be known as facing east; Jupiter and Mercury face north; Saturn faces west; and the Moon, along with the remaining planets, face south. Those facing east have their gaze directed upward; those facing north have their gaze directed to the left; and those facing west [have their gaze directed to the right].

"Those others [the planets] face the Sun with their heads raised. Thus it is stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*. In the *Hemādri*, it is said that there is an option [regarding their orientation]. Having invoked them as endowed with their respective colors, forms, and qualities, one should praise them. Regarding the mandalas of the planets, the *Skanda Purāṇa* states: "One should know the Sun to be circular in shape, the Moon as quadrangular, Mars as triangular, and Mercury likewise as arrow-shaped. One should know Jupiter as quadrangular, and Venus likewise as five-sided. One should know Saturn to be like a bow, and Rāhu likewise as winnow-shovel shaped."

The comets, however, are represented by banners; one should establish Gaṇeśa, who possesses their own form, within the respective colored mandalas, or in images made of copper and other materials, or in heaps of rice—this is the meaning. Hemādri states that there is an option between the mandala and the image. Yājñavalkya declares the mantras for the planets: "Ā kṛṣṇena," "Imaṃ devāḥ," "Agnirmūrdhā divaḥ kakut," and "Udbudhyasva" are the Ṛgvedic verses proclaimed in their respective order. Also: "Bṛhaspate ati yad aryaḥ," "Tad dhaviḥ," and "Annāt parisrutaḥ."

"May the goddess [protect] us," "from the unseasonable [time]," "making this banner," and "these [verses]"—thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa. "By what [path] for us? and "Rāhu" are also mentioned. However, others are stated in the Matsya Purāṇa: "Agni, the messenger" for the Sun; "Soma, you are indeed our king" for the Moon; "O Earth, be pleasant" for Mars; "This Viṣṇu" for Mercury; "Indra among these" for Jupiter; "The light of Śukra" for Venus; "May offspring increase" for Saturn; "Come, O Bull" for Rāhu; and "Brahma, desiring to know" for Ketu. Thus they are established with their respective mantras.

The application (*viniyoga*) of other mantras is according to the principle that "even if only a portion of a mantra is uttered, it may serve as the *aindrī* [mantra]," provided there is no contradiction with other authorities. These same mantras are also used for the fire-oblation (*homa*). Regarding the presiding deities (*adhidevatās*), the Skanda Purāṇa states: One should place Śambhu to the north of Sūrya; Umā to the south of Soma; and one should install Skanda to the south of Aṅgāraka (Mars). One should place Viṣṇu to the west of Saumya (Mercury) and Brahmā to the east of Jīva (Jupiter). Know Indra to be at the southeast corner of Aiṃdrī (Indra’s quarter), and Yama to the southeast of Mandi (Saturn).
One should place Rāhu in the northeast, Kāla—who brings fear to all beings—in the north, and Citragupta in the northwestern direction of Ketu.

One should cause Īśvara to be established with the mantra "Tryambakaṃ ca," Śrī with "Śrīśca te," Pārvatī with "Yadakranda," Skanda with "Viṣṇo rarāṭataḥ," Brahmā with "Ābrahman," Vāsava (Indra) with "Sajoṣā indravāsavā," Yama with "Yamāya tvā," and Kāla with "Kārṣirasīti. Citragupta should be installed with the mantra "Citrāvasoḥ svam. Agni, Āpaḥ, Kṣiti, Viṣṇu, Indra, Aindrī, Prajāpati, Sarpas, and Brahmā are designated as the Pratyadhidevatās and should be established accordingly.

"agnīṃdūtam" (for Agni), "mitraṃ huve" (for Mitra), "agna āyāhi" (for Agni), "varuṇasya skambhanam asi" (for Varuṇa), "ud uttamaṃ varuṇa pāśam" (for Varuṇa), "syonā pṛthivi bhava" (for Pṛthivī), "medinī devī" (for Medinī), "idaṃ viṣṇur vicakrame" (for Viṣṇu), "viṣṇave tvā" (for Viṣṇu), "indrāyendo pari srava" (for Indra), "indro dadhīca" (for Indra)—these are for Indra; "uttānaparṇe" and "śacīsmatrau" (for the two); "vrajāpate" (for Prajāpati); "eṣa brahmā" or "vidhe" (for Brahmā); and the mantra "namo astu sarpebhyaḥ" is prescribed for the installation of the serpents. Gobhila and Vasiṣṭha state that one should place the presiding deities (adhidevas) between the planets and their respective deities (grahadevatās). In the *Madanaratna-saṃgraha*, it is stated: [as above].

The presiding deities (*adhidevatās*) should be placed with effort on the right side, and the secondary presiding deities (*pratyadhidevatās*) on the left, each separately with the *vyāhṛti* mantras. (From the *Utpalaparimala*): One should place the presiding deities on the right side of the planet, and the secondary presiding deities on the north side of the planet. (From the *Launaka*): One should place Kṣetrapāla, the lord of the field, to the north of Bhuja; "Bhuja" refers to Mars (*bhauma*). [One should also offer] food offerings (*naivedya*) and flowers to the planetary deities and other gods.

"The offering of seats for the planets, their installation, and the sequence of the earth [elements] have been described thus; however, in the Vāsiṣṭha [Tantra], it is stated otherwise: "One should install Rudra to the north of the Sun with the *Tryambaka* mantra. To the southeast of the Moon, one should worship Śrī, the daughter of Menakā, with the mantra *Śrīśca te*. One should worship Skanda to the south of Mars with the mantra *Yadakrandah*. One should worship Viṣṇu to the east of Mercury with the mantra *Viṣṇorarāṭam*. And to the north of Jupiter, Brahmā should be installed with the mantra *Brahma jajñānam*."

One should cause Śakra to be established in the east with the mantra "sajoṣā indra" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.4.26.1). To the west of Śani, Yama is to be installed with the verse "ā yātu varuṇaḥ" (Ṛgveda 7.89.5). Likewise, Kāla is to be placed to the north of Rāhu with the mantra "kārṣīr asi" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.7.5.2). Citragupta is for the Ketus, and he is to be placed in the southwest (Nairṛta) with the mantra "citrāvaso" (Ṛgveda 7.101.1). One should install the presiding deities (adhidevatās) between the planets and their respective deities. In the Matsya Purāṇa: "One should likewise invoke Vināyaka, Durgā, Vāyu, and Ākāśa with the Vyāhṛtis; at that very time, one should also invoke the two Aśvins and Kumāra."

In the *Madanaratna*, from the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "To the north of Saturn and the Sun, and to the south of Jupiter and Ketu, one should install Gaṇādhipa, who is saluted by all the gods. In the *Saṃgraha* on that very subject: "The wise man should install Rāhu, Maṅgala (Mars), and the Lord of the Day (the Sun) in due order to the north; and to the south of Gaṇeśa, Durgā, Vāyu, Rāhu, and Ketu, he should install Ākāśa and the two Aśvins—these five. Vasiṣṭha says: "I invoke Vināyaka, the leader of the hosts; I invoke Durgā for the sake of the Vedas."

One should invoke Vāyu with "vāyo yāhi" and offer clarified butter (ghṛta) with "ghṛtam ghṛta. Then, having honored both these horses, [one should proceed]. According to Gobhila: "There are thirty-two deities, the guardians of the quarters, and the elephants of the directions. Yājñavalkya says: "Garments, flowers, perfumes, and offerings should be given according to the respective colors; the incense for the gods is guggulu resin; and there should be rice with jaggery, milk-rice, sacrificial food (haviṣya), and milk-porridge."

A wise person should give these foods to the twice-born according to the sequence of the planets: curd-rice, sacrificial oblation (havis), powdered rice, meat, and variegated food. Or, according to one's capacity and as available, he should prepare them according to the prescribed rite. *Havis* refers to ghee and rice; *cūrṇa* refers to rice mixed with sesame powder. In the Skanda Purāṇa it is said: "Red sandalwood should be given to the Sun and Mars; white sandalwood should be presented to Venus; and sandalwood combined with saffron should be given to Jupiter and Mercury."

One should offer agarwood and sandalwood to Rāhu and Ketu; flowers of the colors corresponding to each planet should be offered with the Gāyatrī mantra, and one should perform the incense offering as follows: kunduruka incense for the Sun, clarified butter and unbroken rice (akṣata) for the Moon, resin of the sarja tree and agarwood for Mars, and sihlaka is prescribed for Mercury. One should give clarified butter and milk-rice (pāyasa) to Jupiter, and sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) to Mars.

One should offer milk-rice (*kṣīraṣāṣṭika*) to Budha; curd-rice (*dadhyodana*) to Guru; and ghee-rice (*ghṛtodana*) to Śukra. To Śanaiścara, the food offering (*naivedya*) should consist of sesame and black gram (*tilamāṣa*) mixed together. One should offer bean-rice (*māṣodana*) to Rāhu, and likewise rice with various condiments (*citrodana*) to Ketu. In the *Matsya Purāṇa*, it is stated that one should offer lentils (*masura*) to Kuja (Mars). Having presented these offerings, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with oblations (*āhuti*) without sloth. Regarding the specific details here, they should be known from my work, the *Dānakamalākara*. [In the] *Matsya Purāṇa*: [as stated above].

One should offer fragrant incense above the canopy. For the presiding deities, one should apply blue lotuses as a garland, and for all the world-protectors (Lokapālas), sandalwood paste as anointment. One should offer śatapatra flowers and guggulu incense. The lamp should be combined with cow’s ghee, and the food offering (naivedya) should consist of ghee and curd. In the Matsya Purāṇa: To the northeast of that, one should place [the vessel] adorned with curd, rice unbroken by threshing (akṣata), joined with a mango sprout, and provided with fruits and a pair of garments.

One should place a water-pot (kumbha) endowed with the five jewels (pañcaratna) and joined with the five sprouts (pañcapallava); therein one should install Varuṇa. O best of Brahmins, having brought earth from the Gaṅgā and all other rivers, from the oceans, lakes, elephants, horses, streets, anthills, confluences, ponds, and cow-pens, and having combined it with all medicinal herbs and sacrificial wood, the knower of dharma should place it there for the bathing of the patron (yajamāna). Yājñavalkya says: Oblations (carus) should be prepared according to the respective deities accompanied by mantras.

According to the statement in the *Gṛhyasūtra*, "together with the various deities," one should cook [the offerings] either together or separately. In the *Mātsya Purāṇa*: "One should commence the oblation (*homa*) with clarified butter, barley, rice, sesame seeds, and so forth. In the *Devīpurāṇa* as cited in the *Hemādri*: "O Brahmin, the first four oblations must be offered to the Lord Gaṇapati; otherwise, it becomes fruitless in this world—of this there is no doubt. Yājñavalkya: "The Arka, Phalgu, Khadira, Apāmārga, Pippala, Audumbara, Amī, Dūrvā, Kuśa, and Śamī [are the sacrificial woods] in their respective order."

For each deity, eight hundred or twenty-eight oblations should be offered with honey, clarified butter, curd, or milk; the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) should be one span (*prādeśa*) long, without branches, and devoid of fruit. For all the deities, the offering should be performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). According to one who knows the supreme truth, the fuel-sticks should be offered individually with their respective mantras. Where ghee and other substances are to be offered, then sacrificial porridge (*caru*), edible offerings, and so forth, should follow. In the *Skanda Purāṇa*, it is stated that the installation mantras themselves are the mantras for the oblation, and this applies likewise to the presiding deities (*adhideva*) and others.

In the Vāsiṣṭha [Saṃhitā] as well: "The installation of the remaining [deities] is performed with mantras, and the oblation (homa) is offered with sesame seeds using the Vyāhṛtis. However, in the Mātsya [Purāṇa], the mantras for the presiding deities (adhidevas) and others are stated: "One should perform the offering and the oblation for Rudra with the mantra 'ā vo rājānam'; for Umā with 'apohiṣṭhā'; and likewise for Svāmisa (Sūrya) with 'syonā'. For Viṣṇu, 'idaṃ viṣṇuḥ'; for Svayaṃbhū (Brahmā), 'tameśa'; and similarly for Yama, 'ayaṃ gauḥ'—thus the oblation is proclaimed. For Kāla, the mantra 'brahmajijñāsa' is praised."

Those who know the Vedas understand that "citraguptasya ca ājñānam" (the command of Citragupta) is [the mantra]. "Agniṃ dūtaṃ vṛṇīmahe" is proclaimed [as the mantra] for Agni. "Bhūmeḥ pṛthivyaṃtarikṣam" is declared by the great sages [to be the mantra] for the Earth. "Sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ" is cited as [the mantra] for Viṣṇu. "Indrāyendo marutvate" is [the mantra] for Śakra (Indra). "Uttānaparṇe subhage" is praised as [the mantra] for Śacī. Furthermore, "Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ prajāpate" is remembered as [the mantra] for Prajāpati. "Namo astu sarpebhyaḥ" is said to be the mantra for the serpents.

"O Brahman, you are worthy of the sacrifice"—this is declared as the mantra for Brahmā; "vināyakasya cātunaḥ" is remembered by the wise as the mantra for Vināyaka. "jātavedase sunavāma" is said to be the mantra for Durgā. In the Skanda Purāṇa: Having offered the remnants of the *naivedya* with the *homamantras*, one should subsequently perform oblations (*homa*) with the *vyāhṛtis*. For each deity, one should offer oblations in due order—either one thousand and eight, or one hundred and eight, or twenty-eight, or even eight times. One should perform the *homa* for each individual deity accordingly.

The offering of the *naivedya* remains; according to the opinion of some, the *homa* [is performed next]. In the *Hemādri*: "Then, according to the rule for taking portions (*avadāna-dharma*), one should offer the *caru* with a *sruk* ladle. A Brahmin should cause clarified butter (*ājya*) to be offered with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *arka* wood smeared with ghee. He should offer sesame seeds with the mantra 'Akṛṣṇena' and with the *vyāhṛtis*. With the *caru*, the fuel-sticks, the clarified butter, and the sesame seeds, in that order, the presiding deities (*adhidevatās*) should be offered oblations there with their respective mantras. Having offered the *caru* with that [ladle] according to the rule for taking portions, some say the *homa* may be done with the hand; that is to be considered."

In the *Mātsya-purāṇa*: "The oblation should be offered, and the overflowing caru, as well as the foodstuffs and so forth; having performed ten oblations with the mantras, one should then perform the homa with the *vyāhṛtis*. The eminent brahmins should face northward. Here, regarding the phrase "with the *vyāhṛtis*," since the plurality and the requirement of simultaneity (sāhitya) are understood through the grammatical rule of *ekaśeṣa* applied to the exception (*dvaṃdvāpavāda*), and because these qualities pertain to the materials to be offered, it is more appropriate to understand that there is a single oblation performed with all the *vyāhṛtis* together. Also in the *Bhaviṣyottara* cited by Hemādri: "In the homa, everything is deposited there by means of the *vyāhṛtis*."

Having offered the food and other items as *naivedya*, and having performed the remaining oblations with the respective planetary mantras using materials such as sesame seeds for ten thousand homas, one should offer ten oblations for each [planet]. Then, by repeating the sequence of the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and the *vyāhṛtis* beginning with *bhūḥ*—both individually and collectively—one completes the count of ten thousand or one hundred thousand homas. This is stated in the *Hemādri* and the *Madanaratna*. However, we do not know the source for this division; the truth is that there is one oblation with the three *vyāhṛtis* together.

It appears that every oblation (*homa*) is indeed performed with this [mantra]. Thus it is stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* within the *Hemādri*: "The ritual for the *lakṣahoma* is remembered as: 'bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ stadhā svāhā'. However, Hemādri is surely mistaken, because there is no contradiction between the earlier and later statements. In the *Matsya Purāṇa*: "Rice-porridge offerings (*caru*) accompanied by mantras should be made for each deity. Having properly offered those *carus*, one should then perform the *homa*. One should cast the final full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the verse beginning 'mūrdhānaṃ divaḥ'."

Then, the consecration (abhiṣeka) should be performed with mantras and auspicious songs. At the conclusion of the *homa*, the sprinkling (snāpana) of the patron (*yajamāna*) should be carried out by four twice-born priests facing the northeast, using that very same full water-pot (*pūrṇakumbha*). In this regard, the mantras beginning with "Sūryo jyotiḥ" and others will be stated in the ritual application. In the *Agnipurāṇa*: "With the mantra 'Mūrdhānaṃ divaḥ' and with a continuous stream, one should offer [the water] while standing; never while seated. In the *Mahārṇava*:

The four mantras for the *pūrṇāhuti* (the final oblation) are stated as: "mūrdhānaṃ divaḥ," "punastvādityāḥ," "pūrṇā darviḥ," and "saptate agniḥ. In the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*, it is said: "O best of men, there is no fixed rule regarding the number of Brahmins here, nor is there a restriction of time; the sacrifice is said to be performed according to one's own desire. Then, wearing white garments and with his face anointed with white unguents, the sacrificer, together with his wife and attended by the officiating priests, is bathed by the eminent Brahmins with all medicinal herbs and all fragrant substances.

One should worship with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) with great effort, free from pride. In the *Vāsiṣṭha*: "Then, for the protection of that consecrated one, one should offer oblations (*bali*); thereafter, one should perform the lustration (*nīrājana*) with various foods and lamps in the cardinal and intermediate directions. In the *Prayogapārijāta*, Vāmana states: "Then, one should receive—with the pouring of water—the fruit of the worship of the planets by the preceptor and others, as well as the fruit of the oblation of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, parched grain, and sesame seeds, and likewise the fruit of their recitation (*japa*)."

Then, sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) should be given to them individually according to one’s capacity. These have been stated by Yājñavalkya: "A cow, a conch, a bull, gold, a garment, a horse, and in order, a black cow, a goat, and a ram—these are the sacrificial fees in sequence. [In the *Mātsya Purāṇa*: "The priests should be provided with sacrificial fees equal in value to gold by the patron; furthermore, he should give a cow to all of them, or to whichever preceptor (*guru*) is satisfied."

All mantras should be recited, and all fees (dakṣiṇās) should be given here. Those mantras are to be known from my work, the *Dānakamalākara*; the ritual application (*prayoga*) for this will also be stated [therein]. Āśvalāyana says in the *Madanaratna*:

For each single oblation (*āhuti*), one should feed a Brahmin with food; for fifty [oblations], a middle-ranking one; and for a hundred oblations, even a low-ranking one should be fed. O Lord, otherwise, it quickly burns [the donor] like fire; of this there is no doubt. Therefore, he who is unable to give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) or even food should satisfy and honor his gurus through recitations (*japa*), prostrations, and hymns of praise. As stated in the *Purāṇa*: "Just as a twice-born man [is honored] by the planets, so too is the knower of ritual who has mastered the Vedas."
Having gratified him with soft garments and other gifts, one should dismiss him once he is satisfied.

Yājñavalkya: A wise man should offer these foods to the Brahmins according to the sequence of the planets: jaggery-rice, milk-rice (pāyasa), sacrificial food (haviṣya), rice with milk and flour (kṣīrapāṣṭika), curd-water, clarified butter, powdered food, meat, and variegated rice. Or, according to his capacity and whatever is available, he should provide excellent food according to the prescribed rite. "Sacrificial food" refers to rice with ghee; "powdered food" refers to rice mixed with sesame powder. Viśiṣṭha: He should take ashes from the northeast corner using either the large sacrificial ladle (sruk) or the small one (sruva).

By means of that [mantra], one should cause protection to be performed for the head, the throat, and the shoulders. In the *Mātsya Purāṇa*: "Having thus completed everything in its entirety, one should dismiss all the deities: 'May all the hosts of gods depart, taking with them this earthly worship, so that my desired wishes may be fulfilled and they may return again. He who performs the worship of the planets according to this rite attains all his desires and, through their favor, is glorified in heaven. But he who causes great affliction before one of little wealth..."

Having worshipped [the principal deities] with great effort, a person should also honor the remaining ones. Likewise: "This sacrifice to the nine planets (Navagraha-makha) is traditionally prescribed as a constant offering of ten thousand oblations (Ayuta-homa). O best of sages, it is for the sake of removing obstacles during marriages, festivals, sacrifices, consecrations, and other rites; likewise during times of distress and portents. For acts of subjugation (vaśya), attraction, and even for expulsion (uccāṭana), one should perform the Navagraha-makha and only then commence the primary rite. Otherwise, the desired fruit may only occasionally be attained by men."

Marvelous events such as earthquakes and the like [occur]. Other specific details regarding this should be understood from my *Prayogadīpikā*. As for what the learned do—performing the recitation (*japa*) of the planetary mantras ten thousand or a thousand times and then performing a fire-oblation (*homa*) with sesame seeds numbering one-tenth of that—it is done only when no specific number of recitations is mentioned. When no number of recitations is mentioned, we cannot say what the root authority for such a practice might be. This concludes the procedure for the ten-thousand-fold oblation. Now, the practical application (*prayoga*).

Even though this was performed by our grandfather, it is nevertheless stated here in brief: Having remembered the place and time, and having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*)—saying either, "Desiring prosperity, or desiring the pacification of planetary afflictions, portents, or disease, or desiring victory over enemies, I shall perform the sacrifice known as the *Navagraha-homa*," or simply, "I shall perform the *Graha-yajña* alone"—and having performed the worship of Gaṇeśa, the worship of the Mothers (*Mātṛkā-pūjā*), and the *Vṛddhi-śrāddha*, and having chosen the officiating priest (*ācārya*), one should pray to him.

"You are my father, you are my mother, and you are my ultimate refuge; by your grace, O Brahmin-sage, may everything that is in my heart be fulfilled. For the sake of my liberation from calamity, perform here without delay a sacrifice known as the *Koṭihoma*, which is incomparable, brings peace, and grants all desires. Then he should choose four officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Or else, the preceptor (*ācārya*) and the Brahman-priest (*brahmā*)—these two—should be chosen according to the ritual manual of their own Vedic branch (*tacchākhayā*), and they should be honored with the honey-mixture offering (*madhuparka*). Regarding this, Viśvāmitra says in the *Hemādri*: "Having honored the officiating priest with the *madhuparka*, one should have him perform the rite."

"Otherwise, it would be fruitless here; of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, the Madhuparka should not be performed with a branch that has already been worshipped (*arcya-śākhā*), for it is stated in that very same [text]: "The Madhuparka is [offered] with a branch that has been worshipped. Then, having constructed a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) of ten or eight cubits, one should make a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring one cubit in its center. Hemādri states that the pit should be in the northeast. To the northeast of that, an altar (*vedi*) should be made, four cubits wide, two spans high, square, and provided with two steps; the first step should be two finger-breadths high.
The second is two finger-breadths high.

Both [the doorposts] should be two finger-breadths wide. Then, wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands and unguents, the preceptor, the officiating priests, and the patron, with auspicious sounds and water-filled jars in their hands, should circumambulate the pavilion while reciting the mantra, "Oṃ bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ... and enter through the western door. "Whatever being is stationed here, having taken refuge in this place, let all of them leave this spot and go wherever they belong."

"May the spirits and Piśācas depart in all directions; may I complete this Brahma-rite without opposition from anyone. Having thus scattered white mustard seeds (*gaurasarṣapa*) and sprinkled the ground with the two verses beginning with *śucī vo havyā* and *āpo hiṣṭhā*, he should mutter the two mantras *svasti na indra* and *tad akṣan*. Then, having prepared the sacrificial altar (*vedikā*) for the Vāstu-ritual to the northeast of the pavilion, he should [recite]: "May the Nāgas and the Guardians of the World enter the surface of the earth from all sides in the four corners beginning with the northeast of the altar."

"May they remain in the pavilion, always bestowing long life and strength"—with this mantra, having planted four stakes, one should then offer oblations of black-gram rice (*māṣabhakta*) at the sides of the stakes starting from the southeast (*āgneya*). With the mantra: "To all the fires, and to those others who are stationed here, I offer this oblation, excellent and meritorious cooked rice"—thus, with these three mantras, having offered the oblations of black-gram rice at the sides of the stakes in the southwest (*nairṛti*), northwest (*vāyu*), and northeast (*īśāna*), [the following are] those mantras: [The mantras are: 1. *maṇṭape 'smin nimitāstiṣṭhantu āyurbalakārāḥ sadā* 2. *agnibhyaḥ atha sarvebhyo ye cānye 'tra saṃsthitāḥ | tebhyo baliṃ prayacchāmi puṇyamodanam uttamam* || 3. *maṇṭape 'smin nimitāstiṣṭhantu āyurbalakārāḥ sadā* || (These correspond to the directions: southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast respectively.)

To the lord of the Nairṛta region and to those Rākṣasas who roam in the southwest, I offer this oblation; may you all accept this offering. Salutations to the protectors dwelling in the wind and to others who depend upon them; I offer this oblation to them; may you all accept this offering. And to all the Rudras and to others who depend upon them, I offer this oblation; may they, ever eager, accept it. Then, with a needle made of gold or other such material, [one should draw lines] upon the cloth over the altar.

Ṣaṃ, obeisance to Śāntā; Oṃ, obeisance to Yaśovatī; Oṃ, obeisance to Kāntā; Oṃ, obeisance to Viśālā; Oṃ, obeisance to Prāṇavāhinī; Oṃ, obeisance to Satyā; Oṃ, obeisance to Sumanā; Oṃ, obeisance to Nandā; Oṃ, obeisance to Bhadrā. Having thus drawn the lines starting from the west and ending in the east, arranged in an upward direction (from south to north).

Again: *Oṃ hiraṇyāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ suprabhāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ lakṣmyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ vibhūtyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ vimalāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ vidyāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ jayāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ kālāyai namaḥ*, *Oṃ viśokāyai namaḥ*. Having thus drawn lines from the south toward the north and from the west toward the east, one should merge the four central squares into one and draw lines in the corners; by this, half-squares are produced.

Then, one should invoke Brahmā and the other deities there, according to the principle that "the gods remain having stepped upon the quadrangular body of Vāstu. Thus, the invocation of each respective deity occurs in their respective positions: there, in the four central squares at the heart, one says "Obeisance to Brahmā" and invokes Brahmā with "I invoke Brahmā. In the two eastern squares at the right breast, one says "Obeisance to Aryaman" and invokes Aryaman with "I invoke Aryaman. In the two southern squares at the lower right, one says "Obeisance to Vivasvat" and invokes Vivasvat with "I invoke Vivasvat."

In the two western feet, on the right side of the belly: *Vivasvate namaḥ*, I invoke Vivasvat. In the two western feet, on the left side of the belly: *Mitrāya namaḥ*, I invoke Mitra. On the left breast of the northern foot: *Pṛthivīdharāya namaḥ*, I invoke Pṛthivīdhara. There, in the place near Brahmā, in the right hand of the two deities of the southeast (Agnēya), are Sāvitra and Savitṛ. There, in the eastern half: *Sāvitryāya namaḥ*, I invoke Sāvitrī.

In the western part, *namaḥ savitre*, I invoke Savitṛ. In the southwestern quarter, in the two parts—the bull (*vṛṣaṇa*) and the penis (*meḍhra*)—are Vibudhādhipa and Jaya. There, in the eastern part, *namaḥ vibudhādhipāya*, I invoke Vibudhādhipa. There, in the western part, *namaḥ jayāya*, I invoke Jaya. In the northwestern quarter, in the two parts—the left arm (*vāmabāhu*) and the hand (*hasta*)—are Rājayakṣman and Rudra. There, in the eastern part, *namaḥ rājayakṣmaṇe*, I invoke Rājayakṣman. In the western part, *namaḥ rudrāya*, I invoke Rudra. [In the northeast,] Īśāna...

In the two quarters of the space, at the mouth of the *rūpa*, are the *āpaḥ* and the *āpavatsa*. There, in the eastern quarter, I invoke the *āpaḥ* with the mantra "Obeisance to the Waters" (*adbhyo namaḥ*). In the western quarter, I invoke the *āpavatsa* with the mantra "Obeisance to the Āpavatsa" (*āpavatsāya namaḥ*). In the southern quarter of the *īśāna*-pad, on the head of Vāstu—

Homage to Śikhin; I invoke Śikhin. To his right, in one and a half squares, at the right eye: Homage to Parjanya; I invoke Parjanya. To his right, in two squares, at the right ear: Homage to Jayanta; I invoke Jayanta. To his right, in two squares, at the right shoulder: Homage to Kuliśāyudha; I invoke Kuliśāyudha. To his right, in two squares, at the right arm: Homage to Sūrya; I invoke Sūrya.

In the two right feet, at the right upper arm, *satyāya namaḥ*; I invoke Satya. In the one-and-a-half right feet, at the right elbow, *bhṛśāya namaḥ*; I invoke Bhṛśa. In the southeast portion of those [feet], at the right forearm, *ākāśāya namaḥ*; I invoke Ākāśa. In the western half of those [feet], at the right forearm, *vāyave namaḥ*; I invoke Vāyu.

To the west of that, at the right wrist (occupying one and a half squares), [I worship] Pūṣan; obeisance to Pūṣan, I invoke Pūṣan. To the west of that, on the right side (occupying two squares), [I worship] Vitatha; obeisance to Vitatha, I invoke Vitatha. To the west of that, on the right side (occupying two squares), [I worship] Gṛhakṣata; obeisance to Gṛhakṣata, I invoke Gṛhakṣata. To the west of that, on the right hip (occupying two squares), [I worship] Yama; obeisance to Yama, I invoke Yama.

To the west of that, on the two feet and the right knee: *Namaḥ gandharvāya*, I invoke Gandharva. To the west of that, in one and a half squares, on the right shank: *Namaḥ bhṛṅgarājāya*, I invoke Bhṛṅgarāja. To the west of that, in the south-western square, on the right tail: *Namaḥ mṛgāya*, I invoke Mṛga. To the north of that, at the feet: *Namaḥ pitṛbhyaḥ*, I invoke the Pitṛs.

Beyond that, on one and a half squares at the left hip: *namaḥ dauvārikāya*, I invoke Dauvārika. Beyond that, on two squares at the left shank: *namaḥ sugrīvāya*, I invoke Sugrīva. Beyond that, on two squares at the left knee: *namaḥ puṣpadantāya*, I invoke Puṣpadanta. Beyond that, on two squares at the left thigh: *namaḥ varuṇāya*, I invoke Varuṇa. Beyond that, on one and a half squares at the left side: *namaḥ śeṣāya*, I invoke Śeṣa.

In the space to the north-west of that, at the left wrist, [I offer] salutation to Pāpa; I invoke Pāpa. In the space to the east of that, on the left upper arm, [I offer] salutation to Roga; I invoke Roga. In the space to the east of that, measuring one and a half squares, on the left upper arm, [I offer] salutation to Āvāya; I invoke Āvāya. In the space to the east of that, on the left elbow, measuring two squares, [I offer] salutation to Mukhya; I invoke Mukhya. In the space to the east of that, on the left upper arm, measuring two squares, [I offer] salutation to Bhallāṭa; I invoke Bhallāṭa.

In the two squares to the east of that, on the left arm: *namaḥ somāya*, I invoke Soma. In the two squares to the east of that, on the left shoulder: *namaḥ sarpebhyaḥ*, I invoke the Serpents. In the half-square to the east of that, on the left ear: *namo 'ditaye*, I invoke Aditi. In the half-square to the east of that, on the left eye: *namo dityai*, I invoke Diti. In the north: *Vāstoṣpati*, Vasiṣṭha, Triṣṭubh; this is the application for the invocation of Vāstoṣpati. *Oṃ vāstoṣpate pratijānīhy asmān tvadāveśo anamīvo bhavā naḥ | yad te mahe pratitanno juṣasva*.

Prosper, O Lord of the Dwelling, for the benefit of our bipeds and our quadrupeds! O Lord of the Dwelling, through that auspicious, golden, and accessible [abode], may we always possess prosperity. May you grant us protection in rest and in exertion. And do you all protect us always with blessings! O Lord of the Dwelling, the dispeller of disease, entering all forms, be a most gracious and kind friend to us. Salutation to Vāstoṣpati in his golden form; I invoke Carakī. In the southeast, salutation to Vidārī; I invoke Vidārī.

In the southwest, obeisance to Pūtanā; I invoke Pūtanā. In the northwest, obeisance to Pāparākṣasī; I invoke Pāparākṣasī. In the directions starting from the east of the mandala: in the east, obeisance to Skanda; I invoke Skanda. In the south, obeisance to Āryamaṇ; I invoke Āryamaṇ. In the west, obeisance to Jṛmbhaka; I invoke Jṛmbhaka. In the north, obeisance to Pilipiñcha; I invoke Pilipiñcha. [Maṇḍala mantra: Oṃ. Regarding the consecration mantras for the house, that which is most firmly established should be recited with a steady voice.
May he obtain cattle today even from afar.
Desiring to bring them home, may he find a firm foundation for his house; may there be a firm foundation for cattle, may there be a most secure foundation, may there be a favorable moment.
Then, having worshipped all [the deities], he should place a water-pot (kumbha) in the northeast corner of the mandala and offer an oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa) in front of the mandala.
It is as follows:
Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā; this milk-rice offering (pāyasa-bali) is for you, svāhā. Oṃ, salutation to Āryaman; this milk-rice offering is for you, svāhā.
Oṃ, salutation to Vivasvat.
Oṃ, obeisance to Mitra;
Oṃ, obeisance to Pṛthivīdara. This milk-rice offering, this milk-rice bali, is for you—obeisance! Oṃ, obeisance to Sāvitra. This milk-rice bali is for you—obeisance!
Oṃ, homage to Savitṛ;
Oṃ, homage to the Lord of the Wise;
Oṃ, homage to Jaya.
Oṃ, homage to Rājayakṣman;
Oṃ, homage to Rudra;
Oṃ, homage to the Waters.
Oṃ, obeisance to Apavatya; Oṃ, obeisance to Śibhi;
Oṃ, obeisance to Parjanya.
Oṃ, homage to Jayanta; Oṃ, homage to Kuliśāyudha;
Oṃ, homage to Sūrya.
Oṃ, homage to Satya;
Oṃ, homage to Bhṛśa;
Oṃ, homage to Ākāśa.
Oṃ, homage to Vāyu;
Oṃ, homage to Pūṣan;
Oṃ, homage to Vitatha.
Oṃ, homage to Gṛhakṣata;
Oṃ, homage to Yama;
Oṃ, homage to Gandharva.
Oṃ, homage to Bhṛṅgarāja; Oṃ, homage to the Deer;
Oṃ, homage to the Ancestors. This milk-rice offering is for you.
Oṃ, homage to Dauvārika; this milk-rice offering is for you.
Oṃ, homage to Sugrīva.
Oṃ, homage to Puṣpadanta.
Oṃ, homage to Varuṇa;
Oṃ, homage to Asura;
Oṃ, homage to Śoṣa.
Oṃ, obeisance to Pāpa; Oṃ, obeisance to Roga;
Oṃ, obeisance to Āhni.
Oṃ, homage to Mukhya; Oṃ, homage to Bhallāṭa;
Oṃ, homage to Soma.
Oṃ, obeisance to all;
Oṃ, obeisance to Āditi;
Oṃ, obeisance to Diti. This milk-rice offering is for you; this milk-rice offering is for you.
Then, one should offer an oblation of black gram rice to Caraka and the others.
Oṃ, homage to Carakī; I offer this bali of black gram and boiled rice.
Oṃ, homage to Vidārī.
Oṃ, homage to Pūtanā.
Oṃ, obeisance to Pāparākṣaṇī; Oṃ, obeisance to Skandā;
Oṃ, obeisance to Āryamṇ.
Oṃ, homage to Jṛmbhaka;
Oṃ, homage to Pilipiñcha; I offer this oblation of black gram rice.
Then, one should sprinkle the pavilion with the Pāvamāna and Rākṣoghna hymns.

Oṃ! May the one who removes evil purify me. With that golden, hundred-streamed, purifying filter belonging to Prajāpati, we who know the Veda purify ourselves as purified by the Veda. May Indra purify us with his leadership; may Soma purify us with well-being; may Varuṇa purify us with his attentive gaze; may King Yama purify us with his crushing powers; and may Jātavedas purify us with his life-sustaining energy.

Oṃ! I strike down the followers of Viṣṇu, the destroyers of demons and the destroyers of spells. Here I cast out this spell. Whatever [spell] a rival has buried against me, that I now render powerless. Whatever a rival has buried against me, that I now render powerless. Whoever, whether a rival or not a rival, digs it up—by means of the Gāyatrī metre, well-supported, I crush the spell. What is auspicious here, let that be for us both. You are the sovereign (Virāj), the slayer of rivals; you are the supreme ruler (Saṃrāj), the slayer of enemies; you are the over-ruler (Abhibhū), the slayer of those who attack; you are the all-ruler (Viśvarāj), the destroyer of all destructive powers.

Then one should perform the worship of the doors. There, at the eastern door: above—*Śriyai enam śriyam āvāhayāmi* (To Śrī, I invoke Śrī). Below—*Dehalyai namaḥ, dehīm āvāhayāmi* (Salutation to the threshold; I invoke the threshold). On the left and right pillars—*Gaṇeśāya namaḥ, Gaṇeśam āvāhayāmi* (Salutation to Gaṇeśa; I invoke Gaṇeśa). *Skandāya namaḥ, Skandam āvāhayāmi* (Salutation to Skanda; I invoke Skanda). Having placed two *takṣaka* water-pots, [one says]: *Gaṅgāyai namaḥ, Yamunāyai namaḥ, Gaṅgā-Yamune āvāhayāmi* (Salutation to Gaṅgā, salutation to Yamunā; I invoke Gaṅgā and Yamunā). Then, having filled them with water...

At the southern gate: [Facing] upward—*namaḥ śriyai*, *namo devālyai*. On the two pillars: *namaḥ puṣpadantāya*, *namaḥ puṣpadantāya*, *namaḥ kapardhine*. "O Puṣpadanta and Kapardin, I invoke you. Having placed two water-pots (*kalaśa*) and having filled them with water: *namo godāvaryai*, *namo kṛṣṇāyai*.

At the southern gate: above—*namaḥ śriyai*; on the threshold—*namo dehalai*; on the two pillars—*namaḥ puṣpadantāya*, *namaḥ kapardhine*. "O Puṣpadanta and Kapardin, I invoke you. Having placed two water-pots (*kalaśa*) and filled them with water—*namo godāvaryai*, *namaḥ kṛṣṇāyai*.

At the western gate: above—*namaḥ śriyai* (salutation to Śrī); *namaḥ dehalyai* (salutation to the threshold); at the two pillars—*namaḥ nandine* (salutation to Nandin) and *namaḥ caṇḍāya* (salutation to Caṇḍa); at the two pitchers—*namaḥ revāyai* (salutation to Revā) and *namaḥ narmadāyai* (salutation to Narmadā). I invoke Revā and Narmadā; fill the water.

At the northern gate: to Śrī above, *namaḥ*; to the threshold (*dehalī*) below, *namaḥ*; to the two door-keepers, Mavākāla, *namaḥ*; to Bhṛṅgin, *namaḥ*; to the two water-jars (*kalaśa*), Vāruṇī, *namaḥ*; to Kṛṣṇaveṇī, *namaḥ*. Then, fill them with water.

Then, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the worship of the archway (*toraṇa*) and so forth," one should proceed as follows: In the eastern direction, at a distance of one cubit outside the pavilion, having installed an archway (*toraṇa*) that is very firm, beautiful-named, or marked with a conch—whether it be a *aśvattha* (pipal) or a *vaṭa* (banyan) tree—one should worship it with the following offerings, beginning with perfumes and ending with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*): "Oṃ, I praise Agni, the domestic priest... [Recite this mantra]. "Salutation to the very firm archway (*sudṛḍha-toraṇa*); I invoke the very firm archway; salutation to the very firm archway. One should worship it with the services (*upacāra*) of perfume, flowers, incense, lamp, food offering (*naivedya*), betel-leaf, and sacrificial fee.

There, one should offer the scents and other ritual services to Rāhu with "Obeisance to Rāhu" and to Bṛhaspati with "I invoke Bṛhaspati. Then, having placed a single water-pot there, one should perform the ritual placement of the mantras at that location of the pot.

Having touched the earth with the words "mahīṃ dyauḥ" (O Earth and Heaven), [he recites]: "Oṃ, may Heaven and Earth sprinkle this sacrifice for us; may they nourish us with their blessings. Having touched the earth.
Having scattered barley with the mantra: "O plants, speak together," [he recites]: *oṃ oṣadhayaḥ saṃ vadante somena saha rājñā | yasmai karoti brāhmaṇas taṃ rājan pārayāsi*.
Having established the *kalaśa* with "akalaśa," [one recites]: *oṃ ākalaśeṣu dhāvati pavitre pariṣicyate ukthairyajñe vardhate*.
Having filled [the vessel] with water while reciting: "O Gaṅgā, this [water] of mine...
and "Oṃ, O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Śutudrī, Marudvṛdhā, Vitastā, Ārjīkīyā, and Suṣomā, may you together attend to my sacrifice," and having cast perfume [into it] while reciting: "Gandhadvārām..."
Oṃ! I invoke here Śrī, who has the fragrance as her door, who is invincible, eternally nourishing, the bestower of prosperity, and the sovereign of all beings.
The plants have gathered together.
Oṃ! The plants hold consultation with Soma, their king; O King, we cause that for which the Brāhmaṇa acts to reach its fulfillment.
"From stalk to stalk," [with these words] he offers dūrvā grass.
Oṃ! From joint to joint they sprout, from stalk to stalk; O dūrvā grass, spread yourself forth with a hundredfold and a thousandfold.
With the mantra "aśvad deva," [he places] five sprouts.
Oṃ! Aśvadeva is the one who settles; the leaf has been made his dwelling. For the sake of cattle, he shall surely accomplish it; may he win the man who is to be won.
The earth is pleasant; let there be fruit here.

Oṃ! Those plants which bear fruit and those which are fruitless, those which blossom and those which are flowerless—may Bṛhaspati, having impelled them, release us from the stroke of the enemy's weapon.
Together with the jewel, these are the five jewels of political ethics (*nīti*).
Oṃ! Savitṛ, the Lord of Fortune, bestows jewels upon the donor; we pray for that manifold portion.
"In the form of gold" means gold.
Oṃ! Of golden form, with a golden appearance, the protector of food, golden-hued; having sat down from his golden womb, may he, the giver of gold, grant food to this man.
One should wrap the openings of these two garments with a thread from the cloth itself.

Oṃ: "Clad in a garment, you have come hither; as soon as he is born, he becomes full of vigor. Wise poets lead him upward, moving with a mind that delights in the divine. Having recited this, one should place the full vessel upon the *paridhi* sticks.
Oṃ! The ladle has flown away full; may it return well-filled once more. O Lord of a hundred powers, bring us food and strength, as you do for the one who desires and acts.
Oṃ, obeisance to Dhruva in the pitcher—I invoke Dhruva; I present these offerings, beginning with water for the feet.

Then, having gone to the south, one should install an archway (*toraṇa*) made of *udumbara* or *plakṣa* wood, auspicious and known by the names Subhadra or Vikaṭa, and marked with the sign of a wheel—reciting: *oṃ iṣetvorjetvā vāyavastho pāyavastha devovaḥ savitā prārpayatu śreṣṭhatamāya karmaṇe*.
Salutation to Subhadrā’s archway. I offer the ritual services beginning with invocation (āvāhana) and the five offerings beginning with fragrance (gandha).
Therein, "Salutation to Sūrya—I invoke."
Homage to Aṅgāraka— I invoke Aṅgāraka.
Salutation to Sūrya and Aṅgāraka; I offer these services, beginning with perfume.
There, having placed one water-pot, [one should say] in that pot: "Obeisance to Dharā; I invoke Dharā; I offer the services beginning with perfume."

Then, having gone to the west—as before—there are water-pots [made from] *plakṣa*, *udumbara*, *vāsukarman*, and *sukhīma* wood, marked with the *vāgda* sign, and other archways (*toraṇa*). [Recite]: "O Agni, come for the sake of the wind, being praised as the giver of oblations; sit down as the Hotṛ priest upon the sacrificial grass."
Salutation to Sukarmatoraṇa; I invoke Sukarmatoraṇa; I offer the services beginning with perfumes (gandha).
There, for Śukra, the white [oblation]—I invoke.
I invoke Budha for Budha—O Śukra, O Budha, obeisance to you—I offer the five services beginning with fragrance.

Then, having gone further north, one should place a Vaṭa, Aśvattha, or Palāśa tree, or a radiant archway (toraṇa) marked with a lotus, dedicated to Suhotra. [Reciting: "Oṃ, may the waters be most auspicious to us; may they be for our refreshment; may they flow gently for our well-being. "Salutation to the Suhotra-toraṇa; I invoke the Suhotra-toraṇa; I offer the services beginning with fragrant scents (gandha)."
Therein: "Homage to Soma—I invoke Soma; homage to Ketu—I invoke Ketu;
homage to Śanaiścara—I invoke Śanaiścara."
*Oṃ somaketu-śanaiścarebhyo namaḥ*: I offer the five services beginning with fragrance (*gandha*).
There, one water-pot (*kalaśa*) should be placed. In that pot, [I say]: *Vighneśāya namaḥ*; I offer the five services beginning with fragrance.

Then, having gone to the east, one should place two water-pots (kalaśas) upon the door-posts according to the *Ṛgvedic* tradition. For each pot, the mantra is repeated: "In these two pots, obeisance to the world-elephant named Airāvata. Having invoked the world-elephant named Airāvata—saying, "Obeisance to the world-elephant named Airāvata"—one offers the services beginning with perfumes (*gandha*). Therein, the *Ṛgvedic* [tradition] is as follows: "The *Ṛgveda* has eyes like lotus petals; its meter is the Gāyatrī; its presiding deity is Soma."
Having chosen each one individually, saying, "O best of Brahmins, you belong to the Atri lineage; please serve as my officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) at this sacrifice," he appointed them.
Maṃ. Oṃ, I worship Agni, the domestic priest, the divine officiant of the sacrifice, the invoker, the bestower of jewels—with offerings of fragrance and other services.

Meditation: Then, one should meditate upon Indra, who is seated upon the thousand-eyed Airāvata, wearing a yellow crown and earrings, with a vajra and a blue lotus held in his right and left hands respectively.
Come, come, O Lord of the Immortals, praised by all the gods and Siddhas!
Having been consecrated with the host of mind-born Apsarases, O Wielder of the Thunderbolt, protect our sacrifice; O Blessed One, homage to you!
O Indra, come here, stay here! I invoke Indra, together with his limbs, his retinue, his weapons, and his powers, into the pitcher at the door.
Om! I invoke Indra, the protector, the deliverer, the one who is present;
I invoke the hero Indra, who is easily summoned at every call;
I invoke the pure Indra, the much-invoked.
May Indra establish well-being for us in this great distress.
Salutation to Indra; I invoke him upon the flag and banner and offer these services, beginning with fragrant scents.

Meditation: To Indra, the most excellent lord of the gods, who holds the thunderbolt in his hand and possesses great strength, the deity who is the master of a hundred sacrifices—to him, perpetual salutations, salutations!
Thus one should perform the salutation.

"O Indra, together with your limbs (Aṅgas), your retinue (Parivāra), your weapons (Āyudhas), and your vehicles (Vāhanas), accept this *māṣa-bali* accompanied by a lamp, offered by me until the completion of the sacrifice. Protect, protect the sacrificer, along with the Preceptor (Ācārya), the officiating priests (Ṛtviks), the Brahmins, the worshippers, the cooks, and all others!"—thus one should say.

Then, having gone to the southeast and having established a water-pot there as before, one should say: "Obeisance to Puṇḍarīka; I invoke him. O Amṛta, I invoke Amṛta. [One should then offer] perfumes and other articles of worship to Puṇḍarīka and Amṛta. Immediately thereafter:
Meditation: Having meditated upon [Agni] stationed in his portion, red in color, holding a spear and a discus in his two right and left hands, and wearing a sacred thread;

[one should recite]: "Come, come, O bearer of oblations for all the immortals, you who are attended on all sides by the most excellent sages! O Lord of the world, together with the hosts of the lords of light, protect my sacrifice; salutations, salutations to you! O Agni, come here, stay here! I invoke Agni, along with his limbs, his retinue, his weapons, and his powers, into this vessel; I offer him the services beginning with fragrance."

[Reciting] the mantra: "Oṃ—We choose Agni as the messenger, the invoker (hotṛ), the all-knowing, the one of excellent wisdom for this sacrifice"—one should hoist a red banner and a red flag. Then [reciting]: "O Agni, you who are wise, may you go as our advocate before the god Varuṇa; being the best sacrificer, the most excellent bearer of oblations, and shining brightly, release us from all enmities. *Salutation to Agni*. I invoke Agni upon the flag and banner. *Salutation to Agni*. I offer the services beginning with the Gaṅgā water.

Meditation: "The person [Agni] is red, consisting of all the gods, and imperishable; O Dhūmraketu, lord of the *rajas* quality, I bow to you eternally, again and again. Having recited this, one should say: "O Agni, together with your limbs (*sāṅga*), your retinue (*saparivāra*), your weapons (*sāyudha*), and your power (*saśaktika*), accept this offering of incense, lamps, parched grain, rice, and food-bali. Protect the sacrifice! Protect the preceptor (*ācārya*), the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the Brahmins, the worshippers, the cooks, and others, along with the patron (*yajamāna*)! Protect, protect! Having thus bowed, one should inform the preceptor.

Then, having gone to the south and having placed two water-pots (kalaśas) against each door-leaf, [one should say] regarding those two pots: "Obeisance to the world-elephant named Vāmana; I invoke the world-elephant named Vāmana. Obeisance to the world-elephant named Vāmana; I offer the services of perfumes and other offerings. There, having appointed two officiating priests (ṛtvij) who are versed in the Yajurveda for the purpose of chanting the Śānti-sūkta at this southern gate, one should say: "The Yajurveda priest named Kātarākṣa, belonging to the Triṣṭubh meter, having Viṣṇu as his deity, and being a descendant of Kaśyapa—O best of Brahmins, I choose you as my officiant in this sacrifice. Thus, having chosen each one individually.

*Maṃ* | *Oṃ ikṣetvorjetvā vāyavasthopāyastha devāva so savitā prārpayatu śreṣṭhatamāya karmaṇe apyāyamadhvo agniyā devabhāgamūrjasvatīḥ payasvatī rasavatīrayakṣmā mā va stena īśata māghaśaṃsaḥ rudrasya hetiḥ parivovṛṇaktu dhruvā asmin gopatau syāta bahvīryajamānasya paśūnpāhi* | Thus, having worshipped each one individually with perfumes and other offerings.

Then, having meditated upon Yama, mounted upon a buffalo, holding a staff and a noose in his two right and left hands respectively, resembling a mass of black collyrium, and possessing eyes like fire;

Meditation: "Come, come, O Vaivasvata, Dharmarāja, you who are worshipped by all the immortals, embodiment of Dharma! O Śubhānanda, Lord of sorrows, salutations for the sake of auspiciousness; protect the sacrifice, salutations to you! O Yama, come here, stay here! I invoke Yama, together with his limbs, his retinue, his weapons, and his power, into the door-pitcher (dvāra-kalaśa). I offer the services beginning with fragrant scents (gandha). The mantra for that is as follows:
[Reciting] the mantra: *oṃ āyaṃ gauḥ pṛśni rakramīd daśanannmātaraṃ punaḥ pitaraṃ ca prayantsuvaḥ*, one should hoist a black flag and a black banner. Then, [reciting] the mantra:

*oṃ sugannaḥ paṃthā mabhayaṃkṛṇotu | yasminnakṣatreyami yajñesmin pūjaye pratigṛhyatāṃ || yamāya namaḥ mayā samarpita sadīpa dadhiyukta māṣabaliṃ bhakṣa yajamāna sahita ācārya-ṛtvik brāhmaṇa arcaka pācaka ācāryādīnāṃ rakṣa rakṣa* (O Yamadeva, may you grant us a good path free from fear; in this constellation, in this sacrifice, please accept this worship; salutations to Yama; consume this offering of black gram with curd and a lamp offered by me; protect, protect the sacrificer, the preceptor, the officiating priests, the Brahmins, the chanters, the cooks, the preceptors, and others). Having said this—
Let him cause [them] to study.

Then, having gone to the southwest and having established a water-pot there as before, [one should say]: "Obeisance to Kumuda; obeisance to Durjaya; I invoke Durjaya-Kumuda. I offer the services of fragrance and the other offerings to both Kumuda and Durjaya."

[The meditation on] Nairṛti: Then, having meditated upon Nairṛti—mounted upon a man, of massive body, sword in hand, possessed of great strength, surrounded by Rākṣasas, blue in color, and adorned with yellow ornaments—one should say: "Come, come, O Rakṣa, O leader of the Gaṇas! O Viśāla Bhairava, together with the hosts of Piśācas, protect my sacrifice from the Piśācas! O Lord of the world, O Blessed One, salutations to you! O Nairṛti, come here; stay here! I invoke Nairṛti into this jar."
I offer the services of perfumes and so forth. With the mantra beginning with "meṣaṇaḥ," one should raise a blue banner and a flag.

Maṃ | Oṃ! Moṣamaḥ, you who transcend both the higher and the lower, whose nature is the manifestation of reality, endowed with steadfastness—along with intense craving, I invoke you upon the flag and banner for the sake of liberation.

Maṃ || Oṃ! "Do not follow the sacrificer; release him from this sin. Do not seek after the thief; desire another instead of us. Thus [the goddess] Nirṛti releases him; let there be homage to you, O Goddess Nirṛti. Homage to Nirṛti. I offer these services of incense and the rest.

Maṃ || Oṃ! Meṣaṇā, Parāparā, Nirṛti, Dhṛpaṇāvatī—O fierce one, may you not seek another through thirst away from us. Homage be to you, O Goddess Nirṛti! Homage to Nirṛti! I offer these services of incense and other offerings.

Dhyāna: "I invoke Nirṛti, who holds a sword in hand and is the sole purifier of all the worlds; may he accept this worship in this sacrifice. Having thus bowed, one should say: "O Nirṛti, with your limbs, retinue, vehicle, and power, please consume this *māṣa*-balī offering accompanied by ghee and curd which has been offered by me. Protect, protect the preceptor, the officiating priests, the Brahmins, the worshippers, the cooks, and the preceptors and others, along with the sacrificer! Having said this, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*).

Then, having gone to the west, one should install two pitchers at the door-jamb as before. In these two pitchers: "Obeisance to the world-elephant named Añjana. "I invoke the world-elephant named Añjana into this pitcher. "Obeisance to the world-elephant named Añjana; I offer the services of perfumes and other articles. There, by means of a Sāmavedin priest: "At this western door, I choose you for the purpose of chanting the Śānti-sūkta."

Having individually chosen them, he said: "O eminent Brahmin, let Piṅgākṣa, who is devoted to the Sāmaveda, wakeful, and has Indra as his deity, be the officiating priest (ṛtvij) at my sacrifice; and you, Bhāradvāja, likewise."

[Reciting] the mantra: "Oṃ, Agni, come for the feast, being praised for the giving of oblations; sit down as the Hotṛ-priest upon the sacred grass (barhis)," one should worship [the deity] individually with offerings such as sandalwood paste and so forth. Then, having meditated upon [Varuṇa], who is situated in a crocodile (makara), holding a noose in his hand, white in color, and wearing a crown.

Meditation: O Lord of the hosts, who are preceded by those who come hither; O Gaṇeśa, together with Parjanya and the Apsarases; you who are praised by the lords of the Vidyādharas and the immortals—protect us, O Blessed One, salutations to you! Oṃ! I invoke Varuṇa, along with his limbs, weapons, powers, and retinue, into the door-pitcher.
With the mantra: "Oṃ, O Varuṇa, hear this prayer of mine; may you be gracious to me today; seeking your protection, I call upon you," one should raise a white banner and a white flag.

Maṃ || Oṃ—To you I approach, praising with a sacred hymn; the sacrificer seeks your favor with oblations. O Varuṇa, being gracious, take heed of this; do not steal away our life, O wide-ruler. *Salutation to Varuṇa*. I invoke [the deity] upon the top of the flag and banner. I present the services of perfumes and other offerings.

[Visualizing: "I invoke Varuṇa, the Lord of the waters, who holds a noose in his hand; may he accept this worship in this sacrifice. Having thus meditated: "O Varuṇa, together with your limbs, retinue, vehicle, and power, please consume this bali-offering consisting of rice mixed with curd and accompanied by a lamp, which has been offered by me. Protect, protect the sacrificer, along with the preceptor, the officiating priests, the Brahmins, the worshippers, the cooks, and others! Having bowed thus, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).

Having gone to the northwestern direction (Vāyavyā), having established the water-pot (kalaśa) there as before, [one should say]: "Obeisance to Puṣpadanta; obeisance to Siddhārtha; I invoke you into this water-pot. [Then: "Obeisance to Puṣpadanta Siddhārtha—I offer the services beginning with fragrance (gandha). Then, one should meditate upon Vāyu, who is mounted on a deer, smoke-colored, wearing variegated garments, youthful, holding an excellent banner, and possessing two hands, the right and the left.

Come, come to my sacrifice for its protection, mounted upon a deer and other [vehicles] along with hosts of Siddhas! O Lord of Life, ally of Kālakavi, accept this worship; O Blessed One, salutations to you! O Vāyu, come here, stay here! Salutations to Vāyu, together with his limbs, his retinue, his weapons, and his powers! O Kaśa, I invoke you; I offer these services beginning with perfumes. A hundred bay horses, youthful and well-nourished, are yours, O Vāyu; or else, O Wind, let a thousand chariots come hither with your splendor.
With this mantra, one should raise the smoke-bannered flag and the smoke-emblem.

Maṃ || Oṃ, O Tvaṣṭṛ, Lord of the Vṛtra-slayer, by the power of Tvaṣṭṛ, the mother of the unmanifest, we choose you as our protector. Salutation to Vāyu; I invoke you upon the flag and banner, and I offer these services beginning with perfumes. I invoke Vāyu, who moves through the sky, who is pure and possesses swift motion; may he accept this worship in this sacrifice. To that venerable Vāyu of the world, who is of great power, who reaches the heavens, and whose course is unseen—I pay homage here. Thus, having spoken.

"Obeisance to Vāyu, together with his limbs, his retinue, his vehicle, and his power; may you accept this *bali* offering of black gram mixed with curd and accompanied by a lamp, which has been presented by me. Protect, protect the preceptor (*ācārya*), the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the Brahmins, the worshippers, the cooks, and others. Having spoken thus, he should offer it to the preceptor.

Then, having gone to the northern gate—having placed two water-pots (kalaśas) at each door-jamb of the northern gate—I invoke the sovereign world-elephants (sārvabhauma-diggajas) into those two pots and worship them with offerings such as perfumes and the like. There, by a priest learned in the Atharvaveda: "In this northern gate, having chanted half of the Śāntisūkta, [I recite] *mahaṃ pṛṇe*. O Bṛhannetra, you who are of the Atharvaveda, in the Anuṣṭubh meter, with Rudra as your deity; O Vaiśampāyana, best of Brahmins, be my officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) in this sacrifice."
Having chosen each one individually.

[Reciting] the mantra: *oṃ śanno devīrabhiṣṭaye āpo bhavantu pītaye | śaṃ yorabhisravantu naḥ*, one should worship [Kubera] individually with offerings such as sandalwood paste (gandha) and so forth. Then, having meditated upon Kubera—seated in a celestial chariot drawn by men, wearing earrings, necklaces, and armlets, holding a beautiful and excellent mace in his two right and left hands, adorned with a crown, possessing a large belly and a massive body, and green in color—one should proceed.

Meditation: "Come, come, O Lord of Sacrifice, for the sake of protecting the sacrifice! O Constellation, dwell here together with the host of stars, with all medicinal herbs, and together with the ancestors. O Blessed One, accept this worship; salutations to you! O Soma, come here, stay here, and accept my worship! I invoke you into the door-jar. [Recite] the sixth mantra: *oṃ āpyāyasva sametu te viśvataḥ soma vṛṣṇyaṃ bhavā vājasya saṃgathe*. With this mantra, one should hoist a green flag and a green banner."

Maṃ || Oṃ, may Soma grant me a milch-cow, Soma a swift steed, and Soma a hero who is skillful in action, worthy of praise, discerning, wise, and whose fame reaches his father—to him who bestows these, [I offer] obeisance to Soma. I invoke [Soma] upon the banner and the flag; I present the offerings of perfumes and other services. "In the midst of all the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), King Soma is established. To that divine Soma, the lord of the lunar mansions, [I offer] obeisance. Having thus bowed, [one should proceed].

To Soma, together with his limbs, his retinue, his vehicle, and his power, I offer this oblation of black gram mixed with curd and accompanied by a lamp, which has been dedicated by me. O Soma, consume this oblation; protect the sacrifice; protect the preceptor, the officiating priests, the Brahmins, the worshipers, and the cooks, along with the patron of the sacrifice—protect, protect! (One should perform the ritual sipping of water.)

Then, having gone to the northeast (Īśānī), one should place a water-pot there as before and perform the following: "Obeisance to Supratīka; I invoke Supratīka. Obeisance to Maṅgala, the deity of auspiciousness; I invoke Maṅgala. Obeisance to Supratīka and Maṅgala; I offer the services beginning with fragrant scents (gandha). Then, one should meditate upon Īśāna, who is mounted on a bull, holding a boon-granting gesture and a trident in his right and left hands respectively, three-eyed, and white in complexion.

Meditation: "Come, come, O Lord of the Universe, together with the trident-bearing protector who holds the *khaṭvāṅga* staff! O Lord of Sacrifice, for the success of the sacrifice, accept this worship; O Blessed One, salutations to you! O Īśāna, come here, stay here, accept my worship, accept it! I invoke Īśāna into the water-pot (*kalaśa*)."

*Maṃ* || With the mantra: *Oṃ abhitvā deva savitarīśānaṃ vāryāṇāṃ sadāvan bhāgamīmahe*, one should hoist a white banner and a white *vajra*. [Recite: "We invoke for our protection the Lord (*Īśāna*) of the moving and the stationary world, the master of the universe, who quickens the intellect; may Pūṣan, knowing the path, grant us prosperity, being the protector for the sake of well-being. "I invoke Īśāna upon the top of the flag and banner. I offer the services beginning with fragrant scents (*gandha*)."

I invoke him who is mounted upon the shoulders of a bull, who holds a trident in his hand, and who has three eyes; may he accept this worship in this sacrifice. To the Lord of All, Mahādeva, the Sovereign, the wielder of the trident, whose eyes are like the sun—to him, eternal salutations, salutations! Having thus prostrated: "O Īśāna, together with your limbs, your retinue, your weapons, your vehicle, and your powers, I offer this oblation of black gram mixed with curds and accompanied by a lamp, which has been presented by me."

"O Bhūta, eat this offering for Īśāna! Protect the sacrifice! Protect the preceptor, the officiating priests, the Brahmins, the worshipers, the cooks, the preceptors, and all others, together with the sacrificer! Having thus spoken, the preceptor [performs the rite].

Then, between the northeast (Īśāna) and east (Pūrva), having visualized Ananta—seated upon his serpent-couch, adorned with seven hoods, holding a lotus and conch in his two left hands and a discus and mace in his two right hands, blue in color—one should invoke him: "Come, come, O Lord of the Nāgas, supporter of the netherworld! You who are sung of by the wives of the Nāgas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, lords of the mountains, and the hosts of the Asura world; O Ananta, protect this sacrificial gate of ours!"
O Ananta, come here; stay here. I invoke Ananta, together with his limbs, weapons, and retinue, accompanied by Naśakti.
Maṃ. Oṃ. The sun, the beholder of all, has stepped forth; he visits his mother again and bestows light upon his father.
With this mantra, one should hoist a white banner and a white flag.

Oṃ, let there be salutation to all those who are on the earth, in the atmosphere, and in heaven; salutation to all of them—salutation to Ananta. I invoke him who is above the banner and the flag. I present the offerings of fragrance and the other services. Salutations again and again to Him who, in His true form, holds the universe with its moving and unmoving beings upon His head like a flower.

"O Ananta! To you, along with your limbs, vehicles, retinue, and powers, I offer this *māṣa*-balī provided with a lamp and clarified butter. O Ananta! Consume this *bali*; protect the sacrifice; protect the preceptor (*ācārya*), the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the Brahmins, the worshipers, the cooks, and others, together with the patron (*yajamāna*). Having thus saluted, [he should offer it] to the preceptor.

Then, between the western and northern directions, facing upward, one should meditate upon Brahmā: four-faced, with a beard and matted hair, pot-bellied, red in color, holding a rosary and a handful of *kuśa* grass in his upper right hand, a sacrificial ladle (*sruva*) and a water-pot (*maṇḍalu*) in his upper left hand, and two lower hands [in the gesture of granting boons]. Having meditated thus, one recites: "Oṃ! Come, come, O Lord of All, O Indra of the Gods, together with the world, the ancestors, and the deities! You are the giver of everything, possessed of immeasurable power; grant us constant favor for our universal welfare."
O Brahman, come here! Stay here! I invoke the Brahman, together with his limbs, his retinue, his weapons, his vehicles, and his powers.

With the mantra: "Oṃ! Brahma, the supreme knowledge, was manifested in the beginning; through his power, he extended the earth and the sky. His highest forms are like the heavens; from him all that moves and stands has come forth"—with this mantra, one should raise a red banner and a red flag.

Maṃ || Oṃ. He is the Brahman among the gods, the path of the sages, the seer among the learned, the buffalo among wild beasts, the hawk among vultures, the bull among the cattle, and Soma among plants—thus he has been praised by Savitṛ and the mortals. [In the Caṇḍīkalpa, it says: "Obeisance to Brahmā; I invoke Brahmā, whose banner is the lotus. I offer the services beginning with perfumes."

Meditation: "Obeisance again and again to him who is the lotus-born, who has four forms, who is the abode of the Vedas, the great source of truth, the lord of sacrifice and the senses, and who has four faces. Having thus bowed down:
I offer this oblation (bali) of cooked rice with black gram and a lamp, dedicated by me to Brahmā, together with his limbs, his retinue, his vehicle, and his power.

"O Brahman, salutations! Consume the offering; protect the sacrifice. O sacrificer, assemble! Protect, protect the preceptor, the officiating priest, the Brahmin, the worshipper, the cook, the preceptor, and the others. Having thus bowed, one should perform prostrations and sip water for purification (ācamana).
Then, in the middle of the pavilion, there was a banner with a very high staff, ten cubits long, three cubits wide, and of variegated colors.

Having established [the deity] with the mantra: *Oṃ indrasya vṛṣṇo varuṇasya rājñā ādityānāṃ marutāṃ śardhaugraṃ mahamanasāṃ bhuvanacyavānāṃ ghoṣo devānāṃ jayatāmudyanmat*, one should offer the services beginning with perfumes (gandha) with the mantra: *Oṃ brahma jijñānaṃ vaḥ | Brahmaṇe namaḥ*. Then, one should worship the sixteen pillars of the pavilion with "Salutation to all the gods," the rafters with "Salutation to the Kinnaras," and the roof-beams with "Salutation to the Pannagas."

Then, having smeared a small portion of ground outside the pavilion in the eastern direction and sitting there, [one should recite]: "Whatever beings there are in the three worlds, both mobile and immobile—may they, together with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, provide protection for these [materials]. May the gods, Dānavas, Sādhyas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas; the Ṛṣis, Munis, cows, the divine mothers, and the Rudras; and Kṣetrapāla along with his hosts—all of them protect the pavilion and slay the Rākṣasas on every side."
Salutation to the stationary beings residing in the three worlds! May the stationary beings residing in the three worlds come to me.

Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmā—I invoke Brahmā, obeisance; I offer the five services beginning with fragrance (gandha). Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu—I invoke Viṣṇu, obeisance; I offer the five services beginning with fragrance. Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva—I invoke Śiva, obeisance; I offer the five services beginning with fragrance.

Oṃ, obeisance to the gods— I invoke the gods; obeisance, I offer the five services beginning with fragrance. Oṃ, obeisance to the Dānavas— I invoke the Dānavas; obeisance, I offer the five services beginning with fragrance. Oṃ, obeisance to the Gandharvas— I invoke the Gandharvas; obeisance, I offer the five services beginning with fragrance.

Oṃ, obeisance to the Yakṣas—I invoke the Yakṣas; obeisance—I present the five services beginning with perfume. Oṃ, obeisance to the Rākṣasas—I invoke the Rākṣasas; obeisance—I present the five services beginning with perfume. Oṃ, obeisance to the Pannagas—I invoke the Pannagas; obeisance—I present the five services beginning with perfume.

Oṃ, obeisance to the cows—I invoke the cows; obeisance—I offer the five services beginning with fragrance (gandha). Oṃ, obeisance to the sages—I invoke the sages; obeisance—I offer the five services beginning with fragrance. Oṃ, obeisance to human beings—I invoke human beings; obeisance—I offer the five services beginning with fragrance.

"Oṃ, obeisance to the Mothers of the Gods (Devamātṛbhyaḥ). Having thus invoked the Mothers of the Gods, I offer the five services beginning with fragrance (gandha). One should present an offering of black-gram rice (māṣabhakta) for each. Then the patron (yajamāna), having had his hands and feet washed and having sipped water (ācānta), together with the preceptor and the officiating priests, should enter the pavilion through the eastern door. The patron should sit to the south of the sacrificial hearth (agni-āyatana). The preceptor, having sat to the west of the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), should make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "In this [specific] rite, I shall perform the installation of the Fire (agni-pratiṣṭhā)," preceded by the Praṇava and the Prāṇāyāma.
Having bowed to the Guru and Gaṇapati.

Having gazed [at the site] with the root mantra, having sprinkled it repeatedly with the water of the general *argha* while reciting "phaṭ," having struck it with *kuśa* grass, and having encircled it with "hūṃ," one should draw three lines with their tips pointing east upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), in order from the center toward the south and north. Upon those, one should draw three lines with their tips pointing north, in order from the center toward the west and east.
