Into those lines, according to the sequence of drawing, one should offer obeisance: "Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ, obeisance to Brahmā; obeisance to Yama; obeisance to Soma; obeisance to Rudra; obeisance to Viṣṇu."
One should worship with "Salutation to Indra.
Then, one should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) upon one's own body as follows:

"Of this glorious Vaiśvānara Mahāmantra, Bhṛgu is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the divine Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandas*), Śrī Vaiśvānara is the deity (*devatā*), *raṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*), and 'Jātavedas' is the pin (*kīlaka*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of success in such-and-such a fire-offering (*homa*)."
Oṃ rāṃ sahasrārciṣe hṛdayāya namaḥ | Oṃ rīṃ svastipūrṇāya śirase svāhā | Oṃ rūṃ uttiṣṭha puruṣāya śikhāyai vaṣaṭ ||
Oṃ raiṃ, to Dhūmavyāpin, for the armor, hūṃ;
oṃ rauṃ, to Saptajihva, for the three eyes, vauṣaṭ; oṃ raḥ, to Dhanurdhara, for the hands, phaṭ.
Now follows the placement of the tongue.

Oṃ sryuṃ, homage to Hiraṇyā—on the secret place; oṃ ṣyūṃ, homage to Gaganā—on the anus; oṃ śryuṃ, homage to Raktā—on the head; oṃ vryūṃ, homage to Kṛṣṇā—on the face; oṃ tryāṃ, homage to Suprabhā—on the two nostrils; oṃ rryuṃ, homage to Atiraktā—on the three eyes; oṃ yryūṃ, homage to Bahurūpā—on all limbs.
Now follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti).

Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Jātavedas, on the head; Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Saptajihva, on the right shoulder; Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Havyavāhana, on the right side; Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Aśvodara, on the right hip; Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Vaiśvānara, on the private parts; Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Kaumāratejas, on the left hip; Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Vaiśvānara, on the private parts; Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Kaumāratejas, on the left hip.
Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Viśvamukha on the left side; Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Devamukha on the left shoulder; Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Agnyāsana on all limbs.
One should visualize the form of the fire of the heart.

Having worshipped the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with the six limbs in the southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest corners, as well as in the center and the cardinal directions, one should draw there the fire-wheel consisting of an eight-cornered, a six-cornered, and a three-cornered [triangle] according to the sequence of entry.

The yantra joined with a dot (bindu) and a triangle, possessing a hexagon and an eight-petaled lotus, and endowed with a *bhūpura* (enclosure of earth), is called Vaiśvānara. Having thus visualized the Vaiśvānara yantra within the mouth of Agni, one should visualize the eight directions within the triangle; therein, starting from the eastern point...

One should worship the pedestal powers (pīṭhaśakti) in order, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise through the cardinal directions and the center: Oṃ, obeisance to Pītā; Oṃ, obeisance to Śvetā; Oṃ, obeisance to Āruṇā; Oṃ, obeisance to Kṛṣṇā; Oṃ, obeisance to Dhūmrā; Oṃ, obeisance to Jvālinī; Oṃ Raṃ, obeisance to the lotus-seat of all powers (sarvaśakti-kamalāsana). Thus one should worship the pedestal power.

Then, in the center of the seat: Oṃ taṃ, obeisance to Tamas; Oṃ raṃ, obeisance to Rajas; Oṃ saṃ, obeisance to Sattva; Oṃ āṃ, obeisance to Ātman; Oṃ paṃ, obeisance to Paramātman; Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Jñānātman.

Then, having worshipped the parents of the fire about to be born—Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara—with the mantra: "Oṃ Hrīṃ, obeisance to the two Vāgīśvarīs" in a triangle, and having meditated upon their state of mutual union; having produced fire from a fire-drill (*araṇi*) or from a sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*), or having brought it from the house of a twice-born (*dvija*); and having placed that fire in an earthen vessel or a copper vessel outside the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in the south-eastern, southern, or south-western direction.

Therefore, having cast a single portion of the fire toward the southwest with the *astra* mantra, "kravyādaṃśamekamagniṃ śalakaṃ phaṭ," having gazed at the fire with the root mantra (*mūla*), having sprinkled it with water while reciting the *astra* mantra, having struck it with *kuśa* grass, having enclosed it with the *kavaca* mantra, and having displayed the *dhenu* mudrā, one should unite the external fire with the internal fire through the intellect by means of the seed-syllable of Vāgīśvarī, using the mantra: "Oṃ raṃ! O Vaiśvānara, Jātavedas, come here; O red-eyed one, cause all rites to proceed; enter the womb of Vāgīśvarī through the seed-syllable of Vāgīśvarī."

Then, having covered [the fire] with fuel sticks while reciting the mantra "Oṃ kavacāya huṃ," and having performed the ritual salutation (*upasthāna*) with: "Oṃ, I praise the blazing Agni, the Jātavedas, the consumer of oblations—pure, golden-hued, well-kindled, and facing in all directions," one should raise the fire with: "Oṃ, arise, O Puruṣa, greenish-brown, red-eyed; accomplish all rites, give and cause to be given, svāhā! Then, with "Oṃ hriṃ," one should establish [the fire] upon the sacrificial mound (*maṇḍala*).

*Oṃ citpiṅgala hana hana daha daha paca paca sarvajñā jñapaya svāhā.* Having thus kindled [the fire] and displayed the *jvālinī-mudrā*, one should meditate upon [Agni] as bearing Vāgīśvarī within his womb. *Oṃ raṃ namaḥ.* To this sacrificial fire (*homāgni*), I perform the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa-karma*) by the name "Homa-devatā Agni," including the rites of conception (*garbhādāna-karma*), the rite for determining the sex of the fetus (*puṃsavana-karma*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana-karma*), and the birth rite (*jātakarma*). *Namaḥ*.

"Oṃ raṃ, salutations! I prepare the rites of the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), the tonsure ceremony (*caulakarma*), the initiation ceremony (*upavītakarma*), the rite of cutting the beard (*godānakarma*), and the marriage rite (*vivāhakarma*) for the divine fire; salutations. Thus, one should worship with these syllables while contemplating each respective rite. Then, having sprinkled water from the general *argha* offering around the fire with the root mantra of the deity, one should adorn the fire.
Having honored [the deity] with mental and verbal rites, one should worship Agni as the yoga-pīṭha.

Oṃ, salutations to Brahmā and the others; salutations to the lineage-sages who are the transmitters of the tradition of Brahman-knowledge; salutations to the gurus. Oṃ, I bow to you, the seat of the hosts. Salutations to the illustrious Mahāgaṇādhipati. Oṃ, salutations to the seven worlds beginning with Atala. Oṃ, salutations to the deities of the pedestal beginning with Maṇḍūka and ending with Paratva. Having worshipped the Fire as the Yoga-pīṭha deity in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa): "Salutations to the deities of the Yoga-pīṭha, the Fire, in the center of the pit."

Then, having performed the *agnimukha* rite as prescribed in one’s own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, one should worship [the fires] in the eight corners, starting from the eastern corner and proceeding clockwise: *Oṃ jātavedase namaḥ* (Salutation to Jātavedas). *Oṃ saptajihvāya namaḥ* (Salutation to Saptajihva). *Oṃ havyavāhanāya namaḥ* (Salutation to Havyavāhana). *Oṃ kaumāratejase namaḥ* (Salutation to Kaumāratejas). *Oṃ viśvamukhāya namaḥ* (Salutation to Viśvamukha). *Oṃ devamukhāya namaḥ* (Salutation to Devamukha). Thus they are worshipped.
In the hexagon, one should perform the six-limbed ritual as follows.

*Oṃ sahasrārciṣe hṛdayāya namaḥ* | *Oṃ svastipūrṇāya śirase svāhā* | *Oṃ uttiṣṭha puruṣāya śikhāyai vaṣaṭ* | *Oṃ dhūmavyāpine kavacāya huṃ* | *Oṃ saptajihvāya netratrayāya vauṣaṭ* | *Oṃ dhanurdharāya astrāya phaṭ*—thus worshiping.
In a triangle.

With the mantra: "Oṃ, O Vaiśvānara Jātavedas, bring [the deity] here; O red-eyed one, accomplish all rites, svāhā!"—one should worship the fire with flowers and unbroken grains (akṣatas). One should perform the purification of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the worship of its girdle and womb.

"Oṃ! May those beings who depart, those beings who remain hidden, and those beings who create obstacles—may they go away to the auspicious fire. Having thus scattered white mustard seeds and having sprinkled the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) while reciting their respective mantras, and having also sprinkled it with water from the *pūṇyāha* rite.
May he purify us who are pure.

Then, taking perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and water, one should invoke [the fire] with: "Oṃ, I invoke that sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) fashioned by Viśvakarman, which is your divine physical body, the wonderful abode of Agni. Having thus invoked, one should worship the pit with the five offerings (pañcopacāra), saying: "Homage to the Pit (Kuṇḍāya namaḥ). Then: "Whatever deities reside in the pit, and whatever deities are in the limbs of the pit, may they all, filled with joy, grant success to the sacrifice."

"O Viśvakarman, this sacrificial pit has been fashioned by you; O Lord, grant us the fulfillment of our desires and the success of the sacrifice. Having thus prayed, one should invoke Viśvakarman into the center of the pit.

Maṃ || Oṃ, Viśvakarman, by means of this increasing oblation, do thou make Indra our protector; for him the ancient people have set their minds, he whom they invoke together at the forefront. Thou art taken with a support; I take thee for Indra. This is thy womb for Viśvakarman; I take thee for Indra and Viśvakarman. Oṃ, obeisance to Viśvakarman. [With] the five services beginning with the Gaṅgā water: "O Viśvakarman, obeisance to thee; do thou destroy all those who are harmful. Having thus prayed.

Upon the upper girdle (*mekhalā*), which is white in color and adorned, one should invoke Viṣṇu with this mantra: "O Viṣṇu, Lord of Sacrifice, destroyer of wicked Daityas! O Protector, accept half of the sacrifice; be present in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Then, having worshipped with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) with the mantra: "Salutation to the girdle, whose presiding deity is Viṣṇu, which is white in color and adorned."

Then, in the middle girdle (*mekhalā*), which is red in color and adorned, one should invoke Brahmā with: *oṃ brahmajijñānaṃ prathamaṃ purastāt*. Having worshipped Brahmā with the five-fold offerings (*pañcopacāra*), [one should pray]: "O God of gods, mounted upon the swan (*haṃsa*), surrounded by hosts of attendants; for the protection of my sacrifice, O Kuṇḍa, be present here. Thus, [one offers] salutation to the middle girdle, whose presiding deity is Brahmā, which is red in color and adorned: *madhyamamekhalāyai brahmadaivatvāyai raktavarṇāyai alaṃkṛtāyai namaḥ*.

Having thus worshipped, one should then invoke Rudra into the black-colored, decorated girdle below: "Oṃ, obeisance to you, O Rudra; be gracious! O Gaṅgādhara, Mahādeva, Maheśvara mounted upon the bull, come, O Blessed Rudra, and be present in this sacrificial pit. Having thus worshipped with: "Obeisance to the third girdle, which is black-colored, decorated, and has Rudra as its presiding deity," one should complete the rite.
Then one should perform the worship of the source (yoni).
Salutation to the Yoni, who is the cause of the world's birth and who is endowed with mental manifestation.
Maṃ || Oṃ, you are the womb of the kṣatriya, you are the navel of the kṣatriya; may I not harm you, and may you not harm me. Having worshipped the womb with perfumes and other offerings...

Meditation: Devas, ṛṣis, siddhas, and humans resort to this great Yoni. Eighty-four hundred thousand species—serpents, apsarases, reptiles, beasts, and birds—all converge here from the earth. Known as "Yoni," she is the cause of the world's origin; the goddess endowed with the power of the mind (Manobhava), she bestows the bliss of Rati. She deludes all the gods; O Sustainer of the World, salutations, salutations! You are the Yoni, possessing universal forms, the primordial nature (Prakṛti) who sustains the universe. You are the abode of desire and the embodiment of desire. Salutations, salutations to the Universal Yoni. Thus one should perform the worship of the Yoni.
Then follows the worship of the throat.
I invoke the neck, which is the source of life for all living beings, the supreme locus for garlands and the like, and the support of the head. Am!

Maṃ || Oṃ: To the Rudras, blue-necked and white-throated, who have resorted to these [mountains], we pay homage with our speech even at a distance of a thousand yojanas. With this mantra, having worshipped the neck [of the sacrificial post] as established in the fire-pit (svarakuṇḍa) in its auspicious form, [one should say]: "The girdles (mekhalās) fashioned by Viśvakarman are arranged all around you. Thus, one should worship the neck with this mantra.
Therefore, there is no worship of the navel.

*Maṃ*. Oṃ! May the navel be consciousness and the mind; may the anus be the organ of excretion. May the testicles be joy and bliss; may the generative organ be the fortune of the Blessed One. Through the two shanks and the two feet, you are Dharma, the universal king, established without opposition. I establish you, O Goddess, in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), honored by the gods. Therefore, you are the goddess who bestows auspiciousness and prosperity. Having thus worshipped the navel with this mantra:
Then, one should perform the Vāstupūjā in the middle of the pit.
I invoke the Lord of Gods, the Puruṣa of great strength, the God of gods, the presiding lord of the Gaṇas, who dwells in the depths of Pātāla.

Maṃ || Oṃ Vāstoṣpati, acknowledge us! Be a gracious dweller for us, free from disease. Whatever we implore you for, favor that for us; grant auspiciousness to our bipeds and prosperity to our quadrupeds. Salutation to Vāstupuruṣa. Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings—Salutation to Vāstupuruṣa—I present this oblation (bali). One should offer the oblation with coconut water. Within his body resides the earth, the Brahmāṇḍa, and the entire cosmic sphere—the pervasive one, of terrifying form, yet beautiful and possessing the universal form.
"O Grandfather, O Chief Son, salutations to you, O Lord of the Site (Vāstupati). Having thus wrapped the thread with the mantra "taṃtu tanvan," [one should proceed].

Maṃ. Oṃ! Spinning the thread, follow the sun with your recitation; protect the luminous footprints fashioned by the intellect. Weave it without flaw for those who sing your praise; become a man of water and give birth to the divine folk. Cover the womb with a red cloth.
One should perform the ritual application of the six vessels. There are four horns.

Having constructed the *sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala for the worship of the planets according to the previously described method, one should invoke the deities therein. Having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and recollected the place and time, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the installation of the deities in the *sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala. Thus having resolved—
"Brahmajijñānam" is by Gautama Vāmadeva; the meter is Triṣṭubh; its application is in the Brahmavāhana rite.

Maṃ | Oṃ. May the wise Vena bring forth from the east the first desire to know Brahman, which shines with splendor; may he, through his awakened intellect, perceive the likeness of this Being and sit upon the womb of the Truth that has been spread out. I invoke Brahman into the center.
Swell up, O Gautama; Soma; Gāyatrī.
Maṃ || Oṃ, swell up, O Soma; from all sides let thy virile power gather, so that thou mayest be present for the attainment of strength. To the northern [direction], obeisance to Soma; I invoke Soma.
"Abhitvājīgah," "Śunaḥśepa," and "Īśāne" are in the Gāyatrī meter.
Maṃ || Oṃ, O divine Savitṛ, lord of desirable things, ever-bestowing, for the sake of greatness, [I invoke] you, the possessor of power.
To Īśāna in the northeast, I pay homage; I invoke him.
Indra is the meter Madhumat; Indra is the Gāyatrī.
Maṃ || Oṃ! We invoke Indra from every side for the sake of our people; may he be ours alone. First, homage to Indra; I invoke Indra.
Kaṇva Medhātithi [saw] Agni the messenger; [the meter is] Gāyatrī.
Maṃ || Oṃ, we choose Agni as the messenger, the invoker, the all-knowing, the one of excellent wisdom for this sacrifice. To Agni in the southeast, obeisance— I invoke Agni.
Yama, following the path, has pressed the Soma.
Maṃ || Oṃ! Press the Soma for Yama; offer the oblation to Yama. To Yama let the sacrifice go, with Agni as the well-prepared messenger. [Facing] south: *namaḥ* to Yama—I invoke Yama.
The terrible Kaṇva, the son of Muṣuṇa, recites this Gāyatrī verse.
Maṃ | Oṃ, may the dispeller, the supreme one, the Nirūrutī who possesses steadfastness, together with her husband Kṣṇatṛṣṇā, come forth. To you, O Nairṛtī, to Virūrutī, obeisance! I invoke Virūrutī.
*Tat tvā yāmi* (Rig Veda 1.24.11). The seer is Śunaḥśepha, the deity is Varuṇa, the meter is Triṣṭubh;

this is the sixth mantra. Oṃ. To you I approach with prayer, worshipping you with oblations; for this the sacrificer hopes through his offerings. O Varuṇa, being mindful, hear us; grant us long life that we may live. In the fifth [offering], salutation to Varuṇa—I invoke Varuṇa.
The deity of this [verse] is Vāyu; it belongs to the Aṅgirases; its meter is Gāyatrī.
Maṃ || Oṃ, O Vāyu, Lord of the wind’s course, wondrous son-in-law of Tvaṣṭṛ, we choose [your] protections. O Vāyu in the northwest, salutation to you—I invoke Vāyu.
By means of the *jyā* [bowstring], Atri and Mitrāvaruṇa; the Vasus [are connected] with the *triṣṭubh*.

Maṃ | Oṃ! Here on earth, the Vasus, the Rantidevas, the radiant ones, purify themselves in the vast mid-air. O you of wide stride, turn your paths hitherward; grant us the hearing of this messenger who has come. Between Vāyu and Soma, homage to the eight Vasus—I invoke the eight Nasūnās.
The eleven Rudras, beginning with Ārudrāsas, are the Śyāvāśvas; the meter is Jagatī.

Maṃ || Oṃ! O Rudras, accompanied by Indra, being of one mind, and possessing golden chariots, come to our well-prepared sacrifice. This prayer of ours is offered to you, like springs of water from the thirsty heavens for one who longs for them. Between the two lords of Soma, obeisance to the eleven Rudras—I invoke the eleven Rudras.
The Sāmaveda, Matsya, the twelve Ādityas, and the Gāyatrī [are associated] with them.
Maṃ || Oṃ, we invoke you, the sovereign Ādityas, for our protection and for our desired aid. Between the two lords, Indra and Īśāna, obeisance to the twelve Ādityas—I invoke the twelve Ādityas.
"Aśvanāvarti" by Rāhūgaṇa; the meter is Uṣṇih.

Maṃ || Oṃ, O Aśvins, lords of rays, come toward us with cattle, horses, and gold; bring hither the identical [treasures]. Between Indra and Agni, salutation to the two Aśvins—I invoke the two deities, the Aśvins.
"Oṃ āsaś carṣaṇīdhṛtaḥ"—this [verse] is by Gṛtsamada; the Viśvedevas are the deities; the metre is Gāyatrī.

Maṃ || Oṃ! You who are sustained by the months, O Viśvedevas, come to the pressed juice of the donor at the offering. [I offer] obeisance to all the gods in the center of the fire; I shall invoke the Viśvedevas.
The Vāmadeva [hymns] are seven; the Atyaṣṭi [meter] has eight syllables.

Maṃ || Oṃ, I praise the divine Savitṛ, the one to be sought with longing, the seer of wisdom, whose libations are true, the bestower of jewels, the beloved thought; whose splendor and light shine upward at his impulse. The golden-handed one of good resolve has measured out the world with his form. To the seven Yakṣas in the midst of whom he shines, obeisance! I invoke the seven Yakṣas.
The verse "āyaṃ gauḥ" is in the Sārvarājī meter; it is a Gāyatrī.

Maṃ || Oṃ: "The dappled cow has stepped forth; she has returned to her mother and to her father, bestowing light. In the midst of Nirṛti and Varuṇa, to the spirits and nāgas—I invoke the spirits and nāgas. Right there.
The *āparāsāma* and *aitasarpaśṛṅga* [hymns] belong to the Gandharvas and Apsarases; their meter is the *anuṣṭubh*.

Maṃ || Oṃ! Moving among the footsteps of the Apsarases, Gandharvas, and wild beasts—O Keśikā, you are his companion in knowledge, most intoxicated by passion. Homage to the Gandharvas and Apsarases! I invoke the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
The mother [carries] the boy on her hip; [the meter is] Triṣṭubh.

Oṃ! When the Mother, having cooked the youth with fire, runs toward the impaled stake after he has been struck down—may he, having taken refuge in the Mother Earth, be granted by the divine Mothers and the Fathers who desire it.
When the most exalted Dīrghatamas, Skanda, cried out, he stood firm in the Triṣṭubh meter.

Maṃ || Oṃ, when you neighed at birth, bursting forth from the ocean, the source of waters—O steed, having praised your two wings like those of a white bird and your arms like gold, may that great being who was born be honored; [I offer] the *brahma* and *soma* between the two, with obeisance. This is the application (*viniyoga*) for the invocation of Skanda.
The Ṛṣabha is indeed the bull; the Anuṣṭubh belongs to the King.

Maṃ || Oṃ! Among those being measured, [I praise] the Bull, the subduer of rival wives, the slayer of enemies, the king of the earth, the lord of cattle, and the Lord of Cows. Between the Brahman and Soma, salutations to the Bull—salutations to Vṛṣabheśvara. I invoke Vṛṣabheśvara.
Aditi is the world, Bṛhaspati is the spear; Mahākāla is the Anuṣṭubh meter.

Maṃ || Oṃ. Aditi was born from Dakṣa as your daughter; the auspicious gods, whose kinsmen are the immortals, were born after her. I invoke the seven groups beginning with Dakṣa into the center of the Īśānī [quarter] of the Brahma [mandala].
Jātavedas, Kaśyapa, Durgā, and Triṣṭubh.

Maṃ || Oṃ, we press the Soma for Jātavedas; he burns up the wealth of the one who acts with hostility. May he carry us across all difficulties, and like a ship, may Agni lead us beyond all misfortunes. Between Brahmā and Indra, obeisance to Durgā—I invoke Durgā.
This [verse] "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ" has Methātithi as its seer, Viṣṇu as its deity, and the Gāyatrī as its meter.
Maṃ || Oṃ, Viṣṇu strode across this; he established his step in three places. His power is gathered in the cave of the sky. To Viṣṇu, between Brahmā and Indra, obeisance—I invoke Viṣṇu.
"May the Śaṅkha rise up; Svadhā! Triṣṭubh."

Maṃ || Oṃ! May the ancestors—the lower, the higher, and those in the middle—worthy of Soma, who have attained the life-breath, who are free from malice and knowers of the Truth (Ṛta), arise. May the ancestors respond to my invocation with praise. In the midst of the sacred fire (Brahmāgni), [I offer] Svadhā; obeisance! I invoke Svadhā.
"O Death, beyond [is] Saṃkuśika; death and diseases are Triṣṭubh."

Maṃ || Oṃ, O Death, go along the other path, that which is different from the path of the gods. To you who have eyes and hear, I speak this: do not harm our offspring nor our heroes. Between Brahmā, Agni, and Yama—salutation to the diseases of death. I shall invoke the diseases of death.
Thee, the lord of hosts, whom the world praises as the one who intoxicates the entire assembly.
Maṃ || Oṃ, you who are the leader of the hosts, the giver of success to the hosts; I invoke Gaṇapati into the midst of this sacred formulation (brahman).
"śanno devī": Ambarīṣa Ṛṣi, Sindhudvīpa Ṛṣi, the Waters (Āpaḥ) as the deity, Gāyatrī Chanda.
Maṃ | Oṃ, may the divine waters be auspicious for our aid, for our drinking; may they flow auspiciously for us. [I offer] salutations to the Waters between Brahmā and Varuṇa—I invoke the Waters.
The Maruts, the troop with unbroken chariot-yokes; the Maruts, the Gāyatrī.

Maṃ || Oṃ! In whose dwelling the Maruts, the most mighty ones from heaven, bestow prosperity—that person shall find a good path. [Offering] obeisance to the Maruts in the midst of Brahmā and Vāyu: I summon the Maruts.
"May the earth be pleasant to our guest"; this verse is in the Gāyatrī meter.

Maṃ || Oṃ, may you be a pleasant earth, free from thorns, providing a secure dwelling; grant us food and protection. I shall perform the worship at the feet of Brahmā. To the Earth—O Earth, I invoke you.
Of this [hymn] beginning with "imaṃ me gaṅge," the meters are *jagatī* for the verses addressed to the Sindhu, Kṣitriya, Yamunā, and Sarasvatī.

Maṃ || Oṃ, O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Śutudrī, Marudvṛdhā, Paruṣṇī, Asiknī, Vitastā, Ārjīkīyā, and Suṣomā—attend to this sacrifice. Homage to all rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā; I invoke all the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā. In that very place.
From abode to abode, Gautama Vāmadeva [saw] the Saptasāgara Anuṣṭubh.

Maṃ | Oṃ, O King Varuṇa, release me from every bond; release me from whatever sin against the waters we have committed, O Varuṇa; release me from whatever sin against the waters we have committed, O Varuṇa—since we implore you thus, O Varuṇa, release me from that. I invoke the seven oceans, beginning with the salt ocean. Above them, salutations to Meru.

Maṃ || Oṃ. These Rudras, the mountains, who are invoked together in the slaying of Vṛtra, being well-pleased—may the thunderbolt given to you as you praised [him], O Indra, and the gods with Indra as their chief, protect us. I invoke Meruparvata.
On the outer enclosure, near Soma and the others, the weapons are placed in sequence in the eight directions: [the *gadā*]. "I invoke the *gadā* near Soma," with the mantra: *gaṇānāṃ tvā sādanam*.

Trident. Maṃ. Oṃ. Since the limbs of the one being roasted over the fire are struck by the trident, may he not strike them while falling upon the mother earth; let that [offering] be given to the gods who desire it. I invoke the Trident in the northeast.

Vajra! Maṃ! Oṃ! Great Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, the sixteenth [deity], grant us protection; may the bountiful one bring us well-being. May he who hates us meet with evil. I invoke the thunderbolt in the presence of Indra.
Śaktim | Maṃ | Oṃ, may there be wealth for me, may there be a dwelling for me, may there be action for me, may there be power for me. I invoke Śakti in the vicinity of Agni.
Daṇḍa | Maṃ | Oṃ, with the Iḍās, the Āditas, and the Sarasvatīs, I invoke Daṇḍa in the presence of Yama.

The Sword [Maṇḍala]: Maṃ. Oṃ! Ruru for Rudra, the chameleon for Śakuni, the Pippakā bird for Tārkṣya, the deer for Śaravyā, the Śārga antelope for Brahmā, the hyena for Īśa, the black dog for the Rakṣas, and the donkey for the Maruts; with the bull, may he drive away the wild beasts of men. Near Nirṛti, I invoke the Sword.

The Noose. Maṅgala: Oṃ. O Varuṇa, loosen the highest noose from us, untie the lowest, and release the middle one. Then, through faith, may we abide in your law, O Āditya, being sinless before Āditya. I invoke the noose into the presence of Varuṇa.

The goad (aṅkuśa). Maṃ. Oṃ āgṃ. May I prosper through my offspring and my rays; may I prosper through my firmness and my lordship. Near Vāyu, I invoke the goad. Outside of that, in the sequence beginning from the north.

Maṃ || Oṃ, O Jātavedas, who art born from the mountains and who art all-seeing, we praise you aloud with splendors that surpass those of the possessor of cattle. [Recite] "uttare ahalyāsahita" (O Uttara, together with Ahalyā). I invoke the sage Gautama.

Maṃ || Oṃ. This is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*): Viśvakarman; his mental faculty is the maker of all (*vaiśvakaraṇa*); the summer season is mental; the *triṣṭubh* meter is of the summer; from the *triṣṭubh* comes the *aiḍa* chant; from the *aiḍa* comes the intermediate space; from the intermediate space comes the fifteen-fold hymn (*pañcadaśa*); from the fifteen-fold hymn comes the *bṛhat* sāman; from the *bṛhat* comes the seer Bharadvāja. With thee, taken by Prajāpati, I take the mind for the sake of progeny. From the northeast, I invoke Bharadvāja together with Suśīlā.

Maṃ | Oṃ Yaṃ. After [the hymn] Viśvacaras, his eye is Vaiśvavyacanas; the years are the Cākṣuṣas; the Jagatī is the Vārṣī; from the Jagatī comes the Ṛk; from the Ṛk, Śukra; from Śukra, the Saptadaśa Stoma; from the Saptadaśa, the Vairūpa Sāman; from the Vairūpa, the seer Viśvāmitra. With you, who are grasped by Prajāpati, I grasp the eye for all creatures. I invoke Viśvāmitra together with Kumudvatī to the east.

Maṃ || Oṃ! That craft of yours which is like that of Kaśyapa, endowed with sensory power, abundant, and of wondrous luster—in which the seven suns are placed together—into that [craft], O King, we shall mix this honey. In the southeast: I invoke Kaśyapa together with Aditi.

Maṃ | Oṃ. This [is from] the Uttara-svastasya; the Śrotra-chant from the Śarad; the Anuṣṭubh from the Anuṣṭubh; the Sāraṅga from the Svāra; the Manthin from the Manthin; the Ekaviṃśa-stoma from the Ekaviṃśa; the Vairāja from the Vairāja; Jamadagni is the Ṛṣi. With you, who are taken for the sake of progeny, I take up the sense of hearing for the sake of my offspring. On the southern side, I invoke Jamadagni together with Veṇukā.

Maṃ || Oṃ. This one is Purobhū; his breath is Bhauvāyana; the spring is Prāṇāyana; the Gāyatrī is Vāsantī; from the Vāsantī Gāyatrī comes the Gāyatra [Sāman]; from the Gāyatra comes the *durāgṃ* [chant]; from the *durāgṃ* comes the *śurupāgṃ* [chant]; from the *śurupāgṃ* comes the *stotra*; from the *stotra* comes the Trivṛt [Stoma]; from the Trivṛt comes the Rathantara [Sāman]; from the Rathantara comes the seer Vasiṣṭha. With you, who are grasped by Prajāpati, I grasp the breath for all creatures. [I invoke] the boat-raft; I invoke Vasiṣṭha together with Arundhatī.

Maṃ | Oṃ. Atri gave [the sacrifice] to Aurva, who desired offspring; he thought himself exhausted, devoid of vigor, and weak. He beheld this four-night rite (caturātra) and sacrificed with it. Thereupon, four heroic sons were born to him: a good Hotṛ, a good Udgātṛ, a good Adhvaryu, and one fit for the assembly. Whoever, knowing thus, sacrifices with the four-night rite—for him I summon these four.

May we, O gods, follow along with our wives, sons, brothers, or even with golden treasures, ascending to the firmament in the world of the righteous, upon the third radiant height of heaven where rain falls. I invoke Arundhatī from the quarter of Vāyu.
That [is arranged] outside, in the sequence starting from the east.

Maṃ || Oṃ. The goddess Indrāṇī is fortunate and well-provided with offspring; she has won a husband by her northern course. Thirty joints are in her loins; Indra bears the aged one upon her lap. I invoke the eastern Indrī.

Maṃ || Oṃ, from these various forms he obtains: one who is excessively short or excessively tall; one who is excessively emaciated or excessively stout; one who is excessively fair or excessively dark; one who is excessively smooth or excessively hairy; one who is excessively crowned or excessively jagged; one who is excessively blind or excessively uneven; a sister for Āśā (Hope); a maiden for Prati-kṣaya (Destruction). To Agni— I invoke Kaumārī.

Maṃ || Oṃ! May [Indra], who is pleased by the sacred word (*brahman*) and who seeks the prize for the yoked pair of bay horses (*haribhyām*), be present. By his greatness, he has rent asunder the two expanses of space; Indra, having struck down the Vṛtras without resistance, has prevailed. I invoke the Brāhmī [Mudrā] on the right.
Maṃ | Oṃ āyaṃgauḥ yaṃtsuvaḥ | I invoke Nairṛtī Vārāhī.
O Mother, O Ambālī, O Ambikā! Let no one harm you; the little horse has fallen asleep.
And in the west, I invoke Cāmuṇḍā.
Maṃ || Oṃ apyāyasva saṃgadhe || I invoke Niṣṇavī from the north-western direction.
Maṃ || Oṃ: That form of yours, O Rudra, which is auspicious, not terrible, and drives away evil—with that form, O Lord of the Mountain, look upon us with favor. In the north, I invoke Māheśvarī.
Maṃ || Oṃ, salutations to the Gaṇas and to the lords of the Gaṇas; salutations! I invoke Vaināyakī from the northeast.

Therein, in the center, for Sūrya: "I invoke Sūryā. On the outside, in the eight directions beginning with the east: for Soma— "I invoke Soma"; for Bhauma— "I invoke Bhauma"; for Budha— "I invoke Budha"; for Bṛhaspati— "I invoke Bṛhaspati"; for Śukra— "I invoke Śukra"; for Śanaiścara— "I invoke Śanaiścara"; for Rāhu— "I invoke Rāhu"; for Ketu— "I invoke Ketu."

Having installed and worshipped these deities according to the previously mentioned method, one should draw a yantra upon a linen cloth using the eight fragrant substances (aṣṭagandha). Having placed it there in the proper sequence, one should install the planets, the primary deities (pratyadhidevatā), and the secondary deities (pratyadhidevatā) therein with saffron and unbroken grains (akṣata). For example: having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), "I shall perform the installation of the deities beginning with Āditya in the maṇḍala," [one should invoke them]. [The deity is] seated on a lotus-throne, holding a lotus in his hand, the interior of a lotus.

"Ā kṛṣṇena": Hiraṇya-stūpa Savitṛ; Triṣṭubh meter. Application (*viniyoga*) is for the invocation of Sūrya. *Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, O Sūrya, born in Kaliṅga, of the Kāśyapa lineage, come here! "Ā pyāyasva": Gautama; Soma; Gāyatrī meter. *Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, O Soma, born on the banks of the Yamunā, of the Ātreya lineage, come here! "Agnir mūrdhā": Virūpa; Aṅgāraka; Gāyatrī meter. *Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, O Bhauma (Mars), born in Avantī, of the Bhāradvāja lineage, come here!

Having awakened, may the gentle Budha, born of the self-awakened, come here—*oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, you who are born in the Magadha country, of the Ātreya gotra, O Budha, come here! O Bṛhaspati, [the seer] Gṛtsamada; Bṛhaspati, the *triṣṭubh* meter—*oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, you who are born in the Siṃdhu country, of the Āṅgirasa gotra, O Bṛhaspati, come here! O Śukra, [the seer] Parāśara, the *dvipadā virāj* meter—*oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, you who are born in Bhojakaṭa, of the Bhārgava gotra, O Śukra, come here!

"Śam agniḥ"—Viśvāmitra is the seer, Śunaḥśepa is the deity, Uṣṇih is the metre. *Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*. O Śanaiścara, born in the land of Saurāṣṭra, of the Kāśyapa gotra, come here! *Kayā naḥ*—Vāmadeva is the seer, Rāhu is the deity, Gāyatrī is the metre. *Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*. O Rāhu, born in the land of Siṃhala, of the Paiṭhīnasi gotra, come here! *Ketuḥ*—Madhucchandas is the seer, Ketu is the deity, Gāyatrī is the metre. *Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*. O Ketu, born in Antarvedī, of the Jaimini gotra, come here! Now, the presiding deities (adhidaivata):

Tryambaka Vasiṣṭha; Rudra, Anuṣṭubh; Gaurī-mimāya Dīrghatamas; Umā, Jagatī. Yad akranda Dīrghatamas; Skanda, Triṣṭubh. Viṣṇor nu kam Dīrghatapas Ātreya; Triṣṭubh. Brahma-jijñānam Vāsudeva; Brahmā, Triṣṭubh. Indram vaḥ Madhucchandas; Indra, Gāyatrī. Yamāya somam Yama; Yama, Anuṣṭubh. Mo ṣu naḥ Aghora Kaṇva; Kāla, Gāyatrī. Uṣo rājan Praskaṇva; Citragupta, Bṛhatī.

The presiding and secondary deities: "Agni, Kaṇva, Medhātithi"—Agni, Gāyatrī. "Ap-sú me, Medhātithi"—Pūṣan, Anuṣṭubh. "Syonā, Medhātithi"—Bhūmi, Gāyatrī. "Idaṃ viṣṇuḥ, Medhātithi"—Viṣṇu, Gāyatrī. "Indra śreṣṭhāni, Gṛtsamada"—Indra, Triṣṭubh. "Indrāṇīm, Vṛṣākapi"—Indrāṇī, Paṅkti. "Prajāpate, Hiraṇyagarbha"—Prajāpati, Triṣṭubh.

This cow belongs to King Sarpī; O serpent, [the meter is] Gāyatrī. "The desire for Brahman" (brahmajijñānam); Gautama, Vāmadeva, and Brahmā; [the meter is] Triṣṭubh. Then, to the north: "Of the hosts, thee" (gaṇānāṃ tvā); Gṛtsamada, Gaṇapati; [the meter is] Jagatī. "To Jātavedas" (jātavedase); Kaśyapa, Durgā; [the meter is] Triṣṭubh.

Tava-vāyu, Śvāṅgirasa, Vāyu, Gāyatrī; Āditya, Sa, Ākāśa, Gāyatrī—this is Uṣas; Praskaṇva, Aśvinau, Gāyatrī. To the north of Vārāha is Vināyaka; to the north of Śani is Vāyu; to the south of Rāhu is Ākāśa; to the south of Ketu are Aśvinau; to the north is Kṣetrasya Patinā, with Vāmadeva as the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapati).

The *anuṣṭubh* [meter]: "O Vāstoṣpati," by Vasiṣṭha; [the deity] is Vāstoṣpati; the meter is *triṣṭubh*. Then, for the *lakṣa-homa* and *koṭi-homa*: "Thou art the embodiment of the sound of the Sāman, the vehicle of Parameṣṭhin; thou art eternally the remover of poison and sin—grant me peace. With this mantra, having invoked Indra (or "Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa... and Garuḍa in the north, and having invoked the guardians of the directions (*dikpālas*) in their respective directions with their respective mantras; then, Śeṣa to the east of the Sun, and Vāsuki in front of the Moon.

One should place Takṣaka in front of Bhauma (Mars); Karkoṭika to the north of Budha (Mercury); Padma to the north of Guru (Jupiter); Mahāpadma to the north of Śukra (Venus); Śaṅkhapāla to the west of Śani (Saturn); Kaṃbala in front of Rāhu; and Kuliśa in front of Ketu. Then, in the east, one should place the seven constellations beginning with Aśvinī, the seven yogas beginning with Viṣkambha, the two karaṇas Bava and Bālava, the seven continents, and the Ṛgveda. In the south, [one should place] the seven constellations beginning with Puṣya.

[He worships] the seven yogas beginning with Dhṛti; in the Kaulava karaṇa, the seven oceans; in the Garaja karaṇa, the seven Vedic impulses (vegās) of the Yajurveda and the Sāmaveda; in the northern [direction], the seven lunar mansions beginning with Abhijit, the six yogas beginning with Sādhya, the Viṣṭi karaṇa, the seven worlds beginning with Bhūr, and the Atharvaveda; in the Vāyu [direction], the Pole Star (Dhruva) and the Seven Ṛṣis; then, according to available space, the seven rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā and the seven principal mountain ranges.

[He should worship] the eight Vasus, the twelve Ādityas, the eleven Rudras, the forty-nine Maruts, the sixteen Mātṛs, the six seasons, the twelve months, the two solstices (ayanas), the fifteen lunar days (tithis), the sixty years, the winged Nāgas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Apsarases, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, and humans. In the case of a *koṭi-homa*, one should meditate on Brahmā in the center of the altar, Janārdana in the east, Rudra in the west, and Skanda in the north.

Then, having invoked Mitrā and Gṛhava with the mantra "ityāvāhya," one should worship them with the Puruṣasūkta using the sixteen types of offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra) and make this prayer: "O Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Maruts, and likewise the Guardians of the World (Lokapālas), Brahmā, Janārdana, Śūlapāṇi, and Bhagākṣaha—may you all be present here in this serpent-sacrifice as partakers of the oblation. May you accept everywhere the worship offered by me with devotion. And may you all, being composed, bring about auspiciousness for the performer of the sacrifice."

Then, having worshipped the water-pot (kumbha) in the northeast of the altar and having made this prayer—“In the conflict between the gods and the demons”—one should perform the anvādhāna, concluding with the offering of clarified butter (ājya) for the two eyes.

With oblations of sacrificial wood (*samit*), parched grain (*caru*), and clarified butter (*ājya*) offered in numbers of one hundred and eight, or one hundred and twenty, or any other [multiple] for the nine planets; or with oblations of barley, rice, ghee, or sesame seeds offered in numbers of ten thousand (*nayuta*), one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*), or ten million (*koṭi*) for the nine planets; and with the remainder for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, and so forth—according to the view that there is only one oblation of *caru* and *ājya* for all [the deities], the drawing of lines and other rites follow accordingly. In the case of the *lakṣa* and *koṭi* homas, one should offer to Garuḍa with sacrificial wood and the rest in numbers such as one hundred and eight; and in the *koṭi* homa, the procedure for Brahmā and the others follows the *Garuḍa-vrata*.

In the case of the *carukāhuti* (oblation of cooked rice), the rule of five-fold portions (*pañcāvadāna*) applies to the calves. When a *lakṣahoma* or similar rite is to be accomplished over many days, the *caru*, the *sviṣṭakṛt*, and other such offerings should be performed on the very first day.

Until the completion of the *homa*, the worship of the planets (*graha-pūjā*) must be performed daily. For every ten thousand oblations in a *koṭi-homa*, a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) should also be offered. At the conclusion of the *homa*, having fully worshipped the fire and performed the rites beginning with the *sviṣṭakṛt* up to the end of the expiatory *prāyaścitta-homa*, one should offer *bali* offerings of black gram and cooked rice to the nine planets around the fire, to the seven deities beginning with Vināyaka and to Garuḍa to the north of the altar (*vedi*) using their respective mantras. Then, the *kṣetrapāla-bali* should be cast by a Brāhmaṇa or a Śūdra at the four corners. Thereafter, having washed one's feet...
The householder should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* with twelve portions of clarified butter taken four times each, accompanied by cloth, coconut, and other offerings. The mantras for that are as follows:
The verse beginning with "samudrā dūrmih" is by Gautama; its deity is Agni, and its meter is Triṣṭubh.
To the ocean, the weaver of the rivers, the lord of streams—salutation! To Viśvakarman, the father of all rivers, offer this oblation which is to be remembered by all people for all time.
The Mūrdhanvatī verses belong to Bṛhaspati; the Vaiśvānara verse is a Triṣṭubh belonging to Bharadvāja.

To me! Oṃ! Agni Vaiśvānara, the head of heaven, the foundation of earth, born for the sake of immortality, the sovereign ruler of men and the boundless one—may the gods establish him as a vessel placed within us.
Again, "Agnirvasu rudrādityā" is a Triṣṭubh verse.

Maṃ | Oṃ! May the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus kindle me again; may the Brahman and the Vasus [kindle] this [sacrifice] through the oblations. O Ghee, cause our bodies to increase; may the desires of the sacrificer come true.
The *pūrṇādarvī* verse, addressed to the Viśvedevas, has Śatakratu as its deity and the Anuṣṭubh as its meter.
Me! Oṃ! Let the ladle fly forth full; let it return well-filled again. O Lord of a hundred powers, bring us food and vigor, bending it to our will.
To you, O Agni, the sevenfold one, to Agni who possesses the seven flames.

Oṃ! Seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni; seven your tongues; seven the Ṛṣis; seven your beloved abodes. May the seven officiating priests impel you in seven ways; fill the seven wombs with clarified butter.
The seer is Vāmadeva; the deity is Water; the metre is Jagatī.

*Maṃ* || *Oṃ dhāmno dhāmno rājannito varuṇonumuṃca yadāpo agniyā varuṇotiśaphāmahe tato varuṇonumuṃca.* Having offered oblations with these [mantras], the renunciation (*tyāga*) is as follows: "This [is for] Agni Vaiśvānara, for the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, for Śatakratu, for the seven [sages], and for Agni; obeisance. Then, one should pour out the remnants of the clarified butter (*vasoddhārā*). The mantras for that are: for the nine verses beginning with *agnim īḷe*, Madhucchandas is the seer, Agni is the deity, and Gāyatrī is the metre.

For the six verses beginning with "viṣṇornuka," Dīrghatamas is the seer, Viṣṇu is the deity, and Triṣṭubh is the meter. For the fifteen verses beginning with "ātepitar," Gṛtsamada is the seer, Rudra is the deity, and Triṣṭubh is the meter. For the ten verses beginning with "svādhī," Madhuchandas is the seer, Pavamāna Soma is the deity, and Gāyatrī is the meter. Having completed the remainder of the ritual, including the Mahāvaiśvānara and Jyeṣṭhasāman chants and the pouring out of the full vessel (pūrṇapātra), etc.:

Having performed the accomplishment of the welfare of sentient beings, he should consecrate the patron—who is seated upon a *bhadrāsana* atop a *svastika* in the northeast portion of the sacrificial pit—with the water from the planetary jars (*grahakalaśa*) using the mantras beginning with "The oceans are the eldest" (*samudrajyeṣṭhāḥ*) and "May the gods [consecrate you]" (*surāstvā*). Here, the wife is on the left. Then the patron, having bathed after being anointed with all medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadhi*), [should recite] the Puranic verses: "May the gods consecrate you—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara; Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, as well as the omnipresent Saṃkarṣaṇa."

May Pradyumna and Aniruddha be for my victory! May Ākhaṇḍala, Agni, the Lord Yama, as well as Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Pavana, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), and Śiva—may all these guardians of the quarters, together with Brahmā, protect me always! Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Medhā, Puṣṭi, Śraddhā, Kriyā, Mati, Buddhi, Lajjā, Vapus, Śānti, Kānti, and Tuṣṭi—the Mothers; may these wives of the gods, having assembled here, consecrate you!
May Āditya, Candra, Bhauma, Budha, Jīva, Śukra, and Arkaja, as well as Rāhu and Ketu when propitiated, sprinkle you with water; may the gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, and Yakṣas [do the same].

"May the Rākṣasas, the Pannagas, the Ṛṣis, the Muses, the Yogins, the cows, the mothers of the gods, the wives of the gods, the trees, the Nāgas, the Daityas, the hosts of Apsarases, all weapons, all scriptures, kings, vehicles, medicinal herbs, jewels, the divisions of time, the rivers, the oceans, the mountains, the sacred fords, and the clouds—may these all consecrate me for the attainment of all desires and goals. Thus it is said.

Then, the performer, facing east, having honored the preceptor and the officiating priests (ṛtvij) who are facing north, shall announce the place and time, and say: "In this *grahayaṣṭi* sacrifice called the *āyutahoma*, performed by me, I hereby bestow this tawny cow (*kapilā-gau*), whose deity is Rudra and which serves as the foundation for the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), together with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), upon all the officiating priests beginning with the preceptor, according to their respective lineages (*gotra*). Having said "I give," he recites: "O Kapilā, you are worthy of worship among all the gods; O Rohiṇī, since you consist of sacred fords and deities, grant me peace."

Thus one should recite. This should be understood as follows: "O auspicious conch, you are the merit of meritorious things and the most auspicious of auspicious things. Constantly held by Viṣṇu, grant me peace. Thus [one offers] the conch to Soma. "You are Dharma in the form of a bull, the cause of joy for the world, the abode of the Eightfold Form (Aṣṭamūrti). Therefore, grant me peace. [One offers] the bull to Bhauma. "The golden seed of the Sun, situated within the womb of Hiraṇyagarbha..."

"Grant me peace, O you who bestow the fruit of infinite merit"—thus [the gift] for Mercury. "Since a pair of yellow garments is dear to Vāsudeva, may Viṣṇu, through the gift of these, be pleased with me and grant me peace"—thus [the gift of] yellow garments for Jupiter. "Since you were born from the nectar in the form of a horse, and are the eternal vehicle of the Moon and the Sun, grant me this peace"—thus [the gift of] a horse for Venus. "Since you are a black cow, dark as a cloud and resembling the luster of hair... [and so on].

"O you who eternally remove all sins, grant me peace below. Thus for Saturn, a black bull. "Since iron implements such as ploughs and weapons are always made from you, therefore grant me peace. Thus for Ketu, a goat. For all [the planets], cows are the sacrificial animals. "Since the fourteen worlds abide within the limbs of cows, therefore may there be auspiciousness for me in this world and the next; thus it should be given. Or, one should give gold to all.

For the pleasure of all, a bed, gems, and land as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given. May these mantras be recited: "Since the bed of Keśava and of Śiva is never empty, may this bed of mine not be empty on the day of my birth. Just as all the gods are established within all these gems, O gods, grant me peace through this gift of gems. Since other gifts do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of a gift of land, may peace come to me through this gift of land."

One should give garments, gold, and jewels according to one's capacity. Then, having performed the subsequent worship of the planets, one should dismiss them with the mantra "yāntu devagaṇāḥ" (May the hosts of gods depart). Having worshipped the fire and applied sacred ash (vibhūti), one should dismiss it with the mantra "gaccha gaccha suraśreṣṭha" (Go, go, O best of gods). Then, having fed the Brahmins the prescribed number of times, one should dedicate the ritual action to the Lord of Karma (Karmeśvara).

Thus ends the procedure for the ten-thousand-fold oblation (ayuta-homa) composed by Kamalākara; now follows the procedure for the hundred-thousand-fold oblation (lakṣa-homa) according to the Mātsya Purāṇa.

This sacrifice has been described; now hear about the *lakṣahoma*, which is considered a *lakṣa-homa* because the wise know it to be for the attainment of all desires. This *lakṣa-homa* was declared by the Self-born One (*Svayambhū*) to be ten times greater than this [previous] one, performed with great effort through oblations and likewise with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). Now, regarding the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), they were spoken of by Bṛhat-Parāśara: "The officiating priests should be an even number, Brahmins who are learned and constantly devoted to silent recitation (*japa*); those twice-born ones should be appointed by him."

[The image] should be made of bulbous roots, roots, fruits, or even more than an *ādhaka* of milk; or it may be made of fish-scale [stone]. It should be two cubits wide, and likewise four cubits long.

In a *lakṣahoma* sacrifice, the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be shaped like a vulva (*yonivaktra*) and provided with three tiers (*mekhalā*). The first tier should be made by the wise to be two finger-breadths (*dviraṅgula*) in height; the second is prescribed there as being depressed by two finger-breadths; and the third should be four finger-breadths in both height and width. A width of four finger-breadths is also recommended for the first two tiers. To the northeast of that [pit], one should prepare a square area measuring three spans (*vitasti*) on each side, sloping toward the northeast, and level throughout.

Viśvakarman has declared that the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) should be raised to half the height of the supporting pillar (viṣkaṃbha) for the installation of the deities, consisting of two tiers (vapra). The first tier is said to be two finger-breadths (aṅgula) in height; above that, the second tier is declared to be three finger-breadths in height. The width of all these [tiers] is stated by the wise to be two finger-breadths. Above that, the wall (bhitti) of the pillar-base (sthaṇḍila) should be ten finger-breadths in height.

In that [rite], one should invoke the deities as before using white rice grains. One who desires prosperity should install Garuḍa there as the preeminent [deity]. He is not to be placed at the end of all the Vedas, but rather in the eastern part, according to the principle of "Bādarāyaṇa being at the end. Then, the mantras for the invocation are: "O you whose body is the sound of the Sāman, the invocation of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin); O remover of poison and sin, grant me constant intoxication and peace. Alternatively, the reading is: *viṣāpaharama ita*.

Having consecrated the water-pot (kumbha) as before, one should likewise perform the fire-oblation (homa). Having offered a hundred thousand oblations, and again [offering] according to the number of fuel-sticks (samidh) and so forth; having offered fuel-sticks, clarified butter (ājya), and sacrificial porridge (caru) as before, and having performed the homa for Garuḍa—the lord of birds—with the mantra "suvarṇo'si garutmān," one should then perform the lakṣa-homa with the Vyāhṛtis—this is the meaning.

Me! Oṃ! You are the fair-winged Garuḍa; the Trivṛt-stoma is your head, the Gāyatra-chandas your eye, the Stoma your soul, the Sāman your body, the Bṛhat and Rathantara-sāmans your two wings, the Yajñāyajñīya your tail, and the metres your limbs. The Dhiṣṇiya hearths are your feet, and speed is your name. You are the fair-winged Garuḍa; go to heaven, fly to the light of the sun!

One should cause a continuous stream of clarified butter to fall upon the fire from a vessel made of udumbara wood—fresh, straight, free of hollows, and one cubit in length—using it as a *sruva* ladle for both [the oblations]. Then, one should properly pour the stream of ghee over the fire while reciting the *Śrāmaṇya-sūkta*, the *Āgneya*, *Vaiṣṇava*, *Raudra*, *Māndava*, *Mahāvaiśvānara*, and the *Sāman*. Regarding "I praise Agni" (*agnim īḷe*), there are nine verses; Madhucchandas is the seer, Agni is the deity, and the *Gāyatrī* is the meter.
For the six verses beginning with "viṣṇornukam," Dīrghatamas is the seer, Viṣṇu is the deity, and the Triṣṭubh is the meter.
For the Svādhiṣṭhāna, the meters are Madhu, Canda, Soma, and Gāyatrī. For the Mahāvaiśvānara Sāman, Vaiśvānara is the seer and the deity; the meters are Jagatī and Bṛhatī.
The *mūrdhan* [verse] is "naṃdi-paḥ"; the *jyeṣṭhā* [verse] belongs to the Sāman; the two Bharadvājas [are the seers]; Vaiśvānara [is the deity]; the *triṣṭubh* [is the meter].

The bathing of the patron and the recitation of the *svasti-vācana* are to be performed as before. The patron should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) in due order, as previously described. Likewise, for a *lakṣahoma*, there should be ten or eight officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), or according to one's capacity, four who are free from envy. Everything regarding the sacrifice to the nine planets applies to the *lakṣahoma* with its tenfold increase. O best of men, having given [the usual gifts], one should also give ornaments according to one's ability. Here, a gift should be given according to one's means by one who desires prosperity. The meaning is that for every hundred oblations, one Brahmin is to be honored, and for every thousand, one [additional] Brahmin.
May they bear fruit.

He is honored in the world of Śiva by the Vasus, Ādityas, and the hosts of Maruts; there he dwells for eight hundred kalpas, and thereafter he attains liberation. He who performs this Lakṣahoma according to the rules with a specific desire obtains all his desires and attains the eternal state. One desiring sons obtains sons; one desiring wealth obtains wealth; one desiring a wife obtains a wife; and a maiden obtains a virtuous husband. One who has lost his kingdom regains his kingdom, and one desiring prosperity attains prosperity.
Whatever desire one may long for, that one obtains in abundance; however, he who performs it without desire goes to the Supreme Brahman and the like. Thus concludes the Lakṣahoma.
Now, the Koṭihoma according to the Mātsya [Purāṇa]:

The *Koṭihoma* has been declared by Svayaṃbhū to be a hundred times more efficacious than this [the *Śatahoma*] in terms of the oblations offered with diligence, the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and the resulting fruit. As before, the invocation and dismissal of the gods of the household should be performed; the *mantras* for the *homa*, as well as those for the bath and the gift, are the same as previously stated. Now, learn the complete details regarding the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*), and the altar (*vedī*). For the *Koṭihoma*, they say it should be four cubits square, constructed with care, provided with two openings shaped like a vulva (*yoni*), and possessed of three enclosures (*mekhalā*).

"One [altar] is in the west and another in the south. This is stated in the *Hemādri* and the *Madanaratna*: "In a *koṭi-homa*, there should be an altar (*vedi*) with four layers of bricks, square on all sides and covered with three cloths. The measurement of the embankment (*vapra*) is as previously mentioned, and the height of the altar should be likewise. Furthermore, there should be a sixteen-cubit platform (*mañca*) with four openings. Having stationed there at the eastern gate one who has mastered the *Bahvṛca-veda* (the Ṛgveda)," and so forth.

A follower of the Yajurveda should be stationed in the south, and a follower of the Sāmaveda in the fifth [direction]. Likewise, a wise man should station a follower of the Atharvaveda in the north. For the purpose of the fire-oblation (homa), he should invite eight Brahmins who are knowers of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. Having brought together these twelve Brahmins, he should worship them with devotion as before, using garments, garlands, ointments, and all types of ornaments. At the eastern gate, facing north, he should remain reciting the Rātrisūkta, the Raudrasūkta, the Pāvamānasūkta, the Sumaṅgalasūkta, and the Ṛcāṃ Śānti.

O King, one should cause a learned reciter of the Yajurveda to chant the Śākra, Saumya, Raudra, Kūṣmāṇḍa, and Śānti mantras at the southern gate. O King, at the western gate, a Brāhmaṇa should recite the Āgneya, the Rudrasaṃhitā, the Jyeṣṭhasāman, and the Śānti hymn. O King, at the northern gate, a learned scholar should recite the Śāntisūkta, the Saura, the auspicious Śākunika, and the Pauṣṭika hymns. There, a Homa sacrifice should be performed by eight Brāhmaṇas as previously described.

O best of sages, the mantras for the bathing and the giving of gifts shall be the same as those previously mentioned. The procedure for the Vasordhārā and the Lakṣahoma will now be described. He who performs the Koṭihoma according to this rule attains all desires and thereafter goes to the abode of Viṣṇu. O knower of Dharma, one obtains from the Koṭihoma that same fruit which one acquires by performing eighteen thousand horse-sacrifices. [It also destroys] thousands of killings of Brahmins and hundreds of millions of killings of foetuses.
They perish through ten million fire-oblations, exactly as it has been spoken by Śiva.

Thus ends the procedure for the *koṭihoma* according to the *Mātsya-purāṇa*. Now follows the procedure for the *nṛsiṃhahoma*, the fire-offering to Nṛsiṃha; specifically, the particular rite of the *nṛsiṃhahoma* for the fulfillment of the Nṛsiṃha vow.
When there is a terrible dream-vision arising from the affliction of malevolent planets, and especially when an image appears to be struck or is ablaze;

O Prince, seeing [the deity] covered in perspiration, one should—whether personally or through wise agents—continuously perform or cause to be performed the *dhārā* (stream) rite upon the head of Lord Narasiṃha during the solstices (*āyana*), the equinoxes (*viṣuva*), and likewise during lunar and solar eclipses. Having propitiated Narasiṃha, one should also cause a *lakṣahoma* (hundred-thousand oblations) to be performed. Likewise, in times of drought, great pestilence, fever, or fear of disease, one should propitiate Narasiṃha through Brāhmaṇas who are masters of the Vedas.

Upon seeing a calamity or the impending death of his subjects or himself, the lord of men should have a *lakṣahoma* performed behind the village. Having properly propitiated with effort in the temple of Narasiṃha—or likewise in the temple of Śaṅkara—he should perform a *koṭihoma*. The characteristic of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is that it should be one cubit in measurement on all sides. A celibate student (*brahmacārī*), endowed with vows, especially for three nights, or having fasted for a day and night, should recite the Gāyatrī mantra ten thousand times.

Free from food, pure, and with all their senses restrained, they should then begin the sacrifice; thereafter, free from sloth, the wise ones should perform the oblation (homa). First, one who is wise should offer oblations with a single-minded focus, mixed with barley, grain, and sesame seeds, accompanied by the Gāyatrī mantra and the utterance of "svāhā. Thereafter, one should offer the sesame seeds and other materials with the Vyāhṛtis. One should continue this for as many days as it takes to complete the prescribed number—whether a hundred thousand (lakṣa) or ten million (koṭi)—preceded by the worship of Acyuta.

One should give food until the homa is completed; when it is finished, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and then sprinkle with water. When this has been done, [it brings benefit] to the village, the king, and the realm.
It always becomes a peace that pacifies all afflictions.
Thus ends the procedure for the Nṛsiṃha-homa;
the procedure for the Lakṣa-koṭi-homa:
one should have a hexagonal Śiva-liṅga made of lapis lazuli, endowed with the proper characteristics.
There was a golden pedestal, richly adorned with beauty, upon which were the Moon, the Sun, and the Mothers.
Carcikā and the others should be fashioned, arranged starting from the east;
there, the worship of the planets should be performed as before.
A Lakṣahoma should be performed to ward off all afflictions,
using the Gāyatrī, the planetary mantras, the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras, and the Jātavedas mantras.
A hundred thousand oblations are prescribed here to be offered with mantras dedicated to Indra, Varuṇa, Agni, Vāyu, Yama, and Soma, along with their respective modifications.
In this regard, the division of the mantras is indeed prescribed as having been proclaimed by the ancients.
The *koṭihoma* sacrifice brings auspiciousness for the destruction of all afflictions;
it consists of barley, rice, ghee, milk, sesame seeds, *kaṅgu*, and *prasārikā*.
Saffron, uśīra, bilva, and mango leaves are prescribed for the oblation.
On that very occasion, Brahmā said:
"I shall describe the hundred-thousand-fold oblation (lakṣahoma) exactly as it was taught there by Śambhu."
When there is an earthquake, when the quarters of the sky are aflame, or even when a planetary conflict has arisen.
Upon the appearance of a comet, during an earthquake of the sun,
when the sun is black in color, or likewise when it is possessed of holes;
Likewise, showers of blood and rivers flow in reverse;
smoke issues forth from the sky, and fire stands amidst the waters.
Likewise,
O Lord of the Gods, when five, six, or seven planets are situated in the same zodiacal sign of a person, various calamities arise in the world.
During an eclipse of the moon or the sun by planets situated in the eighth house, the sun should be worshipped and Śiva should be propitiated; this destroys inauspiciousness.
The Lakṣahoma, Mahāhoma, and Koṭihoma have been previously described;
the gift of cows, land, gold, clothing, horses, and sesame seeds brings auspiciousness.
Milk-rice, curd, milk, and ghee should be offered as the most excellent food offering;
this should be performed at a single linga as well as in the houses of Brahmins.
A single linga devoid of the bull and other [emblems].
O King of the gods, the oblation should be offered into a pit that is either arm-deep or, alternatively, thigh-deep; such is the rule, and not otherwise.
O best of gods, I shall now describe the procedure for the Lakṣahoma sacrifice;
the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should likewise be four cubits in width.
A four-cubit [pedestal] is proclaimed to have a width and height of sixteen finger-breadths each,
and a height of four finger-breadths.
The width of the yoni should be twelve finger-breadths, and its length is said to be double that;
it should be fashioned as part of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), and anything larger is not commended in any case.
Barley, rice, ghee, milk, sesame, and *kaṅgu* seeds, as well as mango wood and *pālāśa* fuel-sticks, O Indra among kings; thus [should they be offered].
The sprouts of dūrvā grass, the excellent śamī tree, the udumbara tree, and the śubhuvaha; likewise, the gāyatrī and the tryambaka—these are proclaimed as being for the sake of Śambhu.
With the *jātavedas* mantra, with the *indra* mantra, or indeed with the *sahasraśīrṣa* [Puruṣa Sūkta], or likewise with the mantra beginning "namo hiraṇyāya."
Likewise, oblations should be offered with Rudra-mantras, Saura-mantras, and those proclaimed in the Pañcarātra Āgamas,
numbering one hundred and eight or a thousand.
Lotus, blue water-lily, wood-apple, and other such substances for the fire-oblation bring auspiciousness;
trembling, perspiration on the body, shedding of tears, and incoherent speech [are signs].
When portents appear that cause the destruction of the deities and the lords of the gods,
one should perform a Lakṣahoma or even a Koṭihoma.
In the abode of Rudra, at Godoha, the great bath brings auspiciousness; otherwise, a terrible outbreak of pestilence arises and there is confusion among the king's subjects.
All those who are gods are grahas, and all those who are grahas are mobile beings;
by their constant worship, a person shall attain long life.
"In this regard, regarding the *lakṣahoma* and the *koṭihoma*, there is a specific rule stated by Bṛhaspati:
'The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should be even in number, Brahmins who are learned,
endowed with self-restraint and vows, and indeed accompanied by kings.'"
The twice-born should always be engaged in constant recitation and the highest [meditations],
subsisting on bulbs, roots, and fruits, or consuming curd and milk, or even drinking [water].
Agni, Soma, and Sūrya, as well as Viṣṇu and Prajāpati;
the Viśvedevas, Mahendra, Mitra, and likewise Tvaṣṭṛ.
And one should offer a hundred thousand sacrificial fuel sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, while reciting the mantras in their proper sequence.
Twenty-four [oblations] with the Gāyatrī, six with the "mānastoke" mantra, eighteen with the mantras beginning with "grahāḥ," and four with those having Viṣṇu as their deity.
One should offer five oblations with *kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras and sixteen with the *kirikeya* mantras; one should perform ten thousand oblations with the verse beginning "jātavedase."
One should offer oblations five thousand times with the deities of the fire;
then again, [one should prepare] a square and rectangular altar measuring one crore [units] and four cubits.
They say that it should also be provided with both a vulva and a mouth, and possess three girdles;
furthermore, for a *koṭihoma*, the altar (*vedī*) should be four cubits in size.
Having leveled the ground into a square, it should be surrounded by three Brahmins;
furthermore, eight officiating priests who are knowers of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas should be appointed.
Thus, these twelve should be worshipped with garments, garlands, and ointments,
O Blessed One, when great portents arise and the earth trembles.
In the event of a thunderclap or a rain of dust, as well as during the affliction of planets and lunar mansions,
when there is suffering from one's birth star, or during fears of drought;
During cruel afflictions by the planets, in times of famine, during regional upheavals,
when diseases and such have arisen, or when the body is excessively tormented;
"Speak, O best of the twice-born, regarding that which bestows health upon men.
Nandikeśvara said: "Listen, O King, I shall describe the most excellent rite of pacification (śāntikarma)."
The incomparable rite known as the Koṭihoma bestows the fruits of all desires;
sins such as the killing of a Brahmin perish at that very moment through it.
Portents subside and great happiness is attained;
I shall describe the ritual for that—listen with one-pointed attention.
One who desires his own welfare should perform [the rite] in a temple, a palace, at a sacred ford, in the presence of Śiva, or on a mountain.
When there is an auspicious lunar mansion (nakṣatra) and a conjunction (yoga), on a day-endowed with all excellent qualities and favorable to the patron (yajamāna),
one should commence the Koṭihoma after having diligently honored a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas.
And with garments, ornaments, perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
Having prostrated according to the prescribed rite, he should offer himself to him, saying:
"You are our refuge, our father, and our mother; you are our goal and our supreme resort."
O brahmin-sage, by your grace, everything that is in her mind shall come to pass; therefore, for my sake, perform this unsurpassed sacrifice.
May you look upon my misfortune. Perform the sacrifice, O best of men.
The priest, wise, pure, and clad in white garments, performed the incomparable rite called Koṭihoma, which bestows peace and grants all desires.
Accompanied by meritorious and composed Brahmins,
he [should perform it] on a level, pure plot of ground that slopes toward the northeast.
One should cause the Brahmins who have performed meritorious deeds to recite the *puṇyāha* formula and worship them well;
thereafter, together with the Brahmins, one should construct an auspicious pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).
In the center of the pavilion, the wise one should also construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
measuring four cubits in length and likewise in width.
Its three girdles should be twelve finger-breadths wide; with a concentrated mind, one should fashion the womb (yoni) to be of that same measurement.
The wise one should construct an altar on the eastern side of the sacrificial pit.

O King, the wise man should diligently construct a square platform measuring four cubits on each side and one cubit in height; there, he should carefully perform the installation of the deities after having smeared the ground all around the pavilion.
One should place water-filled jars there in the four directions,
adorned with sprouts from trees such as the Aśvattha, Plakṣa, and Cūta.
The wise one should arrange a canopy above the pavilion and place archways in all four directions.
Having thus gathered the necessary materials and being well-composed in his mind,
the priest should commence the rite of oblation accompanied by the proclamation of "Auspicious Day" and "Victory."
O subduer of enemies, having established the gods upon the altar as will be described—
placing Brahmā in the eastern portion and the god Janārdana in the center—
Likewise, one should place Rudra in the west, Vasu in the north,
Saumya in the northwest, and the world-protectors (lokapālas) in due order in the northeast.
O best of kings, having thus established the deities in their respective places,
one should worship them daily with garments, perfumes, garlands, and unguents.
With mantras declared in the Vedas, with their respective characteristic marks, and with those spoken in the Purāṇas individually,
[one worships] Āditya, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Maruts, and likewise the Lokapālas.
Having diligently worshipped these deities present there— Brahmā, Janārdana, Śūlapāṇi, Bhaga, and Yama— the wise man [should proceed].
Then, together with the twice-born who had offered praise, he performed the ritual for Mars according to the prescribed rules, using various kinds of food offerings, snacks, fruits, and lamps.
One should perform the purificatory rites (saṃskāras) as prescribed by those who contemplate the Vedas;
thereafter, one should kindle the fire known by the name Ghanārcis.
O best of men, one should employ a hundred brahmins there;
however, if that many cannot be obtained, one should employ as many as can be found.
Householders who have grown old in knowledge and grown old in age, whose senses are restrained;
O Lord of the Gate, there are four faces and seven tongues;
thus, when multiplied by one, that is remembered as the "Sārvakāmuka" (fulfiller of all desires).

The oblation with the Ṛg verses is to be performed facing the east; with the Yajus verses, facing the north; with the Sāman verses, it is to be done facing the west; and with the Atharva verses, facing the south.
There, every oblation is prescribed by the followers of the Ṛgveda with Ṛg-verses and with the Vyāhṛtis;
these are preceded by the Praṇava, characterized by those [specific] marks, and joined with the utterance of Svāhā at the end.
One should offer oblations to all the deities who have been prepared upon the altar;
thus, having performed the sacrifice known as the excellent Koṭihoma.
Black sesame seeds, anointed with ghee and mixed with a small amount of rice, should be offered;
for a *koṭi-homa*, however, fuel sticks made of *palāśa* wood are to be used.
O Lord of the Sages, when the *pūrṇahoma* has been completed, one should offer the auspicious *pūrṇāhuti*;
this is declared to be the *pūrṇāhuti* in the case of a *koṭihoma*.

O best of kings, there are ten thousand [brāhmaṇas] learned in the scriptures; the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is one thousand [gold pieces], and there are a thousand cows, a conch, and so forth. According to the view that "cows belong to all," there are nine hundred cows and one hundred gold pieces. Now, the varieties of the *koṭihoma*—namely, the hundred-faced, ten-faced, two-faced, and single-faced—are described. Saṃvaraṇa said: "O Brāhmaṇa, because of the vastness of the ritual, the *koṭihoma* is extremely difficult to perform."
It is my opinion that the observances, such as celibacy and the rest, are difficult to perform.
The cessation of activities for Brahmins, as well as sleeping on the ground and other such practices, is difficult to perform;
the relative weight of these duties depends on the specific occasion, such as the time of a festival.
Sanatkumāra, the son of Brahmā, spoke this summary of the Keṭihoma sacrifice:
"There are those with a hundred faces, ten faces, two faces, and likewise one face."
The fourfold Great King is prescribed for the *koṭihoma*; having understood the gravity of the task, [one should perform it] with food offerings at the end of the festival.
Listen now to how the *koṭihoma* should be performed in brief:
having prepared one hundred divine sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) as described and as intended by the mind.
In each individual pit, one should employ ten Brahmins;
however, for the Sadyahpakṣa rite, a thousand Brahmins are prescribed.
Just as there may be a multiplicity of sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) in the Rājasūya sacrifice,
or a multiplicity of fires (*agni*) in the Sāṃcayana sacrifice, so too [is it] divided.
Likewise, even if hundreds of groves are employed here with ghee-fed flames,
it becomes a single sacrifice— a *koṭihoma*— without a doubt.
Thus, he who quickly performs [the rite] with Vyānaka mantras due to the gravity of the task should be known as Śatānana; this is undoubtedly the Keṭihoma.

In this context, the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) are one cubit in measure for substances such as ghee that burn quickly; however, for sesame seeds, barley, and the like, the pit should be three cubits for a hundred-thousandth part of a lakh of oblations, four cubits for half a lakh,
and one cubit when ten thousand oblations are to be offered.
"In a *lakṣa-homa* it is double, and in a *koṭi-homa* it is fourfold"—
this should be understood as stated in another mantra.
Thus says Śatamukha:
"When water is scarce during the rainy season, the Koṭihoma should be performed with only a few days;
in that case, O Great One, the Daśamukha [version] should be performed."
There, having divided two hundred Brahmins, one should employ them;
the pavilion, moreover, should be fifty cubits or twenty-five cubits in size.
Thus said the Ten-faced One:
"Having prepared two sacrificial pits there and divided [the fire],
the twice-born should again perform the oblation to Vibāvasu (Fire), having consecrated it according to the prescribed rite."
A hundred Brahmins should indeed be employed there, having been properly distributed;
this should be done every month or half-month when the proper time has arrived.
Then, when the sacrificer wishes to complete the sacrifice at his own will, the wise should perform the Koṭihoma with two openings.
O King, after a long time, it then becomes a single mouth;
the fire situated in a single pit [is served] by those who are concentrated with one-pointed minds.
O best of men, there is no fixed number of Brahmins here, nor is there a fixed time; such a sacrifice is said to be performed according to one's own will.
For one who is obstructed yet desires to perform rites such as the Cāturmāsya,
this sacrifice— which is applicable at all times— should be performed constantly and without interruption.
Whoever among these kings shall live for a long time, since both lifespan and wealth are always established as unstable.
Therefore, the duty that is praised in the performance of dharma should be performed in brief;
then, once the sacrifice is completed, one who is well-composed should cause it to be done.
Then, with the sounding of conchs and trumpets and the roar of Vedic chants,
the servants, warriors, Brahmins, priests, and likewise hundreds of Śūdras [prepared].
O King, one should give a hundred gold coins, various golden earrings, a hundred cows, and likewise a hundred horses.
He should cause a thousand pieces of gold to be given to all of them;
he should honor the family priest with villages, elephants, chariots, and horses.
Then, for the sake of eternal victory, one should bathe with those previously prepared jars while reciting the mantra prescribed for the hundred-thousand-fold oblation (lakṣahoma).
Whoever thus concludes this auspicious Koṭihoma sacrifice shall possess health, beloved sons, and likewise an increase in lifespan.
Fear of drought, fear of portents,
famine, and affliction by the planets— all these are pacified upon the earth.
This merit, which removes sin and bestows the fruit of all actions,
was narrated by the sage named Sanaka to the king.

O King, those men who perform a *koṭihoma* sacrifice for the sake of worldly prosperity within their home find all calamities pacified; they shall attain the abundant enjoyments desired by their minds.
Those pure beings go to the abode of Śakra by means of their radiance.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the *koṭihoma* in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*.
Since it is stated therein that pacification (*śānti*) must be performed for many births, the "birth through the mouth of a cow" (*gomukhaprasava*) is now described.
Garga says:
Having prostrated before the Sun, I shall declare the expiation (prāyaścitta) as remembered from the Jyotir-arṇava, which was taught for the destruction of all undesirable [results].
Whatever misfortune (*ariṣṭa*) arises from the father, from the son, from the mother, or likewise from the birth-star (*nakṣatra*), one should perform this [rite] in that case; such is the meaning.
One should perform the appropriate expiation for the pacification of each respective fault.
In the asterisms of Pūṣan (Puṣya), Aśvinī, Guru (Pūrvaphalgunī), Sārpa (Āśleṣā), Mukha (Mṛgaśirā), Citrā, Indrā (Jyeṣṭhā), and Mūla—
when one is born under these unpure asterisms, one should perform the rite of "birth as a cow" (go-janana).

Likewise, the word "tathā" (likewise) has the sense of inclusion (*samuccaya*). By that, it means: having performed the pacification (*śānti*) for the misfortune of the father, the [birth] asterism, and so forth; this is what one should do. By the phrase "in the misfortune of the father," the [misfortunes] of Mūla and the others are already included. The mention of Mūla and the others again is for the purpose of including those cases where there is an absence [of misfortune] in the fourth quarter (*pāda*) of Mūla and the rest.
On one's birth asterism, or on the three birth asterisms, during an auspicious weekday and an auspicious day,
having performed all the preliminary rites such as anointing the body, preceded by the decoration of the cave-temple;
Then, having smeared the northeastern part of the cave with cow-dung,
one should draw a lotus with eight petals using white colored powders.
Having poured rice grains there according to their respective essential qualities, one should spread a new winnowing basket and a red cloth over the middle of it.
Having placed the child there, one should again encircle him with a thread;
the child, facing east with his feet turned westward, should be positioned upon sesame seeds and *darbha* grass.
Having shown the cow's face, and having [the child] born again from the cow's mouth,
Viṣṇu, being wise in policy, should bathe the infant with that which is derived from the cow.
