One should touch the limbs of the cow with the mantra "gavām aṅgeṣu," and the calf born from the cow with the mantra "viṣṇo śreṣṭha."
The teacher, having taken hold of him, should cause him to gaze at the sun;
then, removing the cloth from his son's face, the father should look upon his face.
In that manner, it should first be given to the father, and then one should cause it to be given to the mother;
the father, having removed the cloth, should then look upon the face of the son.
Then, one should sprinkle the child with cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and clarified butter combined together,
while reciting the mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
Then the father, having smelled the son on the crown of his head with that mantra, [said]:
"From limb by limb you are born; from the heart you arise."
"You are indeed the self named 'son'; live for a hundred autumns.
Having smelled the head of that infant three times, he should then place him down.
Afterwards, having honored them, one should cause the Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas to utter the words "an auspicious day" (puṇyāha) and give those limbs to a poor Brahmin.
One should give cows, garments, gold, and grain in sequence starting from the first day;
likewise, the father should give wealth to the Brahmins according to his capacity.
Then one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the method prescribed in one's own tradition;
having performed the rites beginning with the marking of the ground (ullekhana), one should carry it out up to the first portion (ādyabhāga).
In the northeastern quarter of the sacrificial ground, one should place an auspicious jar upon a heap of grain;
having placed the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in the jar, one should then pour sesame seeds into it.
Having covered the two images with a pair of garments and then worshipped them with perfumes and other offerings according to the prescribed rule,
one should worship Viṣṇu and Varuṇa within the image.
One should touch the pitcher and consecrate it with the mantras beginning with "yata indra".
These are the six verses that constitute the remainder of the hymn [beginning with] "yata indra".
One should diligently perform the oblation (homa) with curds, honey, and clarified butter.
"With 'yuktena' [the state] is expressed; 'vegena' is the meaning.
Then, with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," and with "apsu me soma," and then from the hymn beginning with "tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam" and "akṣibhyām."
With these Rigvedic verses, one should offer oblations verse by verse twenty-eight times;
or, if unable, eight times, consisting of curd, honey, and clarified butter mixed together.

One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) for the planets, beginning with Āditya, accompanied by their respective mantras. Some authorities maintain that one should perform ten thousand oblations of curd for the planets; otherwise, the mention of curd and other substances would be rendered purposeless.
Thus ends the rite for the pacification of childbirth.

"Oṃ adha go pra sa va pra yo gaḥ | I shall perform the *gomukha-prasava* (the birth of the cow-faced rite) for the pacification of the calamities (*ariṣṭa*) indicated by the birth under the constellation [named] so-and-so of this child. Having thus made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*).

Having first worshipped Gaṇeśa, one should choose the preceptor (ācārya). The preceptor, having fashioned a white lotus out of powder upon rice grains in a winnowing basket (śūrpa), and having scattered sesame seeds upon a red cloth therein, places the child in the basket facing east. Having brought a cow’s head near the child with the mantra "veṣaṭmi," and having visualized the birth, he bathes the child with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) using the hymn "viṣṇuryoniṃ kalpayatu. Then, he should touch the cow with the mantra "gavāmaṅgeṣu. The mantra is as follows: *gavāmaṅgeṣu tiṣṭhanti bhuvanāni caturdaśa | yasmāttasmācchivaṃ me syādihaloke paratra ca ||* "Since the fourteen worlds abide within the limbs of the cow, may there be auspiciousness for me in this world and the next."

"Since the fourteen worlds abide within the limbs of cows, therefore may there be auspiciousness for this child; grant him peace. Then the father, having given [the garment] back to the mother and removed the cloth, gazes upon the face [of the child]. Thereafter, the preceptor should sprinkle the child with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) while reciting the three verses beginning with "apohiṣṭhā. Then the father, having smelled the child on the head three times while reciting "aṅgādaṅgāt," [should perform the rite].

"May you, sirs, declare this to be an auspicious day for the birth of this Gomukha. Having thus requested the increase of prosperity and well-being from the Brahmins three times, he should give a cow with her calf to the Preceptor (Ācārya). For the propitiation of the planets, he should give cows, garments, gold, and grain according to his capacity, and even more if possible. Then the Preceptor, having established the fire and the nine planets, and having recited the ritual formulas up to "the two eyes [are offered] with clarified butter" as part of the supplementary offerings (*anvādāna*), performs the principal oblation (*pradhāna*) there four times with water.

Having offered oblations once with curd, honey, and clarified butter to Viṣṇu using the hymn *yakṣmāṇam akṣībhyām* verse by verse—or twenty-eight times in total—and having offered to the planets one by one, he should offer the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation with the remainder at the conclusion of the *ājyabhāga* offerings. Then, having placed a water-pot in the northeast, having poured into it the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), sesame seeds, milk, and decoctions of medicinal herbs, and having wrapped it in a pair of cloths, he should invoke Viṣṇu into a full vessel with the mantra *tad viṣṇoḥ* and Varuṇa with *tat tvā yāmi*.

Having worshipped and touched the water-pot (*kuṃbha*), one should recite the six verses beginning with *yata indra*, whose seer is Kaṇvaputra Pragātha, whose deity is Indra, and whose metre is the Bārhata Pragātha. Having recited these, when the sacrificer has performed the formal renunciation (*tyāga*), one should offer oblations twenty-eight or eight times for each verse with curds, honey, and clarified butter. [Then one recites] *āpo hi ṣṭhā*. [Then] *tad viṣṇoḥ*, whose seer is Medhātithi, whose deity is Viṣṇu, and whose metre is Gāyatrī. [Finally, one recites] *akṣībhyām iti*—the six verses of which Vivṛhan Yakṣmahā is the seer and Anuṣṭubh is the metre.

Having offered twenty-eight or eight oblations with these individual mantras, and having offered one oblation each with the planetary mantras using curd, honey, and clarified butter, and having completed the remainder of the rite beginning with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, one should feed the Brahmins.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the birth of Gomukha.

Now, the pacification rites (*śānti*) for those born during the junctions (*gaṇḍānta*) of asterisms, ascendants, *yogas*, and *karaṇas* are described in order. Among these, the pacification for one born at the junction of an asterism is commenced first. It is of three kinds, arising from the conjunction of lunar days (*tithi*), asterisms (*nakṣatra*), and ascendants (*lagna*). A "junction" (*gaṇḍānta*) refers to the two *ghaṭikās* (forty-eight minutes) of the transition. This is stated in the *Jyotirnibandha*: "The junction between the lunar days named Pūrṇā and Ānandā consists of two *nāḍīs*; that junction (*gaṇḍānta*) brings death in birth, journeys, marriages, and vows, as does [the junction] between Cancer and Leo."

The interval between the constellations Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras and Ārdrā, and Pūrvā-phalgunī and Uttarā-phalgunī is known as Gaṇḍānta; it lasts for half a ghaṭikā and bestows death. In the constellations of Aśleṣā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Maghā, the last sixteen degrees are the source of inauspiciousness. Likewise, in the constellations following them, one quarter (of the first degree) is designated as Gaṇḍānta. Furthermore, in the *Ratnamālā*, another view regarding the constellations is stated: the interval between Maghā and Aśvinī, Āśleṣā and Maghā, and Jyeṣṭhā and Mūla [is also considered such].

That junction (gaṇḍānta) consists of four nāḍīs; it is inauspicious for journeys, births, and at the time of marriage. Herein, the relative gravity of the defects should be understood from the *Ratnasaṃgraha*: "For all those born during a gaṇḍānta, abandonment [of the child] is prescribed; one should keep him out of sight for a year, or likewise for six months. In the case of a junction involving a lunar day (tithi) or a constellation (nakṣatra), there is destruction of the father or mother; if it occurs at a junction in the ascendant (lagna), there is destruction of the son. Such a person lives while destroying all his kinsmen; though living, he becomes a destroyer of his relatives, yet he may possess many elephants and horses.

In the *prayoga* [of birth], Garga and Brahmā state that for Aśvinī, Puṣya, Mūla, and so forth, there are three *ṣaṇḍa*-vacana *nāḍikās*; for Revatī, Āśleṣā, and Jyeṣṭhā, there are two *māna-ṛtu* junctions. Likewise, for Aśvinī, Puṣya, and Mūla, there are two *nāḍikās*; and for Revatī, Āśleṣā, and Jyeṣṭhā, there are indeed two *nāḍikās*. In the first half of Aśvinī, Puṣya, and Mūla, the child afflicts the ancestors; in the first half of Pūrvā-phalgunī, Pūrvā-bhādrapadā, and Jyeṣṭhā, the mother is afflicted, and in the latter half, the infant is afflicted. One born by day is a slayer of the father, while one born at night is a slayer of the mother.

The meaning is that one born at the junction (gaṇḍānta) of a lunar day is "self-destroying" (ātmaghna). One born at the two twilights (saṃdhyā) is "without Gaṇḍa" (nirgaṇḍa) and free from disease. For all those born at a Gaṇḍānta, abandonment [of the child] is prescribed. Avoiding seeing or hearing [such a child], that [defect] lasts for six months. I shall describe its pacification with devotion using the Soma-mantra. One should prepare a bell-metal vessel weighing sixteen palas, or nine, four, or two, or likewise a beautiful one.

In the center of that, one should worship the stainless silver moon within a conch filled with fresh butter and milk-rice (*pāyasa*), using white flowers. Clad in white silk garments and draped in white garlands and robes, and meditating "I am Soma," one should perform the worship without delay. With faith and a concentrated mind, one should recite the mantra a thousand times and also give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the pacification of the defect of the cheek. One should likewise offer a white image of Vāgīśvarī accompanied by a copper vessel.

For the pacification of the defects of Gaṇḍa, a pure person should give [gifts] to one who knows the Vedas. It is further stated that for Jyotiḥ, Vibhaṇḍaka, and Ekadanta, [the rites should be performed]; that which is born by day is joined with the mother, while that born at night is joined with the father; one should bathe [the child] at both twilights for the sake of the ancestors and the mother. To pacify the defects of Gaṇḍa, one should give ghee in a bronze vessel, along with milk, a pearl, a conch, and an auspicious pair of white garments, to one who knows the Yajurveda for the removal of the Gaṇḍa defects.

One should give gifts of grain, gold, and also worship the planets with lamps. Having recited the mantra that increases longevity, one should perform the libation for the Brahmins. In this case, at the birth from the mouth of a cow, the pacification of the nine planets (Navagraha-śānti) must also be performed. Other details are clear and are stated in the ritual manual (prayoga). Thus ends the pacification for those born during the junctions of constellations and so forth, as spoken by Garga.

Now, the pacification (śānti) for one born during a *gaṇḍānta* of a lunar day (*tithi*) or an ascendant (*lagna*). Gārgya says: "For a son born at a *tithi-gaṇḍānta*, a pacification should be performed on that very lunar day or on an auspicious day; until then, one should not look upon the son. In the case of a *tithi-gaṇḍa*, [one should give] a bull; in the case of a [nakṣatra-]gaṇḍa, a cow; and in the case of an ascendant-gaṇḍa, gold. Thus the defect of the *gaṇḍa* is destroyed. The first part concerns the father’s *gaṇḍa*; "the consecration of the three" means the mother, the father, and the infant.

One should perform the worship of Varuṇa, accompanied by two garments, preceded by the recitation of auspicious verses (*svastivācana*), during the asterisms of Uttarāṣāḍhā, Tiṣya (Puṣya), Citrā, or Pūrvāṣāḍhā. The meaning is that one should worship Varuṇa, the lord of the asterism, within a water-pot (*kuṃbha*). At the conclusion of the worship, one should offer oblations (*homa*) with clarified butter, sesame seeds, and barley, along with a hundred medicinal herbs, gems, earth, bark, and sprouts. Then, having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should give a gift of sesame seeds to a family man who is a student of the Vedas; likewise, during the first quarter of Uttarāṣāḍhā, and during Tiṣya, a cow.

One should give away a well-behaved, milch goat with its kid under the Citrā constellation; under Pūrvāṣāḍhā, one should give gold. One should cause barley, rice, mung beans, sesame, and green gram to be offered. Likewise, one should arrange a feeding of Brahmins according to one's means. This rite of pacification (śānti) is prescribed here for the sake of increasing the lifespan of the father. He who performs this rite of pacification properly and with a concentrated mind attains longevity, health, and prosperity day by day.
Thus concludes the rite for pacifying the defects arising from the junctions of lunar days and ascendants (tithi-lagna-gaṇḍānta).

Now, the pacification of the loss of a day (dinakṣaya) and other such occurrences. Gārgya says in the Uttara [section]: "Hereafter, I shall fully describe, especially regarding the time of birth, the names of the *gaṇḍāntas*, which cause great defects. [These include] the loss of a day (*dinakṣaya*), Vyatīpāta, Vyāghāta, Viṣṭi, Vaidhṛti, Śūla, Gaṇḍa, Parigha, Yamakaṇṭaka, Kālagaṇḍa, Mṛtyuyoga, and the most terrible Dagdhayoga. If a child is born when such a *gaṇḍa* day has arrived, it is declared to cause extreme harm, especially if it is conjoined with malefic planets."

The term *gaṇḍānta* is a technical designation used for the end of a day (the transition from one tithi to another) and so forth. One should perform the worship of the deities and the propitiation of the planets; one should devoutly offer lamps with ghee in the temples of Śiva. One should perform the ritual ablution (*abhiṣeka*) for Śaṅkara and circumambulate the horse. Recitation (*jāpya*) that increases longevity and destroys all misfortunes is as follows: the *Mṛtyuñjaya Mantra*, beginning with "āśuḥ śiśānaḥ" and so on—this is the meaning of the word *yapa*. The worship of the Guru, the deity, and the Brahmins increases the prosperity of one's lineage.

To ward off all calamities, one should perform a sacrifice to the planets (grahayañña). That man who, with devotion, offers a lamp to Śiva according to the prescribed rites using unbroken cow-ghee, shall conquer death. That best of men who, with devotion, performs circumambulation of the highly meritorious Viṣṇu-image and the ever-auspicious Aśvattha tree, having overcome untimely death, will certainly attain long life.

By performing the Gāṇapatya, Puṃsūkta, Saura, the auspicious Mṛtyujaya, the Śānti-japa, and the Rudra-japa, one becomes a conqueror of death. Whether during a Mūla-śānti or a Sārpa-gaṇḍa-śānti, one should diligently perform these rites for the increase of longevity and the pacification of the defects of the Gaṇḍas. This is the compendium of the pacifications for Mūla and the others.
Thus ends the pacification of all swellings.

Now follows the pacification of the *viṣaghaṭikā* (poisonous hour). Regarding this, it is said in the *Jyotirnibandha*: "In the lunar days (*tithis*), starting from the first, the numbers of the hours (*ghaṭikā*) are respectively eight, seven, seven, eleven, eight, eight, ten, ten, nine, and twelve; these are known as the 'poisonous' (*viṣa*) periods. Following that, there is a set of four hours called 'safe' (*niṣpa*). Then, in due order, they are twenty, four, twelve, ten, eleven, five, and twenty-five."

On the days of the Sun [Sunday], there are four *ghaṭikās* known as "poison" (*viṣa*) that are impassable (*asaṃtara*). Regarding the constellations (*nakṣatra*), Nārada says: zero, five, forty-four, thirty-eight, thirty, four, fifteen, twenty-nine, nineteen, thirty, and twenty-one.

Two Ramas (32), Sky-Fires (30), Shu-Asvas (20), Asras (20), Kumbha-Bhūs (18), Rupa-Pakshas (26), Vyoma-Asras (20), Veda-Chandras (14), Chaturdashas (14), Shunya-Chandras (10), Shunya-Chandras (10), Veda-Chandras (14), Shad-Akshas (56), Veda-Bahavas (42), Shunya-Asras (20), Shunya-Chandra (10), Purna-Chandra (15), Gaja-Indus (18), Tarka-Chandra (16), Veda-Pakshas (26), Khara-Amas (32), and Ashvi-Bhas (27) follow in sequence from the Ashvins. From these...

The four *ghaṭikās* following [the birth] are known as "poison" (*viṣa*). Regarding one born therein, Vṛddhagarga says: "When a child is born during the 'poison' periods, it brings about all manner of misfortunes and fear; there is no doubt that the father, the maternal uncle, and the self (the child) will perish. Furthermore, for the mother, [death comes] by means of poison, weapons, or missiles, even if the cruel [planet] occupies the lordship of the ascendant. To ward off that defect, one should perform the rite of pacification (*śāntikarma*). Rudra, Yama, Agni, and Mṛtyu are proclaimed as the presiding deities."

Having had images fashioned out of gold according to one's means, each characterized by their respective marks, one should place them upon a mound of a *māḍhaka* measure of rice. Then, having prepared a sacrificial altar (*sthaṇḍila*), one should place a water-pot (*kuṃbha*) filled with water and containing medicinal herbs; after pouring in the water, one should cast in [the images of] the deer and other [animals]. Having wrapped it with two cloths, one should deposit five gems (*pañcaratna*). Then, having placed the four images upon the pot, one should install them there and worship and offer oblations to them in due order with mantras.

The preceptor, together with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), should offer eight thousand oblations, or one hundred and eight, or twenty-eight, for each of the substances—namely, rice and clarified butter—in due order. Then, the knower of rituals should offer sesame seeds to the deities with their respective mantras. Thereafter, the gift of the image should be performed in sequence with Puranic mantras: "May the Blessed Lord Īśa, the wielder of the Pināka bow, whose face is turned in all directions, be pleased. By the gift of this image, destroy my sin."

"O sinful one! May Death, whose face is terrible with fangs, who resembles black collyrium, whose eyes are red, and who holds a mace in his hand, always protect me! With such mantras, one who is composed should perform the gift-giving according to the rules. The wise person should honor the preceptor with cows, land, gold, and garments. By performing it in this manner according to the ritual, the poison's affliction is pacified. Thus ends the *Ghaṭikā-śānti*.

Now follows the pacification (*śānti*) for birth on specific lunar days (*tithi*). Among these, the pacification for one born on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-caturdaśī*) is as follows. Garga, in the *Prayogapārijāta*, states: "If a child is born on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, there are six types of results. One should divide the fourteenth day into six parts; the first part is traditionally held to be auspicious. The second [part] destroys the father, the third likewise the mother. The fourth destroys the maternal uncle, and in the fifth there is the destruction of the lineage. In the sixth, there will be loss of wealth and the destruction of one's own lineage."

Therefore, one should perform the rite for peace with every effort according to the prescribed rules. Having selected the preceptor (*ācārya*) and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and preceded by the recitation of auspicious prayers (*svastivācana*), one should fashion images of the deities beginning with Rudra from at least one *karṣa* of gold, or from half that amount in the form of cows; one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth according to the rules. Having selected the preceptor and the officiating priests, and preceded by the recitation of auspicious prayers, one should fashion images of the deities beginning with Rudra from at least one *karṣa* of gold, or from half that amount in the form of cows, according to one's means.

Having chosen the preceptor and the officiating priests, and having first performed the *svastivācana* (rite for auspiciousness), one should fashion images of the deities beginning with Rudra out of gold weighing at least one *karṣa*, or half of that in the form of cows, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth. O Lord, one should have the image made endowed with all the auspicious characteristics, seated upon a bull, with hands in the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*), resembling pure crystal, and adorned with white garlands and garments. One should perform the worship according to the prescribed rules using the mantra known as *Tryambaka*.

One should place four jars in the intermediate directions according to the prescribed rule; that is to say, beginning from the south-east (Āgneyī) in the intermediate directions, as will be seen later [in the text] with the instruction "beginning from the Āgneya jar. One should arrange them upon a layer of grain, filled with water from sacred bathing places (tīrthas). In the center of those, one should place a jar provided with a hundred holes. Into that, one should deposit five types of earth, five gems, five fragrant substances (tvaks), five sprouts, five grains, and gold, while reciting their respective mantras.

Having placed a hundred medicinal herbs, one should wrap [the vessel] with a white cloth. One should arrange fragrant flowers and white blossoms around it. "May all the oceans, rivers, sacred fords, clouds, and donors of water come to destroy the misfortunes of the patron. Having invoked them according to the prescribed rule with the Vāruṇa mantras and with this [verse], namely: "imaṃ me varuṇa" (RV 1.24.11), "tat tvā yāmi" (RV 1.24.11), and likewise "tvanno agne" (RV 4.1.4).

One should recite the mantra "satvanna" and the hymn known as "ā no bhadra," as well as the "bhadra agne" hymn. Having chanted the Puruṣasūkta, one should then chant the Kadrudra hymn in due order. One should cause the consecration (abhiṣeka) of the Lord to be performed and the worship of the planets (graha-pūjā). Having completed the worship during the rites, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the rules. One should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the northeast direction of the planet-worship area according to the rules; its width, length, and depth should each measure two aratnis.

Leaving a space of one finger-breadth all around the rim of the pit, the height and width of the three girdles (mekhalā) should be four, three, and two finger-breadths respectively. In the middle of the western side, one should fashion the vulva (yoni) according to the prescribed rule. The auspicious yoni should be six finger-breadths wide, twelve finger-breadths long, resembling the leaf of the holy fig tree (aśvattha), slightly depressed, and extending down to the base; this should be constructed according to the ritual procedure taught in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra.

One should perform the oblation (homa) separately with sacrificial fuel (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), cooked rice (caru), sesame (tila), black gram (māṣa), and mustard (sarṣapa)—the meaning being "sesame and black gram together with mustard"—using auspicious fuel-sticks of Aśvattha, Plakṣa, Pālāśa, and Khadira. One should offer one thousand and eight, or one hundred and eight, or twenty-eight oblations of each of these individually. Sesame seeds should be offered with the *Tryambaka* mantra, and subsequently with the *Vyāhṛtis*. The planets (*graha*) should likewise be worshipped and offered oblations according to the procedure prescribed by us.

Having thus offered oblations in sequence, one should complete the remainder of the *homa*. The consecration (*abhiṣecana*) of the three [figures] adorned with all ornaments—namely, the mother, the father, and the child—is performed with water from four jars accompanied by the great jar (*bṛhatkuṃbha*). The great jar has a hundred holes; having placed golden lotuses upon it, one should then perform the inspection of the clarified butter (*ājyāvalokana*). Accompanied by the sacrificer, one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). All of that should be dedicated to the Lord with supreme devotion.

One should present to the Preceptor an image adorned with all ornaments, along with a milch cow and her calf, as well as a pair of garments; for the pleasure of Īśvara, one should feed Brāhmaṇas according to one's capacity. He who thus performs this rite of pacification (śānti) is liberated from all sins, attains all his desires, and shall live long and happily.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, the Peaceful Chapter.

Now, the ritual procedure (*prayoga*): The performer, having performed the *gomukha-prasava* rite for the sake of averting misfortune (*ariṣṭa*) concerning the father and others, shall announce the place and time and make this formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord, by means of dispelling the misfortune indicated by the birth of this boy on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, I shall perform the *Kṛṣṇa-caturdaśī-janana-śānti*, including the propitiation of the planets and the sacrifice. Then, he should perform the worship of Gaṇeśa, the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the *nāndī-śrāddha*, and the selection of the officiating priest (*ācārya*) and the bridegroom (*ṛtvig-varaṇa*).

Then the preceptor, having placed four water-pots in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast (āgneya), and a fifth in the center; and having placed therein five types of earth, five sprouts, five gems, five barks, five grains, gold, and auspicious medicinal herbs; and having wrapped them with cloths and garlands; and having worshipped the image of Rudra—weighed against a full vessel (pūrṇapātra)—with the mantra "Tryambakam" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.5.1); and having established the pots in the corners starting from the southeast.

With the three mantras beginning with "imaṃ me," [one worships] the images in the pitchers located in the corners starting from the southeast (āgneya). Then, with the mantra "sarve samudrāḥ," one worships Varuṇa. One should then recite the Rudra-mantras, the five Śānti mantras, the "anobhadra" verses, the "bhadrā agneḥ," the "sahasraśīrṣā," the "kadrudrāya," and the "āyuḥ" hymns.

Then, having performed the placement of the vessels in front and taken two fuel sticks (*samidh*), one should offer oblations here. O Rudra, with the substances of *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, *palāśa*, *khādira* wood-fuel, clarified butter (*ājya*), cooked rice (*caru*), sesame, black gram (*māṣa*), and mustard seeds, one should perform [the recitation of] the *Tryambaka* mantra eight thousand times, eight hundred times, or twenty-eight times for each substance.

Having prepared the *caru* by means of pouring and other rites in the prescribed order—beginning with the offering to Prajāpati with the mantra, followed by the *vyāhṛtis* both individually and collectively, then with sesame seeds in numbers such as one thousand, and finally the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering with the remainder—the preceptor and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should perform the oblation and other rites up to the distribution of the *bali* offerings; thereafter, they should consecrate [the king] with four jars possessing a hundred apertures, as well as with the jars of the planets.

Then the sacrificer, having assumed his finery, should look at the clarified butter in a bronze vessel while reciting "rūpaṃ rūpam"; together with his family, he should give a cow, a pair of garments, and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor, as well as fees to the officiating priests; after feeding the Brahmins and dedicating the ritual act to Rudra, he should eat.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the propitiation of Kṛṣṇacaturdaśī composed by Śrī Kamalākara.

Now follows the pacification (śānti) for Sinīvālī and Kuhū. In the *Prayogapārijāta*, Uttaragarga states: If a birth occurs on the day of Sinīvālī, it takes away the prosperity even of Indra—the prosperity of slaves, wives, cattle, as well as elephants, horses, and buffaloes. A birth on the day of Kuhū is remembered as causing half the pleasure [of the parents] and bringing about all manner of evils; for whomever these births occur, there is the destruction of their lifespan and wealth. In all such cases, every kind of *gaṇḍa* (fatal conjunction) is present, and the defect becomes exceedingly powerful. Without performing a pacification, especially, there is no way to avoid [the evil results].

In that case, abandonment must certainly be performed; the wise man should perform a propitiatory rite (*śānti*) with learned experts. Even when a propitiatory rite has been performed, abandonment must still be carried out; the meaning is that without a propitiatory rite, abandonment is all the more necessary. This is because of such scriptural statements as: "A wise man should abandon [the object] through delusion, whether for the sake of wealth or even out of ignorance; however, one should abandon a fool even without a propitiatory rite. The meaning is that by association with that [fool], one might destroy something, or one undergoes destruction oneself, due to association with a fool.

A propitiatory rite (śānti) as prescribed in the Kalpa should be performed immediately for the removal of the defect. Rudra, Śakra, the Pitṛs, and the other deities should be worshipped in their proper order. One should have an image of Śambhu fashioned out of one karṣa of gold, or half of that, or even less according to one's capacity, being free from deceit regarding wealth. The image of Śambhu should be made four-armed, with a trident, a sword, and hands in the gestures of granting boons (varada) and fearlessness (abhaya) respectively; it should be white in color, adorned with white flowers, clad in white garments, and seated upon a bull.

When one performs the worship according to the prescribed rule with the *triṃbaka* mantra, [one should meditate on] Indra as four-armed, holding a thunderbolt, a goad, a bow, and an arrow; he is red in color, mounted upon an elephant, [to be worshipped] with the mantra "yata indra. The Pitṛs (Ancestors) are black in color, four-armed, and seated in celestial chariots (*vimāna*), bearing a staff, a rosary, a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), and the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhaya*). Immediately thereafter, one should perform the worship with the mantra "ye te cetaśca," beginning from the south-eastern direction and placing the jars in the corners.

In the center of that, one should place a water-pot (kumbha) provided with a hundred holes. Into those very holes, one should pour the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other substances with their respective mantras. By the word "and others" (ādi), the five types of earth and the five jewels mentioned in the rites for pacifying the fourteenth lunar day are included. The pacification (śānti) prescribed in the Kalpa should be performed; one should perform it quickly according to one's capacity. One should give gifts of cows, garments, gold, and excellent, auspicious land. The ten gifts mentioned are milk, clarified butter, and likewise molasses.

Although the gift of a cow (*godāna*) and others are included within the ten types of gifts (*daśadāna*), they are to be performed twice. One should cause these [acts], including the inspection of the clarified butter (*ājyāvekṣaṇa*), to be performed with their respective mantras. There is an oblation (*homa*) of sacrificial fuel sticks (*samit*), parched grain (*caru*), clarified butter, sesame seeds, black gram (*māṣa*), and mustard seeds; here, sesame and black gram constitute a single substance. [The oblation is performed] with one hundred and eight fuel sticks of the *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, *pālāśa*, *khadira*, and other [specified trees].

The twice-born should offer oblations for each principal [deity] individually. Furthermore, he should offer sesame seeds with the *triyambaka* mantra and with the *vyāhṛti* mantras. Equipped with four jars and accompanied by a large water-pot (*bṛhatkuṃbha*), the twice-born should offer oblations for each principal [deity] individually with the *triyambaka* mantra and with the *vyāhṛti* mantras. He should perform the entire rite according to the *śānti* [ritual] and cause the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) to be performed. The phrase "the fourteenth day is the *śānti*-day" is the meaning of the half-verse.

There, one should also consecrate the father, mother, and children with the Varuṇa mantras; one should perform the consecration of Śaṅkara, feed the Brāhmaṇas, and offer libations to all others as well as to the Brāhmaṇas, according to one’s capacity and means, preceded by the benedictions of the twice-born.
Thus concludes the propitiatory rite for Sinīvālī and Kuhū.

Now, the ritual procedure (*prayoga*): Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus—"I shall perform the *Sinīvālī-janana-śānti* for the sake of pleasing the glorious Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), by means of pacifying all misfortunes indicated by the birth of this child under the asterisms of Sinīvālī and Kuhū"—one should perform the worship of Gaṇeśa, the recitation of the merit (*puṇyāhavācana*), the *nāndī-śrāddha*, and the selection of the officiating priest (*ācārya*).

Then the preceptor, having scattered mustard seeds and sprinkled the ground, places four jars—beginning from the southeast and extending to the intermediate directions—with the mantra "mahī dyauḥ" and so forth; he places one with a hundred holes in the center. Having deposited into them earth from five [sacred sites], five sprouts, five gems, five barks, five grains, and gold, and having worshipped the image of Rudra placed upon the jar with a hundred holes after it has been filled to the brim, he worships Indra to its right with the mantra "yat te indra" and Agni to its north with the mantra "ye ceheha".

Having worshipped the images of the father and mother with mantras, having worshipped Varuṇa in the four jars while reciting the *Ā no bhadraḥ* and *Bhadra* hymns, and having established the sacred fire, one should offer oblations of grains or other substances to the planets.

With the mantra "The two eyes with clarified butter" (*cakṣuṣī ājyena*) at the end, the principal [offering] here consists of *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, *palāśa*, and *khadira* wood, along with clarified butter, *caru*, barley, sesame, and *māṣa* beans. One should perform the oblation for Prajāpati with each of these substances one hundred and eight times, using the *vyāhṛtis* twenty-eight times, and concluding with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering from the remainder. Having thus performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) during the Āditya sacrifice, and having offered the first oblation (*pūrvāhuti*) with the mantra "Upon the head" (*mūrdhānam*) at the conclusion of the food-offering (*balidāna*), one should [sprinkle] with all the water from the jars through the hundred-holed [filter] while reciting the hymn beginning with "That which is in the waters" (*tat tvā yāmi*).

Having been consecrated with mantras, the patron (yajamāna) should give ten gifts to the preceptor (ācārya) and the others. "For the limbs of the cow"—thus [he gives] a cow. "O you who are the refuge of all worlds, the supreme protector of modesty; O giver of beautiful attire, grant me peace through the gift of clothing. Thus [he gives] clothing. "O Hiraṇyagarbha"—thus [he gives] gold. "The earth, the support of all beings, which was lifted up by the Boar; the yielder of infinite crops and fruits, grant me peace through the gift of land. Thus [he gives] land.

"This milk is conch-white, born from the nectar of milk; from milk comes fame, and in milk the vital breath is established. Therefore, by the gift of this milk, grant me peace below. Thus for the milk. "Born from the wish-fulfilling cow, present in all sacrifices, you are the clarified butter of the gods; bring [this] to me, grant me peace below. Thus for the clarified butter. "As among the gods you are the universal self and most excellent, grant me peace below. Thus for the clarified butter.

Just as Janārdana is the foremost among the gods, the Sāmaveda among the Vedas, and Maheśvara among the yogis; just as the Praṇava is among all mantras, and Pārvatī is among women; and just as the juice of sugarcane is always remembered as the most excellent of all tastes—O Jaggery, grant me supreme prosperity forever. (Thus for jaggery.)

Then, at dawn, with the mantra "rūpaṃ rūpam," he, together with his family, should gaze upon his own reflection in a bronze vessel. Regarding the vessel of clarified butter (ājya): "Clarified butter is declared to be splendor; clarified butter is remembered as the destroyer of sin. Clarified butter is the source of strength for heroes; in clarified butter the gods are established. Thus [ends the section on] the vessel of clarified butter.

Then there are ten gifts (*dāna*). And they are as follows: "Cows, land, sesame, gold, clarified butter, clothing, grain, molasses, silver, and salt—these, the wise say, are the ten gifts. Among these, the mantras for six are stated: "For sesame is known to have originated from the lineage of the great sage Kaśyapa; therefore, by the giving of these, may my sin be removed. (Thus for sesame. "Grain consists of all the gods and is the great producer of all prosperity. (Thus for grain.)

"O grain, you are the means of livelihood for living beings; grant me peace. Thus [one offers] grain. "O silver, you are the delight of Viṣṇu and Śaṅkara, and you always bring satisfaction to the ancestors; since you were born from the eye of Śiva, grant me peace. Thus [one offers] silver. "Since all the flavors of food are not superior without salt, and since it is eternally pleasing to Śambhu, grant me peace. Thus [one offers] salt. These [items] should be given along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).

Some place the *dakṣiṇā* (the sacrificial fee) even in the middle of the sequence of recitation. Then, having performed the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of the image of Rudra with the mantra "Tryambakaṃ yajāmahe," having performed the subsequent worship (*uttarapūjā*), having dismissed [the deity] and placed [the image] in the hand of the preceptor (*ācārya*), having dismissed the fire, and having had [the officiant] declare the completion of the rite, one should feed the Brahmins. Regarding the conjunction of *sinīvālī*, *kuhū*, and the new moon (*darśa*), some maintain that there is no deviation [from the rule]; therefore, this pacification (*śānti*) occurs specifically on the day of *sinīvālī*. As for *kuhū*, however, it is said to involve only a defect.

Since the new moon (*darśa*) is defined as the conjunction of the sun and moon, and that [conjunction] is specifically shown to occur on the *kuhū* day, it is only the *darśa-śānti* (propitiatory rite for the new moon) that applies there; the *gomukha-prasava* (birth through the cow's mouth) does not apply here.
Thus concludes the ritual applications for the propitiation of Sinīvālī and Kuhū.
Now, therefore, regarding the poverty of the parents of those born under the Darśa asterism:
I shall always describe a propitiatory rite (śānti) for the purpose of averting that defect.
Having uttered the "Puṇyāha" (auspicious day) formula and made the formal resolve for the ritual (*kratu-saṃkalpa*),
one should prepare either a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or a mandala, and place a water-pot (*kumbha*) in that location.
The *sarvatobhadra* mandala— one should place substances such as curd, milk, ghee, and so forth into its pitcher;
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), cow urine and cow dung are included, as well as [leaves from] the *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *cūta* trees.
Likewise, having placed the five jewels and *nimba* [leaves], one should wrap it in a pair of new cloths.
May all the oceans, rivers, sacred fords, and givers of water come to the sacrificer, bringing about the destruction of his misfortunes.

With the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, with the verse *kayā naścitraḥ*, with the verse *yat kiṃ cedam*, and with the verse *samudra-jeṣṭhāḥ salilasya madhyāt punānā yanty aniviśamānāḥ indro yā...*

May the Vajra-bearing Bull be pleased; may the divine Waters lick me and protect me—those Waters that flow from heaven, those that flow from springs, those dug out by men, and those that arise spontaneously; those that seek the ocean, pure and purifying—may those divine Waters lick me and protect me. In whose midst King Varuṇa moves, beholding the truth and falsehood of men; they who drip sweetness, pure and purifying—may those divine Waters lick me and protect me. Those whom King Varuṇa honors, those whom Soma honors, those whom all the gods and the Sun delight in; those into whom Vaiśvānara Agni has entered—may those divine Waters lick me and protect me.
With the verse beginning "The ocean is the eldest."
Having consecrated water to the north-east of the fire while facing north,
he should then establish the deities of the New Moon sacrifice.
Such is the grammatical connection (anvaya).
Regarding what was stated, "one should construct the mandala," he says:
"With turmeric, red, black, white, and blue—
using the rice grains of these [colors]— one should draw the Sarvatobhadra [mandala] on all sides."
And for the deity named Darśā, who has the nature of the Moon and the Sun,
an excellent image made of gold, silver, or copper [is prescribed].
One should install an image whose form is that of the deities of the Darśa sacrifice, having the nature of Soma and Sūrya; such is the connection through non-difference.
One should install the deity of the Darśa in the center of the Sarvatobhadra mandala, along with a pair of garments in the color of the planets, and fragrant flowers of that same color.
Having likewise worshipped Savitṛ from behind with the mantra "āpyāyasva," and having propitiated him with the ritual services (upacāras), one should then perform the fire-oblation (homa).
Having established the fire and made such a resolve as this:
"For the sake of longevity, health, and prosperity, and for the pacification of all misfortunes."
For the removal of defects arising at the birth of a son,
and for the pacification of all calamities for the mother, the father, and the child.
"For the attainment of those two, Māyā and Śrī, I perform a peace-offering (śānti-homa).
Thus [are] the verses and mantras.
One should offer oblations with the *hunetpa* and *vitṛ* mantras, and with the *somo dhenuṃ* mantra;
with these mantras, one should perform the homa separately one hundred and eight times for each.
By virtue of the plural number in the word "etair" (by these), the oblation to the ancestors (pitṛ-daivatyahoma) is also one hundred and eight.
And the offering to the deity of the Darśa sacrifice is performed twenty-eight times.
Having thus performed the fire sacrifice (homa), one should then perform the consecration with water (abhiṣecana).

One should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) for the mother, the father, and likewise for the child with these mantras: the Śrīsūkta, the Āyuṣya Sūkta, and the verse beginning with "samudra jyeṣṭhāḥ."
Then, after the *sviṣṭakṛt* and subsequent rites, one should complete the remainder of the oblation;
[one should give] gold, silver, and a black cow, along with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Likewise, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should be given to others according to one's ability;
one should feed Brāhmaṇas there and have the benedictory recitation (vācana) performed.
Now, the procedure for the Darśa-śānti:

Having announced the place and time, and having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus—"For the purpose of propitiating the glorious Supreme Lord by means of removing the misfortune indicated by the birth of this child on the new moon day (*darśa*), I shall perform the Darśa-janana-śānti"—one should perform the worship of Gaṇeśa, the recitation of the auspicious verses (*puṇyāhavācana*), the *nāndī-śrāddha*, and the selection of the officiating priest (*ācārya*) and the ritual assistants (*ṛtvij*).

There, the preceptor, having fashioned a *sarvatobhadra* mandala with rice grains of five colors upon a raised mound or a leveled earthen surface to the east, and having placed a water-pot (*kumbha*) in its center, shall deposit the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the barks and sprouts from the roots of the *nyagrodha*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *cūta*, and *nimba* trees, and the five gems; then, having wrapped it in a pair of cloths, he shall consecrate it with the mantra "All oceans... and the verse beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā."

Having consecrated [the vessel] with the mantra "The chariot is variegated; whatever this is, the ocean is its eldest," and having invoked Soma with "May you swell" (*āpyāyasva*) into the full vessel, and Sūrya with "Savitṛ from behind," one should worship them with scents and flowers according to the colors of the respective deities.

Some worship the ancestors in the center, and Soma and Sūrya to the south and north; one should consider the root of that [practice]. Then, having installed the fires and the planets—here the principal ones being the planets, Soma, and Sūrya—with either one hundred and eight or twenty oblations of fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and clarified butter (*caru*), one should perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering with the remnants of the consecration water mentioned in the ritual manual (*kalpa*). One should add the fuel, spread the grass-covering (*paristaraṇa*), and so forth, up until the *ājyabhāga* offerings. Having offered to the planets and others, one recites the verse beginning with "May there be long life and health" (*āyurārogya*).

Having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the two mantras, with the hymn beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*, with the hymn beginning with *āyuṣyaṃ varcasyam*, and with the verse *samudra-jyeṣṭhāḥ*, and having consecrated the mother, father, and child; then, after performing the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the rites ending with the presentation of the oblations (*balidāna*), and having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*); having completed the remainder of the *homa*; and having given silver, gold, and a black cow along with ritual fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor (*ācārya*) according to his capacity, and having given ritual fees to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) according to their capacity; and having performed the subsequent worship and dismissed the deities, he should give the image to the preceptor.
Having extinguished the fire, fed the Brāhmaṇas, and caused the recitation of the Śānti, one should perform the Svastivācana.
Thus ends the *Darśa-śānti-prayoga* composed by Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa, son of Rāmakṛṣṇa Bhaṭṭa and grandson of Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa.
Thus are the propitiations for the lunar days (*tithi*).
First among them is the propitiation for the *Jyeṣṭhā* asterism. Regarding its origin and the resulting effects, the *Brahmayāmala* states:
"If birth occurs under *Jyeṣṭhā*, the mother [is endangered] in the first [case], and the mother and father in the second."
In the third [case], it is the mother; in the case of a brother, oneself; and in the fourth, the mother.
In the fifth [month] he destroys himself; in the sixth, there shall be the destruction of his lineage.
In the seventh, both his family and his elder brother perish.
The lord of the ninth house kills the hero; the tenth-part (daśāṃśaka) kills everything.

O Vasiṣṭha, a woman born under the asterism Sureśa (Jyeṣṭhā) kills her husband’s elder brother; one born under Dvidaivata (Viśākhā) kills her husband’s younger brother; one born under Puraṃjaya (Pūrvaphalgunī) kills her husband’s elder brother; and likewise, one born under Suta (Śravaṇa) kills her own elder brother, even if she has daughters.
The specific details should be understood from the *Nirṇayasindhu*. Regarding the ritual application (*prayoga*), Vṛddhagārgya says in the *Phārijata*:
"Having approached the best of sages, Garga, who was seated comfortably and surrounded by hosts of sages, Pratiśānaka, with palms joined in reverence, questioned him."
I shall duly explain the determination of the defect known as Gaṇḍa arising from birth under the Jyeṣṭhā asterism, as well as its pacification and the performance of rites for its removal.
One ghaṭikā at the end of Kācamaitra and two ghaṭikās at the beginning of Jyeṣṭhā—the junction between these two should be known as Ratijñeya; it is declared to be Śiśugaṇḍa.
A man born in the first, second, or third quarter of the Jyeṣṭhā constellation becomes a Jyeṣṭha (the eldest) even here.
One born under the last quarter of Jyeṣṭhā becomes the destroyer of his own father;
there is no doubt about this, occurring likewise within ten days.
In the third [lunar day], a daughter is born who will quickly kill her elder brother;
I shall describe its pacification for the purpose of neutralizing the defect of Gaṇḍa.
On an auspicious day, under a favorable lunar mansion (nakṣatra), endowed with the strength of the moon and stars, and at the end of the night,
one should perform the Jyeṣṭhā-śānti according to the prescribed ritual.
One should fashion the beautiful god Indra, the lord of the gods and leader of the deities, holding a vajra-hook and accompanied by the elephant Airāvata.
One should perform that ritual with [the image] weighing one *karṣa* in weight, or half a *karṣa*, or even a quarter of a *karṣa*;
one should have it made according to the prescribed rule, without stinginess regarding the expense.
One who has restrained their speech should worship [the deity] upon a pitcher completely filled with śāli rice,
using the mantra "indrāyendo marutvate."
One should worship him, accompanied by the hosts of world-protectors, with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and various offerings of food.
One should worship the Leader of the Gods, who is endowed with two red garments;
there, one should specifically place water-pots in the four directions.
In the middle of that, one should place a water-pot provided with a hundred holes,
filled with auspicious water and wrapped in two pieces of cloth.
The wise one should place the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) with their respective mantras into the jars,
along with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), the five jewels (pañcaratna), and five kinds of earth.
One should place the five types of trees, the five astringent decoctions, as well as the five sprouts,
gold, kuśa grass, dūrvā grass, and excellent medicinal herbs.
One should diligently worship four water-pots with mantras dedicated to Varuṇa;
first one should recite "tvaṃ no agne," and the second with "sa tvaṃ naḥ."
One should worship with the mantra "samudrajyeṣṭhā" and the fourfold "imaṃ me gaṅge," and also worship four water-pots (kalaśas) with a pair of garments and other offerings.
For the sake of pleasing Varuṇa residing in the water-pot (kalaśa),
the best of the twice-born should perform recitation with effort using these mantras;
one should perform the *anobhadra* recitation, and especially the *bhadrā agneḥ*.
Then, having worshipped Indra, the lord of gods, with the Indra-sūkta, the Rudra-sūkta, and the supreme Mṛtyuñjaya [mantra], as well as Varuṇa residing within the water-pot (kumbha).
Having formed a firm resolve according to the prescribed rule, one should then perform the fire-oblation (homa) with one hundred and eight fuel-sticks of the Brahma-tree (Brahmavṛkṣa).
Restraining one's speech, one should offer oblations of clarified butter and *ruṇā* with the root-mantra,
and likewise recite the mantra beginning with "yata indra bhayāmahe."
Having offered sesame seeds one hundred and eight times separately with the Vyāhṛtis,
[he should especially protect] the sacrificer together with his wife and children.
One should perform the consecration with the mantras known as the Vāruṇas,
and also with the "Samudra-jyeṣṭha" mantras, and likewise with the mantra "Oṃ me varuṇa śr̥dhi."
One should perform the consecration with the mantras beginning with "pṛthivī śāntā" and so forth;
once the consecration is completed, the sacrificer, being composed, [should proceed].
Then, having put on white garments, one should perform the gazing at the clarified butter (ājya) with the mantra "rūpaṃ rūpam" or with the mantra "citram tac cakṣuḥ."
Standing before the deity, one should offer incense and lamps;
one should properly give water for sipping (ācamana), as well as betel-leaf and the arghya offering.
Salutations to you, the Lord of the gods; salutations to you, O Consort of Śacī!
Accept this water offering given by me for the pacification of the defect of Gaṇḍa.
Having obtained whatever auspicious result belongs to the worshippers and others, one should offer it to the preceptor; and one should give a well-behaved, milch cow to the teacher.
[One should worship] the red-colored [goddess] accompanied by her calf, adorned with all ornaments,
and covered with a pair of garments according to the extent of one's wealth.
O Lord of Śacī, though you are worshipped by Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Siddhas,
O Lord of Devas, destroy the defect of the Gaṇḍa [birthmark] through this gift.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one should provide a feast for the Brahmins;
then, having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and prostrated, one should bring the rite to completion.
Having performed this Jyeṣṭha-śānti according to the path prescribed by the rules,
a man overcomes the defect of Gaṇḍa and becomes long-lived.
Thus it was stated by Vṛddhagārgya specifically regarding the Śānaka weapon,
for the pacification of the Gaṇḍa defect arising from the Jyeṣṭhā asterism.
Whether due to lack of understanding, or because of a contradiction, or because of an incompleteness in the refutation—
whatever is deficient or excessive therein, you ought to forgive it all.

Thus ends the propitiation (śānti) for the Jyeṣṭhā asterism. Now follows the ritual procedure (prayoga) for the Jyeṣṭhā asterism propitiation: Having performed the "birth through a cow's mouth" (gomukha-prasava), and having recollected the place and time, one should make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "For the sake of pacifying all misfortunes indicated by the Jyeṣṭhā asterism of this child, I shall perform the Jyeṣṭhā asterism propitiation. Having made this resolve, one should perform the worship of Gaṇeśa, the recitation of the auspicious proclamation (puṇyāhavācana), the Nāndī-śrāddha, and the selection of the preceptor (ācārya) and officiating priests (ṛtvij). Then, according to custom: having touched the ground with the mantra *mahī dyauḥ*, having scattered barley with the mantra *oṣadhayaḥ sam*, and [placing] the water-pot (kalaśa) with the mantra *ā kalaśeṣu*.

Having established [the deity], having worshipped with incense, and having filled the pitcher with *śāli* rice grains, he should place a full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*) with the mantra "pūrṇā darvi. Upon that, having fashioned an image of Indra according to the prescribed proportions, he should invoke and worship Indra with the mantra "indrāyendo marutvate" and the other world-protectors (*lokapāla*) with their respective mantras. Then, [he should place] four pitchers in the directions starting from the east, in the middle...

Having established the hundred-pored [jar], and having poured the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), the five gems (*pañcaratna*), the five types of earth (*pañcamṛttikā*), the five sprouts (*pañcapallava*), gold, *kuśa* grass, *dūrvā* grass, and the *śatāvarī* plant into the water-jars of the directions, and having wrapped them with a pair of cloths, one should invoke and worship Varuṇa.
Then, having consecrated the jars starting from the east with the mantras "tvanno agne," "samudra jyeṣṭhāḥ," and "imaṃ me gaṅge," one should recite the "ā no bhadrā" hymn.

May auspicious thoughts come to us from every side—thoughts that are undeceivable, never-failing, and breakers of obstacles. May the gods always be with us for our exaltation, protecting us day by day with their life-sustaining power. May the auspicious favor of the upright gods be ours; may the bounty of the gods turn toward us, O seekers. May I attain the friendship of the gods; may the gods extend our span of life so that we may live. We invoke them with the ancient invocation: Bhaga, Mitra, Aditi, Dakṣa, and Aśvin.

May the noble Maṇi, Varuṇa, Soma, the Aśvins, and the auspicious Sarasvatī grant us that which brings prosperity. May Vāta (the Wind) grant us that medicine which is the source of bliss; may Mother Pṛthivī (Earth) and Father Dyauḥ (Heaven) grant it. May the pressing-stones that extract the Soma grant that which is blissful; O Aśvins, hear this prayer for our long life. We invoke for protection that Lord of the moving world and of all that stands still, the one who quickens wisdom. May Pūṣan, as our guardian and protector, keep us safe and unharmed so that we may prosper.

May Indra, of the vast domain, grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the knower of all, grant us well-being. May Tārkṣya, whose wheel-rims are unharmed, grant us well-being; may Bṛhaspati establish us in well-being. The Maruts with spotted horses, the sons of Pṛśni, who move in splendor and frequent the assemblies, the men whose tongue is Agni and whose eyes are the sun—may all you gods come here with your protection. O Gods, may we hear what is auspicious with our ears; O Holy Ones, may we see what is auspicious with our eyes.

With steadfast colors, praising you with our bodies, may we attain that which is ordained by the gods for our welfare. A hundred autumns indeed do these gods endure, within which they have brought about the aging of our bodies. In this world, sons become fathers; do not harm us in the midst of our journeying life. Aditi is heaven, Aditi is the mid-air, Aditi is the mother, she is the father, and she is the son. All the gods are Aditi, the five peoples are Aditi; all that is born is Aditi, and Aditi is all that is to be born.

Having recited the Rudra hymn and the Tryambaka mantra, as well as "indrāyendo," "yata indra bhayāmahe," and so forth, they should recite these one hundred and eight times, twenty-eight times, or at least eight times. Then, having established the fire and the planetary deities (grahas), he should offer the supplementary oblations (anvādhāna).
In this case, the primary factor is as follows.

One should offer oblations to Indra with *palāśa* wood and clarified butter as the substance, one hundred and eight times, using the mantra "indrāyendo marutvate"; to Prajāpati with sesame seeds as the substance, one hundred and eight times, with the *vyāhṛtis*; and to Sviṣṭakṛt with the remainder, and so forth. Having performed the rites up to the *bali*, the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), and the release of the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra-vimoka*), one should sprinkle [the recipient] for peace with the Vāruṇa hymns beginning with "sahite kṣatram," the four verses beginning with "samudra-jyeṣṭhāḥ," and the verse "imaṃ me varuṇa."

Then the sacrificer, having gazed at the clarified butter with the mantra "rūpaṃ rūpam," and having given that vessel along with the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brāhmaṇa, shall worship Indra, saying: "Salutations to you, O Lord of the Gods; salutations to you, O Consort of Śacī.
Accept this *arghya* offered by me for the pacification of the defect of the *gaṇḍa*."

Having thus presented the *arghya* offering, and having received from the preceptor (*ācārya*) and others the excellence arising from the fire-oblation (*homa*) and other rites, one should dedicate that to Indra. Then, for the preceptor, [one should give] a red-colored cow with her calf, accompanied by two garments;
and [one should pray]: "O Lord of the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Siddhas, you who are worshipped by Śacī’s husband!
O Lord of Devas, through this gift, destroy the defect of the *gaṇḍa*."

One should offer [the oblation] with this mantra. Then, having given sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others, and having performed the concluding worship (*uttarapūjā*), one should dismiss them with the following:
"Whether through ignorance or through knowledge, whether due to deficiency or an excess of wealth—whatever has been deficient or excessive, you should please forgive it all."

Having thus offered prayers and given [the fee] to the preceptor, having worshipped the fire and applied the sacred ash (vibhūti) to both arms, and having dismissed [the deities], one should feed eight hundred Brahmins with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), receive their blessings, and then eat;
this is the procedure for the propitiatory rite (śānti) of the Jyeṣṭhā asterism. Now follows the propitiatory rite of the Mūla asterism.
In that regard, the fault concerning the birth of a daughter:
one should abandon a male child born under an inauspicious *mūlā* asterism until he is eight years old; or else, the father should not look upon his face [before then].
O dear one, if [the Moon] is in the first quarter of that [sign], the father perishes; in the second, the mother falls low;
in the third part, there is loss of wealth; and in the fourth, it brings auspiciousness.
In the case of the Sārpa-bha (Āśleṣā), the fruit is the same as that which occurs at the end of the Prati-pada month.
Regarding *abhukta-mūla*, the elder Vasiṣṭha says:
"One *ghaṭikā* at the end of Jyeṣṭhā and two *ghaṭikās* at the beginning of Mūla are called *abhukta-mūla*; one should avoid [births] occurring therein."
Bṛhaspati, however, says:
"Half a ghaṭikā at the end of Jyeṣṭhā and half a ghaṭikā at the beginning of Mūla—
the nāḍī situated between these two is called 'unconsumed' (abhukta) Mūla."
But Bṛhannārada says:
"The four ghaṭikās beginning with the root (mūla) and the bulb (gaṇḍa) are unenjoyed;
among them, the final two ghaṭikās of Mūla and the first two of Ārdrā are indeed the avayava."
Thus says the Kaśyapa-saṃhitā; however, another root text states:
"The first-born [son] destroys the father, the second-born destroys the mother, the third-born destroys himself, and the fourth-born destroys his friends."
The same result occurs in the case of the Āśleṣā asterism, while the opposite results from the last one (Punarvasu).

Kātyāyana also states in the *Pariśiṣṭa*: "In the first [birth], it is not desired for the father; in the second, for the mother; in the third, it removes wealth and grain; in the fourth, it removes grief from the family; and in the fifth, the person himself shall partake in merit."
Vasiṣṭha:
The *tāuri* sacrifice brings auspicious results; indeed, that very fruit is obtained because the entire world of moving beings exists within the abode of the serpent.
It should be understood from the *Jayārṇava* that [the worship of the tree] brings auspiciousness to one's father and others, as well as to oneself:
"The root, the trunk, the bark, the branches, the leaf, the flower, the fruit, and the crest; likewise the Vedas, the sages, the directions, and the Vasus."
Nine, five, six, six, six, eleven, eleven, and eleven—these are proclaimed as the divisions of the roots.
[The piercing] at the root causes the destruction of the root; at the trunk, it brings loss and the depletion of wealth;
on the bark, it leads to the destruction of brothers; and on the branches, it causes the destruction of the mother.

If it falls on a leaf, one obtains a kingdom along with one's retinue; if on flowers, one becomes a favorite of the king; if on fruits, one attains sovereignty; but if on the crest, there is a short life.

Elsewhere, however, it is stated differently: "In the seven *ghaṭikās* at the root, there is a blow to the root; in the eight at the trunk, the destruction of one's own lineage; in its branches, the destruction of kinsmen; struck by eleven at the twigs, the maternal uncle is killed; by twelve at the leaves, one becomes virtuous; by five at the fruit, a minister; and by three at the flower, a king—but with a short lifespan. Thus, according to the *Sammūlādhruva*, the results for the *ghaṭikās* of the leaves and so forth are considered excellent. This final objection certainly exists, as stated by Bhūpālapallava:

They remember that Taurus, Aries, and Leo are situated in heaven; Gemini, Libra, and Virgo are situated in the sky; and Aries, Sagittarius, Cancer, and Capricorn are situated in the netherworld, while the remaining signs are in the mortal realm.
The result of this *mūla-lagna* is as follows:
if the *mūla* occurs in heaven, there will be sovereignty; if in the netherworld (*pātāla*), there will be the arrival of wealth;
but when the *mūla* is in the world of mortals, one should predict total emptiness.
As Vasiṣṭha says:
"In Vyatīpāta there is loss of limbs; in Parigha, one should predict death;
in Vaidhṛti, there is loss of one's father; and in Śasta, one enters the jaws of fire."

If [the Moon] is in Mūla, there will be the destruction of the family due to the total eradication of the root; if it is in Dhṛti, there will be the destruction of the lineage; and if it is in both Saṃdhi constellations, one will have deformed limbs and be deficient.
Furthermore, a birth occurring on a parvan day brings about all manner of misfortunes and fear;
likewise, the same applies to a child born with teeth already present, as well as one born with feet first.

Therefore, one should perform the pacification (*śānti*) of the planets with a focused mind. Regarding the conjunction of the *śānti* and the *grahayajña* (sacrifice to the planets) during the *vyatīpāta* and other such occasions: that procedure for the commencement of the planetary rites (*grahamukha-vidhāna*) is not taught as a general rule (*anārabhyādhīta*), because it is restricted by its inclusion within the specific context (*prakaraṇa*) of the seventeen *samit* offerings. For the purpose of making the *grahayajñas* necessary in other pacificatory rites (*śāntika*), Śaunaka says:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the beneficial discourse on the origin of the *mūla* [constellations],
for the sake of the welfare of one's mother and father, as well as for the benefit of one's own family.

Either there shall be the abandonment of those born under Mūla, or their appearance [must be] shown after eight years; for those born under Mūla who have not yet experienced its effects, total renunciation is prescribed.
Even if the father is not seen, one should observe the *samāṣṭaka* for eight years;
thus, the wise declare that this is the fruit arising from the root of a daughter.
I shall now diligently declare the primary time for the peace-offering (śāntihoma):
on the twelfth day after birth, or under the natal asterism, or on an auspicious day.
On the eighth day or the twelfth day, the wise man should have a pavilion constructed;
then, having sprinkled it with water consecrated by meritorious mantras.
As for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), Kaśyapa has stated:
"Eight, twelve, or sixteen Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*).
In that regard, [one should place] a water-pot (*uda-kuṃbha*) that is white, free from blackness, and devoid of red stains.
One should fill [the vessel] with pure water that is free from black roots and thoroughly cleansed; for "cleansed" means washed—
one should wrap it with cloth and fill it with water from a sacred ford (tīrtha).
Making it joined with gold and adorned with mango sprouts.
Having placed [the vessel] upon a svastika and having filled it with the sprouts of milk-exuding trees and *droṇa* rice, one should set it down in the northeast.
Having cast in the five jewels together with all medicinal herbs,
and having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should recite the Śrī Rudra while touching it.
One should correctly recite [the mantra] endowed with the six limbs eleven times;
the Ṛgvedins [should recite] with the Rudra-hymns, the Yajurvedins with the Rudra-sūktas, and the Sāmavedins with the Rudra-sāmans.
One should recite according to one's capacity eleven, eight, three, two, or one time;
and by this same number, one should also recite the Rudrasūkta among the Sāman chants.
Therein, one should mutter the *Apratiratha* hymn, the *Śatarudrīya-anuvāka*,
and likewise the meritorious *Rakṣā-mantra* beginning with "O Agni, you are Rudra," while touching [the person] and reciting the *rakṣoghna* (demon-destroying) verses.
The recitation of these [mantras] should also be performed eleven times or more;
one should properly recite the *Tryambaka* mantra one thousand and eight times,
and likewise, while touching [the water], one should recite the *Pāvamānī* verses once.
For the *japa* [of the mantra], there should be five pitchers; or two may be used depending on the availability of leaves.
Including the *rudra-kumbha* and the *nirṛti-kumbha*, which is broken, there are thus seven pitchers.
There is one *rudrakumbha* in the center and four in the four corners beginning with Īśāna, making five in total;
thus it is stated in the *Kaśyapa-saṃhitā*: "In the corners, there are four jars with holes for the [breaths], and likewise five jars—filled with water—in the four corners beginning with Īśāna."
One should place those of red color, combined with the previously mentioned substances.

One should place a large jar with a hundred holes upon the rice; there, the recitation of the previously mentioned hymn is prescribed for them— by Rudra, in the sequence of the auspicious and most auspicious [verses], with great devotion to Agni.
One should worship with the "Ā no bhadrā" hymn and likewise with this very "Pumsūkta."
One should recite each of the eight mantras beginning with "mocanī mūlajā" individually.

Regarding the case of two jars, Kātyāyana has stated that they should be provided with four spouts; having prepared a second water-jar, it should be joined with four spouts, and therein one should place the roots above Varuṇa, having placed them in a bamboo vessel, as indicated by the words "vastre bhadrā". In the case of five jars, there are a hundred roots in the center. He speaks of two jars:
one jar for the Śrī Rudra [mantra] and all the Sūktas therein.
Likewise, one should prepare five jars endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics— having four spouts and likewise five faces—
and one should clothe them with cloth and fill them with water from sacred fords (tīrtha).

Endowed with the five jewels and joined with mango sprouts, [the earth] is taken from an elephant’s footprint, a horse’s footprint, a royal road, an anthill, a confluence of rivers, or from a pool frequented by kula-birds.
Having brought earth from the entrance of the royal palace, one should deposit it;
one should designate the location for gold in the south-western quarter of the pitcher.
On a ground smeared with cow dung, one should prepare an excellent sacrificial altar (sthaṇḍila).
But Kaśyapa said:
"The pavilion should be square, measuring four cubits in dimension,
provided with four doors, and adorned with various arches."
"The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics, [should be situated] outside toward the northeast. Thus [it is said].
Having performed the rites from the drawing of lines (ullekha) up to the fire-mouth (agnimukha) according to one's own school,
and having completed the placement of the full vessel (pūrṇapātra), one should commence the worship.
The form of the lunar mansion deity should be fashioned with effort from gold, weighing one *niṣka*, half a *niṣka*, a quarter, or according to one's own capacity.
Having first had one [image] made according to the characteristics, the wise man,
having placed it at the root of the faded [image], should worship it.
One should remember Nṛbūti, who is dark-complexioned, handsome-faced, and has a chariot as his vehicle;
he is the lord of the Rākṣasas, holds a sword in his hand, and is adorned with divine ornaments.
In the Jyotirnibandha: "The form of Mūla should be fashioned as white, with a dog as his vehicle;
he is fierce, two-armed, holding a sword and a shield, and has the face of a wolf."
And it has been said:
"For the purpose of worshipping the image, one should provide a pair of garments;
one should draw a lotus on the ground with red rice grains."
With twenty-four petals, white or otherwise, and provided with a pericarp;
upon that, one should place another vessel made of gold, silver, or clay.
Having wiped it with a clean cloth, one should place the roots there.
Regarding the "roots" (mūla) and "hundred roots" (śatamūla):
*muṣṇukrāntā*, *sahadevī*, *tulasī*, and *śatāvarī*—
one should take these roots, especially when a hundred cannot be obtained.
One should place in the center of the *kīrṇikā* a cloth adorned with perfumes and other offerings,
together with a *kūrca*, water, saffron, and medicinal herbs.
A *kūrca* is a cluster of *darbha* grass; such is the nature of the vessel for which it is intended—this is the meaning.
A wise person should place the deity of the natal asterism upon the vessel; one should worship the auspicious deities of Jyeṣṭhā, Pūrvaphalgunī, and Maghā.
One should worship [the deities] beginning with Uttaraṣāḍhā and ending with Anurādhā.
The meaning of the ritual procedure is that the twenty-four lunar mansions, beginning with Uttarāṣāḍhā, should be established starting from the east upon the twenty-four petals;
one should worship them by their respective names, extending from the direction of Indra (East) to Īśāna (Northeast).
And one should worship the offerings and so forth with the mantras specific to their respective deities as stated in their own liturgical texts.
But Kaśyapa says:
"The wise man should have an image fashioned from gold according to the prescribed measure, or even half of that, or again half of that, in accordance with his wealth."
The bark and sprouts of the udumbara, vaṭa, aśvattha, plakṣa, and āmra trees; the roots of the hundred medicinal herbs (śatauṣadhī); a conch shell; the nine gems; and various types of earth.
The five nectars (pañcāmṛta) along with the true seed, saffron, yellow pigment, the fruit, costus, spikenard, the two types of turmeric, murā, śaileya, and sandalwood.
Vacā, campaka, and mustā—these are remembered as the ten universal herbs (sarvauṣadhyaḥ).
As for the eight types of earth: those from an elephant’s footprint, a horse’s track, an anthill, a confluence of rivers, a lake, a royal city, and from the threshold of a palace gate.
Sesame, rice, paddy, barley, wheat, and millet,
together with chickpeas— these eight are always known as the "excellent seeds."

Then, one should worship the jars with curd, honey, and unbroken rice (akṣata), using cloths and mantras appropriate to their respective deities; thereafter, one should worship Nirṛti with the mantra "moṣaṇaśceci."
Having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and invoked [him],
one should worship with either the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra) or the five services (pañcopacāra).
With red sandalwood, perfumes, and so forth; with flowers such as the black and white varieties;
with incense such as ram's horn and others; and likewise with lamps of clarified butter.
One should avoid offering liquor, meat, fish, and the like as food offerings (naivedya) and meals; such things as fish, meat, and wine must be strictly avoided for Brāhmaṇas.
If the aforementioned substances and so forth are not available, one should offer whatever is obtained;
having worshipped up to the offering of flowers, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) as prescribed.
If the aforementioned substances and so forth are unavailable, one should offer whatever is obtained;
having duly worshipped even a single flower, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) as prescribed.
One should perform the rites of banishing, sprinkling, and so forth for the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) according to the prescribed rule.
Having taken the oblation, one should offer it to Nirṛti with the three verses beginning with "vithivat."
One should offer milk-rice mixed with ghee one hundred and eight times;
thereafter, one should offer sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice in a number according to one's capacity.
One's own mantra is the name-mantra;
one should then offer *kṛsara* (rice and pulse) with the verses beginning with "kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ," followed by "jātavedase" in the Gāyatrī meter, and "tryambakam," in that order.
They yoke that plough— the fire of Vāstoṣpati and the fire itself—
that which is fire-colored, blazing with ascetic heat, belonging to Virocana, and cherished for the fruits of ritual action.
I declare Durgā Devī as my refuge; salutations to her whose hair is beautifully white.
Likewise, one should worship Kṣetrapati, Gṛhāgnis, and Dūta with the Śrīsūkta.
The wise man, knowing the ritual, should offer the fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and oblation-gruel in sequence— either one hundred and eight times each, or twenty-eight times each,
or in groups of eight, according to his capacity.
They should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) with Soma for you, thirteen times;
and they should offer four ladles of clarified butter with the mantra "yā te rudra" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.5.1).
One should offer oblations of clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle using the *mahāvyāhṛtis* in sequence;
having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, one should thereafter offer the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścittāhuti*).
But according to Kaśyapa:
one should worship Durgā, the planets, Vighneśa, and the world-protectors; at the conclusion of each [mantra], one should offer clarified butter with the formula, "Svāhā to Prajāpati."
Then, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *palāśa* wood fuel and clarified butter with the mantra "sa tvanno agne," or otherwise, one hundred and eight oblations of each respectively.
With the *mūla* constellation, with the *muṣṭi* formulas, and with the two mantras;
and with the mantras originating from the *aśvattha* tree belonging to Agni, Soma, and Nirṛti.
Having offered oblations of fuel-sticks, sesame seeds, and rice with the *avyāhṛti* formulas,
the preceptor or the sacrificer should then offer a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the fire.
One should perform the *prājāpatya* oblation with the hymn beginning "sumudrā dūrmi," and likewise offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the mantras beginning "pūrṇā darvi" and "sapta."
Having completed the remainder of the *homa*, the wise one should then consign the fire [into himself].
Because the mouth of the planets is of a transformative nature, the consignment of the fire is performed with the *smārta* fires.
One should perform the consecration of the water-jar (kumbha) and sprinkle it upon the navel;
