for the sake of pacifying death, one should recite the *Tryambaka* mantra a hundred times.
One should recite the Rudra mantra while touching it with the mantra prescribed for the Rudra-kumbha.

Having performed the touching [of the vessel] to the south of the *rudra-kuṃbha*, the meaning is that one should mutter the previously mentioned recitation (*japa*) by means of the followers of the Yajurveda, Ṛgveda, and Sāmaveda—namely, eleven, eight, three, two, and one times respectively; the meaning is that one should chant the *rudra-sūkta* and the *sāman*. One should offer incense, a lamp, and the food offering (*naivedya*) into the pair of vessels.
The meaning is: in the Rudra-pitcher and the Nirṛti-pitcher—“O God, grant me grace for the sake of this consecration; [accept] the arghya with respect.”
And at the time of the moon's conjunction with the constellation Nirṛti, one who desires prosperity should perform the reception of the planets;
this is praised as being performed either separately or together with a sacrifice to the lunar mansions (nakṣatreṣṭi).
For that very reason, the planet sacrifice (grahayajña) is prescribed separately— meaning it is to be performed together with the rite for pacifying the *mūla* nakṣatra—
I shall now describe the procedure for consecration (abhiṣeka) as proclaimed by all the masters.
While the patron is seated upon the auspicious throne, all the officiating priests should perform the consecration for him, along with his wife, sons, and relatives.
With the hymn beginning with "akṣībhyām," with those beginning with "pāvamānī," with the nine verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," and with the two verses beginning with "yata indra."
Also with the Ṛgvedic verse beginning "sahasrākṣa," with the mantras beginning "devasya tvā," with the Śivasaṃkalpa mantra, and with the mantras that are about to be mentioned.
These will be explained in the verses to be spoken in the ritual application (*prayoga*): "That *śaṃyu-abhiṣeka* [is] the pacifier of all defects,
the bestower of all desires, divine, and the most auspicious of all auspicious things."
Thereafter, the wise one should perform the ritual bathing with two jars covered by cloths.
Then, wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands and unguents,
the patron should satisfy the officiating priests and others with sacrificial fees.
One should give a milch cow with her calf and a bell-metal vessel to the preceptor;
one should cause an image of Nirṛti, a cloth, a water-pot, and gold to be given.
Half of a planet [image], a cloth, and an image—these are the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) prescribed for each;
a black bull should be given with effort to the reciter of the Śrī Rudra.
One should diligently give him that water-pot, garment, and an incomparable image;
and one should also give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the other Brahmins according to one's capacity.
If the aforementioned [fees] are not obtained, one should then give them to the Ācārya, the Brahmā, and the officiating priests (ṛtvij);
their respective base fees (mūla) should be given, or one should cause them to be paid according to one's capacity.
That which is dedicated to the Ācārya, half of that shall belong to the Brahman;
half of the Brahman’s share belongs to the Sadasya, and half of that to the other officiating priests (Ṛtviks).
"One should give a covering, wool, cloth, and so forth, as well as a cow and gold;
at the conclusion of the gifts, the Brahmin should indeed offer all the monetary values there. Thus it is said.

O King, one should take the roots of the *tāla* tree, offer them to those who have been consecrated, and then, having bowed down, one should measure out [the ground]. One should give food such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and feed a hundred Brahmins.
If these are not obtained, then fifty or ten [verses] may be recited;
furthermore, due to that lack, Brahmins should perform the recitation for the pacification of all misfortunes as well as the pronouncing of blessings.
The wise householder should offer an apology, saying, "May Nirṛti be pleased.
When this rite has been performed, peace will certainly ensue.

The same applies at the end of Gaṇḍa; likewise at the middle of Puṣya. The meaning is that when one enters [the house] during the first half of Puṣya, peace (śānti) must be performed in exactly this manner.
"One should diligently perform the propitiatory rite on the eighth day or the twelfth day," so has Manu declared as necessary for the welfare of one born under the Mūla asterism.
Even the wealth of one's mother and father [should be given] for the pacification of the defects caused by kinsmen.
Thus concludes the propitiatory rite for the Mūla constellation as stated in the *Madanaratna* and the *Śaunaka*.
Regarding the hundred roots, these are those demonstrated by Daivajñamanohara in the *Purāṇasamuccaya*:
Barhiśśikhā, śamī, mātuluṅgī, harikrāntā, plakṣa, jayantī,
punarnavā, palāśa, and yavāñjī.
Śārapuṃkhā, aśvattha, puṇḍarīkā, varāhī, cūta, droṇapuṣpī,
kākajaṅghā, audumbara, and kumbhī.
Sulakṣmaṇā, jambū, śrīparṇī,
tumbikā, nadīvṛkṣa, damana, karkandhu, vetasa, and campaka.
Karcūrī, punnāga, padmaka, kāravallikā, arjuna, kāñcanapuṣpikā,
karkocakā, śoka, and siddheśvarī.
Cakranta, vakula, badarī, śvetārka, śamaṃtaka, rājavakṣas,
vyāghrapatrikā, sāla, and dhava.
Rudantī, tāla, kunda,
the root of aśvagandhā, mucukunda, munālī, pāṭalā, and gojihvā.
Garikarṇikā, śrīvṛkṣa, kṣīrakuṇḍukā, induvāru, the two types of bṛhatī, dāḍimī, apāmārga, balā, and bījapūra.
Śaṅkhapuṣpī, atibalā, brāhmī, kumārikā, pāṭhā, mallikā,
pallakī, nāgabalā, and bhṛṅgarāja.
Gandhārī, Jātī, Adhopuṣpī, Nirguṇḍī, Vakula, Matyākṣī,
Devarāśikā, Ketakī, and Cāṭarūpaka.
The banyan tree, plantain, river, guḍūcī, kākajaṅghā, kāśa,
the two types of niśā, barbarī, and ikṣumālā.
One should take śatamūlikā, tulasī, or the root of mustard; or vāgujī, kula, and alābū; or, in their absence, one may take the sap of excellent trees.
In the Madanaratna, Gārgya says on another occasion:
"The wise man himself should pluck [the roots], and his father [should pluck] a hundred roots."
Lakṣmaṇā, śatamūla, śireṣa, vetasa,
sahasrāśvetamūlā, viṣṇukrāntā, and śaṅkhinī.
Sarpākṣī, Mīnanetrā, and Putrapāṇi with palms joined in reverence;
Palāśa, Bilvaka, Rocana, and the two types of Candana.
Kṛṣṇamāṃsī, mura, uśīra, bālaka, as well as āmalā,
gojihvā, tulasī, iṣīkā, śatapuṣpā, and lāṅgalī [are recommended].
Brahmadaṇḍī, Droṇapuṣpī, white Priyaṅgu, white mustard,
Pippalā, Kākajaṅghā, Trāyamāṇā, and likewise Huhū.
Jyotiṣmatī, Gāndhārī, Gandha, Pūrṇakauśikī, Bhaga, Kṣamā, Subhadrā, Guḍūcī, and Indravāruṇī.
Alābukā, rudantī, kadalī, and likewise ketakī;
gokṣura, śataparvī, ariṣṭīkā, and parājitā.
Chinnaruhā, rudrā, śatapatrā, kuṃbhā, suvarcalā,
aśvagandhā, hastikarṇī, and likewise the second type of haridrā.
The camel-thorn, the honey-maker, the holy fig tree, the bakula, the barbarā, the apāmārga, the mandāra, and the atimuktaka;
Mālatī, Svarṇapuṣpā, Śrīparṇī, and likewise its fruit; the root of Darbha, Karavīra, Mudayantī, and Vikantaka.
Pāṭalā, devadāru, and likewise arka-sūdanikā;
the fruit of the manmatha tree and the sprout of the palāśa.
Rāsnā, river-side tree roots, suradāru, nidārikā,
śvetavīryā, śvetapākā, and likewise blue lotuses (nīlotpala).
One should likewise cast in nāgakesara, miṇḍīrī, and kumārī.

*Śatamūlā* is *śatāvarī*. *Sahakā* is *sahadenī*. *Śvetamūlā* is *punarnavā*. *Mīnanetrā* is *matsyākṣī*. *Putrapārā* is *putrajīva*. *Kṛtāñjali* is known as *añjalinīhātā*, commonly called *hodā*. *Palāśa* is the bitter root; it is both white and yellow. *Uśīra* is *vīraṇa*. *Āmalakī* is *bhūmyāmalakī*. *Gojihvā* is commonly known as *galakuṃbhī*. *Brahmadaṇḍī* is *adhaḥpuṣpī*, *droṇapuṣpī*, and *kañcukā*. *Kākajaṅghā* is *ekāṅgī*.

Jyotiṣmatī, Māla, Kāṅguṇī, Gāndhārī, Pūrṇā; Kauśikā, Kośātakī; Bhagakṣamā, Śigru; Subhadrā, Sārivā; Ālaṃbukā, Tuṃbī; Śataparvā, Avāriṣṭakā, Nāgavallī; Chinnaruhā, Apīḍa, Guḍūcī, Śatapattrā, Kamālinī; Nikumbha, Hastibhedaka; Suvarcalā, Sūryaphalā; Hastakarṇī, Heraṇḍa, Uṣṭrapīṭha; Sarjarasa, Bījaka, Ātimuktaka.

Mādhavī is the Jāti flower; Svarṇā is Puṣpākuśalī. Damayantī is Yudhikā. Ardhasūdanī is Vālakya. Manmathavṛkṣa is Ādru, Suradāru, and Devadāru. Vidārikā is Bhūkūṣmāṇḍī. Śvetavīryā is Girikarṇī. Śvetapākā is Guñjā. The rest is different.
Murā, māṃsī, vacā, kuṣṭha, śaileya, the two types of rajanī,
saṭī, campaka, and mustā— this is remembered as the group of all medicinal herbs (sarvauṣadhigaṇa).
Mūrvā, aikāṅgī, māṃsī, jaṭāmāṃsī, śaileya, manaḥśilā, and vacā—these eight, with coraka as the ninth, are the remaining [ingredients].

Regarding the ritual for the Mūla constellation: one should perform the Mūla-vidhāna by preparing a water-pot (udakuṃbha) filled with all medicinal herbs and all fragrances; it should be provided with cloth, incense, and flowers, and further endowed with white *siddhārtha* seeds and blossoms. Having recited the Rudra-hymns over it, as well as the Apratiratha and Rakṣoghna hymns, one should prepare a second vessel of water (modakuṃbha) joined with four streams, and hold roots above it.

Having placed them in a bamboo vessel and bound it with cloth, I shall describe the eighteen principal roots to be put therein: the golden root (*mūla*) weighing eighteen *māṣas*, the seven grains, *kāśmaryā*, *sahadevī*, *parājitā*, *bālā*, *pāṭhā*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *adhaḥpuṣpī*, *madhuyaṣṭikā*, *cakrāṅgikā*, *mayūraśikhā*, *kākajaṅghā*, the two types of *kumārikā*, *jīvantī*, *apāmārga*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, *lakṣmaṇā*, *jātī*, *vyāghrapattra*, *cakramardakī*, *siddheśvarā*, *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *palāśa*, and *plakṣa*.

Having filled [the vessel] with a hundred roots such as *vaṭārka*, *dūrvā*, *rohitaka*, *kāśa*, *mīśa*, *śatāvarī*, and so forth, I shall describe the six [types of] wood for it: one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) therein using wood from the *bilva*, *dhava*, *nimba*, *kadamba*, *rājavṛkṣa*, *ucchu*, *śālā*, *priyāsu*, *dadhipiṭtha*, *kovidāra*, *śleṣmātaka*, *vibhītaka*, *śālmali*, *sarala*, and all thorny trees, while excluding [others].
For the father, the child, and the mother, he spreads out a high seat made of udumbara wood with the formula "By the impulse of the god."

While she is seated there, he sprinkles her with the *sampāta* [remnants of the oblation], beginning from the head and following the hair’s growth, using mantras such as "The glory of the head... and so forth, touching the limbs according to their respective characteristics. After the bath, having poured milk-rice (*pāyasa*) into a vessel in the southwest, and having heated and wiped the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles made of *kāṣmarya* wood, and having offered the two *āghāra* libations and the two *ājyabhāga* portions, he should offer four oblations of the cooked rice with the verse "asunvantam" (RV 10.86.1). Then, he should offer fifteen oblations of clarified butter, each drawn in four ladlings, with the hymn "kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ" (RV 4.4.1–15).

With the two verses beginning with *mā nastoke*, the six verses beginning with *yā te rudra śivā tanūḥ*, the verse *agne rakṣāṃsi sedhati śukrajyotir amartyaḥ śuciḥ pāvaka īḍyaḥ*, and the verse *tvaṃ naḥ soma viśvato rakṣa rājann aṃhaso yaviṣṭha*, as well as from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering up to the end of the consumption [of the remains], he should give to the teacher a black cow, black sesame seeds, and a golden vessel containing the seven types of grain.

One should give a black ox to a Brahmin, or one should give a garment to those who announce the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*); one should give gold to other Brahmins; and one should feed the Brahmins with *kṛsara* rice and milk-rice (*pāyasa*). This is the procedure prescribed by Kātyāyana for one born under the *gaṇḍa* conjunction when the asterism presided over by the Serpent (*sarpa*) is involved; when this is performed, peace (*śānti*) is attained.

Gold weighing eighteen *māṣas* is prescribed; however, some do not read "eighteen *māṣas*. *Madhuyaṣṭikā* is liquorice (*jeṣṭhī-madhu*). *Atibalā* is marked with a discus. The names of the roots are as follows: *kāśmaryā*, *bālā*, *uśīraṃ*, *athapuṣpī*, *kākajaṅghā*, *cidrucirā*, *sulakṣmaṇā* (resembling a doll), *vrāṣupatrī*, *siddheśvarājātī*, *rohitakaṃ* (a fragrant grass), and others well-known. These thirty-two are essential. The others included within the *śatamūla* (the hundred roots) should also be taken.

In the absence of that [obligatory duty], there is an option (vikalpa) regarding those things which are neither prohibited nor enjoined, as well as those which have been enjoined and those which have been prohibited.

Now follows the procedure for the *Mūlāśānti* (propitiatory rite for the Mūla asterism) as taught by Śaunaka: At the prescribed time, having performed the birth-rite (*gomukhaprasava*), one should announce the place and time and make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "I shall perform the *Mūlanakṣatraśānti* according to the method taught by Śaunaka. Then, having performed the worship of Gaṇeśa, the recitation of the *Puṇyāha*, and the *Nāndīśrāddha*, one should select an *Ācārya*, a Brāhmaṇa, a *Sadasya*, and eight or four *Ṛtviks*, and honor them according to one's means with *madhuparka*, garments, ornaments, and other gifts.

Then the preceptor, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) and made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), "In this rite, I shall perform the duties of the preceptor," and having scattered mustard seeds while reciting "yadatra saṃsthitam," and having sprinkled the ritual ground with water while reciting the mantras beginning with "apohiṣṭhā," he should perform the worship of the deities of the pavilion and other rites according to the prescribed characteristics.
Then, having drawn a svastika there in the northeast quarter using colored powders (varṇaka).

Therein, having touched the earth with the mantra "mahī dyauḥ," and having cast into [the vessel] rice grains measuring one *droṇa* with the mantra "oṣadhayaḥ sam," and having placed nine new jars there with the mantra "ā kalaśeṣu," and having filled them with water from a sacred ford with the mantra "imaṃ me gaṅge," and [having added] fragrance with "gaṃdhadvārām," medicinal herbs with "yā auṣadhīyaḥ," barley with "oṣadhayaḥ sama," *dūrvā* grass with "kāṇḍāt kāṇḍāt," five types of sprouts with "aśvatthe vaḥ," five kinds of clay with "syonā pṛthivī," and fruit with "yāḥ phalinyāḥ."

Having placed the five gems along with the jewels, the five products of the cow with the verse beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā," and gold with the verse beginning "hiraṇyarūpam," and having wrapped the jar with a cloth using the verse beginning "yuvā suvāsāḥ," one should place a full vessel made of copper, bamboo, or similar material, using the verse beginning "pūrṇadarvī."

Some, however, based on an examination of the root text, maintain that the traditional practice is as follows: having placed upon rice a pitcher filled with water wrapped in cloth containing the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) along with gold and sprouts; then, after adding fruits, gems, medicinal herbs, and so forth, and performing the worship with perfumes and flowers, one should place four Rudra-pitchers in the four directions. Having touched the ground with the mantra "mahī dyauḥ" and scattered barley according to one's capacity, one should install the four pitchers and perform the rites up to the placement of the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*). In this regard, the mantras are to be repeated for each individual pitcher.

Then, having placed a golden image of Rudra upon a full vessel covered with cloth, one should worship it with the sixteen types of offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra) while invoking it with the mantra beginning with "tryambakam".

Vasiṣṭha is the seer and Rudra is the deity for the Anuṣṭubh [verse]. Then, having touched the water-pot (kumbha), a single officiating priest (ṛtvij) should mutter the Rudraikādaśinī if he belongs to the Yajurveda; a Bahvṛca (Ṛgvedin), however, should recite the four Rudra-sūktas; and a Chaṃdogin (Sāmavedin), the Rudra-sāmans. In this regard, according to one's capacity, the number [of recitations] should be taken as eleven, eight, three, two, or one. Some say that the Rudra [rite] is common to all; others say there is an option between the Susāman and the Rudra for the Bahvṛca and the Chaṃdogin. In that context, the ritual placement (nyāsa) and other details of the Rudra rite should be observed in the *Rudrapaddhati* composed by our own Guru.

For the hymn consisting of twenty-five verses beginning with "rakṣohaṇam," the seer is Āṅgirasa, the deities are Vāyu and Agni, and the meters are Triṣṭubh—with the last four being Anuṣṭubhs. Its application (viniyoga) is for recitation (japa). Here, the number [of recitations] should be taken according to one's capacity, following the previously mentioned method. Alternatively, one should recite the Pavamāna hymns once for each of the four [vessels]; or else, the recitation of these [mantras] may be performed only for the Rudra-vessel. Some say that the recitation for peace (śānti-japa) is to be performed at the four [locations]. Thus, in the event that five jars are not available, having established two jars—in this case, the previously mentioned Rudra-mantras and so forth are to be used for the Rudra-jar.
Regarding the recitation of all [mantras]: having invoked Varuṇa into this water-pot (kumbha), one should perform the recitation of the Śānti Rudra.

Alternatively, there may be only one [deity] in the place of each of the five jars; thus there are four outflows (*prasravaṇa*). In this regard, the rites for the central jar are performed at the center of the opening, while the rites for the four jars are performed at the four outflows—this is the distinction. Then, to the north of the jar previously established in the east, having fashioned [the design] with twenty-four, ten, or five colors—or else with white rice flour—at that point, in the pericarp (*karṇikā*):

Having established the pitcher with the verse beginning "mahīdvau," having filled it with water there using the mantra "imaṃ me gaṅge," and having cast fragrant paste there with the mantra "gaṃdhadvārām," one should deposit a hundred garlands therein.

In its absence, having added *viṣṇukrāntā*, *sahadevī*, *tulasī*, and *śatāvarī*, and having added *kuśa* grass and saffron (*kuṅkuma*), one should perform the rites from the verse beginning with "yā oṣadhīḥ" up to the placement of the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*). Having made a cloth canopy above, one should bathe the image of Nirṛti—made of half a *niṣka* of gold—with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) while reciting "mo ṣu naḥ," and having installed it in the pericarp, one should [worship] Indra to its south with the verse "indraṃ vo" (Rig Veda 10.89.1)—where Mathuṣchaṇḍas is the seer and Gāyatrī is the meter—and [worship] Varuṇa to its north with the verse beginning with "āpsum."

With the verse "medhātithirāpo'nuṣṭup," one should set down the water; the deities are the Viśvedevas, Viṣṇu, the Vasus, Varuṇa, Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pūṣan, the two Aśvins, Yama, Agni, Prajāpati, Soma, Rudra, Aditi, Bṛhaspati, the Sarpas, the Pitṛs, Bhaga, Aryaman, Savitṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, Vāyu, Indra-Agni, and Mitra. Then one should invoke the world-protectors (lokapālas).

Then, having performed the installation of the fire in the southwest (naiṛta), and having invoked the planets along with their respective [deities] in the northeast (īśānya) using their respective mantras, one should perform the anvādhāna.

Namely: having taken two fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and having uttered "for the eyes, with clarified butter" (*cakṣuṣyājyena*), [he offers] to the nine planets (*navagraha*) with a specified number of oblations of fuel-sticks, parched grain (*caru*), and clarified butter; to the presiding deities (*adhidevatā*), the secondary deities (*pratyadhidevatā*), the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), Vināyaka and the others, each with a specified number of oblations of fuel-sticks, parched grain, and clarified butter; to Nirṛti with one hundred and eight oblations of each respective substance; and to Indra and the Waters with twenty-eight oblations of each respective substance consisting of milk-rice porridge mixed with ghee, fuel-sticks, and clarified butter.

With fifteen *ṛc*-verses, eight times with *kṛsara* oblations for Agni, Kṣetrādhipati, Mitra-Varuṇa, and Agni—these being the eight—with *samit*, clarified butter, and *caru* oblations; for Soma thirteen times with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) oblations; for Rudra with clarified butter taken four times (*caturgṛhīta*); for Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, and Prajāpati with clarified butter; and for Sviṣṭakṛt with the remainder—and so forth, having performed the rites up to the placing of the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*), [one should offer] with their respective mantras.

One should perform the worship beginning with Nirṛti: therein, a pair of garments, red sandalwood paste, fragrance, black fragrant flowers, incense of ram's horn, a lamp of goat's fat, and *holikā* for the coarse food offering.

For a Brāhmaṇa, milk mixed with sugar should be placed in the position of *sūrā*, and rice-pudding (*pāyasa*) mixed with salt in the position of meat; for Kṣatriyas and others, these should be the primary offerings if available. Having performed this worship—including the *ācamana* and other rites, as well as the offering of handfuls of flowers—and having cooked the *pāyasa*, *kṛsara*, and *caru* oblations according to the sequence of the *anvādhāna* rite beginning with "amuṣmai," he should perform the rites up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings.
Then, the sacrificer should perform the formal renunciation (*tyāga*) on the right side, dedicating it to all the deities.
Thereafter, the Preceptor (*ācārya*), together with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), should offer the oblations as follows:

Having offered *samidh*, clarified butter, and *caru* in the previously mentioned number with the respective mantras of the nine planets, their presiding deities (*adhidevatās*), and their secondary deities (*pratyadhidevatās*), as well as Vināyaka and others; then, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should offer the four substances in sequence with the mantras of Nirṛti, Indra, and Āpa:

With the fifteen-verse hymn beginning "kṛṇuṣva" (RV 4.4), composed by Gotama Vāmadeva, in the *ṛṣabha* meter, for the destruction of demons (*rakṣohan*), there is the application (*viniyoga*) in the *kṛsara-homa*. One should offer [the oblation] eight times for each verse.

Having offered eight oblations of *kṛsara* with the *Gāyatrī* mantra, [the following are prescribed]: for "to Jātavedas," Kaśyapa is the seer, Durgā is the deity, Triṣṭubh is the meter, and *kṛsara* is the application; for "tryambakam," Vasiṣṭha is the seer, Rudra is the deity, Anuṣṭubh is the meter, and *kṛsara* is the application; for "sīrā yuñjanti," Budha is the Soma-seer, the Ṛtviks are the deities, Gāyatrī is the meter, and *kṛsara* is the application; for "tām agne," Saubhari is the seer, Durgā is the deity, Triṣṭubh is the meter, and *kṛsara* is the application by way of the number eight; for "agnim īḷe," Kāṇva is the Medhātithi-seer, Agni is the deity, Gāyatrī is the meter, and *kṛsara* is the application by way of the number eight.

With the [verses] numbered: for Kṣetra, Vāmadeva is the seer, Kṣetrapāla is the deity, Anuṣṭubh is the meter; with eight repetitions of the number, Kṛsara (rice-and-pulse porridge) is the offering. For Dṛṇānā, Jamadagni is the seer, Mitra and Varuṇa are the deities, Gāyatrī is the meter; with eight repetitions of the number, Kṛsara is the offering. For the verse beginning "Agniṃ dūtam," Aṅgirasa is the seer, Bṛhaspati-Aṅgāraka is the deity, Gāyatrī is the meter; with eight repetitions of the number, Kṛsara is the offering. For the hymn of fifteen verses beginning with "Hiraṇyavarṇām," Ānanda, Kardama, Ṛcīka, Indira, and Suta are the seers; Śrī is the deity; the first three are Anuṣṭubhs; the fourth is a Prastāra.

The fifth and sixth [verses] are *paṅkti*s; the two following are *triṣṭubh*s; the next three are *anuṣṭubh*s; and the final one is a *prastārapaṅkti*. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the oblation (*homa*):
one should offer fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and cooked rice (*caru*) with each verse, using a number of twenty-eight or eight times as many as appropriate.

Regarding the verse *tvanno soma viśvataḥ*, the *pragādha* is Soma, the meter is *triṣṭubh*, and its application (*viniyoga*) is in the milk-oblation (*pāyasa-homa*). Whether by the mantra *tvanno soma viśvagopāḥ* or *tvanno jakṛtuḥ*, for these two [verses], Indra Vimada is the seer, Soma is the deity, and the meter is *prastarapaṅkti*. Then, having taken four portions of clarified butter (*ājya*), one should offer with the mantra *yā te rudra śivā tanūḥ*; Kaśyapa is the seer, Rudra is the deity, and the meter is *svarāḍ-anuṣṭubh*. With this, one should sacrifice.
Then, having offered the *ājya* with the *sruva* ladle using the individual and collective *vyāhṛti* mantras, one should perform the expiatory rites beginning with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.

Thereafter, one should present offerings of *māṣa*-beans and lamps to the guardians of the quarters (*dikpālas*), the nine planets (*navagrahas*), Vināyaka and the others, Nirṛti, Indra, the Waters (*adbhas*), Rudra, and the guardians of the field (*kṣetrapālas*).

Then the preceptor or the sacrificer, having filled the *sruk* ladle and placed fruits and other items therein, should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* (full oblation). The mantras for this are as follows: for the eleven verses beginning with "samiddho agna ūrmiḥ," Gautama is the seer, Vāmadeva is the deity, Agni is the fire, Triṣṭubh is the meter, and the final verse is in Jagatī; their application (*viniyoga*) is in the *pūrṇāhuti* homa.

*Prajāpate*, *Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ*, *Prajāpatiḥ*, *Sṛṣṭyai*, *Pūrṇādarvī*, *Viśvedevāḥ*, *Śatakratuḥ*, and *Anuṣṭubh*; these are the applications (*viniyoga*) for the offering of the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). *Saptate agne*, *Saptavānagneḥ*, and *Jagatī*; this is the application for the offering of the full oblation. Having thus offered the full oblation and completed the remainder of the ritual procedure beginning with the bringing of the *praṇītā* water, if one intends to perform the rite for pacification (*śānti*) within the fire, one should consign [the fire] into it at this time. However, if the sacrifice to the nine planets (*navagraha-makha*) is to be performed together with the pacification rite, then the sacrifice to the nine planets must now be performed separately in that very same fire.
Then, having touched the central pitcher from the right among the four pitchers, one should recite the mantra "Tryambakam" one hundred times.

The Bahvṛcas [should recite] the Rudra-sūktas; the Sāmagas, the Rudra-sāmans; and the Atharvaṇas, at least the Tryambaka mantra. Alternatively, having performed the worship eleven, eight, three, two, or one time, and having performed the secondary ablution (*upasnāna*) with the mantra "tryambakaṃ yajāmahe," the preceptor (*ācārya*), together with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), shall take all the water from the jars into another vessel. Then, having seated the patron (*yajamāna*)—whose limbs have been anointed with unguents and who wears a new garment—to the left of whom is seated his wife, also wearing a new garment and accompanied by their son, he shall proceed with the rites to be described hereafter.

One should perform the consecration with mantras: With the three verses beginning "tribhiṣṭvaṃ deva," Vasiṣṭha is the seer (*ṛṣi*). For the first three verses, Agni is the deity; for the following four, the Viśvedevas are the deities. The first is in the *gāyatrī* meter, the second in the *anuṣṭubh* meter, the next three in the *gāyatrī* meter, and the last two in the *anuṣṭubh* meter. Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the consecration (*abhiṣeka*). With the nine-verse hymn beginning "āpo hiṣṭhā," Ambarīṣa, Sindhu, Dvīpa, and the Waters are the seers. The first eight are in the *gāyatrī* meter, and the last two are in the *anuṣṭubh* meter. The fifth is in the *vardhamānā* meter and the seventh in the *pratiṣṭhā* meter. Their application is in the consecration.
For the two verses beginning with *āpa idu*, the seers are the Seven Sages; the deity is the Viśvedevas; the meter is Anuṣṭubh; the application is for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

For [the mantra] beginning with *sahasrākṣeṇa*, the seer is Prājāpatya; the deity is Yakṣanāla; the meter is Triṣṭubh; the application is for the consecration. With the three mantras found in the *Staṃbaśākhā* beginning with *devasya tvā*, and for the six [mantras] beginning with *yajñagratas*, the seer is Prajāpati; the meter is Triṣṭubh; the application is for the consecration.
Then: May that god Vajradhara, Mahendra, who has the elephant as his vehicle,
dispel the defects born at birth for the child and for the mother and father.
May that god who wields the spear, whose vehicle is the fire,
the seven-tongued forest-fire Agni, dispel the root defect.
May that god Yama, the wielder of the staff, whose vehicle is the buffalo and who is Dharma himself,
dispel the defects of my newborn infant.
May that Lord Khaḍgadhara, the sovereign of the Rākṣasas in the direction of Nirṛti,
pacify the affliction arising from the fundamental [constellations] and produced by the junctions of the Gaṇḍāntas.
May that god who holds the noose— Varuṇa, the lord of waters,
whose vehicle is the crocodile, and who is known as Pracetas— dispel the sin arising from the root.
May that deity who is the life-breath of the world— the Wind-god whose vehicle is the deer—
grant peace and pacify the affliction arising from the root for this child.
May that Lord Vidhipati— the wielder of the sword and mounted upon a horse—
dispel the fundamental defects of the mother, the father, and the child.
May that Lord Paśupati— the wielder of the Pināka bow and whose vehicle is the bull—
swiftly dispel the defect of the Gaṇḍānta occurring at the junctions of Āśleṣā and Mūla.
May Viṣṇu, Śiva, the guardians of the fields, Durgā, the world-protectors, and the nine planets— all who bestow peace— pacify every affliction.

Then, one should consecrate [the patron] with the verses beginning with "tataḥ surāstu... and so forth. The application (*viniyoga*) of "tac chaṃ yoḥ, śaṃ yur viśve devāḥ, śakvarī" is for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*). Then, having been consecrated by the water from the *śānti*-pitcher dedicated to Rudra and Nirṛti, using another [pitcher] with a hundred holes held between [himself and the pitcher], the patron, having put on two washed garments, having applied the *tilaka*, having worn the sacred ash (*vibhūti*), and having worshipped the preceptor (*ācārya*) and others preceded by the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to them.
Therein, he should give to the preceptor a milch cow with her calf as the fee;
and according to Kaśyapa:

It is stated that one should give a bull and a lump of iron to the preceptor (ācārya) along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). A bull should be given to the Brahmin; a black ox to the reciter of the Rudras; and to the officiating priests (ṛtvij), having given sacrificial fees according to one's ability and even more than that, and having performed the subsequent worship for the Nṛttas, Rutyas, and others, one should dismiss them with the words, "O hosts of gods, depart. Having received blessings from the hand of the preceptor, having worshipped the fire, and having dismissed it with the words, "Go, go," one should [feed] a hundred, or fifty, or ten Brahmins.
Having eaten together and caused the recitation of the Śānti Sūkta to be performed, having recited "yasya smṛtyā," and having offered the ritual action (karman) to the Lord (Īśvara), one should eat.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the *Mūla-śānti* in the *Śāntiratna* composed by Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa.
Now, in the *Madanaratna*, as stated in the *Pitāmaha-saṃhitā*:
"Two *ghaṭikās* at the beginning of *Mūla* and likewise two at the end of *Jyeṣṭhā* [are inauspicious]."
That should be known as the "unconsumed root" (abhuktamūla); one should abandon a child born during that time.
In the first quarter of the root [nakṣatra], there is the obstacle (gaṇḍa) of the father; the second is the obstacle of the mother;
the third pertains to wealth and grain; and the final quarter brings auspiciousness.
In Āśleṣā, all results are contrary, just as in Mūla;
so too are Śūla, Vyāghāta, Vajra, Vyatīpāta, and Vaidhṛti.
When [a birth] is joined with the defects of the lunar mansion (pariṣa), the day (vāra), viṣṭi, or the poisonous nāḍīs,
the defect of the root-nakṣatra (mūladoṣa) becomes even more severe.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the auspicious ritual procedure for pacification (śāntikarma):
[one should offer] a sacrifice to Vāyu with a niṣka, or eight [coins], and a sacrifice to Nirṛti with gold.
If a snake-bite occurs, the wise man should fashion a pit in the shape of a serpent;
he should make the pit one cubit in length and likewise one cubit in width.
It is joined with three girdles and is likewise endowed with a yoni.
One should have a pavilion constructed there according to one's wealth and means; then, having proclaimed an auspicious day and made a firm resolve according to the prescribed rite.
The wise man should choose four priests adorned with ornaments;
afterwards, he should choose the preceptor (ācārya), who is likewise adorned with sacrificial garments and other ornaments.
Having brought four well-adorned black-colored jars and a large,
beautifully decorated jar provided with a hundred holes;
Wrapped in thread, one should place it in the center upon the grain;
[therein are placed] herbs such as the hundred-roots, flowers, and nine kinds of jewels.
Clay ten times [the usual amount], likewise five sprouts,
the decoctions of the five trees, and similarly the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
As well as the five fragrant substances, the merchandise, the three metals,
all kinds of grain, and likewise kusha and durva grass.
One should place all the waters of the sacred fords (tīrtha) into all the jars;
I shall now state the roots of those which number one hundred by name.
Sahadevī, śikhā, puṃkhā, viṣṇukrāntā, punarnavā,
candravṛkṣā, white guñjā, dugdhikā, and likewise balā.
Kākabaṃdhu, vāyadūrvā, kākamācī,
śatāvarī, karkara, surasa, brāhmī, nirguṇḍī, musalī, and vacā.
Varṣābhū, śaṅkhinī, pāṭhā, samaṅgā, the two types of bṛhatī,
apāmārga, kuśa, bhṛṅga, kāsakhaṇḍaka, and rūpaka;
The lordly Śrīvṛkṣa, barley, Plakṣa, Brahmavṛkṣa, Udumbara, and mango;
Jambū, Bilva, Murā, Māṃsī, Musta, Ariṣṭa, and the two types of Niśā.
Kadali, ketaki, tāla, śrīparṇī, sallakī, as well as pāṭalā, lodhra, kośara, kośātakī, and agnimantha.
Jīvantī, pomegranate, śāla, tamāla, bījapūraka, punnāga, vakula, kunda, mathura, and mucukundaka.
Mudga, māṣa, balā, nandyāvarta, kuraṇṭaka,
campaka, nyubjaka, kuṣṭha, guḍūcī, and likewise āmalakī.
Uśīra, bāla-khadira, and likewise karañja;
the kanda, the aśvattha tree, karāhvā, and granthiparṇikā.
The girdle, the conch-shell, the snake, the pot-herb,
as well as the lotus, the water-lily, the bud, the blue lotus, and the two large ones.
These hundred roots remove all misfortunes;
in the absence of the hundred roots, one should throw in all medicinal herbs.
In the absence of all medicinal herbs, one should cast in ten specific herbs;
in the absence of all roots, one should cast in a measure of gold.
Devadāru, the two types of niśā, padma, as well as nīlotpala,
kuṣṭha, raudra, priyaṅgu, tagara, and likewise the root.
Emblic myrobalan, vacā, karṇī, mustard seeds, ginger,
as well as mūrvā, māṃsī, caṇḍī, uśīra, and vālaka.
Śailajā, gṛdhraparṇī, śrīkhaṇḍa, and likewise tāraka— these,
together with siddhi and vṛddhi, are proclaimed to be all the medicinal herbs.
Kuṣṭha, māṃsī, the two types of haridrā, mūra, śaileya, candana, vacā, karpūra, and mustā— these are remembered as the ten universal medicinal herbs (sarvauṣadhyaḥ).
One should deposit the medicinal herbs and other items with the mantra "yā oṣadhī," and one should deposit the nine gems along with the jewels using the [appropriate] mantra.
Taking up the earth with the mantra "udhṛtāsī," one should place it down;
and with the mantra "pra vo yajñam," one should cast in the sprouts.
One should cast the *tvak* and *caka* with the mantra "yāścedam," and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) with the *gāyatrī*, and *dūrvā* grass with the mantra "kāṇḍātkāṇḍāt."
With "madhu vātā" one should place honey-flavored [sugar], and with "pavase" sugar;
at the mouth of the jar is Brahmā, in the middle is Rudra, and likewise Hari.
May all the oceans, rivers, sacred fords, and givers of water come to the patron of the sacrifice, bringing about the destruction of his misfortunes.
"imaṃ me varaṇa" is the first; "tvā yāmi" is the second; "tvanno agne" is the third; and "satvanno agne" follows thereafter.
The preceptor should worship the great pitcher with the root mantra;
for the root is progeny, and the root is indeed all this, even unto the serpent.
Within the city of Śatacchidra, one should worship the deity right there;
one should clothe Nirṛti and the Lord of Serpents with a pair of garments.
One should worship Indra and the other world-protectors with their respective mantras;
having thus completed the worship, one should then perform the rite of fire-oblation (homa).
One should properly perform the oblation with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, and sesame seeds—
either one thousand and eight times, or one hundred and eight times.
The root mantra, the mantra for the progeny, and the eight mantras—these are the words for the oblations in their proper order;
thereafter, one should perform the secondary oblation (anuhoma) with clarified butter together with the sacrificial porridge (caru).
With the mantras "Svāhā to Prajāpati" and "Svāhā to the serpents," he should,
being well-composed, perform the oblation of the Vyāhṛtis.
One should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and perform the consecration;
then, having sprinkled [the disciple], one should hold a hundred-holed [vessel] over the head.
They should pour [the water] through a hundred holes with mantras originating from Varuṇa,
with the mantras beginning with "samudrajyeṣṭhāḥ," and likewise with the mantra "devasya tvā."
With the mantra "śiro me śrīḥ," with the three mantras beginning with "āpo hiṣṭhā," and with the mantras "punantu mā devā janāḥ" and "trātāram indram," [he should perform the rite].
Having discarded the wet garments with the mantras beginning with "dveṣaśānti" and also with the mantras mentioned in the *Mātsya-purāṇa*, one should present them to the preceptor.
Having performed the inspection of the clarified butter, one should cause it to be given to a virtuous Brahmin;
likewise, one should give a bull and an iron ball to the preceptor.
One should give as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) a cow with her calf adorned with all ornaments;
half of that should be given to the Brahman priest, and half of that to the officiating priests (ṛtvij).
Thereafter, one should feed the Brahmins according to one's capacity; the man who, full of devotion, performs this rite of pacification according to this injunction [attains his desired goal].
Longevity, health, sovereignty, and fame shall certainly be his.
Thus ends the pacification of Mūla and Āśleṣā, composed by Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa.
Now follows the propitiation for Āśleṣā.
Regarding the results for each quarter (pāda) therein, it is stated in the Jayārṇava:
"The head, the two eyes, the throat, the pair of ears, and the two arms."
The heart, knees, genitals, and feet are the parts of the body that must always be covered.
The channels (nāḍīs) are, in sequence: five, three, two, seven, four, eleven, nine, eight, and five.
Sovereignty, loss of father, destruction of mother, delight in sensual pleasures and activities,
devotion to the ancestors, powerful, wealthy, generous, and an enjoyer of luxuries— in this order.

The specific details should be understood from the *Nirṇayasindhu*; as Śaunaka says regarding the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) for those born under Āśleṣā: "I shall now describe the excellent propitiation for those born under Āśleṣā;
on the twelfth day after birth, one should perform the propitiatory fire-oblation (*śānti-homa*)."
If it is impossible on one's birth star, then on another auspicious day,
having bathed and performed the anointing and other rites, one should select the most excellent brahmins.
According to one's means, there should be five jars for the manifestation [of the deity], or two;
one for the installation of the deity, and one for the consecration with the Rudra-mantras.
Having placed [the image] in a water-pot according to the method prescribed for the root asterism,
one should worship it in a place smeared with cow-dung and beautifully adorned with pavilions.
One should cause a lotus to be made there, endowed with twenty-four petals; or one should have it made with rice grains that are red, yellow, white, and black.
The wise one should place [the deity] upon the pericarp and establish the water-pot (kalaśa) therein;
the ritual installation of the pot within the impurities is prescribed by means of the mantra beginning with "ā".

One should fill [the vessel] with water from a sacred ford (tīrtha) while reciting the mantra "imaṃ me gaṅge," and one should worship the pitcher with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings using their respective mantras.
One should cast pearl-oysters, gems, medicinal herbs, and other such items while reciting the *palinī* mantra into the vessel placed upon the pitcher; then, one should worship the image of Āśleṣā.
Having caused [the image] to be made according to his capacity, either with four feet or without feet,
he should worship it under the previously mentioned asterism in the south and north.

One should worship the remaining constellations, beginning from Indra and ending with Dīśāna, according to the procedure stated for the Mūla [constellation]. The two jars should be consecrated with mantras.
The worship of Rudra in the Rudra-kumbha should be performed as previously described;
this is declared to be the mantra for the worship of the serpents.
He has the form of a serpent, is red, possesses eyes like a woman's, and has two arms; he wears yellow garments, holds a shield and a sword, is fierce, and is adorned with divine ornaments.
Having meditated thus and then performed worship, one should commence the rite of fire-oblation (homa);
the practitioner should perform it according to the path prescribed in his own Vedic branch, or the preceptor may do so.
Having performed the ritual up to the mouth [of the fire] and having taken the oblation according to the scriptures,
one should offer it with the mantra "idaṃ sarpebhyo juhomi" and perform the rites for the Sādhi and Pratyadhi deities.
Alternatively, one hundred and eight or twenty-eight [times],
one should perform the sequence of the fire-oblation (homa) according to the procedure prescribed for the root asterism (mūlanakṣatra).
Having performed the rites ending with the *pūrṇāhuti* offering and likewise the *saṃpāta*,
one should cast them into the pitcher during the recitations and then perform the consecration (*ābhiṣeka*).
The preceptor, together with the officiating priests and his own sons, should likewise consecrate the sacrificer along with his wife and children, as previously described.
One should perform the consecration with the waters from the consecrated jar;
likewise, one should sprinkle [the disciple] with the sprouts while reciting Puranic mantras.
May all the defects of the mother, father, wealth, kinsmen, brothers, relatives, family, and position of one born under the asterism Āśleṣā be dispelled.
May that presiding deity named Vāgeśvara, Bṛhaspati,
dispel the Gaṇḍānta for the mother, the father, and the child.
May the ancestors always protect all the brothers, the father,
the wealth, the kinsmen, and the relatives of one born under the constellation of the serpents (Āśleṣā).
When the consecration has been performed in this manner, the pacification of the serpent [deity] will certainly occur.
Thereafter, the patron, wearing white garments and well-adorned, [should proceed].
Then, one should satisfy the learned brahmins with gifts as if they were the very root;
by this knowledge thus spoken, may all misfortune be dispelled.
All desires shall be fulfilled, and one's lifespan shall be as declared in the Vedas.
He spoke the mantra for the water-offering (arghya):
"O Lord of Serpents, O Sovereign of the hosts of Nāgas, salutations to you!"
Accept this water offering given by me for the pacification of all misfortunes.
One should perform [the rite] as in the case of the Mūla asterism; in the Sarpagaṇḍa, it is according to its own name.

Regarding the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one should perform the modification of the ritual as follows: "for the pacification of the defects arising from birth under the *gaṇḍānta* asterisms of Āśleṣā and Mūla.
This is according to Śaunaka. Now, the procedure for the *Āśleṣā-śānti*:
The application (*prayoga*) is as follows: [Insert specific ritual details here].

At the appointed time, having performed the *gomukhaprasava* rite, and having proclaimed the place and time (*deśakāla*), one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) as follows: "For the sake of pacifying the portents of danger to my father and others indicated by the birth of this boy under the asterism of Āśleṣā, and for the pleasure of the Lord Śrī Parameśvara, I shall perform the sacrifice to the nine planets (*navagrahahoma*) and the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) for the birth under the asterism of Āśleṣā. Having thus resolved, one should perform the worship of Gaṇeśa, the recitation of the *puṇyāha*, the worship of the Mothers, and the *nāndī-śrāddha*; thereafter, one should select the Preceptor (*ācārya*) and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

Then the preceptor, having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), "In this rite, I shall perform the duties of the preceptor," and having scattered mustard seeds while reciting "yad atra saṃsthitim," and having sprinkled the ritual ground with the mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," and having drawn a svastika with five colors in the northeast direction, and having touched the earth there while reciting "mahī dyauḥ," and having poured in a measure of one *droṇa* of rice while reciting "oṣadhayaḥ saṃ vadante," and having placed the water-pot there while reciting "tatrā kalaśeṣu," and having filled it with water while reciting "imaṃ me" and "gaṅge," [he should recite] "gandhadvārām."

Having cast in perfumes and flowers; with the verse "yā oṣadhīḥ," medicinal herbs; with "samit" (the word *samit*), barley; with "kāṇḍāt kāṇḍāt," twigs; with "aśvatthe vaḥ," the five sprouts (*pañcapallava*); with "syonā," seven types of earth; with "yā phalinīḥ," fruit; with "sa hi ratnāni," the five gems (*pañcaratna*); with the three verses beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā," the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*); and with "hiraṇyarūpa," gold—having thus placed these in and having wrapped [the vessel] with cloths while reciting "yuvā suvāsāḥ," one should set down a full vessel with the verse "pūrṇād arvaḥ."

Then, having invoked Mṛtyuñjaya into a golden image of Rudra placed within a vessel situated upon a full vessel (pūrṇapātra) with the mantra "Tryambakam," one should worship him—of this [mantra], Vasiṣṭha is the seer, Rudra is the deity, and Anuṣṭubh is the meter.

Then, one of the officiating priests (ṛtvij), having touched the water-pot (kumbha), should recite the Rudraikādaśinī. If the sacrificer (yajamāna) is a follower of the Yajurveda, he should do so; if he is a Bahvṛca (Ṛgvedin), he should recite the four Rudra-sūktas; if he is a Chandoga (Sāmavedin), he should recite the Rudra-sāmans. Regarding the number of recitations for the Sūktas and Sāmans, the counts eleven, eight, three, two, and one are to be taken respectively. Some say that the Rudra [mantra] is common to all, whereas for the Bahvṛca and Chandoga, there is an option between the Sūkta and the Sāman along with the Rudra [mantra]. It is precisely in this manner that the learned perform it. In that regard, the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Rudra-mantras and other details should be observed in the *Śrīgururudrapaddhati*.

Regarding the Rudra-hymns: the nine verses beginning with *kadrudrāya* have Aghora as the seer, Kaṇva as the deity, and Gāyatrī as the meter; the single verse beginning with *imā rudrāya* has Kutsa as the seer and Rudra as the deity—the first three are Jagatīs and the last two are Triṣṭubhs; the fifteen verses beginning with *ā te pitar* have Gṛtsamada as the seer and Rudra as the deity, in the Triṣṭubh meter; the verse *tam u ṣṭuhi* has Bhaugotra as the seer and Rudra as the deity, in the Triṣṭubh meter; the verse *bhuvanasya pitaraḥ* has Ṛjiśvan as the seer and Rudra as the deity, in the Triṣṭubh meter; and the verse *tryambakaṃ yajāmahe* has Vasiṣṭha as the seer and Rudra as the deity, in the Anuṣṭubh meter. The details regarding the seers and other elements for the Rudra-sāman are found in the *Tulāpuruṣa-paddhati*.
It should be observed: then one should recite "Tryambaka" one thousand and eight times, and the *Pāvamānī* verses over the central pitcher.

Then, over the eastern pitcher, one should recite the thirteen verses beginning with "Āśuḥ śiśānaḥ"; Indra is the *ṛṣi*, Indra is the deity, *triṣṭubh* is the meter, and the final verse is *anuṣṭubh*. Over the southern pitcher, [one should recite] the section beginning with "Tvaṃ hyagne rudraḥ"; Havyavāṭ is the *ṛṣi*, the self of Agni is the deity, *jagatī* is the meter. Over the western pitcher, [one should recite] "Rakṣohaṇam"; Vāmadeva is the *ṛṣi*, Agni is the deity, and *triṣṭubh* is the meter.

In the northern pitcher (*uttarakuṃbha*): for the twenty-five verses beginning with *rakṣohaṇam*, [the seers are] Aṅgiras; [the deities are] Vāyu and Agni; the metre is *triṣṭubh*, and the last four are *anuṣṭubh*. The application (*viniyoga*) is for recitation (*japa*).

Here too, the previously mentioned number should be taken according to one's capacity. In the absence of five pitchers, having placed a pitcher with four streams and five faces, one should perform everything right there.
Then, having made a twenty-four-petaled lotus of five colors to the north of the pitcher, one should place it in the pitcher on the pericarp as before.
In that regard, there is no restriction concerning the rice grains:

one should scatter the "fruit-bearing" gems and herbs, saying "yāḥ phalinīḥ. Then, upon the full vessel placed on top of the pitcher, one should invoke the serpent named Āśleṣa with the mantra "namaḥ astu sarpebhyaḥ."
Then he was entirely red, three-eyed, and two-armed, wearing blue garments;
he held a shield and a sword, was fierce, and adorned with divine ornaments.

Having thus meditated upon the serpent, one should invoke Bṛhaspati into his image to the south with the mantra, "Bṛhaspate gṛtsamadaḥ, bṛhaspatistriṣṭup," and then invoke the Pitṛs into the image of the Pitṛs to the north with the mantra, "Udīratāṃ śaṅkhaḥ pitarastraiṣṭubham. Then, starting from the east among the twenty-four lotus petals, one should invoke the lunar mansions (nakṣatras) beginning with Pūrvaphalgunī and ending with Punarvasu, along with their respective deities.

Namely: Aryaman, Bhaga, Savitṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, Vāyu, Indra-Agni, Mitra, Indra, Nirṛti, the Waters, the Viśvedevas, Viṣṇu, the Vasus, Ājaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pūṣan, the Aśvins, Yama, Agni, Prajāpati, Soma, Rudra, and Aditi.

Then, having invoked the World-Guardians (Lokapālas), the Preceptor (Ācārya) shall establish the Fire, the images, and the Planets (Grahas), and then perform the supplementary offerings (Ānvādhāna): to each of the Nine Planets with a specified number of oblations of fuel-sticks (samit), parched grain (caru), and clarified butter (ājya); to Bṛhaspati and the Ancestors (Pitṛs) with twenty-eight oblations of each substance consisting of ghee-mixed milk-rice (pāyasa), fuel-sticks, and clarified butter; and to the twenty-four deities beginning with Bhaga, each with eight oblations of milk-rice and clarified butter; [and finally] to the Rakṣohaṇa.

With fifteen *ṛc*s beginning with "kṛṇuṣva," with eight offerings of *kṛsarā* for each verse, one should worship Savitṛ, Durgā, Tryambaka, the praise of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), Vāstoṣpati, Agni, Kṣetrapati, and Mitra-Varuṇa—each with eight oblations of *kṛsarā*, fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice; Soma with thirteen oblations of milk-rice (*pāyasa*); and Rudra with clarified butter taken four times (in the ladle), as well as Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya.

Having performed the oblation to Prajāpati with clarified butter, followed by the *sviṣṭakṛt* with the remainder, and so forth, up to the placement of the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*), he should cook the milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and the *kṛsara* porridge, and perform the rites up to the portioning of the clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*). Then, the sacrificer, standing to the south, should perform the renunciation (*tyāga*) dedicated to all the deities.

The preceptor, together with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*). It is as follows: having offered oblations to the nine planets, the presiding deities (*adhidevatā*), the secondary deities (*pratyadhidevatā*), Vināyaka and others, and the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) with their respective mantras; having offered the fourfold substances to all of them with the mantra "Salutation to the serpents" (*namo astu sarpebhyaḥ*), to Bṛhaspati, and to the ancestors (*pitṛ*) with their respective mantras according to the prescribed number; one should offer oblations eight times to the twenty-four deities beginning with Bhaga using their individual name-mantras.

Then, for the *kṛsara* oblation: the application (*viniyoga*) of the fifteen-verse hymn beginning with "kṛṇuṣva" is by Gotama; it is addressed to Vāmadeva, is for the destruction of demons (*rakṣohan*), and is in the *triṣṭubh* meter.
The application of the *gāyatrī* verse to Savitṛ, the verse to Jātavedas, and the verse to Kaśyapa-Durgā is for the *kṛsara* oblation in the *triṣṭubh* meter.
The application of the verse "tryambakam" by Vasiṣṭha, addressed to Rudra, is for the *kṛsara* oblation in the *anuṣṭubh* meter.

For the verse beginning with *sīrā yuñjanti*, the seers are Budha and Saumya, the deity is Ṛksuti, the meter is Gāyatrī, and its application is in the *kṛsara* oblation. For the verse beginning with *tām agnivarṇām*, the seer is Saubhari, the deity is Durgā, the meter is Triṣṭubh, and its application is in the *kṛsara* oblation. For the verse beginning with *vāstoṣpate*, the seer is Vasiṣṭha, the deity is Vāstoṣpati, the meter is Triṣṭubh, and its application is in the *kṛsara* oblation.
The application (*viniyoga*) for the *kṛsara* oblation is as follows: for the verse beginning with "gṛṇānā," Jamadagni is the seer, Mitra and Varuṇa are the deities, and Gāyatrī is the meter;
for the verse beginning with "agnim dūtam," Aṅgiras is the seer, Virūpa is the deity, Agni is the deity, Gāyatrī is the meter, and its application is in the *kṛsara* oblation;

and for the hymn (*sūkta*) consisting of fifteen verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇām," Ānanda, Kardama, Cīklīta, and Indirāsuta are the seers, Śrī is the deity, the first three verses are in the Anuṣṭubh meter, and the fourteenth is in the Prastārapaṅkti meter.
The fifth and sixth verses are *triṣṭubh*s; then follow eight *anuṣṭubh*s, the last of which is a *prastārapaṅkti*. This is the application (*viniyoga*) for the oblation (*homa*):
one should offer fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and cooked rice (*caru*) eight hundred and sixty-eight times according to that number.
With the verse beginning "tvannaḥ soma," one should offer the cooked rice (*caru*) eight hundred and sixty-eight times according to that number.

The mantra "tvanno soma viśvatogopā" (or alternatively, "tavannaḥ soma sukratuḥ") belongs to Indra Vimada; its meter is *prastārapaṅkti*. Then, having taken four portions of clarified butter (*ājya*), one should offer it with the verse "yā te rudra" [RV 7.59.12], for which Kaśyapa is the seer, Rudra is the deity, and *svarāḍanuṣṭubh* is the meter. After that, having offered clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle using all the *vyāhṛtis*, one should perform the rites beginning with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering up to the end of the expiatory oblations (*prāyaścitta-homa*).
Then, one should offer oblations together with lamps to the guardians of the directions, the nine planets, Vināyaka and the others, to Nirṛti, Indra, the Waters, Rudra, and Kṣetrapāla.

Then the preceptor or the sacrificer, having taken four portions—or indeed twelve—of clarified butter, filling the *sruk* ladle and placing fruits and other offerings therein, should offer the *pūrṇāhuti*. The mantras for this are as follows: eleven verses from the hymn beginning with "samudrād ūrmiḥ," attributed to Gautama Vāmadeva, in the *triṣṭubh* meter (the last being in *jagatī*), are applied to the *pūrṇāhuti* homa; and the verse "prajāpataye hiraṇyagarbhāya," addressed to Prajāpati Hiraṇyagarbha, in the *triṣṭubh* meter, is applied to the *pūrṇāhuti* homa.

Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* with these [mantras], and having performed the remaining rites such as the removal of the *praṇītā* water and so forth, he should touch the central jar from among the four jars on the right side; if the sacrificer belongs to the Yajurveda, he should also mutter the *tryambaka* mantra and the *rudraikādaśinī*.

The Bahvṛcas [should recite] the Rudra-sūktas; if he is a Sāmaga, the Rudra-sāmans; if he is an Ararvan, only the Tryambaka mantra. Here too, the Rudra-japa is performed according to the numbers eleven, eight, three, two, or one; for all, there is a hundred-fold recitation of the Tryambaka mantra. Then, having worshipped the Rudra serpents with the five offerings (pañcopacāra) and having performed the ritual salutation (upasthāna) with the words "May Tryambaka bow to all," the preceptor (ācārya), together with the officiating priests (ṛtviks), takes water from all the vats into another vessel and [sprinkles] the patron (yajamāna) with all the medicinal herbs.

Having dressed the husband in new garments and seated his wife, who is likewise anointed on her limbs and accompanied by their son, he should sprinkle them with the mantras to be recited hereafter. For the six verses beginning with "atribhyām," Kaśyapa is the seer; "kaśyapo vivṛhā yakṣmanāśa" is the application for the sprinkling. For the seven verses beginning with "tribhirvaṃ deva," Vasiṣṭha is the seer. For the first three, Agni is the deity; for the following four, the Viśvedevas are the deities. The first is in the Gāyatrī meter, the second in the Anuṣṭubh, the next three in Gāyatrī, and the last two in Anuṣṭubh. This is the application for the sprinkling.

*Āpo hi ṣṭha*: Navanāmbārīṣa Siṃhudvīpa is the seer; the waters are the deity; the meters are *gāyatrī*, with the last two being *anuṣṭubh*; the fifth is *vardhamānā* and the seventh is *pratiṣṭhā*; its application (*viniyoga*) is for consecration (*abhiṣeka*). *Āpo ha*: the two *ṛṣis* are Naptar; the Viśvedevas are the deity; the meter is *anuṣṭubh*. *Sahasrākṣeṇa*: Prajāpati is the deity; Yakṣmanāśin Yakṣmahan is the seer; the meter is *triṣṭubh*.
Then—
may the god Yīsa (Viṣṇu), the wielder of the thunderbolt, and Maheṃdra, whose vehicle is the elephant,
remove the defect of the infant born from the lineage of serpents for the sake of the mother and father.
May that god who wields the spear, the consumer of oblations whose vehicle is a ram,
the seven-tongued divine Fire, dispel the evil influence of the serpent.
May that Lord Yama, the wielder of the staff, who is Dharma himself and whose vehicle is the buffalo,
dispel the defects caused by the infantile afflictions of the serpent-born for me.
May that god who bears the sword, Dharma, whose vehicle is a buffalo,
pacify the affliction arising from the *gaṇḍānta* [juncture], which is elevated by serpents.
That god who holds a noose was born at the junction of the Gaṇḍānta.
May the wise Nakravāha, rising from the serpent, dispel all evil.
May that god Māruta, the life-breath of the world, who has a deer for his vehicle and bestows peace, pacify this affliction caused by the serpent in the child.
May that god Nidhipati, who bears a sword and has a horse as his vehicle,
dispel the evil influence of serpents for [my] mother, father, and children.
May that Lord Paśupati, the wielder of the Pināka bow who has the bull as his vehicle,
dispel the defect of the Gaṇḍānta occurring at Āśleṣā and Mūla.
May Vighneśa, Kṣetrapa, Durgā, the world-protectors, and the nine planets all pacify the affliction caused by the serpent and bestow peace.
May the constellation Āśleṣā dispel all the misfortunes of one born under it— of his mother, father, wealth, brothers, kinsmen, family, and position.
May that presiding deity named Vāgeśvara, Bṛhaspati,
dispel the Gaṇḍānta for the mother, the father, and the infant.
The Pitṛs are the presiding deities, Bṛhaspati is the overlord;
the serpent-constellation brings as wealth a mass of serpents, as well as kinsmen and relatives.

Having consecrated [the patron] with the mantras beginning with "surā, stu" and so forth, and with the verses "kacchayoḥ śaṃyuḥ" and "viśve devāḥ," the application (*viniyoga*) is for the sprinkling (*abhiṣeka*).

Then, having been consecrated by the water from the *kalaśa* of Rudra and the serpents, as well as from another vessel with a hundred holes (*śatacchidra-dhārā*), the patron (*yajamāna*) shall give a cow to the Preceptor (*ācārya*), a bull to the Brahman priest (*brahmā*), a black ox to the reciter of the *Rudra-mantra*, and an image to the *ṛtvij*s; and having given sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) according to his capacity, and having performed the subsequent worship of the serpents, he should take the respectful offering (*arghya*) consisting of fruits, flowers, and other items in a copper vessel.
O Lord of all, salutations to you, the sovereign of the hosts of Nāgas;
accept this water-offering given by me for the pacification of my misfortunes.

Having thus offered the *arghya*, having dismissed [the deity] with "Arise," having presented [the offering] to Ācāryamahat preceded by a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), having worshipped the fire, and having dismissed [him] with "Go, go," one should feed the Brahmins according to one's capacity and eat while accompanied by friends.
Furthermore, regarding the specific results for each constellation,
it is stated in the *Nṛsiṃhaprasāda*:
"For the purpose of painting and so forth, [one should act] during Puṣya, in the middle of two quarters, in the first quarter, or in the third quarter of Dhiṣṇya."
A son born under Uttarā Āṣāḍhā brings about the destruction of the longevity of his mother, father, and brother.
This rising [of the moon] in Uttarā-phalgunī results in two months; in Puṣya, three months;
in Pūrvā-āṣāḍhā, eight months; and in Citrā, the fruit is six months.
One should avoid seeing one's son during the ninth month of Āśleṣā, for eight years after Mūla, and for fifteen years during the month of Jyeṣṭha.
Where no propitiatory rite (śānti) is mentioned, there a sacrifice to the planets (grahamakhā) should be performed;
therefore, one should perform the propitiation of the planets with a focused mind.
Thus it was said by Vasiṣṭha to all.
In the *Mātsya-purāṇa*, Garga says:
"If a mare gives birth during the day, especially in the month of Śrāvaṇa, or if a buffalo cow gives birth on the new moon day of Māgha or on a Thursday," [it portends a calamity].
If cows give birth to lions, they bring death to their owners;
likewise, if a stationary being is born from a moving one, or a moving being from a stationary one, the same result follows.
When there is such a reversal of the *yoni*, there will be the arrival of a foreign army;
yet by performing abandonment, exile, or rising up, one will quickly obtain auspicious results.
If a mare, an elephant cow, or a cow gives birth to twins,
or if there is a cross-breed or a deformity, that animal shall die within six months.
All [animals]— with the exception of mice, cats, fish, and dogs— engage in sexual union with those of a different species;
they should be known as the bringers of famine, for they consume the flesh of their own kind.
Due to the excessive rutting season at an improper time, there is danger from other species to the four-footed animals and birds; this is especially true for cows and dogs.
If a male buffalo should mate with a female buffalo,
or a cow with a cow, or if a cow mates with a bitch, or a bitch with a cow— or even vice versa.
In the animal realm or among humans, there may be the arrival of a hostile army;
if non-humans and humans are incited against one another, they will wage war.
Or she may give birth to a deformed child, or there may be the arrival of a foreign army;
therefore, one who understands [the situation] should practice renunciation, luxury, or charity toward them.
One should satisfy the Brahmins with food and have the *bali* offerings performed;
worship of the lords of the thirty gods should be conducted with drums, mṛdaṅgas, and most beautiful paṭaha drums.
In that case, the ritual should be performed according to the prescribed rules, and much food should be given to the twice-born Brāhmaṇas.
Nārada says in the *Adabhutasāgara*:
"If a cow gives birth while the Sun is situated in Leo..."
His death is declared to occur in six months; of this there is no doubt.
One should cause that cow to be given to a Brahmin immediately after she has calved;
thereafter, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) with mustard seeds smeared with ghee.
Then, one should offer ten thousand oblations of ghee-smeared offerings with the Vyāhṛtis;
this is the homa, and Prajāpati is the deity of the mantra, according to the statement regarding the status [of the deities].
Having observed a fast with diligence, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin;
one should cause a pair of garments, barley, and gold to be given as well.
If a buffalo is born in the month of Pauṣa, or likewise a mule on that same day, then whatever has been lost will be recovered; for its pacification, one should perform a propitiatory rite (śāntika).
One should offer oblations of sesame seeds and clarified butter one hundred and eight times, using the hymn beginning with "anyavāme" and the mantra beginning with "tad viṣṇoḥ."
One should perform the oblation according to the prescribed rite of Mṛtyuñjaya as it has been taught;
thereafter, one should bathe with the Śrīsūkta or again with the Śāntisūkta.
Whether at midday or at midnight, when the lowing of a cow occurs—
whether in a village or even in one's own home— one should perform the propitiatory rite (*śāntika*) as previously described.
Thus, the birth of a *baḍadā* (a female who has borne six children) in the month of Śrāvaṇa is forbidden; this is stated by Garga in the *Pariśiṣṭa* of the Atharvavedins:
"In Māgha, on a Wednesday, one is a *mahiṣī*; in Śrāvaṇa, during the day, she is a *baḍadā*."
If cows give birth to lions, they bring about the death of their master.
In this regard, the pacification rite (śānti) called Amṛta, as stated therein, should be performed—
the specific details of which are to be known from the Nirṇayasindhu—
thus concludes the pacification for the birth of a child from a lion-man or a cow-man, and so forth.
Nārada said:
A black cow with a tawny tail, or a tawny cow with a black tail—
these should be given by men to a Brahmin for the sake of peace, and they yield their fruit instantly.

Then one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) for the sake of pacification using barley and sesame seeds, with the mantra "namaste rudra"; thereafter, one should cause the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be bestowed.
In accordance with one's wealth, peace shall then arise;
one should likewise mutter that mantra with which the oblation is to be offered.
The knower of mantras should offer oblations with the mantra "śatāvarta," and then he should offer sacrificial fuel-sticks placed upon a leaf-plate as an offering to Śiva.
The recitation of the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times is the most excellent;
for the sake of pacification, a Brahmin should recite "idaṃ viṣṇurvicakrame."
One should perform the recitation (*japa*) with the *Sahasraśīrṣā* mantra for the sake of prosperity and pacification.

Āpastamba states: "That which has four feet or five feet becomes deficient; all these are portents having the Sun as their deity, and they require expiations (*prāyaścitta*). Having offered the cooked oblation (*sthālīpāka*) with the mantra 'ud u tyaṃ jātavedasam,' one makes offerings of clarified butter (*ājya*) with five oblations."
"Swāhā to Sūrya! Swāhā to Gṛhapati! Swāhā to Kirapāṇi! Swāhā to Īśvara! Swāhā to the pacifier of all sins! Having offered oblations with these *vyāhṛtis*, he then sings the *Sāman*.
Thus ends the rite for pacifying the birth of deformed offspring from father and son, in the *Śāntiratna* composed by Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa;
[this also applies] when two brothers or a father and son are born under the same lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*).
It is certain that death shall come to one of these two first.

The meaning of "of the two brothers" (*bhrātroḥ*) is "of the brother and the sister. The meaning of "at the lunar mansion of the parents" (*pitroḥ nakṣatre*) is "if there is the birth of a son or a daughter.

In the case of "of the two brothers and the two sons" (*bhrātroḥ putrayoḥ*), the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) is applied as "brother and son" (*bhrātṛ-putrau*) and "sister and daughter" (*svasṛ-duhitṛbhyām*).

In the case of "of the parents" (*pitroḥ*), the *ekaśeṣa* is applied as "father and mother" (*pitā-mātā*). This is an *Amdana* compound, which is a type of *madhyamapadalopa* (elision of the middle term) and is considered incomplete (*asamasta*).
In the *Jyotirnibandha*:
"O Goddess, when two fathers and their sons, or two sisters, or two kinsmen are born under the same asterism (*samānabha*), then there is the destruction of the elder."
When one performs the prescribed propitiatory rite (*śānti*) and consecration (*abhiṣeka*) for the destruction of those defects,
one should worship an image of the lunar mansion (*ṛkṣa*) before it and then give gifts according to one's wealth.
In this regard, I shall proclaim the rite of pacification according to the consensus of all teachers:
on an auspicious lunar mansion and an auspicious day of the week, when the moon and the stars possess strength.
On the day of commencement, the wise man should avoid the *riktā* and *viṣṭi* lunar days; he should first choose an Ācārya and four of the most excellent brahmins.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) to be made, one should perform the rite of pacification (*śānti-karma*);
then, in the portion of Agni-Ṛśāna, one should [place] the image of the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra-pratimā*).
One should perform worship over the water-pot (kalaśa) with the mantra "tattadṛk-ukta.
The Nakṣatra mantras for those belonging to the Āpastamba Śākhā are well known through eight statements in the third Aṣṭaka.
In that case, the ritual procedure must be performed, including the worship of the birth constellation.
For it is stated in the Nibandhas that when performing the worship of the lunar mansion deity (*nakṣatradevatā*), it must be preceded by the worship of the presiding deity (*adhipratyadhidaivata*).
Having bound [the image] with a red cloth, one should wrap it with a pair of garments;
then, one should perform the fire-offering (agnimukha) according to the path prescribed in one's own Vedic school.
With this very mantra, one should perform the oblation one hundred and eight times;
the meaning is that it should be done with the respective [substances] as prescribed, using sacrificial fuel-sticks, rice, and so forth, for each [deity], up until the conclusion of the expiation.
Then the preceptor should perform the consecration for both the father and the son;
furthermore, he should honor the preceptor with gifts of clothing, ornaments, and cows.
One should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests consisting of three māṣas of gold;
furthermore, there is the gift of an image of the deity along with gifts such as clothing and other articles.
One should give vehicles, beds, seats, and so forth, as well as three māṣas of gold;
one should feed all the brāhmaṇas, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth.
Now, the ritual procedure (*prayoga*):

Having performed the *gomukha* birth-rite for the parents and the birth-star of the brother, and having announced the place and time, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), saying: "For the sake of pacifying all calamities indicated by the birth under the same star as the father and others of this child, I shall perform the *ekanakṣatra-janana-śānti*. Then, after the worship of Gaṇeśa and the selection of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the preceptor (*ācārya*) should establish a water-pot (*kalaśa*) in the northeast. Therein, upon a red cloth, he should worship the image of the birth-star with the mantra of that star, using a pair of garments and other offerings.

Then, having established the fire and the planetary deities (grahas), one should perform the principal offering here to the specific nakṣatra or its presiding deity with sacrificial wood, parched grain, and clarified butter, each eight times; then, with the remainder, one should perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation and so forth, up to the presentation of the bali offerings.
In the *Jyotirnibandha*, however, it is stated:
"With devotion, [one should worship] the auspicious deities Hari and Hara, made of gold and silver.
Having thus spoken, one should fully worship Hari and Hara.
The parents of the universe, possessing manifold forms and faces turned in every direction.
"May both the gods Hiraṇyagarbha and Hari be pleased by this gift of the image.
Having said this to the preceptor, and having given another sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), he should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka).
It is stated that after the gift and the fire-oblation (homa), there is an ablution following the giving.

Having performed the *pūrṇāhuti*, the removal of the *praṇītā* vessel, and so forth, and having sprinkled [the recipient] with water from the ritual jar (*kalaśa*), the preceptor (*ācārya*) should give garments, ornaments, and three *māṣa*-measures of gold to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Having performed the concluding worship (*uttarapūjā*) and offered the dismissal (*visarjana*), he should place [the offerings] into the hand of the preceptor. Then, having given grain, clothing, vehicles, beds, and seats to the preceptor, the officiating priests, or others according to his capacity, he should feed the Brahmins.

Thus ends the ritual procedure for the pacification of being born under a single asterism (*ekanakṣatra-śānti-prayoga*) in the *Śāntiratna* composed by Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa, son of Rāmakṛṣṇa Bhaṭṭa, son of Śrī Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa.
Now follows the pacification for the *vyatīpāta*, *vaidhṛti*, transits (*saṃkramaṇa*), and birth [under these conditions], according to Śaunaka:
Now, therefore, Śaunaka shall fully proclaim this supreme pacification (śānti);
for at the conjunction of the moon and sun (vaidhṛti) and during the Vyatīpāta yoga, a great defect arises.
O Prince, if at the time of birth there occurs Vyatīpāta,
Vaidhṛti, or a transit (saṃkrānti) of the sun, one born then will be a cause of poverty.
Poverty brings great suffering, affliction by disease, and immense wandering;
one meets death through dependence—there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
It would cause grief, suffering, and total destruction for women;
therefore, extensive propitiatory rites (śānti) must be performed, as there will be no fault whatsoever in that case.
One should perform the Gomukha rite of delivery and diligently perform propitiatory rites (śānti),
specifically including recitation (japa), consecration (abhiṣeka), giving gifts (dāna), and the propitiatory fire-offering (śānti-homa).
One should perform a sacrifice to the nine planets (navagraha-makha) for the pacification of its defects;
first, one should undergo rebirth through the Gomukha rite, and thereafter perform the propitiatory rite (śānti).
On the eastern side of the house, having smeared it with cow dung and made it well-adorned in a suitable spot, one should prepare a heap of rice.
One should provide five *droṇas* of grain, half of that in rice, and half of that again in sesame seeds; one should arrange these for one another.
The wise one should draw an eight-petaled lotus within the triangular heap of materials;
having first caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), he should then choose the preceptor (ācārya).
One should present the five-fold ornament, a silk cloth, and a finger-ring;
and the pitcher, which is flawless, very beautiful, and established upon the [appropriate] zodiac sign.
Having collected water from sacred bathing places along with abundant medicinal herbs and sprouts,
together with cow products, fragrances, and gems, one should wrap it in a pair of garments.
Having placed a fine vessel upon its edge and joined it with a fine cloth,
the wise one should install the image, together with the presiding deity and other deities.
One should worship Candra and Āditya on the two sides and Vaidhṛti in the middle;
likewise, one should worship Vaidhṛti, its presiding deity Rudra, and similarly Vyatīpāta for the sake of pacification during a solar transit.
One should worship Rudra to the north of Bhānu and Agni to the south.

In the *vaidhṛti* yoga, Rudra is in the middle; the Sun and Moon are in the south and north respectively. In the transition (*saṃkrānti*) and the *vyatīpāta* yoga, the Sun is in the middle; Agni and Sūrya are in the south and north respectively—this is the meaning.

A wise person should have an image fashioned according to their own capacity, even for the price of a full *niṣka*, half a *niṣka*, or even a quarter of one, characterized by its respective specific features; and that has been stated by me in the section on the rules for giving gifts (*dānaparibhāṣā*).
For the purpose of worshipping the image, one should offer a pair of garments;
Sūrya is the presiding deity (adhidaiva), and Candra is the counter-presiding deity (pratyadhidaivata).
One should worship with the respective mantra completed by the corresponding vyāhṛtis;
one should worship the principal image with the Tryambaka mantra.
One should perform the worship of the Sun with the mantra "utsūrya," and one should perform the worship of the Moon with the mantra "āpyāyasva."
It is worshipped with the sixteen services, or else with the five services,
by means of perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as fruits, food offerings, and betel.
One should touch the principal image with the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra,
reciting it either one thousand and eight times or one hundred and eight times.
One should thus recite each of the twenty-eight mantras according to one's own capacity;
then, having recited all those pertaining to the Sun, one should recite half [of the portion] for Soma using the Soma mantra.
One should recite the hymn beginning with "ā no bhadraḥ," the hymn of Agni beginning with "bhadrāḥ," the Puruṣasūkta, and thereafter the Tryambaka mantra.
