Having touched the pitcher, the officiating priests should perform the recitation (japa) in the four directions;
then, one should prepare the fire on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to the west of the pitcher.
One should cause the consecrated fire to be prepared according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra,
and with the Tryambaka mantra, one should offer sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice-oblation (caru).
One should perform either one thousand and eight oblations, or one hundred and eight,
or twenty-eight oblations, according to one's own capacity.
One should perform the oblation of sesame seeds with the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra;
then, having offered the Sviṣṭakṛt oblation, one should cause the Abhiṣeka (consecration) to be performed.
With the mantra "samudra jyeṣṭhā," with the mantras beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā," with the hymn "ākṣībhyām," and also with the Pāvamānī verses.
One should perform the consecration with the mantra "tryambakena hi," reciting "utsūrya āpyāyantu" according to the ritual manual, and using the mantra "sūrās tvam asi."
Thereafter, one should honor the preceptor with garments, gold, and finger-rings;
specifically, the gift of a cow, the gift of clothing, and the gift of gold [should be offered].
To pacify those defects, one should offer them to the preceptor;
one should give a concealing cloth, and thereafter peace will prevail.
He should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins who perform the recitation to satisfy them,
and he should bestow abundant fees upon the poor, the blind, and the miserable.
One should feed a hundred Brahmins with pure foods; then, together with one's kinsmen, one should eat according to one's means and capacity.
Thus, the mortal who performs this shall never encounter suffering;
he shall obtain long life, health, and prosperity, as well as for his mother, father, and even his child.
There shall be the cessation of all suffering, the increase of sons and grandsons, and one attains all desires; having become happy, one shall dwell for a long time.
Thus ends the *Vyatīpātādi-śānti* according to the *Śaunakīya*. Now, the ritual procedure (*prayoga*):

Having performed the "birth through the mouth of a cow" (*gomukha-prasava*), and having proclaimed the place and time, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord (*Parameśvara*), and by means of pacifying all misfortunes indicated by the birth under the *Vaidhṛti* yoga, I shall perform the *Vaidhṛti-janana-śānti* for this child. In this manner, if the *Vyatīpāta* and the *Saṃkrānti* (solar transit) occur on the same day, there is only a single combined *śānti* performed together. However, if the *Vaidhṛti* yoga occurs on the day of the *Saṃkrānti*, two separate *śāntis* must be performed because of the difference in the presiding deities; after that, [one worships] Gaṇeśa.
One should perform the worship, the recitation for an auspicious day, the *nāndī-śrāddha*, and the selection of the officiating priest and the sacrificial priests.

Therein, the preceptor, having scattered grains of rice there, having sprinkled the ground with water, and having touched the earth while reciting "mahī dyauḥ" (the great heaven), then, having prepared a heap of sesame seeds measuring five *droṇas* while reciting "oṣadhayaḥ saṃ vadante," and having leveled it on top, he should fashion an eight-petaled lotus there using five colors. Having established the water-jar there while reciting "kalaśeṣu" (in the jars), and having filled it with water from a sacred ford while reciting "imaṃ me gaṅge," he should place therein seven types of earth, all medicinal herbs, five sprouts, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and eight [other substances].

Having cast down perfumes and the five jewels, and having covered [the vessel] with a pair of cloths, one should first invoke Tryambaka in the eastern part of the cloth covering the full vessel for the pacification of Vaidhṛti, using the verse "tryambakaṃ vasiṣṭho rudro 'nuṣṭup" (TS 4.5.10.3); then, in the middle, one should invoke Rudra; to the south of that, invoking Sūrya with the verse "utpūrya" (TS 1.4.28.1); and to the north of that, one should invoke Soma with the verse "āpyāyasva" (TS 1.4.32.1).

Then, having worshipped with the sixteen offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra), while touching the image of Rudra, one should recite the *Pativrata-jaya-mantra* eight thousand or twenty-eight times. Then, while touching the image of Sūrya, one should recite all the mantras dedicated to Sūrya.

In the *Udutyam* hymn of thirteen verses, the son of Kaṇva, Praskaṇva, is the seer; they are all in the *gāyatrī* meter, except for the last four which are in the *anuṣṭubh* meter. In the six verses beginning with *citraṃ devānām*, Kutsa the descendant of Aṅgiras is the seer; they are in the *triṣṭubh* meter. In the two verses beginning with *indra mitra*, Rocadhyo Dīrghatamas is the seer; they are in the *triṣṭubh* meter. In the verse beginning with *haṃsaḥ śuciṣat*, Vāmadeva, the son of Gautama, is the seer; it is in the *jagatī* meter. In the verse beginning with *yattvā sūrya*, [Vasiṣṭha] is the seer; it is in the *triṣṭubh* meter. In the single verse beginning with *yadadya sūrya*, and in the three verses beginning with *utsūrya*, [the respective seers are] as follows; these are the *udvayantīya* verses.

Of four [verses] together, "ud u tyaṃ jātavedasam" and three others are addressed to Mitra-Varuṇa; they are in the Triṣṭubh meter, with the final verse being a Bṛhatī-śīrṣa—the term "śīrṣa" here meaning a Sato-bṛhatī—and "tat cakṣur devahitam" is a Pura-ukta.

The *brahmahā* [is the seer] of the first two; Agni is the seer of the third; the *bṛhatī* is the metre of the first two, and the *anuṣṭubh* of the latter two. "Samo mitrasya" consists of twelve verses; Sūrya is the deity, and *abhitapāḥ* is the metre. For the five hymns beginning with "Sūryo dīpyate," Sūrya is the deity, and *jagatī* is the metre. For the four verses beginning with "Vibhrāṭ bṛhat," Sūrya is the son, *cakṣus* is the deity, and *gāyatrī* is the metre. For "Vibhrāṭ," *jagatī* is the metre. For "Vibhrājam," *prastārapaṅkti* is the metre. For "Āyaṃ gauḥ," *sārparājñī* is the deity and *gāyatrī* is the metre. Sūrya is the deity for all of them.

Then, touching the image of Soma, one should mutter the mantra "āpyāyasva. For the pacification of the *vyatīpāta* yoga and the sun's transit (*saṃkrānti*), first there is the recitation of the *saura-mantra*; then the recitation of the *mṛtyuñjaya-mantra*. Then, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) in the four directions, having touched the water-pot (*kuṃbha*), should recite the hymn beginning with "avobhadrā," the hymn beginning with "bhadra agneḥ," the *puruṣasūkta*, and the *tryambaka-mantra*. Thereafter, the Preceptor (*ācārya*), having installed the fire and the planetary deities (*graha*), should perform the ritual addition of fuel (*anvādadhāti*).
The primary [offering] is as follows:

for Rudra, one should offer fuel sticks (*samidh*) and clarified butter (*ājya*) using the *tryambaka* mantra, with a quantity of eight thousand, eight hundred, or twenty-eight; for Sūrya and Soma, likewise with fuel sticks and clarified butter using the *rudra* mantra, in a number of twenty-eight. However, during the *vyatīpāta* yoga and at the sun’s transit (*saṃkramaṇa*), for Sūrya, Rudra, and Agni-Rudra, one should perform the rites with a number of twenty-eight. For Mṛtyuñjaya, using the *tryambaka* mantra and sesame seeds (*tila*) as the substance, one may offer in a number of eight thousand, eight hundred, or twenty-eight, or alternatively, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering with the remainder of the materials.

"Thus, etc."—Then, having performed the aforementioned *homa*, having performed the *mṛtyuñjaya-homa* with sesame seeds (*tila*) in all rites for pacification (*śānti*), and having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) at the conclusion of the offering of the sacrificial portions (*balidāna*), they should perform an ablution (*abhiṣeka*) with the hymn "The ocean is the eldest" (*samudrajyeṣṭhā*), with the hymn "O waters, you are indeed... (*āpo hi ṣṭhā*), with the hymn "From the eyes... (*akṣebhyaḥ*), with the verses beginning with "Pāpamānī," with the mantras of Rudra, Sūrya, and Agni, and with the Puranic mantras beginning with "Surāṃ tvā... Then the patron (*yajamāna*), having consecrated the clarified butter (*ājya*) with the mantra "Rūpam," and having given that vessel along with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a Brahmin, [he should give it] to the Preceptor (*ācārya*).

Having given two garments, a cow, oblations, a ring, and so forth, as well as gold and a cloth for covering, and having given sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and other gifts to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and having performed the concluding worship (*uttarapūjā*), one should dismiss [the deities] by consigning them into the hand of the preceptor (*ācārya*), and after dismissing the fire, one should feed a hundred Brahmins and the officiating priests.

Thus ends the ritual procedure for the pacification of Vyatīpāta and other [inauspicious planetary conjunctions], composed by Jamālākara Bhaṭṭa, son of Kṛṣṇa Bhaṭṭa and grandson of Śrī Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa.
Śaunaka says:
If birth occurs during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, there will be suffering from disease; likewise, if it occurs at the onset of the menses for women.
For one in whom this [sign] arises, death will undoubtedly occur;
there shall be affliction by disease, poverty, hunger, and strife.
Out of a desire for the welfare of all beings, I shall declare the pacification for those [planets] when an eclipse occurs specifically under a particular lunar mansion (nakṣatra).
One should fashion the image of the lord of that lunar mansion out of gold;
during a solar eclipse, one should fashion the image of the Sun out of gold according to one's means.
The wise man, during an eclipse of the moon, should especially fashion the form of the Moon out of silver;
the eloquent one should likewise fashion the form of Rāhu out of lead.
Regarding the Naga and Sisa: one should diligently smear a clean spot with cow dung;
upon that, the wise one should place a very beautiful new cloth.
One should cause the installation of three deities there,
adorned with white garments, white garlands, and white perfumes and ointments.
The wise man should worship the Sun with the mantra "Ā kṛṣṇena," and likewise during a lunar eclipse, he should worship properly with the mantra "Ā pyāyasva."
One should worship Rāhu with effort using the mantra beginning with "svarbhānoḥ";
thus, by worshipping him in this manner, the wise man [should offer oblations] with fuel-sticks produced from the śrīvṛkṣa tree.
A person should offer oblations with *pālāśa* fuel-sticks during a lunar eclipse;
a wise man should offer oblations with *dūrvā* grass for the complete propitiation of Rāhu.
The wise one should offer oblations for the remainder with fuel-sticks of the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree;
thereafter, he should offer with clarified butter, sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and sesame seeds.
This [is offered] to the serpents.
With the five products of the cow, the five jewels, the five barks, the five sprouts, water, and the paste of medicinal herbs, combined with the waters from the ritual jars.
One should diligently perform the consecration of the patron with the three Vāruṇa mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
When the consecration has been completed with this mantra, "imaṃ me gaṅge," and by means of the mantra "tattvā yāmi," the sacrificer, being composed in mind, [should proceed].
Thereafter, being well-composed and having conquered his senses, he should honor the teacher;
therefore, with devotion and great effort, he should offer three circumambulations.
The sacrificer, being composed, should give a cow as the sacrificial fee;
having performed the pacification ritual properly and especially according to this procedure.
He shall not encounter untimely death, grief, or the torment of disease;
rather, he obtains constant happiness, mental well-being, and good fortune.
This, which destroys all calamities for those born under a planetary eclipse,
was taught by Bhārgava to the high-souled Śaunaka.
Thus concludes the pacification for planetary seizures and childbirth; now follows the pacification for the birth of twins, as stated by Vṛddha Gārgya in the Bhārata:
If twins are born from a cow or a mare, one should know that it portends death;
therefore, one should perform the Mārutī Śānti rite.
One should cause a *lakṣa*-homa to be performed and cause many gifts to be given;
one should provide food for the Brahmins and also give a cow as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Upon the occurrence of impurity in my chief queen, or upon the birth of others as well,
one should offer the *aindrī* oblation or cause her to be banished from the country.
Kātyāyana.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the expiation for the birth of twins.
His atonement shall be as follows: his wife, a cow, a maidservant, a buffalo, or a mare may give birth to a deformed offspring within ten days;
he should then collect the milky sap of trees that yield astringent (kāṣāya) resin.

Having filled eight jars with Plakṣa, Vaṭa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, Śamī, Devadāru, and white mustard seeds, along with gold, Dūrvā sprouts, and young shoots; having bathed the couple with all medicinal herbs using the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," the two verses beginning with "kayā naścitraḥ," and the verse "idaṃ āpaḥ pravahata" while pouring five Droṇas of Varuṇa-water; having adorned them and made them enter through the Darbha grass; having there cooked a Māruta Sthālīpāka (oblation for the Maruts) and performed the Ājyabhāga offerings, he offers oblations of clarified butter.
With the previously mentioned bathing mantras, he offers oblations with food cooked on the spot:

*svāhā* to Agni; *svāhā* to Soma; *svāhā* to Pavamāna; *svāhā* to Pāvaka; *svāhā* to Marut; *svāhā* to Māruta; *svāhā* to the Maruts; *svāhā* to Yama; *svāhā* to Antaka; *svāhā* to Mṛtyu; *svāhā* to Brahmā; *svāhā* to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
Thus, O gods, regarding these portents occurring in the house: if an owl, a vulture, or a dove should enter the house, or if a hawk should alight upon a pillar, it is a great omen.

If there is an anthill or a honeycomb [on the roof], if a water-pot should break, if the seat, bed, or vehicle should catch fire, if a house-lizard, tortoise, chameleon, or a snake enters the body [of the householder], if the umbrella or banner is destroyed, during the *gaṇḍa-yoga* in the *sarpa* or *naiṛta* [asterisms], or during other such portents, as well as during earthquakes, the falling of meteors, and so forth—in these cases, one should likewise perform the house-purification (*gṛha-śānti*) according to the prescribed rite. Having given a boon to the preceptor (*ācārya*), having fed the Brahmins, and having caused them to pronounce blessings (*svasti*), one should receive their benedictions.
To that extent, it is stated in the Bahvṛca-kārikā:
Furthermore, if his wife or a cow should give birth while impure,
he should likewise prepare a *caru* offering for the Maruts and also perform the *pūrṇāhuti*.

One should offer a cake on thirteen potsherds to Brahmāṇaspati, Soma, Agni, and Agni Marutvat; or, as it is stated, one may offer oblations instead. In this case, for one who has established the sacred fires, the Śrauta rite involving the cake on thirteen potsherds for the Maruts is combined with this [Smārta] rite.
Thus ends the *Yamaśānti* for a child born under [the asterism] Yama;
now follows the *Trikaprasavaśānti*.
This is from the *Śāntisarvasva*.
When three sons or three daughters are born to men at that time,
it will become a great misfortune for both the mother and father, as well as for their family.
On the eleventh day after birth, or on an auspicious twelfth day,
having invited and chosen the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), he should perform the sacrifice preceded by the *graha* offerings.
One should worship the images of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, made respectively of gold,
placed upon heaps of grain atop water-pots, according to one's capacity.
In the fifth pitcher, one should worship Rudra with the Rudra-saṃkhyā [mantras],
the four Rudra-sūktas, and all the Śānti-sūktas in their entirety.
There, the preceptor should offer fuel sticks, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and cooked rice (caru),
either one thousand and eight times or one hundred and eight times.
And from the gods beginning with Brahmā, preceded by the planets in the various directions,
[one should offer oblations] with the mantras of Brahmā and others, and with the mantra "yata indra bhayāmahe" for Indra.
Then, having offered the sviṣṭakṛt oblation, the bali offering, and the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti),
and having performed the consecration (abhiṣeka) of the household, one should worship the preceptor.
Then, having given gold and one cow as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests (ṛtvij),
and having performed the inspection of the clarified butter (ājya), he should cause the recitation of the peace-mantra (śānti-pāṭha) to be performed.
Thus concludes the pacification for the birth of triplets (trika-prasava-śānti).
Now follows the pacification for the birth of twins (sadaṃta-janana-śānti), as stated by Puṣkara in the Pādma Purāṇa and the Viṣṇudharmottara:
Now, learn from me the characteristics of children born with teeth:
that infant whose teeth first appear above [the gums]—
O best of the Bhārgavas, one may have teeth along with the birth [mark] in the second,
third, fourth, or likewise in the fifth [house].
When teeth grow and there is great fear even in one's mind,
it concerns either the mother, the father, or one's own body and self.
In this regard, I shall proclaim the rite of pacification; listen as I speak it.
One should have a hundred young elephants, or [images] situated on a boat, bathed by twice-born brahmins.
In the absence of that, O knower of dharma, [one should place him] upon an excellent seat made of gold,
with all medicinal herbs, all fragrances, as well as seeds, flowers, and fruits.
Immediately thereafter, one should worship the Sustainer (Dhātṛ) with cooked food.
In this rite, the *saptāpa* should be performed, as well as the feeding of Brahmins;
on the eighth day, a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should likewise be given to the Brahmins.
Gold, silver, horses, land, or even wealth—
[these are given] as a pacification (śānti) for the occurrence of a perpetual portent, as stated in the *Padma Purāṇa* within the *Ādbhutasāgara*.
Now listen further to the procedure for bathing when the eruption of teeth is common;
having thus seated [the child] on a *bhadrasana* seat, with roots and fruits likewise placed upon its head.

At that very time, one should bathe and worship [the deity] with all medicinal herbs, all seeds, and all fragrances; and here, one should perform the fire-oblation (vahnihoma) and the wind-rite (samīraṇa).
One should likewise offer oblations into the fire according to the prescribed rite for Parvata, as well as for the renowned god Keśava; indeed, one should sacrifice to these very ones.
And a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the Brāhmaṇas according to one's ability.
In the *Adbhutasāgara*, Bṛhaspati states:
If a child’s teeth begin to erupt in the eighth month, or again in the sixth month thereafter, the mother dies; if they erupt in the eighth month, the father dies.
There, the child will suffer and may even die of its own accord;
thereafter, one should offer fuel-sticks of the *aśvattha* tree smeared with curd, milk, and ghee.
The wise knower of mantras should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times;
he should also give a cow as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and thus it becomes auspicious.

In the *Jyotirnibandha*, however, it is stated that [the appearance of teeth] in the eighth month and so forth is auspicious; specifically, "the eruption of teeth during the eighth month and subsequent months brings good fortune. This refers to the pacification (*śānti*) for one born with teeth.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara* and the *Matsya-purāṇa*: "Women who give birth out of season, as well as those whose offspring die prematurely,
those who have deformed births, and likewise those who give birth to twins."
If non-human beings, those with unshaven heads, those born of unknown lineage,
or those with deficient or redundant limbs are born, or even if there are others such as these;
One should predict the destruction of that region and its people, as well as the beasts, birds, and reptiles.
The king should banish them from his own realm;
thereafter, that best of Brahmins becomes beloved and worthy of honor through physicians, Brahmin-satisfactions, and offerings.
Then his evil attains pacification.
Uśanas says:
Where a human woman gives birth to animals with two or three heads, a severe danger arises within six months; of this there is no doubt.
And in the Vārāha [Purāṇa] it is said:
"One should know that non-human beings, humans, and likewise even superhuman beings are born when there is the arrival of a foreign army."
When even a single offspring is born from a bull, a donkey, a dog, a boar, or a camel, or from Rākṣasas and Piśācas;
A fourfold, terrible fear will swiftly arise.
Bhārata, Mayūra, Vṛddha, and Gārgya state:
When there is an inversion of the fetus among humans or even among animals, and when they give birth to portents, that indicates the ruin of that country.
In this case as well, pacification (śānti) must be performed immediately by fifteen wise men for humans,
and for other humans, cows, goats, horses, deer, and birds.

They were born with various distinctions of birth; some had teeth, while others were toothless; likewise, they were deformed—some having many heads, some being headless, some having many ears, and some being earless.
There were humans with one horn, two horns, and three horns; likewise, some had three or four arms;
others had long ears, large ears, or even goitrous ears.
Where humans, beasts of prey, tigers, cats,
and scorpions are born together in a harsh manner, one should predict a battle in that place.
From that [neglect], there is the destruction of royal fortune, as well as of wealth, family, and the strength of men,
elephants, and horses.
Then one should perform the Brahma-śānti rite, because Brahmā is the bestower of peace;
one should offer ghee into the fire one thousand and eight times.
With fuel-sticks of *palāśa* wood, he should satisfy the twice-born as before,
accompanied by male and female servants and provided with cattle, grain, and fruit.
One should give gold, a bull, and clothing as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin;
likewise, one becomes a king of horses, or similarly a king of two or three islands.
One should understand the miracle of the sun by worshipping the Maker of Day with fuel-sticks produced from the Arka tree,
combined with curd, clarified butter, and honey.
One should give a golden cow and a garment as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin;
thereby all defects are destroyed and auspiciousness is attained.
Bṛhaspati produces deer, serpents, frogs, and even humans; this is a marvel, and one should worship that seed.
Standing firm in his observance, he should offer fuel-sticks of the *udumbara* tree mixed with curd and clarified butter into the fire for the sake of pacifying the afflictions.
One should give clothing, gold, and a cow as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin;
[otherwise] there may be a miscarriage of the woman's fetus, or twins, or even female offspring.

If children are born with six teeth, or if they are born already laughing, one should recognize this as a portent from the planet Mercury; one should cause that [child] to drink [the consecrated] water.
One should give clothing, a cow, and gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a brāhmaṇa.
Thus end the wonderful propitiatory rites (*śānti*).

Now, regarding the remedies for the alleviation of suffering (*sukhaprasavaupāya*) in the *Madanaratna* by Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭa: "If the head of a cow becomes stuck in the birth canal within the maternity chamber..."
At that time, a favorable wind blew, making the labor for a comfortable delivery.
Only the bones remain; this refers to the half-verse beginning with "the cow's head.
One should prepare the roots of the *upodakī* plant mixed with oil;
this should be applied as an ointment to the vagina, and the woman will give birth easily.
Having ground together the bark of bamboo and neem, the root of *tulasī*, the leaf of *kapittha*,
and the seed of *karapīra*— all weighed in equal measure with buffalo milk— and having smeared that paste mixed with oil upon the sword, you [shall succeed].
This mantra extracts a dead fetus; it is wonderful for a comfortable delivery.
Thus ends the method for an easy delivery.
Now, regarding the protection of the infant: during the first days, the child should be kept away from perfumes and those who possess them.
Elevation of the limbs, loss of appetite, and twisting of the neck due to saliva.
At midnight, with dhātakī, lodhra, mañjiṣṭhā, tāla, and sandalwood, one should offer incense made from mahiṣākṣa; then that seizure-grasper releases [the victim].
In that very place, [one should worship] with fish, meat, liquor, non-edible substances, perfumes, blood, incense, and lamps. As for the mantra, it is stated in the *Prayogasāra*:
Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One Cāmuṇḍā, O lightning-tongued one, svāhā! Depart, O wicked graha, huṃ!
Let them go away from this place to another location, as Rudra commands, svāhā! Lightning-tongued one, hāṃ hīṃ huṃ huṃ, release, release, svāhā!
It is recommended for the offering of oblations when performing rites for the child-seizing spirits.
In the Nārāyaṇīya [section], this is the mantra.
This *bali-mantra* is prescribed for all cases of seizure by *bālagrahas*.
In the *Prayogasāra*: "The *kadaṃba*, *cakaraṃja*, *vibhītaka*, and *nimba*..."
The Aśvattha, the Udumbara, the Śleṣmātaka,
and the Vaṭa are declared to be the trees of the Mothers, situated respectively from the east to the northeast.
At every sacred site, at every body of water, at every tree, and even at a well,
one should offer an oblation to the Mothers wherever they may be.
Having performed the ritual offering of bali according to the rules up to the end of the Vināyaka-rite, he should summon the child there,
touch his head with water accompanied by mantras, and sprinkle it with flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata).

Having cast [the offerings] before the deity with well-recited mantras accompanied by songs according to the ritual procedure, one should perform the rite in their presence; thus the afflictions of evil planets go to dissolution like snow in the heat.
The mantra for the Nirijana rite is as follows:
"May Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Skanda, and likewise Vaiśravaṇa, quickly protect the child; release him, release the young boy!"
Having performed the protection rite by means of praise, one should touch the body of the child down to the feet from the head with this mantra.
In the *Kaumāra-tantra*, composed by the son of Rāvaṇa, regarding the *Majjana-ratna*:
"Having fashioned an image one cubit in measure from two types of earth from the confluence of the rivers."
She has three eyes, holds a trident and a skull-cup in her hands, wears matted locks, and possesses a body like that of Rudra;
she is adorned with serpents, her limbs are radiant with ashes, and she has accepted the playful sport of the saliva from Śeṣa.
Having invoked Rudra, the lord of all grahas, into this formless [image],
one should worship him, along with Skanda and others together with Pūtanā, using sandalwood paste and other offerings.
One should fashion two square enclosures within a winnowing basket using unhusked rice;
having established [the vessel] there facing east, one should perform the ritual procedure for that [vessel].
Then, with various mantras and diverse implements,
one should place that [image], complete with its appurtenances, at a crossroads.
Cotton seeds, peacock feathers, *bṛhatī*, *nimba* blood, *paṇḍītaka*, *kulya*,
human excrement, goat dung, *vacā*, snake skin, *keśa*, and *śāhivirmoka*.
An incense made from equal parts of nāgeṃdra, dvija, hiṅgu, bhṛṅga,
and marica is known to destroy piśācas, rākṣasas, asthma, and fever when offered to Skanda.
On the second day of the month, year, or season,
the Yoginī Pūtanā seizes the child, O Svastika, unless he drinks [the protective remedy].
Then fever arises, preceded by a contraction of the hands and feet;
he gnashes his teeth incessantly and closes his eyes.
One does not take food and weeps day and night;
there will be eye disease, vomiting, and fear again and again.
And emaciation shall arise; this is the characteristic of a child.
Then, having fashioned a little girl out of rice flour paste, one should [proceed].
Thirteen banners and lamps, *svastika* offerings, and oblations of strength; fish-shaped cakes made from flour measured by a *prastha*, and worship for the attainment of success.
One should cast all this, including the meat, in the western direction;
and during the evening twilight in the west, one should offer these three oblations.
On the third day, month, or year, the one called Pūtanā may seize the child; first, fever shall arise in him.
Then, one should have a small image fashioned from flour measuring one *prastha*;
there should be red rice, a twice-born man with red [garments], and a *svastika* that is also red.
With red flowers, red fragrance, and likewise red unguents,
one should offer the bali-oblation in the western twilight toward the north.
On the fourth day of the month, or at the end of the year, she seizes the child;
she is the Pūtanā named Tuṣamaṇḍanikā, or a Yāginī.
Then, for him, first there arises a fever known as Bhīṣaṇa,
along with a breaking of the limbs, a crushing pain in the head, discoloration, and the closing of the eyes.
Incoherent speech, labored breathing, trembling, and weeping are the signs [of possession].
Having fashioned a doll out of sesame paste and *balvika* thorns, one should perform the rite.
One should arrange an eight-petaled white flower; the white banner is Arjuna. Above the svastika are cooked rice prepared on a stand, fried cakes, and pastries.
One should diligently offer oblations in the western direction at the three junctions of the day;
[the substances for this are] a cow’s horn, a snake’s slough, garlic, and neem leaves.
Human hair, cat hair, and likewise ghee produced from the milk of a goat;
One should fumigate with these during the three twilights of a single night;
likewise, on the fifth day of the month or year, [one protects] the child from Pūtanā.
In the one known as Bikālikā, first fever arises, followed by cough,
asthma, colic, and a breaking pain in the limbs.
Having fashioned a little girl out of a prastha of ground rice,
one should provide her with white wealth, five banners, and five svastikas.
The five [fires] are blazing.
One should cast five lamps, white flowers, and sandalwood at the foot of a tree in the western direction during the afternoon.
In the *Madanaratna*, it is stated that even a lamp [offering] is prescribed for four days during the five *Utsava* festivals.
On the sixth day, during the month, or even in the year, immediately thereafter, the spirits named Pūtanā and Śakunī seize the child.
Fever, agitation, emaciation of the limbs, dyspnea, and loss of appetite,
as well as cough and contraction of the hands, feet, and eyes— these are the symptoms.
Then, having fashioned a figurine from a prastha of ground rice,
one should offer black rice, five banners, five black items, and five auspicious objects.
Then, having fashioned a little image of Kṛṣṇa as before, one should offer minced meat roasted on a spit.
Fish, *parpacikā* insects, and a *prastha* measure of blood should be offered as a bali-oblation in the northeast during the morning twilight for the sake of pacification.
On the seventh day, month, or year, the Pūtanā Aśuṣkā-Rēvatī seizes the child; then, first of all, there occurs fever.
Then, having fashioned a small female figure from flour measured by a *prastha*, one should offer it while reciting the *vidveṣa* hymn and the *kaṃparodana* mantra.
One should offer seven banners, the seven islands, svastikas, and seven vaitathas;
as well as flowers, fish, meat, and cooked rice.
On the eighth day, year, or month, the one named Bijālaka Pūtanā attacks the child; from that, fever arises for him.
Emaciation of the limbs, loss of luster, weeping, closing of the eyes, dryness of the tongue, eruptions on the head, and likewise aversion to food;
Then, one should have an effigy fashioned from a prastha of ground rice;
[and prepare] milk-rice, honey, clarified butter, milk, parched grain, and fried cakes.
Guggulu, mutton, and likewise parched grain;
four lamps with banners, and various kinds of perfumes as well.
And red *sumana* flowers—this is the offering (*bali*) prescribed here;
one should quickly present it toward the southern direction at the evening twilight.

On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, being self-restrained, one should [perform the rite] for the child on the ninth day of the month or even the year, using this mantra which is about to be stated.
Immediately after that, Pūtanā, named Nandanā, seizes [the child],
as do Jvara, Riddhi, Ghrṇā, Jñāna, Kāsa, Śvāsa, and Tṛṣṇatā.
Lameness of limbs and piercing pain—these are the signs in the child;
having fashioned a doll from one *prastha* of ground flour, [one should perform the rite].
One should place boiled rice, fish, meat, flat cakes, sugarcane,
and radish as an offering in the northern direction during the morning twilight.
The mantra for that is as follows:
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One Vāsudeva, huṃ phaṭ svāhā!
On the tenth day, in the month of Māgha, he bathed the young boy.
Then the one named Pūtanā, also known as Revatī, seizes the child;
fever, vomiting, dyspnea, cough, and pain—these are said to be her symptoms.
One should fashion a small image there from flour measuring one *prastha*;
one should bury eight [offerings] there with thorns of the *bilva* tree;
and there should be jaggery-rice, clarified butter, and twenty-five banners.
And exactly twenty-five svastikas and lamps.
One who stands in the southern direction should scatter four red flowers during the three junctions of the day with the mantra that will be recited hereafter.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One Vāsudeva! Strike, strike! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
On the eleventh day, month, and year, Pūtanārcikā [is subdued].
Afterwards, a fever arises in the child who has been seized;
there is an aversion to food, parchedness of the mouth, breaking pain in the limbs, and weeping.
"Even one whose gaze is directed upwards"—this is the characteristic of that householder.
The *putrikā* is dyed with the flour of black gram (*māṣa*), as is the white cooked rice;
the flowers are also white, and there are twenty-five banners.
And twenty-five lamps in the shape of svastikas—
all this one should offer at the morning twilight according to the prescribed rule.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One who holds a vajra in his hand; oṃ phaṭ svāhā!
On the twelfth day, month, or year, Pūtanā afflicts the infant;
there is constant crying, gnashing of teeth, and redness of the eyes.
The bristling of his hair and perspiration—this is the complete set of his characteristics.
Having fashioned a small image there from a prastha of ground rice, [one should proceed].
Thirteen svastikas, thirteen banners and lamps,
intoxicants, fish, meat, and likewise fried cakes—
all of this one should cast toward the southern direction with the mantra.
Oṃ, homage to Nārāyaṇa! Strike down the wicked beings! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
In the *Prayogasāra* of the *Madanaratna*: "In the thirteenth year, the Yakṣiṇī Bālagrahī seizes [the child]."
Having performed that rite and muttered the mantra, one should offer oblations of heart-pain, fever, weeping, and laughter,
along with boiled rice, wine, meat, fish, and variegated parched grain.
One should offer a *kṛsara* oblation in a winnowing basket as a *bali* for three days at midday;
thereafter, one should drink clarified butter, and then the seizure is released.
In the fourteenth year, one who seizes a child by name is called Svacchandā; her characteristic action therein is the shedding of blood.
If there is pain in the region of the navel, there is no remedy for it.
It is stated that for the pacification of malevolent planets, this very previously mentioned ritual deposit (nidhāna) is to be employed.
In the fifteenth year, the Vāruṇī Graha seizes the child;
its symptoms there are lassitude, fever, sleepiness, and loss of appetite.
With kulmāṣa, kṛsarā, pūpa, holikā, pāyasa, and āsava.
One should offer a bali-oblation with areca nuts and incense it for three nights;
then, with sandalwood mixed with clarified butter, the planet-seizer releases [the victim].
In the sixteenth year, the invincible Balagrahī seizes [the child].
And thus, she repeatedly spoke these words out of anger: "I shall become a laughingstock."
One should offer a bali-oblation with kulmāṣa, kṛsarā, cakes, sesame, flour-cakes,
and rice-grits, along with curd, for three days in the northeast direction during the night.
In the seventeenth year, a spirit seizes the child;
cough and dyspnea are to be recognized there, and no remedy exists for it.
These [periods], beginning with the year and the planets, are the joints (*parvan*) of the maiden's stages; hereafter, the rest is the same.
Thus ends the *Bālagrahaśānti* (Rite for the Peace of Child-Spirits) as declared in the *Madanaratna*, within the *Śāntiratna* composed by the illustrious Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa.
Furthermore, regarding the ritual procedure for the *pūtanā* [demoness], in the *Skanda-purāṇa*, in the section on the birth of the *lubdha* [greedy demon], Skanda said to the Sun:
"By what action does the seizure (*graha*) of infants arise?"
I shall tell you all of that; ask me, O Divākara.
In Laṅkā, there is one named Rāvaṇa, a descendant of Pulastya and lord of the rākṣasas. That hero has twelve sisters who are exceedingly formidable.
By them, a terrible deed was performed that brought fear to all the worlds;
thus, the entire universe was oppressed by those powerful ones through their might.
Rudra, having been propitiated by them through austerity and the power of their vows, became pleased;
then the God granted this supreme boon to them.
Rudra said:
"O night-rangers, I am the granter of boons to you who are worthy of boons;
therefore, choose as your food that which is produced from the bodies of children."
Fat, blood, flesh, marrow, bone, pith, and semen—O Lord, all this belongs to the one who consumes; do not bring harm to the one who gives.
Having heard those words of theirs, the Supreme Lord became enraged.
Born into the lineage of Brahmā and devoted solely to the practice of austerity,
how could there be such a transformation of the mind toward the slaughter of children?
That which is esteemed by the whole world should be given when requested by those who are wise.
The Rākṣasīs said: "If you are pleased, O Blessed One, grant us this favor, O Auspicious One:
that we may be satisfied with the fat of all these children."
Rudra said: "O girl, she who bathes at the onset of night, touches [impure things], or eats, and who, out of negligence, does not apply oil massage at the time of childbirth— "
Or she sleeps naked at night, having recently engaged in sexual intercourse;
her child—especially during the month or year following birth—is [at risk].
On the first day, month, or even year, O Deliverer,
may they be freed from the masses of pain caused by fevers and other ailments through my grace.
The second is named Mohinī, Sunandā is the third;
in the fourth is Pūtanā by name, and in the fifth is Surī; in the sixth, however, is Piśācikā.
In the ninth [month], let the goddess Pāśinī quickly seize the infant;
in the tenth, Mahāmārī; and after that, Kālikā.
In the twelfth year, the goddess Bhāginī will be intent on causing affliction;
O children, you yourselves must inflict suffering upon the enemy in battle.
On his own day, month, or even year, or on various specific occasions,
or even when the Rākṣasa’s child is born,
whoever offers you a complete and supreme sacrificial gift;
Even though you have seized that child, release him with contentment.
Having obtained boons, all these [planets], being well-disposed, afflict children according to the measure of days, months, and years; no further deliberation is required in this matter.
On the first day of the month, the goddess Vimocanī rains; for children, her affliction arises as intense pain—
a fever at first, followed by a burning sensation, and thereafter an eye disease.
The infant does not take the breast; he becomes one who vomits while clinging to the lap.
With great force he clenches his fists and bites his teeth excessively with his teeth.
In this way, O Sun, suffering arises from Vimocinī.
I shall describe her worship, which brings peace to children:
[offerings of] oleander, arka flowers, sandalwood, red flowers, sandalwood, and red cloth.
Incense is known as *śivanirāmalya*, and the *bilva* leaf with clarified butter is prescribed;
five lamps are to be understood [as required], and likewise five *polikā* cakes.
Five types of fist-fights are to be known, and five banners, all yellow;
there is betel-leaf with five *vaṭaka* sweets accompanied by *pūgī* nuts.
O wise one, red rice and cooked food mixed with ghee and jaggery should be offered; all of this must be placed in a new earthen bowl.
Then, one should fashion a doll from the clay of both banks of a river.
There, the wise man should place [the image] covered with yellow garments;
a devoted person should worship it, adorned with a yellow thread around its edge.
With the previously mentioned requisites, such as perfumes, flowers, and so forth, the wise man, being composed,
should offer it with the mantra to be described hereafter.
Therein is the mantra: Oṃ namo bhaktavatsale vimocani svāhā.
Having thus recited this mantra, one should perform worship for all.

On the twenty-first night, having placed the doll [there] and having performed the services of worship with perfumes, betel, and so forth, one should take five sprouts, remove them from the limbs of the child, and wash them with water. Then, having again performed the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*), one should recite the mantra and lift up all of that during the night. Those sprouts are:
those of the *jambu*, *āmra*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *vaṭa* trees.
When pain arises for the child, having emerged from all its limbs, the learned say:
"One should cast this [effigy] into a river or at a crossroads."
In this manner, being well-composed, one should perform the giving for three nights.
The wise man should always go out from the village toward the north during the first part of the night.
One should recite the mantra at that place for the sake of pacifying children;
thus the affliction of the infant comes to rest without doubt. This is the procedure for pacifying afflictions on the first day, month, or year, as stated by Skanda in the Lubdaja-tantra.
Skanda said:
O Divākara, on the second day of the month and likewise of the year,
the goddess named Mohinī inflicts affliction upon the child.
It causes fever, eye pain, cough, and especially asthma;
it also brings about constant vomiting and aversion in the child.
In this regard, I shall explain in brief both the pacification and the ritual distribution.
Worship with *mālatī* flowers, sandalwood from the Malaya mountains,
divine saffron (*kesara*), and camphor for anointment.
With divine devotion and virtuous conduct, one should likewise offer ten-ingredient incense;
the food offering (naivedya) should be presented as before, and the ritual actions should likewise be performed as previously described.
Having fashioned a doll as before, he should perform all this with focused concentration.
The mantra for that is as follows:

"O Sovereign of All, beloved of all people, protect, protect the entire world! Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed Lady, svāhā! Having performed the entire ritual procedure with this very mantra, [one should proceed].
It should be performed during three nights outside the village in the west;
that which is done during the first watch of the night bestows happiness.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for pacifying afflictions on the second day.
Skanda said:
Listen to the procedure for the third day, month, and year, O Rāma.
There, a goddess named Sunandā causes fear among children;
that passionate woman brings about a terrible state of being.
Heart disease, vomiting, and asthma arise together with fever;
the child contracts his limbs and cries day and night.
In this manner, the obstacle known as Sunandā arises from anger;
I shall now describe the procedure for its pacification in brief.
A hundred lotus petals, flowers, an ointment of sandalwood,
turmeric, saffron, nāgakeśara, and yellow pigment (rocanā).
One should offer incense made of fragrant substances combined with guggulu,
having thoroughly heated the sun-god [the image] with pieces of khadira wood smeared with clarified butter.
Having fashioned a doll as before, one should place it within a jar;
[one should offer] three handfuls of cooked rice mixed with ghee.
Five lamps, five *polīkā*s, and five handfuls (*muṣṭikā*) are prescribed;
the banners (*dhvajāḥ*) should be known as being accompanied by five [offerings] and five sprouts (*pallava*).
One should collect the entire sacrificial offering with the *maṃdra* [chant] that will be described hereafter.
In this regard, the mantra is as follows:
Oṃ namaḥ sunandāyai huṃ phaṭ svāhā. With this very mantra, one should cast [it] to the east of the village.
For three nights, during the first watch of the night, [one should perform this] for the pacification of the child;
when this rite is performed in this manner, every disease is destroyed.
The child grows like a god and prospers happily like a lotus in the bright fortnight; "Abja" refers to the Moon. This is the third-day rite for the pacification of afflictions.
Skanda said: O Vibhākara, on the fourth day, month, and year,
a goddess named Pūtanā inflicts affliction upon the child here.
First, a burning sensation arises, followed by diarrhea;
then one clenches the fists, and trembling occurs again and again.
I shall now describe the procedure for its pacification during the affliction caused by the hot-rayed one (the Sun).
Having fashioned an effigy as before, one should place it inside a shallow bowl.
One should wrap it with a red thread and anoint it with saffron;
worship should be performed with *dhattūra* flowers together with *barbarī* leaves.
Fish, meat, and incense, combined with ghee and clarified butter—
these three lamps are for the three corners;
three banners are likewise declared for them, and no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
O Prabhākara, three handfuls of rice are prescribed;
that cooked rice, mixed with clarified butter, should be placed upon a platter.
Having paid homage to the doll clothed in a red garment,
and having placed curd, unbroken grains, and other offerings upon it, one should deposit it with a concentrated mind.
One should wipe the child on all limbs with five sprouts. The mantra is:
Oṃ! Homage to you, Mother Pūtanā! Having accepted this beautiful offering, release the boy with haste, being delighted by the gift of the oblation.
Having recited this mantra, one should offer all the bali-oblations. Listen now to the procedure for the sevenfold rite performed at the moment when night has begun.
Taking recourse in the southern direction, one should cast [the remains] outside the village.
When the *bali* offering has been performed correctly in this manner, the child shall obtain happiness.
Thus concludes the ritual for pacifying suffering caused by the four classes of spirits, as well as by days, months, and so forth.
Skanda said: O Prabhākara, on the fifth day of the month and likewise of the year,
a goddess named Asurī afflicts the child severely here.
In that regard, O son of Bālā, I shall describe the signs that arise:
first there is fever, followed by hiccups, and then the affliction of *gṛdhra*.
Excessive binding of the tongue, delirious speech, aversion to food,
and likewise severe headache— these are the symptoms of *rave*.
Having fashioned a doll according to the prescribed ritual, one should wrap it with yellow thread;
dressed in yellow garments, one should place it within a conch shell at nightfall.
Having performed an oil massage and anointment, and having applied a paste of turmeric,
one should then perform worship with *karavīra* flowers.
With hibiscus flowers, bandhujīva blossoms, and likewise with putrajīvaka and nakha fruits.
Its surface should be smeared with sandalwood paste and adorned with divine fragrances;
for this [image], incense made from mustard seeds mixed with ghee is recommended.
There should be seven lamps, as many mirrors, and the same number of banners; likewise, there should be seven types of fist-shaped cakes, round cakes, and cloth strips smeared with clarified butter.
The offering for the food-oblation (naivedya) consists of cooked rice with ghee;
one should perform the sprinkling (mārjana) of the child with sprouts as was done previously.
Having recited this mantra three times, one should perform worship there.
The mantra is:
O auspicious goddess, bestower of good fortune, repeller of all enemies,
O Rākṣasī, bring peace to this child by means of this offering.
Having uttered this, one should first cast [the offering] at midnight for three days;
then, having taken recourse to the western direction, after half a watch (yāmārdha) of the sun has passed.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for pacifying the affliction caused by the Asurī on the fifth day and subsequent days.
Skanda said:
"Furthermore, O Sun, on the sixth day of the month, and also during the year,
a deity named Revatī seizes the infant without a doubt."
At the outset, pain arises for him in the head of the infant;
fever, dryness of the mouth, and thirst indeed manifest.
The limbs tremble and one weeps again and again;
regarding that, I shall declare the pacification—listen with a concentrated mind, O Sūrya.
Having fashioned a doll as before, one should place it in a shallow bowl;
having bathed it with water from the Gaṅgā, one should wrap it in a white cloth.
Clad in white garments, adorned with white garlands and unguents,
white incense is prescribed here, O sinless one, along with bilva leaves.
O Soul of the Universe, five lamps anointed with clarified butter are thus proclaimed.
That many were the orders from Muṣṭika, brought together with fried cakes.
A meal of cooked rice made from three *prasṛtis* of *vrīhi* grain is thus prescribed.
One should offer this oblation, which consists of a most enchanting betel leaf smeared with curd and jaggery,
accompanied by five twice-born brahmins.
And with concentrated mind, one should cast [the offering] while reciting the mantra that is about to be described.
The mantra for that is as follows:
Accept this entire offering and release the child, O lady of auspicious countenance;
grant security to this world and be gracious, O Revatī.
Having consecrated [the offering] with this mantra, one should present the bali-oblation at the boundary.
Having bathed the child with five types of sprouts while remaining well-composed,
one should offer the bali-oblation to Revatī in a region to the north of the city.
In this way, O Prabhākara, the affliction of the ignorant comes to complete pacification.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for pacifying afflictions beginning from the sixth day.
Skanda said: "O Sun, on the seventh day of the month,
the terrible bird named Nāmadevī seizes the child."
Fever first manifests as heat, and after that, as pain in the head.
Incoherent speech, diarrhea, and vomiting that lasts until the end [of life] occur;
furthermore, the eyes close and trembling arises in the limbs.
In that regard, I shall describe the propitiatory rite (śānti) which increases the pleasure of the Seven-Horsed One (the Sun):
one should fashion an effigy as previously described, its limbs smeared with red sandalwood paste.
A wise person should diligently worship with flowers that bloom out of season;
incense made of guggulu is most excellent, and five types of lamps are prescribed.
Five very beautiful *polikās* and five *muṣcikās* should be offered;
the sacrificial food (*naivedya*) is considered to consist of rice mixed with ghee, served in handfuls (*prasṛta*).
O best of gods, one should prepare the rice grains consecrated with mantras.
The mantra is: "O you with large eyes like lotus petals, take away the impurity!
Resorting to the southern direction, perform the rite that bestows peace."
O best of gods, when this rite has been performed in this manner for three nights, the child shall be freed from disease; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
Thus ends the procedure for pacifying afflictions beginning from the seventh day.
On the eighth day of the month, the goddess Pilācikā rains.
Indeed, it afflicts children with fever, wandering pains, and headaches;
eye pain, contraction of the limbs, and heart disease may also arise.
Listen to the remedy for that, by which even the Piśācī may be satisfied;
and within three nights, one should perform the pacification that removes the child's suffering.
Having fashioned a doll as before, one should place it within a shallow earthen bowl;
having bathed it with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one should bring it down from heaven together with the child.
With her limbs anointed with sandalwood paste, one should worship her with white flowers.
The seven types of fried cakes known as *polikās* are praised as being like the seven mothers.
The muṣṭikās should also be known; they are considered auspicious when smeared with turmeric, well-prepared with yellow-colored cloth and thread.
In this rite, an incense made from the powder of *vijayā* smeared with clarified butter is prescribed.
One should offer lamps fueled by sevenfold clarified butter after first performing the preliminary rites,
specifically offering three handfuls of cooked food smeared with clarified butter.
The wise one, well-endowed with devotion, should offer the food-oblation (naivedya) to the gods;
and betel-leaf with camphor should be respectfully presented nearby.
Furthermore, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given according to one's capacity for the pleasure of the Sun-god.
By the mantra that is about to be recited, the accent itself is prescribed.
The mantra:
Oṃ, salutations to you, O mistress of all beings, O beautiful one, O Piśācikā!
Having accepted this offering, release the child quickly.
The respectful offering of the five sprouts should be performed just as before.
For three nights, at the onset of night, one should offer an oblation (bali) outside the village;
when this rite is performed, the pacification of disease occurs.
Thus ends the pacification of obstacles beginning from the eighth day, as declared in the Brahmayāmala.
Skanda said: O Prabhākara, on the ninth day, month, and year,
the goddess named Pāśinī causes great affliction to children.
In this regard, O Divākara, I shall explain the signs in brief:
fever, vomiting, pain in the throat, and likewise contraction of the eyes;
the joining of the index and middle fingers causes great distress through the two thumbs.
Through the renunciation of food and contentment, a fragrance arises in the mouth.
In that regard, I shall proclaim the peace for the propitiation of Pāśinī:
having first fashioned a sacrificial cake (*pūpa*) of white rice flour, one should place it upon a stone slab;
it should be wrapped with a white thread and encircled by a white cloth.
One should worship with white flowers, such as mandāra and others that are fragrant.
Having prepared food mixed with half-portioned sandalwood essence and fragrant roots,
he cooked various kinds of cakes and the finest rice-porridge.
One should give as many handfuls of rice as there were [measures], and likewise sacrificial ladles; nine *prasṛtis* of this excellent rice-porridge should be measured out.
Sprinkling with curd and milk, one should prepare the sacrificial offering;
at the three middle watches of the night, one should cast the bali-offering to the west of the village.
By this master, the wielder of the noose, preceded by the recitation of the mantra— the mantra is as follows:
Oṃ, salutations to her who holds a noose in her hand, who has been granted boons by Rudra, and who is auspicious! Accept this offered bali; release the child from disease.
By this much procedure, the child shall become free from disease;
furthermore, the ritual with the five types of sprouts is performed as previously described.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the propitiation ceremony beginning on the ninth day, as spoken by Brahmāyāmīśa.
Śrī Skanda said:
O Divākara, on the tenth day of the month and likewise of the year, the Rākṣasī Mahāmārī of terrible form, Śaktiratnā, [appears].
It produces a fever that is like death and colic day and night; it excessively causes constipation, as well as hiccup, cough, and the three types of mental distress.
I shall describe its pacification out of a desire for the welfare of children:
having fashioned a doll as before, one should place it inside a shallow bowl.
One should bathe her with flowing waters and anoint her with sandalwood paste;
she is then clothed in yellow garments and adorned with flower garlands.
One should offer incense consisting of ten ingredients for the sake of warding off great pestilence;
five lamps are to be recognized, and there should be as many handfuls of flour-cakes.
Five fistfuls of the five auspicious banners are highly desirable; there is cooked rice prepared with ghee and an abundance of fine grains.
For the purpose of the food offering (naivedya), one should place that most beautiful [flower] there in a shallow dish (śarāva).
O Bhānu, [offer] that along with betel-leaf and likewise with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
in the southern half [of the vessel], a new cloth and silver, or according to one's ability.
One should offer all the oblations (bali) accompanied by five sprouts;
one should perform the oblation from midnight until dawn for three days.
Taking recourse in the southern direction, outside the village to the west,
[the following] mantra [is recited]:
Oṃ, homage to you, O red-eyed one, whose face resembles a red lotus,
with red lips and red teeth, O Great Plague, O Great Terror!
O you of great strength, of great body, who wards off great fear!
Be pleased by this offering of bali, O most beautiful one!
"O Supreme Goddess, protect [the child] afflicted by disease;
what need is there for further deliberation here?
Thus ends the procedure for pacifying afflictions on the tenth day, as stated in the *Brahmayāmala*.
O Divākara, on the eleventh day of the month or even year,
the goddess named Kālikā afflicts the child here.
First there is fever, then heart disease;
thereafter comes dryness of the mouth, great exhaustion, and then mental distraction.
They strike all his limbs with their feet again and again;
this condition, resembling death, arises from untimely anger.
In this regard, I shall proclaim the rite of pacification out of a desire for the welfare of children:
having fashioned an effigy as before, one should place it within a shallow earthen bowl.
Having bathed [the image] with the water of the Gaṅgā, one should anoint it with sandalwood paste;
one should worship with karavīra flowers and with leaves of the barbara grass.
One should fumigate the hell with human hair, sloughed-off snake skins,
and *narṣapa* seeds, combined with *vacā*, *laśuna*, *phena*, and *varjaka*, all mixed with clarified butter.
Having performed the lustration ceremony with five lamps resembling the sun,
one should offer as an oblation milk-rice, milk, rice flour cakes, sesame sweets, and modakas.
One should prepare five cakes, five small pastries, and five large cakes;
the banners are to be known as five; all of this [is placed] in a shallow bowl.
Having established it all, one should offer it to the goddess Kālikā with this mantra,
O Saptāśva, which will be spoken by me to you.
Oṃ, salutations to you of terrible form, O fierce one, O you of fearsome appearance!
Protect the entire world, O Mother; release this child, O beloved one, for he is powerless.
One should perform such a rite as previously described, including the ritual with sprouts;
when this procedure is performed, the child shall be liberated from disease.
At the time of evening twilight, outside the village to the south,
one should place [the offering], recite the mantra, and perform the rite of protection with holy ash (vibhūti).
Thus ends the pacification of afflictions for eleven days, months, and years as declared by Brahmā in the Yāmala.
Skanda said: O Divākara, on the twelfth day, month,
or year, the one named Bhāmisī here afflicts the child incessantly.
At first it causes fever, and thereafter heart disease;
then cough, dyspnea, diarrhea, delirium, and likewise excessive salivation.
All the limbs tremble and there is stiffness of the eyes;
thus, various kinds of diseases arise in children.
In that regard, I shall proclaim a rite of pacification that brings benefit to children:
having fashioned a doll as before, one should place it inside a shallow bowl.
One should offer to the Earth goddess fragrances, flowers, unbroken grains of rice, incense, various kinds of lamps,
and diverse types of food offerings.
A fine garment, a banner, an umbrella, and boiled rice accompanied by milk-rice (pāyasa),
together with cakes, parched grains, and milk-mash.
One who is devoted should prepare the food offering during the evening twilight at the close of day;
one should offer the bali-oblation in a place to the north of the village, without a doubt.
Thus, for the sake of liberation from disease, this should be performed within five days;
with this mantra, one should consecrate the *sarvatobali* seven times.
Accept this offering from the child; remove, remove his disease!
By the grace of the Five-faced One, may Bhavabhāminī become gracious.
When this rite is performed, the child shall attain well-being;
thus, O Sūrya, has the propitiatory rite for the Lubdha-jātaka been described to you.
Thus is the procedure for the pacification of *hīḍā* as taught by Skanda for the twelve-day periods, months, and years.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for Pūtanā.
Now, regarding the pacification of constellations (*nakṣatra-śānti*) at the onset of fever:

therein, in the *Madanaratna*, Ātreya said: "I shall now describe the thorough knowledge of the constellations. Aśvinī has three stars; it is feminine; its symbol is two horses facing each other; it is yellow in color; its tree is the *kāñcī*; its bird is the golden-winged one; it is light; its deities are the Aśvins; its class is the divine host; its womb is the horse; its letters are *ā* and *ākāra*; and one should perform the seasonal approach to a wife (*ṛtugamana*), the tonsure ceremony (*caula*), the giving of food (*śrāttha*), the wearing of clothes, the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), medicine, sowing seeds, building a house, planting sugarcane, and the collection of goods."

At the end of the fifty *nāḍīs*, there are four poisonous *nāḍīs*: in the month of Makara, it is *śūnya*; on Wednesday, the *mṛtyu-yoga*; on Sunday, the *ānanda-yoga*—some desire [this] to be a time of conflict; on Tuesday, the *siddhi-yoga*. Having partaken of food with *mudrās*, one should set out on a journey and collect one's weapons. If at that midday a red cloud appears, there will be rain within five days or on that very day. If on that day, which is a Tuesday, fever arises, [the result lasts for] ten days.

Pīḍā: Blue lotus flowers; Pūḍā: Guggulu incense; Kṣīra-laḍḍuka (milk-sweets) as the food offering; the ritual procedure for worship with the mantra "devasya tvā"; wood from milk-trees as the primary fuel for the fire sacrifice; having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the Gāyatrī mantra, one should present an offering of curd-rice (dadhyodana). From the eleventh day until the end of the twenty-fifth day, one will become well. During the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti), this is the medium price. Here, the performer, having remembered the place and time, [should declare]: "It is indicated by my birth-star that fever has arisen."

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "For the sake of pacifying all misfortunes (*ariṣṭa*), for the sake of quickly attaining health and success, I shall perform the pacification rite (*śānti*) for such-and-such constellation," he should worship Gaṇeśa and choose an officiating priest (*ācārya*). The officiating priest, having touched the ground to the northeast of the place of the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the mantra *mahī dyauḥ*, having scattered barley with the mantra *oṣadhayaḥ saṃ vadante*, having placed the water-pot (*kuṃbha*) with the mantra *ā kalaśeṣv*, having filled it with water with the mantra *om me gaṅge*, [he should add] fragrance with the mantra *gaṃdhadvārām*, all medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadhīḥ*) with the mantra *yā oṣadhīḥ*, and *dūrvā* grass with the mantra *kāṇḍāt kāṇḍāt*.

Having cast five sprouts with the mantra *aśvattheva*, seven types of earth with *syonā pṛthivī*, fruit with *yāḥ phalinīḥ*, five gems with *sahiraṇyāni*, and gold with *hiraṇyastūpaḥ*; having wrapped it with cloth using *yuvā suvāsāḥ*; and having placed a twelve-petaled lotus upon the cloth over a full vessel with *pūrṇā darvī*—one should invoke the deity of the lunar mansion (Nakṣatra-devatā) along with the syllable *Māyā* (*Hrīṃ*) using its respective mantra, and [invoke] the twelve [deities] beginning with Saṃkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva around the twelve petals.

Having invoked the deities and the guardians of the directions (dikpālas), and having worshipped them at their respective places with the prescribed perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings (naivedya), one should establish the sacred fire (agni). Then, using the materials specified for that purpose, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations (āhutis) with the Gāyatrī mantra to the deity of the lunar mansion (nakṣatra-devatā), and eight, four, or one oblation each to Saṃkarṣaṇa and the others. After performing the rites from the Sviṣṭakṛt offering up to the dismissal of the Praṇītā vessel, one should present the bali offering with the ritual substances, give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor (ācārya), perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) with water from the pitcher, and finally dismiss the image and other objects.

Having given [the fee] to the teacher and dismissed the fire, one should feed the Brahmins; this is the summary of the ritual procedure. It should be understood in the same way for what follows as well.

Bharaṇī consists of three stars; its shape is triangular; it is female and faces downward; Yama is its presiding deity; it is fierce; its group is that of humans; its source is the cow; its tree is the Āmalaka; its bird is the cock; its syllables are *i* and *ī*; if a red cloud appears at midday, there will be rain on the sixteenth day; on Tuesday, there is an obstacle; one should perform the accumulation of wealth, the use of the *bṛhatī* and *kāravallikā* plants, and the act of staying still; the twenty-four *nāḍīs* at the end are poisonous *nāḍīs*; [this applies] in the month of Phālguna.

The month is empty. On the seventh lunar day of Mercury (Budha-saptamī), there is the Viṣa-yoga. On Wednesday, it is the Nāśa-yoga; on Sunday, Yamakaṇṭaka; in other parts [of the week], it is Dinamṛtyu. In the Cancer or Sagittarius ascendant, in the portion of Mars (Kuja-aṃśa), one should collect grain; in that same ascendant, one should engage in agriculture. If fever arises, there is death or doubt [of recovery]. One should offer molasses as the sacrificial food (naivedya) and black fragrant flowers. The incense is Mahiṣākṣa. "Tryambakam" is the mantra for worship. [The oblation is] ghee and honey in equal measure.

Regarding the materials for the *homa*: at the end of five days, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the *Gāyatrī* mantra. At the end of twenty-one days, there will be prosperity. If there is no peace, death will occur. Except for the ninth lunar day (*navamī*) in the months of Taurus, Scorpio, and Virgo, and except on the days of the Moon, Mars, and Mercury, one may view land when the [planets] are rising; during a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), the price of land is low.

Kṛttikā consists of six stars; its shape is like a razor; it is female and faces downward; its presiding deity is Agni; it is of a mixed nature; its attendant is the Rākṣasa host; its color is yellow; its source is the womb; its tree is the Udumbara; its birds are the Krauñca and the crow; its letters are the syllable *u* and the vowel *u*; one should go on a journey with curd; one should offer green gram (*mudga*) and *śyāmāka* grain; one should give ornaments; at the end of thirty *nāḍīs*, there is a poisonous *nāḍī*; in the month of Kārttika, it is empty; on Wednesday, there is the Mṛtyu-yoga.

One should place coconut, areca nut, cardamom, and clove [as offerings]. If there is fever, for nine days one should offer cooked rice with ghee as the *naivedya*. Worship should be performed with jasmine flowers (*mallikā*), and ghee should be used for incense. The worship mantra is: "punantamā devajanāḥ. One should offer one hundred and eight oblations of curd-rice while reciting the Sāvitrī mantra. This is the ritual procedure for the day.

Rohiṇī consists of five stars; it is triangular in shape, feminine, and faces upward. Its presiding deity is Prajāpati. It is stable, yellow in color, belongs to the human class, and has its origin in the serpent. Its tree is the Jambū. Its two auspicious birds are the peacock and the cock. Its two seed-syllables are the letters *ṛ* and *ṝ*. One should perform the following rites under this asterism: entering the womb (*ṛtugamana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first feeding (*annaprāśana*), the tonsure (*caula*), the initiation (*upanayana*), the commencement of studies (*vidyārambha*), the consecration of the water-pot (*kalaśasthāpana*), and the preparation of fermented liquors (*sādukarman*). In the month of Caitra, it is void; it possesses forty *ugra-yogas*; and on Thursday, it is a *viṣi-yoga*.

On Friday, there is Mṛtyuyoga; on Saturday, Siddhayoga. If Saturn is situated in a fixed sign in the ascendant, one should engage in the collection of grain. If there is fever, it will last for three days, and there will be pain from a new well. Milk-rice is the offering (*naivedya*). Lotus-flowers with ghee and all kinds of grains are the materials for the fire-oblation (*homa*). Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the Sāvitrī mantra, one should present a bali-offering of milk-rice to Prajāpati. Starting from the second day until the end of the ninth day, one will become well. During a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), there is an increase in the value of offerings (*argha*).

Mṛgaśiras has three stars; its figure is that of a deer; it is neuter; Soma is its deity; it is of the Mṛdu (soft) quality; its group is that of the gods; its origin is the serpent; its tree is the Khadira; its bird is the peacock; its syllable is *lṛ*, *kā*, and *ra*; its face is turned sideways; one should travel after eating deer meat; if a rainbow appears on a day when the moon is in this asterism, there will be rain; [auspicious for] approaching one's wife during the fertile period, the *sīmantonnayana* rite, the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first feeding (*annaprāśana*), the commencement of Vedic study, sacrifices, the beginning of learning, ear-piercing, ceremonial baths, marriage, sowing seeds, and royal consecrations.

One should perform the collection of earth for the building site and the *śrāddha* ceremony at the end of the fourteen *nāḍīs*. At the end of the *viṣaghaṭikā*, there is a void; on Thursday in the month of Kārttika, there is the *maraṇa-yoga*; with the sixth [lunar day], there is the *ugra-yoga*. On Sunday, there is the *ānanda-yoga*; on Monday, the *siddhi-yoga*. On Tuesday, at moonrise, one should perform the installation in the Taurus ascendant (*vṛṣa-lagna*); the increase of fruit will follow. In this ascendant, one should collect the clay from the wedding ground; it brings success to oneself.

One should prepare a seat of grain. If there is affliction from fever for five days, the food offering (*naivedya*) should be milk-rice (*pāyasa*); worship with *kumuda* and blue lotus flowers; incense consisting of ten ingredients; and the mantra for worship is "navo navo" (RV 10.85.19). Mudga beans, sesame seeds, and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) are the materials for the fire oblation (*homa*).

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the *Sāvitrī* mantra, one should present a sacrificial offering (*bali*) to Candra and the other deities using mudga beans and sesame seeds. From the fifth day until the end of the ninth day, one will become well. During the transit (*saṃkrānti*), the middle *argha* [is prescribed].

Ārdrā has one star; its deity is Rudra; it is feminine, sharp, and yellow in color; its face is turned upward; its group is that of humans; its animal is the dog; its tree is the black Khadira; its bird is the Piṅgala; its seed-syllables are *e* and *aikāra*; its poisonous hour consists of twenty-one *ghaṭikās*. Having drunk [the water] from this [hour], one should set out on a journey. If there is a rainbow, there will be no rain. If there is a cloud-cluster in Aries (*meṣa-lagna*), rain will fall on the fifth or seventh day. At that time, if there is a wall-like rising [of clouds], and in Taurus (*vṛṣa-lagna*), there should be the gathering of wealth.

One should perform the commencement of studies (*vidyārambha*), ear-piercing (*karṇavedhana*), and the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*). On Thursday (*guruvāra*), there is the *mṛtyuyoga* (death-configuration). On Saturday with the Sun in conjunction (*sanaṃdārke*), there is the *maraṇayoga*. In the second part of the day, it is the time of death. On Saturday with a Saturday rising sign (*mandodaye*), one should construct a bridge (*setubandha*). On Sunday or Tuesday, under the Cancer ascendant (*karkāṭakalagna*), one should administer medicine. Under this same ascendant, the commencement of studies should be performed; however, if there is fever, it leads to death. There will be suffering for thirty-one days. [The remedy involves] the *dhattūra* flower, the *narakarañji* tree, *agaru* incense, and the mantra "Namaḥ Śambhave."

The mantra for worship: clarified butter is the substance for the fire-oblation (*homa*). Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the *Sāvitrī* mantra, one should present an offering (*bali*) of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) to Rudra. Beginning from the fifth day until the end of the tenth day, one will become happy; otherwise, death occurs. At the time of the solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), there is great danger.

Punarvasu consists of six stars; its shape is that of a boat; its deity is Iditi; its divine group is Cara; its source is the cat; its tree is the bamboo; its companion wind is Vāyu; its letters are *o* and *au*; it is masculine; its direction is the intermediate (diagonal); one should perform the seasonal union, the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first feeding (*annaprāśana*), the tonsure (*caula*), the initiation (*upanayana*), the commencement of studies (*vidyārambha*), medical treatment for a woman who has recently given birth, house-consecration rites (*vāstukarma*), the installation of deities (*devatāpratiṣṭhā*), the wearing of clothes and ornaments, consecrations (*abhiṣeka*), the sowing of seeds, journeys, and so forth. At the end of thirty *nāḍīs*, there is the *viṣanāḍikā*.

One should perform the pilgrimage and other rites during the month of Mithuna. At the end of the thirtieth nāḍī, there is the Viṣanāḍikā. In the month of Mithuna, the Śūnya [period] occurs. On Thursday, there is the Amṛtayoga; on Sunday, the Arthasādhanayoga; and some say there is also the Siddhiyoga. If there is fever, the affliction lasts for seven days. The food offering (naivedya) should be rice with jaggery (guḍa). Worship is performed with Mallikā flowers. Sandalwood (malayaja) is the incense. "Aditir dyauḥ" is the mantra for worship. Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of ghee and rice with the Gāyatrī mantra, [one offers] to Aditi.

One should offer an oblation with perfumes, garlands, and wealth; starting from the seventh day until the end of the twenty-seventh day, one will become happy; there is an increase in prosperity during the transits.

Puṣya has eight stars, is shaped like an arrow, is masculine, faces downward and upward, has Bṛhaspati as its deity, belongs to the light divine class, has Ajayoni as its source, the Aśvattha tree as its sacred tree, the Jīvañjīva bird as its symbol, and the letter *ka* as its seed-syllable. One should undertake a journey after consuming clarified butter. The poisonous hour (*viṣanāḍī*) occurs at the end of the ninetieth *nāḍī*. It is auspicious for the following rites: seasonal unions, the *sīmantonnayana*, *nāmakaraṇa*, *annaprāśana*, *cūḍākaraṇa*, *upaniṣkramaṇa*, *karṇavedhana*, the commencement of studies, ceremonial baths, consecrations, the sowing of seeds, and the laying of foundations.

One should perform the wearing of clothes and ornaments, the installation of cows and deities, and the ancestral rites (*śrāddha*). In the month of Kārttika, [the *yoga*] is empty; on the tenth day, there is the *ugra-yoga*; when the Moon and Sun are in conjunction, it is *yama-kaṇṭaka*; and when the Sun is in Jupiter, it is *siddhi-yoga*. On this day, having built a house, one may perform its consecration and the painting of murals. If a birth occurs during this time, death follows. In the third part [of the day], everything is auspicious; in the fourth part, there is the death of a kinsman. If there is fever, there will be affliction for seven days. [The remedy is] the *khaṇḍamuṇḍaka* offering and *mallikā* flowers.

One should offer a lotus flower and perform worship with *guggulu* incense. The mantra for the worship of Bṛhaspati is "bṛhaspate atīti. Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter and iron filings while reciting the Sāvitrī mantra, one should present an offering (*bali*) to Bṛhaspati consisting of perfumes, garlands, and boiled rice. Beginning from the third day until the end of the seventh day, one will become happy; there is an increase in prosperity during the transit (*saṃkrama*).

Now, Āśleṣā consists of four stars; its shape is like a plow; its presiding deity is the Serpent; it is sharp, female, and downward-facing; its group is that of the Rākṣasas; its source is the cat; its tree is the Nāga (Strychnos nux-vomica); its bird is the crow; its letters are *ra* and *ka*; one should set out on a journey after consuming milk-rice (*pāyasa*). At the end of thirty *nāḍīs*, it is the hour of poison (*viṣaghaṭikā*); death occurs at the third part of the day; there is victory over enemies; on Saturday, it is a yoga of death; on Tuesday and Wednesday, it is the "Thorn of Yama" (*yamakaṇṭaka*); some desire destruction on Tuesday.
