The Mṛtyu-yoga (death-configuration) occurs with Tuesday: when the sun rises amidst black and red clouds, within one *ghaṭikā* of this time, rain will fall from seven days once the sign of Sagittarius (*Kārmuka*) has risen; it becomes beneficial to oneself when Jupiter rises in its [specific] degree. All undertakings and the accumulation of wealth succeed quickly in this asterism. One should perform the digging of wells and such works under this asterism. If there is fever, the affliction will cease within nine days. The offering should be milk-porridge (*pāyasa*), worship with flax flowers (*atasī-puṣpa*), and the food-offering (*naivedya*) should consist of ghee and rice-cakes (*muṇḍaka*).

Guggulu incense; "maduvātā" is the worship mantra. One should offer the Nāga-bali with *kṛsarā* rice. If there is no peace, death will occur on the eighth day; there is a great obstacle at the transit (*saṃkrānti*). || ||

The constellation Māghī has four stars and the shape of a yoke; its presiding deity is the Pitṛs (Ancestors). Its lord is Ugra, its class is Rākṣasa, and its source is the rat. Its tree is the jackfruit (*panasa*), and its seed-syllable is the letter *Gha*. It is female and faces downward. One should undertake a journey after eating the meat of the partridge (*tittiri*). At the end of thirty *nāḍīs*, there are the "poisonous" (*viṣa*) periods. By performing plowing, sowing seeds, gathering grain, marriage, and the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice during this time, one’s grain yield will be a thousandfold. One should not incur expenditure; the month of Kārttika is void on a Friday.

The Yoga of Death (maraṇayoga): When the Sun [is in a certain position], it is the Yoga of Death; when the Sun and Moon [are so placed], it is Yamakaṇṭaka. On the fifth lunar day, there is the yoga of death together with the native. At the rising of the Moon, one should undertake all undertakings; in this ascendant, at the wedding site, one should also perform the taking of earth. If there is fever, it leads to death. There will be suffering for twenty-one days. The offering (naivedya) should consist of ghee, molasses, and sweetmeats; worship with Campaka flowers; incense of guggulu; the mantra "pitunastoṣam"; and offerings of sesame seeds mixed with ghee and honey, along with unbroken rice grains and banyan leaves.

Regarding the ritual substance: having offered one hundred and eight oblations of unbroken rice (*akṣata*) and sesame seeds with the *Sāvitrī* mantra, one should present the sacrificial offering (*bali*) to the ancestors. If there is no pacification and death occurs at the end of ten days, the long duration [of the obstacle] will persist.

Puṇya and Phalgunī are each two-starred constellations. Their deity is the female Adomukhī; their presiding deity is Bhaga; they belong to the Ugra class of beings; their animal source is the rat; their tree is the *phalāśa*; their bird is the crow; and their seed-syllable is the letter *ca*. Having eaten *śyāmaka* grain, one should set out on a journey—victory will ensue. One should pay off debts. In the month of Āṣāḍha, this constellation is empty. On Friday, it forms a *mṛtyuyoga* (death-configuration). One should perform the accumulation of gold, the commencement of learning, and the plastering of a house. In this month, under this asterism, if there is a halo around the sun or moon, [it portends a specific result].

If it is seen on the tenth day, there will be rain; at the end of twenty *nāḍikās*, there is the *viṣaghaṭikā* (the fatal hour). If there is a fever, there will be affliction for five or seven days. Incense of *bilva* fruit [should be offered]; "To the god Aryaman" is the mantra for worship. Having offered oblations of *priyaṅgu* grain with ghee one hundred and eight times while reciting the *Sāvitrī*, one should present an offering (*bali*) to the Sun with perfumes and flowers. Starting from the sixth day until the eighth day, one will be well. If there is no pacification, death occurs. At the transit (*saṃkrānti*), the price is middling.

Uttaraphalgunī consists of two stars; its gender is female; it faces upward; its presiding deity is Aryaman; its fixed nature (dhruva); its group is that of humans; its source is the bull; its bird is the crane (krauñca); its syllables are *cha* and *jā*. One should undertake a journey after drinking milk. At the end of eighteen *ghaṭikās*, there is a period of poison (*viṣaghaṭikā*). It is auspicious for the following rites: entering the womb (*ṛtusaṃgamana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), naming (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first feeding (*annaprāśana*), the tonsure (*caula*), the initiation (*upanayana*), the commencement of studies (*vidyārambha*), marriage (*vivāha*), the ceremonial bath (*snāna*), wearing clothes and ornaments, entering villages and such places, and the sowing of seeds and building foundations (*vāstu*). [One] cow.

One should perform rites of attraction (*saṃgrahaṇa*) and nourishment (*pauṣṭika*). In Mārgaśīrṣa, the *śūnya* [period] is for wearing clothes and ornaments; there is great success. On Sunday, it is a *siddhi-yoga*. Some say it is *śūnya*. In four [days], there is the *sahamṛtyu-yoga*. On Friday, there is the *kalaha-yoga*. When a halo or a rainbow is seen, there will be rain on the fifth or seventh day. There will be fever and suffering for twenty-one days. The food offering (*naivedya*) should be *kṛsara*; worship with white *karavīra* flowers and incense of *bilva* fruit. Or, it is said, "it is not so."

The mantra for worship: having offered one hundred and eight oblations of sesame, black gram, mustard, rice, and barley with the Sāvitrī mantra, one should present the *bali* offering to Aryaman with those same materials. From the eighteenth day until the end of the twenty-first day, there is liberation from fever; with each transition [of a day], there is an increase in intensity.

The Hasta nakṣatra has five stars—some say three—is masculine, faces obliquely upward, has Savitṛ as its deity, is light, and has the luster of a pigeon; its seed-syllables are *jha* and *ña*, its divine host is the Āriṣṭas, its tree is the Āriṣṭa, and its bird is the Ghaṇṭakī. One should set out on a journey after eating milk, rice, and meat; at the end of thirty-two nāḍīs, there is a Piṣaghaṭukā.

Auspicious acts such as sexual union during the fertile period (*ṛtu*) and so forth are as previously described. In the month of Makara, there is an *śūnya* (void) period. On Saturday, there is the *maraṇa-yoga* (death-configuration); others call it the *viṣa-yoga*. On Sunday, there is the *siddhi-yoga*; there is great success in wearing clothes, ornaments, and the like. Together with the seventh lunar day (*tithi*), there is the *maraṇa-yoga*; together with the fourth, there is the *mṛtyu-yoga*. On Thursday, there is the *kalaha-yoga* (conflict-configuration). On Wednesday, there is the *ānanda-yoga* (joy-configuration); one should perform the installation of deities, the appointment of generals, and so forth. One may give wealth or receive it; one may collect [taxes] from the gods and the people.

In the first portion, death occurs within a day. When a rainbow is seen, rain will fall on the twenty-first day. If there is a corpse, it indicates death; otherwise, there is doubt, and for fifteen days there will be suffering. The offering consists of cakes (*apūpa*). Worship with red *karavīra* flowers, incense of ten ingredients (*daśāṅga*), and the mantra "ud u tyam" should be performed. Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of curd and ghee while reciting the *Sāvitrī*, one should present the *bali* offering with perfumes and flowers. From the fifteenth day until the end of the twenty-first day, one shall become happy. During the transit (*saṃkrama*), the oblation is of medium quality.

The mind is one-pointed; the face is turned toward the animals; the presiding deity is Tvaṣṭṛ; the temperament is gentle; the animal source is the tiger; the class of beings is the Rākṣasas; the tree is the Bilva; the bird is the swan; the letters are Ṭa and Tha. Having eaten variegated food, if one sets out on a journey, it will take twenty-one *nāḍīs*; the poison-hour (*viṣanāḍikā*) occurs at the end. One should perform the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), piercing the ears (*vedhana*), the tonsure (*caula*), the initiation (*upanayana*), wearing clothes and ornaments, consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the Śrāddha rite, sowing seeds, and planting trees. The month of Vaiśākha is empty; Tuesday is a destructive conjunction (*nāśayoga*).

On Saturday, Sunday, and Tuesday, there is a *carayoga*. On Monday with the second lunar day (*dvitīyā*), there is a *sahaviṣayoga*. On the thirteenth lunar day (*trayodaśī*), there is a *maraṇayoga*. On Wednesday, there is *yamakaṃcaka*. On Saturday, there is a *nāśayoga*. If rain occurs in the morning during the first half of the month of Māgha, there will be fever and suffering for five days. The offering (*naivedya*) should be sweetmeats (*modaka*); worship with *japā* flowers; incense consisting of ten ingredients; and the mantra for worship is "citram devānām. The substances [for the offering] are water, rice, ghee, and variegated cooked rice (*citrodana*). [The number of recitations is] one hundred and eight times the *sāvitri*.

Having offered one hundred oblations of ghee to Tvaṣṭṛ, one should present an offering (bali) of water; beginning from the seventh day until the end of the twentieth day, one will become well. During a transit (saṃkrama), the price is middling and high.

Svātī consists of one star; its color is red; it is female; its presiding deity is Vāyu; its movement is toward the northwest (carātir-yajmukhī); its divine group is the Devagaṇa; its source is the buffalo; its tree is the Unmatta; its bird is the peacock; having eaten the Āmalaka fruit, one should set out on a journey. At the end of fourteen *nāḍīs* there is a poisonous (*viṣa*) period. Auspicious rites such as approaching a wife for intercourse are performed as before. The month of Vaiśākha is empty. On Monday there is the Siddhi-yoga; on Saturday there is the Amṛta-yoga; on Sunday there is the Siddhi-yoga; on Friday there is Yamakaṇṭaka.

The conjunction of death on the thirteenth lunar day; the excellent conjunction of Sanandā Kuḍyau—one should not give wealth; victory on the fifth day of the bright fortnight; one should effect imprisonment on a Saturday when Taurus is rising; the syllable *ḍa* and the *ṛk* verse; if there is fever, suffering for sixty days; boiled rice with curds as the sacrificial offering; worship with *damanaka* flowers; incense of white aloe-wood; the mantra for the sacrifice is "sanaḥ pite"; the substance is barley-gruel smeared with ghee; having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the Sāvitrī mantra.

One should offer a bali-oblation to Vāyu with fragrant flowers; starting from the tenth day until the fortieth day, one will become happy. During a transit [of the sun], the price is middling and high.

Viśākhā has four stars; it is feminine, shaped like a winnowing basket, and faces downward. Its presiding deities are Indra and Agni. Its mixed source is the tiger; its tree is the Vaikaṅkata; its bird is the Piṅgala; and its letters are Ṛ and Ḍha. One should undertake a journey after taking food consisting of flour and water. On the fourteen-nāḍī creeper, it is a poisonous nāḍī; auspicious rites are as previously stated. One should perform the sowing of seeds and the taking of clothes and ornaments. One should not give wealth, but should certainly receive it. In Mārgaśīrṣa, it is empty.

The Ārknāśa Yoga: Some desire this to be the Viṣa Yoga. On the days of Mercury and Jupiter, it is Yamakaṇṭaka; on the second degree, there is death during the day. On Friday, when Venus is rising, one should commence agricultural work; if one sees an enemy at that time, it becomes auspicious. On Saturday, in this Lagna, if Cancer, Scorpio, or Sagittarius is the ascendant and Mars is present, one should undertake the collection of grain; at that time, if there is a dispute over land, victory will be achieved. If a rainbow is seen, rain will fall within eight days; if there is fever, suffering will last for twenty days. [Regarding] molasses...

The food offering (*naivedya*) consists of *baṃdhūka* flowers; the incense is *devadāru*; the worship mantra is "śanna indrāgnī"; the substances for the fire oblation (*homa*) are milk, rice, and ghee. Having performed one hundred and eight oblations with the *Sāvitrī*, one should offer food mixed with milk, along with perfumes and garlands, to Indra and Agni. Beginning from the tenth day until the end of the twentieth day, one will become well; the transit (*saṃkrānti*) will be short and auspicious.

Anurādhā consists of six stars, has the shape of a garland of wheels, is masculine, faces the intermediate directions, has Mitra as its presiding deity, belongs to the class of gods, and its source of birth is the deer. Its tree is the *vakula*, its birds are the cuckoo and the crow, and its letters are *ta*, *tha*, and *da*. Poison is fatal at the end of the twelfth *nāḍī*. One should undertake a journey after consuming wholesome food. One should perform the seasonal union (*ṛtusaṃgamana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first feeding (*annaprāśana*), the initiation (*upanayana*), the commencement of studies (*vidyārambha*), the ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), the sowing of seeds (*bījāvāpana*), and other such rites.

In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, the [lunar] day is empty; on a Sunday, it is a *maraṇa-yoga* (death yoga), though some consider it a *mṛtyu-yoga* (death yoga); on a Wednesday, it is a *mṛta-yoga*; on the tenth lunar day, it is a *mugra-yoga*. Death occurs during the third part of the day. At that time, if one collects grain under a Capricorn ascendant (*cāpa-lagna*) in a portion of Mars (*kujāṃśa*), there will be victory in business dealings. One should collect clay at a wedding site. If a cloud resembling a *karavīra* flower is seen, rain will fall on the third day; if it is otherwise, it will be on that very day.

There will be suffering for twenty days, or perhaps ten days. The worship mantra is "mitrasya carṣaṇī. The offerings are saffron, sandalwood paste, lotus flowers, milk-rice with ghee as the food offering, sandalwood incense, and the suraṇa tuber as the primary substance for the fire sacrifice (homa). Having offered one hundred and eight suraṇa tubers while reciting the Sāvitrī mantra, one should present an offering of milk-rice with ghee, along with a vessel of black gram (māṣa) and a bali-offering, to Mitra. From the eighth day until the end of the fifteenth day, one will become happy. This is the arghya for the middle of the transit (saṃkrama).

Jyeṣṭhā consists of three stars; its form is that of a woman wearing a bodice; it faces obliquely; Indra is its presiding deity; it is sharp; its source is the deer; its tree is the poison-tree; its bird is the cock; its seed-syllable is the letter *Dha* and the *Kṣa-ra*; having eaten sesame seeds, one should set out on a journey. At the end of fourteen *nāḍikās*, there is the *viṣaghaṭī*. Some say it is for the commander-in-chief, for *śrāddha*, and for sowing rice. In the month of Phālguna, it is empty (*śūnya*). On Sunday, it is a conjunction of destruction (*nāśayoga*). On the first lunar day (*pratipad*), Jupiter's day, it is a *viṣayoga*. On Monday, with Mars in the ascendant, it is suitable for digging wells and similar works.

One should perform the digging rite—if a cloud resembling a *karavīra* flower is seen on the tenth day, there will be rain; if there is fever, it portends death or doubt [of death]; suffering for five days or more [will follow]. The offering (*naivedya*) should be variegated rice; worship with *paṭolī* flowers; incense of *karpūra* and *agaru*; the mantra is "Indrava. The substances for the fire-oblation (*homa*) are *sūraṇa* root and *kuṇḍa* root mixed with ghee. Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the *Sāvitrī* mantra, one should present a sacrificial offering (*bali*) to Indra with perfumes and flowers. If peace is not attained, there is death; if the transition [of the illness] occurs, there is a reduction of the affliction.

The root is Navatārā; the animal form is the Paśvākṛti; the color is Haṃsa (white); the face is downward-facing; the gender is neuter; the deity is Sīṛṛti; the temperament is Tīkṣṇā (sharp); the group is Rākṣasa; the birth-source is the dog; the tree is Sarjara; the bird is Jīvañjīvaka; one should set out on a journey after eating Śyāmāka grain—some say after eating Tila; its duration is twenty Nāḍīs; its poison-period is the Viṣaghaṭī; death occurs at the end of the day; it is auspicious for the seasonal union, the naming ceremony, the first feeding, the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, and marriage.

One should perform the sowing of seeds and the gathering of cattle; one should perform fierce rites; one should not give away wealth but should certainly take it; let there be no emptiness in the cow-pens. On Sunday occurs the *mṛtyuyoga* (death-configuration); on Saturday and Tuesday occurs the *varayoga* (auspicious configuration). The founding of a city should take place when the sign of Sagittarius (*kārmuka*) is rising. If a red cloud appears with a fierce aspect, there will be rain on a favorable day. If there is fever, there is death or doubt [of recovery]; suffering lasts for ten days. Fish, meat, wine, and *polikā* cakes are the offerings (*naivedya*). The performer should worship with *aśoka* flowers and black *śevantikā*.

Regarding "flower," [it is described] in the *Hemādri*: "meṣaśṛṅga" (ram's horn) is the incense; the mantra is "moṣaṇaḥ parāparā"; and "brāhmaṇaḥ saravidāna" is [stated] in the *Hemādri*. Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of the root-substance of the kanda with ghee while reciting the Sāvitrī mantra, one should present a bali-offering of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) to Nirṛti. There is an increase in the number of oblations for each step.

Pūrvāṣāḍhā consists of two stars; its deity is female; it faces downward; its presiding deity is Water (Āpa); it is fierce; its group is that of humans; its source is the monkey; its tree is the monkey-tree (*vānara*); its bird is the parrot; its letters begin with *sa* and end with *va*; if one sets out on a journey after eating human flesh, there is a "poison-hour" (*viṣaghaṭī*) at the end of twenty-four *nāḍīs*. One should engage in the gathering of cattle and the sowing of rice; one should also undertake the digging of wells and the like, the commencement of learning, the entry into vows, the construction of water-houses, and the building of boats. However, one should not give away wealth.

One should indeed undertake [the work]: in the month of Śrāvaṇa, on a Sunday, there is the *śūnya* yoga; on a Tuesday, during the *yamodaya* yoga, one should begin the construction of a wall. In this *lagna*, one may dig wells and the like. If it is seen by a reddish cloud and rains for five days, there will be fever and suffering for twenty-five days. The offering (*naivedya*) should be *maṇḍaka* cakes; worship with *kalhāra* flowers; incense of realgar (*manaśśilā*); and the mantra for worship is "Āpo hi ṣṭhā. Using red rice as the substance, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations (*homa*) with the Sāvitrī mantra and present an offering (*bali*) of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and clarified butter (*ājya*) to Varuṇa, starting from the fourteenth day.
At the end of twenty days one shall become happy; during the two transits (saṃkrānti), there is a long period (of illness).

Uttarāṣāḍhā consists of two stars; its gender is female; it faces upward; its presiding deity is the Viśvedevas; its *dhruva* (fixed) group is the human class; its source is the Gaurī-yoni; its tree is the jackfruit (*panasa*); its bird is the piṅgala; its seed-syllable is the letter *Bha*; one should engage in the selling and riding of elephants; having consumed sesame seeds, one may set out on a journey; the Viṣaghnī-ṛtu-saṃgamaṇa and other auspicious rites should be performed; it is void in the month of Vaiśākha; and there is a "death-yoga" (*maraṇayoga*) on Monday.

On Sunday, Siddhi-yoga; on Tuesday, Kalaha-yoga; on Saturday, Mṛtyu-yoga; on Friday, Ānanda-yoga. On the third lunar day, there is the Marana-yoga. If a red cloud is seen, rain will fall on the eleventh day; if there is fever, suffering will last for twenty days. The offering consists of five types of food. Worship with flowers of various colors. Lākṣā (lac) is the incense. The mantra for worship is "Viśvedevāsa āgata. The materials are ghee and pieces of sallakī wood. Recite the Sāvitrī mantra one hundred and eight times.

Having offered oblations, one should present a *bali* offering of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) to the Viśvedevas; beginning from the eleventh day until the end of the twentieth day, one will become happy. During the *saṃkrānti*, there is an increase in the duration [of the ritual].

Śroṇā consists of three stars and has the form of a staff. It is masculine, faces upward, and its presiding deity is Viṣṇu. Its group is the Caras, its source is the monkey, and its tree is the Nyagrodha. Its bird is the peacock, and its artisan is Atri. At the end of the Maśa-nāḍī, there is a period of poison for sixty ghaṭikās. If one undertakes a journey after drinking water during this time, one should perform the seasonal rites, the union of husband and wife, the *sīmantonnayana*, the naming ceremony, the first feeding of solid food, the tonsure, the initiation (*upanayana*), consecration, the wearing of ornaments, agriculture, the sowing of seeds, ear-piercing, and so forth; as well as marriage, ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), sacrifices, and acts of wisdom.

In Mārgaśīrṣa, it is empty [inauspicious]. On Sunday, there is Siddhi-yoga; on Monday, there is Mṛtyu-yoga. On the fifth lunar day, one should undertake the collection of grain when the ascendant is Leo, Cancer, Scorpio, or Sagittarius, and during the portion of the Moon. There will be loss through theft. Having commenced the building of a house at sunrise on Monday during the second part [of the day], one should perform the consecration ceremony. If clouds are seen, rain will fall. If there is fever, there will be suffering for two months, or else doubt [regarding recovery]. Milk, sugar, ghee, and *maṇḍaka* cakes should be offered as the sacrificial oblation (*naivedya*).

For the worship with *jātī* flowers: ten-ingredient incense (*daśāṅga-dhūpa*); the worship mantra is "Ātodevā"; red rice is the substance for the fire oblation (*homa*). Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the *Sāvitrī*, one should present an offering (*bali*) to Viṣṇu with fragrant flowers. At the end of the month or the end of the year, one shall become happy; at the transition of the sun (*saṃkrānti*), there is an increase in prosperity.

Dhaniṣṭhā consists of five stars; its form is distinct, shaped like a mṛdaṅga drum; it is female and faces upward; its presiding deity is Nāsavya; its group is that of the Rākṣasas; its source is the lion; its tree is the śamī; its syllable is *makāra*; having consumed barley meal (*saktu*), one should set out on a journey; at the end of ten nāḍīs there is a poisonous nāḍī; the junction of the seasons and other auspicious rites are as previously stated; in the month of Āṣāḍha it is void; on Tuesday there is the Viṣa-yoga; some say it is the Nāśa-yoga; on Saturday, during the rising of Saturn, one should gather land for a garden.

One should act thus: one should engage in battle at this *lagna*; during the rising of Mars (*kujodaye*), one should engage in business, the accumulation of wealth, and battle. Death occurs through the first portion (*ādyāṃśena*). When a red cloud is seen, there will be rain in twenty days; if there is fever, there will be suffering for five days. The offering (*naivedya*) should consist of salt. One should perform worship with a hundred thousand flowers, offer *guggulu* incense, and recite the mantra "trāyantāṃ mihadevāḥ. The sacrificial materials (*samidh*) should be from *bilva*, *udumbara*, and *aśvattha* trees. Having offered one hundred and eight oblations (*homa*) with the *Sāvitrī* mantra—

One should offer a bali-oblation to the Vasus with green gram mixed with ghee; starting from the tenth day until the end of the fifteenth day, one will become happy, or by the end of the thirteenth month. At the transit [of the sun], the price is middling.

Śatabhiṣak (the Hundred Stars) constellation has the appearance of a cluster of flowers; it is neuter, faces upward, and has Varuṇa as its presiding deity. Its group is the Caras, its source is the horse, its tree is the Kadamba, and its bird is the Kaṇṭakī. Its letters are *ra* and *la*. One should perform the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), the tonsure (*caula*), the rite for a male child (*puṃsavana*), ear-piercing (*karṇavedhana*), the kindling of the sacred fire (*agnisaṃdhāna*), the threshing of grain (*dhānyāvaghāta*), ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), and the commencement of weapons (*śastrārambha*) during this asterism. It is empty in the month of Proṣṭhapada. On Tuesday (*kuja-vāra*), it forms a yoga of death; some say it is a yoga of death on Saturday (*manda-vāra*).

— *Yamakaṇṭaka*: This is a yoga of death for Saturn and Mars. On Thursday, it is a yoga of death (*mṛtyuyoga*). If Cancer is the ascendant on Sunday or Tuesday, one may administer medicine. In this ascendant, one should perform the planting of crops. Having eaten cakes (*apūpa*), one may set out on a journey. After eighteen *nāḍīs*, there is the *viṣaghaṭī* (poisonous hour). If there is fever, one should offer oblations for ten days and present a *bali* offering with milk-rice (*pāyasa*). From the sixth day until the end of the twelfth day, one will become well. At the transit (*saṃkrānti*), there is a great obstacle.

Pūrvābhādrapadā consists of two stars; its gender is female; it is downward-facing; its presiding deity is Ajaikapād; it is fierce; its group is that of humans; its source is the lion; its tree is the mango; its letters are *a* and *kṣa*; its animal is the pigeon; one should undertake a journey after eating molasses. At the end of sixteen *nāḍīs*, there is a poisonous hour (*viṣanāḍikā*). It is auspicious for acquiring horses, gathering cattle, and commencing studies. One should not give away wealth, but may certainly receive it. On Tuesday, it is a yoga of destruction. In its final degree, there is the *nāgavallī* (betel vine) and so forth.

Installation: On the second lunar day, during the rising of Venus, one should dig a well or similar excavation. If blood-colored clouds are seen on the desired day, there will be rain; if there is fever, it portends death, or else suffering for twenty-two days. The offerings should consist of curd, ghee, and sacrificial food (naivedya); worship with *arka* flowers; incense of all medicinal herbs; the mantra "śanno devīr abhiṣṭaye" (or "śanno aja ekapād"); and the substance of ghee and pieces of *kūṣmāṇḍa* fruit. Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the *Sāvitrī* mantra, one should present a bali offering to Aja Ekapād with perfumes, garlands, and food, as well as to Indra and the other deities.
And if there is no pacification, death occurs; at the transition (saṃkrama), it is middling and severe.

Uttarābhādrapadā: second night; male; facing upward; Ahirbudhnya as the deity; the class of humans; stable; the womb of Gaurī; the Nimba tree; the Cakravāka bird; the letters *a* and *kṣa*; having eaten meat, one may go on a journey; at the end of twenty-four *nāḍīs*, it is poisonous; one should perform the union for conception (*ṛtusaṃgamana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first feeding (*annaprāśana*), and the gathering of cattle (*gosagrahaṇa*); if a sick person bathes, he will become well; [the asterism] is empty in the months of Śrāvaṇa and Mārgaśīrṣa.

The conjunction for death with the third lunar day: on Tuesday, it is a yoga of death; on Sunday, a yoga of success. Death occurs during the third quarter of the day. If seen by a red cloud, there will be rain on the eleventh day. If there is fever, there will be affliction for ten days. The food offering (naivedya) should consist of rice with molasses. The leaves of the *karañja* tree are the flowers; ghee is the incense. "Viṣṇor-ṇo" is the mantra for the oblation. The substance is black gram and green gram soaked in ghee. Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the *Sāvitrī* mantra, one should present the *bali* offering to Ahibudhnya with perfumes and flowers. There is an increase in prosperity through the *saṃkrānti*.

Revatī is the thirty-second lunar mansion (tārā). It is masculine, yellow in appearance, and faces obliquely. Its presiding deity is Puṣan; its temperament is mild (mṛdu); its divine class is that of the gods (devagaṇa); its source is the elephant (gajayoni); its tree is the Madhūka; its bird is the Piṅgala; its syllable is the letter *ha*. One should set out on a journey after consuming milk. At the end of thirty nāḍīs, there is the Viṣaghaṭī. In the month of Proṣṭhapada, it is empty (śūnya). One should perform the rites prescribed for Uttarā Bhādrapadā, such as sexual union during the season. On Sunday, it is the Siddhi-yoga; on Wednesday and Monday, it is the Viṣa-yoga; and on Saturday, [it is the same].

Nāśayoga: conjunction with the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī). Viṣayoga: on Friday. Siddhiyoga: conjunction with the seventh lunar day (Saptamī). Ugrayoga: if there is fever, suffering for twelve days. The food offering (naivedya) should consist of ground sesame seeds and rice; the flower is Mandāra.

The worship consists of guggulu incense; the mantra is "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat"; the substances are plantains together with ghee and mango fruits. Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the *sāvitrī* mantra, one should present the *bali* offering to Pūṣan with perfumes, flowers, and other articles. Beginning from the fifth day until the end of the twentieth day, one shall become happy. Regarding the transit (*saṃkrama*), Gārgya, Māṇḍavya, and others maintain that the *argha* [offering] is moderate, while others hold that there is an increase in the *argha*.
Thus ends the knowledge of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) as stated in the *Madanaratna* within the *Śāntiratna*.
In the *Vasiṣṭhasaṃhitā*:
"I shall now proclaim the pacification of diseases for embodied beings afflicted by illness."

When disease arises for men under whichever constellation (dhiṣṇya), then worship of that constellation must be performed for the complete satisfaction of its presiding deity through bali offerings, ancillary fire-sacrifices (homa), recitation of mantras (japa), and the feeding of Brahmins.
Having fashioned an image according to one's means, using half a pala of gold, or half of that, or even half of that again,
one should draw it in the northeast, southeast, east, or northern direction upon the sacrificial site.
A lotus with eight petals is drawn upon a mandala made of cow dung.

Having bathed [the image] separately with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and waters while reciting their respective mantras, one should then install the image using the mantra prescribed in the ritual manual (kalpa). Having placed it firmly upon the pericarp (karṇikā) and meditated upon the deity, one should worship it.

One should worship that with colored garments, perfumes, and the like, along with flowers, incense, and offerings; likewise, a pitcher of reddish color, provided with five sprouts, white cloth, gold, gems, and a hundred medicinal herbs.

Having placed the deity to the east, one should worship him with his respective mantras using earth, the five products of the cow, auspicious seeds, fruits, substances, and kuśa grass. Then, one should duly establish the fire upon an altar (sthaṇḍila) to the east of that.
At the conclusion of the rite, one should perform eight thousand oblations with the prescribed substance—
the aforementioned substance for the pacification of each respective lunar mansion (nakṣatra), as will be described later—
and one thousand and eight oblations of sesame seeds with the Vyāhṛtis.
One should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* following the proper recitation of mantras; then,
for the patient who is comfortably seated and facing the east,
one should sprinkle him with water from a jar purified by mantras, or with water consecrated by the *liṅga-mantras*.

Having arrived at the place of worship with a purified mind, he should perform the ritual cleansing (mārjana) preceded by a formal resolve (saṃkalpa). Then, having offered the lustration ceremony (nīrājana),
he should bow with devotion to the god Agni and pray as follows:
You are the sole Lord of Sacrifice, born from the nectar of immortality, the Supreme Self;
protect me from disease, for you are the one who wards off the afflictions of the gods.
Having prayed thus, he should then devotedly give the image, together with a garment and a priestly fee (dakṣiṇā), to the preceptor who maintains a household; thereafter,
he should feed the Brāhmaṇas according to his capacity.
And having performed the worship of the lunar mansion (nakṣatra), as well as of the lunar day (tithi) and the day of the week (vāsara).
One who is ill attains all desires and is freed from disease;
having performed the previously mentioned rite on the specified lunar day and weekday, one should perform the propitiatory ceremony (śānti)—this is the meaning.
A disease that has arisen under Aśvinī is released after seven nights.

For the mantra beginning with "devasya tvā," the seer is Kāśyapa, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deities are the two white-colored Aśvins. One should offer jars filled with nectar, along with separate vessels of food, sandalwood, blue lotuses, flowers, clarified butter, and guggulu resin; these are pleasing to Guja.
The two of them were eaters of milk-laddukas, and their sacrificial fuel was produced from milk and water.

Clarified butter and guggulu incense, as well as an oblation with fuel-sticks—thus it is also hereafter. One should offer a bali-offering of rice mixed with jaggery together with lamps at the beginning of the night.
A disease arising under the asterism Bharaṇī brings wealth within a short time;
however, it releases the patient after a month—such is the crooked course of destiny.
The seers, meters, and deities for the mantra of Tryambaka have been declared.
Sandalwood, *karavīra* flowers, and guggulu incense are prescribed;
likewise, ghee for the lamp, and for all [the offerings], molasses and rice constitute the *naivedya*.
Red in color, holding a noose and a staff, mounted upon his buffalo mount, he should carry an offering of clarified butter, honey, unbroken rice grains,
oblation (havis), and *kṛsarānna*;
one should cause the offering to be properly presented with the mantra that will be recited hereafter.
In Kṛttikā, a disease arises at dawn and leaves after three nights;
[the deity] holds a sacrificial ladle (sruk) and spoon (sruva), grants boons, belongs to his own class, and has a ram as his vehicle.
The *medhātithi* hymn, the *jagatī* meter, the deity Agni, and the verse beginning with "punantu mā"—
for these, sandalwood, jasmine flowers, ghee, and *sugandha-guggulu* incense are prescribed.
The food offering (naivedya) should consist of sesame, black gram, and rice, combined with fried cakes and clarified butter;
there, one should present an oblation of jaggery-rice as the sacrificial offering (havis), along with a bali-offering of milk-rice (pāyasa).
A disease that has arisen under Rohiṇī is released after ten nights.
"Obeisance to Brahmā"—this is the mantra; Gāyatrī is its meter, and Īśvara is the presiding deity.
He is white in complexion, holding a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), a sacred thread (yajñopavīta), and displaying the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons;
[the offerings are] sandalwood, a lotus flower, incense, and ten-parted guggulu resin.
This milk-rice offering with ghee shall always be the sacrificial oblation (havis) consisting of all kinds of food.
A disease arising from the lunar mansion of Candra is released after five nights; [its deity is] Śveta, who holds a boon-granting hand and has a chariot as his vehicle.
He becomes ever new; his [mantra] is the Gāyatrī, Gautama is his seer, and the Śaśin is his deity.
Sandalwood, the kumuda flower, the ten-ingredient incense (daśāṅga), and milk-rice are the offerings.
One should offer the oblation with the *mandaka* flower mixed with honey,
combined with sugar and curd, along with white rice.
A disease arising under Ārdrā brings suffering for a long time;
it releases after a month, for the course of destiny is crooked.
[The deity] resembles pure crystal and bestows the sword, protection from fear, and desired objects.
For the mantra "namaḥ śaṅkarāya," the seer is Bṛhatīśa Vidhi.

One should offer there sandalwood, fragrant flowers, the ten-ingredient incense (daśāṅga), and milk-rice; the sacrificial oblation (havis) should consist of honey and clarified butter, and one should present an offering (bali) of curd-rice.
Furthermore, that disease born of ill fortune is released after seven nights;
he always carries a water-pot, a rosary, a sacred thread, fuel-sticks, *darbha* grass, a large sacrificial ladle, and a small sacrificial spoon.
Aditi is the deity of the mantra "aditirdyauśca," which is in the Triṣṭubh meter; its seer is Druhiṇa and its deity is Diti.
Haridrā, saffron, fragrance, flowers, śāmaṃtikā, and so forth.
One should offer incense made from ground sandalwood, ghee-rice, yellow pigment,
rice smeared with ghee, and oblation-food (havis) together with yellow food as the sacrificial offering (bali).
A disease that arises under the Puṣya asterism is released after seven nights.
He is yellow in color, holding a staff, a water-pot, and a rosary, with his right hand raised in the gesture of granting fearlessness.
For the hymn beginning with "bṛhaspate tītī," the seer is Jīva Āṅgirasa in the Triṣṭubh meter;
the offerings are saffron, lotus flowers, honey, clarified butter, and milk-rice (pāyasa).
This same offering should consist of pancakes combined with jaggery;
one should cause an oblation (bali) to be presented there with pancakes and ghee-rice.
In Āśleṣā, a disease that has arisen well will release one from suffering after a month;
by reciting the mantra "Namo astu" [to the serpent], the fire-eater, the king of serpents, [is appeased].
The sword and shield are auspicious when honey-colored and provided with a bowstring;

the incense should have the fragrance of *kaṅkuṣṭha* and *agaru*; the flower should be that produced by the *agastya* plant; the smoke offering (*dhūpa*) should be ghee and *guggulu*; and the food offering (*naivedya*) should consist of milk and clarified butter.
One should offer as the oblation clarified butter, well-prepared rice with curd, and a sacrificial gift of curd-rice.
One who has risen from the *ṛtambhara* stage bestows immediate liberation;
for one who holds the staff of smoke and the sacred grass, peace is attained within half a month.
May the Gāyatrī be for our benefit, may the Triṣṭubh be ours, and may the Jagatī be born from the Pitṛs.
[I offer] sandalwood, campaka flowers, incense, and guggulu resin mixed with honey.

The sacrificial offering consists of rice mixed with ghee, rice with sesame seeds, oblation with ghee, rice with sesame and clarified butter, and rice with mung beans; this is the bali-offering when the ancestors are satisfied.
A disease occurring under Pūrvāphālgunī is released after one month;
Bhaga alone is the eternal lord, and this is the rule for the three-year cycle.
Padmā, Bhayakara, Padmavraṇa, seated upon a lion-throne;
sandalwood, mālatī flowers, bilva, incense, ghee, and curd.
The sacrificial offering (naivedya) should consist of sugar, cakes, and sweetmeats;
there, one should present as an oblation (bali) clarified butter, curd, and milk-rice (pāyasa).
The disease born of Āryaman releases its hold within a month.

[He who is] lotus-colored, seated upon a lotus, and possessing a luster like the interior of a lotus—[this is the deity of] the mantra "Āryamāya. Āryaman is the seer, the Triṣṭubh is the meter, and the lotus-born [Brahmā] is the deity.
Camphor, saffron, fragrance, and the flower known as vakula.
Here, the incense is guggulu mixed with clarified butter, the food offering is milk-rice cooked in clarified butter,
the substance for the fire-oblation is rice cooked in clarified butter, and one should present the bali-offering with śāli rice.
A wind arising from the hand releases [the disease] within nine nights;
the fragrance is of saffron and the flower known as the blue lotus (rājīva).
Here, the incense is guggulu resin, and the food offering consists of ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa).
One should offer as an oblation honey, flowers, sesame, clarified butter, and cooked rice, together with dūrvā grass;
likewise, one should present a bali-offering of jaggery, sugar, honey, clarified butter, and flour-based food.
A disease that has arisen under Citrā is released after ten nights.
"The wondrous [work] of the gods..."—this verse belongs to Mitra; Tvaṣṭṛ is the father of Triṣṭubh, the great one.
One should scatter flowers of variegated colors, fragrant with saffron and agaru, along with a thread that bestows fearlessness.
The sacrificial offering (naivedya) consists of sweetmeats, clarified butter, rice mixed with sesame, ghee, and oblation;
one should present the bali-offering with that food for the removal of all diseases.
If a disease arises under the Svāti asterism, it always bestows wealth;
one is released from it after one, two, three, four, or five days.
For the mantra "sanaḥ pite," the meter is Gāyatrī, and the seers are the Maruts and Aṅgiras.
The sword and shield are black; the fragrance is black aloe-wood;
the flower is *damanaka*; the incense is sandalwood, aloe-wood, and *guggulu*;
the food offering is milk-rice with clarified butter—by means of these one should present the oblation.
If a disease occurs for two days, it will be released after one month;
indeed, [one should recite] the Gāyatrī verse beginning with "indrāgnī āgatam."
Honey, sandalwood, the lordly sages, fire, and their upward [flames] as before;
for those two, sandalwood paste, fragrance, and the lotus flower.
Devadāru wood is the incense for these two; the sacrificial food consists of ghee and milk-rice.
That same food is the oblation there; one should present the bali offering with variegated rice.
A disease that has arisen from a friend departs within ten nights;
one should indeed perform this [rite] for him with the verse "mitrasya carṣaṇī" (RV 3.59.6), which is in the Gāyatrī meter.
The sage there is named Hiraṇyastūpa, and Mitra is the presiding deity.
He has two arms, possesses the luster of the interior of a lotus, holds a lotus, and is seated upon a lotus.
[One should offer] saffron, the flower known as the white lotus (puṇḍarīka), incense, and sandalwood.
The sacrificial offering should consist of milk-rice with clarified butter; the oblation is the kandarba and sūraṇa roots.
A bali offering should be presented there with honey, sugar, and milk-rice.
Rice mixed with black gram, accompanied by mung beans and preceded by ghee.
If a disease arises in Jyeṣṭhā, it is death itself; of this there is no doubt.
Or else, after one month, it surely leaves; of this there is no doubt.
For the mantra beginning with "indraṃ vaḥ," the seer is Droṇa Āṅgirasa and the meter is Gāyatrī.
Indra, as before, offered sandalwood paste, auspicious flowers, camphor incense, an oblation of food, and most enchanting, variegated delicacies.
One should offer the oblation with *sūraṇa*, *karaṇa*, *madhukanda*, and excellent milk-rice (*pāyasa*), along with curd-rice (*dadhyanna*) and the fragrance of various flowers.
A disease arising from the root is released after half a month;
it is a lord who is black, bearing a sword and shield, with a terrifying face.
The *moghāṇa*, the *agrayatri*, the terrible *kaṇya*, and *nirṛti*;
the scent is black aloe-wood, and the auspicious flower is the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*).
The incense is black aloe-wood; the food offering consists of beans and rice.
That same food serves as the oblation there; one should present the bali-offering with the bean-rice.
A disease arising from the Vāribheda yoga brings death to the patient;
it is released by subtracting two, three, six, five, or seven from that [number].
For the mantra "āpyāyasva," the meter is Gāyatrī, the deity is Brahmā (Padmaja), the water is the offering substance,
the form is golden, he has two arms, his hand holds a lotus, and the fragrance is sandalwood.
The lotus, śaileya, and dūpa are the offerings; the oblation consists of ghee and milk-rice.
For the sacrificial offering (havis), one should present a bali with masūra flour-cakes and that same food.
A disease arising from Viśvabhuj is released after one and a half months;
its meter is Gāyatrī, its deity is the Viśvedevas, and it belongs to the Viśva-group.

Holding a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), a lotus, and displaying the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), seated upon *kuśa* grass, [he should offer] sandalwood, a lotus flower, incense, and clarified butter;
with *nicula* wood for the fuel, he should present the sacrificial offering (*bali*) with that food.
The disease arising from hearing [inauspicious sounds] is released after ten nights;
for this, the Gāyatrī metre is prescribed as the *prapada* for the mantra "atodevā".
Clad in white garments, dark-complexioned, and bearing the conch, discus, and mace;
[he is worshipped with] sandalwood, mālatī flowers, incense, camphor, and guggulu resin.

He should offer as an oblation rice of the *śāli* variety endowed with the six flavors, together with various kinds of foods to be chewed and eaten; this sacrificial offering (*havis*) may also consist of milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and with that he should present the bali.
A disease arising from Vasubheda leaves one after ten nights;
may the Trāyantīya mantra protect me here—this is the well-composed *anuṣṭubh* verse of Vyāsa, the best of the Vasus.
Holding a bow and arrow, with white fragrances such as camphor and sandalwood;
incense consisting of lotus and guggulu resin; and an offering of ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa).
One should offer to Pāpī an oblation consisting of fuel-sticks of Udumbara wood, jaggery, milk-rice,
sweetmeat balls (laḍḍuka), cakes, honey, clarified butter, sesame flour, and other offerings.
A disease arising from Varuṇa is released after eight nights;
for the verse "imaṃ me varuṇa," the meter is Gāyatrī and the seers are Kaṇva and Vāripā.
The glorious one holds a serpent-noose, adorned with nine jewels;
his fragrance is like that of agaru from the Malaya mountains, and his flowers are the lotus and the water-lily.

One should offer camphor, sandalwood, incense, and an oblation of ghee-filled *polikās*; for the sacrificial food (*haviḥ*), one should use fuel-sticks of the *aśvattha* tree and present the *bali* offering with various kinds of cooked rice.
Ajaikapāda (the one-legged goat) is disease, which always bestows death;
or else, it releases [the native] after many months or days.
When the left foot and hand are on the earth, the other two [feet] are in the sky.
Extending his hands in añjali, he stood facing the Lord himself while meditating upon him.
The mantra "śam agniḥ" has Ājyaikapāt as its deity, the Gāyatrī meter, and Caturānana (Brahmā) as its seer;
its materials are saffron, sandalwood paste, fragrance, and flowers from the white Arka tree.

The incense should be mixed with medicinal herbs; the sacrificial food (naivedya) should consist of curd and milk-rice (pāyasa); the oblation (havis) should be pieces of kūṣmāṇḍa fruit; and one should offer the bali-offering with curd and honey.
The disease born of Ahibudhnya releases one within a fortnight;
by reciting "namaste rudra," everything is established right there.

One should offer sandalwood and camphor as fragrance; auspicious flowers such as the lotus and water-lily; incense including *bilva* and *guggulu*; an offering of clarified butter and milk-rice (*pāyasa*); and oblations consisting of mung beans, black gram, sesame, rice, barley, and *vrīhi* grain mixed with clarified butter.
With this curd mixed with water, one should offer the bali-oblation to the deities of the sacrificial food.
A disease that has arisen under the asterism Revatī is released after eight nights.
For the mantra beginning with "pūṣātva," the meter is Jagatī and the seer is Gautama.
And Pūṣan is the deity; his color is auspicious like that of a conch, he is the bearer of seeds, and his fragrance is red sandalwood; his flower is known as mandāra.

The incense should be guggulu mixed with clarified butter; the food offering (naivedya) should be rice-pudding (pāyasa) with ghee; that same oblation (havis) should be offered with water; and one should present the bali-offering with curd-rice.
Since the Lord of Beings has followed you, O Jvara, the lord of diseases,
protect me from this illness and accept this supreme offering of all kinds of food.
Having performed the worship of the lunar mansion (nakṣatra), as well as of the lunar day (tithi) and the day of the week (vāsara),
one should likewise offer oblations to the sixfold group beginning with the zodiac sign (rāśi), and to their presiding deities.
Whoever performs the bali offering correctly is liberated from disease;
thus ends the pacification of diseases arising from the lunar mansions (nakṣatras).
The affliction that has arisen against one is released after twelve days;
Agni is the deity there, and one should offer an oblation of *kṛsara* rice.
If an illness should occur on the second lunar day, it is released after five nights;
Brahmā is the deity there, and one should offer an oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa).
If the affliction occurs on the third lunar day, it is released after seven nights;
Girijā is the presiding deity there, and one should offer an oblation of rice cooked in ghee.
On the fourth day, the disease arises and is released after ten nights;
Gaṇeśa is the deity there, and one should offer an oblation of rice cooked in ghee.
A disease that has arisen on the fifth day is abandoned after nine nights;
Sarveśa is the deity there, and one should offer a bali-oblation of food difficult to obtain.
A disease arising on the sixth day is released after four nights;
one should offer an oblation of mung beans there to the deity Skandanu.
A disease arising on the seventh day is released after eight nights;
Āryamā is the deity there, and one should offer an oblation of molasses and rice.
A disease that arises on the eighth lunar day is released after eight nights;
one should offer an oblation of jaggery-rice to the deity there.
If one recovers on the ninth day, the illness will surely lead to death;
Vasu is the deity there, and one should offer an oblation of sesame and rice.
A disease arising on the tenth day departs after five nights;
the deity there is a Nāga, and one should offer an oblation of rice cooked with ghee.
A disease arising on the eleventh day is released by a woman within a night;
Dharma is the deity there, and one should offer an oblation of black gram (māṣa) food.
If a disease arises on the twelfth lunar day, death will certainly occur;
even if one is liberated from that illness, one goes to the realm of Yama.
On the thirteenth day, Bhava causes illness, from which one is released after seven nights;
Kāma is the presiding deity there, and one should offer an oblation of sweetmeat balls (laḍḍukas).
If [the planet] is on the fourteenth day, there will be a dual disease and it will grant death within two months;
one should offer an oblation of flour-cake (piṣṭānna) to release all misfortune (ariṣṭa).
If a woman falls ill on the full moon day, she is released within three nights;
Candra is the deity there, and one should offer an oblation of curd-rice.
A disease born of the new moon (Amāvāsyā) is released after one month; or else, one afflicted by fever and burning sensations born of the lunar orb (Maṇḍala) is released after one full cycle.
Or he may face a great death, or he goes to the realm of Yama.
In this regard, I shall declare the rite of pacification for the sake of alleviating all defects:
an image of the ancestors should be fashioned from gold weighing one *karṣa*.
One should perform the fire-oblation with sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, sesame seeds, black gram, parched rice, and clarified butter,
either one hundred and eight times or twenty-eight times.
A black cow should be given to the preceptor along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
afterwards, one should feed eleven Brahmins according to one's ability.
For the sake of pacifying all calamities, one shall become long-lived and happy.
On Sunday, there may be double illness, yet one shall not be afflicted by fever or burning sensations;
the Sun is the presiding deity there, and one should offer an oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa).
If [the affliction] occurs on Monday, it will be cured within seven nights;
Soma is the deity there, and one should offer an oblation of ghee and rice.
On a Tuesday, there may be illness, leading to loss of hair or even death;
Mars is the deity there, and one should offer an oblation of red food.
If it falls on Wednesday, there will be illness leading to distress and even death;
since Mercury is the presiding deity there, one should offer an oblation of mung beans.
If there is illness on Thursday, it will be released after five nights;
Jupiter is the deity there, and one should offer an oblation of turmeric rice.
If [the affliction] occurs on a Friday, it will be cured within seven nights;
Bhṛgu is the deity there, and one should offer an oblation of turmeric and rice.
If illness occurs on a Saturday, one is released from it within half a month;
Saturn is the deity there, and one should offer an oblation of black gram (*māṣa*) food.
One should offer oblations to the lords of the six divisions (ṣaḍvārgapa), beginning with the zodiacal sign, for the attainment of happiness.
He who performs the oblation properly is liberated from disease;
[one should do so] in the houses called Dāsa, Nidhana, Pratyaga, Janma, and Vipat.
A disease born under a lunar mansion leads to affliction and even death.
[The asterisms] Āśleṣā, Ārdrā, the three Pūrvās, Yama, Varuṇa, Marut, Śakra, Tārā, and Anala—these are the twelve; on the twelfth day, Skanda and Riktā [are unfavorable].
And for those [born] on lunar days associated with Saturn, Mars, or the Sun, and on Saturdays;
If [the Moon] is born in the eighth house from the Ascendant, one will soon attain the supreme state; likewise,

if the Moon is in the eighth house from the natal sign, or if it occupies the eighth house from the house of kinsmen, or if it is situated in the eighth house from the house of kinsmen, or in the eighth house from the Ascendant, [disease arises].
Thus ends the section on the pacification of birth-stars and other factors regarding the onset of diseases such as fever, composed by Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa in the *Śāntiratna*.
Now follows the ritual for the pacification of the planets, beginning with the Sun.
In the *Madanaratna*, the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* states: "Henceforth I shall proclaim this supreme secret,
by which prosperity, fortitude, contentment, nourishment, and splendor are produced."
The wise practitioner, having first grasped the hand at the solar aperture (ādityāvāra),
should perform all rites for the Sun, such as worship and so forth, according to the procedure prescribed in the mantra.
Having performed seven nights of worship for each sun with devotion,
a person should then, when the seventh [night] has arrived, provide a meal for the Brahmins.
Having carefully fashioned a sun-god out of pure gold,
a person should bathe it in a copper vessel and worship it well with red flowers.
Covered with a pair of red garments and provided with an umbrella and a pair of sandals,
one should bathe it with ghee and offer sweetmeat balls (laḍḍukas).
The knower of mantras should perform the homa with ghee and sesame seeds while reciting the name of the Sun,
using one hundred and eight or twenty-eight sacrificial twigs (samidhs).
It should be offered with honey and clarified butter, as well as with curd and ghee.
The fuel-sticks are the rays of light.
One should cause it to be given to a Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the mantras.
O Primordial God, homage to you, O seven-rayed Maker of Day!
O Ravi, deliver us from this ocean of saṃsāra.
O Indra among kings, through this vow one attains supreme health; the knowers of the Purāṇas declare that it also brings wealth, prosperity, and the birth of sons.
This propitiatory rite brings about the attainment of one's desires and bestows nourishment upon men;
when performed for the severe affliction caused by the Sun, it grants auspiciousness.
Thus ends the propitiation of Āditya.
Now follows the propitiation of Candra—in that same work: "Likewise, on the Citrā [nakṣatra], the wise man, having observed Monday..."
By this very same method, one should perform the worship and other rites for the Sun.
Then, when the seventh [fast] has been reached, one should provide a meal for the Brāhmaṇas on the seventh *nakta*.
Having placed wealth in a bronze vessel, one should install Soma fashioned from silver,
covered with a pair of white garments, and worshipped with white flowers.
Provided with sandals, shoes, an umbrella, food offerings, and a seat,
the knower of mantras should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with ghee and sesame seeds, using the mantra named Soma.
One hundred and eight fuel sticks, or twenty-eight,
should be offered with honey, clarified butter, curd, and indeed ghee.
The fuel sticks are made from *pālāśa* wood.
O Indra among kings, having offered curd-rice to the Moon, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa,
being fully endowed with devotion, while reciting this mantra.
O Mahādeva, you whose beloved consort is Umā, you who are white as cow’s milk and like a flower;
O Soma, be gentle toward us—O Giver of All, salutations, salutations!
When this is done, there will be great peace, and Soma will become a bringer of well-being.
Thus concludes the propitiation of Candra.
Now, the pacification of Bhauma (Mars): When Mars is in the constellation Svāti, one should eat only at night;
when the seventh [day] has arrived, one should place [the image] in a vessel made of gold or copper.
It was covered with a pair of red garments and anointed with saffron.
Having offered *kusara* with devotion, along with flowers, incense, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*),
the knower of mantras should perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with ghee and sesame seeds while reciting the mantra by the name of Mars (*Kuja*).
One hundred and eight, or twenty-eight,
fuel-sticks should be offered with honey, clarified butter, curd, and ghee.
The fuel sticks are made of Khadira wood.
With this mantra, one should give it to a brāhmaṇa who maintains a family:
"Though you are born from the earth and Kṛttikā, you are Maṅgala (Auspiciousness), O reciter, you are recited."

O Mangala, having quickly destroyed inauspiciousness, grant auspiciousness, O Mangala! When this is done, O Bhauma, whatever evil deed has been committed shall attain peace; therefore, one must perform the propitiation of Bhauma with mental offerings for the sake of one's sons.
Thus concludes the propitiation of Aṅgāraka.
Now, the pacification of Mercury (Budha-śānti)—in that same [text]: "If one perceives Mercury in the Viśākhā nakṣatra, one should worship him for seven nights.
Having fashioned an image of Mercury, it should be placed in a bronze vessel."
Covered with a pair of white garments, adorned with white garlands and unguents,
and accompanied by molasses and curd, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa.
Obeisance to the son of Soma, who is the state of Buddhahood, the progenitor of the Buddhas, the possessor of awakening for all beings, and who brings about the realization of reality.
As before, one should perform the fire-oblation with ghee, sesame seeds, and *apāmārga* fuel-sticks while reciting the name of Budha.
This propitiation of Budha has been proclaimed as the destroyer of Budha’s portents.
In the case of a fault involving Mercury, a propitiatory rite (śānti) should likewise be performed, which bestows desired blessings.
Thus concludes the propitiation of Budha.
Now, the pacification of the Guru:
A person should worship the Guru under the constellation Anurādhā with devotion,
according to the previously mentioned ritual procedure, and should likewise observe seven nights of fasting.
Having placed Bṛhaspati in a vessel made of gold,
one should represent him as covered by a pair of yellow garments and wearing a yellow sacrificial thread.
One should worship him, adorned with sandals, shoes, an umbrella, and a water-pot,
anointed with saffron, and honored with yellow flowers.
One should present before the Guru offerings of incense, lamps, and other substances, as well as fruits, sandalwood, rice grains, and sweetmeats such as sugar-candies.

O knower of the true meaning of the Dharmaśāstras, you who have reached the further shore of knowledge and realization; O teacher of the gods, the inconceivable remover of the suffering of the wise—salutations to you!
The fire-oblation (homa), however, is as before.
When Jupiter is in an unfavorable position, men should perform this great propitiatory rite (mahāśānti) with oblations of ghee and sesame seeds, along with fuel-sticks bearing the name of Jupiter.
Thus concludes the pacification of the preceptor.
Now, the pacification of Venus (Śukra-śānti):
Having observed Venus in conjunction with the Jyeṣṭhā constellation, one should eat only at night on the ground,
following the procedure taught by the Guru and by means of the gratification of the twice-born.
On the seventh day, however, one should place silver wealth and have it fashioned as bright as white;
having placed it in a bamboo vessel, one should worship it with flowers born of white lotuses.
In the absence of those, one should offer before him flowers desired [by the deity], betel leaves, sandalwood paste, and milk-rice mixed with ghee.
Bhārgava, the son of Bhṛgu, Śukra, who is learned in the Śrutis and Smṛtis,
having removed the defects caused by the house, [bestows] longevity, health, and freedom from disease.
With this mantra one should offer oblations; the fire sacrifice is to be performed as before, using ghee, sesame seeds, and *udumbara* wood, while reciting the name of Śukra.
Thus concludes the propitiation of Śukra.
Now follows the pacification ritual for Saturn and the others: one should place images of Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu in vessels made of iron;
black aloe-wood is prescribed as incense, and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given according to one's means.
The sacrificial fuel (samidh) is prescribed to be made of śamī, dūrvā, and kuśa grass respectively;
on the seventh day, however, one should have golden [fuel] prepared.
The wise man should have each [image] covered with a pair of black garments;
having anointed them with musk and offered *kṛsarā* rice,
he should, at the conclusion of the fire oblations (*homa*), present all of that to a Brāhmaṇa.
One should perform the *homasūktas* with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) while reciting their respective names:
"O Śanaiścara, obeisance to you; likewise, obeisance to you, Rāhu."
And salutations to you, O Ketu; grant all peace.
With this mantra, one should offer [the oblation].
Thus concludes the propitiatory rite for Saturn and the other [planets].
Now, regarding the gifts for the nine planets and so forth, it is stated in the *Jātakabharaṇa* and the *Sārāvalī*:
"The planets become auspicious when they have reached their positions through their course (*gocara*) and their various divisions (*varga*)."
Because he has become exceedingly pleased by my acts of giving and so forth, I shall now explain the ritual procedure for giving.
Rubies, wheat, a young calf, a milch cow, saffron-dyed cloth, molasses, gold, copper,
red sandalwood, and a lotus— these they say are the gifts to be given to Virocana.
He gave to the Moon a vessel containing six parts of rice, camphor, pearls, and auspicious cloth,
a pair of oxen suitable for a yoke, silver, and a jar filled with ghee.
Coral, wheat, lentils, a bull, red cloth, jaggery, gold,
crimson garments, karavīra flowers, and copper— these they declare to be the gifts for Mars (Bhauma).

Silk cloth, indigo, bronze, bell-metal, mung beans, clarified butter, emerald, all kinds of flowers, a female servant, a staff, and an elephant— these the learned declare to be gifts that lead to the delight of [the gods].
Sugar, red lead, a horse, yellow grain, yellow cloth,
topaz, salt, and gold are offered for the pleasure of the Preceptor of the Gods (Bṛhaspati).
A multicolored garment, an exceptionally white horse, gold, a diamond, silver of divine hue,
jasmine flowers, the finest clarified butter, and fragrant substances— these they declare to be the gifts for the son of Bhṛgu.
Black beans, oil, a pure sapphire, sesame seeds, horse-gram, a great cow, iron,
and a black cow— these they declare to be the gifts for the Sun’s son when he is in an unfavorable state.
Gomedha gems, four-cornered iron, very dark-colored cloths, blankets made of hair, sesame seeds, oil, and indeed iron mixed with these— these they declare to be the eight treasures of the earth.
A lapis lazuli gem, sesame with oil, a woolen blanket, and the fat of a musk deer,
as well as a weapon for the sake of propitiating Ketu— the gifting of goats and elephants has been prescribed by the lords of sages.
Furthermore, in the *Ratnadhāraṇī*, it is stated therein:
"The ruby belongs to the Sun; the pure pearl to the Moon; the emerald to Mars; the sapphire to Mercury; the topaz to Jupiter; the diamond to Venus; and the blue sapphire to Saturn."
When the sun and moon are eclipsed, one should indeed offer a gomedha and a vaidūryaka gem.
Regarding the baths for the removal of evil influences (*atharvagraha-snāna*),
the *Viṣṇudharmottara* states:
"Madder, an intoxicated elephant, saffron, and red sandalwood..."
The ritual bath for the Sun is prescribed to be performed with a full copper vessel.
Intoxicated elephant, elephant-ichor, uśīra, śirīṣa, saffron, and red sandalwood—
this bath prepared with conch-shell ash destroys the defects caused by the moon.
Khadira wood, Devadāru, sesame seeds, and Āmalaka fruits,
when placed in a full pitcher made of silver, destroy the affliction caused by Mars.
O wise one, waters from the confluence of rivers together with the earth from that place,
when placed within an earthen pitcher, destroy the affliction caused by Mercury.
O wise one, placing udumbara, bilva, vaṭa, and āmalaka fruits upon the earthen pitcher destroys the affliction caused by Budha.
Gorocanā, nāgamada, śatapuṣpā, and śatāvarī,
when placed within a water-pot, shine forth as the destroyer of afflictions caused by semen.
Sesame seeds, black gram, priyaṅgu, as well as perfumes and flowers,
when placed in a copper vessel, destroy the affliction caused by Saturn.
Guggulu, cinnabar, realgar, and auspicious yellow orpiment,
when placed in the horn of a buffalo, destroy the affliction caused by Rāhu.
Tāla is yellow orpiment.
O King, earth from the peak of a mountain as prescribed by Varāha,
as well as goat’s milk in a rhinoceros-horn vessel, destroys the affliction of Ketu.
This is declared to be the planetary ablution (grahasnāna), which destroys all afflictions.
Thus end the ritual baths for the planets.
In the Madanaratna, Pippalāda said: "I shall proclaim the worship of the Guru as it was formerly declared by Brahmā;
this is for the benefit of the worlds and for the pacification of all calamities."
At the time of a daughter’s marriage, for one whose purity is not established;
and at the initiation of a Brāhmaṇa,
for one whose Guru has passed away— by these, worship of the Guru must be performed according to the rules, being permeated by devotion.
Madantī flowers, kāma flowers, palāśa leaves, and ṛṣapa seeds.
Madaṃtī is yūthikā; it is the subduer of passion. Guḍūcī, apāmārga, viḍaṅga, śaṃbhinī, sahā, devī, viṣṇukrāntā, sarvauṣadhī, and śatāvarī [are the herbs].
Kuṣṭha, māṃsī, the two types of haridrā, murā, śailēya,
candana, vacā, kacorā, and mustā are proclaimed to be the "all-herbs" (sarvauṣadhi).
Likewise, there should be branches of the *aśvattha* tree, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), water,
and a new water-pot accompanied by a yellow cloth.
One should place five gems joined together, situated in the northeast,
and cast all of them into this [pitcher] with the mantra "yā oṣadhīḥ. Then, having placed Bṛhaspati upon the upper portion of the pitcher.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, [one should place] a golden image within a golden vessel.
One who is free from the stinginess regarding wealth should have [the image] made according to his ability,
covered with a pair of yellow garments and wearing a yellow sacred thread.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and then perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
One hundred and eight fuel-sticks of the *aśvattha* tree should be offered;
furthermore, one should offer sesame seeds mixed with rice and barley in the proper sequence.
With the mantra "Bṛhaspate," accompanied by its seer and meter.
One should diligently offer oblations of grain with this mantra as previously described;
then, at the conclusion of the homa, one should worship Bṛhaspati.
Then, with devotion, [one should worship] with yellow perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps;
and the food offering (naivedya) should consist of curd-rice accompanied by fruits and betel-leaf.
O son of Kuntī, with this mantra one should offer oblations again and again:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of Girijā, and to Bṛhaspati, the Lord of Speech."
Salutations to the one who leads those afflicted by cruel planets to immortality;
having worshipped the Preceptor of the Gods, one should thereafter present the *arghya* offering.
O Lord, worshipful to the gods, you of profound and firm form and noble intellect!
"Salutations to you, O Lord of Speech, O Great Lord; this is the arghya for the pacified planets.
This is the mantra for the arghya offering.

Having offered the *arghya* to the Preceptor of the Gods (*surejya*), one should complete the recitation (*japa*) and the fire-oblation (*homa*). With devotion, one should perform the hospitable rites for the Teacher of the Gods, such as the oblation, worship, and other honors.
"O Lord of Speech, accept this prepared offering for the sake of peace; salutations, salutations to you!
This is the *saṃkalpa* mantra.
Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) with this mantra, the king then offered his prayer.
Jīva, Bṛhaspati, Sūri, Ācārya, Guru, and Aṅgiras;
"May Vācaspati, the divine minister, always bring me auspiciousness.
This is the mantra of prayer.
In this manner, O Yudhiṣṭhira, one should indeed pray thus and worship the preceptor,
together with the image, accompanied by all ritual offerings.
Having prostrated, he should present [the gift] to the teacher, who is yoked to speech;
then the teacher, being self-restrained and having reached the further shore of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas, [should accept it].
Taking the water from the jar, one should sprinkle it upon the sacrificer and his wife— whose minds are tranquil and whose senses are subdued— with these mantras.

One should sprinkle this with water while reciting the mantra "tām agnim" and likewise with the verse "yā oṣadhīraśvāvatīḥ. One should also perform the consecration with the Kaṣmāṇḍa mantras. Afterwards, O Yudhiṣṭhira, one should feed the Brahmins according to one's capacity.
Having thus performed the worship of the Guru, one shall obtain all desires.
O son of Kuntī, by performing the worship of Bṛhaspati during the solar transits as well as on one's own auspicious occasions, one shall obtain the desired fruit.
At the transit [of the sun], at the transit of Jupiter.
Thus ends the worship of the Guru; now follows the procedure for each Friday according to Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha:
A journey undertaken when Venus has set, or when the Moon has set,
as well as during childhood or old age, brings fear and disease.
A pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā) is forbidden when Venus, Mercury, or Mars are in retrograde; however, such a prohibition does not apply when Venus is merely heliacally set.
Among the Kaśyapas, the Vasiṣṭhas, the Bhṛgus, the Aṅgirases, the Bharadvājas, and the Vatsas, there is no one who rivals Śukra.
In the presence of others there is a fault, but regarding Śukra, it applies to everyone at all times;
having performed a propitiatory rite with great effort, one should thereafter perform everything else.
Having observed a fast on a Saturday until the rising of Venus,
one should have an image of Bhṛgu fashioned from pure silver.
One should draw an eight-petalled lotus in a bronze vessel with rice grains;

there, one should worship the image with white flowers, unbroken rice, and perfumes. Having offered the ritual services (upacāras), one should then offer the oblation with the verse beginning "śukraṃ te anyat."
One should perform the recitation (japa) one hundred and eight times with that mantra;
then, with devotion, one should offer the arghya water using milk, scented paste, unbroken rice grains, and flowers.
The minister of the Daityas was the divine-sighted Uśanas Bhārgava, also known as Kavi.
"O Śukra, whose orb is white, son of Kavi, [you who are] the ordinance for Bhṛgu—salutations to you!
Having offered this arghya with diligence, one should pray with devotion:
'O Śukra, by this worship of yours, be favorable and auspicious.'"
O storehouse of splendors, quickly destroy our faults while protecting us.
Then one should give the image, together with a white cow, to an astrologer;
when this is done, the evil influence will depart and the twice-born man shall become victorious.
There is also a distinction regarding the fish.
Now, therefore, O protector of the earth, listen for the sake of the pacification of Śuka.
And at the commencement of a journey, at the time of departure, as well as when Venus has risen;
O Bhārata, listen to the manner in which the worship of Śukra is to be performed.
Either in a silver vessel, or one made of gold, or again in a bell-metal bowl,
provided it is joined with white flowers and cloth and filled with white rice.
Having placed a bright, pure silver vessel filled with pearls upon a great white bull, one should present it to the singer of the Sāman hymns,
saying: "O Lord of all the worlds, O descendant of Bhṛgu, salutations to you!"
O Sage, for the sake of accomplishing all goals, accept this water offering; homage be to you!
O son of Kuntī, having offered the guest-water (arghya) and prostrated, one should dismiss [the deity];
for as long as the worship with all the ritual offerings has not been performed for Śukra.
By means of small cakes, parched grains, wheat, and even chickpeas,
women may obtain as much fruit as is desired for the accomplishment of their aims.
O Bhārata, those who perform journeys and other such activities when Venus has risen,
as well as before the arrival of the new moon, shall obtain their desired goals.
In that same manner, O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall describe the worship of Vācaspati.
O Lord of the Immortals, a golden vessel was placed upon a golden [stand].
Having bathed with mustard seeds and wearing yellow flowers and garments,
one should [worship] him with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and sesame seeds, which completely shatter the hope for fruits.
Bhaṅga is a sprout.
Clad in yellow garments and possessing a golden hue, he should cause the oblation of clarified butter to be performed.
Having prostrated, one should offer half of the cow to a Brāhmaṇa, saying:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of the Aṅgirases, O Bṛhaspati, Lord of Speech!"
Salutations again and again for the sake of the immortality of those afflicted by cruel planets;
this is the mantra for the water offering (arghya).
O Kunteya, when a transference [of merit] has occurred, during pilgrimages, and on occasions of prosperity.
By performing worship of Bṛhaspati during the transit of Jupiter, one attains all desires. During the transit of Jupiter...
Alternatively, having examined pearls that are well-rounded and large,
one should present those very ones [to the bridegroom] according to the custom of Bhārgava and Āṅgirasa.
O descendant of Kuru, by the offering of pearls with devotion— and not otherwise—
ugliness never arises for men at any time.

O Bhārata, for those partakers of merit who, having attained the rising of Śukra (Venus), offer garments, flowers, and worship with undivided minds, no obstacle arises in their homes while they dwell there during the period of Śukra’s presence.
Thus concludes the worship of Guru and Śukra.
In the *Madanaratna*, the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* states: "Then, on the day of Maṅgala (Tuesday), a bath preceded by an oil massage should be performed;
and oil should be given to a Brahmin for the purpose of an oil massage."
But that man who, for the duration of a year, [performs this] on every day of Saturday when it arrives—
Or he gives oil to the Brahmins according to his capacity, having honored them as well.
Then, at the end of the year, when that day arrived once again, [he performed it].
One should place the Sun-god, inscribed upon a copper plate, into a jar filled with sesame oil.
It may be made of iron or clay, and it should be provided with a pair of black garments.
He was accompanied by a black cow as his sacrificial fee and was reclining upon a blue woolen blanket.
Having bathed after having conquered one's own self, one should worship him with black flowers,
fragrant scents, flowers, kṛsarā rice, and sesame-rice.

Having worshipped the son of the Sun, O twice-born one, the god Śanaiścara [should be propitiated] with devotion by means of this mantra, saying "Forgive me" again and again, for Kṛṣṇa, the foremost of the twice-born, or in his absence, for Viṣṇu.

May that Śanaiścara protect us— he who, through his fierce aspect and the cruelty of his planetary nature, does not grant a new abode, yet when pleased, bestows wealth, gold, and happiness; he who, moreover,
was satisfied by a man whose kingdom had been lost.
In a dream, he gave his own kingdom; O descendant of Sura, may he perish along with it.
I bow to Śanaiścara, who resembles black collyrium, who moves slowly and spreads his influence, and who is born from the shadow of the Sun.
Obeisance to the son of the Sun, to Śanaiścara, who has the hue of frost and the appearance of collyrium;
having heard this secret, you, the son of the Sun, are the bestower of existence and the granter of fruits.
Homage be to the King of the Pretas; salutation indeed to him of emaciated body. Homage to Śanaiścara, the cruel one, who bestows pure intellect.
He grants satisfaction to whoever praises Him by these names;
however, fear of Him shall come upon that person even in his dreams.
Having bowed to Śani according to this procedure, one should dismiss him.
In this way, those men who shall constantly practice that vow, [shall attain success].
As long as every day that arrives for a full year passes thus,
there shall be no affliction from Saturn for them, nor even in their country.
