Whoever, out of devotion, places an image of King Yama fashioned from black metal into a small vessel filled with sesame oil and gives it to a Brāhmaṇa on a Sunday, the affliction caused by Śanaiścara shall not oppress him.
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
When Saturn, the lord of all planets, is situated in the twelfth or eighth house from birth.
What should be done by men, or what else should be performed, for the sake of pacifying suffering?
Skanda said: When the auspicious Saturday has arrived in the month of Śrāvaṇa,
one should fashion an image of Śani out of iron and bathe it with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
One should worship the most excellent of the planets in due order with these names, using eight kinds of flowers, incenses, and especially fruits.
Koṇastha, Piṅgala, Babhru, Kṛṣṇa, Rudra, Yama, Antaka, Saurī, Śanaiścara, and Manda— thus was he praised by Pippalāda.
One should worship everywhere with the Vedic mantra "śanno devī";
and having worshipped, one should then present the food offering (naivedya) in the proper sequence.
One should offer cooked rice with lentils as the first oblation and auspicious milk-rice (pāyasa) as the second;
one should worship [the deity] everywhere as "Devī" according to the Vedic rites.
Having performed the worship, one should then present the food offering (naivedya) in due order.
On the first day, offer black gram rice; on the second, auspicious milk-rice (pāyasa);
on the third, you should perform the bali-offering; and on the fourth, auspicious fried cakes (pūrikā).
A gruel made from *āmalī*, buttermilk, rice,
and flour is to be consumed on the first and subsequent days.
Thus concludes the propitiation of Śanaiścara.
Now, regarding the hymn to Śanaiścara and others from the Nāgara-khaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa,
Nārada says:
"Householders, cows, kings, and especially Brāhmaṇas..."
They honor her who has been honored, but when insulted, they utterly consume [the offender].
Therefore, O Lord, the boy offered praise to the Sun according to his own ability. The boy said:—
Piṣpalāda, having prostrated himself again and again before that best of the twice-born, spoke.
Salutations to you who reside in the heart; salutations to you, O Piṅgala.

Salutations to you, O Babhru-rūpa; salutations to you, O Kṛṣṇa. Salutations to you whose body is fierce; salutations to you, the Ender. Salutations to you known as Yama; salutations to you, the son of the Sun, O All-pervading Lord.
Salutations to you, O Śanaiścara, known by the name Mañca; salutations to you.
"O Lord of Gods, show favor to me, who am wretched and prostrate before you.
Śanaiścara said:
"I am now well-pleased with you, my child, by this hymn of praise."
O child, choose a boon; I shall grant you your heart’s desire.
Pippalāda said:
"O son of the Sun, from this day forward, you must not cause suffering to children,
O illustrious one, even for the sake of your own sustenance."
O son of the Sun, by my word, as long as the rains last, you shall be born from a lotus;
and with this hymn, you shall praise me every morning when you have arisen.
O son of the Sun, you must not cause him any suffering;
O mighty-armed one, you must not harm him, but rather grant him gain.
When the yoga of the half-eighth (ardhāṣṭamikā) is established in your [system], a person [attains success] in exactly seven years; thus it is the "half-eighth."
"O Lord, she has arrived to offer you sesame and rice mixed with water;
you should give her according to your capacity, and no harm should be done to her by you."
Let the Brahmin sing the Kṛṣṇa-gītā for the sake of extending his life;
you must not cause him any suffering on the eighth day of the lunar fortnight.
Whoever should offer an oblation with *śamī* fuel-sticks dedicated to you,
as well as with black sesame seeds, black flowers, and unguents;
He who performs worship for you and offers *guggulu* incense—
encircling it with black cloth— by him you have been conquered in battle.
Sūta said:
Having been addressed thus by Śani, and having replied "So be it," he took leave of Nārada and went to his own abode.
In the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa of the Madanaratna:
"Furthermore, he who is endowed with faith, pure, and composed in the morning..."
Having worshipped my iron image with śamī leaves,
one should offer boiled rice mixed with black gram and sesame seeds, along with iron as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
"Whosoever shall give a black-limbed bull or even a cow to a brahmin,
I shall never cause him any suffering whatsoever.
Thus ends the hymn to Śani.

Now, the pacification of Rāhu. According to the *Jyotiṣya*: "If the planet Rāhu should move by the power of its transit through the first, last, fifth, fourth, eighth, ninth, second, seventh, or tenth [sign] from one's birth, it causes agitation, fear of the king, ruin, destruction of half [one's possessions], the onset of disease, exile, and the fear of fire and death."
In the *Mātsya*: "If the Moon is in the *horā* or the *nata* of whichever [sign] belongs to a particular asterism,
one encounters a risk to life or meets with death."

If the moon and the sun are eclipsed here during one's birth asterism, there will be suffering for those born under it, as people are devoid of peace. If an eclipse occurs while the moon is situated in one's [natal] sign, [the same result follows].
I shall now describe his ritual bath, accompanied by mantras and medicinal herbs.
Having encountered a lunar eclipse and performed the recitation by Brahmins,
one should honor four Brahmins with white garlands and unguents.
Having first gathered medicinal herbs and other necessary items for the eclipse,
one should place four jars before [the image] in the directions starting with the east (representing the oceans).
Having brought earth from an anthill, from a confluence, from a lake, from a herd of cows,
and from the entrance of a king’s gate, one should deposit it there.
The five beds, the five jewels, the five-fold *kṛñca* sprout,
yellow orpiment, *padmaka*, conch, saffron, and red sandalwood.
Pearls, crystal, water from a sacred ford (tīrtha), white mustard seeds, guggulu resin, madhuka, devadāru, viṣṇukrāntā, and śatāvarī—
Having cast all of this— balā, sahadevī, and the ten-fold niśā—
into the jars, one should cause the bulls to carry them away.
May all the oceans, rivers, sacred fords, and givers of water come here,
bringing about the destruction of the sacrificer's sins.
O Gaṅgā, perform the *dhīḥ*.
May that god Vajrabhara, who is considered the lord of the Ādityas and possesses a thousand eyes, dispel the affliction caused by the moon and the planets.
May Agni— the mouth of all the gods, possessing seven flames and immeasurable luster— dispel the affliction arising from the lunar eclipse.
May he who is the witness of the actions of the worlds, the Dharma whose vehicle is a buffalo,
dispel my suffering arising from the lunar eclipse.
May the Lord who holds the serpent-noose and whose vehicle is always the sea-monster [Varuṇa] [protect me].
May Varuṇa, who is dear to the deer and whose form is the vital breath of all worlds, forever remove the turbidity caused by the lunar eclipse.
May Vāyu dispel the affliction caused by the planets arising from the lunar eclipse. May Dhanada, the lord of treasures, who bears the sword, trident, discus, and mace,
dispel the misfortune of the lunar eclipse.
That god who bears the crescent moon, the wielder of the Pināka bow, whose vehicle is the bull.
May Śaṅkara ward off the evils of the lunar eclipse;
and may he protect all beings in the three worlds, both the stationary and the moving.
"May Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Sun, resplendent with light, burn away my sin.
Thus one should invoke the deities with these Vāruṇa mantras.
One should likewise inscribe these very mantras upon a gold plate,
or having written them upon a copper plate, one should do so nine times in that same manner.
The most excellent brahmins should place upon the head of the patron the water-pots filled with substances and endowed with the essence of various sacred fords (tīrthas).
Having taken it, one should place it secretly upon a noble throne;
with the very mantras previously mentioned, one should present a gold plate.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and a gift of a cow according to one's ability.
One should worship with perfumes, garlands, incense, and lamps for the satisfaction of the deity;
furthermore, a fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with sesame seeds and the vyāhṛti mantras.
Having completed the fire-offering according to the rules, one should especially give gifts to the Brahmins according to one's capacity, if one desires one's own welfare;
during a solar eclipse, one should recite mantras associated with the name of the Sun.
Whoever performs the ritual bath during an eclipse according to this procedure will never suffer from the defects caused by the eclipse.
Thus ends the pacification of planetary afflictions as stated by Matsya.
In another work within the Madanaratna.

One should perform a ritual bath with *dūrvā* sprouts, *uśīra*, *śamī*, *śilājīta*, gems, all-purpose substances (*sarvārtha*), all medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadhi*), and the five earths (*pañcamṛt*) during the eclipses of the sun and moon; thus, the suffering that arises from the affliction comes to peace, and the evil is removed.
For light.
For men, the eclipse of the sun or the moon occurring when they have reached the third, sixth, or tenth house will be auspicious.
Āyu has eleven syllables; Nandana has nine; Iṣaṇa has five.

In the *Madanaratna*, Garga states: "When the Moon is situated in the seventh, sixth, twelfth, or tenth house from birth, Rāhu, being aspected [by it], bestows misfortune; so too when he is in the natal asterism, the eighth, or the twelfth (the *rippha*)—the twelfth being the end, and the 'mark' (*aṅka*) being seven according to the reckoning of the stars. And in the *Viṣṇudharma* section of the *Pṛthvīcandrodaya*: 'Whichever asterism Rāhu has entered, and which the Moon and Sun eclipse, those born under that [asterism] shall suffer affliction; for them, pacificatory rites (*śānti*) are prescribed.'"
Likewise, in another Purāṇa:

"If at the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), or during an eclipse of the moon or sun, a person's birth star (janmanakṣatra) is afflicted, he may suffer from disease or even death. For him, one should perform charity, fire-offerings (homa), worship of the deity, and the recitation of mantras (japa), as well as the ablution (abhiṣeka) prescribed for eclipses; thus there will be peace. Having fashioned the form of a serpent either out of gold or ground flour, one should give it to a Brāhmaṇa; by that act, his disease and other afflictions will cease. The stars of the birth, the tenth, and the twentieth [from the birth star] are the 'trijanma' (three-birth) stars."
Of Rāhu, who possesses all those forms.
In the *Adbhutasāgara*, Bhārgava states:
"If Rāhu appears in the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) of a king,
one should predict the ruin of his kingdom, the destruction of his friends, and his own death."
This refers to the meaning that for the royal consecration (*rājyābhiṣeka*) of a kingdom, one should consult the *Bārgavārcanadīpikā*.
In the ocean of luminosity.

One should have a golden elephant made from one *pala*, half a *pala*, or even down to a quarter or an eighth of a *pala*; then, one should place a pearl upon its trunk [or forehead] weighing one *paṇa*, or half, or a quarter, or even an eighth of a *paṇa*.

Having placed it especially in a copper vessel filled with ghee— or in one of bell-metal, or bronze, or another metal— one should give it as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). However, during a lunar eclipse, one should give an image made of silver along with a sacrificial fee.
An elephant made of silver, a golden disc during a solar eclipse,
a horse, a chariot, a cow, land, sesame seeds, clarified butter, and gold.
In the Examination of Time.
A Brahmin should present a golden image of a serpent, along with sesame seeds, a bronze vessel, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and a new cloth.
Having fashioned an image of yourself out of gold or silver according to your means, O Goddess,
one should offer it for the sake of severing the afflictions born of the eclipse.
The mantra, however, is as follows:
Homage to Yama, the greatly formidable one, the crusher of Soma and Sūrya!
By the offering of the *homatārā*, grant me peace.
"O Acyuta, son of Siṃhikā, let there be obeisance to you, O Vidhuntuda;
by this gift of the serpent, protect me from the fear of being pierced by a thunderbolt."
The specific details, however, should be understood from my own work, the *Nirṇayasindhu*.
In astrology.
If Rāhu, as a planet, moves by the power of its motion through the fifth, fourth, eighth, ninth, second, seventh, or eleventh house from the natal ascendant,
it causes agitation, fear of the king, destruction of wealth, disease, exile, death, and the fear of fire.
In this wonderful ocean of the Mayūra-citra [grammar],
there occurs at an improper time (apavārṇi) a great eclipse named Viṣṭi, wherein the moon and the sun appear simultaneously.
The dark one veils [the world] in darkness for the ruin of all the worlds;
a wise man should offer eight thousand *jāduṃbara* fruits as oblations.
Having anointed those [objects] with honey while reciting the verse beginning with "jātavedase," one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin, as well as a cow and likewise a bull.
Thus ends the great peace.
Regarding the greatness of that result, it is stated in the Viśiṣṭasaṃhitā:
"Because the rising and setting of Ketu cannot be known through calculation."
These three kinds of comets in the world are celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial.
They are seen as having one hundred and one divisions, or even a thousand divisions;
due to their nature as portentous forms, they appear as many or likewise as one.
Those born from the stars and planets in the sky are known as celestial comets (*ketu*), which yield results upon the earth;
they are renowned as *varipa*, *peṣaṇa*, *indravara*, *dhunu*, *ulkā*, *gandharva*, and *nagara*.
That which arises from a modification of the sky yields middling results, as does the atmosphere;
those born of the earth are terrestrial, while those that arise from moving and stationary [beings] are likewise so.
I shall describe the fruits and forms of those three dharmas;
they reach their full maturation sequentially by year, month, and fortnight.
With a glossy and serene form, resembling white, gentle like a staff held in the heart,
Ketu brings about abundance and happiness at both its rising and setting.
A comet resembling smoke, known as Dhūma, brings about calamity;
one having the form of Indra’s bow or resembling a pillar portends fear of rain in the month of Samyak.
With many incomparable crests, resembling lightning, jewels, necklaces, and gold,
they appeared from the western direction like great fires at the quarters of the world.
If those sons of Agni, resembling parrots or the bandhūka flower, and appearing red and rough like blood,
are seen in the direction of Nala— even though they are so many— they too are bringers of fear.
The daughters of Death, with crooked crests, black and harsh, causing great joy [to their kin], are seen; they too, O slayer of people, bring fear to the southern region.
His arrows, numbering thirty-two, are like polished mirrors;
they cause hunger and fear, possess heads, bring death, and are as massive as mountains.
The moons resembling flowers, and those resembling the kunda flower, the moon, milk, or silver,
appearing in the northern quarter at the end of the Śikhin [fire] era, bring about abundance for living beings.
Having three points, endowed with three colors, the son of Brahmā, resembling the staff of Brahmā,
with light radiating in indefinite directions— this is known as the Brahmadaṇḍa, which brings about peace.
The six white and straight comets known as the sons of Śani and called Tārās are seen for two or three days; though they appear auspicious, they bestow great fear.
The sons of Jupiter known as Vikaca, white, star-like, and glossy,
situated in the southern direction, are always the bringers of many calamities.
The fifty-five [asterisms] known as Budha, Tanaya, and Chora are white and subtle; they arise in whichever direction one desires, yet they constantly cause disease and fear to living beings.
The sixty sons of Kujā, resembling fire mixed with blood and bearing tridents, are stationed in the southern direction and cause fear through hunger.
The Tāmasa, Kālaka, and Saṃjñā planets, as well as the sons of Rāhu, when seen in the solar disc—
their entire fruit is correctly established even on a Sunday.
The sons of Agni were one hundred and twenty in number, possessing forms like the fire of universal dissolution;
they scorched the earth with their fiery glances.
Known as the Aruṇas, resembling dark clouds, and possessing various mixed forms,
these sons of Śukra are seventy-seven in number and bestow fear of weapons and hunger.
The eight known as the Daṇḍakas are like stars, the sons of Prajāpati;
the one hundred and forty-two Tōras are the sons of Vidhātṛ, who bestow evil.
Those known as Karka, having the nature of Varuṇa, numbering thirty-two, resembling a staff with two clusters [of nodes],
produce the state of being a daughter of the stars (Tārājanya), possessing a luster like that of the moon.
Their number is eighty-nine thousand; they resemble headless trunks (kabandhas), bear those same names, and cause the world to suffer from the affliction of boils and consumption.
The pure stars appearing in the ten directions are like crests; thus there are a thousand Vedas. I shall now describe the specific distinctions regarding their sins.
Arising in the western direction and bowing toward the north, the gentle Ketu,
white in color and exceedingly glossy, brings about incomparable and excellent prosperity.
When Ketu is in the south, bowing toward the south, it likewise causes distress;
being harsh, it produces fear of hunger or indeed brings about the fear of hell.
Resembling smoke, located in the southern quarter, the Ketu named Kapāla is most excellent when glossy;
appearing in the cardinal and intermediate directions, it causes fear of famine and brings about diseases of the eyes.
Arising in the eastern quarter, it revolves clockwise like a wheel, being harsh in appearance;
that Cakraketu yields results identical to those of Kapālaketu at all times.
Arising from the west and moving clockwise toward the southern direction,
the comet named Viṣama, resembling smoke, brings about even the removal of the earth's burden.
Having traveled for a few days, that which resembles smoke ceases its course;
known as Sacakra, it causes the destruction of the world through conflict among kings.
Three-quarters as long as the sky, dark-hued, and causing fear to the gods,
it moves in a straight line and then a curved path, gradually taking away one-third of the world.
And among the utensils of kings, in temples of the gods, among trees, festivals, and palaces,
that which has fallen invariably comes into view only as something destined for destruction.
The one resembling a white water-lily, named Kumuda, was seen by the wise six days later in the western quarter;
he who is in the north-eastern direction is auspicious, like a stream of milk.
The star Tāroparimaṇiketū, when seen once in the southern direction at the time of sunrise or sunset,
brings auspiciousness or misfortune like a stream of milk.
When he is seen by others with a crest that is straight yet slightly curved like a stream of water,
he is the Water-Banner (Varuṇa), resembling water, and brings about an abundance of food for all living beings.
A banner resembling the tail of a monkey or like the hair of a scorpion brings fear of many diseases; however, one shaped like a serpent always brings [such] danger.
Furthermore, Padmaketu was like a lotus, resembling the interior of a lotus;
he brought security to kings and bestowed excellent sustenance upon all living beings.
The bright, white comet known as Āvartaketuka, moving counter-clockwise,
brings about the reversal of auspiciousness and causes incomparable fear and disease.
Having pervaded the entire sky, the comet named Saṃvarta,
resembling smoke and appearing like a trident fixed upon a tree, repeatedly portended fear for the world.
Those resembling white are givers of auspiciousness, while those that are black bring inauspiciousness to the world;
having thus declared the results of the comets, I shall now describe the results for those born under the crooked planets.
If Ketu is born in Aśvinī, it destroys those who live by horses;
in Bharaṇī, the ruler of the Mlecchas; and in Kṛttikā, the ruler of Kaliṅga.
In Rohiṇī, Ketu destroys those of incomparable strength; in Śūraṇa, he destroys the lord of men;
in Auśī, the chief of men; in Saumya and Raudra, aquatic creatures.
One becomes the lord of the Aśmaka region under Āditya; the lord of Magadha under Puṣya;
the lord of the Āryas under Āśleṣā; and the lord of the Pāṇḍyas under Māgha.
In the constellation of Bhaga, one should install all the leaders of the sages; in the northern asterism (Uttaraphalgunī), all the staff-bearers;
in the constellation of Hasta, the preeminent treasurer; and in Citrā, all those born of the Kuru lineage.
Jātaketu also [conquered] the preeminent Kāmboja king;
the destruction of the Ikṣvāku dynasty occurred under Dvidaiva-bha, and the lord of Gauḍa under Mitrabha.
If one is born under Jyeṣṭhā, he is considered the lord of all auspiciousness;
under Mūla, the lord of Bhadra and others; under P.ūrva-Phalgunī (Daiva), the lord of water; and under Kṛttikā (Kaliṅga), the lord of the earth.
The Ghūrgharikā constellation destroys the temples of the gods; Vaiśvādhi destroys the sacrificers; Śravaṇa destroys the Kekayas; and Vasubhava destroys all the Dravidas.
A planet situated in the ninth house from the ruler of the year destroys the king; one in the sixth house destroys physicians; one in the tenth house destroys the Pāñcālas;
one born in the asterism of Ahirbudhnya (Śatabhiṣaj) destroys the Saṃkarikas; and one born in the asterism of Kirāta (Kṛttikā) destroys the Koṇas.
The comet arising in the asterism of Puṣya destroys the dharma-path of the twice-born people;
that arising in the asterism of Abhijit likewise destroys the night-stalkers in the land of Koṅkaṇa.

Those born under the Aśvinī nakṣatra, as well as those born under the nakṣatras beginning with Aśleṣā, and those born under the nakṣatras beginning with Svāti, produce various sharp results; however, when they are joined with their respective planets and nakṣatras, they become givers of general results.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), [the list includes] Dhruva, the Seven Sages (Saptarṣi), and so forth;
others as well, such as Calaketu and Gadaketu, are mentioned among those arisen from the ocean.
At the time of questioning.
Due to earthquakes, thunderclaps, or the falling of dust, or during an eclipse of the sun or moon lasting up to seven nights,
or where there are falls of meteors, halos, and rainbows— in that region, the destruction of the king shall occur.
If the banner of the Fire-god (Agni), whose crest is smoke, should joyfully fly toward the crest of this [city],
or if any other banners of Rudra should do so, they shall slay the king in that very place.
When the Sun is situated in Jyeṣṭhā and conjoined with Kuja (Mars), and Rāhu and Ketu have risen,
then at that very time, a sovereign of the earth meets his destruction through disease or from battle.
In this case, either the previously mentioned *koṭihoma* should be performed.
Thus ends the propitiation of Ketu.
Regarding the meteor (ulkā): Dārada says that those forms which are meteors on earth are indeed the forms of those who have fallen from heaven.
The firebrand, lightning, thunder, and stars are recorded as the fivefold [types of light].
The *pīḍā*, *uṣṭra*, *gomāyu*, *khara*, *go*, *gaja*,
*daṃṣṭraka*, *kapi*, *godhā*, and *dhūmanibha* [planets] are of various kinds that bring suffering to men.
A meteor falling at the rising or setting of the sun or moon bestows auspicious results;
however, one that is white, red, yellow, or white destroys the twice-born along with the meteors themselves.
Do not grant your favor for the destruction of the king and the kingdom;
there shall be suffering for the masters in their homes, and for kings upon the mountains.

There will be suffering for the lords of the various directions in their respective quarters, for cultivators in the threshing floors, for the owners of cattle in the cow-pens, and for artisans in the waters.
A circular comet destroys the city; one shaped like an umbrella destroys the priest; those shaped like bamboo, shrubs, or creepers cause the kingdom to flee, as does one that is bent.
In this regard, the pacification of the transformations of the stars as previously stated by Garga should be performed.
Then the sun, variegated with peacock feathers, spoke: "When the rising sun is seen as such a reflection,
there will undoubtedly be destruction within three years or even half a month."
Now, regarding the halo (pariveṣa): when the rays of the sun or moon are struck by the wind and raised up, they form a circular shape;
thus a halo of various colors and forms appears around the moon and the sun.
When halos repeatedly vanish while bestowing full results,
and when they possess many shapes and colors, they bring about the end of kings.
If the head is within a triple halo, it portends the death of the king; likewise, a planet situated within a triple halo brings about strife among rulers.
Two planets positioned within a halo (pariveṣa) cause discord between kings.
Three planets situated in a halo cause quarrels and misfortune;
four situated in a halo bring about the death of the king;
five planets situated in a halo are the destroyers of the world.
A halo appearing individually around Mars and the other planets portends the destruction of men.
A halo during the rainy season and autumn bestows water;
however, in most other seasons, it yields the results described for those specific times.

Elsewhere also: "If there is a halo around the sun and moon in the first watch of the day, there is suffering; if there is a halo around the sun and moon in the middle watch, there is excessive rain; if there is a halo around the sun and moon in the third watch, there is destruction of grain; and if there is a halo around the sun and moon in the fourth watch, there is the ruin of the kingdom."
Now, regarding the battle of the planets— Garga, in the *Adbhutasāgara*,
states: "Obscuration (*chādana*), obstruction (*rodhana*), likewise the obstruction of rays (*raśmirodhana*),
and eclipsing (*grahaṇa*)— these four are said to be the types of planetary battle."
This applies to the sun and moon;
however, it is otherwise for others.
For it is said: "The five conjunctions of the planets with the stars are declared according to their yoga."
Likewise.
One who, having encountered a planet that has seized another, becomes extremely dark,
clearly suffers loss, and repeatedly trembles.
Its fruit is not stated here for fear of prolixity.
Nārada said:
When the rays of various colors are struck by clouds and wind within that very sky,
the form of Indra’s bow is seen.
Or else, [it was] born from the long-standing confidence placed in him by all the lords of the nāgas.

A bow produced from the intermediate directions brings rain to that direction; one that is not bent deeply, is unbroken, and is well-proportioned is favorable. Two bows [of such quality] are auspicious.

If the elephant (Gaja) should be unfavorable to the king, it brings about his end; however, if it is favorable to the Vedas, that is auspicious. Regarding this, the pacification (śānti) spoken by Garga will now be described.
Now, regarding the yoga of the six planets and so forth, and the pacification of its effects, it is stated in the *Brahmayāmala* within the *Madanaratna*:
"I shall now fully explain the pacification (śāntika) of planetary yoga."
If, on the new moon day or other such occasions, there occurs a planetary conjunction (graha-yoga) in the same asterism,
or in different asterisms within the same zodiac sign, or even when there is a difference in both the zodiac sign and the asterism;
When [the asterism] is joined with the Moon and Sun and accompanied by three planets, there will be famine and other fears; likewise, when it is accompanied by four planets, the same occurs.
There will be the fear of great diseases, the destruction of the kingdom, the failure of rains,
famine, and the like, when five planets are in conjunction.
Human corpses and the destruction of fetuses occur, bringing about the death of people;
when the six planets are in conjunction, the death of ministers shall take place.
There will be fear from cattle, horses, and the like; everything from social disorder to the destruction of the people; the loss of the chief queen, or perhaps even fear of the enemy.
When the conjunction of the seven planets occurs, the death of the lord of the earth is certain;
indeed, it is like the dissolution of the world, for then the world becomes devoid of men.
Beyond this, there will be great portents, agitated by various sufferings;
if the Sun is distinct from that [alignment], then such a conjunction is a great marvel.
Even a yoga occurring without the Moon causes distress to the world; for living beings born under those lunar mansions, it brings great disease, great fear, loss of wealth,
loss of position, destruction of honor, and suffering.
Great suffering and great fear arising from wind, bile, and other [humors].
The lack of harmony among householders always brings about faults.
Furthermore, within six years, one's lifespan, sacrificial oblations,
and prosperity [decline] when the birth asterism occurs in the eighth, twelfth, fourth, or fifth house.

One should diligently perform the propitiatory rite for this vow here, according to the aforementioned results and in accordance with the specific fault; one must not practice stinginess regarding wealth.
Having diligently fashioned each of those grasping instruments out of gold— using one *pala*, half of that, a quarter, or even the smallest amount—
Men should not practice stinginess with their wealth according to their capacity;
they should certainly not fail to have an image of Gṛha fashioned according to the previously mentioned characteristics.
For each planet, one water-pot should be prepared, in accordance with the prescribed measurements for planetary conjunctions.
Or one should have a single water-pot made, free from cracks, very firm, and new.
In the northeastern direction of the planet's location, on a pure site and level ground,
one should perform the fire oblation (homa) according to the prescribed rules, either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or upon an altar (sthaṇḍila).
To the northeast of that, one should designate a place for the preliminary installation.
One should prepare a square sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring one cubit, using water.
One should draw the forms of the planets there and place their images accordingly;
one should then set down the presiding deity and the counter-presiding deity to the south and north.
Then, one should prepare [the offerings] with the aforementioned perfumes and flowers using their respective mantras;
one should worship them with the specific mantras prescribed for each planet, as previously stated.
Having first performed the *svastivācana* together with the preceptors and officiating priests,
and having completed the worship of the planets (*grahapūjā*) and other rites, one should present the food offering (*naivedya*).
Then one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra;
thereafter, one should perform the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa), ending with the dative case.
One should fill [the vessel] with pure water according to the previously mentioned procedure,
along with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the five barks, and the five sprouts (pañcapallava).

Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) with the respective mantra for each, one should cast in the medicinal herbs; having gathered the roots on the days specified for each particular planet, one should deposit them.
The preceptor should fill the pitcher with water possessing the qualities of the *ab* syllable;
then, according to the prescribed rule for each respective planet, he should perform oblations with the corresponding mantras.
Thereafter, one should offer oblations of clarified butter and perform the oblations of sesame seeds as prescribed;
then, having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, one should bring the remainder of the *homa* to completion.
The officiating priests should perform the consecration with the water from the ritual jar upon the patron who is seated on the auspicious throne.
The nine planets are [propitiated] with their respective mantras,
and the nine grahas are [propitiated] with their specific mantras, beginning with the five starting from Jātavedas.
With the mantra "Tryambaka," as well as with the "Kṣetrapati" mantra and the eight oblations to the world-protectors beginning with "Yata indra bhayāmahe."
One should perform the consecration with the mantra beginning "sūrāstvā" and with other meritorious mantras, in the proper sequence for the gods and others.
One should present to the preceptor a garment moistened with the consecration water (*abhiṣeka*). Then, wearing white raiment, he should perform the gazing at the clarified butter (*ājyāvalokana*).
He should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), such as cows, conch shells, and other items.
In its place, one should cause gold to be given according to one's ability.
Thereafter, one should feed the Brahmins according to one's capacity and means. He who performs this with devotion becomes free from the afflictions of the planets;
liberated from the aforementioned defects, he shall possess sons and live in happiness.
Endowed with long life and sovereignty, that excellent person shall live for a hundred years;
having become happy in this world, he shall thereafter go to the city of Śiva.
Thus ends the pacification of the conjunction of the six planets in the Madanaratna.

Now, regarding the results of an earthquake and its pacification: the occurrence of an earthquake arises from the resting of Śeṣa, the lord of serpents, who is weary from bearing the burden of the earth. Furthermore, such an earthquake always brings misfortune to the worlds.
Nārada said:
An earthquake occurring during the watches of the night is unfavorable for the twice-born;
at night, it is unfavorable for Vaiśyas and Kṣatriyas, and during the two twilights, it is unfavorable for Śūdras.
If there is an earthquake during the four asterisms beginning with Āryamā, as well as during Citrā, Svātī, and Puṣya,
or during the Vāyavya-maṇḍala,
it brings about the destruction of kings, merchants, and artisans, even without rain.

Puṣya, Viśākhā, Bharaṇī, Svātī, Mūla, Pūrvaphalgunī, Āśleṣā, and Kṛttikā—this is the circle of Agni. If there should be an earthquake in this [circle], it leads to the destruction of the king and to disease; yet, just as a cat kills mice, [it destroys] the enemies.
The verses beginning with "mūlāhi," "rbudhnya," "varuṇa," "pauṣṇī," "indrāṇyah," and "ahibhānu" [are to be recited].
If there is trembling in this Varuṇa-maṇḍala,
it portends the destruction of the king and strikes down the Pauṇḍras, Cīnas, and Pulindas.

The conjunction of the planets destroys the king, rain, and wealth, and kills the disciples and the mixed castes; this occurs when the moon is in the asterisms of Abhijit, Śravaṇa, Vaiśvadeva (Uttarāṣāḍhā), Maitra (Anurādhā), or Viṣṇu (Śravaṇa).
If there should be an earthquake within this Vāsava-maṇḍala,
it generally portends misfortune for all sovereign rulers due to the universal upheaval.
An earthquake occurring at six measures yields the fruit of burning; one occurring at two measures yields the fruit of fire.
Those not mentioned [occurring] at five measures yield the dust-fruit at that time.
The introductory verse of mine:
Some say it arises from the jar and fire; some say it arises from the impact of wind;
others say it arises from the tossing of the waves of the ocean, or from the species of fish therein.
We declare that this earthquake arises from the shaking of the multitude of heads of the lord of serpents, caused by the rain produced as he draws upward the series of Hari’s virtues.
The root, however, should be known as belonging to Vārāhī.
In that very [text] it is said:
"O lord of men, death is predominant in the fire and wind mandalas, while calamities occur in those two."
And people are indeed tormented by hunger, fear, and drought.
In this world, there shall be abundant rains from Varuṇa and Indra, bringing auspicious showers;
cows shall yield much milk, and kings shall have turned away from enmity.
Agni yields fruit within four fortnights, Varuṇa within seven days, and Devarāja (Indra) immediately; however, it is said that these do not bear fruit when they arise at an improper time.
If an earthquake occurs on the third or fourth day, or after five days, or within a month, a fortnight, or even three fortnights,
it brings about the destruction of the sovereign king.
In this case, either the previously mentioned *lakṣahoma* or the *koṭihoma* should be performed.
Thus ends the section on earthquakes.
Arathaja— Nārada:
When villages, forests, and mountains are covered by white dust,
then the kings perish and their wealth goes away.
In this very direction, however, there is destruction for one born on earth;
here, in the season of winter, the dust becomes full and yields fruit.
Thus ends the section on *rajas*.

Now, regarding the "burning of the quarters" (digdāha): Bṛhaspati says—when a flame of fire is seen while the sun has already set, one should know that to be the burning of the quarters; thus it was spoken by Bhārgava.
In the *Adbhutasāgara*, Nārada states:
"If a fire-colored glow appears in the quarters of the sky, it portends fear for the lords of the earth."
In the *Adbhutasāgara*, regarding the victory over the peacock:
"With sesame seeds, dūrvā grass and the like, as well as with beans, lentils, and barley."
The rite of oblation (āhuti) should be performed with grains, fruits of the udumbara tree, and bilva fruits;
at its conclusion, having partaken of a meal, one should direct the gazing upon the image of the man.
If a man perceives the sun situated in the midst of the sky,
he should, being pure, offer ten thousand oblations of curd, salt, and ghee.
Having fasted and performed a fire-oblation with *arka* wood, one should give a cow to a twice-born man.
Now, regarding the time for the results of portents, Parāśara states in the *Adbhutasāgara*:
"Among those, a celestial portent yields its fruit after a full year;
likewise, a terrestrial or atmospheric portent yields its fruit in eight or four months."
A thunderclap [predicts death] in three months; likewise for a city of Gandharvas.
Fire [predicts death] in seven nights, and a meteor falls within a month.
In the case of the destruction of ancient shrines and the like, during the shifting of cities,
and upon the collapse of city banners and such, the fruit [of these omens] ripens within two months.
A portent is ripened within six months for the sake of its fruit;
likewise, grief that is exceedingly intense ripens immediately.
Whatever fruit ripens for insects, mice, and snakes among bees and other such creatures, that is ripened in two months; honey, however, ripens in seven.
The omen of horses, elephants, birds, and likewise dogs,
as well as that of the owl, must be observed for three days.
O Yakṣa, the hearing and seeing of Rākṣasas while in Videha,
as well as whatever deformity occurs among animals, ripens for you in this very place.
In matters concerning meat, preparations of oil, the secretions of the body,
and varieties of clothing, the result shall be known on the seventh day.
In the case of a variegated work, [the penance lasts] for two months; for a bed, it is six monthly periods;
for an anthill, it is six months; and likewise, in cases of loss or increase, it is three [monthly periods].
When there is victory over those who are superior, when sacrifices are broken, when there is a deformity in the sacrificial vessels,
and when there is a change in the Soma-banner, such a transformation occurs after seven months.
In the case of threads and seeds, in modifications, and in the yawning of a king's weapons.
For lotuses, water-lilies, fruits, and the like, the fee shall be six māṣas.
In their destruction, those [karmas] become fruitless at the time of ripening.
Garga says: The period of the Sun is one fortnight; that of the Moon is monthly;
that of Rāhu is remembered as two months; and that of Ketu is measured by women.
However, Mercury and Jupiter should be understood as having their fruition within a year.
An earthquake occurs every six months; a solar eclipse occurs every five months;
a lunar eclipse occurs every three months; a meteor fall occurs monthly; an earthquake occurs every eight months; and a thunderclap (nirghāta) ripens [its effects] in three months.
Flowers and fruits that do not appear in their proper season ripen after six months.
For birds, insects, and moths, one should predict the result after ten days;
for ghee, oil, and fat, the result is said to be immediate.
O Indra, having seen the rainbow at night, there is a reversal of the king's character.

The fruit of the cries of monkeys and men, as well as of elephants and horses, and of various musical instruments, ripens within a month. The fruit of the cries of vultures, jackals, and lions ripens within a month.
Having heard the sound of cats, mongooses, boars, and tigers in the sky, the fruit ripens after one month.
Parāśara [says] in the *Adbhutasāgara*:
In the king’s person, in the world, in the city, the wife, and the domestic priest; likewise in the sacrificial fires, the magical arts, the treatises, as well as in the treasury and the vehicles.
If a favorable rain should fall due to a portent arising from me,
it should be known that within seven days that portent will become fruitless.
In that regard, peace through propitiation is described in the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā:
"Mars is pacified by propitiation, while Venus, born in the intermediate space (the sky), attains mildness."
A divine [merit] is obtained through gifts of fire-offerings, food-grains, land, and ten million oblations;
likewise, there is the great offering to Rudra preceded by the gift of a cow.
As long as the boat remains upon the surface of the earth, adorned with its banks— even if it reaches a divine state— what need is there to mention the other two?
In that very place:
"A pavilion (maṇṭapa) sixteen cubits square on all sides should be constructed from sacrificial trees or from the wood of chariot-fittings."
Then, in the middle of the four cubits, a square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be constructed.
It was dug with hands and teeth, and endowed with the conviction of certainty.
The six-cornered [pit] is elevated by twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas) and its base is twenty finger-breadths wide; the first girdle (mekhalā) is one finger-breadth [high],
and the pit must not be otherwise than as prescribed.
Ten finger-breadths in length at the middle, it is well-expanded to eight finger-breadths [in width].
It is fourteen finger-breadths in height and four finger-breadths in width.
A third enclosure wall should be constructed to the west of the two [other] enclosures.
It should be fourteen finger-breadths long and sixteen finger-breadths high;
it must not be made shorter or taller than that, and its width should be eight finger-breadths.
The characteristics of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) for a Koṭihoma are always as follows:
an altar (vedī) should be constructed in the northeast, measuring one and a half cubits;
indeed, because it embodies all the gods, the worship of Śiva must precede [the rite].
Then, having seized them, one should worship them there according to the previously mentioned procedure;
at the conclusion of each [mantra], one should separately offer one hundred oblations of palāśa wood, clarified butter, and cooked rice.
One should perform oblations with the Aghora mantra and cause the planetary (graha) homa to be performed;
then one should offer oblations of sesame seeds soaked in ghee with the Vyahṛtis.
At the gates, the reciters of their respective Vedas should perform the complete recitation (pārāyaṇa) in due order;
and the auxiliary reciters should chant the Camaka, the Namaka, the Sūkta, and the Puruṣasūkta.
At home, the rite should be performed with nine Brahmins who are free from transgression;
thereafter, the offering should be made, preceded by the recitation of the peace-mantra (śāntivācana).
Afterwards, one should feed the Brahmins together with one's own kinsmen.
Then, one should spend the remainder of the day with stories concerning Śiva and Viṣṇu.
In this manner, one should perform the rite without sloth until ten million oblations (koṭi-homa) have been completed;
or else, half of that, or even a hundred thousand oblations (lakṣa-homa).
The ritual should be performed according to one's means, avoiding stinginess regarding wealth;
at the conclusion of the fire-offerings (homa), one should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to twenty-four officiating priests (ṛtvijas).
One should give an ornament for each twice-born person, or two hundred niṣkas along with their contents, or half of that, or half of that again, according to one's wealth.
Thus has been described the common propitiatory rite; hereafter follow the portents by name.
Portents and their respective pacifications shall also be explained here individually.
Garga, in the *Adbhutasāgara*, states:
"An expert [in ritual] should perform one hundred thousand oblations with the Sāvitrī mantra for the sake of pacification."
Cows, land, gold, grain, and likewise clothing.
And one should give a village, a cow, or a pair of garments to the preceptor;
by this rite, the wise man should pacify the portents arising from the earth.
Thus concludes the pacification of terrestrial portents.

This same procedure is to be known for portents occurring in the intermediate space (antarikṣa). There is a specific distinction regarding the Sāvitrī: one should perform ten lakhs of oblations. One should perform the oblation with a concentrated mind, wearing a woolen blanket.
Regarding the one who has donned a woolen blanket, it will be said:
"Twelve cows, together with a hundred *niṣkas*, should be given; the preceptor should bring this wonderful *udumbara* vessel. Thus ends the *Āntarikṣa-śānti*.
When divine and miraculous events occur, those who have assembled should perform a *koṭihoma*;
furthermore, a thousand cows must be given as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor according to the rite.
This procedure has been correctly declared for the removal of celestial portents (*ariṣṭa*).
Thus ends the *Divyādbhutaśānti*.
When all these [rites], even those that are divine and wonderful,
have been performed with self-restraint, the wise man should perform the Great Peace (mahāśānti), which is immortal and the universal medicine.
Amṛtā is well known in the Atharvaveda;
however, some say it refers to the Mahāśānti mentioned in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa.
It will be seen that Viṣṇudharma and Atharvamūrti are remembered by the wise as Amṛta even among all the extraordinary [Purāṇas].
In the Niṣṇudharma: "The one called Amṛtā, Abhayā, and Smṛtā pacifies all portents.
In the Nāradasaṃhitā:
In a temple or in one's own home, one should prepare a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) endowed with the proper characteristics and surrounded by tiers (mekhalā), located in the northeast or even in the east.
There, one should establish the sacrificial fire according to the secret injunctions;
at the conclusion of the portion of clarified butter, one should offer oblations separately one hundred and eight times.
Since we fear from Indra, O Giver of Well-being, with non-terrible mantras,
one should then offer fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and caru-oblation of rice and sesame seeds, accompanied by the vyāhṛtis.
One may perform ten million oblations (koṭihoma), half of that, or even a hundred thousand oblations (lakṣahoma);
or else, according to the extent of one's wealth, one may perform a smaller number such as ten thousand and so forth.
One should perform the fire-sacrifice (homa) for twenty-one nights, or for a fortnight, or even for half a fortnight, or for five nights, or for three nights.
Then one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor and his family;
[and one should worship] the deities Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapāla, Arka, Durgā, and the Earth.
For their gratification, one should perform recitation (japa) and the bodily rites; the remainder should be performed as previously described.
One should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to sixteen officiating priests according to one's own capacity.

Thus ends the General Propitiation (*sāmānya-śānti*) in the *Prayogaratna* composed by Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa. Now follow the propitiations for various portents (*nānotpāta-śāntayaḥ*). Varāhamihira says: "I shall describe those portents which Garga has proclaimed."
This is their summary: a portent is a deviation from nature;
an affliction arises for men through misconduct and the accumulation of evil.
These portents—celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial—indicate [the coming events].
Due to the neglect of gems, the deities become disaffected and create these [calamities];
therefore, O King, the ruler should employ propitiatory rites within the kingdom for their destruction.

The celestial consists of abnormalities in the planets and constellations, meteors, thunderclaps, winds, halos, as well as cities of the Gandharvas, Indra’s bow, and so forth; that which belongs to the intermediate space is the atmospheric.
Terrestrial [portents], whether moving or stationary, when struck by propitiatory rites, attain pacification;
those not terrestrial do not attain softness, for some say they are divine and cannot be stilled.
Even divine affliction comes to rest through abundant gifts of gold, food, cattle, and land;
yet for Rudra, that [affliction] is removed on earth by the milking of a cow and by ten million fire-oblations.

O King, destiny, imagined by others, ripens in eight ways for a monarch: toward his own self, his sons, his treasury, his vehicles, his city, his wife, and his domestic priest, as well as toward the world at large.

O Lord of the Seas, the appearance of portents such as earthquakes, the falling of sweat and tears, and incoherent speech from the various images and temples of the gods leads to the destruction of the lands.

The worship of deities, auspicious journeys, favorable glances, the acquisition of a pair of wheels, the destruction of enemies, the fall [of adversaries], the overturning of thrones, the attainment of means, and association with the virtuous— these bring welfare to the ruler of the land.

That which arises from the sages, the Dharma, the ancestors, and Brahmā, as well as that which is produced by the Rudras and the world-protectors— whatever modification occurs among the twice-born, or whatever is undesirable among animals, that [is the result].

The [muhūrta] arising from Jupiter and Venus is for priests; that born from Jupiter and Saturn is for the worlds; that arising from Mars and Mercury is for regional rulers; and that arising from Mars and Venus is for the lords of the gods.
When the minister Vedavyāsa, the commander Vināyaka,
and the creator Viśvakarman have undergone transformation, the worlds are destined for destruction.
Whatever transformation may occur in the appearance of divine youths, maidens, or women,
that pertains to the king’s sons, daughters, wives, and retinue.
This alone is to be declared for the Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Guhyakas, and Nāgas;
and for all of them, the ripening of the fruit occurs within eight months.
Having ascertained the deformity, the pure domestic priest, having fasted for three nights and bathed,
shall worship the image with baths, flowers, ointments, and garments.
The domestic priest should attend upon [the guest] according to the rules with the honey-mixture (madhuparka), edible offerings, and oblations;
he should offer the cooked rice (sthālīpāka) according to the ritual procedure with mantras indicative of that [deity].
Thus, for those who have pacified the afflictions of the wise for seven nights—
those songs, dances, and festivals performed by hosts of twice-born ones and gods,
and those commissioned by kings according to the prescribed rites— [may there be peace].
The ripening of evil deeds occurs when it is obstructed by sacrificial gifts.
Thus ends the section on the modifications of the *liṅga* and other components.
In whose kingdom the fire does not blaze forth, or blazes though it possesses fuel,
the suffering of that lord of men along with his entire realm is to be recognized.

A blazing fire amidst water and flesh portends the death of a king; its fierce appearance in weapons during battle indicates destruction in the army, the front lines, and the cities, while causing fear among the people.
If palaces, houses, archways, banners, and so forth are consumed by fire without wind,
or if lightning strikes, the arrival of a foreign army will certainly occur within six months.
Dust and darkness arising from fire and smoke, as well as the appearance of stars during the day—these portend great danger;
likewise, the sight of them at night when there are no clouds causes harm during the day.
They say that for cities, quadrupeds, birds, and jewels, smoke, fire, and sparks portend fear and calamity; when these appear on the bed, on garments, or within the treasury, they signify death.
If weapons exhibit portents such as flaming, hissing, moving about, emerging from their scabbards, or quivering,
or if other extraordinary signs appear in the arms, one should declare that a fierce and tumultuous battle is imminent.
The fire should be offered oblations with mantras using fuel-sticks from milk-producing trees, along with rice and ghee;
thus, when the pacification of Agni and the other deities has been performed, gold should be given to the Brahmins.
Thus ends the section on abnormalities of the fire element.
Why should one indicate from the branches and limbs of trees the preparation for war?
Laughter portends exile from one's country, and weeping indicates an abundance of diseases.

The destruction of the kingdom occurs through untruth; the slaughter of children occurs when there is excessive flowering; the oozing of milk from trees and the total exhaustion of all wealth come to pass.
If it falls in the middle, there is loss of vehicles; in blood, battle and disease of women;
in oil, fear of famine; and if it issues out as water, there is great danger.
There is no wasting away of strength in those who are dry and parched; there is freedom from pain for those being dried up;
there is the rising up of those who have fallen, and fear born of fate.
Indeed, when flowers and fruits appear out of season on trees that have been worshipped, it is indicated as portending the death of the king;
likewise, if smoke or even a flame should arise from them, it leads precisely to the king's death.
When trees slither like serpents or utter harsh cries, the destruction of people is predicted; when there is a deformity of trees, the ripening of the fruit occurs within ten months.
When serpents slither or when people chatter excessively, the destruction of the populace is foretold;
indeed, for trees, the ripening of their fruit occurs after ten months.

For the worship of the tree with garlands, perfumes, incense, and garments, an umbrella and treasures should be offered at its base; having performed this, the recitation of the Rudra-mantra for the sake of auspiciousness should be undertaken, and here the six-limbed oblations (ṣaḍaṅgahoma) are to be made "to the Rudras."
One should feed the Brahmins with milk-rice and honey; a king [should do so] with ten thousand measures of ghee.
Thus has the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) been declared for an abnormality caused by trees by those seeking welfare.
Thus ends the section on the Vṛkṣavai-kṛta.
In which [month] do two or three stalks, lotuses, barley, and so forth appear, or does death occur?
This indicates the same for their presiding deities, as well as twins born and flowers or fruits produced.
If there is excessive growth of grasses and the production of various fruits and flowers on a single tree, the arrival of a foreign army will certainly occur.
When the oil of sesame seeds becomes heated, it would still possess its nature as oil; yet if even that were to change into something else, one should know that a very great danger is imminent.
A deformed flower or fruit, or [something similar] outside the village or city, should be employed here;
for the sake of pacification, a gentle fourfold rite should be performed, or an animal should be offered as a libation.
If one observes a deformity in the nose, that very field should first be given to the twice-born;
by performing a *caru* sacrifice for Bhauma (Mars) in the center of that very spot, the knower of the rite incurs no fault.
Thus ends the section on abnormalities of crops.
Famine arises from drought or excessive rain; there is fear of hunger and fear of enemies.
There is danger from diseases and from the seasons, and obstruction by the king occurs when [the moon] is in conjunction with the asterism Bharaṇī.
When cold and heat occur in an abnormal reversal and the rains do not fall properly,
there will be fear of the kingdom, fear for the world, and fear arising from divine causes within six months.
During the rainy season, if there is continuous rain for seven days, there will be the death of the chief king;
if it rains blood, weapons, or effort [is directed toward them], there will be a plague caused by flesh, bones, fat, and the like.
One should know that there will be fear from rainfalls of grain, gold, bark, fruit, or flowers;
however, by rainfalls of charcoal and dust, that city shall meet its destruction.
When living beings are struck by waterfalls that produce loud echoes,
or when crops are excessively rained upon, it causes great distress and fear.
If there is a rain of milk, ghee, honey, curd, blood, or hot water, the destruction of the country should be known; and in the case of a rain of blood, there shall also be war between kings.
If the shadow of the sun is not seen on a clear day, or if it is seen cast in the opposite direction,
then one should declare that a great danger has come upon the king.
When a shimmering rainbow is seen during the day or at night,
whether in the east or in the west, then there shall be very great fear of famine.
The conjunction of the sun, the moon, the clouds, and the winds is traditionally held to cause a change in the rainfall at that time;
therefore, gifts of grain, food, cattle, and gold should be given, whereby the evil is pacified.
Thus ends the section on rain.
The departure of the distressed brings about the emptiness of the city in no time; likewise, the drying up of rivers and other such bodies of water renders them parched.
Rivers that flow against their current, turbid with mud and carrying an abundance of oil and blood,
indicate the arrival of a foreign army within six months.
Flames, smoke, boiling water, and loud wailing from wells,
as well as singing and chatter, are declared to portend a plague among the people.

If water appears where there is no pit, or if there is a perversion of its smell and taste, or if the waters undergo a transformation in a reservoir, there will be great danger; for this, the following pacification rite is prescribed.
In the event of a water-related affliction, one should perform worship of Varuṇa with mantras dedicated to Varuṇa;
by performing recitation (japa) and fire-oblation (homa) with those very same mantras, that evil comes to an end.
Thus ends the anomaly of water.
In the case of women, when there is a disorder of childbirth occurring after two, three, four, or more [conceptions],
or when it occurs at an excessively full or empty time, the offspring will be one born of a specific region or family.
If twins are born from a mare, a camel, a buffalo, a cow, or an elephant, their death occurs;

if born after six months, the result is miscarriage. Regarding the pacification [of these omens], there are two verses spoken by Garga: "If twins are born from a mare, a camel, a buffalo, a cow, or an elephant, their death occurs; if born after six months, the result is miscarriage. One should perform the rite of pacification for them with great effort, as prescribed by the sages. "By performing the rite of pacification according to the rules, one obtains the fruit of a hundred cows; by reciting the *Gāyatrī* mantra ten thousand times, one attains the supreme state."

A woman who has been abandoned by her husband because she was attached to another man should be released from that state; he should satisfy the twice-born with their desired objects and likewise cause propitiatory rites to be performed here.
Quadrupeds should be released from their own herd into foreign lands;
otherwise, the herd might destroy the city and its lord.
Thus ends the section on abnormalities of the secretions.
The approach of choice-bulls to the cows of the animals is indeed pleasant;
or else, a bull drinks from this [udder] while the dog licks the son of the Surabhi.
Within three months, one will undoubtedly know of his departure;
these two verses are taught by Garuḍa for the purpose of striking him down there.
Relinquishing, casting out, and giving—that shall quickly become auspicious for him;
he should satisfy the Brahmins here and cause recitations and fire-offerings to be performed.
The domestic priest should worship Dhātṛ with an oblation cooked in a pot and with an animal sacrifice,
using the Prajāpatya mantra, and provide abundant food as the sacrificial fee.
Thus, indeed, the four-footed [verse] was performed.
If a vehicle moves without its draft animals, or fails to move when joined with them,
or if there is a breakage of the wheels, then danger shall arise for the kingdom.
If the sound of the unstruck musical instruments should not arise when they are struck by the wind,
or if there is a change in their sound due to the wind, it portends either the death of the king or his departure.
If one hears the sounds of singing and musical instruments while wandering in a forest fire, it portends stability followed by change;
if one hears such sounds and musical instruments at the time of death, it indicates an affliction and defeat by an enemy.
If there is the sound of a jackal near a vessel, a ladle, a winnowing basket, or other such household implements,
as well as the cry of a jackal, then, according to the words of the Sage, there will be danger from weapons.
In these rites dedicated to Vāyu, the king should worship Vāyu with parched grain (saktu);
the five verses beginning with "āvaha" should be recited by the self-restrained twice-born.
One should satisfy the Brahmins with excellent food and sacrificial fees;
furthermore, abundant food, sacrificial fees, and oblations must be performed with great effort.
Thus, O Vāyu, it has been done.
The city-dwellers, like forest-dwelling birds, abandon their homes for the wilderness;
those who roam by night now wander during the day, while those who roam by day frequent the nights.
Deer or birds, forming circles at both twilights,
or crying out together while facing a blazing direction, portend danger.
Dogs howl as if weeping at the gate, and jackals cry out with blazing mouths;
or perhaps a young owl or an owl enters the palace of the lord of men.
The crowing of cocks at dawn, the warbling of cuckoos at the beginning of winter,
and beasts of prey such as lions moving in circles against the natural order in the sky are portents that bring fear.
The gathering of flocks of birds at domestic shrines, on battlefields, or at gateways, as well as the emergence of bees, anthills, or lotuses from such places, portends destruction.
O King, if dogs enter a temple by thrusting their bones or carcasses into it, or if they bark while holding weapons, death will occur; such is the word of the sages.
In the event of abnormalities involving wild animals or birds, one should perform burnt offerings (homa) accompanied by sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā);
furthermore, the hymn beginning with "devāḥ kapotaḥ" should be recited by five twice-born men.
With the mantra "sadevā" and likewise with the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās),
one should mutter the Ākhu-sūkta and place the heads upon the altar.
Thus ends the section on the portents concerning beasts and birds.
O King, if there is a breaking of the semen-banner, the lord-pole, the wedge, the pillar, the door, or the water-trough,
as well as the breaking of the door-panels, the archway, or the banner, death for the monarch occurs.

The blazing of the two twilights and the appearance of smoke from the forest fire indicate the absence of the light of consciousness; the splitting and terrifying trembling of the earth likewise signify this same condition.
When a king is devoted to heretics and nihilists, abandons virtuous conduct, is prone to anger, envious, cruel, and has a mind intent on conflict, that country perishes.
Even there, children with sticks, stones, and weapons in their hands, shouting "Strike! Strike! and "Cut! Break!", quickly become a source of fear.
In that [place] where there is the depiction of deformed spirits with charcoal, ochre, and other pigments,
or where the hero is painted, one’s lifespan does not perish for long.

A house that is variegated with cobwebs and spider-webs, where worship is not performed during the two twilights, which is filled with quarrels, and where women constantly eat from the same vessel as their husbands, goes to ruin.
When Yātudānas are seen, one should declare that death has swiftly arrived;
for their counteraction, one should perform the Garga-śānti rite.
Then, one should perform great propitiatory rites (mahāśānti) and offer very extensive oblations (bali);
furthermore, one should cause Maheṃdra and Māheṃdrī to be worshipped.
Thus ends the section on the portents concerning the banner of Śakra, the Indra-kīlaka, and so forth.
When Ketu rises in the ruler’s country, or when it is conjoined with Saturn or Mars, there is the occurrence of portents at their respective seasons; yet this does not lead to any calamity.
An astrologer shall recognize, through these verses composed by his son and expressed in brief, the portents produced by the faults of women that arise from the nature of the seasons.
There were thunderbolts from the Vraja region, earthquakes, twilight, the roar of portents,
halos around the sun, dust, smoke, and the sun appearing blood-red at both sunrise and sunset.
The trees, as if with the essence of nectar, produce abundant flowers and fruits; likewise, there is an increase in the vigor of cattle and birds during the auspicious months of Madhu and Mādhava.
The orb of the sun and moon at Kampila was obscured by the falling of meteors and stars,
while a mass of smoke and dust, though not ignited by fire, was driven away by the wind.
Seeing the sky red as a lotus or the dawn, resembling an agitated ocean,
and observing the drying up of the waters of rivers during the summer, one should predict auspicious results.
A halo around Indra’s weapon, the withering and regrowth of lightning,
trembling, overturning, and deformity, as well as the churning and splitting of the earth.
In the rainy season, the swelling and overflowing of lakes, rivers, and wells,
as well as the shifting of mountain peaks and caves, do not bring about danger.
The wondrous sight of celestial women, spirits, and gandharvas in their aerial chariots,
and the vision of the planets, lunar mansions, and stars in the divine sky.
In the autumn season, the sounds of songs and musical instruments resound through the forests and mountain ridges;
there is an abundance of crops, the waters are clear, and it is remembered as being free from calamities.
The presence of cold winds and frost, the crying of beasts and birds,
the sight of beings such as Rākṣasas and Yakṣas, and the speech of non-human beings.
In the winter season, the quarters of the sky shrouded in the darkness of smoke, along with the clouds, forests, and mountains,
as well as the high rising and setting of the sun, are considered auspicious.
The sky, with its winds and gusts from the Himalayas, appeared strange and wondrous to behold;
it shone like black collyrium, turned tawny by the falling of meteors and stars.
The birth of variegated offspring among women, cattle, horses, deer, and birds, as well as the budding of leaves on trees and creepers— these transformations in the winter season are inauspicious.
These [omens] born of the nature of the seasons are seen to bestow auspicious results when occurring in their proper season;
however, when portents appear out of season, they are seen to be exceedingly terrible.
Whatever verses are uttered by the insane, whatever speech is spoken by children, and whatever women say— there is no deviation from that [truth].
Having first sported among the celestial delights, she later descends to the human world;
for this Sarasvatī, whose speech is truth, does not speak unless impelled.
Even one devoid of mathematical calculation, by understanding portents, becomes renowned and a favorite of kings;
this secret teaching of the Sage has been declared, knowing which a man becomes a seer of the three times.
Thus end the propitiations for the portents described in the Vārāha [Purāṇa].
In the Madanaratna, Garga said:
"The deities certainly become displeased due to the transgressions of men;
and from the displeasure of the deities, calamity ensues."
It is proclaimed to be threefold: celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial.
Learn from me the celestial and atmospheric portents concerning the planets and the stars:
namely, the fall of meteors, the burning of the quarters, and likewise the appearance of halos.
A city of Gandharvas, as well as distorted rain—
such things as these in this world one should designate as the atmosphere (antarikṣa).
That which is stable on earth, earthquakes, and whatever originates from the ground,
as well as the abnormalities of reservoirs of water, are proclaimed to be terrestrial (bhauma).
When [the planet] is on the earth (bhauma), its fruit is known to be great and ripens after a long time;
when it is born from the clouds (abhraja), it yields moderate fruit and bestows its results during the middle period.
When a portent has arisen in the atmosphere, if the rain should become auspicious,
it should be known that within seven days that portent will have perished and will bring benefit.
When a portentous transformation and destruction are seen within three years, it should be known that this will cause a very great terror.
In the bodies of kings, in the world, in the city, as well as in the wife and the house;
it ripens in their sons, and likewise in the treasury or the vehicle.
O Indra among kings, the seasons possess inherent natures that are designated as marvelous; they are to be understood as auspicious when occurring in their proper time—listen now as I describe them:
thunderbolts, meteors, earthquakes, halos around the sun and moon, and the sounds of atmospheric portents.
Halos, dust, smoke, a reddish sun, and so forth;
trees that are split by men, lack of moisture, and the abundant production of crops and fruits.
In the months of Madhu and Mādhava, the appearance of cattle, birds, and slow-growing plants is auspicious;
however, it is inauspicious if they are defiled by falling meteors or if the discs of the sun and moon appear tawny.
Without fire, it blazed; without being struck, it emitted sparks and smoke; the sky, crimson as a red lotus, resembled the agitated ocean at twilight.

Seeing the drying up of the waters of the rivers, one may predict a favorable summer. The appearance of Indra’s bow (a rainbow), a halo around the sun, the rising of Jupiter and Venus, trembling, upheaval,
and the shaking and sinking of the earth— these are the portents.
The waters of the ponds become sweet with fresh rain, young frogs leap upward, and the decayed parts of trees sprout anew; thus the rainy season is exceedingly beautiful.
Furthermore, there is coolness amidst fire, the state of frost, and the crying out of beasts and birds.
There is the sight of Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, and Piśācas, or the speech of non-human beings.
In the winter season, smoke in all directions, the sound of thunder, clouds together with mountains,
and the high rising and setting of the sun are considered auspicious.
There was the wondrous sight of celestial women, Gandharvas, and divine chariots; the vision of planets, constellations, and stars; and the appearance of superhuman speech.
The sounds of song and musical instruments on forested mountain ridges,
and the arising of aesthetic flavors through the increase of newness— these are remembered as the flavors of the autumn season.
There were portents of snow and portents of rain, with sights both deformed and marvelous;
the sky took on the luster of black collyrium, and it was turned tawny by the falling of meteors and stars.
The birth of variegated offspring among women, cattle, horses, deer, and birds,
as well as the auspicious transformations of leaves, flowers, and creepers, occur during the cool season (śiśira).
When the king heard that a son had been born at an auspicious season accompanied by wonders, he immediately performed the birth rites;
thereafter, for the sake of the child's welfare, the King of the Earth (the Lord of the World) spoke these words of pacification.
Garga said:
The images of the deities dance, tremble, or blaze;
they ascend, climb, perspire, and even laugh.
They rise up, sit down, run about, and move about;
they perform strange movements that dispel the fear of human beings.
They stand facing one another, wandering from place to place;
they vomit fire, as well as smoke, fat, blood, and marrow.
Such transformations arising from one's own nature are seen in the various images and shrines; therefore, one should not desire to dwell there.
If the king suffers misfortune there, the entire country perishes;
having seen divine processions and great portents, one must certainly predict fear.
The components related to the journey include the axle of the cart, the banner, the bamboo frame, and so forth.
Among these, the [axis] of animals is to be known as born of Rudra, while that of kings is born of the World-Guardians (Lokapālas).
It is stated in the *Arghya* [section]: "The breaking of the image of Rudra brings about danger for the animals."
Thus it should be understood in all cases:
from the destruction of the generals arises that which is born of Taksan and Viśākha;
and for the worlds, that which originates from Viṣṇu, Vasu, Indra, and Viśvakarman.
The origin of the Vināyakas should be known as being for the sake of the attendants of the Gaṇas;
their messengers are the gods, and their servants are the wives of gods and the wives of kings.
This should be understood to apply to the Vāsudeva images in the houses [of devotees], and not otherwise;
for the worship of the deities in temples, the domestic priest, having bathed and purified himself, [should perform it].
Having gone to the image of the deity, one should bathe it, clothe it,
and worship it according to the rules with the madhuparka offering immediately thereafter.
And with the mantra bearing that [specific] characteristic, one should diligently offer oblations of cooked rice (*sthālīpāka*) into the fire according to the prescribed rule for seven nights.
O lord of men, the Brahmins should be honored for seven days with sweet foods, drinks, and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā);
by the gift of cows along with gold, one attains the desired state on earth and one's sin reaches pacification.
Thus ends the rite for the pacification of deformities in the image of the deity.
Garga said: O King, when fire blazes excessively in a kingdom,
or if a fire possessing fuel does not blaze, that kingdom is afflicted.
Or if fire is wet with water, or likewise if one dreams of eating earth;
or if one sees a palace, an archway, a gate, a royal residence, or a temple of the gods.
Where these [signs] are burnt, one should predict fear of the king;
where they are scorched by lightning, there too there is fear of the monarch.
Where there is an extremely intense heat without water or dust,
and where there is smoke not born of fire, one should know that a great danger is present.
If there is lightning and clouds in the sky when it is devoid of rain,
one should predict danger from the gods at that very moment, even if the stars are visible in the sky.
If there is a transformation involving iron weapons, one should predict a battle there;
in that case, the priest, being well-composed, should fast for three nights.
One should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with the wood of milk-exuding trees, mustard seeds, and ghee,
using the Agni-mantras, and should also feed the Brāhmaṇas.
One should likewise give excellent colors, cows, and garments to the twice-born;
when this is done, O lord of the twice-born, that calamity arising from the abnormality of fire comes to an end.
Thus ends the pacification of abnormalities of the fire.
Garga said:
"In the cities, those trees that are seen as if impelled by fate—whether they are weeping, falling, or vomiting blood upon the ground; [these are omens]."
If it is weeping, disease approaches; if it is dwelling, there is confusion in the region;
and if it forms a canopy of branches and clouds, it causes the fall of warriors in battle.
The death of children occurs due to fruits and flowers of children;
out-of-season fruits and flowers cause the division of one's own kingdom.
If milk is found everywhere, it indicates deep-seated affection; if there is a lack of oil, it is a sign of famine.
If vehicles increase in number amidst these conditions, one should anticipate war.
When there is an excess of honey and an excess of water, it rains;
the drying up of health should be known as the characteristic of a Brahmin famine.
Vigor sprouts even in the withered, yet food is withheld;
for those who have fallen, there shall be fear of rising and of internal division.
One should predict the ruin of the country when there is movement from place to place;
likewise, there is loss of wealth when trees are chattering or making sounds.
When this [omen] occurs upon trees worshipped by all kings, it ripens for the king;
likewise, one should predict the death of kings through flowers or fruits that have become deformed.
And among other trees, being vigilant toward those that have sprouted unexpectedly,
one should cover that tree and adorn it with perfumes and garlands.
Likewise, one should place a parasol above the tree for the pacification of evil;
however, some say that in the event of a portentous shaking of the tree, the tree should be cut down—this [latter view] must be rejected due to its contradiction [with the former].
One should worship the god Śiva and offer an animal to him;
saying "to these," that is, to the Rudras, one should then recite the Rudra-hymn after having performed the sacrifice.
