Having honored the Brahmins and Lord Bhava with milk-rice (pāyasa) prepared according to my ritual manual, one should offer it;
likewise, for the sake of destroying sin, one should worship that Lord Hara with song and dance.
Thus concludes the pacification of abnormalities in trees.
Now, the pacification of the evil birth of the plantain tree (*kadalī*):
*Umo vā ca*.
When the first fruit of a plantain tree is seen, [one should perform this rite].
The wise man, facing south, does not indeed obtain various fruits.
"O King, for whom does fruit arise even among farmers?
Śrī Mahādeva said:
When the goddess Kadalī bears fruit facing the southern direction..."
Then, it brings about the destruction of the village headman; of this there is no doubt.
When such a calamity has arisen, one should perform the prescribed rite therein.
Even one who has been defiled by birth-impurity (sūtaka) should desire to approach [the deity] with a plantain tree;
having performed a vigil for that purpose, a fire-oblation (homa) must then be performed thereafter.
The oblation should be performed with Ṛg Veda mantras proclaimed by the Vaiṣṇavas;
the eloquent one should recite the mantra a thousand times, and perform the recitation for peace many times over.
Viṣṇu is the deity there, and the mantra associated with his signs is recited;
various kinds of the seven grains should be given to the Brahmins.
The king should give that plantain tree to a wise and eminent brahmin.
When the ritual has been performed in this manner, peace shall arise for the brahmins; and when the most excellent of brahmins has been honored, the performer shall attain happiness.
Thus concludes the rite for pacifying the evil fruiting of the plantain tree.
Now, regarding the pacification of abnormalities in rainfall,
Garga said: "Excessive rain, drought, famine, and so forth— therefore, there is fear."
But if it rains excessively during the day outside the proper season, it will lead to disease and fear.
And those who belong to the Anabhraka heaven alone should be known as the slayers of kings.
Unnatural thundering and the like [are portents]. When there is an inversion of cold and heat seasons, there is fear born of enemies.
Wherever blood rains down, there shall be the danger of weapons. Likewise, when fruit and flowers wither prematurely, they lead to fear.
During the showers of dust, insects, and fruits, there is danger arising from disease.
The rain did not fall through the gaps, yet the crops flourished excessively; though free from dust and devoid of foul odors, no shadow was seen.
If a contrary shadow is seen there, there will be danger in that place;
"contrary" means an unfavorable shadow, which is to say, a reversed shadow.
Where it rains continuously, there shall be fear of enemies;
likewise, if at night there is a cloudless white light toward the south or the north, [the same danger follows].
Likewise, having seen Indra’s bow, as well as the fall of meteors,
the burning of the quarters, portents of grinding destruction, and a city of Gandharvas;
One should recognize the fear of foreign armies, as well as regional calamities, the burning of the quarters, halos around the sun or moon, and likewise the city of the Gandharvas.
One should give grains, cows, and gold as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the twice-born for the sake of destroying poverty.
Thus ends the Vaikṛta-śānti for excessive rain.
Now, regarding the pacification of portents concerning reservoirs of water, Garga said: "If they move away from the city or approach it closely,"
Rivers, streams, springs, and waterfalls become devoid of flow.
They carry water that is discolored, turbid, heated, swirling in eddies, and agitated; it flows with milk, oil, wine, and blood, its waters thrown into confusion.
Within six months, they know there will be fear of an enemy army there;
by that very [omen], the reservoirs of water somehow burst into flame.
In that manner, O Brahmin, it emits flames, smoke, and dust;
like water arising where there was none, or like reservoirs filled with living beings.
The sounds of music are seen; know them to be the fear of birth and death.
Know this divine and great terror to be merely the sprinkling of honey.

Vāruṇa mantras should be recited, and with them, the oblation (homa) should be performed in water. Here, milk-rice mixed with honey and clarified butter should be given to the twice-born for their meal. Furthermore, cows accompanied by white garments, as well as large water-pots, should be given for the pacification of all sins.
Thus concludes the pacification of abnormalities in reservoirs of water.
Now, regarding the pacification of portents concerning vehicles and other equipment,
Garga said:
"If vehicles yoked with other animals move toward the right side, or if those already yoked should pass beyond the axle-pin..."
Being urged by those staying there, it was brought near out of fear of me.
Musical instruments that were being played did not play, nor did those not being played;
mountains seemed to move, yet they did not move, and what was moving did not move at all.
If there is the sound of musical instruments in the sky and the singing of gandharvas,
or if wood, ladles, axes, and other such objects undergo transformation;
If one sees a plough, a trident, or a collection of weapons, or women, or even a woman who strikes [one],
or if one is deformed by household utensils and the like, there will be terrible weapons and fear.
O twice-born one, having performed the worship of Vāyu with barley-meal (saktu), one should recite the mantras with focused concentration;
one should offer excellent food (paramānna) along with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the spirits (bhūtas), and for you there shall be no misfortune.
Thus ends the Upaskara, with its peace-chanting completed.
Now, regarding the pacification of portents involving wild animals and birds,
Garga said: "If, for every twenty villages, wild animals and birds [behave abnormally]..."
Village-dwellers go to the forest, and those born of water go to dry land.
Terrible jackals, dwelling without fear, come from the land to the water;
they howl at the king’s gate and the city gates, bestowing both auspiciousness and inauspiciousness.
Whether they be nocturnal creatures wandering by day, or diurnal creatures wandering by night,
if they abandon their village or the domestic animals leave it, one should declare that place to be empty.
Where the radiant garments and the celestial spheres appear like the twilight,
and where all musical instruments resound— there too one shall obtain that same fruit.
If a cock cries at dusk in its roost, or a cuckoo in winter,
or if a jackal howls facing the sun at sunrise, it portends danger.
If a dove enters the house during a planetary transit, or if a flesh-eating bird alights upon the head,
or if honey-bees make honey [there], death will befall the master of the house.
If a carnivorous beast should take refuge in the gate-houses of the ramparts, in archways, marketplaces, or streets, or among umbrellas, weapons, and the like;
O Lord, if an anthill arises and exudes honey,
then that region will go to ruin and the king shall die.
Upon seeing mice and locusts, there will be great fear of hunger;
[the omens] abounding in pieces of wood, firebrands, bones, and horns portend the suffering of dogs and monkeys.

Famine is to be known by the signs of crows meditating with their faces turned upward and so forth, as well as by people overpowering one another and those who perceive themselves as being in a fearless wilderness.
If a white crow is seen engaged in sexual union,
the king will die there, or the entire region will perish.
If an owl is seen at the king’s gate or likewise in one’s house,
it should be known that there will be death for the master of the house as well as the loss of wealth;
in the event of such portents involving beasts or birds, one should perform a fire sacrifice accompanied by ritual fees (dakṣiṇā).
The verses beginning with "devāḥ kapota" should be recited by five twice-born men, and the verse beginning with "sudeva" by one; cows should also be given as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Recite the Kuṇṭhasūkta, the Sama-veda, and the Vedaśiras;
these mantras are well-known in the Ṛg-veda, beginning with "namo brahmaṇe."

The Upaniṣads, which are the heads of the Vedas, should be given according to the prescribed rule; likewise, cows along with gold, and upper garments together with clothing, should be given to the twice-born.
When this is done, the evil comes to rest, as has been declared by the deer and the twice-born.
Thus ends the pacification of portents involving beasts and birds.
Now, regarding the propitiatory rite for portents mentioned by Mātsya,
Garga said: "In palaces, archways, gates, gateways, ramparts, and dwellings..."
But a sudden fall of firm trees portends death by lightning.
When the quarters of the sky are completely obscured by the dust raised by the king's army,
and the sun, moon, and stars become discolored, it portends an increase in fear.
Where Rākṣasas are seen, where Brāhmaṇas act contrary to the Dharma, where the seasons are disordered, and where the unworthy are honored by people;
The separation of the lunar mansions is a sign of great danger; so too are the rising of Ketu, the retrograde motion of the planets, or an eclipse of the moon or the sun.
Wherever there is an anomaly in the planets or the stars, one should predict fear there as well;
women engage in quarrels, and children kill other children.
Where the failure of rites that have been performed is observed,
and where the fire, though being offered oblations during propitiatory ceremonies, does not blaze up;
Flesh-eating spirits indeed go there, as do those from the north;
full jars leak, or the sacrificial oblation is scattered.
Where auspicious sounds are not heard on all sides, or where sneezing afflicts one, or where there is the roaring of those who are incited to violence;
One should not behave with hostility toward either [the enemy] or toward the Brahmins;
or else, let the sounds of the Vedas and musical instruments be played extensively.
Where those who hate their teacher and friend are always devoted to honoring their enemies; where the Brahmin is honored as a friend, yet the people hold him in contempt.
In rites for peace and auspiciousness, if one harbors atheism or feels contempt,
the king will die there and the astrological prediction will perish.
When the king’s own destruction was imminent, these signs appeared:
he first showed hatred toward the brahmins and reviled the brahmins.
He seizes the property of Brahmins and seeks to kill Brahmins;
he does not remember those who have served him in times of need, and he becomes enraged at them.
He delights in their censure and does not rejoice in their praise;
likewise, O twice-born ascetic, he regards greed as something difficult to overcome from the very beginning, even when it brings pleasure.
Cows should be given to the assembly of the twice-born, as well as land, gold, and garments;
likewise, a fire-oblation (homa) should be performed for the sacrifice of the twice-born; when this has been done, the sin attains pacification.
When a portent has arisen, if auspicious rain falls,
it should be known that within seven days the portent will become fruitless and beneficial.
Thus concludes the extraordinary rite for pacification as spoken by Matsya.
Now, regarding the pacification of various portents, Garga says in the *Madanaratna*:
"Listen now to the great pacification for portents as it truly is."
Where there is disease, drought, or a foreign army has arrived.
Famine, death among the people, diseases, and even death itself [shall prevail];
for that, the sequence of pacification is proclaimed: one should perform a great sacrifice here, and a fire-oblation (homa) must be performed again according to the system of Bṛhaspati.
On that very day cows should be given as gifts; on that very day the wind shall blow favorably;
on that very day the king’s consecration should be performed, and likewise the sacrificial priests.
Having fasted for either three nights or seven nights,
the domestic priest shall duly burn one hundred fuel-sticks made of *udumbara* wood.
One should feed the Brahmins there and offer them abundant sacrificial fees;
likewise, one should perform oblations with droṇas of barley grains smeared with ghee.
One should give ghee to the twice-born until peace is attained;
for a king or a preeminent person, a drona-measure of ghee is prescribed.
One should bestow eleven bulls upon Brahmins;
thus, sons and daughters alike will flourish within the lineage.
And there, one should employ ritual action for the benefit of all living beings;
one should have the rite performed with the Sāvitrī mantra, whereby sin is then pacified.
Excessive heat and excessive cold, excessive rain and drought, flowers and fruits out of season, and an excessively strong wind;
There shall be excessive death among draft animals and an abundance of mice;
or else, there will be a great wind that scatters herds of deer in the forest.
The beasts and birds cry out with excessive terror;
there is the roar of lightning and thunder, and rain falls even though there are no clouds.
The sight of lions, tigers, and hyenas at a crossroads—
through such omens and portents as these, one should foresee total destruction;
elsewhere a king is born, and likewise another high priest.
In this regard, I shall proclaim an auspicious rite of pacification that quells all evil:
one should offer one hundred and eight fuel-sticks of the Udumbara tree.
Having offered one hundred thousand oblations of [materials] mixed with milk and anointed with ghee, using the auspicious groups of great mantras, one shall attain supreme peace.
But where a pestle or even a mortar cracks,
or where beings and spirits likewise cause fear in the house as well as in the temple;
Where the earth suddenly quivers as if it were shaking,
or where that which is joined or unjoined runs about in a manner inconsistent with its nature;
Where the immovable wavers and there is dispute among the ministers,
and where the officials likewise argue excessively with the Brahmins;
In such omens, one should proclaim great danger;
one should predict fear for merchants, caravan leaders, and ministers.
One should predict disputes among the populace and among ministers;
regarding that, I shall declare the pacification known as the Prājāpatya.
Having offered fuel-sticks of the Aśvattha tree smeared with ghee and mixed with honey,
one should consecrate them with the Sāvitrī mantra eight thousand times and with the Prājāpatya mantras.
One should feed the twice-born with milk-rice and give abundant sacrificial fees at the conclusion of the meal;
then the sin is pacified, according to the doctrine of Prajāpati.
And auspicious twin-born [beings] appeared upon their own mounts,
as well as those with shaven-faced heads, the cruel, and the corpse-eaters.
Among humans, elephants, wild animals, and birds,
there are born those with upper teeth, as well as horses with deformed faces.
With many heads or no head at all, with many colors or no color;
with one horn or no horn, and likewise with four arms or no arms.
With long ears or no ears at all, with the face of a goat, or likewise with the form of a spotted tiger’s face, or with a high, protruding cat’s face.
O Gautama, wherever such ill-omened sights are seen, one should declare from those omens a great and destructive fear arising from battle.
Regarding the destruction of people, the slaughter of citizens, and likewise the killing of guilds,
I shall there proclaim a peace that destroys all sins.
Being well-composed and acting according to the rules, he should duly burn one hundred and eight fuel sticks of Khadira wood with the Nirupaksha mantra.
Regarding "Virūpākṣa, Agnimūrdha," and so forth, Virūpākṣa is the seer (ṛṣi) therein.
One who desires peace should give a tawny cow at the conclusion of the fire-oblation;
then that sin is pacified, just as when the sacrificial fire has grown strong.
When improper deeds arise, the king punishes those who should not be punished;
those unworthy of honor are honored, and even those worthy of respect are held in contempt.
The ox should drink from the cow, and the cow should drink from the ox;
the cow does not welcome her newborn calf with a lowing.
The remaining [signs] are the newly-calved cow with her calf (vatsagaurī) and the inverted coitus; [so too are] the mating of deer and birds at the wrong time.
Brahmins who do not abide by their boundaries do not persist in any ritual acts.
From such signs and portents, one should know the upheaval of the country;
a terrible conflict arises, along with famine and pestilence that kills the people.
There will be the destruction of the king and his ministers, as well as great fear for the citizens;
in that regard, I shall proclaim a peace-rite that destroys all sins.
Having kindled the sacrificial fire with fuel-sticks of the *aśvattha* tree and having prepared a great altar-covering,
the wise man should offer one thousand and eight fuel-sticks of the *udumbara* tree.
One should offer oblations into the fire according to the prescribed rite and shall attain supreme peace;
one should also bestow a house, together with male and female servants, upon a twice-born man.
Then, just as by the word of Gautama, evil is pacified wherever there are black ants in villages and cities.
Indeed, they are seen in great numbers perched upon bamboo poles,
as well as in houses, temples, and likewise in the palaces of kings.
Then, houses were seen everywhere above in excessive numbers;
moreover, flies, mosquitoes, and gadflies appeared in great abundance, causing extreme terror.
Through such signs and portents, there shall be great fear of thieves;
one should predict the seizure of goods and the arrival of a foreign army.
In that regard, O Śāntila, I shall describe the rite shown by Viśvāmitra:
having offered one hundred and eight oblations of *aśvattha* wood fuel.
At the conclusion of the fire-oblation, one should give full vessels and abundant sacrificial fees;
one should also give a house, complete with all household utensils, to a member of the twice-born caste.
A vessel of sesame seeds should be offered; by offering sesame seeds, one attains prosperity.
Where there is no fire, it blazes; where there is no smoke, there is the appearance of smoke.

Where the young princes engage in quarrels together with their forces, there constant strife shall arise among the cattle and other livestock, as well as among the inhabitants of the cowherd settlements.
Wherever a quarrel arises among traveling merchant caravans,
there will be the destruction of the king and his ministers, as well as great fear for the citizens.
In this regard, I shall proclaim the rite of pacification according to the words of the Grandfather (Brahmā):
one should offer one thousand and eight oblations of palāśa wood into the fire.
There, one should feed the Brahmins with excellent food soaked in ghee;
then, in accordance with the words of the Grandfather (Brahmā), one shall pacify the sin.
Whether on the ramparts of a city, in a delightful palace, or upon the watchtowers; whether on the main roads, at crossroads, or in the temples of the deities.
Where cranes, crows, owls, vultures, cuckoos, and wild beasts and birds make their dwelling;
He perceived the terrible quarrel and likewise the words of the Siddhas;
he perceived them through his reasoning.
In that regard, I shall proclaim the rite of pacification characterized by the *nārada* [mantra],
performed before the fire with fuel-sticks of the *aśvattha* tree smeared with clarified butter.
Having offered well-prepared blood with the Vāyavya mantra, the sin is then pacified; such is the word of Nārada.
If a man who has died and been carried to the cremation ground returns to life and should ever enter a house, he shall remain there.
One whose wife and possessions have been stolen soon attains peace;
I shall explain the means for that peace according to the doctrine of Dharmarāja.

Having offered into the mouth of the fire oblations of sacrificial wood smeared with clarified butter according to the rule, the wise man shall have performed the rite of pacification using vessels made of udumbara wood.
One should perform the milk-appeasement (kṣīraśānti) with eight thousand recitations of the Sāvitrī mantra;
and this milk-appeasement applies to the "red ones," the "single-colored ones," and so forth, which will be described hereafter.
At the conclusion of the fire-oblation, one should give a tawny cow, sesame seeds, and bell-metal as abundant sacrificial fees;
then that sin is pacified, according to the doctrine of Dharmarāja.
Whether it be a dog, a jackal, a vulture, a crow, or even a human,
having taken flesh from the cremation ground, one should cause it to be brought into the middle of the city.
Whether it be a city, a town, a village, or even a house,
in no long time at all, it will become a cremation ground.
There will be the arrival of a circle of thieves and the onset of a foreign army;
there will be ill health, drought, famine, and pestilence that kills people.
One should predict that there will soon be a battle involving a multitude of weapons;
therein, I shall proclaim a rite of pacification that brings peace to that evil.
Having taken fuel-sticks of the *aśvattha* tree and sesame seeds mixed with honey,
[he should worship] Virūpākṣa, who is deep red, with the *virūpākṣa* mantra.
One should offer sesame, leaves, and water, and perform a rite for peace;
then that sin is pacified when it is according to the doctrine of Prajāpati.
The Sautrāmaṇi, the Pākayajña, the Paśubandha,
and likewise the other sacrifices proceed for one who has attained the dawn [of knowledge] even without having studied [the Vedas].
When these occur in such a manner— whether out of anger, greed, or even fear—
and when the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is not properly given, it is truly a sign of a great portent.
Illness, drought, famine, and pestilence;
fever, cough, asthma, leprosy, ringworm, and cholera.
Diseases of the head, hemorrhoids, jaundice, and throat-obstruction,
among others, manifest through the signs of evil dreams.
In this matter, O Bṛhaspati, I shall declare the means of pacification;
let the domestic priest, having fasted for three nights and subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya), deliberate upon it.
One should burn a hundred fuel-sticks smeared with clarified butter;
if a thunderbolt or a flash of lightning should fall upon the blazing fire, [the rite is successful].
If one should perceive great danger even in the city and the surrounding countryside,
then within a year or more, one should expect a great loss of people.
The king will suffer destruction along with his ministers; of this there is no doubt.
In that regard, I shall declare the propitiatory rite (śānti) according to the words of Indra and Agni.
One should burn one thousand and eight fuel-sticks of Apāmārga;
one should feed two Brahmins milk-rice (pāyasa) and perform a rite for peace with milk.
O Brahmin, the knower of mantras should offer a hundred oblations with the Māhendra mantra and then prescribe the milk of red cows that have failed to produce color.
O Brahmin, the knower of mantras, having offered a hundred oblations with the Māhendra mantra, should prescribe the milk of cows possessing the color of gold and excellent jewels.
At the conclusion of the fire-oblation, there was a vast sacrificial fee consisting of heaps of gold and jewels;
likewise, by the word of Indra and Agni, that sin was consumed.
The great rivers flow with their currents at dawn from their reservoirs,
and they bring forth waters that travel along paths out of their proper courses.
The lotus ponds and reservoirs discharge water onto the earth,
and rivers become the source of the flow for lilies and blue lotuses.
There is the sight of the seven sages, of the serpents reclining in the water,
of sacred trees, and of great meteors that bear flowers and fruits.
The stench of pus and blood became fragrant for those possessed of compassion,
while the priest was cut to pieces and rained upon by worms and blood.
O Gautama, wherever such omens exist, one should know that an invasion by a foreign army is imminent, bringing fear to all the world.
One who is composed should declare fear of the king and his ministers, and great fear for the citizens,
by means of fuel-sticks from the Udumbara tree offered according to the prescribed ritual.
Having offered one thousand and eight oblations with the *indrāgneya* mantra,
the knower of mantras should perform the recitation of the Rudra hymns and the *vāyavya* hymn on all sides.
In all the temples of the gods, amidst the sounds of various musical instruments,
one should have the Brahmins recite benedictions (*svasti*) with sweetmeats, unbroken rice grains, and leaves.
At the conclusion of the fire oblation, a thousand cows shall be given as abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the twice-born;
furthermore, whatever terrible fears there may be, such as portents and the like, shall be dispelled.
According to the opinion of Prajāpati, [sins] are pacified by the gift of a cow,
as well as by vows, fasts, restraints, fire-offerings, and the satiation of Brahmins.
When celestial portents have arisen, one should perform the *caru* sacrifice to Mahendra;
likewise, a sacrifice to Varuṇa for those occurring in the atmosphere, and a sacrifice to Agni for those on the earth.

Likewise, at the time of battle, for the sake of warding off blows, one should utter "evam" and so forth; thus [the mantra] is applied to that which arises from the divine, the terrestrial, and the atmospheric realms in the world.
Through observances, vows, fasts, and rites for pacification, he attains tranquility;
the deities are worshipped, as are the astrologers and domestic priests.
"The planets and constellations are the gurus; they declare this to be an auspicious sign.
Thus, in the *Madanaratna*, are the pacifications for portents as spoken by Garga.
O Sage, due to the misconduct of the world and the harm caused by the wicked, they create a deity for the purpose of destroying those who have turned hostile.

When various kinds of portents—celestial, terrestrial, and atmospheric—occur, or when the eastern quarter revolves [unfavorably], or when his jeweled jars, pots, or vessels break; or when his umbrella, bed, seat, residence, chariot, banner, or the tip of his standard breaks; or when his chief horses perish—all such occurrences are portents presided over by Indra. For these, the expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) are as follows: having offered one hundred and eight oblations of cooked rice (*sthālīpāka*) with the verse "Indra vo viśvataspari," he should offer five oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the formulas: "To Indra, Svāhā! To the Lord of Śacī, Svāhā! To the wielder of the thunderbolt, Svāhā!"
He offers oblations separately with the words "Svāhā to Īśvara, svāhā to the allayer of all evils, svāhā," and with the vyāhṛtis.

Then he turns toward the southern direction. Now, whatever unpropitious things appear among his offspring or his cattle within his body—namely, various kinds of diseases, excessive sleep, bad dreams, overeating, laziness, indigestion, a crow going to the door of the house, a dove entering or perching upon the body, a black woman [seen], or seeing such things in a mirror—all these are portents presided over by Yama. Having offered one hundred and eight *sthālīpāka* oblations with the verse "In the vault of heaven, the gold... (*nāke suvarṇam*), [he should perform the rite].

He offers five oblations with the words: "Svāhā to Yama! Svāhā to the Lord of the Departed! Svāhā to the One who holds the Staff in Hand! Svāhā to Īśvara! Svāhā to the Queller of All Evils! And he offers separately with the *vyāhṛtis*.

O Lord of the East, he does not turn back from his goal, for in whose fields, houses, or dwellings various kinds of extraordinary calamities appear—such as mice, locusts, ants, *mathvaka*, *bhaumaka*, parrots, *śakabhaka*, *saukṣmaka*, and so forth—all these, O Varuṇa, become [manifestations of] the *daityas*.

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations from the *sthālīpāka* with the verses beginning "ghṛtavatī" and "varuṇasyottaṃbhanam asi," he offers five oblations of clarified butter with the mantras: "To Varuṇa, svāhā! To the Lord of Waters, svāhā! To the One with noose in hand, svāhā! To Īśvara, svāhā! To the Queller of all sins, svāhā! and he also offers separately with the *vyāhṛtis*.

The sun and moon turn back; there is a loss of gold, silver, diamonds, lapis lazuli, pearls, and gems; the *rambhā* plant withers; friends become estranged; honey comes from gourds; anthills rise up; dry trees sprout; oil solidifies at night; smoke arises from a blazing fire in a cremation ground during the day; a female donkey conceives—such are the omens, O Śravaṇa.

Marvelous things occur through the Dhaivata [chant]. Having offered one hundred and eight oblations from the cooking pot with the hymn "Abhitvā deva" (RV 10.99), he offers five oblations of clarified butter: "To Vaiśravaṇa, svāhā! To the pacifier of all sins, svāhā! and he offers separately with the Vyāhṛtis.

The earth revolves for him; when his earth cracks, slips, trembles, blazes, weeps, smokes, or suddenly vomits forth water, floats, sinks, or, having sunk, rises up again, and produces flowers and fruits out of season—such portents as these occur due to Agni as the presiding deity. Having offered the *sthālīpāka* with the verse "Agni is the messenger" (*agnir dūtaḥ*), he offers five oblations of clarified butter with the following: "To Agni, svāhā! To the radiant one, svāhā!"

He offers oblations separately with the mantras: "To Śaktipāṇi, svāhā! To Īśvara, svāhā! To the Pacifier of All Sins, svāhā! and also with the *vyāhṛtis*. Then he contemplates the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). When there are winds blowing from all sides, when water-forms are seen in the machines and clouds, when there is a gathering of ravens, cranes, vultures, herons, pigeons, owls, hawks, and crows; when rains of flesh, insects, animal meat, animal bones, and blood fall; and when the mating of crows is seen at night, or a rainbow appears in the sky.

If one should see twenty rabbits, trees shedding blood in the sky, or such other portents as these, they are omens presided over by Vāyu. Having offered the *sthālīpāka* with the mantra "May the wind blow" (*vāta āvātu*), he offers one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with five mantras: "To Vāyu, svāhā! To the Lord of Great Omens, svāhā! To the Swift-handed One, svāhā! To Īśvara, svāhā! To the Remover of All Sins, svāhā! After offering with the *vyāhṛtis*, he should then sing the *Sāman*.

When the moon appears as if it were the sun, when stars rain down and meteors fall, when the quarters of the sky smoke and burn, when comets arise, when smoke issues from the horns of cows and blood flows from their udders, and when excessive frost falls—when such portents concerning Soma occur—one should offer one hundred and eight *sthālīpāka* oblations with the mantra "Obeisance to King Soma," and then offer five oblations of clarified butter with the following: "Svāhā to Soma! Svāhā to the Lord of the Constellations! Svāhā to the Cold! (and so forth).
He offers oblations separately with the mantras "To Pāṇi, svāhā! To Īśvara, svāhā! To the remover of all sins, svāhā! and with the vyāhṛtis.

The entire world turns back; the abodes of the gods tremble; the deities cry out in distress, dance, sing, burst asunder, suffer, open their eyes, close their eyes, and retreat; even the rivers flow backward.

At that time, water is seen in the sun, and it becomes heated; comets, banners, umbrellas, thunderbolts, and horned animals appear blazing; embers rain down from the sky; and wondrous portents related to the deity Viṣṇu occur, such as these: "Viṣṇu is here," "Viṣṇu is here," and "Viṣṇu is here. Having offered the *sthālīpāka* oblation with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇur," he offers five oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the following: "Svāhā to Viṣṇu! Svāhā to the Lord of all beings! Svāhā to the wielder of the discus! Svāhā to the Sovereign! Svāhā to the remover of all sins! [He then recites] the *vyāhṛtis*.

Having offered oblations with the *Bhūr* mantra, one should then sing the *Sāman*. The earth is purified by four means: digging, burning, scraping, and treading; and fifthly, by smearing. Having brought the ritual materials (*saṃbhāras*) while circumambulating from left to right and having had the Brāhmaṇas recite auspicious blessings (*svastivācana*), one should sprinkle water over that which has been touched by the materials; thus it becomes pure here. One should feed the Brāhmaṇas and give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) consisting of gold, a cow, clothing, and so forth.

Then, when his thoughts turn toward the six directions, and when his cows, buffaloes, and camels give birth to offspring with fat limbs, yet their bodies appear empty or deformed, and even immovable things like mountains begin to shake, and other such wondrous portents presided over by Rudra occur—having offered one hundred and eight oblations from the *sthālīpāka* with the hymn "Ā vo rājānam," he offers five oblations of clarified butter to Rudra Paśupati, Śūlapāṇi, Īśvara, and Sarvapāpahara; then, having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis*, he chants the Sāmaveda.

When the quarters of the sky revolve upward and so forth, or when his mind becomes afflicted with distress; when mountains split asunder, the earth falls from the sky, great trees tremble, stones dry up, and four-footed creatures become five-footed—when such portents occur, these being omens pertaining to the deity Sūrya—one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of cooked rice (*sthālīpāka*) with the hymn *ud u tyam*, and then offer five oblations of clarified butter (*ājya-huti*) with the following verses: "To Sūrya, the lord of all planets, the drinker of rays, the Sovereign."

Having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* for the purpose of removing all evils, one should then sing the *sāman*. Then, when the quarters of the sky turn turbid, or when women give birth to twins, or when a white crow or a mating of crows is seen, or when there is a conflagration of all the quarters—[in these cases, one should perform the rite].

Piśācas and Rākṣasas are born among cattle, goats, sheep, and camels; fire breaks out among livestock; humans become like animals; and all kinds of beings are born among human beings. Through the actions of body and mind, one hates Rudra; there is promiscuity between men and women; and the intellect turns toward all manner of sins—such are the portents presided over by Rudra that occur. Having offered a *sthālīpāka* with the verse "viśvataścakṣuḥ," one should offer five oblations of clarified butter.
He offers oblations with the heart-mantras beginning with "To Rudra, the lord of Umā, the wielder of the trident, the Sovereign who pacifies all evils."

Earthquakes, the burning of the quarters, and planetary conflicts arise; a comet is seen in the sky, and the sun itself trembles. A hole appears in the sun, and it turns black in color. Rivers flow in reverse and carry blood. Song is heard from the sky, and thunderous roars occur. All such portents as these come to pass, and for them there are expiations: in every house there should be peace, and brothers should perform sacrifices and offerings.

One should constantly perform charity, recitation, and worship of Rudra and Bhāskara (the Sun). Puṣṭihita [should perform] a *lakṣa-homa*, a *koṭi-homa*, and a *dūrvā-homa*. The gift of cows, land, gold, clothing, food, and sesame seeds brings auspiciousness. Rice-milk (*pāyasa*), curds, milk, and ghee should be offered as food for those who desire nourishment.

Then, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation), one should bring together *dūrvā*, *darbha*, *śamī*, *vīraṇa*, and so forth; clarified butter, mustard seeds, *phalinī*, *apāmārga*, sesame, barley, and rice; and sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*). Having bathed and smeared the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should prepare the following separate sacrificial porridges (*caru*): curds with honey, *kṛsara* (rice and peas), barley, parched grain flour (*saktu*), and milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with curds, honey, and ghee. For all of these, one should offer the milk-rice into the kindled fire, reciting: "Indra, all have strengthened thee"; "The eagle in the vault of heaven"; and "Thou art the support of Varuṇa."

We choose you, O God Savitṛ; we choose Agni as our messenger. "Viṣṇu strode through this [universe]. "The all-seeing eye. "Gaurī has lowed. "From joint to joint. "You are firm; may this [man] be firm. "He who knows, lead him; they are known. "May he dwell here; may he not perish. "Agni has given back the wife together with life and luster. May her husband, possessing long life, live for a hundred autumns."
Thus end the marvelous propitiatory rites declared in the Devīpurāṇa within the Madanaratna.
Now, regarding the pacification of the breaking of a temple, a pinnacle-vessel, or a linga: Nārada, the Ocean of Marvels, says—
wherever in a temple a thunderbolt falls, or a vulture [alights], or again...
Upon the falling of a heron and likewise upon the sight of fire on a crest of grain.
Where the *liṅga* splits or trembles without cause,
where the crest-jewel (*cūḍā*) breaks, or likewise where the image (*pratimā*) is split;
If there is a destruction of the village, one should predict the death of its master;
in that case, I shall declare a pacification by which auspiciousness is attained.
Having constructed the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the prescribed rules, one should then perform the fire-oblation (homa).
Having prepared the sacrificial porridge (caru) dedicated to one's chosen deity according to the ritual injunctions, one should proceed.
One should not undertake the ritual work with a hand that has gold [on it];
rather, one should then offer one hundred and eight fuel-sticks smeared with clarified butter as oblations.
One should perform five thousand oblations with these— black gram, mung beans, and sesame seeds, together with ghee and honey— using the *śakti* seed-mantra.
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice (homa), one should satisfy the twice-born with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), meals, and so forth;
as well as land, a cow, a bull, gold, and grain, accompanied by the dakṣiṇā.
Then, having prepared the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the twice-born man should bathe in the temple,
having offered an oblation with secretions, along with kṛsara and milk-rice (pāyasa).
One should install Īśāna there after offering a bali-oblation according to the prescribed rule;
by performing the rite in this manner, a person becomes one who has fulfilled his duty.
Likewise, for the walls of a pavilion, the pinnacle of a temple, a mound of earth,
and similarly for a clay image;
If [the fire] should suddenly fall out or tremble without a visible cause,
then [one should offer oblations] of Aśvattha fuel-sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
The knower of mantras should offer one hundred oblations with the mantra "imā rudrāya" for one who has been bitten;
he should also give a cow as a sacrificial fee, along with a vessel of sesame seeds together with gold.
Thus ends the pacification of the destruction of the worship of the *liṅga* and so forth, from the *Śāntiratna*.
In the *Mādanaratnapariśiṣṭa*:
"If a pillar sprouts in the middle of a house, or if a pigeon falls into the middle of the house, or if a crow enters the house..."
If a cow enters the house, or if one climbs onto an anthill, these [inauspicious] things arise.

If a white ox leads him away, or if he scratches the sky with his horns while naked, or if smoke arises from a fire that has no flame, or if resinous exudation is produced; or if a frog is seen in his dwelling, or if he dreams of the falling out of his teeth, or if the master of the house meets with misfortune along with his wife; or if other portents occur in the house—having performed the rites beginning with the scratching of the sacrificial ground for the gods up to the "mouth of the fire" (the invocation of Agni), he offers oblations from the *sthālīpāka*.

Having recited the *puronuvākyā*, "yata indra bhayāmahe," he offers the oblation with the *yājyā*, "svasti dā viśpatiḥ. Then he offers additional oblations of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*) with the verses: "vāstoṣpate," "śaṃ na indrāgnī," "kayā naścitra ābhuvat," "ko adābhyaḥ," "vataṃ naḥ samanasaḥ," and "ā līl̥a. From the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, the procedure is established until the gift of the cow. Then, in front [of the fire], he places the remnants of the oblation upon *śamī* leaves with the verse, "śaṃ no devīrabhiṣṭaye"; likewise, he places the wash-water from the cooking pot, the remnants of the clarified butter, and the remnants of the water.
Having brought [the food] into a vessel, one should sprinkle it with water while reciting "tac chaṃ yoḥ ā vṛṇīmahe";
then, having prepared the food, honored the Brahmins, and instructed the disciples, he said, "May there be auspiciousness. Thus the extraordinary [rite] has been explained.
Regarding the pacification of the *janamāra*, great pestilence (*mahāmārī*), and so forth,
Garga states in the *Hemādri*:
"I shall declare the origin of the *janamāra* along with its pacification."
When kings, possessed by greed, oppress their subjects.
He sports excessively and does not abide by the Dharma;
the subjects follow his word because he is blind to righteousness.
Overcome by anger and greed, and devoid of virtuous conduct,
they do not constantly worship the gods, the Brahmins, or their well-wishers.
When those women were overcome by unrighteousness, Rudra became enraged;
yet this Blessed One is pleased even with the lowest of beings.
And it produces various kinds of modifications that serve as causes:
the stars, the planets, comets, meteors, Rāhu, and the Vīrakas.
Nor [should one see] the sun at dawn or twilight appearing distorted, or terrifying portents involving deer and birds,
earthquakes, meteors, lightning strikes, and abnormalities of cold, heat, and wind.
There shall be excessive rain or a total lack of rain, and likewise a reversal of the seasons; during this inversion of the seasons, the medicinal herbs will be devoid of their essence.
Deprived of their flavor and potency, they then give rise to diseases;
furthermore, divine, terrestrial, and atmospheric portents appear as indicators of impending calamities.
Then, terrible diseases that kill people arise;
because they are born from the wrath of Rudra, they are called "the killer of people" (janamāra).
And all of them, moreover, were overcome by him due to a derangement of their intellects.

Vitality, strength, and even the natural constitution generally undergo transformation in living beings due to the theft of a Brahmin's property, treachery toward a guru, and the killing of the virtuous.
It is heard that this plague has arisen;
therefore, for the sake of pacifying this pestilence, [offer] that which is the source of Rudra’s power.
Therefore, with a concentrated mind and established according to the ritual prescribed by those who know the divine, one should strive to propitiate the God of gods, Maheśvara.
One should perform the propitiation according to the Gāṇapatya ritual, as well as the Ātharvaśiras,
and by means of the Yāmala procedure.
One should mutter the Śiva-stuti, the Umā-stuti, and the Śatarudriya;
one should also offer various oblations of water and present them at the crossroads.
I invoke you, Rudra with his retinue, or Śiva himself;
one should satisfy the Brāhmaṇas with edible foods, meals, and sacrificial fees.
When Rudra is thus propitiated, the plague of people ceases;
for this [plague] does not have various deities as its cause, nor can it be averted by other diverse rites.
When the power arising from Rudra’s wrath was forcibly pacified by Śakti, he therefore resolved with effort: "May there be welfare for the world."
When Śiva is well-pleased, there is welfare for all creatures;
he is devoted to righteousness, auspiciousness, and virtuous conduct, and is a devotee of the gods, the Brahmins, and the learned.
The king, with his senses restrained, was devoted to recitation and fasting.
One should perform the fire-oblation with discipline, according to the prescribed rule.
For a king who acts in this manner, the successful accomplishment of his undertakings arises;
for faith, O King, is said to be the very root of that action.
Having stayed overnight, the man— having bathed and donned white garments and having performed his own self-protection— should then employ the rite for peace.
The king is the soul of dharma and the royal priest is the knower of dharma among those who know dharma;
when the king possesses these qualities, their welfare increases therein.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Likewise, the recitation of the Rudra-mantras destroys all sins;
the fire-oblation (*homa*) fulfills all desires and likewise bestows peace in every respect."
[He knows] the [number] of goats and sheep, of horses and likewise of elephants,
of cows, of men, of kings, and even of children and women.
O Bhārgava, knower of dharma, [you have described] the calamities of villages and cities,
as well as those that have arisen from diseases.
When death is imminent, or when there is fear from enemies or other such dangers,
the Rudra-homa performed with milk-rice and ghee brings supreme peace.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "During times of affliction for men, may my majesty pacify the outbreak of great pestilence as well as the three kinds of portents."
In this context, it should be understood that the *lakṣahoma* and *koṭihoma* are to be performed with the previously mentioned *Nṛsiṃhagāyatrī*.
Thus ends the pacification of the Great Plague that kills people and other such calamities.
Now follows the pacification of the mating of crows,
according to Garga in the *Adbhutasāgara*:

One should observe the mating of crows; if a crow alights upon the head, it portends death to the head; likewise, if it scratches the head with its claws, it indicates the destruction of one's wings (or followers).
If one performs an investigation and touches the vehicle,
then one should announce death or even a great calamity (mahāriṣṭa). In that case, one should perform a propitiatory rite (śānti) according to the prescribed injunctions.
One should perform the pacification of misfortune (ariṣṭa-śamana), preceded by a formal resolve (saṃkalpa).
Having established the fire upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) one cubit in size in a pure place,
and having placed it according to one's capacity upon a water-pot over an eight-petaled lotus in the northeast of that [mound];
Having worshipped an image of Indra fashioned from gold, accompanied by the guardians of the world (Lokapālas),
according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Vedic branch, one should partake of the sacrificial oblation (caru).
Having performed the rites up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, one should offer the oblation (*havis*) in sequence:
fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood, *vrīhi* rice, fried grain (*caru*), and clarified butter (*ājya*), according to the proper order.
One should offer one hundred and eight, or one hundred thousand,
or indeed one hundred and eight oblations to the world-protectors with the mantra beginning "yata indra".
Having offered oblations according to one's capacity, one should offer the expiatory oblations (*prāyaścittāhuti*) prescribed in one's own Vedic branch (*svaśākhā*);
thereafter, one should present the *bali* offerings to the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), beginning with Indra and Agni.
One should offer the bali-oblation to the crows with the *aindravāruṇa* mantra:
"O those belonging to Indra, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, Agni, and Nirṛti."
May the ancestors accept this earth, which has been offered by me.

Then, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* oblation, one should worship the preceptor (*ācārya*). Then, the principal officiant (*yajamāna*) should be consecrated with the water from the ritual jar (*kuṃbha*) according to the detailed procedure.
Then the preceptor should give an image of Indra along with its appurtenances;
furthermore, he should give abundant gifts according to his capacity and provide a feast for the twice-born.
One hundred, or fifty, or twenty-five, or even ten [drops] may be emitted if semen is present;
however, if white [semen] is seen, it is joined with passion (kāma).
Thus says Garga in the Hemādri:

some, however, maintain that the defect seen in the sight of a white crow mating is not merely that; if it is seen by two-footed beings (humans) through repeated observation, then because of the resulting mental affliction, they die from that knowledge, and thus [the sight] is to be avoided.
Thus ends the pacification of the crow's mating.
Now, the pacification of the crow from the Mānava-saṃhitā:
I shall now fully declare [the rite] when a crow enters the house.
One should enter through the gate and depart; one should remain for one month and then leave.
If it should enter through another door, one must abandon [the site] for six months;
if it enters a temple, the destruction of the king and the village will occur.
At the time of entering a house, a crow causes the destruction of the entire household;
if a dog or a cat should go there, or a crow should enter the house [at that time], it is likewise inauspicious.
One should know that death occurs for the householder and total destruction may happen in the home;
I shall describe, in brief, the pacification of these various defects.
Then, in the house at the site of entry,
one should first choose a Brāhmaṇa teacher who has mastered the Vedas.
One should place a smooth, unblemished jar filled with a *droṇa* measure of rice,
combined with the five sprouts and accompanied by the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Having purified it with water from sacred fords and joined it with the five jewels,
one should place the Lord of Śacī in the form of a crow upon that vessel.
Then, having worshipped with at least a karṣa of gold, or according to one's own capacity even with a quarter of that, using the mantra "yata indra," the knower of the deity [should proceed].
One should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) in order, beginning with Indra and ending with Īśana;
one should perform the consecration of the pillar and chant the Śrī Rudra while touching it.
One should perform the rite of fire-oblation (homa) according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*;
with the two mantras beginning with "yata indra," one should offer fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and cooked rice (*caru*).
One should offer one hundred and eight thousand, or indeed one hundred and eight,
oblations of sesame seeds with the Tryambaka mantra.

One should perform the oblation of parched grain (lājahoma) with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," and then, having performed the oblation of rice grains (vupahoma), one should offer oblations with the Mahāvyāhṛtis.

"Oblation to Indra, Svāhā! Oblation to the bird-omen, Svāhā! Oblation to Śamana, Svāhā! Oblation to Śānta, Svāhā! Then, having offered the Sviṣṭakṛt oblation, he should complete the remainder of the Homa.
Having been consecrated with the splashes [of water], one should give a pair of cows as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
then, having performed the inspection of the clarified butter (ājya), one should recite the Mahāśānti.
Thus ends the pacification of the crow: Nārada says—there is destruction of one’s prosperous kinsmen, loss of wealth, as well as infamy;
distress for relatives, loss of sons, anxiety regarding one’s wife, and madness.
In the forenoon, seeking fruits,
[one should bathe] the head of Indra with the five barks, sprouts, gold, the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and fruit water.
By anointing [the body] with mantras consecrated by recitation, one is released from the defect of the bath.
In the same way, [these are inauspicious] when there is a firebrand on the head, when the middle of the head is defiled,
when there is a breaking of teeth, when a crow or a hawk strikes, and also upon the falling of a lizard.

If a lizard or a monitor lizard falls upon a wall, it bestows gain; if it occurs otherwise, it is an expenditure. A throbbing on the right side brings profit, while a throbbing on the left is the opposite.
The opposite is true for women—as stated in the *Rāmāyaṇa*: "Sītā was the protector of the monkeys' eyes, while their proud eyes were the protectors of Sītā. Thus they shine upon one another.
Thus ends the rite for the pacification of the crow.
Now, regarding the pacification (*śānti*) for seeing crows mating, as spoken by Nārada in the *Madanaratna*:
"Whether by day or by night, he who should see crows mating..."
A person meets with death, or else the destruction of their position.
Or else, he should observe the Kāghāta vow for a year;
indeed, with devotion, he should greet the twice-born daily as if they were his own fathers.
One who has conquered the senses and subdued anger, being devoted to truth and righteousness,
should perform rites of pacification (śānti-karma) in order to neutralize those defects.
One should designate the place for the fire-oblation (homa) in the northeastern part of the house;
there, having established the sacrificial fire according to the procedure prescribed by one's own *gṛhya-sūtra*.
At the conclusion of each mantra, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of fuel-sticks, rice,
and clarified butter with the Tryambaka mantra and the two Apamṛtyu mantras.
The two mantras beginning with "apamṛtyum" and "apakṣudham" are well known in the Taittirīya [Āraṇyaka].
One should perform the Jaya and other oblations with the Vyāhṛtis and grains of rice.
The performer, being pure and well-adorned, should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti);
[he should also give] a black, milch cow with golden horns, auspicious hooves, and a beautiful tail.
Accompanied by garments and ornaments, and provided with twelve *niṣkas*,
or half of that, or half of that again, or even provided with ten thousand [coins].
O slender one, according to one's wealth, one should not make excessive preparations;
one should give a cow to a teacher who is a learned Vedic scholar and maintains a household.
Since you, O Earth, constantly remove all death from one who has suddenly fallen into a fire-like state, therefore grant me peace.
He should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) according to his ability to distinguished Brahmins,
and afterwards he should feed the Brahmins, preceded by the recitation of the Svasti-vācana.
Thus, he who acts in this way is liberated from the fault of insulting the Tathāgata.
In the Madanaratna, Vṛddhagārgya states:
"The attainment of sovereignty and prosperity on the head; the sight of kinsmen with the eyes;
good fortune on the nose; and the eating of delicious food in the mouth."
A constant embrace of a beloved is indicated by the throat; victory is certain for the two shoulders;
gain of wealth for the pair of arms; and the accumulation of half [one's desires] for the hands.
On the chest, there is good fortune; on the heart, the increase of love for one's son;
on the belly, the attainment of a son; and on the navel, the increase of fame.
If it is on the back, there will be gain from a companion; if on the thighs or knees, there will be a vehicle;
if on the shanks, there will be lack of effort; and if on the feet, there will be wandering.
If one performs circumambulation starting from the feet and ascending up to above the head,
or even circumambulates the body itself, one will likewise obtain a kingdom.
If the *gī* moves from the head down to the feet,
or from the feet upward, or even circumambulates the limbs, one should predict loss and grief.
If a lizard falls on all parts of the body at any time, there is loss;
if it moves upward or downward, it bestows prosperity upon the family.
Thus, the wise should understand this to be the fruit of the wife’s downfall;
one should know that this very same fruit results from the growth of another's [offspring].
If a wife falls down or a lizard grows on [the head],
for five nights he will suffer from the affliction of disease, especially so.
If an ascent occurs immediately after a fall,
the fruit of the fall becomes supreme, whereas the ascent would be fruitless.
If there is ascending with the face upward and descending with the face downward [one hundred] times a thousand, that fruit will certainly arise.

In the conjunction of death (mṛtyuyoga), on a day of burning (daddha), during the fall of the planet (pāta), when Kaṇṭaka is present, when the Moon is in the eighth house, at the time of death (nidhana), and during the poisonous minutes (viṣanāḍikā) of one's birth star— these are the times for such rites.
If the lord of the eighth house is conjoined with a malefic planet, or is associated with the Viṣa, Aṣṭami, or Vaidhṛti yogas,
or occurs during a Durnimitta or Nidhi-utpāta, death certainly occurs.
Upon merely touching those two, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on.
Having consumed the five products of the cow, one should perform the purification with clarified butter and water.
Or, as if instructed by a teacher, if one desires prosperity for oneself,
one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited and then perform the rite of pacification (*śāntikarman*).
One should fashion a suitable image out of gold according to one's means,
wrap it in a red cloth, and worship it with perfumes and flowers.
Having prepared the fire-pit, one should perform the oblation according to the prescribed rules,
using auspicious fuel-sticks of Khadira wood while reciting the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra.
One should perform the oblation of sesame seeds with the Vyāhṛtis one thousand and eight times,
or one hundred and eight times, according to one's financial means.
One should perform the Mahāvyāhṛti oblation with clarified butter and milk;
thereafter, one should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) upon the head of the patron.
One who performs the supreme rite of pacification (śānti) should bestow a cow along with a cloth, accompanied by meritorious Vāruṇa hymns and mantras for peace and other purposes.
For such a person, longevity, victory, prosperity, fame, and nourishment arise;
the pacification of the *pallī* and *saraṭa* [omens] is established by the *lauṇaka* system.
It has been proclaimed, together with its fruits, by the wise Vṛddhagārgya.
Thus concludes the pacification of the pallī and the lizard.
Now follows the pacification of the lizard falling from a wall as spoken by Nārada.
Nārada said:
"Upon the falling of a lizard from a wall and its regrowth thereon..."
One should discern the auspicious and inauspicious according to the specific nature of that particular place.
The falling of the wife's [hair] likewise yields auspicious or inauspicious results;
on the head it brings sovereignty or fortune, while on the forehead it increases power and prosperity.
Victory is declared when [the breath] is in the left arm; great danger when in the right;
and likewise, gain of wealth when in the right side of the abdomen.
Wealth is said by the ancient seers to be located in the left side of the abdomen;
there is the acquisition of friends in the right hand, while sound is in the left hand.
In the right side of the abdomen, the attainment of good sons is said to occur;
in the left side, there is great disease; and on the right hip, there is great fame.
If [the shadow] falls on the left hip, there will be loss caused by kings or venomous creatures;
one should know that it is likewise for the knees, and on the left foot, it portends the removal of auspiciousness.
The great seers have declared that movement with the left foot first is auspicious;
however, for women, one should declare the result to be the opposite.
One should know that the climbing of an anthill and the falling of a lizard upon all parts of the body are inauspicious; one should perform a propitiatory rite according to one's ability.
If there is the attainment of auspiciousness in an auspicious place, or if there is inauspiciousness in an unfavorable place,
its true nature is like gold, and likewise, it is the form of Rudra.
One should worship the chariot with garments and other offerings while reciting the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra;
having established the sacred fire there, one should offer oblations of sesame seeds mixed with rice flour.
There, the preceptor should perform the consecration with hymns dedicated to Varuṇa;
[he shall also worship] Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapāla, Arka, Durgā, the Earth, and the deities of the limbs.
For their gratification, the recitation of mantras should be performed; the remainder should be carried out as before.
One should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests and should not act with stinginess regarding wealth.
Thus concludes the pacification of the Pallī-saraṭa (the lizard of the hamlet) as spoken by Nārada.
Now, regarding the pacification of the arrival of pigeons, tawny birds, and so forth, Nārada states in the *Madanaratna*:
"If a pigeon should ascend upon one's house or enter it..."
He shall suffer a loss of his position, just as there is a succession of misfortunes.
For one who is afflicted by defects, for the sake of wealth, for the poor,
and for the sake of auspiciousness, its pacification should be performed according to the rules of recitation and fire-oblation.
There, one devoted to the performance of Śrauta and Smārta rites should invite sixteen, twelve, or eight Brāhmaṇas, preceded by the recitation of auspicious benedictions (svastivācana).
The wise man, having diligently prepared a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the procedure prescribed in his own Gṛhya-sūtra, should mutter the five verses beginning with "devāḥ kapota".
One should establish the fire in the northeast and, at the conclusion of the [main] rite, perform one hundred and eight oblations with sacrificial fuel (samidh),
clarified butter (ājya), and cooked food (anna), each preceded by the Praṇava (Om).
One should offer oblations of sesame seeds with the three mantras beginning with "yata indra bhayāmahe," "svasti na indro vṛddhaśravāḥ," and "svasti no bṛhaspatirdadhātu," together with the vyāhṛtis.
Then, with devotion, the performer himself should offer the Jaya and other oblations, as well as the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti);
he should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins, and thereby the pacification of defects shall occur.
After feeding the Brāhmaṇas, one should then eat oneself together with one's kinsmen;
he who performs this with devotion is liberated from that sin.
Likewise, even in the cry of a Piṅgala bird, there is honey in an anthill;
in a full house there is loss, while in an empty dwelling there is auspiciousness.

The fruit [of the omen] pertains to the village chief within the walls, at the city gate, in palaces and the like, or on the main roads; and for the boundary-guardian within the boundary, there is peace. All ritual actions should be performed according to the sequence previously described.
Thus ends the propitiatory rite for the arrival of pigeons, tawny birds, and others.
Then, on the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, there is the worship of Revanta;
the mantra for this is prescribed by Śālihotra.
Homage to the god who is the primordial deity of gods, who moves with the strength of a horse,
the son of the Sun, the god who is the benefactor of horses.
O you who are surrounded by a multitude of horses, who burn away the sins of men and elephants; O you whose field is filled with horses and devoid of other horses, I go to you for refuge.
And in the Rūpanārāyaṇīya, there is an alternative procedure established by tradition:
"O son of the Sun, O mighty-armed one, O delighter of Chāyā’s heart!"
Bring peace to the horses; salutations to you, O Revanta!
Right there, [the hymn] for Brahmā.
In the bright fortnight of Āśvina, on an auspicious day under the Svātī conjunction,
the first horse named Ucchaiḥśravas was brought forth by the Sun.
Therefore, he should be worshipped there with one's own horses and men with such faith;
indeed, the arenas should be honored until the ninth day.
Peace, well-being, and various benefits accrue to them day by day;
likewise, grains, *bhallātaka*, *kuṣṭha*, *vacā*, and *siddhārthaka* [should be used].
Then, one should bind them with a five-colored thread,
using mantras dedicated to Vāyu, Varuṇa, Sūrya, Śākha, and Viṣṇu.
Likewise, the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice must be performed day after day;
and the horses should be guarded by men with weapons in their hands.

In that regard, they should never be struck, nor should they be harmed in any way. When the conjunction with Svātī occurs in the morning during the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, starting from that time until the ninth day—
The meaning is that, having first performed the worship of Revanta before the image,
one should worship Ucchaiḥśravas and then worship the other horses.
In the *Śālihotra*: "When the horse has been consecrated with the *nīrājana* rite, when the *lohabhisārikā* sacrifice has been performed,
and when the royal horse has been sprinkled with water, then [the blood] of the horses shall flow."
On the lunar day beginning with the second of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, for seven nights,
the constellation Svāti, in the form of a mare, draws the chariot of the Sun.
Overcome by pride and enraged, she gazes upon others with sharpness;
she seizes their entire essence of splendor and all their strength.
Therefore, when the moon enters Svāti, there will be great suffering for horses;
thus, its conjunction is declared to last for seven nights.
In that regard, the horses should be kept where they are not touched by the rays of the sun—
a stable that has been smeared with cow dung, is pleasing to the mind, and is shielded from the sun's rays.
On the second day, horses adorned with various kinds of flowers and perfumed with incense should bathe in that pool, having been honored and worshipped.
They must be guarded for seven days by men with weapons in their hands.
[The substances are: guggulu, asafoetida, barley, the bark of *sthāṇu*, *apāmārga* grain, and iron.
Siddhārtha [white mustard] on the garment, Āryā on the necks of the horses,
barley, āmalakī, and rice as seed.
Having prepared the altar, one should offer oblations into the fire in its center according to the prescribed method;
there, one should perform the homa with this mantra as declared by Śālihotra.
O Rohitāśva, O highly fortunate one, O carrier of oblations,
O best of gods, O smoke-bannered one, O sustainer of sacrifices, you are renowned on the path to heaven.
Arise, take up the oblation, and perform the pacification (śānti) among the horses;
with the mantra "svāhā," offer the first oblation there.
There, [he offered] to Prajāpati and Indra, to Soma and Varuṇa, to Vivasvat,
to Kubera, to Suṣeṇa, and to Hiraṇyaretas.
To the Ādityas, as well as to the Aśvins, to the Rudras together with the Vasus,
and to Viṣṇu, the Viśvedevas, and the Sādhyas along with Varuṇa.
One should offer the first oblation with the utterance of "svāhā" into the fire;
then, a single oblation should be offered to all the deities beginning with Prajāpati and ending with Rudra.
Thus says Rūpanārāyaṇa:
[this applies] to the Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and the hosts of lunar mansions and stars;
to the serpents headed by Vāsuki; and to the deities of the full-moon days and the rivers.
One should offer oblations with the exclamation "svāhā" to the lords of the ocean-dwellers.
"svāhā to the other gods"—with these words, he offers three oblations.
He should constantly employ musical instruments and singing in the stables for the mounts.
And having passed seven days, on the eighth day one should cause [the image] to be bathed with compassion.
Having offered the *bali* oblation to Varuṇa, one should subsequently immerse [the image] with water;
"on the eighth" means on the second, the eighth, and so forth, up to the ninth lunar day (*tithi*).
Then, on the ninth day of the bright fortnight, having gone outside the city; the meaning is that this occurs on the tenth day, after the ninth has passed.
And so says King Bhoja:

"The king should, in due order, arrange for a long festival procession and the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the welfare of both the young and the old on the eighth day and subsequent days of the month of Āśvayuja."
In the north-eastern direction, in a pure place sloping toward the east,
one should erect there an archway ten cubits high.
It was declared to be eight *iṣṭas* in width, adorned with banners and arches; then, having bathed in pure water, the mounts were bathed according to the daily rites,
amidst the sounds of the proclamation of merit, the chanting of the Vedas, and the resonance of songs and musical instruments.
Well-adorned and being praised by bards, panegyrists, and celestial musicians,
they were escorted by men with swords in hand and by those who subsist on horses.
Being protected by those very [guards] there, near the archway,
the domestic priest offered oblations into the fire at the southern corner of the pillar.
Eight men, free from physical defects and equipped with torches in their hands,
should ignite the torches by means of that exchange of fire.
Having sprinkled the royal horse with the remainder of the oblation (havis), he should satisfy it;
"he should satisfy" means that he should offer a sacrificial ball (piṇḍa) to the steed with the remainder of the cooked rice (caru).
May the King of Horses and Viṣṇu stand as your priest before you; may he who holds the noose of Varuṇa in his hand stand behind you and protect you from the rear.
May Vaivasvata and Kubera protect [him] on both sides;
may the Moon and the Sun protect the backbone, and the Mountain that supports the earth protect the navel.
O Gandharva, protect the sacrificial offering; Indra gives it to you.
Having bound Bali, destroy him entirely for the sake of the king’s victory.
Having also consumed the *taṇu* [oblation], the enemy of Pūru, Jāmbava,
should place this ear-ornament upon his ear.
Born of a noble lineage and distinguished by auspicious marks and characteristics, may you protect your husband; welfare shall be yours. O best of horses, forgive me for this punishment of the whip.
Thus addressed, the horse, resounded with the chanting of the Veda, [proceeded].
Then, being sprinkled with water poured from kusha grass and consecrated by mantras,
the king, together with his ministers, [should enter] through the middle of the archway.
Having proclaimed this, he should proceed with horses that have been groomed and followed by attendants;
all these rites, especially those pertaining to the month of Āśvayuja, should be performed.
Thus ends the ritual for the pacification of horses as taught by Śālihotra and composed by Rūpanārāyaṇa.
Now, regarding the pacification ritual in the *Madanaratneśvara*:
when portents or omens appear, or when horses fall ill,
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) there on the northern side of the horse-stable.
Having fasted there for three nights, the domestic priest (purohita) should perform a rite of pacification (śānti);
he should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) covered with new garments and having four corners.
Four water-jars should be placed in the four directions,
along with as many vessels of flavorful liquids as there are full jars among them.
With a concentrated mind, one should offer oblations of clarified butter into the fire for Pitāmaha, Rudra, Skanda, and Varuṇa.
With a concentrated mind, one should offer oblations of clarified butter every day to Pitāmaha,
Rudra, Skanda, and Varuṇa.
And likewise to the two Aśvins, to Śarva, to Śakra, and to Agni;
to Vāyu, to the two Haris, and also to the goddess Śrī.
The *Soma*, *Ucchaiḥśravas*, and others belong to the *Gandharvas*;
in that case, she becomes the cause of a portent for the deity.
Having recognized the mandala, one should then worship the bali offering;
having performed one hundred and eight oblations for each deity, one who is well-disposed should proceed day by day.
Then one should perform worship, especially of the deities,
with milk-rice, cakes, lamps, incense, garlands, and ointments.
The Brahmins should be fed with honeyed milk-rice (madhupāyasa) along with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā),
dedicating the offering to each deity individually, whether it be ten, seven, or five times.
Gold, sandalwood, garments,
cows, and bell-metal should then be accepted as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the sake of atonement by the king for three nights.
And the priest should worship all [the deities] with benedictions recited by the best of the twice-born;
for this rite bestows peace and destroys all calamities.
This merit grants victory to the king and increases his wealth and grain.
Thus ends the peace ritual from the Madanaratneśa.
In the *Madanaratna* and the *Gāruḍa*:
"Now, a king should perform a fourfold propitiatory rite for elephants and horses afflicted by the *māyā* [planetary] influence when its rising occurs."
When one does not take up a blanket and lets go of the earthenware vessel at that time,
one is then afflicted by diseases arising from that [negligence].
Then one should perform a propitiatory rite for the elephants and likewise for the horses;
for the sake of the peace of the elephants and horses, a square pavilion should be constructed.
One should cause it to be made extended according to the measure of twelve *aratnis*;
one should construct a fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) with three ridges, either circular or square.
To the east, south, west, and north of that,
one should then construct a quadrangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit in size.
Likewise, in the corners, one should fashion a circle, a semicircle, and a triangle;
[these should be made] from *arka*, *khadira*, *pālāśa*, *bilva*, *aśvattha*, and *vaṭa* wood.
Audumbara and Apāmārga wood are the best fuel-sticks for that [rite];
alternatively, one may use all kinds of fuel-sticks in the middle, or those made of Palāśa, Bilva, and Vajra wood.
With sesame, rice, parched grain, flour, white mustard, and śāla flowers,
as well as barley smeared with the three sweets— in the center, this is the established rule for all.
With curd, milk, ghee, and honey,
as well as with clarified butter in the corners, and in the center upon the water-pot (kalaśa).
Then, one should place eight jars in the eight directions,
covered with pairs of cloths and provided with mustard seeds and medicinal herbs.
Then, having prepared four jars filled with all the auspicious substances and mixed with perfumes, flowers, and water, he should place them there equally in the four directions.
One should place water-pots filled with water, cloth, and other offerings in the corners;
and in the principal pot, one should meditate upon Hari in the form of Narasiṃha.
The conch, discus, mace, lotus, shield, sword, arrow,
and spear should also be placed in the pitchers, following the sequence starting from the east.
Outside, one should worship the guardians of the directions, such as Śakra and the others;
and there, in front of the principal pitcher, one should prepare a circular maṇḍala.
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods there, one should subsequently perform the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites;
likewise, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) may be at the front of the water-pool, or at the front of the pitcher, or even within the pit itself.
In all these cases, one should perform the consecration of Nala according to the rites prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra;
for the sake of perfecting the fire, one should offer a thousand oblations of clarified butter with the mantra.
Having offered oblations of fuel-sticks and clarified butter according to the prescribed form, the practitioner, being composed in mind,
should perform a hundred thousand oblations of clarified butter by means of the *sampāta* method.
Then, having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* and subsequent rites according to the rules,
he should touch the water-pot and recite the mantra ten thousand times.
Having touched the pitcher in the east, one should recite [the mantra] there one thousand times;
in the subsequent pitchers, one should recite with the Gāyatrī or with the Praṇava.
There, the officiating priests (ṛtvij) should simultaneously perform the oblation (homa) as previously described;
and touching each jar, he should recite [the mantra] one thousand times.
One should worship the world-protectors and the others with perfumes and other offerings without weariness;
then the king should duly consecrate Nṛsiṃha and the others in their proper order.
One should consecrate [the king] with the water from the pitcher before the deity while reciting that mantra;
likewise, one should surround him with jars and with royal vehicles such as elephants and the like.
With the remaining water, the wise man, being fully composed, should cause all other mounts and elephants to be bathed.
There, the practitioner should bathe [the deity] with water from an external pitcher;
the knower of mantras should perform the lustration (nīrājana) of the king and the mounts.
Having given abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests (ṛtvij), the king should present garments, vehicles, land, and other such items to his preceptor (ācārya).
The preceptor himself should cause the king to lie down in the royal palace;
having previously bathed with water from a jar by Vasiṣṭha, he, being a knower of mantras, [performs the rite].
Having sprinkled water upon the elephant stable and likewise the horse stable,
he should scatter white mustard seeds, rice, sesame seeds, and flowers over them.
Then, having entered the middle of the hall and offered an image of Nṛsiṃha and the Sudarśana discus to the preceptor,
the guru, and having given a cow, one should perform worship.

just as armor serves as a defense against the streams of weapons.

Any other person who is made of clay, even if they are entirely young and foolish.
