Then, up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings,
one should perform the ritual completion of the *avadāna* with the ten verses beginning with "anobhadrāḥ kratavaḥ."
With the verse beginning "imaṃ stomaṃ marhate," with sixteen verses starting with "jātavedase," and likewise with the verse beginning "ṛcā," he then offers the iṣṭakṛt oblation.
Then, having completed the remainder of the *homa*, one should feed the Brahmins;
after the twice-born have pronounced the benediction (*svasti*), one should offer them food and give a cow as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Thus is the *āyuṣya-homa*.

[The mantra: "May he who extracted the life-force (*āyus*) from the hymn, who extracted the sacred word (*brahman*) from the priests, the one clad in skins, the wielder of the *pināka* bow—the Lord (*Īśāna*), the God—grant us long life. To him I offer here oblation with ghee; *svāhā*! This is for Īśāna."

Shining from the midst of the body, radiant with the luster of the sun, the god has come here for the sake of life, having driven away the terrible noose of death and the curse; may he, the consumer of ghee, accept this offering of ghee. To the one of solar radiance, this!

The great light, the embryo which the consort of Brahman conceived—the many-formed, victorious, golden one, the sun, the object of worship—let us honor him; we increase his life-span with clarified butter. This [is for] the light of Brahman.

We invoke Śrī, Lakṣmī, Maupālā, Ambikā, Gā, Ṣaṣṭhī, Jayā, and Indrasenā; we satisfy that Vidyā, whose source is Brahman and who is of like form, with clarified butter for the sake of long life—this [offering] is for those whose source is Brahman.

The daughters of Dakṣa, belonging to all wombs, belonging to their own womb, by the thousands, of universal form and of various forms—along with their sons, along with their husbands, along with their troops—may they, the life-sustaining ones, enjoy this clarified butter; [this is] for the daughters of Dakṣa.

May the divine hosts, many-formed and ancient, who cut short the life-span, the heroes, wake up from their slumber. To them I offer oblations in many ways with clarified butter; do not harm our offspring nor our heroes—this [is for] the Dākṣāyaṇīs.

He who alone was here in the beginning, from whom the protector of the world arose—he to whom all this world returns at the final transition—may that God, who is well-established, grant us prosperity. This [is] for Īśāna, for Brahman.

Having offered clarified butter for the sake of long life, we perpetually magnify the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Maruts, Sādhyas, the Bhūts, the Nakṣatras, Gandharvas, Pitṛs, Viśvedevas, Bhṛgus, Sarpas, and all the Aṅgirases—this [is] for the Vasus and the others.
O Viṣṇu, grant us your closest protection and your conquering shelter. Your streams, dripping with sweetness, draw forth an inexhaustible spring—this [is offered] to Viṣṇu.
Thus ends this single oblation.

Every month, every year, or on the anniversary of one's birth, on the new moon day (kuhū), on Saturdays, during the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign (saṃkramaṇa), during lunar or solar eclipses, and so forth; or when there is a conjunction with one's birth asterism (janmanakṣatra) or during affliction by fever and other major diseases—one should perform the Āyuṣya-homa for the purpose of averting untimely death (apamṛtyu).

The formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is as follows: "Preceded by the worship of Vighneśvara, I shall perform the *āyuṣya-homa* for the purpose of removing the defect of [limited] lifespan. In the case of employing a preceptor (*ācārya*), one should choose the preceptor with the words: "I choose you as my preceptor to perform the rite known as the *āyuṣya-homa* for the purpose of averting the affliction of such-and-such [person]. Having thus chosen the preceptor, the preceptor [should say]: "I choose you as my preceptor to perform the rite for the purpose of removing the defect of such-and-such person, who was born under such-and-such asterism, in such-and-such zodiac sign, and is named such-and-such Śarman. Having thus chosen the preceptor...

The preceptor, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of removing the defects of short lifespan for [Name] Śarman, born under such-and-such constellation and in such-and-such zodiac sign, I shall perform the rite known as the *āyuṣya-homa*," and having performed the drawing of the lines for the sacrifice to the gods and the installation of the fire up to the pouring of the *praṇītā* water, he should prepare a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with rice grains in the northeast portion of the fire. Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus upon it, he should place upon it a vessel filled with water from a holy bathing place (*puṇyatīrtha*) scented with musk, saffron, and the like, along with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the five sprouts (*pañcapallava*).

Having placed a decorated jar together with a pair of coconut cloths, and having placed within it an image of the deity Mṛtyuñjaya fashioned from one karṣa of gold and purified with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other means, one should invoke the deity Mṛtyuñjaya with the mantra "Tryambakam," worship him with all ritual offerings (upacāras), and then cook the Prāṇa-caru and Āyuṣmat-caru individually according to the rules of sacrificial offering (nirvāpaṇa). Having sprinkled clarified butter over them and moved them [from the fire] toward the east or north, one should establish them.

Having performed the rites beginning with the *mabhighā* (sprinkling) and *brahmajya* (preparation by the Brahman priest), up to the end of the *agnimukha* (oblation to Agni), he should take portions from the *āyuṣmat-caru* according to the rule for portions (*avadāna-dharma*). Having recited the *puronuvākyā*: "O Viśvāvasu, enter into us," and having offered with the *yājyā*: "Agni, giver of life," he takes a portion for the *sviṣṭakṛt*. Then, having placed the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) to the south, he chooses eight, six, or four Brahmins. With them, using the eight *ghṛtasūkta* hymns beginning with "yo brahmā" and so forth, he offers one thousand and eight oblations of clarified butter (*ājya-huti*). In the final round, he recites: "viṣṭotvanno antama."

Having thus spoken, he who offers one thousand and eight oblations of clarified butter with the *Ghṛtasūktas* beginning with "Brāhmaṇam" and so forth, and having offered the final verse "vi ṣṭvā no antamaḥ," pours the remainder of the clarified butter from each oblation, accompanied by the exclamation *svāhā*, as a *saṃpāta* into the *prāṇacarū*. [He says: "May the death of such-and-such a person perish; may his lifespan increase. Having thus offered "vi ṣṭvā no antamaḥ," he pours the remainder of the clarified butter from each oblation, accompanied by the exclamation *svāhā*, as a *saṃpāta* into the *prāṇacarū*. [He says: "May the death of such-and-such a person perish..."

One should offer oblations with each mantra using the *vyāhṛtis* both individually and collectively, increasing the number by one for each; then, having offered to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with the mantra "havyavāham," and having completed the remainder of the ritual procedure beginning with the *jaya*-oblations, one should perform worship again upon the water-pot (*kuṃbha*), dismiss the deity, sprinkle with water using mantras dedicated to Varuṇa and those containing the word "water" (*abbliṅga*), and pour out the remnants of the sacrificial food outside the sacrificial enclosure to the east of the fire, over *dūrvā* grass and unhusked rice (*akṣata*), saying "namo astu nīlagrīvāya" (salutation to the blue-necked one) as an offering to Rudra, and then pour out more water with unhusked rice over that as before.

Having offered the cooked rice mixed with the life-force (saṃpātita-prāṇa-caru) while reciting "yad asya pūrvam" and so forth, he should consume it together with his family; then, having sipped water (ācamya), he should touch his belly while reciting the two verses beginning with "yata indra svasti dāḥ. Then, having given a water-pot, a garment, an image, and other items to the preceptor (ācārya), and having given sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests (ṛtvij), he should offer sesame seeds and black eggs according to the degree of the fault, for the purpose of warding off untimely death (apamṛtyu).

The venerable Bodhāyana has stated that one should give gifts such as woolen blankets and black wool, perform extensive offerings, and feed the Brahmins. Some, having offered the oblation for the gift of the long-lived preceptor (*āyuṣmac-ācārya*), perform the secondary oblations (*upahoma*) with the verses beginning "O Brahman" (*yo brahmā*) using that same food, fuel-sticks, and clarified butter; the remainder is the same.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the longevity-oblation (*āyuṣya-homa*).

Now, regarding the ritual procedure for pacifying untimely death (*apamṛtyu-śāntividhāna*), known as the *Mṛtyuñjaya-vidhāna*: it is extremely necessary to perform this when one has fallen victim to untimely death, or when afflicted by the onset of diseases for a long duration. It is a means for attaining welfare and the prevention of untimely death.
Regarding the prevention of untimely death, Bodhāyana states in the *Madanaratna*:

Now we shall explain the ritual procedure for Mṛtyuñjaya (the Conqueror of Death). On one's birth star or on an auspicious lunar mansion, having satisfied three Brahmins with food to ward off rebirth, and having caused them to pronounce "Auspicious Day," "Welfare," and "Success," one performs the rites beginning with the drawing of the lines for the sacrificial ground for the gods and ending with the "mouth of the fire" (the invocation of Agni). One offers oblations of cooked barley-grains with the Sāvitrī mantra. Taking fuel-sticks of Tisra, Dūrvā grass, and Udumbara wood, each a span in length, one offers eight thousand or eight hundred of them. Having mixed together curd, honey, ghee, and milk, and having anointed the sticks with this mixture, one places them [into the fire].
May death depart far away; may I not be subject to pride; [may there be] protection for my offspring; [I praise] Tryambaka.
"These thousand," he says, and then he offers oblations of clarified butter: "May death perish; may life increase; may there be well-being, svāhā!"
O Death, perish; may life increase—Bhuvaḥ Svāhā! O Death, perish; may life increase—Bhuvaḥ Svāhā! O Death, perish; may life increase—Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ Svāhā!

Thus, from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, the rite is established up to the granting of the boon to the cow. Then, to the south of the fire, he places an offering of the remnants of the oblation upon a clump of *dūrvā* grass with the verse, "I choose that which is most auspicious for us. Then he gives a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), consisting of a cow, a bull, an ox, a horse, gold, or bell-metal; so says Ābhodāyana.
Now the procedure:

Having honored eight, four, or two Brahmins and caused them to pronounce the *puṇyāha* (day of merit), having established the *saṃkalpa-agni* (the fire of the ritual resolve) and performed the pouring out of the oblation (*nirvāpaṇa*) and so forth, one should cook the *caru* with the *Sāvitrī* mantra. At the conclusion of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, taking a portion of the *caru*, one recites the *Sāvitrī* and offers it immediately. Then, having offered six portions taken in six ladlings of clarified butter mixed with three types of *dūrvā* grass and cow’s curd, using the six verses beginning with "apaitu mṛtyuḥ," at the end of the dismissal of the *brahmā*, one pours water containing *kṣata* (barley) onto a clump of *dūrvā* grass in front of the fire, and offers a *bali* with the remainder of the oblation while reciting "tac chaṃyoḥ."
Having offered water with unbroken grains (akṣata) and poured it out, and having worshipped the fire and paid homage to the Sun, he should feed the Brahmins.
Thus, regarding one's own agency— according to the view of the teacher— the planet sacrifice (grahayajña) should be performed by the sick for three days;
it should be performed every day as long as the disease of the planets persists until its cessation.

Now, regarding the Homas of the Great Mṛtyuñjaya, Durvā, and Guḍūcī: we shall now explain the Great Mṛtyuñjaya Homa—one should perform it during illness, sorcery, chronic disease, affliction by planetary influences, when facing death, during a great malady, or in times of great calamity; also during the eclipses of the moon or sun, at one’s birth star (janmanakṣatra), during the poison-veins (viṣanāḍī), or in the Kuhū conjunction, or for the sake of averting other great diseases. Desiring long life, one should perform it month by month on one's birth star at the prescribed times, or once a year, either through a preceptor or by oneself.

Having bathed, caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, and performed breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "Desiring long life for [the patron] named So-and-so Śarman, I shall perform the Mahāmṛtyuñjaya Homa. Then, at the time of preparing the vessels for the kindling of the fire, one should place down three blades of *dūrvā* grass, six *śatapatra* flowers, and thirty-six pieces of *dadhi* (curd).

Having seated a Brāhmaṇa to the south upon Darbha grass, [the sacrificer] places pieces of jaggery measuring four finger-breadths. Having silently threshed rice grains, having washed them, and having prepared the clarified butter, he performs the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circling with fire) together with the *caru*. Having prepared the *sruva* and *sruk* ladles by wiping them, and having performed the *paryagnikaraṇa* together with the *caru*, he performs the wiping of the *sruva* and *sruk* ladles; then, for one who follows the five-fold division (*pañcāvattin*), the oblation is to be sprinkled with clarified butter.

Having recited the *puronuvākyā*, "May Śacīpati depart from here toward death," he offers with the *yājyā*, "O Death, go away to the far distance; leave our heroes behind," while making the renunciation (*tyāga*) with the words, "To Death, svāhā! Having spread an underlayer of clarified butter from the eastern part and having taken the portions, he recites the *puronuvākyā*, "Stride out, O Tawny One, as you carry away the tawny one," and offers with the *yājyā*, "Do not cut us off from the world of the living," while making the renunciation with the word "svāhā" for both [the *puronuvākyā* and the *yājyā*]. He cuts the portions as before. He then offers with clarified butter and the *mahāvyāhṛtis*.

Having offered five oblations with the five [mantras] beginning with "Bhūr agnaye pṛthivyai ca mahate ca svāhā," he then offers three blades of *dūrvā* grass with [the mantras]: "May death depart; immortality has come to us. O Death, go away by another path, leaving behind the heroes, svāhā! May I attain the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and long life, svāhā! May there be existence in the world beyond, and may we be united with those who have attained glory through their powers, svāhā! With the *śalā* [grass], to Agni, to the Great One, svāhā! Taking up the golden [blades], stride forth with valor, svāhā! This is for the gods."

"Do not strike me, do not kill me; spare me, Svāhā! To Rudra, this [offering]. "O Prajāpati, you [are] the lord of riches, Svāhā! "From whatever we fear, O Indra, destroy it, Svāhā! "The giver of well-being, the creator of fearlessness, Svāhā! "To Tryambaka—may he not abandon me, Svāhā! "Against untimely death—the thousandfold [protection], Svāhā! "To that [deity], from the waters, Svāhā! "To that [deity], Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ, Svāhā! With these twenty-one mantras, one should offer oblations in sixteen rounds.

There are three hundred and thirty-six oblations. Then, with clarified butter (ājya), one should offer twenty-one mantras for each of eight rounds; there are one hundred and sixty-eight oblations. Again, with this same [mantra], one offers twenty-one mantras for sixteen rounds of guḍūcī; there are three hundred and thirty-six oblations. Furthermore, with this same sequence, one should offer guḍūcī verse by verse using twenty-one mantras.

Having again offered oblations with the Mahāvyāhṛtis, he then takes a portion for the Sviṣṭakṛt sacrifice and offers the Sviṣṭakṛt oblation with the mantra: "We invoke Havyavāha, the subduer of enemies; O Agni, may this be well-offered; [may there be] long life, Svāhā! Then, having offered the Jaya and other oblations, and immediately thereafter having performed the anointing of the enclosing sticks (paridhi), and having completed the rites from the silent recitation (japa) up to the final sprinkling (pariṣecana), he places the remnants of the offering upon the wooden posts to the east of the fire with the two mantras: "May everything be Rudra; let it be equal to that Rudra" and "May all beings be [favorable]. He should thus make the offering.

"O Agni, giver of life, may you protect this one; Svāhā!"—with these words, he places a fuel-stick (*samidh*) into the fire. Having performed the ritual salutation (*upasthāna*) with the verse "To Jātavedas, who moves by day... and so forth, he offers the remainder of the oblation and the remainder of the clarified butter (*ājya*) while reciting the five verses beginning with "Agni is long-lived. Then, having consecrated all the remaining *caru* with the twenty-one verses beginning with "Agni is long-lived" and "Thou art life, thou art all-life... may I attain," he consumes it. Having sipped water (*ācamana*), he touches his stomach while reciting the same twenty-one verses beginning with "Thou art life, thou art all-life... may I attain."

Having consumed the remainder of all the sacrificial offerings (caru) and sipped water for purification, he touches his belly with the two verses beginning with "yata indra svasti-dāḥ. Having given a choice gift to the Guru, having gazed at the clarified butter (ājya) with the mantra "rūpaṃ-rūpam," and having offered the clarified butter, he shall give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests (ṛtvij) and to the Brāhmaṇas, and then feed the Brāhmaṇas with cakes, clarified butter, and milk-rice (pāyasa). By doing this, one becomes possessed of long life; by performing ten thousand oblations (ayuta-homa), one becomes long-lived; by performing one hundred thousand oblations (lakṣa-homa), one becomes a thousand-year-lived. Thus ends the Mṛtyuñjaya-śānti as taught by Baudhāyana.

In this consecrated fire (*anvāhita-agni*), beginning with the *samidh* for Jātavedas and ending with "with clarified butter (*ājya*) in the eye," the principal offerings here are as follows: [offerings] twice to Mṛtyu, and with *rudravya* (the Rudra-material) to Agni, to Pṛthivī, to Mahat; to Vāyu, to Antarikṣa, to Mahat; to Āditya, to Dyau, to Mahat; to Candramas, to Dyau, to Nakṣatras, to Mahat; and to the Devas, Pitṛs, Bhūḥ, and so forth, with clarified butter. Furthermore, the principal offerings here are to Vaivasvata, Śacīpati, the Aśvins, Agni, Hari, Mṛtyu, Rudra (twice), and Prajāpati.

[One should worship] Indra the Maghavan; Indra the bestower of fearlessness; Tryambaka; Agni Mṛtyu; Jātavedas Agni; Jātavedas Pāvaka; Vaiśvānara Vaidyuta Agni; Vāyu; Sūrya; and Prajāpati—each with their respective verses. [This is done] with sixteen offerings of pieces of *guḍūcī* combined with three types of *dūrvā*.

Having offered those same verses verse by verse eight times with clarified butter (*ājya*), again those same [verses] verse by verse sixteen times with pieces of *guḍūcī*, and again those same [verses] verse by verse eight times with clarified butter—herein the principal offerings are: Agni for the greatness of the earth; Vāyu for the greatness of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*); Āditya for the greatness of heaven (*dyu*); Candramas for the greatness of the stars and so forth; and the gods, the ancestors, the earth, and so forth, with the remainder of the clarified butter. With the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, using the binding-cord of the sacrificial wood (*idhma-sannahana*), one offers to Rudra, Jaya, and the others.
Thus, in the Āyuṣya-homa, there is the propitiation of Guḍūcī.
In the *Ṛgvidhāna*:

"One who is overcome by a disease that is fierce and life-threatening should fast on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight and offer a sacrificial oblation (*caru*) with the *raudra* hymn, remaining pure and restrained in speech, reciting it verse by verse. Having first offered oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*), he should then place [the vessel] before Śaṅkara. He should subsist on the remnants of the oblation in solitude and remain vigilant. When the month is complete, he shall conquer death and be liberated from diseases. In that same work: "A twice-born man should worship King Yama with the [Yama] hymn."

One should prepare a *sthālīpāka* offering for the two fortnights dedicated to Yama; on the eighth and fourteenth days, one should sacrifice with an oblation while employing the hymn and mantra beginning with "pareyuvāṃ saṃgama."

Now, if there is no increase in lifespan through easy means, I do not know the remedy for one who fears death before their time has come. Nevertheless, having reflected upon the scriptures, I shall declare a peace that brings happiness: one should offer oblations with the mantra of the hymn dear to Dharmarāja; this rite should be performed regularly on the full moon day of Vaiśākha.

In that very place it is said: "A twice-born man, eating with moderation, eating what is available, always spreading his own seat, and always sweeping it, should utter the *paramamṛtyu* mantra while muttering [it] as if facing death itself."

One does not die before one's allotted lifespan; therefore, O son, do not lead [your] progeny [to ruin]. One who subsists on fruits, who is self-controlled, and who observes moderation in food, may conquer death within three years. Or, as it is said in that very same [text]: If one considers some dear friend to have reached the end of their life, one should bathe well and strike the head of that person with a blade of *kuśa* grass while reciting the mantra "yatteyaṃ" five thousand times over five days; thus he shall obtain long life. Furthermore, one should anoint him with ghee using the *Sindhu-dvīpa-sūkta*. He should lie down upon his bed every day and constantly recite this mantra.

One living in the household should always employ this [mantra] with the thought, "I live. By anointing one's limbs with flowing water, one becomes happy and free from fever. Other matters, such as the worship of Lakṣmī and the King (Lakṣapārthiva), performed for my sake, are to be understood from my previous work, the *Kamalākara*. Likewise, the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with sesame oil according to the *Rudra* rite also wards off untimely death; we shall explain the procedure for the *Rudra* rite hereafter.
Thus ends the prevention of untimely death.
Now follows the removal of drought and the pacification of drought. In the *Ṛgvidhāna*:

"One desiring rain should employ the hymn beginning with 'athāva' (RV 5.53). Wearing wet clothes and carrying a vessel for water, he causes it to rain. Having offered ten thousand oblations of cane-wood sticks smeared with milk into the fire, he obtains a great rain by means of this hymn during the rainy season. In that same work: "Having plunged into water up to the navel, facing east, self-restrained and pure, one should worship the Sun with the two hymns known as the *Trivṛt*. This refers to the three utterances beginning with 'parjanya ehi' (RV 5.83.1–3)."

One who desires rain should diligently recite [the mantra] while fasting; after five nights have passed, he shall obtain a great downpour. In that same context: "One desiring rain, with his diet restrained, should take refuge in Bṛhaspati, accompanied by an offering of milk-rice (pāyasa) and oblations. Having recited 'O Bṛhaspati,' one seeking rain should employ [this rite]; and having paid homage to Parjanya, he obtains auspicious rain."

Thus says Ānāvṛṭi Vaikhāyana: We shall explain the rain when Parjanya has not given rain. Having first honored Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas, having worshipped Varuṇa-pratighā, and standing in water while meditating on Varuṇa, one recites the five verses beginning with "tatsavitur," the *ṛk* for the offering of oblations, and the introductory mantras of the Vedas. One recites the five verses beginning with "mamme varuṇa," the six verses beginning with "uduttamam," the two verses beginning with "yadanti" and "yaccha," the verse beginning with "udāyuṣā," the verse beginning with "mahaṅg indra," the verse beginning with "oya ojasā," the verse beginning with "vācam indriyāṇi," the ten verses beginning with "vānas tadam," the verse addressed to Mitra-Varuṇa, the verse addressed to Sārī, and [verses] to Varuṇa, Prajāpati, and Varuṇa.

Having recited the two sections beginning with *vāyurveta*, the two golden-hued ones (*dve hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*), *pavamāno vṛṣāsaḥ*, *āgṃśuḥ*, *sindhujaḥ*, *sauyopaḥ*, *sūdi*, and all the sections from *suvarṇam* and *sahasraśīrṣādbhyaḥ* up to *ādityo vai pṛthivī sam*, one should go out from the water, face the east, and mutter eleven times the section beginning with *pīvonnām*. Then, having muttered the four sections beginning with *punarmārutaṃ asi*, [one recites] *ehi parjanya*.

One should loudly recite the mantra: "ehivaruṇa—come, O Lord of Waters! Produce the eastern wind, produce it! Calm the western wind, calm it! May Parjanya immediately bestow good rain! with a loud voice.

The illustrious son of Nibhaṇḍaka [instructed] Ṛṣyaśṛṅga: "To Yaśmakeśa, one should offer the two-fold Maitrāvaruṇī oblation; one should chant the four Anuvākas beginning with 'māruta masi'; for Parjanya, one should chant the Pragātha; it is the bestower of rain. Having cast away the [old] garments and donned white clothes, one should make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), saying: 'I shall perform the Parjanya-homa. Then, according to the ritual rules, having established the fire, one should offer oblations twenty times with the verse beginning 'purovāto varṣan'. Thus spoke the Sage.

The renunciation [of the offering] is with the dedication "To Vāta. Then, having offered the *jayā*-oblations and the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should recite the peace-chant (*śāntipāṭha*). A statue of Varuṇa is given to the preceptor (*ācārya*), and sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); such is the general procedure for Parjanya.
Thus ends the Parjanya-śānti.
Now, the general rule for the mantras employed in the *Ṛgvidhāna* is stated in that very same work: "Furthermore,
the recitation of the Vedic *caraṇa* at the beginning brings about the successful accomplishment of rituals."
Having had his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved off, he bathes and becomes pure.
One should remain standing during the night, pure, silent, and restrained;
speaking only the truth, one should then recite purificatory mantras and the Vyāhṛtis.
Having recited hymns beginning with the syllable *oṃ*, as well as the *Sāvitrī*, the verse *tat savituḥ*,
the hymn *apohiṣṭhā*, the *Śuddhavatīs*, and the *Aghamarṣaṇī*.
The words *śaṃvatyaḥ*, *svastimantryaḥ*, and likewise *pāpamānaḥ* should be employed everywhere at the beginning and at the end of ritual actions.
One should recite the *śamatha* mantra one thousand times, or one hundred times, or twenty-one times;
or else, ten thousand times the *oṃkāra*, the three *vyāhṛtis*, and the *sāvitrī*.
Likewise, one should satiate the preceptor, the *ṛṣis*, the *chandases*, and the deities with water offerings.
Saying "Prapadye," one should mutter the group of Raudra mantras dedicated to Virūpākṣa.
One should not speak with non-Aryans, nor with Śūdras, nor with those who are censured;
one should not travel in the same vehicle as non-Aryans, outcasts, or men of the lowest castes.
The king, accompanied by his ministers and teachers, should bathe three times a day;
at the end of twelve nights, he should prepare a *śrāddha* offering of cooked rice (*stālīpāka*).
One should offer oblations to Agni and Adhasoma with the third [verse],
and likewise to the Viśvedevas and Rudra in the north.
To the Lord of the End, likewise to Mamatā, and another to Dhanvantari;
and also [offerings] for the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
The tenth [verse] is addressed to Brāhmaṇaspati; it is remembered as being for the sake of the sacred formulation (brahman).
Sarasvatī is the offering for that [deity], and "Oṃ" is likewise the offering for the Sviṣṭakṛt.
First, having offered oblations of clarified butter, and then having again offered the sthālīpāka into the fire,
one should satisfy the Brahmins by making offerings into the fire and then present the portions to the ancestors.
Pure and restrained in speech, one should eat the remnants of the oblation according to the prescribed rule;
likewise, having performed the Prājāpatya-kṛcchra, as well as the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances.
With his self purified by these vows, he should perform his duties without sloth;
consequently, he attains all desired objects—of this there is no doubt.
Each of these—grains, oil-cake, and buttermilk—serves as a purifier.
Having thus purified his actions, he should perform the rites with mantras as follows:
first, for all rituals, one should fast for three nights.
One should not perform the three nocturnal acts; thereafter, one should commence the ritual action.
Likewise—
Śaunaka says that one should always give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) or a gift that bestows success; for there is no ritual act whatsoever that is without a fee.
One should understand that this is commensurate with one's capacity or a full vessel;
one should give ten bulls, by which the Guru is satisfied.
Thus ends the procedure for the mantra-sādhana as stated in the *Ṛgvidhāna*.
Now follows the procedure for the *Śrīsūkta* according to the *Ṛgvidhāna*:
In the *Ṛgvidhāna*:
He who desires the goddess Śrī, the giver of boons, who is eternally established within his lineage,
should, having become pure and restrained in three ways, offer clarified butter (ājya) daily.
One desiring prosperity should constantly recite the fifteen-verse hymn of Śrī.
One should invoke Śrī into a lotus or even into golden [images] with five [verses].
One should prepare white foods, both primary and secondary offerings, as well as milk,
curd, and a pot-cooked meal of śāli rice with milk.
One should quickly undertake the Cāndrāyaṇa vow with self-restraint;
having bathed in waters containing all medicinal herbs and their essences, as well as purifying substances.
"May I approach as a friend of the gods"—with these words is the consecration for a king;
"As one who desires the mind"—with these words is the consecration for one desiring cattle.
One who desires offspring, being pure and observant of vows, should bathe with the verse beginning "kardamena.
One who desires sovereignty, being pure and observant of vows, should bathe with the verse beginning "aśvapūrvām."
A Brāhmaṇa should bathe on a red hide according to the prescribed rule;
a Kṣatriya king on a tiger skin, and likewise a Vaiśya on a ruru deer skin.
Immediately thereafter, the Vaiśya should perform the oblation upon a hide of a goat;
the twice-born man should offer lotuses as numerous as the moon, accompanied by clarified butter.
By this verse beginning with "ādityavarṇa," the offering of wood-apple (bilva) is prescribed;
the fire itself should be situated within the wood-apple tree, and the twice-born man should offer the cooked oblation (sthālīpāka) therein.
The first rite for one desiring prosperity is the oblation of ten thousand [offerings];
having duly offered a million, one shall obtain infinite prosperity.
By reciting it one hundred thousand times, one attains prosperity;
indeed, one finds eternal and infinite prosperity that is ever-present within the heart.
Reciting this very mantra ten thousand times without attachment is superior; having properly recited it ten million times, one attains infinite prosperity.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, one attains prosperity;
O Keśinī, one should daily offer ten thousand lotuses as oblations.
Having seen that splendor, the twice-born man indeed became indifferent due to his lack of desire;
he ate bilva fruits, dwelt in a bilva tree, and [offered] pure bilva fruits with clarified butter.
Within twenty-one nights, one attains supreme accomplishment;
likewise, Satyakāma obtained lotuses and even wood-apples.
In this regard, regarding the Viṣṇudharmas, Puṣkara said:
"O twice-born one, the fifteen verses beginning with 'hiraṇyavarṇām' which carry away [all sins] are called the Śrīsūkta; it is meritorious and increases prosperity, as declared in the Ṛgveda."
Regarding the chariot, the horses, and the spoils of war, there are likewise four verses;
this hymn, which increases prosperity, is declared in the *Vajurveda*.
This *Śriyam-iti* Sāman is proclaimed in the Sāmaveda;
likewise, it is stated in the Atharvaveda as "O Śrī, give me prosperity."
The one who recites the Śrīsūkta with devotion finds that his misfortune perishes;
and he who knows the Dharma should especially offer oblations of sacrificial food (haviṣya).
O best of the Bhṛgus, that man who, endowed with devotion, performs ten thousand oblations of lotuses smeared with ghee into the fire while reciting the Śrīsūkta;
Lakṣmī, with two lotuses in her hands, attends upon him who worships;
likewise, he who offers oblations of ten thousand lotuses into the water [attains the same].
Fortune does not depart from his family, just as the fortune residing on the chest of Viṣṇu never leaves him;
likewise, by offering ten thousand oblations of bilva fruits smeared with ghee to Rāma,
one obtains wealth according to whatever one desires.
By performing a hundred thousand oblations of bilva fruits, one attains the prosperity of one's lineage;
one should likewise perform ten million oblations of lotuses or bilva fruits.
Having duly worshipped the boon-granting Goddess with white lotuses, or with flowers such as these, one certainly attains Satyaloka and even the status of Indra among the gods.
By means of milk, incenses, and offerings of rice-pudding (paramānna), one obtains prosperity and wealth in abundance.
Thus ends the ritual for the Śrīsūkta in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Then, at that very place, Puṣkara said to King Nīrajana: "In the north-eastern direction from the city, there is a most enchanting spot."
The king caused a vast and enchanting pavilion to be constructed.
Covered with mats, strewn with kusha grass, and adorned with banners and flags;
the triple archway was auspicious, decorated with weapons and the sound of conchs.
O best of the Bhṛgus, sixteen [units] should be marked out there;
therein the work should be performed according to the support on the southern side of the archway.
In the absence of an image of the deity, the rite of offering oblations into the fire should be performed there;
[the altar] should be made beautiful with a five-colored thread having a hundred knots.
At the middle archway, one should place a hundred nooses;
having covered it with *kuśa* grass, one should then joyfully cover it once more.
And every living being should strive to avoid leaping over it;
for as long as it has not been leaped over by the first royal elephant, [so long does its power remain].
When, having left Citrā, the Sun enters Svātī,
from that point onward the rite should be performed as long as the Sun remains in Svātī.
O best of the twice-born, every day the gods should be worshipped in the pavilion:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śambhu, Śakra, Soma, Anila, and Agni.
O highly fortunate one, [he addressed] Vināyaka, Kumāra, Varuṇa, Dhanada, Yama,
the Viśvedevas, and likewise Ucchaiḥśravas.
Eight great elephants are to be worshipped; hear their names:
Kumuda, Airāvata, Padma, Puṣpadanta, and Vāmana.
Supratīka, Janman, Nila, Etoṣṭva, and Devayoni—these are the lords of the constellations;
worship should be performed for them, as well as for the domestic asterisms and the city-protectors.
Then, with a concentrated mind, the priest should offer oblations into the fire with the mantras of the deities of the Vimata class, using those [mantras] designated by their respective signs.
And so it is said, O mighty-armed one: for those who lack the mantras, there are fuel-sticks from milky trees as well as white mustard seeds, [to be used] with the *praṇava*.
O performer of the sacrifice, having offered clarified butter, sesame seeds, and likewise unbroken grains (akṣata),
one should prepare water-pitchers filled with water and combined with grain.
On the western side of the archway, [one should place] bhallātaka, kali, siddhārtha, vacā, kuṣṭha, and priyaṅgu, using pitchers previously prepared.
Then, having bathed those most excellent elephants with waters purified by mantras,
he likewise adorned the highly fortunate horses that had been praised.
Then follows the consecration of the Nāga and likewise of that horse;
thereafter, the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) and food should be offered by the family priest Abhimanyu.
Upon the king’s rejoicing at this, his victory is proclaimed.
One should know that a great danger has already arisen for him;
therefore, first let out a roar from the gateway.
There too, first [one should worship] Rāma, the consecration, and the supreme elephant;
before that, an elephant or even a five-nailed beast should be brought.
If one should leap over it, one should predict the death of the king;
or if that elephant of a king should leap over it with his forefoot.
The queen, the domestic priest, the ministers, and the princes—
whenever it would be detrimental [to the state], they should utter the king’s name and then proceed with their attack.
He announces victory to the king;
they should all emerge from that [city] by crossing to the south, facing eastward with their elephants in battle array.
Then the horse, O highly fortunate one, and then the best of men;
then the parasol and the banner, as well as whatever other emblems of royalty there may be.
Having established them in the pavilion and other locations, one should worship them according to the rules;
those [lines] which have been made with five-colored threads are known as *patisarās*.
O Bhārgava, the domestic priest should fumigate with incense using the mantra "dhūrasi" and bind it upon all the king's elephants and horses.
The elephants, together with the horses, should be led to their own stables while the sun remains in the constellation Svāti, until they are situated in the shadows.
One should constantly worship [the royal insignia], neither reviling nor striking them;
one should always worship all the emblems of royalty within the temple.
Varuṇa and Bhūti,
the two priests for the year, lived constantly in the hermitage with their excellent attendants during the night.
They shall be preeminent as physicians for horses and likewise as the most excellent healers of elephants;
furthermore, they must remain consecrated and observe the vows of celibate students.
When the sun, having passed through Svāti, enters Viśākhā,
one should especially adorn the mounts in that forest.
O knower of dharma and knower of the proper time, one should consecrate with mantras the elephant, the horse, the parasol, the sword, the vehicle, the drum, the banner, and the flag.

In this regard, the mantras for the parasol and other items should be known: having consecrated them all with mantras, one who has mounted an elephant or a horse should then place a heap of firebrands and immediately set it ablaze.
The king, accompanied by his fourfold army and all his retinue, should perform circumambulations for three nights with a well-concentrated mind.
Having gone alone to his home, the king, preceded by his army,
should honor Janvā and then abandon everything else.
This rite of propitiation through the waving of lights (nīrājanā) brings peace as well as the increase of well-being.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, the King said: "O Lord, please explain to me the peace known as *ghṛtakaṃbaśala*."
Puṣkara said:
One should cause a sacrificial hall to be constructed in the north-eastern quarter;
the mantras for the consecration ceremony have been previously declared by me.
One should first arrange the stations for those beginning with the gods;
then, having fasted, one should perform the invocation and the ritual bath there.

He should perform the worship of the deities with all the requisite offerings such as perfumes and garlands for all those who have maintained the sacred fires, as well as for the minister and the domestic priest.
Having performed the worship in this manner, those three, while observing the fast,
should rise during the last third of the night and perform the propitiatory rite.
Having performed these tenfold rites there, one should bathe that foremost of men;
likewise, the preliminary bath should be performed with white mustard seeds as previously prescribed.
At this time, the knower of the proper occasion [should perform the rite] with a full jar of ghee while reciting the mantra:
"Clarified butter (ājya) is declared to be splendor (tejas), the supreme remover of all sins."

Clarified butter is the food of the gods; in clarified butter the worlds—whether of the earth, the atmosphere, or the heavens—are established. Whatever sin has come upon you, O wind, [may it be removed] by this clarified butter.
"May all that perish through contact with the clarified butter (ājya).
Then, O Virūpākṣa,
let him go to the front of the altar along with the lord of the chariot (Indra), preceded by the astrologer and the family priest."
The bathing altar should be constructed by the king, adorned with flowers and beautifully decorated in the intermediate directions with four full water-pots.
He should wear four skins, including the necks, which are equal and free from defects:
those of the leopard, the tiger, the lion, and likewise the panther.
O Rāma, one should place a *bhadrāsana* for those attendants;
there, upon a well-spread seat, one should cover the king with new cloths—
first with cotton ones, then with those from Avanti, and thereafter with those produced by insects (silk).
Then, one should consecrate him with all those jars filled [with water];
eight jars, or even twenty-eight, should be prepared.
Alternatively, O Rāma, there is this superior method of increasing their number by eight hundred;
then, on that altar, the family priest [places] the sacred threads and garments.
Filled with wrath, one should break an earthen vessel with a trident and cast the royal umbrella away;

thereafter, one should offer the king’s water-pot from one's own shoulder for a year. Then, the king’s consecration should be performed with mantras, using a well-honored, prepared, and sturdy vessel.
Then I bow to Jyotiṣmatī, Trāyamāṇā, Abhayā, Aparājitā, Jīvā, Viśveśvarī, Pārā, Namagā, and Abhayā.
One should place Sahā, Sahādevī, Pūrṇakośā, Vaśatāvarī, Ariṣṭikā, Śivā, and Bhadrā into the water-pot (kalaśa) there.
The *brāhmī* plant, the three types of *avakā*, all seeds, gold,
auspicious items as they may be available, juices of all medicinal herbs, gems, all fragrances, the *bilva* fruit, and the *vikaṅkata* tree.
Having likewise seen his own reflection in ghee or in a mirror,
and having performed the auspicious touching [of the limbs], he, wearing washed garments and composed in mind, [should proceed].
Then, having performed the individual worship of the gods and others separately,
one should subsequently offer oblations into the fire for them by means of their names in the dative case.
One who has a beneficial domestic priest should offer clarified butter preceded by the syllable *oṃ*.
Thereafter, the worship of the weapons and the worship of the mounts should be performed.
Having performed worship at midday and adorned one's own body,
one should apply an ointment consecrated with the mantra "Gantu dvāre."
"Bestow the wealth consisting of minerals"—this mantra should be used with a well-disposed mind;
likewise, the mantra "rāyaspoṣa" is prescribed for the purpose of adorning with ornaments.
Having performed the worship of the hair and the navel, one should then proceed to the place of the fire with the vajra;
on the northern side of the fire, upon the skin described as having its neck facing east.
One should place a lion-throne upon the back, provided with a costly covering; having spread over it the skin of a bull, one should likewise place the skin of an elephant.
After that, [he saw] a lion and a tiger above those two.
One should place the skins of these animals, beginning with the deer, in front;
then, with the *dhruva-ādya ṛtī* mantra, one should cause the king to lie down there.
Then, being pure, one should offer clarified butter into the fire with the Brahma-mantras,
as well as those dedicated to Rudra, Viṣṇu, Vāyu, Śakti, Soma, and Varuṇa.

Then the astrologer, being self-restrained, should perform the ritual procedure known as the "Northern" (uttara) according to the teachings of Bṛhaspati; he should then perform the dismissal of the deities and,
having fed the Brahmins with food, should give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Thus ends the procedure for the offering of a woolen blanket (*kaṃbala*), as recorded in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
I shall describe the bath that accomplishes all goals and brings about peace; listen.
A wise person should cause one who has entered the house to bathe on the bank of a river.
In a temple during an outbreak of fever, in a house afflicted by Vināyaka,
at a sacred ford of knowledge, in a lake, in one's home, or at a bathing place for one desiring the fruit of recitation.
If one bathes a lotus plant with milk, then a child will be conceived;
and by reaching the vicinity of an Aśoka tree, the birth of a child occurs.
May there be holy places that bestow merit, and for those with sons, may there be an ocean [of joy] in their homes; and for all, may there be good fortune and beauty in the presence of Viṣṇu.
On the day of Viṣṇu’s birth (the eleventh lunar day), on Revatī, and on Puṣya, bathing is most excellent for all.
Listen now to the procedure for the preliminary offering for one desiring to perform the ritual bath, which should be done seven days prior.
Furthermore, one should take punarnavā, vacā, rocanā, śatāhvā,
the bark of the aruṇa tree, madhūka, the two types of haridrā (rajanī), tagara, and nāgakesara.
Asura, mañjiṣṭhā, māṃsī, yava, and samardaka; priyaṅgu, sarṣapa, the meritorious vacā, brāhmī, and kuṅkuma.
Having rubbed [the body] with the five products of the cow mixed with barley meal, one should perform the ritual bath.
In the center of the mandala, upon the pericarp, one should worship Viṣṇu and Brahmā;
in the middle, the destroyer of desire, and in the directions starting from the east, in due order, with mantras.
One should place Indra and the other gods, equipped with their weapons and their vehicles,
within the bathing mandala in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
One may likewise offer oblations for thousands of Viṣṇus, Brahmās, Īśas, Śakras, and others.
For each [deity], there are eight hundred fuel-sticks together with sesame seeds;
[the attendants are] Bhadra, Subhadra, Siddhārtha, Kalahā, and Puṣṭivardhana.
One should install these jars: Amoda, Citrabhānu, Parjanya, and Sudarśana, along with the two Aśvins and the hosts of Maruts.
May the Viśvedevas, as well as the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the sages,
along with the lords of the Śrāddha and all other deities, be well-pleased.
One should place medicinal herbs into the pitcher: jayantī, vijayā, jayā, śatāvarī, śaṅkhapuṣpī, viṣṇukrāntā, and aparājitā.
Jyotiṣmatī, balā, candana, śīra, kesara,
musk, camphor, vāluka, patra, and ketu.
The best of the twice-born should place nutmeg, fragrant substances, earth, and a pala-measure of cow-products in the center upon the auspicious seat.
Having performed the king’s consecration as prescribed in the mantras and the separate oblations to the gods,
one should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor.
In ancient times, Indra, having been consecrated by his preceptor, slew the Daityas;
therefore, he is called the Guardian of the Quarter (Dikpāla), for he was victorious over them in battle.
Thus ends the "Peace for the Accomplishment of All Aims" in the Agni Purāṇa.
In the *Vīrasiṃhāvaloka* and the *Rudrayāmala*, regarding the ritual bath with *kañcukavastra* (silk cloth):
Śambhu, having been entreated by Śukra, prostrated before the Teacher of the World.
O Lord, please explain to me in detail the procedure for wearing a single garment.
Listen attentively, O Bhārgava, to that which destroys the suffering of widowhood;
when this rite involving cloth is performed, the state of barrenness goes to its dissolution.
When the sun has not yet risen, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus in sequence with white rice grains while reciting the mantra beginning with "śivo nāma."
According to the rites prescribed in the Vedas, with mantras and hymns according to Vedic injunctions,
[he worshipped] the Lord of Pārvatī, who has five faces, ten arms, and three eyes.
One should worship the deity named Śiva on the nose with the mantra "padma midhyen," and Indra in the southeast corner with the mantra "indraṃ viśvā."
One should perform the worship of Yama in the south with the mantra "ye cettha";
one should place Sanaka and the others in the southwest with the mantra "ye devā";
and one should install Varuṇa in the west with the mantra "tattvā yāmi."
With the mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā," one worships Gaṇeśvara; with the mantra "vāyusya" and the Abhigotra mantra, one worships the Mothers of the Embryo in the north.
One should install all the planets in the northeast according to their respective mantras;
one should remember that one should place the Ṛtu-mantras in the east.
Therefore, one should place the pitcher in the center and fill it with water from sacred fords;
it should be accompanied by a full vessel and provided with all medicinal herbs.
Having first performed the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) accompanied by gold, cloth, and a coconut, one should perform the worship with mantras.
There, one should recite the Śrīrudra along with its six ancillary limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) according to the prescribed rules;
thereafter, worship should be performed by both the woman and the man as if for a treasure.
Having worshipped according to the proper rite and performed his ablutions, he then—
Furthermore, this Nāndīmukha Śrāddha should be performed according to the rules;
one should then consume the middle piṇḍa with the mantra, "Thou art the embryo" (garbho 'si).
The Prayer for Recitation:
O Lord of the western quarter, O King, O Sovereign of the ocean!
You from whom lost embryos are restored—grant me the desired offspring.
Rivers, streams, lakes, and likewise other reservoirs of water do not shine at all without you; O Lord of Waters, bestow your seed.
Whatever evil or misfortune was committed by me in a previous birth, or whatever was done by myself through all [means],
may you be gracious to me as I remain here in the water within this womb.
You are the lord of sixty-six million rivers and streams;
even the seven great oceans have their source within you.
You alone are the noose-handed one; you indeed are the lord of the waters. Water is the life-force of living beings; bestow the embryo upon me, be gracious!
In your left hand is the water-offering (arghya), and in your right is the life-giving elixir;
with matted locks tawny at the crown of your head, bestow the embryo and show compassion.
Having utterly destroyed all obstacles, bestow the embryo and show compassion.

Thus is the prayer for water—the prayer for medicinal herbs: "O Great Herb, you who are the eternal treasure of all the luminaries and planets of the world, O Lord, I am your servant; grant me a conception."
One who knows all mantras should cause a branch of the fruit-bearing udumbara tree to sprout for a woman desiring a son, using the mantra: "O herb, queen of soma! (oṣadhe somarājñi).
One should hang a branch from the heart-center (the chest) while remaining pure in mind;
having taken dūrvā grass, coconut, and unbroken rice grains in one's hand,
one should perform the worship of Varuṇa, being intent on the recitation of the hymn (sūkta).
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Soma, Kandarpa, and the bull-vehicled Śiva;
Pārvatī, Subhagā, Bhadrā, and Sāvitrī are the deities of the site.
With these two white garments, unblemished and sacred to the Guru,
beautiful with all ornaments, there shall be auspiciousness through their binding.
With mung beans, rice, wheat, barley, kangu, and excellent śāli rice,
as well as with black gram and udida, the wise man should worship his own vessel.
Having placed a lamp there, as well as a heptad of fruits,
one should perform the meditation-bath with the mantra "dhānāvantā."
The coconut, the orange, the pomegranate, the citron, the wood-apple, the betel nut— these are known as the seven, with the *damana* flower as the seventh.
A coconut with a back like the shell of a tortoise, filled with milk and water,
possessing three eyes, and having Śambhu as its presiding deity, bestows a son.
Round, with the luster of gold, possessing excellent seeds, and most enchanting;
as cool as snow, this orange grants me offspring.
The citron fruit is like the orb of the moon, well-sprinkled with many seeds;
it is fragrant, presided over by the deity Soma, and bestows offspring.
The flower of which is like the rising sun, its fruit resembles vermilion,
and whose interior is like a citron— may that pomegranate grant me a child.
The fruit-bearing thread, presided over by the deity of the wheel, is like a unique likeness;
may it fulfill the state of being an embodied soul, the supreme embryo born of wisdom.
May the betel nut, whose deity is the Sun and which possesses a luster like lac-dye,
being fresh and the most excellent among fruits, always grant me its inner essence.
In all festivals, the fruit of the Madana tree— which has the luster of yellow orpiment, bestows auspiciousness upon all deities, and grants offspring— is auspicious.
Thus, for auspicious results— the medicinal bath at the beginning:
*vārḍāvarā*, *carā*, *snāyī*, *ekākī*, *vacā*, *kī*, as well as *dhānyā*, *niśā*, and *bahulā*— these are remembered as the "all-medicinal" (*sarvauṣadhī*) herbs.
O Bhārgava, with the mantra "yā oṣadhī," perform the consecration with all medicinal herbs; then, O descendant of Bhrigu, place the bamboo vessel upon the hand on the head.
Then the wise man, having recited each of all the mantras declared in the Ṛgveda preceded by the words "tad āyāmī," should bathe the couple.
The purifying mantras beginning with *vāruṇī*, then *varuṇastvottabhanam*,
these [mantras] numbering one hundred, and likewise *idam āpaḥ punantu mā*.
Having approached these Yajurvedic mantras with the Nirukta,
one should recite repeatedly the *ghṛtavatī*, the *bhuvanānām*, and the *pāvamānī* verses.
Varuṇa [is the lord] of the Sāman, and Sarasvatī [is the mistress] of the purifying Sāmans.
The ritual bath is declared to be performed with the "śanno devī" verse and the Atharva-mantras.
Therefore, one who desires a son should perform the ritual bath following the recitation of the Rudra hymns.
Then Bhārgava, having established the fire upon an auspicious sacrificial altar (sthaṇḍila),...
According to this procedure prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras, one should cause the patient to drink milk-rice (pāyasa).
There, the two libations (āghāra) and the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga) should be offered as oblations of ghee.
"Apām pṛṣṭham," "ni hotā," "ā ca punas tvā"—with these [verses], the fuel-stick is likewise offered.
O Agni, may strength be before you; you shall consume the embryo as well.
Then, having entered Sarasvatī, his source, he remained there with his wives for a long time.
With the mantra "Thou art the girdle of Aditi," he should tie it on for both the man and the woman.
He is the embryo of the herbs, and the mantras are his oblations in due order.
Having offered oblations with these mantras, one should then perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
One should give a bull to the Brahman priest and likewise a cow to the teacher;
furthermore, one may give to other Brahmins at their own discretion according to their protection.
Then one should perform the consecration with the waters from the jars purified by sacred threads.
Together with the Brahmins, he [should perform the rite] with purifying mantras beginning with "surāstvām" and so forth.
One should receive the sevenfold fruit by means of mantras that grant all desired objects.
Taking the vessel along with the lamp, he should go to the temple of Civa.
Having placed a bamboo vessel before Śiva and having prostrated, [one should proceed].
O God of gods, O Consort of Gaurī, O Maheśvara!
O Lord of Existence, Great God, obeisance to you; be the bestower of sons.
There are eight faults for women, and the ninth belongs to the man.
To destroy those defects, one should perform a ritual bath accompanied by his wife.
Whatever bodily transformation occurs that causes suffering to one's progeny is [the result of] *vikṛta*.
May all that be reduced to ashes; may she be faultless and possess a virtuous son.
And he is the Lord who effects the purification of the sins of living beings, [bestowing] the state of Varuṇa upon them.
By the power of your sacred ford, grant me abundant progeny.
Then, one should cause [the deity] to enter the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) with the mantra beginning "mādhatra," and so forth; having fed the Brāhmaṇas, one should grant a boon and dismiss them.
This, though baseless, is mentioned because it is current among the Gurjaras.
Thus ends the ritual bath with mantras as declared in the Rudrayāmala within the Vīrasiṃhāvaloka.
Aruṇa said:

"O you who wear but a single garment, regarding the rules for bathing and the performance of propitiatory rites (*śāntikarma*), those who do not practice contentment, the worship of the lineage, and devotion with faith and other such virtues—though they may perform these acts, their progeny will perish and their lineage will not flourish. These rituals are indeed difficult to perform; for one who does not endure the hardship, there is no fruit. However, for one who endures it, great fruit indeed flows forth."

O Lord, regarding that which was previously described—the single-cloth consecration (*ekavastrābhiṣecana*) for a married couple, which is the supreme pacifier of misfortunes such as barrenness—please explain its procedure (*vidhi*) exactly as it is set forth in the scriptures. Who is the deity (*devatā*) therein, what are the mantras, and what is the fruit resulting from it? Furthermore, what kind of cloth is it, and how should it be worn by both of them?
How may success in the husband-wife relationship be achieved for both man and woman when that [rite] has been performed?
The illustrious Sūrya said:

Formerly, at the beginning of this kalpa, when the Creator—the ordainer of the Vedas and Smṛtis—desired to bring forth creation, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) meditated in his mind upon the seven sages. When they, though afflicted by austerity, were unable to accomplish the task of creation, those sons of Prajāpati, desiring offspring, propitiated Śiva through penance and, being pleased, entreated him: "O Blessed One, O Lord of Creatures, we, the sons of Prajāpati, are exhausted by our austerities; [grant us progeny]."

"O Śiva, because of our ignorance in performing the cooking without removing the husks, the success of our progeny has not arisen. We have sought refuge in you for the sake of offspring; tell us the means that will bring about that success. Then Śambhu, being thus entreated, reflected for a moment and said to them: "Listen, all you sages, to the cause of the non-appearance of progeny. O sages, with the eye of knowledge, I have seen the karma performed by you during the previous dissolution (saṃplava) which results in childlessness."

Whatever misfortune remains after eating at the proper time, that evil resides in the body; likewise, the loss of mantras and other [powers] is divided between both [the husband and wife]. Having clothed that pair of bodies with a single garment, perform the ritual bath according to the rules, which destroys misfortune. From the nails to the fingertips, until the entire limb is as pure as clarified butter—thus does misfortune perish. This [misfortune] is proclaimed to be of five kinds. Regarding its removal, the procedure for the bed and seat is performed together with a separate garment for each.

"Having bathed properly, O sons of Vidēdha, you shall obtain the highest good for your lineage. When Śambhu had spoken thus and vanished, the sages performed the great rite of bathing from the beginning, wearing only a single garment, according to the rules as seen and heard through the eye of knowledge from the Śruti scriptures, on an auspicious month, during the bright fortnight, on a day when the planets were favorable.

At the confluence of two rivers, or even at the junction of two great rivers, at dawn, having established oneself in spiritual perfection (*siddhi*) according to the prescribed rule, and having performed various rites along with one’s wife, being endowed with faith, one should offer worship and recite this mantra: "O Lord of the universe, whatever incomparable misfortune known as the suffering of widowhood may have existed for me in a previous birth—fivefold in nature—for its destruction, I perform this unsurpassed ritual procedure."

"O Lord, together with my wife, protect me from the afflictions of the day and grant me success here. Having spoken thus, he should take that great garment, which consists of twenty parts, measuring two and a half cubits in length and twenty-five finger-breadths in height. It is woven with smooth, spread-out threads, and within it is placed a wonderful cloth. Consecrated by the mantra "yuvā suvāsāḥ," it is offered upon the divine altar. Having properly received that, he should wear the garment along with its cloth. It is firm, unbroken, and made of double-folded thread.

Then she, standing on his right side, accompanied by her husband and her virtuous daughter, and with her head covered, should carefully place [the vessel] upon it. Having swept and hidden the *kuśa* grass, she follows behind them. Sitting down at the water’s edge, both husband and wife wash their hands and feet; being self-restrained and having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), they become pure before me. Both Vedic and worldly duties are fulfilled by those who have offered oblations and whose senses are conquered. Even among all sacred fords (*tīrthas*), the Lord is the foremost of the gods.

"O Lord, grant me a child, for all living beings depend upon life. Whatever sins exist here that cause childlessness, O Lord, having destroyed them all, grant me a child, O Master! Whatever great sin was committed by us both in a previous birth due to suffering, having completely removed that from me, grant me a child, O Lord! All rivers and reservoirs of water are presided over by you alone; they purify even the most wicked sinners—grant me a child, O Lord!"

"O highly fortunate one, we pray for progeny that purifies the world. O Lord, my Master, being well-pleased, grant me a conception. Whatever spirits, ghosts, piśācas, and others may cause obstacles to my progeny—having bound them all with a noose, O Lord, grant me a conception. Having thus prayed, the couple should forcibly emerge from those waters. Having bathed well, the husband should stand facing the east and cause the mantra to be heard [by his wife].

Having caused these auspicious verses from the *Maṅgīrasa* and *Āditya* hymns to be recited on earth by worthy recipients, he should bow down to them. Then, having put on two bright, pure garments, he should sit upon a beautiful, auspicious seat, honored with holy garlands and sandalwood paste. Thereafter, the twice-born man should touch gold and ghee; then, having performed the prostration, he should complete all the remaining rites. The preceptor, however, should act according to the injunctions as approved by the astrologer.

Then, on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring one cubit (hasta), he should place a water-pot (kalaśa) that is free of cracks, filled with milk, and adorned with gold, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata). He should place there a full vessel (pūrṇapātra) filled with flowers, fruits, and unbroken grains. Having consecrated it with their respective mantras, O Maheśa, [addressing] Umā’s husband, those who are knowers of the mantras of the Vedas should mutter them before it according to the five-limbed ritual (pañcāṅga-vidhi), using the Rudra-sūktas and Yajurvedic hymns. Then the preceptor (ācārya), according to his own rules, should properly offer the sacrificial oblation (caru).

Having offered the two *āghāra* libations and the two *ājyabhāga* portions, and having worshipped the guardians of the directions (the *dikpatis*) all around with their respective mantras while remaining composed, he should recite the *prajāpate* mantra toward the southeast and the other, "garbhaṃ dhehi," as well as "apāṃ pṛṣṭham" and the seven verses addressed to Varuṇa beginning with "imaṃ me. Then, having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, he should perform the remainder of the ritual. At the conclusion of the *homa*, the learned officiant (*ṛtvij*), having worshipped Śiva along with Śivā according to the rules, should offer the recitation (*japa*) and the *homa* to Him in accordance with the prescribed rites.
Then, to a learned and self-controlled Brahmin, he should give an excellent milch cow together with her calf, accompanied by clothing and a ritual fee (dakṣiṇā), and with all her limbs adorned.

Having first given a bull endowed with auspicious marks, the couple, subsequently gladdened by the astrologer, should utter the mantra as prescribed by the learned according to the ritual rules: "O God of gods, O Lord of the universe, O Destroyer of the multitude of all sins! By this rite and by this gift of a pair of cows, being forever satisfied, O Lord, grant me progeny. Thereafter, one should present a lute (vīṇā) before Śiva.

The ritual requisites should be offered to the preceptor according to one’s own capacity. Having presented two garments to the guru, one should complete the remainder of the rite. After bowing to the deities and dismissing them according to the rules, the Brahmins, being attentive, should then consecrate the performer with the water from the pitcher using Vāruṇa and Saura mantras, as well as those for peace (śānti) and prosperity (svastyayana), and various Purāṇic mantras that bestow manifold fruits. Thereafter, one should commence the Śrāddha ceremony according to the Nandīmukha rite.

One should utter the consecration (*saṃskāra*) with the mantra "namo vaḥ. There are seven Tantric mantras, five Vedic mantras addressed to Varuṇa, and the mantras beginning with "tvaṃ naḥ," as well as the two subsequent Varuṇa mantras. With these Varuṇa hymns (*sūktas*), such as "tvanno agne," "satvanno agne," and "tat tvā yāmi," one should consecrate that water, praise it with mantras, and bow down. Having immersed oneself and emerged again, one should perform the ritual bath (*tantra-snāna*) once more.

Having performed the ritual application according to the rules for the fulfillment of the desire for a son, [the husband] should say: "We shall bathe; may the Blessed One, the Lord of Progeny, be pleased with us. Then the two should perform the bath with substances consecrated by mantras: with fine clay, cow dung, cow urine, curd, milk, and ghee; with ground sesame and *āmalaka* fruits, and with water containing all medicinal herbs and *kuśa* grass. Having completed the bath according to the rules, both husband and wife should be bathed; then the wife should be bathed with each of the collections of substances individually.

The king and queen, accompanied by their offspring, should have themselves bathed according to the prescribed rites with seven chariots filled with jars brimming with the seven medicinal herbs (saptauṣadhi) purified by mantras. The wise priest should perform the consecration using the *Audumbara* branch—which bears many fruits and was given by the husband with preceding mantras—along with the following seven herbs for the ablution: *Vardhamāna*, *Karaja*, *Carā*, *Snāyu*, *Devīśatāvarī*, *Elā*, and *Lakṣmaṇā*. Furthermore, the *Yājyānuvāka* hymn should be recited during the consecration with the seven medicinal herbs.

Then, one should place a bamboo vessel filled with seven kinds of grain—consisting of mung beans, rice, wheat, barley, śāli rice, kaṅgu, and māṣa beans—therein with the mantra "yāḥ palinīriti. Furthermore, one should place these seven fruits: coconut, orange, pomegranate, citron, utpala, betel nut, and the jambīra fruit as the seventh.

With the seven previously mentioned worldly mantras and the *Śiromanyavākya*, one should perform the bath to dispel the misfortune that has previously arisen. One should sprinkle [water] from the tip of the thumb up to the tip of the hair, saying: "By this bath, drive away all the deities. Having thus petitioned Varuṇa and me as witnesses to the commencement of the rite, one should with a single-minded focus meditate upon Lord Śiva together with Umā. Then, [one should likewise meditate upon] these very gods, humans, and ancestors.

Having gratified the ancestral deities (pitṛ-devatās) according to the Nāndīmukha rite, he should then perform the worship with the *vibhrāṭ* anuvāka while holding his hands cupped with fruits and flowers. After that, he should complete the remainder of the ritual. Then, placing that Vaiṣṇava vessel upon his head and touching it with the tip of a blade of kuśa grass, he should recite auspicious mantras for peace. Thereafter, for the sake of well-being and repeated pacification, the wife—urged by the astrologer—should eat the middle piṇḍa.

Having consecrated [the water] with the mantra, "The ancestors have placed the embryo," and having sipped water (ācamana) like a treasure, he should afterwards complete the remainder of the ritual. He should feed one hundred other twice-born men, satisfying them according to his capacity. Thus, the two of them shall have fulfilled their duty and be endowed with the happiness of sons and grandsons.
Thus ends the procedure for bathing while wearing a single garment, from the Dialogue between Sūrya and Aruṇa.

In the *Dharmaśāstra-nibandhana* titled *Adbhutasāgara*, Garga states: "If a horse neighs upwards after twenty years have passed, it portends the death of its master. If it neighs upwards before that time, one should perform a propitiatory rite (*śānti*) and satisfy the Brahmins with offerings. Having fasted for one night, bathed, and purified his mind, the devotee, being clean, should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times. Then, having consecrated water with the mantra, he should sprinkle it [over the horse]."

One who knows the true nature of elephants should perform the auspicious elephant-bath (*gajasnāna*), which removes all defects, on that day with the sounding of musical instruments. Having performed the preliminary rites in the forenoon with a hundred jars of water, one skilled in the ritual of fire-offerings (*homavid*) should then perform the *homa* according to the prescribed rules: "Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Rudra! Svāhā to the Lord of Elephants! Svāhā to Varuṇa! Svāhā to Bṛhaspati! Svāhā to Śukra! Here, bathing with a hundred jars [of water] destroys all calamities.

First, there should be the worship of the twice-born (Brahmins). [One should offer] water mixed with jaggery, along with barley and *yāvaka* (barley-gruel), and then repeatedly fumigate the *piṇḍa* with honey. Having performed the rites of worship, one should quickly pay homage to Gaṇādhipa. [The mantra for the *naivedya* is: "O Lord, born from the forehead of the Great Wealth (Śiva), having been offered this, please partake of the *naivedya* yourself. This is the *naivedya* mantra.
Thus ends the pacification of elephants and so forth occurring at improper times.

When a female elephant emits a fragrant ichor and even discharges her reproductive fluid; when she stands in the city, the kingdom, the forest, or the house while intoxicated; when she remains standing while voiding urine and excrement; or when she is fought in battle by another intoxicated elephant—then there shall be great danger for that country and its city. In such a case, the king’s priest, together with his ministers and kinsmen, should fast and offer a cow adorned like an elephant and equipped with two horns.

Then, having led this female elephant away, one should separate her from the enemy's kingdom; in this very manner, she should remain dwelling in the forest at night. Alternatively, having performed the rites as before and having performed the pacification (*śānti*), one should split the forest with well-heated gold. This is the pacification of the rut of cows and elephants.

Now, regarding the propitiatory rites (*śānti*) for the *Dhaniṣṭhā* asterism, the *Tripuṣkara*, and so forth: O performer of the rite, this is extremely necessary. For those born under *Dhaniṣṭhā*, the *Pañcaka*, and other such [periods], as well as for those who have died, for children, women, and the elderly, there are fears; therefore, the primary concern is the protection of the house. Having understood these [matters] from the *Āndaruṇu*, the *Yājakula-mūlam*, the *Neṟiṅgiyuṇḍaginadi*, the *Madanaratna*, and the *Gāruḍa*: [The following verses follow: "O Lord, the *Dhaniṣṭhā* [asterism] is the most terrible among all the asterisms. It is said that it causes the destruction of the family and the lineage. Therefore, one must perform the *Śānti* for the sake of the welfare of the household. Having first identified this group of five constellations beginning with Dhaniṣṭhā and ending with Revatī as always inauspicious for the rite of cremation, one should then place four effigies made of *darbha* grass near the corpse, consecrated with the mantras of the respective constellations. Then the cremation should be performed together with those effigies. At the end of the period of impurity (*sūtaka*), an auspicious and nourishing rite of pacification (*śānti-pauṣṭika*) should be performed using leaves. A person who dies during these five constellations does not attain a [favorable] state; therefore, one should offer sesame seeds, gold, and ghee dedicated to that deceased person.
In the *Kriyānibandha*:
"A vessel, sandals, an umbrella, and a golden seal—these should be given as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to Brahmins; it liberates one from all sins."
In the *Madanaratna*, Gārgya states:

"If the Bhadra-tithis (the 4th, 9th, and 14th lunar days) coincide with Sunday, Tuesday, or Saturday, and there is a conjunction of three-quartered asterisms (*tripāda-ṛkṣa*) with two of these [planets], it is a *puṣkara* yoga. When there is a conjunction of two or three *puṣkaras*, death brings about the end of liberation; indeed, in the case of death during a *tripuṣkara*, the suffering is tripled. Even in the case of burial, it is exactly the same. To pacify this defect, one should then have a body fashioned from sesame paste or barley, place it in a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), adorn it, and cremate it upon the paternal fire."

Bodhāyana says: One should burn sesame flour with the mantra "asmāttvam". By three *kṛcchra* penances, one removes the affliction caused by two or three *puṣkaras*. If death occurs in the north (Vāsava), it will happen at home; if it occurs again, it is a re-death. One should give gold as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), or even wear black clothing.

If one's death occurs while the Moon is situated in Vāsava (Śravaṇa), Dhaniṣṭhā, Brāhma (Rohiṇī), or in the signs of Aquarius or Pisces, no upward movement (ascension) is seen for that person; rather, constant misfortune shall prevail. A cremation must be performed for such a person, even if it results in the destruction of one's own kin. Alternatively, the cremation should be performed according to the prescribed rites on the following day. If Jīva (the planet Jupiter) is in the five stars of Dhaniṣṭhā when someone dies, or if it is during a Tripuṣkara yoga or under the constellation Yāmya (Bharaṇī), it will certainly kill those born in the family. To destroy such inauspiciousness, the following ritual procedure is proclaimed.

Images made of darbha grass should be fashioned and wrapped with threads of five-colored wool; these should be smeared with barley flour, and with them one should burn the corpse. Pretavāha, Pretasakha, Pretapa, Pretabhūmipa, and Pretahartā as the fifth—these are the five names in sequence.

Having worshipped the images here, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the head, eyes, left side, navel, and feet in sequence with their respective mantras. Having offered clarified butter (*ājya*) into the fire, the Bhaṭṭas maintain that one should offer it into each [image] respectively with the two mantras: "māyasomaṃ" and "tryambakam". Then, at the end of the period of impurity (*sūtaka*), the son should perform a propitiatory rite (*śānti*) and a rite for prosperity (*pauṣṭikī*). He should look upon oil placed in a bell-metal vessel and give it to a twice-born (*dvijana*). Thereafter, he should do so for the pleasure of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, Indra, and Varuṇa.

For the pacification of the fault, one should perform the gift of black gram, mung beans, barley, rice, and millet; the gift of gold; the chanting of the Rudra-mantra; a hundred-thousand-fold fire-oblation (lakṣahoma); the honoring of Brahmins; and the gift of cows and land, each consisting of a sixth part [of the total penance].
In the *Aparārka*, another Smṛti states:

"If death occurs during the five stars beginning with Dhaniṣṭhā, one should place five gems in the mouth [of the deceased], offer three oblations there with the mantra 'vahavapām,' and then perform the *nirvapaṇa* (offering of funeral cakes). This is the rule for one who maintains the sacred fire (*sāgni*). For others, one should simply bury the body or cast it into water. If death occurs during the three stars beginning with Pūrva-bhādrapadā, likewise place pieces of gold in the mouth; then one should fashion a three-part human figure out of flour. One should perform the oblation facing each part of the figure with the mantra 'vahavapām.'"

Having offered black sesame, cotton, and flowers to Kārṣṇa, one should consign [the body] to the fire after performing the *agni-saṃskāra*, or otherwise cast it into the earth or into water. In that very context: "Gold, diamond, sapphire, topaz, and pearl—this is declared by the sages to be the 'five jewels' (*pañcaratna*) to be given. In the absence of gems, however, gold weighing one *karṣa* should be used; and in the absence of gold, clarified butter (*ājya*) should be known as the substitute by the wise."
In the Madanaratna it is likewise stated:
"One should give to a Brahmin, according to one's ability, a bell-metal vessel with eighty-one fruits, or half of that, or a quarter of that, or even with nine, six, or three fruits."
Elsewhere it is also stated:
