"Having performed the installation of the fire according to the ritual prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, then [perform] the placing of the fuel, the offering of oblations (*nirvapaṇa*), and likewise the sacrifice to the deities: to Yama, Dharmarāja, Mṛtyu, Antaka, Vaivasvata, Kāla, Sarvabhūtakṣaya, Audumbara, Dadhna, Nīla, Parameṣṭhin, Vṛkodara, Citra, and Citragupta—having performed the invocation according to the rule, one should offer one oblation for each."

One should give to a peaceful Brahmin a black-limbed [image] dressed in black cloth and adorned with a golden *niṣka* coin, saying, "May Yama be pleased with me. The same applies even for the constellation of the three-footed (Pūrvaphalgunī).

In the *Aparārka*: "Punarvasu, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Kṛttikā, Uttaraphalgunī, Pūrvābhādrapadā, and Viśākhā—these are to be known as the 'three-quarter' [nakṣatras]. Regarding the death of a celibate student (*brahmacārin*), the death of one afflicted by leprosy, the death of a pregnant woman, a menstruating woman, or a woman who has recently given birth, as well as the specific rules for the gift of the body, they should be understood from my own work, the *Nirṇayasindhu*.
Thus ends the section on the pacification of death occurring during the five stars of Dhaniṣṭhā, the Tripuṣkara, and so forth."
Now follows the procedure for death-omens such as the *tripuṣkara* and others, as taught by Vasiṣṭha.

O Mṛtyuñjaya, the ritual procedures (*vidhāna*) appropriate for each specific time are capable of warding off untimely death (*apamṛtyu*). However, those who are wise and crest-jewels among theists (*āstika*), though intent on investigating the truth, do not perceive this clearly; they do not consider the rituals such as *homa* and the like, which are the means to ward off diseases caused by untimely death, nor do they know the protective rites (*rakṣā-vidhāna*) that exist elsewhere. Thus, they fall into calamity.
Having summarized what is stated in the Vasiṣṭha-kalpa, the procedure for Mṛtyuñjaya is now being declared; thus it begins:
"O lords of sages, I shall proclaim the ritual procedure of Tryambaka."

That which was previously declared by Brahmā through the *uktavidhi* (the method of recitation) is the *mṛtyuñjaya* (conqueror of death), proclaimed to be threefold: the first is known as *mṛtyuñjaya*,
then *mṛtasañjīvinī*, and thereafter *mahāmṛtyuñjaya*.
The *Mṛtajīvanī* is formed by joining [the syllables] to the solitary *Mṛtyuñjaya*;
when joined with the *Tāra*, the three *Bījas*, and the *Vyāhṛtis*, it becomes the *Tryambaka*.
This is declared as the *Mahāmṛtyuñjaya* by those proficient in all mantras.
First, one should recite the *mṛṣasañjīvinī*, the *tāra* (om), and the *vyāhṛtis*;

then the *triṃbaka* mantra, and finally, at the end, one should recite that [mantra] again. This is declared by the most excellent knowers of mantras to be either the *mṛtyuñjaya* or the *yama* [mantra].

Then there are Māyātārā and the others, followed by the three *vyāhṛtis*. The mantra of Tryambaka is considered the "Reviver of the Dead" (*mṛtasaṃjīvinī*). That mantra which possesses the seed-syllable (*sabīja*) is indeed known as Mahāmṛtyuñjaya.
One should first recite the Praṇava and the Vyāhṛtis, preceded by the Praṇava;
then the Tryambaka mantra, followed by the Vyāhṛtis at the end;
and finally, one should utter the three seed-syllables, the Praṇava, and the Vahnijāyā (Svāhā) at the conclusion.
At the end of the *praṇava* (Oṃ) is *prasāda*, which indeed removes death.
Then follow the *vyāhṛtis* beginning with *bhūḥ*, and thereafter the verse "Tryambakam.
Reversed, that is the three seed-syllables; then the word "Tvam" and the three *vyāhṛtis*.
This mantra, ending with "svāhā," was propitiated here in ancient times by Śukra;
it is celebrated throughout the three worlds as the "Great Conqueror of Death.
It is joined with six and indeed fourteen *oṃ* syllables.
By worshipping Mṛtyuñjaya according to the prescribed rule, one shall obtain one's desired object.
Likewise, the assignment of the six limbs may be performed by dividing [the mantra] with three syllables;
the heart is said to consist of three, the head is declared to consist of four,
the crest is specified as eight, and the armor is considered to consist of nine.

The five-eyed weapon is proclaimed; it is described as having three faces. Immediately thereafter, its eastern, western, southern, and lunar (northern) faces [are described], and then its upper face, which is known as Tryambaka, possesses the complete mantra.
[One should place them] on the head, the neck, the face, the pair of eyes, the navel, the heart, the back, the belly, the penis, the anus, the thighs,
the roots of the thighs, the two knees, and thereafter on the two shanks,
the two calves, the two sides, and again on the two feet.
One should place the mantra-syllables in sequence upon the two hands, the two nostrils, and the head; having placed the eleven words upon the head, the pair of eyebrows, and the eyes,
one should again place them on the mouth, the pair of cheeks, the heart, and the belly.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) in this manner upon the secret parts, the thighs, the knees, and the feet.
The manifestation of this application will become clear:

first, having uttered the seed-syllable of the palace (prāsādabīja), then the syllable "ha" which removes death, and the heart-mantras, one joins the "traṃbaka" mantra; this very first [mantra] again removes death.
Having performed the sixfold assignment (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) and visualizing Rudra— the bestower of nectar— entered within the maṇḍala,
the yogi conquers death through the grace of the primordial seed-syllable (śukram).

One who desires the fruits [of mantras] should recite the three syllables beginning with *vedādibhūḥ* (the source of the Vedas), and in between, the *tryambaka* mantra which removes death; then, having applied the *prāsāda* mantra according to rule, one should recite it encased within the *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra.
One should know that the syllable *oṃ* begins the triad and the syllable *oṃ* ends the triad;
likewise, there is the triad of *vyāhṛtis* and the triad of *prāsādas*.
By means of the syllables *oṃ*, numbering as many as the mantras, one should understand [the practice] for the sake of all success.
Mahāmṛtyuñjaya, Mṛtyuñjaya, Tryambaka,
and the mantra of Tryambaka— preceded by [the syllable] Om and concluded with two [syllables],
these are the Mahāmṛtyuñjayas; through the propitiation of Śukra, one certainly attains them in this world.
And that which is devoid of seed-syllables (bīja) is called the pure Mṛtyuñjaya.
Others say there is a mantra called Mahāmṛtyuñjaya which, like this [previous] mantra, bestows the three [goals].
Likewise, it is stated elsewhere:
"The seed-syllable known as Prāsāda consists of the fourteen vowels joined with the letter *ha* and the *bindu*;
[alternatively] it consists of the letter *ja* and the *bindu*."
The seed-syllable known as Mṛtyuñjaya is the supreme remover of death;
it is proclaimed as the Savior (Tāraka), consisting of the letter *sa* with the visarga.
It is the essence, stable, joined with the ear (the letter *r*), the moon (the bindu), and the visarga of Bhṛgu (*ha*).
The mantra consisting of syllables is said to be of the nature of the conquest of death.
Thus ends the procedure for Mṛtyuñjaya as proclaimed by Vasiṣṭha:
On the eastern side of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is proclaimed Kālījihvā;
in the southeast is Karālī, and in the south is Sulohitā.
Manojavā belongs to the Nairṛtas, and Dhūmravarṇī belongs to Varuṇa.

One should perform pacification (śānti), protection (rakṣā), and prosperity (puṣṭika) rites with Visasphuliṅgī in the northwest, and with Viśvaruci in the northeast; or alternatively, one may perform them with Kālī or Karālī.
For the pacification of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and the like, one should use Lohitajihvikā.
The performance of malevolent rites (abhicāra) is prescribed for the tongue called Mano-jayā;
one who desires rain should offer oblations into the smoke-colored [tongue].
However, they know that the tongue characterized by sparks is for the purpose of pacification (uccāṭana).
Let Viśvaruci-jihvā go from the northern part of the sacrificial pit;
she is called Sarvārthasādhikā by those most skilled in mantras.
The wise know that the tongue in the northeast is indeed another, called Sudhārā.
The central portion of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is declared to be the mouth of the fire;
in that place, one should perform all rites except for killing.
Having brought the aupāsana fire, one should deposit it into that pit.
Alternatively, one should cause a learned Brahmin (śrotriya) to recite the Veda within the sacrificial hall.

One should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas), beginning from the east and proceeding clockwise. Having performed everything up to the portioning of the clarified butter (ājyabhāga) in the fire-pit (kuṇḍa), including the marking of the lines (ullekhana) and so forth;
One should perform the oblation with milk-rice (pāyasa) according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra;
however, if desiring long life, one should offer oblations into the fire with clarified butter (ghṛta) in the number of one hundred thousand.

One should offer oblations of honey and the three sweets (madhuratriya) either ten thousand times, or a thousand times, or one hundred and eight times, using three blades of dūrvā grass for each offering.
Or the wise man should offer oblations with pieces of *guḍūcī* four fingers long, or with sesame seeds and *taṃjula* fruits that have been husked;
or he may offer oblations with sesame seeds that have been washed and soaked in cow's ghee.
Having offered oblations of *palāśa* fuel-sticks, one shall obtain a full lifespan;
or else, being composed, one should satiate the deity with water.
One desiring health should offer oblations of *arka* wood soaked in clarified butter.
One should also offer oblations with milk, or again with other substances rather than clarified butter;
likewise, for the pacification of all diseases, one may offer fruits or fuel-sticks.
For fever, one should offer oblations with *ācchidrā* leaves or mango leaves smeared with milk.
Alternatively, one should offer oblations with pieces of *guḍūcī* soaked in cow’s ghee;
for urinary disorders (*prameha*), the oblation may be performed with honey, milk, or ghee;
or the oblation may be made with *audumbara* wood fuel or with *āmalaka* fruits.
For abdominal tumors (gulma), a homa with black sesame seeds or with ghee,
or a homa with *vardhamāna* fuel-sticks, shall instantly remove colic pain (*śūla*).
Alternatively, one may perform a homa with *karañja* fuel-sticks or even with *nirguṇḍī* fuel-sticks.

One should perform an oblation after anointing [the body] with oil for the pacification of wind-diseases (*vātaroga*). One should offer oblations with *śamī* fuel-sticks for the pacification of excessive wasting (*atisāra*).
For the purpose of pacifying eye-disease (*akṣiroga*), fuel-sticks of *palāśa* are prescribed.
Having offered oblations of *usmanta* fuel-sticks, one is released from the waters.
For pain in the eyes, one should offer oblations with *kuberākṣī* and *indravallī*;
at that very time, having anointed [the area] with oil, one should also offer oblations with pieces of diamond (*vajra*).
An oblation of Mātaliṅga and Guḍūcī destroys jaundice;
through an oblation of the three sweets (madhuratraya), there shall be peace from consumption and pulmonary diseases.
And by an oblation of fruits and roots, diseases of the womb are pacified.
For leprosy (kuṣṭha) and smallpox (masūrikā), one should offer oblations of *ṛṣī* mixed with the three types of honey,
or of *chinna-utpala* flowers soaked in ghee along with *lāśa*;
or alternatively, one should offer oblations of white mustard seeds combined with oil.
Furthermore, whatever other diseases of the mouth or diseases of the head there may be,
they all reach pacification through sesame seeds soaked in ghee and offered into the fire.
For one desiring the alleviation of all abdominal diseases, [this same rite should be performed].
O best of the twice-born, an oblation with fuel-sticks of the *bilva* tree should be performed;
then one should offer oblations with clarified butter soaked in the juices of all the herbs,
or one may offer oblations with *dūrvā* grass as prescribed, or with sandalwood.
One should perform the oblation with the fuel-sticks of the *aśvadha* tree,
or else with cow’s ghee alone, for the pacification of bloody diarrhea (*raktātisāra*).
This applies to all other diseases as well, including throat ailments and abdominal enlargements (*mahodara*).
One should offer oblations with three sweet substances soaked in honey, milk, and ghee;
this triple-sweet oblation is for the pacification of all diseases.
Whatever remedy has been prescribed in the Āyurvedas for a particular disease [should be employed].
To pacify that disease, one should perform oblations with various [mantras],
or else with the *namas-mantra* or indeed with the *pāvamāna* hymns; then, being composed, one should consecrate the Goddess of Gods with water from a sacred ford (*tīrtha*).
For the pacification of all fevers caused by spirits (bhūta), as well as those caused by planetary influences and others,
one should perform a libation (tarpaṇa) with the aforementioned mantras in the previously stated number;
or else, being self-controlled in diet and composed in mind, one should recite the mantra.
In this manner, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) and recitation (japa), or the libation (tarpaṇa) and recitation alone.
For the sake of attaining long life and health for oneself or for another,
[one may observe this vow] for one day, or three days, or ten days, or twelve days; or for a fortnight,
a month, two months, or even three months.
Alternatively, having resolved, "We shall wander for four months or six months," one should remain concentrated for that long period; however,
for a very short time, one may perform the triad of offerings, such as the *juhū*-oblation and so forth.
Whatever items, such as beds and seats, were used during the period of illness,
one who has been freed from disease should never use them again.
Hereafter, I shall describe the means for overcoming untimely death.
The wise one should offer oblations with *dūrvā* grass mixed with the three sweets (*madhuratraya*),
either a thousand, ten thousand, or one hundred and eight times;
or alternatively, he may offer oblations with white *arka* flowers or with cow’s ghee.
The wise one should offer oblations with *apāmārga* twigs, black sesame seeds, barley, and *dūrvā* grass mixed with the three sweets (*madhuratra*),
either a thousand, ten thousand, or one hundred and eight times.
One may also perform the oblation with white *arka* flowers or with cow’s ghee;
or with *apāmārga* fuel-sticks, black sesame seeds, and barley;
or alternatively, one may offer the oblation with cow’s ghee alone or even with milk.
The wise praise the milk and ghee of a tawny cow.
On a Saturday, touching water, one should mutter this mantra.
If a twice-born man were to do so even while dying, he would attain liberation; how much more so if he performs it himself!
Alternatively, having sprinkled him with water or indeed with clarified butter,
one should offer oblations with fuel-sticks of *palāśa*, *khadira*, or *aśvattha* wood,
or even with those produced from the *bilva* tree; he too is liberated from death.

Alternatively, O best of the twice-born, by offering a caru-oblation to Rudra and performing one hundred and eight oblations, a man conquers death. Now I shall describe another means that directly averts death.
A wise person should construct an altar measuring one cubit in size;
in its center, he should place a water-pot wrapped with yellow thread. He should surround it on all four sides with a square area filled with rice and grains.
Having wrapped it in a pair of garments and filled it with pure water,
one should cast into it sprouts of milk-trees or mango sprouts;
then, having adorned it with perfumes, garlands, unbroken grains, and other offerings.
There, having invited the great god, the three-eyed Lord Tryambaka,
one should worship him with perfumes, flowers, and offerings using the verse beginning with "tryambakam."
Then, the knower of mantras should consecrate this pitcher with this mantra one thousand and eight times, and subsequently bathe the person [with its water].
By means of the *dvāthakūrca* at the time of death, one should completely conquer the king [of diseases];
for such a person, there is no fear of death nor any fear caused by the five types of disease.
Out of greed for wealth for the sake of others, or through delusion or ignorance,
if one performs the *mṛtyuñjaya* recitation, one shall meet death oneself.
Except for one's mother, father, son, king, and teacher, [one should never... always.

In the ritual procedure for the Great Conqueror of Death (Mahāmṛtyuñjaya), the rite for protection is now described; it overcomes the fear of all beings. Having taken the fire from the domestic hearth (aupāsanāgni) produced by the fire-sacrifice (agnihotra), one should perform the rite at the time of birth.
Whether it be a thousand or even a hundred [repetitions] performed for Mṛtyuñjaya,
one should then consecrate that [water] with mantras and touch the limbs of the image according to the prescribed ritual.
I shall proclaim the foundational rite which removes the fear of disease and death;
through it, no fear arises from planets, spirits, serpents, and the like.
If one should have a ring made of pure gold,
it should not be made of the five metals, nor of nine metals, nor even of three metals.
Then, with a concentrated mind, he worshipped the Lord of Gods with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains of rice, and other offerings, using the mantra "Tryambaka."
An expert in mantras, having offered oblations according to the prescribed rite into either a sacrificial pit or upon a consecrated mound using cow’s ghee, should worship the god Janārdana.
A hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, or even a hundred thousand [coins], according to reality,
should be placed on the right side of the Hotṛ priest, made either of gold or silver.
Whether it be a vessel of bell-metal or even one of clay,
the wise man offers the remnants of all oblations into that [fire] as a finger-ring.
Touching the ring, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times;
for the sake of total protection, one should wear the ring upon a finger.
By this very method, one should always wear all new ornaments; thus, one shall live happily for a hundred years.
Now, O best of the twice-born, I shall proclaim the pacification that destroys all calamities, as well as [the rites for] all portents and evil dreams.
Upon the manifestation of divine, celestial, and terrestrial wonders,
appearing directly before one in all their various forms from every direction;
Likewise, when there is apprehension of possession by bhūtas, pretas, or piśācas,
one should place fire in the midst of the planetary spirits and cook the pāyasa caru.
Therefore, one who is self-restrained should offer oblations into the fire with his own arm, using this mantra,
either sesame-rice or boiled rice mixed with honey.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations with mantras, using either cow’s ghee or [fuel sticks] produced from the palāśa, khadira, aśvattha, bilva, and udumbara trees.
One should offer oblations with *apāmārga* fuel-sticks, or else with sesame seeds;
or alternatively, one may have someone perform the fire-sacrifice (*homa*) with this mantra.
One should know that with cow’s ghee, barley, rice, and sesame seeds,
having taken fire, one should offer oblations of sacrificial wood, parched grain, clarified butter, and so forth.
The bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and whatever other grahas and such there may be—
all of them depart from the house by means of the oblation, the fragrance, the touch of the incense, and the power of this mantra.
Alternatively, one who desires [success] should prepare a full water-pot; having consecrated it with this mantra, he should sprinkle the entire house with that water.
Now, O great sage, I shall describe another method of ritual placement (nyāsa) for this mantra;
there are thirty-three deities within this mantra.
One should know that there are eight Vasus at the beginning, and eleven Rudras in the subsequent [group].
And thereafter, the Prajāpati who is the twelve Ādityas,
as well as the Vaṣaṭkāra, are Śiva, the protector of all beings.
Thus, these forms of the gods have indeed been described;
the practitioner, being composed, should assign the syllables to all the limbs.
One should first place the pentad in the five locations beginning with the crown of the head,
and likewise in the five locations of the right hand.
Then, five more [syllables] are placed on the left hand;
thereafter, on the right foot, in five locations.
Having placed five others, one should likewise place them on the left foot.
Then, on the right side, from the left side in sequence,
one should place three [syllables] on the back, the anus, the private parts, and the belly.
One should place the Mātṛkās in the middle of the eyebrows, on the head, the neck, and the heart;
having thus performed the placement of all [the letters], one should then recite the Praṇava mantra.
With a concentrated mind, one should install the deity and the mantra upon one's own limbs;
however, if one is unable to do so, one should have the best of the twice-born perform the protection.
Now, I shall briefly declare the rites for specific desires.
One who desires prosperity [should perform them] with the sacrificial fuel-sticks or fruits of the *bilva* tree.
Or, by offering oblations with its leaves, one may attain great prosperity;
one desiring cows obtains a cow that yields abundant milk through oblations made with milk.
A seeker of knowledge who performs oblations with rudrākṣas soaked in cow’s ghee will thereby obtain knowledge, long life, and wealth; of this there is no doubt.
One who desires other primary things should offer oblations of food thus drenched in ghee;
having offered fuel-sticks of *palāśa*, one shall attain spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*).
One desiring rain, having worshipped the God of gods, Tryambaka,
should consecrate the deity with water for the guest-offering (arghya), water for washing the feet (pādya), and other offerings, using mantras related to the god.
With the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," likewise with those beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ," with the Pavamāna section, and with this verse beginning with "tryambakaṃ."
One should offer oblations with fuel-sticks of reed soaked in milk;
or one may offer ten thousand or even a thousand oblations with milk alone.
One should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made, feed the Brahmins, and thereafter, within ten days, rain will surely fall; of this there is no doubt.
Those desiring rain, dressed in wet garments, should offer oblations with fuel-sticks produced from the vaṭa tree; by means of the mantras, they shall obtain immediate rain.
Standing in water reaching up to the navel and meditating, one shall indeed obtain nourishment;
by reciting the three-syllabled mantra, one shall obtain great nourishment.
Having taken the Agnihotra ladle and the finest white and black ashes,
one should offer them into the water with this Ṛgvedic verse and thereby ward off rain.
The meaning is "having caused [the fire] to blaze.
A man desiring a son, however, should offer milk-rice mixed with ghee;
having himself consumed the remainder of the oblation, he obtains a son.
Having offered sesame seeds smeared with ghee on the full moon day of the month of Pārṇamāsa, one attains happiness;
having smeared a surface of ground measuring a *gocarma* with cow-dung, one should perform the rite.
Having poured out a heap of grain, the wise man should place [the image] in its midst,
surrounded by twenty water-pots encircled with white thread.
The wise man should worship the jars, filled with water from sacred fords and adorned with sprouts and other ornaments, while reciting the mantra beginning with "Tryambaka."
Having consecrated the jars, the wise man should then mutter the hymns (*sūktas*);
furthermore, he should [consecrate] the barren woman with those mantras beginning with "akṣibhyām."
Having recited the *Tryambaka* mantra and performed the ritual cleansing of each limb with sacred waters,
one should place her facing east and consecrate her with water-pitchers.
O son, you will soon obtain a long-lived and illustrious [son].
One who desires clothing should offer oblations with flowers that bloom in their proper season.
By offering flowers of whatever color, one shall obtain clothing of that same color;
by offering grain mixed with sesame and clarified butter, one shall obtain a daughter.
One who desires the favor of the deities should offer oblations of kṛsara mixed with ghee,
or alternatively, milk-rice (pāyasa), one thousand and eight times.
Having himself consumed the remainder of the oblation, he, with his senses composed, should again recite this mantra while directing it toward the deity and the sacrificial fire.
In this matter, the goddess Bhūtāsā bestows the desired boon;
thus one should perform the rite for the welfare of the world under a lunar mansion presided over by Rudra.
By offering one thousand and eight oblations of *karavīra* wood fuel sticks, smeared with either oil or ghee, one shall indeed cause enemies to be driven away. Likewise,
by using [fuel sticks] produced from *nirguṇḍī* and equal in quantity to white *arka* sap...
One should cause a fire-oblation (homa) to be performed there; as it is being performed, the enemy wanders about. If one offers fuel-sticks of *unmatta*, the expulsion of the city will occur.
Whatever cruel acts, such as killing and so forth, are prescribed in the Kalpas,
all of that must never be performed by a Brahmin or even by a king.
In the thirteenth chapter of the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Liṅga Purāṇa,
Sūta said:
"With the Tryambaka mantra, [one should worship] the God of gods, Tryambaka."
One should worship [the Lord] either in a Bāṇaliṅga or in a self-manifested (svayambhū) one.
At the Ṛṣitīrtha and Devatīrtha,
he worshipped Śaṅkara with one thousand and eight lotuses (puṇḍarīka) in due order.
Having worshipped with a thousand red lotuses as well as blue lotuses,
and having offered milk-rice along with rice cooked in ghee once again;
He partook of fragrant foods consisting of mung beans mixed with honey,
and performed extensive fire-offerings according to the rules as prescribed in the past.
One should properly recite the mantra one million times with the previously mentioned flowers and especially with *caru*, for the sake of pacifying untimely death.
One seeking subjugation should offer three million oblations with *jātī* flowers;
O twice-born one, one should perform attraction using *karavīra* flowers with clarified butter.
One should effect incantation for enmity with *dālāhala* poison itself;
incantation for eradication is said to be performed with oil, and that for immobilization is remembered as being performed with honey.
Enchantment is said to be performed with sesame seeds, and striking with blood;
likewise, in due order, the immobilization of a donkey, an elephant,
or a camel is achieved with mustard seeds, and cleaving with garlic.
O you of excellent vows, killing and expulsion are accomplished by means of the seed-syllable of malice;
binding is performed with the leaf of the *snuhī* plant, and the paralyzing of an army follows thereafter.
With clarified butter, all success is attained; it is said that milk-rice with curd is likewise effective.
With sesame seeds there is the destruction of disease, and with lotuses wealth shall arise.
One should perform the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra with Madhūka flowers thirty thousand times;
beginning with the recitation and ending with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, it should be understood as being performed according to the previous procedure.
The same applies to the Rudrādhyāya—thus says the Vasiṣṭha-kalpa.
One should place [the mantra] "dā na he mā drau śau na kaḥ triyaṃbakaṃ yajāmahe" upon the topknot (śikhā).
"O fragrant one, increaser of nourishment"—with this [mantra], he places [the flower] on the heart;
"like a cucumber from its stem"—with this, on the two arms.
"From death" is at the secret place; "may I be released from immortality" is at the navel;
and [the mantras] are at the ankles, the shins, the knees, the thighs, the hips, and the genitals.
At the navel, on both sides of the abdomen, on the flanks, on the two thighs, on the two breasts,
at the heart, on the shoulder, on the belly, and on the elbow and the wrist.
The little finger, the ring finger, the middle finger, the forefinger, and the thumb [are placed] upon the hands;
[and one touches] the throat, the chin, the mouth, the nose, and the ears.
One should place the syllables of the mantra on the forehead, the head, and the topknot.
In the Devīpurāṇa: "Oṃ jūṃ saḥ"—this mantra is proclaimed as Mṛtyuñjaya (the Conqueror of Death).
This god is Mṛtyuñjaya, four-armed and three-eyed;
the god holds a rosary in his right hand.
In his left hand he should hold a nectar-pot filled with ambrosia;
granting boons, with hands [also] displaying fearlessness, and adorned with divine ornaments.
White and dressed in beautiful blue garments, he is seated upon a lotus;
his head is known to be the syllable *Tāra* (Oṃ), and *Hauṃ Juṃ Saḥ* is used for the worship of Śiva.
Furthermore, the eight Śaktis, conjoined with the five-syllable mantra, are to be worshipped:
Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, and Aparājitā.
Śiva, the conqueror of death, is to be worshipped with the mantra "Oṃ Jūṃ Saḥ."

Now, the ritual procedure (*prayoga*): Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*)— “For the sake of my own living body, without conflict, through the total eradication of such-and-such disease, by means of the removal of untimely death, for the purpose of swift recovery from illness, I shall perform the recitation of the *Mahāmṛtyuñjaya* mantra [or] have it performed through a Brahmin in such-and-such a number”— and having performed the worship of Gaṇeśa, the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkā-pūjana*), and the *Vṛddhi-śrāddha*, one should choose a preceptor (*ācārya*) with garments and other offerings.

Then the preceptor, having sipped water (ācamana) and restrained his breath (prāṇāyāma), having declared the place and time, shall say: "By the command of such-and-such [person], for the sake of quickly curing the disease of this person, I shall perform the worship, recitation, and other rites of Triambaka."

Having said this, one should prepare the seat with the mantra "Pṛthvi" and expel the obstructing spirits with "Apasarpantu. Then, having performed the three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma)—filling [the breath] through the left nostril with the root mantra and "Nala" repeated twelve times; holding [the breath] with the root mantra and "Yama" repeated sixteen times; and exhaling with the root mantra and "Rama" repeated thirty-two times.

With the twelve-fold repetition of "Yam"—having dried the body, burnt it with the fire-seed-syllable "Ram," and flooded it with the nectar-seed-syllable "Vam"—one should contemplate the emergence of the body from the Self according to the sequence: from space comes air, from air comes fire, from fire comes water, and from water comes earth. Having thus visualized the birth of the body and caused the nectar of "Vam" to flow, one should establish the foundation in the heart, contemplate "I am Śiva," bow to the chosen deity, and bow to the left-hand Guru, the Paramaguru, the Parāparaguru, and the Parameṣṭhiguru by uttering their respective seed-syllables and names; then, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra.

Now, for the great mantra of the illustrious Mṛtyuñjaya: Vasiṣṭha is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ). Its application (viniyoga) is in the recitation of the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra. *Tryambaka* is the pure seed-syllable (*bīja*), *Aṃ* is the power (*śakti*), and *Vaṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*)—according to the *Mantrakośa*. Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the seer and other elements upon the eyes, head, face, heart, private parts, and feet, and having purified the hands with the root mantra, one should place the *Praṇava* (*Oṃ*) on the palms of both hands. *Oṃ Agnaye hṛdayāya namaḥ* (Oṃ, salutation to the heart, [addressed to] Agni). *Tribakāya śirase svāhā* (To the three-eyed one, salutation to the head, *svāhā*). *Trinetrāya śikhāyai* (To the three-eyed one, [salutation] to the crest-lock).
To Vasiṣṭha, the armor, *huṃ*. To the Anuṣṭubh meter, the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*. Rudra is the deity; to the weapon, *phaṭ*.

Now, the six-limbed [mantra]: "Tryambakam" is for the heart; "Yajāmahe" is for the head; "Sugandhim puṣṭivardhanam" is for the tuft (śikhā); "Urvārukam iva bandhanāt" is for the armor (kavaca), with *huṃ*; "Mṛtyor mukṣīya" is for the three eyes, with *vauṣaṭ*; and "Māmṛtāt" is for the weapon (astra), with *phaṭ*.

Now, the ritual placement of the feet (pādanyāsa): Oṃ *tryambakaṃ yajāmahe*, salutation to the eastern face. Oṃ *sugandhiṃ puṣṭivardhanam*, salutation to the western face. Oṃ *urvārukam iva bandhanāt*, salutation to the southern face. Oṃ *mṛtyor mukṣīya mā amṛtāt*, salutation to the northern face. Oṃ, [the mantra] consisting of all the ṛcs, salutation to the upward-facing face.
The assignment of individual syllables (*adhākṣaranyāsa*):

everywhere, the sequence begins with *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ends with *namaḥ*. *Tryaṃ* at the base of the right foot; *baṃda* at the right knee; *kaṃ* at the right ankle; *yaṃ* at the bases of the toes of the right foot; *jāṃ* at their tips; *maṃ* at the base of the left foot; *haṃ* [at its tip].

*Suṃ* on the left knee; *gaṃ* at the roots of the toes of the left foot; *diṃ* on their tips; *puṃ* in the private parts; *ṣṭiṃ* at the base (ādhāra); *vaṃ* in the abdomen; *rdhaṃ* in the heart; *naṃ* in the throat. With the mantra "urvārukam" [and others], these are placed on the joints of the right arm; with "vabaṃdhanāmṛṃ" on the joints of the left arm; *tyoṃ* on the mouth; *rmuṃ* and *kṣiṃ* on the right and left nostrils; *yaṃ* on the two eyes; *māṃ* on the two ears; *mṛṃ* between the eyebrows; *tāt* on the head. Thus, having spoken these [syllables] below.

*Tryambakam* for the head; *yajāmahe* for the middle of the eyebrows; *sugandhim* for the eyes; *puṣṭivardhanam* for the mouth; *urvārukam* for the cheeks; *iva* for the heart; *bandhanāt* for the belly; *mṛtyoḥ* for the ankles; *mukṣīya* for the thighs; *amṛtāt* for the feet. Now the placement of the syllables (*akṣaranyāsa*): *Oṃ triṃ* for the head, salutation to the Atharvan; *yaṃ* for the two eyes, *baṃ* for the ears, *saṃ* for the nostrils, *kaṃ* for the mouth, *yaṃ* for the face, [and] *anilāya* for the face.

JĀṂ to Ānala, at the base of the right arm; KUṂ to Pratyūṣa, at the elbow; HEṂ to Prabhāsa, at the right wrist; SUṂ to Vīrabhadra, at the bases of the fingers of the right hand; GAṂ to Śambhu, at the tips of those fingers; DHIṂ to Giriśa, at the base of the left arm; PUṂ to Acaikapāda, at the left elbow; ṢṬIṂ to Ahirbudhnya, at the left wrist; VAṂ to Pinākin, at the bases of the fingers of the left hand, [and] RDHAṂ to Aparājita, at the tips of those fingers—[to all these] obeisance!

Naṃ, salutation to Bhuvanādhīśvara at the base of the right foot; uṃ, salutation to Kapālī at the right knee; rvāṃ, salutation to Sthāṇu at the right ankle; ruṃ, salutation to Bharga at the bases of the toes of the right foot; kaṃ, salutation to Thātṛ at their tips; miṃ, salutation to Aryaman at the base of the left thigh; vaṃ, salutation to Mīna at the left knee; baṃ, salutation to Varuṇa at the left ankle; dhaṃ, salutation to Dharma at the left foot; nāt, salutation to Bhaga at its [the foot's] toes; mṛṃ, salutation to Indra at the right side.

*Rtyoṃ* to Yama for the left side; *muṃ* to Pṛṣvā for the back; *kṣīṃ* to Parjanya for the eyebrows; *yaṃ* to Tvaṣṭṛ for the forehead; *māṃ* to Viṣṇu for the head—*namaḥ*; *mṛṃ* to Prajāpati for the throat; *tādvaṣaṭkārāya* for the heart—one should mutter the *praṇava*.

Now, another [method]: one should place these syllables of the *Triṃbakam* mantra on the front, back, right, and left sides of the face: *jāṃ* on the chest for auspiciousness; *heṃ* on the mouth; *su* on the two eyes; *ghiṃ* on the navel; *puṃ* on the heart; *ṣṭiṃ* on the back; *rthaṃ* on the two armpits; *naṃ* on the penis; *uṃ* on the anus; *rvāṃ* on the two thighs; *rudhakaṃ* on the two knees; *miṃ* on the two shanks; *baṃdhaṃ* on the two breasts; *nāṃsmṛṃ* on the two sides; *tyoṃrmuṃ* on the two feet; *kṣīṃ yaṃ* on the two hands; and *māṃ mṛṃ* on the two nostrils.

*Tāt* on the head. Below, the placement (*nyāsa*) as spoken by Śaunaka: *Tatpuruṣāya vidmahe* on the forehead; *mahādevāya dhīmahi* on the throat; *tanno rudraḥ pracodayāt* on the heart. *Tat* on the head; *ambakaṃ yajāmahe* on the crest-lock (*śikhā*); *sugandhiṃ puṣṭivardhanam* on the heart; *urvārukamiva bandhanāt* on the arms; *mṛtyormukṣīya mā'mṛtāt* on the navel. *Tyaṃ* on the feet; *baṃ* on the ankles; *kaṃ* on the shanks; *yaṃ* on the thighs; *jāṃ* on the hips; *maṃ* on the waist; *haṃ* on the penis; *suṃ* on the navel; *gaṃ* on the belly; *dhiṃ* on the sides; *puṃ* on the chest; *ṣṭiṃ* on the breasts.

*Vaṃ* at the heart; *dhaṃ* on the two shoulders; *naṃ* at the throat; *uṃ* on the two elbows; *rvāṃ* on the two wrists; *ruṃ* on the two little fingers; *kaṃ* on the two ring fingers; *miṃ* on the two middle fingers; *vaṃ* on the two index fingers; *baṃ* on the two thumbs; *dhaṃ* on the two palms; *nāṃ* on the two cheeks; *mṛṃ* on the chin; *tyoṃ* on the mouth; *rmuṃ* on the two nostrils; *kṣiṃ* on the two ears; *yaṃ* on the two eyes; *māṃ* on the forehead; *mṛṃ* on the crown of the head; *tāt* on the crest-lock (*śikhā*). These [syllables] alone are the mantras for conquering death.
O Lord, this same [mantra] is also used for the Mahāmṛtyuñjaya; however, one should utter the three Vyāhṛtis preceded by the Praṇava for every single syllable, as previously described.

Oṃ bhūḥ—Oṃ bhūvaḥ—Oṃ suvaḥ—Oṃ tryambaka. One should utter "Hauṃ," "Oṃ," "Juṃ," or "Oṃ Saḥ" at the beginning of each syllable or each word at the root of the right foot. Alternatively, this is the six-limbed (ṣaḍaṅga) mantra: Oṃ hauṃ oṃ juṃ oṃ saḥ oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya śūlapāṇaye svāhā—obeisance to the heart. Oṃ hauṃ oṃ juṃ oṃ saḥ oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya amṛtamūrtaye māṃ jīvaya—[obeisance] to the head.

Oṃ hauṃ oṃ juṃ oṃ saḥ oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya caṃdraśirase jaṭine śikhāyai | Oṃ hauṃ oṃ juṃ oṃ saḥ oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya tripurāntakāya hrīṃ hrīṃ kavacāya | Oṃ hauṃ oṃ juṃ oṃ saḥ oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya trilocanāya ṛgyajussāmamaṃtrāya svāhā netratrayāya vauṣaṭ |

Oṃ hauṃ oṃ juṃ oṃ saḥ oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya pralayāgnirudrāya netratrayāya jvala jvala māṃ rakṣa rakṣa aghoramūrtaye astrāya phaṭ. Now, the third six-limbed [mantra]: Oṃ hauṃ oṃ juṃ oṃ saḥ oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya triyaṃbakāya trinetrāya tripurāntakāya tryambakaṃ hṛdayāya.

Oṃ hauṃ oṃ juṃ oṃ saḥ oṃ. Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, Rudra, the blue-necked one, whose crest is adorned with the moon, who showers nectar; we worship you for the head. Oṃ hauṃ oṃ juṃ oṃ saḥ oṃ. Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, Rudra, who is clothed in a tiger skin, the one with matted locks; [we offer] the fragrant [incense] that increases the mass [of hair] for the tuft.

Oṃ hauṃ oṃ juṃ oṃ saḥ oṃ. Homage to the Blessed Lord Rudra, the wielder of the Pināka bow, adorned with serpents, bearer of the staff and garland, [who cuts] the armor-like bondage as if it were a gourd; huṃ. Oṃ hauṃ oṃ juṃ oṃ saḥ oṃ. Homage to the Blessed Lord Rudra, whose mantra is the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, who is the form of light, the essence of knowledge; may I be liberated from death; [homage] to the three eyes.

Oṃ hauṃ oṃ juṃ oṃ saḥ oṃ. Homage to the Blessed One, Rudra, whose seed-syllable is fire, who wards off malevolent planets, the one with matted locks, whose form is non-terrible (Aghora). Blaze, blaze! O Rudra, wielder of the spear and trident, protect me, protect me from all directions! To the Non-Terrible One, to the immortal weapon, Phaṭ! Then, having drawn the yantra: a circle in the center of the pedestal, outside that a square, outside that a hexagon, outside that two sets of eight petals, and then a square.

For Dharma, for Knowledge, for Dispassion, for Sovereignty; for Adharma, for Ignorance, for Non-dispassion, for Non-sovereignty; for Kṛta, for Tretā, for Dvāpara, for Kali; for Sattva, for Rajas, for Tamas; for the Solar Orb, for the Lunar Orb, for the Orb of Fire; for Fire—having thus worshipped.
This god is Mṛtyuñjaya, possessing four arms and three eyes;
the god holds a rosary in his right hand,
while with his left he holds a water-pot filled with nectar.
Bestowing boons and granting prosperity, with hands in the gesture of protection, adorned with divine ornaments,
clad in white and deep blue garments, he is seated upon a lotus.
Thus, in the Hemādri.
In her two hands resting upon her lotus-feet, she holds two full jars;
with two others, she holds a rosary and a water-pot, both of which are eternally full.
May that very Lord, who bears upon His head the beautiful crescent moon dripping nectar from those two [streams],
and who possesses a multitude of ornaments, enter into our prosperity forever.
Thus, according to the method of the *Prapañcasāra-mantrakośa*.
Or one may meditate on the Lord as having tawny matted locks, adorned with serpent ornaments,
twelve eyes, five faces, and eighteen arms.

I worship Lord Śiva, who is seated upon Kailāsa, who bathes his head with the nectar-essence from two jars held in his hands, who holds a deer-skin and a rosary with two other hands, who carries a supreme vessel of nectar placed upon his two arms resting on his lap, who is adorned with a crown of the new moon, possesses three eyes, and dwells within the heart of the devotee.

Thus, having visualized [the deity] at the root of the tongue and through the path of the tip of the nose, one should invoke the deity into the center; then [perform] the rites of installation (sthāpanī), bringing near (sannidhāpanī), and confinement (sannirodhinī).

Having displayed the mudrās, one should offer the seat (āsana), water for the feet (pādya), water for the face (arghya), water for sipping (ācamana), honey-mixture (madhuparka), the bath (snāna), clothing (vastra), the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), fragrance (gandha), and flowers (puṣpa) with the root mantra.
One should perform the *āvaraṇapūjā* (peripheral worship):

Īśāna in the center; Tatpuruṣa at the eastern face; Vāmadeva in the south; Aghora in the west; Sadyojāta at the northern face. Then, in the six corners: *hrāṃ* to the heart; *hrīṃ* to the head; *hrūṃ* to the crest-lock; *hraim* to the armor; *hrauṃ* to the three eyes; *hraḥ* *hasta* *phaṭ* [to the weapon]. In front [of the deity], in the southwest, [worship] Pratiṣṭhā; in the [other] corners, Vidyā and Śānti. *Gaṃ* obeisance to Gaṇapati.

*Maṃ* to Mṛtyu, *namaḥ*; *maṃ* to Durgā, *namaḥ*; *kṣaṃ* to Kṣetrapāla, *namaḥ*. Thus on the four petals. On the eight-petaled [lotus], [offerings] to Brāhmī, Maheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, and Cāmuṇḍā. Outside of that, to Cañcabhairava, Krodhabhairava, Unmattabhairava, Kapālabhairava, Saṃharabhairava, Āpaduddhārabhairava, Kālabhairava, and Gaurabhairava.

Outside of that: *Laṃ* to Indra; *Raṃ* to Agni; *Yaṃ* to Yama; *Naṃ* to Nirṛti; *Paṃ* to Varuṇa; *Vāṃ* to Vāyu; *Saṃ* to Soma; *Īṃ* to Īśāna. Between Īśāna and Indra: *Āṃ* to Brahmā, *namaḥ*. Between Nirṛti and Paścima: *Hrīṃ* to Viṣṇu, *namaḥ*. Having thus worshipped, one should perform the offering of incense, lamp, food (naivedya), betel leaf, and the priest’s fee (dakṣiṇā), followed by the waving of lights (nīrājana), circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa), and prostrations (namaskāra).
O Great Rudra, conqueror of death, protect me who have come to you for refuge;
I am afflicted by birth, death, old age, and disease, and bound by the fetters of karma.
O Mṛḍa, I am always yours, my life is centered on you, and my mind is fixed upon you.
Having thus addressed the Lord of Gods, one should then mutter the supreme *Mṛtyuñjaya* mantra; having performed that recitation, one should again perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*).

One should offer the recitation (*japa*): ten thousand times for the *Vunascaraṇa* mantra. Then follows the ritual application (*prayoga*). Now, the extraction of the mantras (*mantroddhāra*): *oṃ bhūḥ | oṃ bhuvaḥ | oṃ suvaḥ | oṃ tryambakaṃ yajāmahe sugandhiṃ puṣṭivardhanam | urvārukamiva bandhanān mṛtyormukṣīya mā'mṛtāt | oṃ suvaḥ oṃ bhuvaḥ oṃ bhūḥ oṃ*—this is the *Mṛtyuñjaya*. With the verse alone: *oṃ jūṃ saḥ* is the first part; *oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ* is the second; *oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ* is the third. At the end, [the sequence is] in reverse order everywhere. Or, as for the *Mahāmṛtyuñjaya*: *oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ tryambakaṃ yajāmahe sugandhiṃ puṣṭivardhanam | urvārukamiva bandhanān mṛtyormukṣīya mā'mṛtāt | oṃ bhūḥ oṃ bhuvaḥ oṃ suvaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ sva

Oṃ hauṃ jūṃ saḥ oṃ bhūḥ oṃ bhuvaḥ | Oṃ svaḥ oṃ tryambakam ṛk | Oṃ svaḥ | Oṃ bhuvaḥ oṃ bhūḥ oṃ saḥ oṃ jūṃ oṃ hauṃ oṃ svāhā. This is the fourteen-fold *praṇava*. In the *Ṛgvidhāna*: "Restrained for three nights and fasting, one should cook a *caru* of milk-rice (*pāyasa*). With that, a twice-born man should offer a full hundred oblations of clarified butter, dedicating them to Mahādeva with the verse 'tryambakaṃ yajāmahe'. Having performed all this a hundred times, he shall live happily for a hundred years."
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the Mṛtyuñjaya [mantra].
Now, the repetition of the Puruṣasūkta; next, the ritual procedure for the Puruṣasūkta. In the Viṣṇudharmottara, Puṣkara said:
"O highly fortunate one, that which is remembered as the Puruṣasūkta is prescribed for each deity."
This purifying hymn to Madhusūdana, which grants all desires, should be known;
having bathed, one should offer handfuls of water while reciting each verse individually.
By reciting this Pauruṣa Sūkta while submerged within the water, one is liberated from all sins.
Freed from all impurities, he attains his desired destination;
having bathed with each individual verse, he should offer the merit to a Brahmin.

O Rāma, by bathing with even a single verse, one is liberated from all sins; having offered [the oblation], O Rāma, one obtains the fruit [of the rite] and attains all desires whatsoever that one wishes for in the mind.
Prāṇāyāma performed with the Pauruṣa Sūkta yields great fruit;
likewise, O Rāma, japa and homa destroy all impurities.
One who drinks liquor, one who kills a Brahmin, and likewise one who violates the preceptor’s bed,
shall be liberated from their sins by reciting the Puruṣasūkta.
Having previously purified himself thoroughly, he should go into the water at midday;
while bathing, he should daily recite the Pauruṣa Sūkta without sloth.
O Lord of Gods, O highly fortunate one, by subsisting for a year on vegetables, roots, and fruits, he himself shall enter into Vāsudeva.
O best of the Bhṛgus, he obtains whatever desire his mind longs for— supreme prosperity, as well as beauty and long life— and even the powers of aṇimā, laghimā, prāpti, and mahimā.
Whether one desires the removal of suffering or anything else whatsoever,
O Viṣṇu, by chanting this mantras of Puruṣa, one attains the supreme state.
This is supremely auspicious, most purifying, and the destroyer of the flood of suffering in saṃsāra;
it is declared to bestow happiness upon men who know the Dharma and to fulfill their heart's desires.
In the *Mahārṇava-Ṛgvidhāna*:
"I shall describe the procedure for the recitation of the *Puruṣasūkta*,
as well as the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), the rules for silent recitation (*japa*), and the hymn (*stotra*) consisting of that very [sūkta]."
Having bathed according to the prescribed rule, the wise one with a purified mind should place the first [mudrā] on the left hand and the second on the right hand.
One should place the third [step] on the left foot and the fourth on the right;
the fifth on the left knee and likewise the sixth on the right.
The seventh [syllable] is on the left hip, the eighth likewise on the right;
the ninth is in the middle of the navel, and the tenth likewise in the heart.
One should place the eleventh [tithi] on the throat, the twelfth on the left buttock,
the thirteenth on the right, and the fourteenth in the region of the anus.
One should place the fifteenth [syllable] on the right arm and the sixteenth on the head.
Having performed the ritual of placement (nyāsa) in this manner, one should perform the assignment of the five limbs (pañcāṅga).
The assignment of the five limbs is performed with the Rigvedic verses beginning with "brāhmaṇo'sya".
The heart, the head, the crest, the armor, and the weapon—these are the five limbs.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the prescribed rule upon the deity just as one does upon the body, [one should proceed].
First, having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should perform the two types of ritual placement (nyāsa).
For this hymn (sūkta): Nārāyaṇa is the seer (ṛṣi); Puruṣa is the deity;
Anuṣṭubh is the meter for the first verse, and Triṣṭubh for the others; its application is in recitation (japa).
In that regard, the Lord has declared that for both recitation (*japa*) and fire-oblation (*homa*), the *ṛc* mantra alone is mandatory. One should invoke the God Puruṣottama with the first [verse],
offer a seat with the second, and likewise offer water for the feet (*pādya*) with the third.
The fourth offering (arghya) should be presented, and likewise the fifth with *mana*.
One should perform the bath on the sixth day, and the clothing on the seventh.
On the eighth day, the sacred thread; likewise, on the ninth, ornaments;
on the tenth, the offering of fragrant paste; and on the eleventh, a garland.
On the twelfth day, one should offer incense; on the thirteenth, a lamp;
on the fourteenth, an offering of food (naivedya); and on the fifteenth, a prostration.
The dismissal (udvāsana) belongs to the sixteenth [rite], while the ritual services (upacāra) are sixteen;
one should offer water for rinsing the mouth (ācamanīya) during the bathing, the clothing, and the food offering (naivedya).
Whoever should offer even a handful of flowers with the Puruṣasūkta, [attains the supreme goal].
By him indeed, the entire triple world, including all things mobile and immobile, is honored;
therefore, one should cause sixteen verses to be offered according to one's ability.
Then one should perform circumambulation and recite prayers with a concentrated mind;
having recited according to one's capacity, one should offer the hymn to that deity.
On the right side of the deity, one should have a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or a leveled altar (sthaṇḍila) prepared;
first, one should perform the worship, and then the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) with the third [mantra].
The third [verse] is for the measuring of the fire-altar; the fourth is for the kindling of the fuel;
the fifth is for the preparation of the clarified butter, as well as for the hearing of the praise.
Having visualized the center of the Nala [lotus], one should conceive of it as a lotus-mind;
there, one should meditate upon the Lord of Gods, whose splendor is equal to that of Kālanala.
One should offer perfume, flowers, incense, and a lamp to the one with the mouth turned upward, whose head is turned outward, and who has a red face and red eyes.
Then one should perform the [offerings] with the twenty-fifth [verse], starting from the seventh [verse] in due order;
the meaning is that one should worship in the fire.

First, one should offer oblations with fuel-sticks (samidh) verse by verse, using those that have been sprinkled with ghee; thereafter, one should offer oblations with clarified butter (ghṛta), and then again with the sacrificial porridge (caru).
Having thus performed the oblation and then having requested permission in due order,
one should recite the hymn of praise in the presence of the Blessed One, the Fire-god.
Victory to you, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, O creator of the universe!
Salutations to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, Great Puruṣa, Primordial Being!
Salutation to Hiraṇyagarbha, whose form is both primordial matter (pradhāna) and the unmanifest;
Oṃ, salutation to Vāsudeva, whose nature is pure knowledge.
I go for refuge to you, the common presiding deity of both gods and dānavas, whose conduct is universal and who transcends all dualities.
May you alone be the creator and destroyer of this world,
its supervisor and its permitter, veiled by the *māyā* of the *guṇas*.
Having taken refuge in you alone, the wise cross over the terrible ocean of saṃsāra and the endless destruction of afflictions.
You have no form, no appearance, no weapons, and no abode;
nevertheless, you manifest in the form of a person for the sake of your devotees.
Nothing at all, whether hidden or manifest, belongs to anyone;
nor is anything at all established as dual for anyone.
The wise declare you to be the primordial cause of all effects, the supreme sentence of all words, and the ultimate perfection attained by yogins.
O Lord of Gods, O lotus-eyed one, I am terrified in this fearful cycle of existence; I do not know any other supreme refuge from this sinner.
O Acyuta, at all times and in all directions,
even when the body has perished, these two great fears continue to persist.
Other than your lotus feet, there is no other cause for even a single virtuous deed in future births,
by which I might attain a good rebirth.
O Lord, may this consciousness which has been attained, which is devoid of [worldly] knowledge,
not suffer destruction for me in another birth.
Even for one born into a low state, you are the refuge; you are my intellect.
If I were to find even a fraction [of this], by that alone I would always be fulfilled.
This unblemished night stands at my feet;
may that Vaiṣṇava reality alone be mine throughout all births.
Having praised the God day after day with this very hymn of praise,
one should offer oneself to the God, saying, "What shall I do?"
One who subsists on gathered fruits should daily recite this hymn to Puruṣa Hari, which leads to heaven, bestows wealth, and brings fame, while perceiving the Self within the self.
Subsisting on fruits, he should observe fasts; he should not associate with people, but dwell constantly in the forest as a sage, muttering this mantra of the Ṛṣi.
At the time of the three daily libations (triṣavaṇa), one who is composed should recite the Ṛṣi-mantra in the waters;
this means that during the bath, one performs the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) with these [verses] and the Aghamarṣaṇa.
One should always stand facing the sun while reciting this hymn;
having offered oblations of clarified butter with this very hymn, one should thus meditate upon the Ṛṣi.
The seer who perceived this hymn is Nārāyaṇa;
one who subsists on fruits for a month and recites this for three years [attains success].
Devoted to Him, with his mind fixed on Him, and remaining single-minded for ten years,
he shall behold that very Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is free from all affliction.
Even when feeling distressed, one should treat a devotee with gentle humor;
by being compassionate toward his devotees, the Blessed One becomes the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Whatever desire one may have, if one recites [the mantra] with constant effort, that desire will be attained; this is for one who acts with faith and whose prosperity is fully realized.
One should perform a fire sacrifice (homa), or recitation (jāpya), or an offering of honeyed oblation (madhucarū),
by whatever desire one seeks to attain its fulfillment.
Preeminence among kinsmen, great wealth, fame in the world,
the supreme goal, and liberation from sin— all this would come to pass, yet it remains accompanied by doubt.
Now, the ritual for one desiring a son is declared:
it should be performed during the bright fortnight, on a Friday, under an auspicious lunar mansion and a favorable planetary conjunction.
On the twelfth day, one who desires a son should prepare a Vaiṣṇava caru;
meanwhile, the couple should observe a fast on the eleventh day in the temple of the gods.
Having properly worshipped Janārdana with sixteen Ṛg-verses,
O son, one whose mind desires offspring should cook the sacrificial oblation (caru) with the Puruṣasūkta;
such a son shall indeed soon obtain a Vaiṣṇava lineage capable of perpetuating the family.
On twelve occasions of the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), one should offer a sacrificial oblation (caru) prepared with pure milk;
he who performs this a thousand times goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Having properly offered oblations into the fire according to the rules with the sixteen Rigvedic verses, the wise man attains the highest state.
Having joined his palms in reverence, he should employ these hymns of praise.
They know Keśava in Mārgaśīrṣa, and Nārāyaṇa in Pauṣa;
Mādhava in the month of Māgha, and likewise Govinda in Phālguna.
One should know Viṣṇu in Caitra, Madhusūdana in Vaiśākha,
Trivikrama in Jyeṣṭha, and Vāmana in Āṣāḍha.

In the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should know [the form] as Śrīdhara; after that, as Dṛṣikeśa; in Āśvina, as Padmanābha; and after that, as Dāmodara. One should offer oblations to these twelve names every month.

One should prepare a *caru* oblation in milk according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra* at the time of the *Śravaṇā* asterism; then, reciting the entire hymn (*sūkta*), one should offer it as a single oblation, and thus perform a thousand-fold *homa*.
And it should not be performed after ten thousand recitations—
having commenced on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight and recited ten thousand times,
one should fast as a couple on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight and [perform the rite] on the twelfth day.
"One should offer a thousand oblations"—thus says the Mahārṇava. Now, there is another method: fasting on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī).
For a married couple, this Puruṣasūkta should be recited at the proper time without conflicting with their daily obligatory duties;
one should recite this Sūkta continuously on every Ekādaśī.
In this manner, one should offer a caru oblation with milk on each of the twelve twelfth days;
likewise, there is no rule for fasting on the eleventh day or for offering clarified butter without first performing the fire sacrifice.
The wise Vatsātreya,
having joined his palms in reverence, should employ those [mantras] consisting of sixteen Ṛg-verses while facing the fire.
Having offered fuel-sticks from the *aśvattha* tree, one should again offer clarified butter;
then, meditating upon Madhusūdana, one should perform the propitiation (*upasthāna*) of the Fire with the mantra "agne naya" (O Agni, lead us), according to the Great Ocean [of Tradition].
But it is proper [to worship] with the Puruṣasūkta alone.
Being pure and restrained in speech, one should continuously perform the offering of the oblation according to each verse-verse (ṛc).
One should offer clarified butter with the hymn, as before, at the beginning and at the end.
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa, her husband, the woman should eat the remainder of the sacrificial offering;
having consumed the remnants of the *havis*, she should sleep on the ground—this is the meaning.
Then, O twice-born one, having performed the *āvid* rite, the libation (*tarpaṇa*) must be performed.
He should desist from a second woman until she conceives a child.

One should not approach another woman, even during her fertile period (*ṛtu*), having abandoned the woman with whom this ritual act was performed; however, there is no fault in performing the vow together with all [wives].

Even during the fertile period, there is indeed no fault in not approaching another wife—though it is a minor transgression. In that regard, if one is capable, the *prājāpatya* penance applies; if incapable, the three-night or two-night fasts and so forth. A woman who is childless or whose children have died should procreate through a *niyoga*. As Ṛṣyaśṛṅga has declared: "She shall quickly give birth to a son."
Bṛhat-Parāśara has likewise declared this rule:
at the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa), one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of a cow, clothing, and sesame seeds.
Land, gold, and foodstuffs, according to their availability.
Thus the person is described according to the prescribed rule.
Furthermore, in rites such as the recitation of mantras (*japa*), the installation of a lamp must be performed; it is as follows:
one should first write the pairs of vowels, and having written the classes of consonants (*varga*) beginning with *ka* in their proper sequence.
The sages declare that the place where the imperishable yantra, beginning with the syllables *sthā* and so forth, resides is the location of the lamp.
This very thing is the tortoise-wheel (*kūrma-cakra*), whose division is determined by the first letter of the name;
it is called "the mouth of the tortoise" (*kūrmamukha*) in the *Śivacandrikā*.

One should place the eight vowels beginning with *a* and the pairs of consonants (*svaradvandva*) starting from the east and so forth. One should always place the letters beginning with *u*, *ga*, and *d* in the ten directions, excluding the intermediate points (*chidra*). Furthermore, one should determine which direction the final letter of the village's name occupies.
In that regard, the tortoise-faced [lineage] is to be known as being among the other limbs and elsewhere;
one should know that the accomplishment of mantras resides in the mouth, while the fruit in the hands is slight.
Futility occurs between the two feet, and indifference resides in the feet;
moreover, killing, imprisonment, and poverty arise in the region of the tail.
Thus, some say that [the recitation] is for the feet of Rudra; others, however, state that because this pertains to non-tantric *japa*, it follows the rules of Vedic *japa*.
An exception to this is stated in that very same work:
One should not consider the installation of a lamp at Kurukṣetra, during a ritual performance, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, at Mahodaya, or in Kāśī.
Thus ends the section on the location of the lamp.

The procedure for the *puraścaraṇa* of the Rudra-mantra is here set forth after examining the commentaries of Saccidānanda Bhāratī, Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara, Vidyāraṇya, and the *Mahārṇava* of Hemādri, among others. In this regard, the employment of the Rudra-mantra is seen in the Vedas, Smṛtis, and other texts for recitation (*japa*), burnt offerings (*homa*), and ritual ablution (*abhiṣeka*). Regarding this, the Jābāli Śruti asks: "Tell us, by what recitation do we attain immortality?"

"By means of the Śatarudrīya, by these invocations of the immortals, one becomes free from sin"—thus it is said in the Kaivalya Upaniṣad: "He who studies this Śatarudrīya becomes purified from the theft of gold, purified from the murder of a Brahmin, purified from the performance of malevolent magic, and he attains the fruit of liberation."
In the Hemādri, Bodhāyana states:
"Now we shall explain the procedure for the recitation, fire-oblation, and worship of the five-limbed Rudras.
The word "procedure" (vidhi) is to be construed with each of the acts, beginning with recitation.
Worship and consecration constitute the great ocean; thus says Parāśara.
Having drunk liquor, having approached the wife of his guru, having committed theft,
and having even committed the murder of a Brahmin—
covered in ashes and lying upon a bed of ashes.
By reciting the Rudrādhyāya, one is liberated from all sins.
This should be understood as being for one month, performed with great care.
"One should become a reciter of the Rudrādhyāya with devotion for one month without sloth;
this shall be the expiation for the secret [offense], there is no doubt"—thus from the Parāśara Purāṇa.
In the *Śivagītā* within the *Padmapurāṇa*:
"One should constantly mutter the Rudra-mantra while meditating on my form."
Or, with body free from impurity and senses conquered, he should recite the six-syllabled mantra or the *praṇava*,
or else the *Atharvaśiras* mantra or the *Kaivalya* [Upaniṣad], which is most excellent.
With this very body, Śiva is certainly attained.
In the *Vāyanīya*: "In all defects caused by the planets, upon seeing bad dreams or portents,
a Brahmin who recites the *Rudras* even once is liberated from all defects."
Yama said:
By reciting the Pañcabṛhat, the Vālakhilyas, the Nivids, the Preṣas, the Vṛṣākapi, the Hṛcchūnas, and the Rudras once, one is liberated from all sins;
especially so by reciting the Śukriyas, the Āraṇyakas, the Dvāpas, and the Gāyatrī.
For these, as well as the Rudraikādaśinī, are indeed the removers of all sins.
Hemādri quotes Kauśika and Bodhāyana:
"This Rudraikādaśinī bestows the fruits of all desires; it causes the destruction of all sins and grants all forms of peace."
In the Viṣṇudharmottara as well:
"Likewise, the recitation of the Rudra-mantras brings destruction to all [obstacles];
the fire-oblation (homa) fulfills all desires and likewise bestows peace everywhere."
Of dogs that have not been born [of their own kind], as well as of elephants, cows, humans,
kings, children, and even women.
O Bhārgava, knower of dharma, [you have described] the instruction regarding villages, the Sagaras, and regions,
as well as calamities and those who are afflicted by disease.
When one has encountered death, enemies, or likewise fear,
a fire-offering (homa) of blood brings supreme pacification, as does an offering of milk-rice (pāyasa) or clarified butter (ghṛta).
In the *Kālikā Purāṇa*, as cited in the *Hemādri*:
"Furthermore, he who constantly worships the Moon-crested Lord with devotion..."
One who always recites and meditates upon the Rudrāṇī attains the supreme state.
In this world, there is some fruit, and likewise, abundant fruit in the hereafter;
indeed, by reciting those very [mantras] while remaining pure and composed,
one desires to make this entire world as white as the moon.
Then one should mutter the Rudra-mantra while meditating upon Maheśvara;
by that, the Rudra is said to be threefold: the Japa-Rudra, the Homa-Rudra, and the Abhiṣeka-Rudra.
The first is twofold: consisting of recitation (japa) and the limb of fire-oblation (homa).
In this regard, Atri and Aṅgiras say:
"Even one who has committed the eleven sins, by reciting the Rudra hymns, becomes a knower of dharma;
even if touched by great sins, he is liberated—of this there is no doubt."
"All sins are destroyed by the Rudraikādaśinī," as stated in the Kālikā Purāṇa and other texts, where it is taught that [the result comes] from mere recitation (japa).
From the japa, the homa is said to be one-tenth; likewise, from the homa, the tarpaṇa;
and from the tarpaṇa, the mārjana is indeed prescribed as one-tenth.
One should also feed Brahmins with a tenth part of the number used for the ritual sprinkling (mārjana);
furthermore, there is the recitation of mantras (japa), worship (arcā), the preliminary fire sacrifice (homa), the crossing over (tarapaṇa), and the consecration (abhiṣecana).
The worship of the Brahmanas (Bhūdevas) and the preliminary rites (puraskriyā) as described in the fivefold method;
if one is unable to perform the fire-oblation (homa), one should perform recitation (japa) four times the number of oblations.

"Upon the performance of the *ekakṛta* (single-time) rite, the supreme accomplishment (*siddhi*) of the mantra arises," for it is stated in the *Puraścaraṇacaṃdrikā* and other works that when there is mere recitation (*japa*), the fire-oblation (*homa*) should be performed with a tenth part of that number.
By that [offering], the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and so forth are also accomplished;
however, in the case of *homarudra*, the libation and so forth are not at all necessary.
Others, however, maintain that according to those [texts] which state "by mere recitation" (*japamātre*), this procedure is indeed the *puraścaraṇa* itself;
for that very reason, there is no mention of libations (*tarpaṇa*) and so forth in the *Hemādri*, the *Mahārṇava*, and other such works.
Therefore, it has been said by him: "The burnt offering (homa), the recitation (japa), and the feeding of Brahmins—these three must be performed," so say the elders. The elder Yājñavalkya says:
A drinker of liquor, a stealer of gold, and one who recites the Rudra-hymn while standing in water,
as well as one who recites the Sahasra-śīrṣa hymn, are liberated from all sins.
For these, as well as the Rudraikādaśinī, are indeed removers of all sins;
by reciting the Veda even once, one is purified from that very moment.
In the *Kālikāpurāṇa* within the *Hemādri*:
"When one desires a great fruit pertaining to the world beyond in these worlds,
then one should constantly recite the Rudra-mantra while meditating upon Maheśvara."
And whoever should give away the earth, bounded by the oceans, together with its gold;
Therefore, even more than that, for him there shall be the merit arising from the recitation of the *Kṛrudra*.
In the *Vāyupurāṇa* it is likewise stated:
"The *Namaka*, the *Camaka*, and also the *Puruṣasūkta*."
One who constantly employs these three is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
One should also recite the Camaka, the Namaka, and the Puruṣasūkta;
he shall enter Mahādeva just as the master of a house enters his home.
Even one who possesses passion and is sinful, having conquered his senses by chanting the Rudra-mantra, [is purified].
Released from disease and sin, he enjoys incomparable happiness. In the fifty-third chapter of the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Liṅga Purāṇa:
"O best of the twice-born, I shall describe the procedure for conquering death; listen, O you of great power."
Restrained and following the prescribed order, one should perform [the rite] with ghee according to the ritual of the Rudrādhyāya.
With sesame seeds mixed with ghee, with lotuses,
and effortlessly with two spoons of honey mixed with ghee and cow’s milk.
One should offer oblations with ghee alone or even with milk;
this is proclaimed as the remedy for untimely death.
In the Sūtasamhitā: "He who, endowed with constant faith, daily practices the Śatarudrīya,
[is liberated] from the theft of gold, the drinking of liquor, and likewise from the performance of evil deeds."
"One is released from the murder of a Brahmin," so say the followers of the Kaivalya branch.
In the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"The self-controlled one performs intense austerity for thousands of years."
He who recites the Rudra mantra even once obtains the same fruit that one attains by making a gift of ten million cows according to the prescribed rites for the Guru.
There is nothing superior to the Rudras—neither recitation, nor meditation, nor sacrifice, nor austerity. It is thus.
In cases of defects such as childlessness and the like, and in cases of possession by Śākinīs and other spirits.
The recitation of the Rudra-mantra is determined for the destruction of all fevers;
Āpastamba says: "Rudra does not afflict the offspring or the cattle of one who performs it."
The ritual procedures for the hymns of the *yajña* and so forth are to be understood from the commentary on the *Rāva*.
In that regard, the vow is first described in the *Kālikā Purāṇa* within the *Hemādri*:
"Having first performed the *kṛcchra* penance oneself, one should likewise perform the *parāka*."
Having performed this study, O Mahādeva, one should practice thus again:
having bathed and worshipped Īśa, and having stayed for seven nights,
one should constantly recite the Rudras and consume that food which has been offered as an oblation.
When the next day has dawned, having thus completed the vow,

one should face the sun, fix one's gaze upon him, and recite [the mantra]. Furthermore, on the following day, having worshipped Rudra according to the prescribed rites, one should perform what remains to be done.
One should perform the oblation to Rudra with bilva leaves smeared with clarified butter.
Thus, by performing [the rite] correctly, that twice-born man becomes a performer of what is complete;
then, as the Great Radiance himself, he shall accomplish his desires.
Regarding the *śāntihoma*, Kauśika states:
"I, the twice-born Śaunaka, shall proclaim exactly that which was spoken by Bodhāyana."
For those with desires, it is half of all their desires; for those without desires, it is the Śatarudriya.

Having bathed at the sacred ford (tīrtha) according to the prescribed rite, either by means of the two *liṅga* mantras or with the mantra "mūrdhakeśa," one should tie a protective knot (*rakṣārdha*) in the topknot of the hair on the head.
One should request the elements with the mantra, "May they arise for that purpose," then,
having sat down in a pure place and restrained one's speech, one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Whatever is intended for the purpose of recitation, chanting, and fire-offerings is thus declared;
at that time, the *anuṣṭubh* meter of the *Rudrapraśna* becomes the sacrificial ladle (*sruva*).
Aghora, the destroyer of all sins, whose supreme deity is Āditya;
having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) and so forth with [mantras] ending in "namaḥ" and accompanied by the syllable Om (praṇava).
One should assign Īśāna with the eight mantras beginning with "Bilādya," which bestow auspiciousness;
Bhava at the feet, and Śarva in the middle of the thighs.
One should place Īśāna in the secret region and Paśupati at the navel;
having placed Rudra in the heart, one should place Ugra in the mouth.
One should place the Bhīma [mudrā] on the forehead and the Mahānta [mudrā] on the head.
One should perform the great kavaca-rite with each individual supreme weapon-mantra;
likewise, being pure, one should do so with the twelve mantras of the final section.
The first [syllable] should be placed at his feet, and the second in the region of the knees.
Having placed the third [digit] on the thighs, the fourth at the region of the anus,
the fifth at the region of the navel, and one should place the sixth on the heart.
The seventh [syllable] is in the region of the throat; the eighth, which is supreme, is in the mouth;
the ninth is in the nose; and the tenth is in both eyes.
One should place the eleventh [syllable] on the forehead and the twelfth on the head;
having placed the thirteenth as "huṃ" on the armor, one should then place "phaṭ" on the weapon.
Having thus performed the rite of ritual placement (nyāsa), one should then display the mudrās;
"This is your portion, O Rudra"—thus is the display of the mudrā.

One desiring prosperity should [worship] on the head; one desiring preeminence, on the forehead; one desiring splendor, on the eyes; one desiring other primary desires, on the face; and for the destruction of disease, on the neck.

One desiring all desires should show [the mudrā] at the heart; one desiring knowledge should show it on the nails; one desiring progeny should show it in the secret place; and one desiring cattle should show it on the shanks.
One who desires a village should show it at the knees; one who desires a kingdom at the feet;
and one who desires subjugation should show it at the left hand.
Or, when there is the destruction of evil, or likewise the departure of disease,
one should perform [the rite] outside the body while recollecting the command of Śiva.
Having thus demonstrated [the visualization],
one should then perform the meditation upon [the deity] who has three eyes, four arms, and is adorned with all ornaments.
Clad in an elephant hide with a tiger skin as an upper garment,
he is mounted upon the hump of a bull and wears the crescent moon upon his head.
Immersed in the nectar of immortality, peaceful, with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament,
resembling pure crystal, and adorned with a crown of matted locks.
Having thus properly meditated upon Hara, the remover of sins, who has hands granting boons and fearlessness and who bestows the fruits of all desires— the twice-born [attains his goal].
One who is fully devoted to devotion should perform the sacrifice of the limbs;
having recited the *Hṛdaya* mantra upon the heart, one should recite the *Puruṣasūkta* upon the head.
Having recited the Śukriya, the Uttara, the unsurpassed Nārāyaṇa,
and the invincible Kavaca, one should then recite the Śatarudriya.

Having recited the limbs (aṅgas), one should recite the peace-mantra (śānti) three times and utter "śānti" three times. [The mantras] beginning with "śāntiḥ," "śanno vātaḥ," and "namo vāce"—these three types of Rudras—should each be recited five times.
Rudra, Rudrī, Rudra, Mahārudra, and Rudra—these are the names;
therein, both the Namaka and Camaka constitute the form.
On another day, Tapa said: "The Rudra-ekādaśinī consists of six limbs;
from Rudra come eleven Rudras, and by means of these eleven, the Mahārudra is proclaimed."
He who consists of eleven great Rudras is called "Aitarudra."
Together with them, he is like a great, vast ocean.

Having recited the eleven *namaka* sections from the previous placement (*pūrvanyāsa*), one should recite the first *makānuvāka*. Having recited those again, one recites the second *makānuvāka*; thus, by this repetition eleven times, it is called "Rudra."
"Rudra is the eleventh," is the [Vedic] section; thus says Baudhāyana.
"One should mutter the eleven *anuvākas* beginning with *namaste rudra manyave*, and one *anuvāka* from the *camaka* section beginning with *agnāviṣṇū sajoṣasā*.
This means that after reciting all the *namaka* hymns, one should recite each *camaka-anuvāka* individually.
Therefore, there is no distinction; all should recite the Camaka in a single form.
By means of those eleven Rudras, it is called "Rudrī."
That very same Laghurudra is also called the Rudraikādaśinī.
