With those eleven [verses], it is the Mahārudra; with eleven repetitions of those, it is the Atirudra.
Hemādri quotes this very same [view] from Kauśika and Bodhāyana:
"The five-faced [forms] beginning with Sadyojāta, and likewise the eleven Rudras."
Having recited all the Rudra hymns, one should recite the Camaka at the beginning and at the end;
then one should recite all of this again, as well as the second Camaka.
This is the eleven-fold rule of Rudra, which bestows the fruits of all desires,
effects the destruction of all sins, and grants all forms of peace.
This very [power] is called Rudra when possessed of eleven qualities;
however, when the elevenfold qualities are greatly increased, he is here called Atirudra.
One should recite the Rudra and the Mahārudra according to the gravity of the task at hand;
this is the method for the Mahārudra and other such rites, following the procedure of the Ekādaśinī Rudra.
The rules for the time of recitation and for the consecration ceremony are the same for all branches of the Veda.
However, we shall now describe the elevenfold division of the Camaka hymns according to the followers of Kāṇva and Kātyāyana.
Likewise:
"Then one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with the mantra 'namaḥ śambhave'.
Having recited the Rudra eleven times, one should offer thirty-three oblations."
Then, the Laghurudra is said to consist of sixty-three [verses];
likewise, four thousand and seven hundred Rudras,
as well as forty-four thousand, are to be offered as oblations.
It is certain that there are seventy-eight minus one [seventy-seven] in the Atirudra;
it is for the destruction of sin, for the removal of obstacles, and likewise for liberation from disease.
The fuel sticks should be made of *pālāśa* wood, except in the event of seeing an omen;
likewise, there may be fuel sticks of *audumbara* wood, or those smeared with honey, or unbroken grains.
For one desiring food and drink, milk-rice (pāyasa) should be accepted for the sake of prosperity and peace;
for all desires, fresh grain should be accepted; and sesame seeds are prescribed for the sake of long life and intelligence.
One desiring splendor should offer dūrvā grass smeared with ghee;
one desiring cattle should offer rice grains; and one desiring a kingdom should offer barley.
If one sits in a pure place upon a clump of dūrvā grass and recites the mantra,
or performs oblations with white flowers, he brings the entire universe under his control.
The man who, having touched [the ashes], recites the Rudraikādaśinī one hundred times,
shall destroy diseases such as fever and dysentery, even those caused by the Lord of Creatures (Ulūpin).
Homa should be performed with fuel-sticks of *palāśa* mixed with honey;
furthermore, when the enemy's army approaches, one should perform it for the eleven Great Rudras.
One should recite the mantra eleven times; the fire-oblation (homa), however, is prescribed according to the ritual rules.
One should perform the rite with sesame seeds sprinkled with ghee, as taught in the Vedas.
In the recitation of the Rudraikādaśinī, one hundred is considered equal to one;
likewise, ten thousand Rudras are equal to one Nayāyuta.
In this way, the threefold form should be performed for Mahārudra and Atirudra;
it should be employed by one desiring rain, or for the pacification of diseases affecting elephants and horses.
For the emergence of wonders and for the pacification of the afflictions caused by the planets and the like, sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter should be offered when the contrary occurs.

At the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa), for the sake of all desires, one should offer clarified butter according to the prescribed rite with the Kuṣmāṇḍa mantras and likewise with the Mahāvyāhṛtis.

Then, having sprinkled water around the fire and worshipped it with the mantra "tat tvā yāmi," one who is pure should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) using mantras containing the syllable *svāhā*.
Having first worshipped Śiva together with Pārvatī at the beginning and at the end,
and having worshipped the world-protectors (lokapālas) like a treasure-trove in the presence of the Lord, [one should proceed].
Having bathed Gaṅgā and Durgā according to the prescribed rite with mantras and the offering of water for the ablution, one should quickly perform a salutation.
Having gratified the pure Brahmins, who are themselves pure, with two kinds of food, or with milk-rice (pāyasa) and milk, saying,
"May Śambhu be pleased," and having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to those at the end [of the row],
he should bow down and dismiss them.
When this is done, that Blessed One bestows the objects of their desire for joy.
For one who is without desire, there is no need for deliberation regarding the fruit of liberation;
however, this mantra spoken by Bodhāyana is for the fulfillment of all desires.
Thus ends the Rudra-vidhi in the Hemādri; this method of the Rudraikādaśinī belongs to the Āpastamba Śākhā and is intended for those devoted to the Rudra.
However, for those of the Mādhyandina and Kaṇva Śākhās, there is an absence of the eleven Anuvākas in the Camaka.
Having divided the *ccamakāna* into eleven parts, one should perform the *yājyaikādaśinī* by offering each single part in the *namaka* verses.
In the *Homepya*, it is stated that here the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is optional; some say this is because of the statement "of the five-limbed Rudras.
Regarding the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), there are six [limbs] according to that [text], while others say there are five. Thus says Mahārṇava.

The placement of the five limbs (*pañcāṅganyāsa*) is performed with the *bodhayana* mantras from the Taittirīya branch, while the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is for those of the Vājasaneyī school and others; furthermore,
according to some, it is performed with the mantras spoken by Bṛhat-Parāśara.
Beyond the uninitiated Rudra-pareti rite,
there is that which is found in the Sāmavidhāna Brāhmaṇa of the Chāndogas.
The *Āvorājā*, the *Tadvovarga*, the *Ājyadohāni*, and the *Devavratāni*— this collection is named the *Raudrī*. It has been stated that by employing this, one pleases Rudra.
The *āvo rājā* is a single *sāman*; that constitutes one section; there are four [sections].
The three Ājyadohas and the three Devavratas—
this constitutes another ritual application (prayoga) for half a palāśa leaf.

However, there is no authoritative basis for these [practices] regarding the performance of the Mahārudra and other rites. Therefore, the performance of the Mahārudra by the Ghūrjaras using the twelve Sāmans,
as well as that performed by the Ṛgvedins using the Rudra-sūktas, is without foundation.
One should disregard the notion that [the mantra] is merely a supreme delusion or a conceit;
furthermore, because it serves as a substitute, for this very reason Bṛhat-Parāśara states: "One should perform the ritual procedure."
It has been stated that [the ritual] for the Rudras is commensurate with the Yajurveda.
Now follows the specific rule for the Kātyāyanas as stated by Bṛhat-Parāśara: regarding the mantras beginning with "iṣe" and ending with "khaṃ brahma."
Regarding the rites performed with the ten *praṇavas*:
a *praṇava* should be placed at the beginning of the mantra and another *praṇava* at the end of the mantra;
then, joined with the *vyāhṛtis*, these constitute the ten *praṇavas*. This is one view. Another, however, is as follows:
First, having uttered the *praṇava*, then all the *avyāhṛtis*;
the *praṇava* should be employed at the beginning of the mantra, and the *praṇava* again at the end of the mantra. Thus it is said:

One should first remember that group of five mantras beginning with "manojyotir juṣatām agniḥ," "agnirmūrdhā," "mūrdhānam," "marmāṇi te," and "jātavedāḥ," as well as the "mānastoke" mantra for the secret parts.

Then, having performed the first nyāsa of the ten-syllable mantra with the words beginning with "tato yāte rudra" and the second with those beginning with "trātāram," he spoke according to the tradition of Bodhāyana regarding the *sampuṭa* (encasement).
"Then one should eject the guardians of the directions, such as Sūtrāmāṇ and the others, from the east and so forth;
having performed that very *raudrīkaraṇī* [rite], one is liberated from sin.
Since this has been stated in such passages—
One should meditate upon the five-faced Soma as one's own self, adorned with all ornaments,
bearing the deer-mark on his head, and resembling pure crystal.
He wears a crown of matted locks from which the seven-flamed fire blazes forth, adorned with a crest and a garland of the lord of serpents, who hisses with a thousand hoods.
He was resplendent with a thousand arms, adorned with a khaṭvāṅga staff and other ornaments;
he was brilliantly shining, possessing three eyes like the blazing fire of the moon and sun,
and he held a vibrating damaru drum whose sound deafened the world.
Adorned with armlets upon the heads of lordly serpents and shining with jewels,
it was resplendent with the tinkling sound of pearl strings and girdles of small bells.
With anklets making an indistinct gurgling sound as they moved,
she wore a blue silk cloth and a tiger-skin upper garment.

The twice-born, having meditated upon himself as being fully endowed with the deities of the quarters and saluted by gods and demons, should contemplate his own self as truly having the form of Rudra.
Having completely destroyed all obstacles, he should then begin the sacrifice.
On a secret and well-anointed spot the size of a cow-hide,
having drawn a sacrificial diagram (sthāṇḍila) shaped like the moon, he should then inscribe that mantra upon it.
The meaning of "ten-syllabled" is as follows: there, one should perform the worship and other rites with the mantra "namaḥ śambhave."
However, as for those [texts] which omit the installation of eleven jars and,
therein, omit the worship of Rudra and the consecration with the Rudra-mantras,
that is another optional ritual application (*kāmyaprayoga*).
We shall explain that [mantra] up to the end of the Rudra section:
the twice-born should recollect the established mantra, "mā no mahāntam" and so forth.
One should also perform the secret placement (nyāsa) with the mantras containing the syllable *oṃ*, beginning with "mā nastoke."
With the mantra "śambhavāya," one should offer a vessel of scented water,
and having presented incense, food offerings, lamps, and so forth, according to what is available.
With that very same ten-syllable mantra, the twice-born should again offer salutation;
for that Rudra, the Śikhā-mantra is remembered as the Uttaranārāyaṇa.
The *Puruṣasūkta* is the head; the *Śivasamkalpa* is the heart; the *Kavaca* and *Aghamarṣaṇa* are the armor; and the *Vibhrāṭ*, *Bṛhat*, and *Amṛta* are the two eyes.
One should employ the Śatarudrīya weapon as the weapon of the deity.
Regarding the Śatarudrīya—the Rudradhyāya—it is specifically that [text] which states: "He offers the Śatarudrīya."
Because it is also designated by the term "Śatarudrīya."
Likewise, for the Taittirīyas as well, the Śatarudrīya— beginning with "O Agni, you are the great ocean" and ending with "O Rudra"— is indeed found in the Brāhmaṇa:
"The twice-born man should meditate upon the five fires and mutter the eight Praṇavas."
The five faces, beginning with Sadyojāta and so forth—as stated in the Hemādri:
"Having extracted the Lord with the *praṇava*, one should dismiss him with the *vauṣaṭ* syllable.
Having performed worship in this manner, one should perform the recitation (*japa*).
In that case, for the Ekādaśinī, there is no Camaka;
rather, there is an elevenfold repetition of the Rudradhyāya alone.
From the eleven Purāṇas—
"Having recited the Rudras, one attains the state of Rudra"—
thus [it is said] by Bṛhat-Parāśara and others, who prescribe the recitation of the Rudra alone.
Some, however, maintain that this is because the Camakas do not possess the designation of the word "Rudra."
Therefore, because that [procedure] belongs to another application, the Rudra-ekādaśinī is not included here;

for in the case of the Mahārudra and other such forms, only the recitation (japa) is mentioned by those who follow the Kāṇva school and the Kātyāyana tradition, and thus there is no occasion for the fire-oblation (homa) therein.
Having divided the eight *camaka* sections into eleven parts, one should recite them by returning to each individual portion; this indeed is the correct method.
Likewise, in the *homam*, the division of the *camakas* is as follows:
first, there are four *anuvākas*; then, "aśmā camu" and so forth, which comprise four [sections].
"Agni is our [friend], Indra is our [friend]"—these are three verses.
"Come hither, O bright one," and so on—these are three [verses].
"agniśca me dharmaśca me" and "amaḥ"—these two [verses].
"Ekā ca me tisraśca me"—this is the first [verse].
"Three sheep and one sheep for me"—this is one [verse].
And "traviśca me" and "trivṛdme" are two [verses].
The eighth [chapter] is "vāyajasayāha."
"Āyurjajñenaṃ," "iti dyauḥ," and "iyam tayorāṭ."
Let him try.
And [the formulas] beginning with "Soma" and "Yajus."

The root source for this is as follows: "Then he offers the *ardhendra* oblations; then he offers the *graha* oblations; then he offers this *yajñakratu* oblation; then [the mantra] 'atha heyaḥ te rāṭ'; then he offers the *kalpa* oblations; then [the mantras] beginning with 'athā hasto maśca yajuśca' and so forth; and 'ye yajāmahe' etc. Indeed, this eleven-fold division in the Śruti pertains only to this subject, because there is no other subject [to which it applies]. As for its true nature: since there is no sequential order (*anukrama*) among the divisions, one should join each [mantra] to a single *anuvāka*; thus it is stated in the Bodhāyana Sūtra, Hemādri, and other works.

Regarding the application of the *bhāgahara* (the portion-taker) by way of the sequence of the *vākya-anuṣaṅga*: it is proper that there be a triple repetition of the *vākya* itself within the *camakas*. As for the mantras beginning with "aṣṭākapālam," "indrāgnī," "upa sāmane," and those used when there is an increase in the *stoma*, one should recite twenty-one; so says [the tradition]. Since elsewhere the *camakas* are established through the rule of *prasidhyāgama*, and because the repetition is already obtained due to the eleven *prayājas*, and because Āpastamba has stated, "there is either an omission of the end or an increase," [the conclusion follows].

As for that which the Kātyāyanas and the Kāṇvas recite from the text of Paraśurāma: "One should recite the Rudra with its ancillaries (*sāṅga*) in the *dudra* [version]; however, in the *navāntara*, it is *kevala* [without ancillaries]. Some say the last form is *saśīrṣaka* (with the head), while others call it *viraṅga* (without ancillaries). Regarding this, some say that after reciting the final form, one should recite the ancillaries. Others, however, because there is no authority for the *saṃpuṭa* (enclosing) method, state that the ancillaries come first, followed by the Rudra, just as in the first recitation mode. They further state that the eight verses beginning with *vayam̐ some* constitute the head (*śīrṣa*), and the seven [verses] beginning with *ugraśca* are for the recitation of the Rudra. Such is their statement.

"O Lord, may my existence be uprooted; O Supreme One, may I be regarded as nothing more than the beyond (parā-mātra). May my heart be the *Śivasaṃkalpa*, my head the well-spoken *Puruṣasūkta*, and they say my tuft (*śikhā*) is the *Nārāyaṇīya*—meaning the *Uttaranārāyaṇa* beginning with 'adbhyaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ'.
May my armor (*kavaca*) be the *Āśuśiṣa* and my eyes the *Bṛhatsāman*;
may the *Śatarudrīya* be my weapon (*astra*)—this is declared to be the sequence of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*)."
O high-minded one, those who know the ritual procedures state that, according to their own scriptures, the six limbs of Rudra are: the heart, the crest, the armor, the eye, and the weapon.
The source for this is stated by Bṛhat-Parāśara:
"The sages, deities, and meters of these have not been mentioned at all. — Bṛhat-Parāśara.
One should first offer unbroken rice grains, sesame seeds, barley, or even fuel sticks,
sprinkled with clarified butter, into the fire while reciting "To Śambhu."
The twice-born practitioner should offer oblations five by five, or six, or eight, or eighteen, or ten by ten, or eleven.
One who is devoted to recitation, libation, fire-offerings, and so forth, should perform the recitation for one year.
Now, he states other applications:
"One desiring success, being self-controlled and subsisting on roots, tubers, and fruits..."
One should subsist on cow urine, barley gruel, milk, curd, vegetables, and clarified butter.
That Brahmin who subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya) and eats nothing else,
while performing recitations, fire-oblations, and other rites, shall obtain the fruit as it has been described.
The seven and eleven [deities] together with Rudra are certainly at the head of all mantras for that Brahmin who acts according to what has been taught.
Having duly brought those eleven auspicious jars,
together with gold, accompanied by cloths, and adorned with fruits and flowers;
One should worship them with devotion using scented water and unbroken grains (akṣata);
then, one should consecrate each [liṅga] individually with the eleven Rudra mantras.
Having thus fully worshipped those jars, and having paid homage and performed the consecration (abhimantrya),
one should worship either the eleven high-souled ones or a single benefactor.
Or, for one afflicted by Vināyaka, one should perform the Kākapaddhati bath;

for a woman whose children have died or who is barren, one should perform the bath and offer the oblation of rice (caru) with ghee. One should also give a bull, a garment, and a cow along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Upon the completion of the rite, one should likewise feed twenty Brahmins;
for the mantra beginning with "namo gaṇebhyaḥ," a single Brahmin should be engaged.
Having recited [the mantra] and offered oblations with bilva fruits (*śrīphala*), one becomes successful in all undertakings.
By repeating the mantra "namo astu nīlagrīvāya" seven times,
one should consecrate water and place it upon the ear of one afflicted by poison.
One is immediately freed from poison; even one bitten by a fatal snake survives.
Likewise, one afflicted by planetary spirits, ghosts, rākṣasas, or corrupted by śākinīs is liberated.
With the mantra "pramuñca dhanvan" (Release the bow), one should strike [the target] with ashes and mustard seeds while saying "muñca muñca" (Release, release!); it will be released very quickly.
Having recited the mantra beginning with "namaḥ saṃbhava" ten thousand times, the twice-born brahmin should then offer oblations one thousand times with fuel-sticks of khadira wood.
One should properly recite the mantra over the *kuṭaja* leaves for such-and-such a person;
by offering them into the fire with the utterance of "phaṭ," the one whose affliction is destroyed shall become happy.
If [the mantra] is recited one hundred times in the midst of water, immediate rain is said to occur.
Having entered water reaching up to his navel, the Brahmin should offer oblations into the water;
through the great majesty of the mantra, he shall thoroughly transform the earth into a single ocean.
This is how it should be understood—now follows the ritual procedure (*prayoga*):

having remembered the place and time, and having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus—"I shall perform the recitation and fire-oblation (*japa-homa*) of such-and-such a Rudra for the sake of such-and-such a desire, either myself or through a Brāhmaṇa," one should perform the worship of Gaṇeśa, the proclamation of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkā-pūjana*), and the *nāndī-śrāddha*, and then choose the preceptor (*ācārya*), the Brāhmaṇas, and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Then the officiating priests, remembering the place and time, should say: "For the sake of such-and-such a person’s such-and-such desire, I shall perform the recitation of the Rudra."
Having said this, they should perform the other [rites].
In this regard, the five types of nyāsa mentioned by Bodhāyana are common to all;
however, other nyāsas are mentioned in the Kātyāyana Pariśiṣṭa.
At the commencement of the Brahmayajña,
having bathed according to the rule, one should place the Chandas-puruṣa within one's body;
having said this, [one places] the Camasa [vessel] obliquely and upwards.
The foundation is his two eyes, O Gautama Bharadvāja.
One should assign Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni to the ears; Vasiṣṭha and Kaśyapa to the nostrils;
Atri to the voice; and Gāyatrī, the *chandas*, and Agni as the deity to the head.
One should assign Uṣṇih and Savitṛ to the necks, and Bṛhatī and Bṛhaspati to the chin.
The Bṛhatī is outside, the Rathantara is outside;
Indra is in the middle, with the Triṣṭubh.
Upon the two thighs [he places] the Jagatī and Āditya; upon the penis, the Atichandas and Prajāpati;
upon the two knees, Agni and the Yajñāyajñīya.
Vaiśvānara [is assigned] to the thighs; the Anuṣṭubh meter to the anus; the Viśve Devas to the stomach; the Pakti meter to the past; and Viṣṇu to the two feet as the Dvipadā meter.
He offers to Vāyu with the Prāṇeṣu verse.

By applying [the rules] to all the limbs—whether they are deficient or redundant—such as [assigning] a meter with fewer syllables or the waters (*apaḥ*) as the deity, one becomes composed of the Veda and becomes capable of both cursing and bestowing grace.

Brahmanic splendor proceeds; he finds no fear from anywhere. He who consists of the *Ṛg*, the *Yajus*, the *Sāman*, the *Atharvan*, the *Tejas*, and the *Amṛta*—having been born, he attains Brahman itself. Therefore, one should not speak this to one who is not a *brahmacārin*, nor to one who is not an ascetic (*tapasvin*), nor to one who has not dwelt for a year, nor to those who do not proclaim it. This [text] is thus [to be used] in the *brahmayajña* and in all recitations (*japa*) according to the prescribed sequence. We do not know what [fruit] comes from merely reciting this *Rudra* for a month.

Likewise: *jātavedase* is the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*); *catuḥsraktiḥ* is the seat; *mano jyotiḥ* is the heart; *abhodhyagniḥ* is for the head; *mūrdhānaṃ divaḥ* is for the crest-lock (*śikhā*); *marmāṇi* is the armor (*kavaca*); *viśvataścakṣuḥ* is the eye; *mā nastoke* is the weapon (*astra*). This is the assignment of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*). Among these, the first is the thirty-one-fold limb-assignment beginning with the crest-lock and ending with the weapon; the second is the ten-fold limb-assignment beginning from the head and ending at the feet; [the third] begins from the feet and ends at the head.

The third is the five-limbed assignment (pañcāṅganyāsa) from the secret parts to the head; the fourth is the five-limbed assignment from the heart to the weapon (astra); the fifth is the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa); and according to the system of sixteen limbs, the sixth is the sixteen-limbed assignment starting from the generative organ.
In the *Hemādri* and the *Mahārṇava*, Bodhāyana states:

"We shall explain the procedure for the recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), worship (*arcana*), and consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of the five-limbed Rudras, preceded by ritual placement (*nyāsa*). With the mantra 'Yā te rudra' [one places it] on the crest-lock (*śikhā*); with 'Asmin mahaty arṇave' on the head; with 'Sahasrāṇi' on the forehead; with 'Tryambakam' between the eyebrows; and with 'Haraṃ saśśuciṣat' on the eyes."

One should apply the mantras as follows: *ātrakātyāyanā nāmagnirjotiḥ* for the eyes; *namaḥ srutyāya* for the ears; *mānastoke* for the nose; *avatatya* for the mouth; *nīlagrīvau dvau* for the neck; *namaste astvāyudhāya* for the two arms; *yā te hetiḥ* for the forearms; *ye tīrthāni* for the hands; the five *anuvākas* beginning with *sadyojātam* for the five fingers; *namo vaḥ kirikebhyaḥ* for the heart; *ye vṛkṣeṣu* for the stomach; and *namaḥ śambhave* for the belly. *Namaḥ*.

On the back: "To the hosts" (gaṇebhyaḥ); on the two sides: "Homage to the golden-beamed one" (namo hiraṇyabāhave); on the belly: "The bow of knowledge" (vidyaddhanuḥ); on the private parts: "The golden embryo" (hiraṇyagarbhaḥ); on the anus: "The king born with the head" (saśirājātavedāḥ); on the thighs: "Do not harm us, O great one" (mā no mahāntam); on the knees: "He comes" (eṣata); on the shanks: "The conqueror of the enemy" (sagṛṣṭajit); on the ankles: "All that has become" (viśvaṃbhūtam); on the feet: "Those who [protect] the paths" (ye pathām); as armor: "Today he has spoken" (adya vocat); as the secondary armor: "Homage to the pot-bellied one" (namo bilmine); as the third eye: "Homage be to the blue-necked one" (namo astu nīlagrīvāya).

"Release the bow"—with this [mantra] one performs the *astra* (weapon) rite; "as many as these"—this constitutes the *digbandha* (binding of the directions). Thus is the *pradadyonnyāsa* (placement upon the womb).

One should perform the *samaskāra* (consecration) placement with: *oṃ namo bhagavate rudrāya*. Having placed the syllable *oṃ* on the head, the syllable *na* at the tip of the nose, the syllable *mo* on the forehead, the syllable *bha* in the middle of the mouth, the syllable *ga* in the region of the throat, and the syllable *va* on the heart—one should place the syllable *te* on the right hand and the syllable *ru* on the left. This is the second [placement].

In this regard, Kātyāyanī speaks of a third alternative method of placement (*nyāsa*): "One should place Rudra on the head, and Caṇḍeśvara on the forehead; one should place the three-eyed Lord Bhairava on the eyes, and Śiva on the nose."
One should place the god Śaṅkara on the nose, Paśupati on the face,
Nīlakaṇṭha at the region of the throat, and one should place the Pervasive Lord (Vyāpaka) upon the heart.
One should place the god Gaṅgādhara Śiva in the hand and in the navel.
One should place Mahādeva in the secret parts and Tryambaka on the shanks;
one should place Sarvajña on the feet and Śiva everywhere.
Thus, that [view] is rootless— according to Bodhāyana:
"Having placed Sadyojāta on the two feet, Vāmadeva in the middle of the thighs,
Aghora on the heart, one should place Tatpuruṣa on the mouth."
Having placed the name Haṃsa upon the head of Īśāna, he is ever Śiva;
he who should utter "Haṃsa, Haṃsa" is indeed the one named Haṃsa, the eternal Śiva.
Having thus performed the rite of nyāsa, one should then commence the saṃpuṭa.
From here, the third [section]:

"A protector, Indra" (RV 8.61.13), "O Agni, for us a path easy to traverse" (RV 1.90.1), "To him who presses [the Soma]" (RV 1.91.1), "That you come with your teams" (RV 1.84.15), "We [choose] that Soma" (RV 1.91.17), "The Rudras are with us" (RV 2.41.11), "Gentle is the earth" (RV 1.22.15)—having performed this encapsulation (*saṃpuṭa*) of Indra and the others in the directions, one should likewise effect the transformation of oneself into Rudra (*raudrīkaraṇa*).

One is liberated from all sins residing in the skin and bones and becomes unconquered among all beings. Then, [one should protect oneself] from the afflictions and injuries caused by Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, Brahma-rākṣasas, messengers of Yama, Śākinīs, Ḍākinīs, serpents, beasts of prey, thieves, and so forth; let them all behold me as a blazing Māra. Having consecrated the secret parts—the navel, heart, mouth, head, and face—with the mantra: "The mind is the light, Agni is the sky, Agni is the head, the head is the vital point, the vital point is the splendor, the splendor is the foundation," one should perform self-protection with the mantra: "O Brahman, you are my own self, created by yourself."
Thus, in four ways:

one should recite once the five-limbed [rite], consisting of the *Śivasaṃkalpa* as the heart, the *Puruṣasūkta* as the head, the *Uttaranārāyaṇa* as the tuft (*śikhā*), the first half-verse of "Āśuśśiśāna" as the armor (*kavaca*), and the *Śatarudrīya* as the weapon (*astra*). Having prostrated with the eight-limbed [salutation], one should recite the verses beginning with "Hiraṇyagarbho yaḥ prāṇataḥ," "Brahma jajñānam," "Mahī dyauḥ," "Upaśvāsaya," "Yā agne," "Naya yā te," "Agnim īḷe," and "Imaṃ yama prastaram. One should meditate upon oneself in the form of Rudra. Regarding this, in some places a half-verse is mentioned;
in all cases, however, this is the Taittirīya reading.

The *upabāhu* (forearm) is the *prakoṣṭha* (wrist). In the five fingers, beginning with the thumb and the index finger (*aṅguṣṭha-tarjanī-ādi*), there is the connection (*anuṣaṅga*) of the phrase "to the hearts of the gods" (*devānāṃ hṛdayebhyaḥ*) following the mantra "namo vaḥ kirikebhyaḥ" and so forth. In the mantra "namo hiraṇya... and so forth, the sacrifice ending in "namaḥ" is the head; "jātavedāḥ" is the downward part (*apāna*). For the sake of this meaning: for the verse "jātavedase sunavāma," [the mantra is] "agne tvam naḥ. For the verse "tām agnivarṇām," [the mantra is] "agne tvaṃ pāraya viśvāni no durgāṇi pṛtanājitam ugram sahamānam. This is the *ṛc*.

The group of four is called the "head"; with this, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the five verses beginning with *jātavedase* using the breath of inhalation (*apāna*). Having consecrated them with *oṃ namaḥ*, one should perform the placement as follows: *oṃ mūrdhne namaḥ*, *naṃ nāsikāyai*, *moṃ lalāṭāya namaḥ*, and so forth. For the third [placement], one should place the five mantras beginning with *sadyojātaṃ prapadyāmi* upon the five locations.

Therein, one should place [the mantra] "Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām" and "Sadāśivoṃ Haṃ" upon the head. Regarding this, Kātyāyana and Hemādri state that one should assign the five faces with the five [mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta; their visualization is described by the five verses beginning with "White as the snowy mountain, the moon, and the kunda flower," and they say that the assignment of the thirty-eight digits (kalās) starting with Buddhi is taught in the *Pratiṣṭhā*. However, here, according to the sacrificer, Kātyāyana and Hemādri state that one should assign the five faces with the five [mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta, [visualizing him] white as the snowy mountain and the moon...

The meditation [on the deity] is described in five verses beginning with "kuṇḍadhavala," which they call the installation of the thirty-eight digits (kalās) starting with Intellect (buddhi); however, this should be disregarded as it is stated in the *Pratiṣṭhā* [treatise] to be merely a deception of the patron and entirely without foundation.

With the ten mantras beginning with "caturthestrātāramindram" and those beginning with "indrāya namaḥ," one should offer a *añjali* (joined palms) to Indra and the other deities in the directions starting from the east. Regarding this, the *Mahārṇava* states: "Having formed a *saṃpuṭa-añjali* (a hollowed-out joined-palms gesture) with these [first set], one should again circumambulate and pay obeisance with these [second set]. [The specific mantras for the limbs are: "manojyotiḥ" and "guhyaṃ" for the navel; "abhodyagniḥ" for the navel; "agnirmūrdhā" and "udaraṃ mūrdhānaṃ divaḥ" for the heart; "marmāṇite" for the mouth; "jātavedā yadivā pāvakaḥ" and "adbhyāvavṛtsva" for the head.
This indeed is called "Self-Protection" (*ātmarakṣā*):

having recited the six verses beginning with *pañcamanyā setur yajñānām*, one says *śirase svāhā* over the head; then, at the end of the verse *tathā lokān akalpayan*, one recites the two verses beginning with *vedāham etaṃ puruṣaṃ mahāntam* and ending with *dhātā purastād yam udājahāra*; then, having recited the entire *Uttaranārāyaṇa* beginning with *adbhyaḥ saṃbhūtaḥ pṛthivyai rasāt* and ending with *man niṣāṇe man niṣāṇa*, one says *śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*; and finally, the fifteen-verse hymn beginning with *āśuḥ śiśānaḥ*.
Recite from "viśvāhā śarma yaccha tvā" until the end; then, according to Kātyāyana, having recited the seventeen-verse hymn (*sūkta*), say "kavacāya hūṃ."

Thus, they say that the *kavaca* (armor) is "kātyeyanāstu," and the two eyes are the mantra "vibhrāṭ" consisting of eighteen verses. Then, with the *anuvāka* beginning "tvamagne rudra" from the *Śatarudrīya*, ending with "bhūrbhuvaḥ suvaḥ svāhā," [one offers] for the *astra* (weapon). This is because, at the beginning of the *Śatarudrīya*, by the word "Śatarudrīya" itself, only Rudra is denoted. As for what is stated in the Śrauta-sūtra regarding the Sāvitra-cayana—that "tvamagne rudra" is the form (*rūpa*) of the *Śatarudrīya*—the term "form" is used in a figurative sense (*gauṇa*). There is no authority for accepting a figurative sense here; therefore...

The weapon is indeed joined with the Rudrādhyāya; this very matter has been explained in the Mahārṇava: "In this regard, the placement (nyāsa), the limbs, the meters, the deities, and the variations in the readings of the other [mantras] are to be known from the Mahārṇava."
It is not stated in detail— Kātyāyana, however,
says that the sixteen verses beginning with "namaste rudra" constitute the Rudra-homa;
thereafter, having prostrated with eight limbs before the hymn beginning with "hiraṇyagarbha," [one should proceed].
As for the meditation: [one should visualize the deity] resembling pure crystal, with three eyes and five faces.
Gaṅgādhara, with ten arms, adorned with all ornaments,
blue-necked, marked by the crescent moon, and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread.
[He saw the Lord] with a tiger-skin upper garment, the most excellent bestower of fearlessness,
endowed with a water-pot and a rosary, holding a trident in his hand,
blazing with tawny matted locks and crests that illuminate all.
He was not immersed in the nectar, yet he was joyful; he bore the heart of Umā’s body,
seated upon a divine lion-throne, endowed with divine enjoyments,
accompanied by the deities of the directions, and attended by gods and demigods.
Accompanied by the deities of the quarters, saluted by gods and demons,
eternal, perpetual, pure, fixed, imperishable, and undecaying;
the all-pervading Lord Rudra, who possesses a universal form.
Thus, having correctly placed the mantras of the elements [on the body], one should then begin the sacrifice;
this concludes the placement of the five limbs.

Regarding the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) taught by Śātātapa, five [placements] have been mentioned therein; the sixth, however, is: "May Brahmā abide in the organ of generation. For the purpose of the word "may they abide" (*tiṣṭhetām*, *tiṣṭhaṃtu*), one should recite it everywhere. [Specifically: Viṣṇu in the feet, Hara in the hands, Agni in the stomach, Śiva in the heart, the Vasus in the throat, Sarasvatī in the mouth, and Vāyu in the nostrils.

May the Sun and Moon be in his two eyes; the Aśvins in his two ears; Rudra on his forehead; the Ādityas on his head; Śiva on his crown; Pinākin on his back; the Wielder of the Trident (Śūlin) in front; the Handsome-Handed One (Śivaṃśakarau) at his sides; Vāyu everywhere; and may he stand outside, surrounded on all sides by garlands of flames of fire. May all the deities remain in their respective places in all the limbs; may they protect me. With the mantras beginning with "Agni has taken refuge in my speech," one should touch the limbs according to their characteristics—just as: "Agni has taken refuge in my speech; speech in the heart; the heart... [and so forth].
In me, who am the immortal—the immortal being Brahman.

Thus: "The tongue is supported by my speech"—this is the placement on the tongue; "the vital breath is supported by my heart"—this is the placement on the heart; "the sun is supported by my eye"—this is the placement on the chest; "the quarters are supported by my ears"—this is the placement on the ears; "the waters are supported by my semen"—this is the placement on the secret organ; "the earth is supported by my body"—this is the placement on the body; "the herbs and trees are well-supported by my hair"—this is the placement on the hair; "the hairs are supported by my heart."

Thus for the body hairs: "Indra is seated in my strength"—for the heart; "Strength is seated in my arms"—for the two arms; "Parjanya is seated on my head"—for the head; "The head is seated in the heart"—for the head; "Īśāna is seated in my fury"—for the mind; "The Self is seated in the self"—for the heart. That is the same: "May my self come back to me, may life come back, may breath come back, may intention come back; may Vaiśvānara, increasing with his rays, stand within as the guardian of immortality. Thus for all the limbs. This is the six-limbed [rite].

In the Hemādri, Kauśika, having stated "the resolve (saṃkalpa), recitation (japa), and oblation (homa)," describes two types of ritual placement (nyāsa) as follows: "One should perform the placement with [mantras] beginning with 'bhava' and ending with 'namaḥ', preceded by the syllable Om."

Placing Bhava at the feet, one should place Śiva between the thighs; Īśāna in the secret region, and Paśupati at the navel. One should place Rudra in the heart and Ugra in the mouth. Thus, being pure, having performed the Nyāsa with the twelve mantras of the Anuvākas in reverse order—excluding those used for malevolent rites—one should place the first mantra at the feet and the second at the knees.

Having placed the third on the two thighs, the fourth at the secret place; the fifth at the region of the navel, and the sixth one should place upon the heart; the seventh at the region of the throat, and the eighth, most excellent, in the mouth; the ninth on the nose, and the tenth on the two eyes; the eleventh on the forehead, and the twelfth one should place upon the head.

Having performed the thirteenth [rite] as armor with the weapon-mantra "phaṭ," [one proceeds]. Now, generally, regarding the seers and other [constituent elements] of the Rudra [hymn]: therein, for all [of these], the Lord Agni is the seer (ṛṣi); Rudra Śambhu is the deity; Mahāvirāṭ is the meter (chandas); and for the Camaka-anuvākas, Agni is the seer of the section (kāṇḍarṣi).

The first [verse] is in the Gāyatrī meter and is addressed to Agni; the remaining portion is in the Yajus style and is addressed to Viṣṇu. Vāja and the others are the specific deities for the food-offerings. This is the application in recitation (japa).
Now, specifically:

as for the first [lineage], it was Kaśyapa, then Ātreya, then Kaśyapa; then for two [generations] it was Gautama Dhūmra, then Kaṇva, then for two [generations] it was Kaśyapa Marutvān, then the Blessed One (Bhagavat), and then for three [generations] it was Bhavavān.

In the second *anuvāka*, Maṇḍūka; in the third, the Blessed One; in the fourth, Durvāsas; in the fifth and sixth, the Blessed One; in the seventh *anuvāka*, Hemakośa; in the eighth and ninth, up to "namo vaḥ kirikebhyaḥ," the Blessed One and Vasiṣṭha; in the tenth *anuvāka*, Agni; [in the section] beginning with "drapsaḥ," the Blessed One Nārada; [in the section] beginning with "atriḥ," Stuhipratama, Vaiyaughra; [in the section] beginning with "pari no rudrasya," the Blessed One; then Vairāja; then Pulaha; then Nārada; then for four [sections], Durvāsas; [and finally] Devala with the concluding verses.
Thus say the sages; then the deities: "He who is Tāmra"—these two have Āditya as their self.
"O Rudra, go away"—this is the self of Skanda; "Do not harm me, O Great One"—this is the self of Sandīśvara.

"O you who possess chariots, go forth; let there be food for the blue-necked one"—these are the fourth, fifth, and sixth sections. "From afar, O most bountiful one," and the two beginning with "May he be auspicious" and "Your weapon," these three are the eighth section. And in the ninth, from "Homage to you, O Kirika" up to "Do not harm our offspring" and "Around us, O Rudra," the deities of these are the venerable Vasiṣṭha, Nārada, and Rudra. Now, as for the meters: "He who is copper-colored and extends," "Upon the son," and "He who creeps along"—these six-footed verses are in the Jagatī meter.

The four verses beginning with *imā rudrāya* are Jagatīs; the three beginning with *ārāt te* are Triṣṭubhs; *mīḍhuṣṭama* is a five-footed Triṣṭubh; in the second Anuvāka, [the verse] is a Mahāgāyatrī; in the third, a Bṛhatī; in the fourth, an Uṣṇih; in the fifth and sixth, a Mahāvirāj; in the seventh, a Mahāpaṅkti; and in the eighth and ninth, a Mahātriṣṭubh. The remaining portions are Yajus formulas. Their application (*viniyoga*) is for recitation (*japa*).

Now, regarding the recitation of the five-limbed (*pañcāṅga*) Rudras during the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), according to the rules for *homa* and worship stated by Baudhāyana, the previously mentioned five-limbed assignments (*nyāsa*) indeed take place. Furthermore, they are prescribed by the words "Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for the bath and worship of Rudra" and so forth, as well as by the verses of the sixth assignment beginning with "O Brahman, be established in the organ of generation" (*prajanane brahman tiṣṭha*). Thus, there is a combination [of these]. Therefore, having performed the aforementioned sixfold assignment ending with "Agni is in my speech" (*agnirme vāci*) and so on—touching the limbs according to their respective signs—the [deity] is worshipped.

Having mentally invoked me with the thought, "I worship you with devotion—whether by humans, *siddhas*, gods, asuras, and others; O Maheśvara, accept me," and having honored me with the five services (*pañcopacāra*) beginning with fragrance (*gandha*), one should then worship him with the mantra "We sacrifice to Tryambaka. The meaning is that one should perform the invocation either with five or six [mantras] excluding the invocation [itself], or with five or six including the invocation "Tryambakaṃ yajāmahe. Alternatively, if the invocation is omitted, one should perform the invocation using this very "Tryambaka" mantra. [Then recite: "May the bay horses bring thee hither."

"O conscious one, come quickly with your white horses—those possessing banners, swift as the wind, powerful, and fleet as thought—to my oblation, O Śarva! Having thus invoked [the deity] by joining [him] with a flower upon the pedestal-liṅga at the right nostril, he should perform the invocation with the mantra: "I take refuge in Sadyojāta. The seat is offered with: "Omb Triambaka, obeisance to Sadyojāta, obeisance, obeisance. The water for the feet (pādya) is offered with: "Omb Triambaka, in existence, in non-existence, and beyond existence, be our protector, O Bhava.
The bath is performed with the *abliṅga* mantras and [the verse]: "Omb Triambaka, obeisance to the source of existence (Bhavodbhava)."

With the verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, he then satiates [the deities] with water: "I satiate the god Bhava; I satiate the god Śarva; I satiate the god Īśāna; I satiate the god Paśupati; I satiate the god Rudra. "I bow to Tryambaka, the eldest"—with this, he offers water for sipping (*ācamanīya*). "I bow to Tryambaka, the most excellent"—with this, he offers honey-mixture (*madhuparka*). "I bow to Tryambaka, Rudra"—with this, he offers fragrance (*gandha*). "I bow to Tryambaka, Kāla"—with this, he offers flowers (*puṣpa*). "I bow to Kalavikaraṇa"—with this, he offers incense (*dhūpa*).
"To Bali, for the act of offering, obeisance"—with this, the lamp; "To Bali, obeisance"—with this, the food offering (naivedya).

"Salutation to Bala-pramathanā," with these words, [offer] betel; "Salutation to Sarva-bhūta-damanā," with these words, [perform] the lustration (*nīrājana*); "Salutation to Mano'smanā," with these words, [offer] the flower-arrow (*mastra-puṣpa*); and the salutation is performed with the verse beginning "To the non-terrible ones" (*aghorebhyaḥ*).
In all cases, there is the covering of Tryambaka. Now, these are the flowers: "Obeisance to the god Bhava; obeisance to the god Śarva;
to the god Īśāna; to the god Paśupati; to the god Rudra."

"To the fierce god, to the wandering god, to the great god, obeisance! Then, with the three mantras beginning with "ebhyaḥ" [of the *Gaurī-vidyā*] and the mantra "Sadāśivo 'ham," he worships the form of Aghora. He should then pour a continuous stream from a golden vessel onto his head.

With honey, clarified butter, milk, sugarcane juice, coconut water, or mango juice—or in their absence, with water—one should mutter each of the eleven sections (anuvākas) beginning with "namaste rudra manyave" and ending with "agniṣṇusajoṣasaḥ. Or, one may mutter them all together; at every repetition, the act of propitiation is accomplished anew.

One who desires the destruction of evil, one who desires eloquence, one who desires prosperity, one who desires peace, one who desires a son, one who desires nourishment, and one who desires union [with the divine] should perform this rite; by performing it, he attains success. He gives a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor: ten cows with their calves, adorned with gold, and an eleventh as a bull. In the absence of these, he should give one cow; thus says the venerable Bodhāyana.

Now, regarding the *mahāsnāna* (great bath), as stated in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa* within the *Hemādri*: "The fruit of a [regular] bath is known to be one hundredfold; an *abhyaṅga* (oil massage) is twenty-five fruits; but the *mahāsnāna* is proclaimed to be two thousand fruits."
Having bathed the Liṅga with honey and cow-derived ghee,
having cleansed it with all substances, and having sprinkled it thoroughly;
when a great calamity has occurred, the bath performed with clay is eightfold more efficacious.
With water alone, or with scented water according to one's capacity, and with that entire anointing substance weighing exactly twenty-five palas,
one should duly offer śamī leaves, bilva leaves, and lotuses.
The food offering (naivedya) may consist of ten *droṇas* or even eight *droṇas*;
the merit of the *māḍhaketu* is ordained to be equal to ten *droṇas*. For a devotee who lacks wealth, there should be no hesitation in this matter.
There, one should cause the vigil to be performed and petition [the deity] in due order; having prayed to the Liṅga of Maheśvara along with dances and circumambulations,
O Goddess of the Suras, even by those who are destitute of wealth, deficient in mantras, or lacking in faith.
O Śaṅkara, you should look upon both what has been done and what has not been done;
the specific details regarding this should be understood from the Vratakalpalatā.
Thus ends the Great Nyāsa and the ritual bathing.
Now follows the Rudra-homa; this Rudra-homa is of two kinds.

The *namaskāra-homa* (homage-oblation) is of two kinds: that which is primary (*pradhāna*) and that which is ancillary (*aṅga*). Regarding the first, the source is the root text itself: "We shall explain the procedure for recitation (*japa*), oblation (*homa*), and worship (*arcana*). As for the primary oblation, statements from the *Bodhāyana-vidhi*, *Viṣṇudharma*, and other texts have been cited previously, such as: "For supreme peace, [one should perform] an oblation with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and ghee," and so forth. However, the ancillary oblation consists of one-tenth or one-hundredth part [of the recitation]. The *Mahārṇava* states that it should be performed with sesame seeds and other materials. Although the root text does not explicitly state this here, it is nevertheless established by the general rule regarding the recitation of mantras.

When no specific substance is prescribed, clarified butter (*ājya*) is ordained for the *homa* offering; this is stated by way of a general rule. Because of the general statement, "When no specific substance is prescribed, clarified butter is ordained for the *homa*," it might follow that [other substances] would not be used. However, that [clarified butter] serves as the standard measure when *tila* seeds are the substance. For this very reason, Hemādri has stated that the *homa* which is an ancillary (*aṅga*) to the recitation of the Rudra-mantras is indeed [performed with clarified butter], but not with a tenth part (*daśāṃśa*) or the like. As Bodhāyana says in that same context: "Then one should perform the *homa* with the mantra 'namaḥ śambhave'."

It is declared that there are eleven *Rudras* and thirty-three oblations (*āhutis*). In the *Laghurudra*, there are four; in the *Mahārudra*, there are four; and in the *Sahasrarudra*, forty thousand minus seven [thousand] (i.e., thirty-nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-three) should be performed. Furthermore, the subsequent [oblations] should be less by seven each; this is the settled rule regarding the *Rudra* [rite]. Hemādri states that this homa should be performed with the mantra "Namaḥ śambhave. It appears appropriate, however, that it should be performed with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) or ghee, as mentioned in the previously cited *Viṣṇudharma*.

Therefore, according to the view of Homādri, there is no division of mantras at all. Furthermore, this is indeed a *homa* that is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the recitation (*japa*), because it is understood through the locative case in the word "in the *japya*" (*japye*), just as in the expression "the *mandrapāyaṇīyā* [is performed] in [this manner]. However, since this [division] is possible in the case of the entire *homa* which constitutes the primary act (*pradhāna*), the division of mantras stated by Mahārṇava for each *sūkta*—as found in the *Kalpasūtras* and other texts within the section on the *cayana* rite—is what should be adopted.

In the *Mahārṇava*, however, because the division of mantras is not observed in the context of the entire *homa*, this very [division] is to be adopted as part of the *japa*. It has been stated that this is because it depends upon the established rules (*klṛpta-tad-vāda*). Furthermore, it has been upheld by the learned (*śiṣṭa*); that [division] is now being explained. In that regard, the division of mantras consists of five ways, three ways, sixteen ways, forty-eight ways, and the position of one hundred and sixty-nine ways. The first is called the "per-mantra" (*prati-mantra*) position.

In this regard, there is one position: he offers the first four *anuvākas* into the first brick, the next four as the second portion, and the final three *anuvākas* as the third portion. Alternatively, there is another position: beginning from "samaste rudra" up to "sabhāpatibhyaśca vo namaḥ," and then the *anuvākas* ending with "tena rudramasyavaḥ"—one should divide these here into three portions. In this case, there are two positions: the first four *anuvākas* constitute one portion, and the subsequent four constitute the second portion.

The three final *anuvākas* constitute the third part; this is one view. Alternatively, one part consists of the section beginning with "Obeisance to you, O Rudra" (*namaste rudra*) and ending with "And obeisance to the lords of the assemblies" (*sabhāpatibhyaśca vo namaḥ*). The second part begins with "Obeisance to the horses" (*namo aśvebhyaḥ*) and ends with "To the desirable one" (*vāryāya ca*). The third part begins with "Obeisance to the furtherer" (*namaḥ prataraṇāya*) and continues until the conclusion. Regarding the division into six parts, the scripture states: "He offers the three subsequent oblations; they become six, for there are six seasons."

In the *Sacāśīti*, a sixfold division of the *svāhākāra* offerings is described. For instance, beginning with "To the Carpenters" (*namas takṣabhyaḥ*) and standing in water reaching up to the knees, one offers; then beginning with "And to the Wheelwrights" (*rathakārebhyaś ca vaḥ*) and standing in water reaching up to the navel, one offers with "To those with good weapons" (*namaḥ svāyudhāya*). Having offered the remainder as before up to "To the Fishermen" (*namo 'psavyebhyaḥ*) while standing in water reaching up to the mouth, and having offered the ten subsequent additions (*anupaṅgavat*) beginning with "Thousands by the thousands" (*sahasrāṇi sahasraśaḥ*), one performs the *anvāroha* offerings.
"Salutation to the Rudras who are on earth, whose food is [this]"; holding it at knee-height, [he recites]: "Salutation to the Rudras who are in the intermediate space."

There are three positions currently in practice: one offers at the height of the navel with the mantra "yoṣāṃ vāta" (The woman, the wind...), saying "namo rudrebhyo divi yeṣām" (Homage to the Rudras who are in heaven); another offers at the height of the mouth with the mantra "varṣam" (The rain...); and yet another [offers] at the height of the mouth. Now follows the forty-eight-fold position. In this regard, there are fifteen mantras in the first section; then eight sections containing eight *yajus* formulas each, ending with the ninth, which makes twenty-three; in the tenth [section] there are twelve, making thirty-five; and in the eleventh there are ten mantras and three *yajus* formulas, making forty-three; thus, [with the addition of the first five], there are forty-eight.

Thus, this is the summary: fifteen are declared in the first [section], twelve are recorded in the tenth; eleven in the eleventh, and eight *yajus* mantras in the twelfth. According to the view that there is one mantra per verse, however, there are one hundred and seventy-one mantras. Among these, there are fifteen mantras in the first *anuvāka*; thirteen in the second; and seventeen in each of the third and fourth. These, from the second to the fourth, are mantras containing salutations (*namaskāra*) on both sides.

In the fifth and sixth [sections], there are fifteen mantras each; in the seventh, sixteen; in the eighth, seventeen; and in the ninth, nineteen. In these [sections] from the fifth to the ninth, the mantras are preceded by the *namaskāra* (salutation) formula. Therein, the four subsequent mantras beginning with "devānām gṛhebhyaḥ" (*from the houses of the gods*) are to be appended. This application is divided in this manner specifically for the fire-oblation (*homa*) and similar rites. However, in cases such as recitation (*japa*) or consecration (*abhiṣeka*), because there is no division, the recitation follows the order of the traditional study (*adhyayana*).

In this same way, the application [of the rule] should be understood elsewhere as well: there are twelve mantras in the tenth [section], and thirteen in the eleventh. As for what Śākapūṇi says—that in the sections beginning with the second and ending with the ninth, the *yajus* begins with a salutation (*namas*) and ends with a salutation—therein, in those cases where there are salutations on both sides, the division is clear: there is one mantra consisting of the word "namas," such as: "Salutation to Bhava and Rudra; salutation to Śarva and Ugra."

In that regard, the word *namaḥ* (salutation) in the second [section] is connected to both as a primary element, with the first [section] being by means of *tat-tva* (thatness) and the second by means of Āditya. Alternatively, it refers to the second, third, and fourth sections; for Yāska says, "The single *yajus* begins with salutation. The *Mahārṇava* states that this refers to everything from the fifth section up to the end of the *Sava*.
Now, this is the summary:

five, one, three, two, seven, one, nine, one, fifteen, six, two, eleven, and twelve—these are recorded as the total number of earths (units) for all the *grahas*. Regarding these divisions within the *camakas*, Bodhāyana says: "Having offered four spoonfuls with the mantra, 'O Agni and Viṣṇu, being of one accord,' he offers the continuous *vasordhārā* with the formula, 'May vigor be mine, may impulse be mine,' until the completion of the mantra. The mantras are [to be recited] together; or rather, they are to be recited separately at the beginning of each speech.

Having offered with that [first] *camaka* section today, one should offer a single oblation with all the *camakas*, or one oblation for each *anuvāka*. Thus there are two oblations; or, because it is required even in the *vasordhārā* rite, it should be understood that this applies to the *homa* as well.

Alternatively, according to the statement of Bodhāyana—"one should mutter each one of the eleven *anuvākas*"—just as there is a repetition of each individual *camaka* in the *japa*, so too in the *homa*. Thus, having offered with the entire first *camaka*, one offers with the others individually, resulting in eleven oblations. These three options have been stated in the *Mahārṇava*.

In this context, the number of oblations (*āhuti*) for the ten-part offering (*daśāṃśa-homa*) and the complete offering (*samagra-homa*)—according to the forty-eight-fold division, the single-form division, and the mantra-by-mantra division—is stated. Among these, a single-form ten-part offering is not even to be considered, because of the absence of division; in the case of the eleven-fold set (*ekādaśinī*), the offering is of a single form. Since division is impossible in the remaining single form, there is no ten-part offering in the *Mahārudra* and similar rites—so says the *Mahārṇava*.
According to our own view, however, in the forty-eight-fold division, there are [the following] oblations: [the specific count follows]. And the mantra-by-mantra division... [is as follows].

There are seventeen oblations. They should be performed with the initial mantras; it is said that "the end [of the mantra] is elided, there is expansion, and there is the suppression of the enemy" (Antāllopo vivṛddhirmetāpastambhokteḥ). However, that [rule] applies only where a specific number is heard in the scripture, such as "three potsherds" or "seven potsherds. Since such a number is absent here, that [rule] is not applicable. For this very reason, because there is no equal division and no basis in the root text, the oblation and so forth are not joined [by those rules]; rather, the oblation is performed solely according to the scriptural injunction with the root mantra "Namaḥ śambhave," and not by a tenth part. This is stated by us having accepted the Mahārṇava.

In this regard, there are these verses: "In the Rudra [rite], for each mantra, ten parts (the *daśāṃśa*) are desired; in the forty-part [rite], they are thirty-four. In a complete homa, it is there by the number of 'sky-veda-arrows' (540). For the *daśāṃśa* of each individual mantra, one should offer oblations numbering 'sky-mountain-moon' (170). In a complete homa for every mantra, it is 'arrows-mountain-wealth-moon' (185). This is the count for the eleven Rudras.

In the *Lakṣa Rudra*, one should offer oblations at the tenth part (*daśāṃśa*) in the measure of "sky, digits, arrows" (1050); the mantra is "namo grahāya eva dāmyaham. In the *Laghu Rudra*, it is remembered as "moon, mountains, arrows, sky, pairs" (25111). In the *Laghu Rudra* and the *Mahārudra*, one should offer oblations at the tenth part; specifically, in the tenth part, there are six thousand, one hundred arrows, and forty (6150). In that very [rite], for the *Sarvahoma*, the oblations are "fire, arrows, seasons" (653). In the *Mahārudra*, one should offer oblations at the tenth part for each individual mantra.

"Twenty-two thousand, six hundred, and ten—this is the number I offer for every mantra in the Mahārudra, in the case of a complete oblation (sarvahoma). Two lakhs, twenty-six thousand, two hundred, seventy-one—this is declared to be the count. Thus ends the calculation of the oblations in the Mahārudra. Now, regarding the Atirudra, in the forty-four-fold division, the tenth part [is as follows]:

For each mantra, at the ten-part offering (daśāṃśa), there are seventy-one thousand eight hundred and eighty-four with a quarter added; for every mantra in the complete homa, twenty-five lakh [offerings] are prescribed, less eleven thousand in the case of the Atirudra—thus it is declared. In some instances, my teachers consider a slightly smaller number not to be counted as a deficiency. This is stated in the Taittirīya Śākhā.

However, for those following the Vājasaneyi-Kāṇva and other branches, according to the view that each mantra constitutes a separate offering, the number of divisions should be known as one hundred and sixty, or slightly less, when the *namaḥ śambhave* mantra is included in the oblation. This is the total number of offerings including the *vasordhārā*. One should cause the *vasordhārā* (stream of wealth) to fall upon the fire using vessels of ghee. Having fashioned a ladle (*sruva*) made of Udumbara wood—moist, fresh, free of hollows, and measuring the length of an arm—one should place it upon two pillars and pour a stream of clarified butter from it over the fire. Thus, one should cause the flow of ghee to descend upon the sacrificial fire.

"One should cause [the officiant] to recite the Āgneya, Vaiṣṇava, Raudra, and Aindava Sūktas, and one should have him study the Mahāvaiśvānara Sāman and the Jyeṣṭhasāman," as stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*. Regarding the Āgneya Sūkta and others, they should be understood as those previously mentioned in the *Bodhāyana* tradition, to be recited at the conclusion of the entire *Camaka* section. Although the *Vasordhārā* is mentioned only in the context of the *Lakṣahoma* in the *Matsya Purāṇa*, nevertheless, because it is observed in the *Cayana* (fire-altar construction) and because it serves as a means to attain results, the *Mahārṇava* states that it should be performed for Rudra; and that should be performed immediately after the *Pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation).

Having recited the *launakopi-āyāśca* and other mantras, and having offered oblations from the *samudra* up to the *ūrmisūkta*, one should then perform the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation) ending with the continuous stream of clarified butter (*ājyadhārā*). Regarding this, some say that after the *pūrṇāhuti*, the stream of clarified butter should be offered silently; however, it is more appropriate that it be the *vasordhārā*. For this very reason, the *vasordhārā* is prescribed everywhere after describing its origin in the *Hemādri*, the *Madanaratna*, the section on propitiatory rites (*śāntikāṇḍa*), and the *Devīpurāṇa*. Here, the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be constructed according to the number of oblations. As stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "It should be one *ratni* in measure..."

For fifty [oblations], the pit should be one *aratni* in measure; for a hundred, it should be two *aratnis*. Furthermore, when a thousand oblations are to be offered, one should make the *kuṇḍa* one cubit (*hasta*) in size. Likewise, for ten thousand oblations, it should be two cubits; for a hundred thousand oblations (*lakṣahoma*), four cubits; and for a million oblations, they prescribe six cubits. As stated in the *Mātsya Purāṇa*: "The *kuṇḍa* should be two cubits wide and likewise four cubits in length; for a hundred thousand oblations, it should have a womb-shaped opening (*yonivaktra*) and three enclosures (*mekhalā*). For the offering of ghee and milk quickly, it should be known as two cubits for a hundred thousand oblations."

Regarding the four-cubit [fire-pit] for offerings such as parched barley and the like, the *Siddhāntaśekhara* states: "For a hundred thousand oblations (*lakṣa*), a pit of three cubits is prescribed; for ten thousand oblations (*ayuta*), one of four cubits; for a million oblations (*daśalakṣa*), one of five cubits; for twenty lakhs, one of six cubits; and for a crore (*koṭi*) of oblations, one of seven cubits. In this regard, it is ordained that even when the number of oblations exceeds the capacity of a smaller pit, the sacrifice may still be performed.
Thus, according to the verses from the *Kuṇḍaratnākara*:

"The intermediate oblation (antarālika-homa) should be performed in a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) that is smaller than the prescribed number. And that [pit]—the altar (vedi) should be in the northeast of the pit and in the middle of the pavilion (maṇḍapa). There, a single altar should be made in the center of the sacrificial pavilion; it should be raised to a height equal to the distance between the central pillars."
Some say that Paraśurāma [stated]: "Having reached the north-eastern region, one should cause a beautiful pavilion to be built;

one should construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the rules, endowed with the auspicious moments. This is because it is stated in the *Ayutahoma* and because it appears in the writings of Hemādri and others. However, our teachers maintain that the statement regarding Paraśurāma is rootless. In the middle of the pavilion, the expert should also construct the sacrificial pit.

Thus, according to the verses of Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha and the *Matsya Purāṇa*: "To the northeast of the pit (garta), having reached the middle region—meaning the center of the pavilion (maṇḍapa) which is superior to the northeast—the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is located. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the *Matsya Purāṇa*, which states: "To the northeast of the pit, a sacrificial altar (vedi) one span (vitasti) high and one cubit (hasta) wide is for the worship of the Lord of Gods (Deveśvara) during the planetary rites (graha-ādi). Furthermore, they say that in the *Lakṣahoma* sacrifice, the pit is in the middle of that [altar], because it is a modification (vikṛti) of it. And the altars (vedīs) in the directions are only for the *Tulādāna* and similar rites; they are not used here, as there is no utility for them.

The Rudra altar is located in the northeast; it is obtained through a different procedure from the Graha altar, or it may be tantric in nature. Even though the Rudra sacrifice is performed for a specific desire, it serves as a modification (vikṛti) of the Graha sacrifice.

As for what Paraśurāma says—"The pavilion [should be] eight times the [size of the] pit, according to the requirements of the *homa*"—this is baseless and a practice of fools, since it is ignored because no such proportion is mentioned for a thirty-two-cubit pavilion in relation to a four-cubit pit; on this point, some say there is a contradiction.

As it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa: "Having prostrated before the Lord of the worlds, who assumes the body of Umā for her sake, I shall describe the extraction of the yantra according to the Rudrakalpa. Having drawn a circle in the center, one should place the ten-syllable mantra in its middle. Outside of that, a lotus with eight petals, then one with sixteen petals, then one with twenty-four petals, and likewise one with thirty-two petals; then a circle with forty petals, radiant like the sun, and a fifth circle consisting of five lotuses, as well as a square house divided into sections."

Enveloped on all sides by the three qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—it has four gates, and at each gate it is surrounded externally by serpents. One should install one hundred and forty deities; this is the ten-syllable mantra that bestows the fulfillment of all desires and purposes. It begins with the *praṇava* (Om) and ends with *namaḥ*. Following that are the five faces: first Sadyojāta, then Vāmadeva, then Aghora, then Tatpuruṣa as declared next, and finally Īśāna in sequence as the fifth.

One should place the eight deities beginning with Sūrya on the petals in order, starting from the east. When drawing the yantra, the east is defined as the direction between the worshiper and the object of worship. First, one should worship Mahākāla, Gaṇeśa, and Vṛṣabha in sequence, followed by Bhṛṅgiriṭi, Skanda, Mātaṅga, and Caṇḍa. Then, on the sixteen-spoked lotus, one should worship the second enclosure: Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śiva, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śikhaṇḍin, and Vāmadeva.

Likewise, the eldest and the most excellent [should be placed]. In the third enclosure, on the twenty-four-petaled lotus, one should likewise assign the eight siddhis: *aṇimā*, *mahimā*, *laghimā*, *garimā*, *prāpti*, *prākāmya*, *īśitva*, and *vaśitva*. Then, in the fifth sequence, one should install the deities beginning with Brāhmī: Brāhmī, Mahīśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Aindrī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Caṇḍikā, in that order. [The Bhairavas are] Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, and Unmattabhairava.

Kālabhīṣaṇa and Saṃhāra are proclaimed as the eight Bhairavas. On the thirty-two petals, the eight Bhavas are first declared: Bhava, Śarva, Īśāna, Paśupati, Rudra, Ugra, Bhīma, and Mahān—these are renowned as the eight Bhavas. Following that are Ananta, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Kulīraka, Kārkoṭaka, Śaṅkhapāla, Kaṅka, and Aśvatara.

Then, one should place in order upon the eight petals [of the seventh circle] Dvainya, Pṛthu, Haihaya, Arjuna, Śākuntaleya, Bharata, Nala, and Rāma. Thereafter, one should place the seven principal mountain ranges (kulācala) upon the eight petals of the eighth circle: Himavat, Niṣadha, Vindhya, Mālyavān, Pāriyātraka, Malaya, Hemakūṭa, and the one known as Gandhamādana. Then, in the fifth enclosure, one should place [the deities] upon the forty petals of the lotus in that fifth enclosure.

One should worship Indra and the other eight world-protectors (Lokapālas) who have destroyed their impurities and afflictions—one should place Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kubera, and Īśāna upon the eight petals. Then one should place the eight Śaktis of Indra and the other Lokapālas: Śacī, Svāhā, Vārāhī, Khaḍginī, Vāruṇī, Mṛgārūḍhā, Kauberī, and Śūlinī as the eighth. After that, one should place the eight weapons, beginning with the thunderbolt (Vajra), belonging to those eight.

One should obtain the weapons of the world-protectors (lokapālas) in sequence: the vajra, the spear (śakti), the staff (daṇḍa), the sword (khaḍga), the noose (pāśa), the goad (aṅkuśa), the mace (gadā), and the trident (triśūla). Then one should obtain their eight mounts in the same order: Airāvata, the ram, the buffalo, the corpse-demon (preta), the crocodile (makara), the deer, the man, and the bull. Following that are the eight elephants of the directions (dig-gajas): Airāvata, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Kumuda, Añjana, [Puṣpadanta], Sārvabhauma, and Supratīka.

Puṣpadanta, Sārvabhauma, and Supratīka are the elephants of the quarters. Outside the five lotuses are the eight guardians of the directions, beginning with Indra. One should place Virūpākṣa in the southeast (Āgneyī) through conjunction with Agni; one should place Viśvarūpa in the southwest (Nairṛtī) through conjunction with Nairṛta. Likewise, one should worship Paśupati in the northwest (Vāyavī) through conjunction with Vāyu. Similarly, one should place the upward-facing Liṅga in the northeast (Īśānī) through conjunction with Īśāna, following the sequence starting from the east.

The remaining [serpents], beginning with Śeṣa, are to be drawn outside the subterranean chamber (bhūgṛha). Having placed Śeṣa in the east, adorned with a thousand hoods; Takṣaka in the southeast; and in the west, Yuta, endowed with seven hundred hoods; Kambala in the north, endowed with thirty-seven hoods; and likewise Kārkoṭaka in the northeast, white and possessed of thirty hoods—this entire Rudrapīṭha is prescribed for rites pertaining to Rudra. It was personally declared by Śambhu out of a desire to bestow grace upon his devotees.

Or else, one should write it with saffron, agallochum, camphor, and betel leaves; when worshipped with devotion, this bestows the fulfillment of all desires and aims. One should invoke and worship these deities using their respective name-mantras ending in the dative case followed by "namaḥ."
The source for this must be considered:

the elders say that one should place the Rudra-kalaśa in the northeast, worship Varuṇa there, and appoint a Brahmin to recite half of the *Rudraikādaśinī*. Then, when the sacrificer has performed the formal renunciation (*tyāga*), having offered oblations to the deities of the house and its limbs as in the *Grahayajña*, and having offered clarified butter (*ājya*) to the Rudra-pīṭha deities during the *Rudra-homa*, he should perform the *Sviṣṭakṛt* and other rites; at the conclusion of the expiatory oblations (*prāyaścitta-homa*), he should give balls of black gram and rice (*māṣabhaktalīn*) to the guardians of the directions (*dikpālas*) and the nine planets, etc., with the verse beginning "samudrād ūrmir."

Having again offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the verses "mūrdhānam," "punastvā ādityāḥ," "pūrṇādaviḥ," and "saptate dhāma," and having performed the *vasordhārā*—preceded by the *camaka* section, the nine verses beginning with "agnim īle," the six verses beginning with "viṣṇornu kam," the five verses beginning with "ā te pitar," the ten verses beginning with "svādiṣṭhayā," and the two Sāmans, "mahāvaiśvānara" and "jyeṣṭhasāman"—and having completed the remainder of the rite starting from the release of the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra-vimoka*), he should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests. Here, having completed the remainder of the rite starting from the release of the full vessel, [he should give the sacrificial fee] to the officiating priests.

One should give [the fee]. Here, regarding the Rudramahānyāsa, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) mentioned by Bodhāyana is that one should give gold, a garment, or a bull; a bull is the fee for the Rudra [rite]. Śālīka says one should give eleven cows. [The bed] is covered with gold, made of thread, with a silver mattress—a golden [bed] with a hundred holes. The *Mahārṇava* states that the fee for the various types of Rudra rites is as follows: therein, ten thousand gold *niṣkas* is the highest [fee].

For that purpose, the middle [measure] is said to be three thousand; the superior is three hundred, while two hundred is considered the middle. One hundred is to be known as the inferior; another method is now proclaimed: the superior is sixty-four, the middle is half of that, and twenty-four is for the other. Then, the patron, consecrated by the water from the jars of the planets and other deities, having performed the subsequent worship of the house and so forth, should dismiss [the deities].

For the pleasure of Śrī Rudra, for the cessation of all misfortunes that have occurred, and for the complete attainment of my prayed-for desires, I offer this golden image of Śrī Rudra, accompanied by a pair of garments, to you who embody Śrī Rudra, according to the prescribed rite; may the fruit as described be mine.

Thus, having given an image of Rudra to the preceptor, having worshipped the fire and dismissed the Brahmins, and having fed three or one Brahmin in the *Rudraikādaśinī* rite, one should perform the dedication of the work to the Lord (*karmeśvarārpaṇa*). Regarding the Mahārudra rite for the sake of obtaining a son, we shall explain the specific details concerning the removal of the lack of progeny in the section on the ripening of karma (*karmavipāka*). As for other mantras, the ritual applications (*prayoga*) as stated in the commentaries and by Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara are to be understood from the *Mahārṇava*; they are not mentioned here due to their lack of current practice.
Thus ends the Rudra-vidhāna, the Veda-pārāyaṇa, within the Śāntiratna composed by Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa, son of Rāmakṛṣṇa Bhaṭṭa, who was the son of the venerable Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa.
Now, regarding the complete recitation of the Vedas (*vedapārāyaṇa*):
first, the installation of the water-pot (*kalaśa*) and other rites are described in the *Mahārṇava*:
"In a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), a temple, or a house that is auspicious and well-adorned..."
There, one should place a very firm pitcher, well-polished and beautifully adorned with flowers,
sprouts, garlands, sandalwood, and kumkuma and other substances; then,
one should set it down in the middle of the altar, mixed with clay and cow dung.
With fifty [units], Brahmā, the sole object of the Kula, stands facing west;
he is bathed and established in the jar, four-armed and four-faced. When the calf is positioned on the knees, the offering substance is said to be honey.
Having offered the Brahmopadhāna, one should then recite the Svastyayana;
thereafter, one should perform the consecration (Pratiṣṭhā), after which the materials for worship are described.
One should worship the Grandfather (Brahmā) with the sacred thread, food offerings, garments, sandalwood paste, saffron, garlands, incense, lamps, betel leaves, and protective amulets.
One should worship the speech beginning with "brahma jijñānam" three times;
then the teacher, having performed the worship, should recite according to the text.
The meaning is that, having performed the homa and other rites to be described hereafter, one should recite [the mantra].
Regarding this very point, Bodhāyana says:

Having prepared a sacrificial mound and kindled the fire, and having strewn grass around it, he offers oblations of clarified butter to these [deities]: to Agni, to Soma, to the Viśvedevas, to Brahmā, to the Ṛṣis, to the Ṛg-verses, to the Yajus-formulas, to the Sāman-chants, to Faith (Śraddhā), to Pity (Medā), to Retention (Dhāraṇā), to Prosperity (Śrī), to Modesty (Hrī), to Sāvitrī, to Savitṛ, to Prajāpati, to Soma the Ṛṣi of the Section (Kāṇḍarṣi), to Agni the Ṛṣi of the Section, to the Viśvedevas the Ṛṣis of the Section, and to Anumati and Sviṣṭakṛt, each with a separate utterance of "svāhā."

Having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* and having offered again, he sprinkles [the water] around. He satisfies these [deities] together with the *yajus* formula. Thus, for the sections (*kāṇḍas*) of the Ṛgveda—excluding the seers (*ṛṣis*) and so forth, up to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering—in their place [he offers to]: Śāntārcis, Mādhyma, Gṛtsamada, Viśvāmitra, Vāmadeva, Atri, Bharadvāja, Jāmadagnya, Gautama, Vasiṣṭha, the Pragādas, the Pāvamānas, the Kṣudrasūktas, and the Mahānāmnīs. Then, beginning from the beginning of the Veda, he continues uninterruptedly.

"One should study it," said the venerable Bodhāyana: "Now we shall explain the rule for the complete recitation (pārāyaṇa) while fasting. Until its completion, one should not eat; or, according to one's ability, having consumed only milk, fruits, boiled rice, or merely sacrificial food (haviṣya), one should study the remainder during that night. Having gone out from the village toward the east or the north, and having established the sacred fire..."

Having strewn the sacrificial grass, from the offering of the fuel up until the end of the "mouth of Agni" (the introductory oblations), he offers with clarified butter to these deities: to Agni, to Soma, to Indra, to Prajāpati, to Bṛhaspati, to the Viśvedevas, to Brahmā, to the Ṛṣis, to the Ṛg-verses, to the Yajus-formulas, to Faith, to Wisdom, to Retention, to Intelligence, to the Lord of the Assembly, to the Earth, to Fortune, to Modesty, to Sāvitrī, to Savitṛ, to Prajāpati, to Soma, to Agni, to the Ṛṣi of the Section, to the Viśvedevas, and to the Ṛṣis of the Sections pertaining to the Saṃhitās.

Having offered oblations with the *svāhā*-utterance separately for the deities of the *upaniṣads* belonging to the sacrificial rites, for the deities of the *upaniṣads* belonging to Varuṇa, for Havyavāha, for all the deities of the *upaniṣads* belonging to Varuṇa, for all the gods, and for Numaṭī and Sviṣṭakṛt, he should again offer the *vyāhṛtis*.
He sprinkles around; he sits down together with these [deities] and satisfies them with a *yajus* formula. At the very end, he should satisfy Agni and Soma with a *yajus* from the *Yajurveda*.

Alternatively, the *Mahārṇava* states that one should satisfy the fire and other deities after having performed the libation with the *yajus* mantra beginning with "I satisfy the gods who are the earth" (*yad vā bhūdevāṃs tarpayāmi*).
