In this manner, for those who know the *Mṛgveda*, excluding the *kāṇḍa-ṛṣis* and so forth, from the *āsviṣṭakṛt* section up to the point ending with "to the Mahānāmnīs" (beginning with "to the Śatarcins"), it is as before. Then, beginning from the start of the Veda, one should recite it continuously; for him there is no suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) in the interval, nor is he impure due to births or deaths occurring in the interim. The meaning regarding the cause of impurity is as follows: "One should not interrupt in the middle"; wherever one might pause, one should continue reciting until the end. The sense is that as long as one is reading, one should not stop in the midst of it nor recite anything else.

If one should stop in the middle, O Sage, having restrained the breaths or while uttering the *praṇava*, he should recite it with a Brahmin until the time [of completion]. Then, having omitted the entire night, the interval between nights, battle, forest, and water, he should wear [the garment] around [himself]. "Omitting the intervals between nights" means that he should complete [the study] after skipping the twilight-nights and so forth. At the beginning and at the end, he should give a meal to a Brahmin and a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). He who studies the Veda according to this rule becomes purified by the Veda and attains purity of mind.

The meaning is that he becomes one whose form is the Veda. By two complete recitations (*pārāyaṇa*) and by [reciting] the *Ṛg-veda* verses, one is here liberated from falsehoods; by three, from the acts causing loss of caste (*patanīya*); by bathing in the waters of the Gaṅgā after having discharged semen in a Śūdra woman, one becomes purified; by four complete recitations, from eating the food of a Śūdra and from serving him; and by five, from officiating at a sacrifice for one who should not be sacrificed for (*ayājya*) and from accepting what should not be accepted (*agrāhya*).

O Brāhmaṇa, by six [repetitions] one is liberated from the sins of stealing gold, causing the three-fold redness [of the tongue, teeth, and nails], killing a cow, stealing gold, and associating with the fallen; by eight from neglecting prescribed duties and failing to wear the sacred thread; by twelve from violating the Guru’s bed and approaching a woman in her menses; by nine from drinking liquor; by ten from not drinking Soma; by eleven from killing a Brāhmaṇa; and by twelve, one is released from all sins committed in previous and present lives and attains the heavenly world.

He goes to the world of heaven; he has performed sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma and other rites. He should always be a student of the Vedas, free from evil, truthful in speech, and pure. Whatever desire he may wish for, he shall accomplish it by means of the Veda. For there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be attained through the Brahman; indeed, its fruit is great.

In the *Ṛgvidhāna*: "At the very outset, one should perform the ritual with the Sāvitrī for the sake of peace; for the sake of satisfaction, for the acquisition of cattle, and for the gain of wealth, O King. For this Saṃhitā, consisting entirely of Brahman and threefold in nature, was seen through fierce austerity by the wise Viśvāmitra. One should always perform oblations (*homa*) and the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) in that manner; it fulfills all desires and one is liberated into the Supreme Brahman. This same [Saṃhitā], when recited in reverse order, is a destroyer of enemies.
When the syllables are reversed, it is recommended for the performance of incantations (*abhicāra*). The oblation should be performed verse by verse according to the entire Saṃhitā."
With clarified butter or sesame seeds—
clarified butter is prescribed as the substance in oblations when no specific material is designated.
Thus, according to the *Brahmottara*:

"A fire-oblation (*homa*) that removes all sins is praised everywhere," and as stated in the *Viṣṇudharma*: "The complete recitation of the three *Rudra* hymns, likewise the complete recitation of the Veda, a thousand oblations of sesame seeds, and this salutation (*namaḥ*); these four together [bring about purification]. Śātātapa says: "The complete [recitation of] the three *Rudras* and likewise the complete recitation of the Veda, a thousand oblations of sesame seeds, and this salutation—this quartet [is effective]."
Thus ends the ritual for the Vedic recitation (*vedapārāyaṇa*) at the birth of a son, composed by Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa; [as stated] by Śaunaka:
This hymn beginning with "jātavedase" is the accomplisher of all aims;
it bestows long life, health, and happiness, grants prosperity, and destroys enemies.
Whatever a mortal desires, he obtains that very thing without a doubt;
one who is pure, wearing white garments and holding a water-pot, should offer oblations with this hymn.
Or, being self-controlled, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), and with senses subdued,
one who desires cattle, sons, or wealth should practice the mantra one hundred thousand times for each.
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) without lethargy, either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or upon a leveled altar (sthaṇḍila).
The pit should be square and provided with two enclosures (mekhalā).
One should arrange the sacrificial ritual (yajñatantra), beginning with the preparation of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and ending with the portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga).
One should invoke Durgā into the water-pot (kumbha), [visualizing her] with weapons and eight great arms.
Then, let that goddess— who is dark like a blue lotus and adorned with a crown and other ornaments— be worshipped in that place endowed with the waters of the sacred ford.
Having invoked [the deity] with this oblation and with various fuel-sticks,
one should offer one hundred and eight oblations individually while reciting this mantra.
Then, having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, he should complete the remainder of the fire sacrifice.
Then, rising up, he should recite this mantra, endowed with faith:
In the *Ṛgvidhāna*:
"One should always recite the hymn beginning with 'jātavedase' as a source of well-being;
for one who has set out upon a difficult path, there shall be no fear of enemies."
Even if accused in various ways for treason or for fighting against the king,
a Brahmin who is incapable [of defending himself] must be protected by other Brahmins, even in a life-threatening situation.
By muttering this verse beginning with "jātavedase," one is liberated from them;
likewise, one who desires to accomplish [a goal] should mutter it while setting out with such a mind.
For the sake of accomplishment, one who is fortunate should not be harassed by thieves on the road;
having achieved his purpose, while staying in his own home, he should always practice this very [mantra].
One should recite these when the sun has risen, and likewise when it has set.
This auspicious prayer for well-being is recommended by day; at night, when one has seen a bad dream, one should constantly recite this [hymn], which destroys evil dreams as soon as one has awakened.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for Jātavedas; next is the Tvaritarudrakalpa, and then Tvaritarudra.

Having performed the worship of Śiva and restrained the breath (prāṇāyāma) by means of the root mantra and the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should proceed as follows: "Of this auspicious Tvaritarudra mantra, Adharvaṇa is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ), Tvaritarudra is the deity (devatā); 'Namaḥ' is the seed-syllable (bīja), 'Astu' is the power (śakti); its application (viniyoga) is in recitation for the sake of pleasing Tvaritarudra. Then, having performed the purification of the hands with the root mantra and having placed the Praṇava (Oṃ) upon the palms of both hands, one should perform the assignment of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).

Namely: Oṃ, to Rudra who is in the thumbs, salutation! Oṃ, to him who is in the fire, salutation to the index fingers! Oṃ, to him who is in the waters, salutation to the middle fingers! Oṃ, to him who is in the plants, salutation to the ring fingers! Oṃ, to Rudra who has entered into all beings, salutation to the little fingers! Oṃ, to that Rudra, salutation to the palms and backs of the hands! Thus is the placement of the heart and other limbs (hṛdayādinyāsa).

Oṃ, he who is Rudra, to the heart, namaḥ. Oṃ, he who is in Agni, to the head, svāhā. Oṃ, he who is in the waters, to the crest-lock, vaṣaṭ. Oṃ, he who is in the herbs, to the armor, huṃ. Oṃ, he who is Rudra who has entered into all beings, to the three eyes, vauṣaṭ. Oṃ, obeisance be to that Rudra, to the weapon, phaṭ. Thus is the binding with the weapon-mantra.

Now, the ritual placement of the feet (*pādanyāsa*): *Oṃ yaḥ*, salutation to the two feet; *oṃ rudraḥ*, salutation to the two shanks; *oṃ agnau*, salutation to the two knees. *Oṃ yaḥ*, salutation to the two thighs; *oṃ apsu*, salutation to the two ankles; *oṃ yaḥ*, salutation to the penis. *Oṃ oṣadhīṣu*, salutation to the navel; *oṃ yaḥ*, salutation to the belly; *oṃ bhuvanāmukhāya*, salutation to the face of the world; *oṃ viveśa*, salutation to the nose; *oṃ tasmai*, salutation to the three eyes; *oṃ rudrāya*, salutation to the space between the eyebrows; *oṃ namaḥ*, salutation to the forehead; *oṃ astu*, salutation to the head.
Now, the meditation:

One should meditate upon the god Rudra as four-armed and three-eyed, bestowing boons and fearlessness; holding a trident and a *ḍamaru* drum with his two upper hands, and Umā seated upon his lap in a lotus posture, holding [flowers] with her two hands and bearing a water-pot and a *mātuliṅga* fruit in her two lower hands.

Having meditated thus, one should perform the invocation and other rites with the root mantra using the sixteen modes of worship (ṣoḍaśopacāra), and daily recite it one hundred and eight times. "This is your portion, O Rudra"—this is the mudrā.

Now follows the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homavidhi*): Sitting facing the *liṅga*, one should offer oblations of clarified butter (*ghṛta*). When this is performed, the preliminary purification (*puraścaraṇa*) is accomplished. One desiring liberation should offer oblations of clarified butter and unbroken rice (*akṣata*); one desiring long life, with *dūrvā* grass; one desiring a maiden, with *ulaja* seeds; those desiring prosperity, with *apāmārga*; one desiring subjugation (*vaśya*), with honey-flowers (*madhupuṣpa*); one desiring fortune (*śrī*), with *bilva* fruits (*śrīphala*); one desiring nourishment, with white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*); the cessation of fever occurs through pieces of *guḍūcī*. One should offer eight thousand oblations of blue lotuses (*utpala*) along with curd, honey, and clarified butter.

Prosperity becomes available as desired. By performing a thousand oblations with *bilva* leaves smeared with curds, honey, and ghee, one destroys fever. One should offer a thousand oblations with *śālmali* fuel-sticks smeared with rabbit blood; the immediate death of enemies will occur. Wearing unwashed clothes and facing the sun, having recited [the mantra] a thousand times for one month, one brings yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, and others under control. After two months, one brings Indra and the other gods under control. Within one month, the gods beginning with Brahmā arrive;
Mahādeva himself, accompanied by Virūpākṣa and surrounded by hosts of spirits, appears.
"It is so," said the Blessed One; salutations to Bodhāyana.

In the *Śāntikāṇḍa* of Hemādri’s work, Bhīṣma said: Now, for the sake of attaining all perfections (*sarvasiddhi*), the sequence of the placement (*nyāsa*) and mudrās of Tvaritarudra, as well as the entire procedure of recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), and so forth, is being described.
Salutations to Him in whose belly the entire universe—both the stationary and the moving—is contained; salutations to that Brahman, who is the very self of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
The meter is Anuṣṭubh and the Atharva; the Ṛṣi is known as Tvarita; the deity is Rudra Tvarita; the seed-syllable is [the name of] the deity, and the power-mantra is "namo astu."

In a temple, on a riverbank, or in a pure place, the wise man, remaining silent and having restrained his senses, should sit down, control his weapon, and perform the ritual according to the prescribed rule.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) on both hands with the root mantra;
then, the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) should be performed in sequence starting from the heart and so forth.
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the heart and other limbs with five mantra-words:
having placed the mantra "yo rudro agnau" on the heart, one should place "yo apsu" on the head;
and "viśvā bhuvanāni viveśa" is declared to be for the eyes.
With the remainder [of the mantra], one should bind the armor upon him, and with the *vyāhṛtis*, one should bind the directions;
having placed the tips of the fingers together with the root-mantra, one should press them with the thumb.
The *sāmudrā* is declared to be the *subhagā*; thereafter, one should practice meditation.
"This is your portion, O Rudra"—thus is the display of the limb-mudrās (*aṅgamudrā*).
One desiring prosperity should place it on the head; one desiring splendor, however, on the eyes;
one desiring food and drink, on the mouth; and for the destruction of disease, on the neck.
One who desires happiness [should place it] in the heart; it becomes a bestower of knowledge when at the navel;
one who desires offspring [should place it] in the secret organ; and one who desires cattle [should place it] on the shanks.
One who desires a village should show it at the knees; one who desires all things, in the secret place (guhya); and one who desires subjugation, on the left arm.
For the destruction of evil, for the attainment of supernatural powers, or likewise for the removal of disease,
one should perform [the rite] outside the body while recollecting Śiva in his presence.
Four-armed and three-eyed, resembling pure crystal,
with two upper hands holding jars filled with nectar.
With both hands forming the mudrā of yoga, seated in a steady posture,
I meditate upon the Lord of the Mountains— Śaṅkara, the source of compassion, who bestows all desires, who is peaceful, yet possesses a fierce form in his terrible deeds.
Two-armed, holding a serpent-noose and a trident in his hand, and wearing matted locks.
Having meditated thus upon Mahādeva and having worshipped him with devotion,
one should sleep on the ground, conquer anger, observe celibacy, and eat sacrificial food (haviṣya).
One should first recite [the mantra] twenty thousand times, worship Śiva every day,
perform oblations with one-tenth of that number, and offer libations with one-fifth of that number.
The purification (mārjana) should be performed with a tenth part of that [number], followed by the feeding of Brahmins;
having thus completed the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) and worshipped Śaṅkara, one should quickly recite the Rudra-mantra, which bestows the fruit of all desires.
One who desires prosperity or one who desires peace should recite [the mantra] a hundred thousand times without sloth;
for the sake of prosperity, one should use fuel-sticks of *bilva* wood, and for the sake of peace, those made of *śamī*.
One should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) and likewise the sprinkling (mārjana) with oblations mixed with clarified butter;
thus, for all desired objects, one should offer barley at the conclusion of the fire-sacrifice (homa).
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, one who desires a son should then offer an oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa).
For the sake of wealth, one should offer *moma* with *śrīphala* fruits; for the increase of longevity, with *mārnayā*;
likewise, one desiring splendor should offer *tila* seeds mixed with clarified butter, indeed with *ghṛta*.
One desiring cattle should offer with rice; likewise, one desiring a kingdom should offer with barley.
For all desires, one should offer milk-rice mixed with sugar.
For the destruction of acute fever, one should offer clarified butter with *guḍūcī* leaves smeared with honey, while reciting the mantras of the Mahābhūtas and Ābhāsvaras.
For the destruction of all diseases, one should recite [the mantra] facing the sun;
one should recite it twenty thousand times, and the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with auspicious *arka* wood and *śamī* wood.

One desiring food should offer oblations with *udumbara* wood, and one desiring luster with *khadira* wood; through the offering of fuel-sticks of *apāmārga*, evil spirits and calamities are destroyed.
For the destruction of domestic afflictions, one should recite the mantra in the vicinity of a horse;
the sacrificial fuel sticks should be made from *aśvattha* wood, which is salty, cool, pungent, and fierce.
One should utter the mantra ending with "svāhā" while offering fuel sticks moistened with curd;
having offered fifteen oblations, one should exclaim, "Go, go!"
As long as the oblation and offering are given in an amount equal to a man’s meal,
a man or a woman, having acted thus, shall be liberated from the great seizing spirit.
If a person wishes to conquer someone, he should recite [the mantra] while facing that very spot;
he should offer oblations of palāśa leaves, and the wicked one shall meet his destruction.
One desiring a daughter obtains a beautiful daughter through the oblation of parched grain (lāja-homa).
Furthermore, when parched grain mixed with honey, white flowers, gold,
and food offerings are sacrificed, the entire world comes under his control.

The wise practitioner, desiring to bring women under his control, should raise his left side [of the body]. For the purpose of pacifying ailments of elephants and horses, he should place a single water-filled jar at the site of the fire-oblation (homa) together with sesame seeds and clarified butter.
Having recited the mantra eight thousand times, one should place a mango branch [upon them];
with that branch, their consecration is performed, as prescribed, while circumambulating it.
The pacification of the planets, the village deities, and so forth, should be performed by all [the officiants] as before;
and the worship of Vāstu should be performed with the eighty-one auspicious squares.
An offering (bali) should be made to Īśāna and likewise to the Lord of Beings (Bhūtānāṃpati);
when this is done, one shall obtain peace for both cattle and progeny.
And during all miraculous events at night outside the village,
one should sit and quickly recite the Durga mantra along with Bali.
A fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with palāśa wood combined with clarified butter;
an offering (bali) should be made to Īśāna in whichever direction the marvel occurred.
To him he should offer oblations to Tvaṣṭṛ, to Pūṣan, to the Lord of Hopes (Āśāpati), and likewise to the Lord of Cattle (Paśupati).
One who desires prosperity should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times and perform a fire-oblation with sesame seeds mixed with ghee.
An offering and worship should be performed for Śiva and Varuṇa;
furthermore, in all desired aims, there should be the rapid recitation of the Tvarita-mantra.
It may extend from twenty thousand up to one hundred thousand, but not beyond that.
When it is performed in this manner, success shall be attained; one who is free from desire shall attain the Divine.
Having enjoyed the pleasures of both this world and the next, he shall attain union with the Absolute.
Thus ends the procedure for the Tvaritarudra rite as proclaimed by Gāṅgeya in the Śāntikāṇḍa of the Hemādri; now follow the dreams and their results.

In that regard, having stated that one should worship the astrologers and the deity, Parāśara says in the *Adbhutasāgara*: "Having worshipped with mantras, the domestic priest should restrain [the king] on the ground; having placed a flower as a pillow at the head toward the east or west, the lord of the earth, eating only once that day and lying on his right side, should examine the dream according to the instruction: 'O Śambhu, salutations!'"

Salutations to the three-eyed one, who has hands granting boons, to the dwarf, to the multiformed, and to the lord of dreams! O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, wielder of the trident, whose vehicle is the bull—tell me, the eternal one, what is auspicious or inauspicious for me in this dream while I sleep. Clad in a single garment, lying upon a bed of *kuśa* grass with a restrained mind, one sees at the end of the night a dream that is either auspicious or inauspicious during the day.
Varāha states in the *Bṛhadyātrā* regarding auspicious dreams:
"Mountains, palaces, and peaks, as well as mounting a bull, are beneficial."
And likewise, the tracing of the moon, the stars, and the planets.
On the earth, there shall be the devouring of grain-stores, the slaying of enemies,
victory in disputes, success in gambling, and likewise victory in battles.
The eating of meats, fish, and likewise milk products;
the sight of blood, or even bathing with blood.
The drinking of wine, blood, and meat, as well as milk itself,
wrapped in an intestine upon the ground— likewise, the stainless sky.
The milking of buffaloes and cows is praised when it is done with ease;
likewise for lions, elephants, and mares.
O Lord, favor toward Brahmins and gurus brings auspiciousness.
Furthermore, the consecration with waters should be known as beneficial and bestowing sovereignty.
Likewise, there shall be royal consecration as well as the cutting off of the head,
death, the acquisition of fire, and burning by fire during the planetary periods.
Likewise, the crossing of waters, the ripening of dense and bitter fruit,
and the birth of female elephants, mares, and cows within the house [are auspicious].
Mounting lordly elephants, as well as weeping, is auspicious;
likewise, the acquisition of another's wife and bowing down [to others] are favorable;
so too are being bound with fetters, grain, and the smearing of ordure.
One may even behold seeds, kings, and friends.
These have been declared pure and as bestowing the attainment of sovereignty.
Parāśara, in the *Adbhutasāgara*, says:
"If a crow should seize one by the neck with its beak, or if one should stand holding fire in one's arm, or a parasol..."
Whether it be the Creator, or even a divine Brāhmaṇa, [this is] the ascent to Mount Rohaṇa by means of an elephant.

The eating or touching of the sun, moon, or stars; the falling off of one's own head; the mounting of a bull, a planet, a king, or a white lion—these three types of occurrences grant the sovereignty of the earth. Victory through extensive battle-struggles, gambling, or speech; the acquisition of cattle, deer, or men; and traveling along a road; the eating of excrement, smearing oneself with it, approaching a forbidden woman, or sexual intercourse; the obtaining of a peacock, the sight of crops, and so forth [are the results].

The sight of white, fragrant, and pleasing ointments, garlands, and garments; the sight of twice-born Brahmins, the preceptor of the gods (Bṛhaspati), and kings; and their blessings; as well as gems, silver, gold, and food eaten from vessels—ghee, curd, and *paramānna* (milk-rice)—all of this is auspicious.
In the Bṛhaspati-saṃhitā:
"He who has a white mark on his right arm shall obtain a thousandfold profit on the tenth day."
If even a serpent, a scorpion, or a jackal should bite him;
One should predict victory, the attainment of wealth, and a son for him who,
having encountered a young hen, a cock, or a female crane, perceives it [favorably].
One obtains land extending for a *krośa*, or a wife who speaks sweetly;
one drinks blood in a dream, or sometimes drinks liquor;
a Brāhmaṇa obtains knowledge, while another obtains wealth.
If one drinks milk in a dream, or if froth appears during milking,
that person shall have a drinking of Soma, or one should predict great wealth for them.
Upon obtaining curd, one gains wealth; upon obtaining ghee, one surely gains fame.
There is great suffering in consuming clarified butter, but fame comes from eating curd;
through wheat or barley, there is gain as well as the accomplishment of one's goals.
When flowers are obtained, one should know there will be wealth; when fruits, there will be unsurpassed prosperity.
On a seat, in a bed, on a vehicle, in the body, in a carriage, or in a house.
If one awakens while it is blazing, his prosperity shall face every direction.
The Boar:
Biting by a scorpion and so forth, gems, jewels, gold, a water-pot, a lamp, a young calf, a swan, a hare, and the like grant gain; [the sight of] cattle, elephants, and so forth grants wealth.
In the Viṣṇudharma: "Whether auspicious or inauspicious, whatever is seen during a single night, one should then predict its fruition to occur therein."
Now, regarding bad dreams— Devala states in the *Adbhutasāgara*:
"If one goes facing south, wearing red perfumes, garments, and garlands,
or mounts a donkey, a camel, or a buffalo, one does not live beyond three months."
In a dream, one may fall into a chasm or find oneself at the entrance of the womb.
He who does not tremble before that [death], his life ends with that very moment.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
If one vomits urine or feces, or likewise gold or silver [into water], [one must perform purification].
In this regard, one who dreams of liquor, meat, or sleep shall live for ten months; likewise, one who dreams of hair, charcoal, ashes, a serpent, or a river without water [shall live for ten months].
If one sees in a dream ten days before death,
being struck with stones by terrifying, hideous, black men with upraised weapons on the eleventh day, one's death will certainly occur immediately in that very dream.
A woman wearing red and black garments, singing and likewise laughing,
who leads one toward the south in a dream— even such a person does not live.
Varāha says:
O lady with thighs like a deer, wandering on the back of a lion leads to death; on the back of a man, it leads to becoming a pig;
on the back of a camel, there will be prosperity; and on the back of an elephant, [there is great success].
Vatsya and Viṣṇudharma state:
wearing soiled garments, anointing with oil, being covered in mud,
falling from a height, and likewise riding on a swing.
The falling of Śakra’s banner, the falling of the moon and the sun,
as well as the wrath of gods, brahmins, kings, and the common people.
Embracing virgins, sexual intercourse with widows,
the loss of one's own kinsmen, a beloved woman around the neck of a hero,
the acceptance of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), approaching women during their menses, and likewise being afflicted by diseases— these are [the omens].
The offering of fruits, as well as the clearing of the grassy plots,
the gathering [of materials], the breaking [of branches], and likewise the sweeping of the house.
O Piśāca of play, O flesh-eater, O monkey, O Aśvatara!
That practice of wearing saffron robes is likewise a mere toy for you.
One should also point out as bad dreams drinking oil, climbing up trees, and wearing garlands and ointments, as well as other such [omens].
Parāśara:
Anointing the body with oil that has been drunk by turbid water,
or eating cooked food with a tongue and teeth like those of a young child, brings about the onset of consumption and bestows half of one's grief.
The Liṅga Purāṇa states: "A man who has disheveled hair, who is naked, and who sings and dances [is liberated]."
If one goes from here toward the southern direction, that shall be the end of his life.
Other instances of such effort are to be known from the Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa, and Parva sections of the *Yuddhakāṇḍa*, as well as from the *Mahābhārata*, the *Rāmāyaṇa*, and other works.
And in the Matsya and Viṣṇudharmottara:
"The fruit [of the vow] shall be realized at the end of the year, during the first watch of the night."
In the second [case], the result occurs in six months; in Triyāmaka, in three months;
and in the fourth, in just one month—the fruit comes to pass, and not otherwise.

Parāśara: Dreams occurring during the four watches of the night— lasting for half a year, one month, three months, and one month respectively, with each subsequent watch increasing by a quarter of the preceding duration— yield results that are either undesirable or desirable according to their nature.
Varāha states: "In the first year, fruition occurs in half a year; in the second year, in half of a half-year (one quarter); in the third year, fruition occurs after one month;
and at the end of the Śarvīrī [period], fruition occurs in a dream—thus it has been proclaimed by the wise."

In his dream, he sees a man with formidable teeth who kills him; a boar kills him; a monkey makes him leap; a wind swiftly carries him away; having swallowed gold, he vomits it up; he eats [the fruit of] a single *puṇḍarīka* lotus; he travels in vehicles yoked to formidable asses and boars; he sees a black cow with a black calf; wearing a garland of *nalada* grass, he walks facing south. Whosoever sees even one of these things, that person will meet with misfortune. Having cooked a mess of rice (*sthalīpāka*), he should spend the night...

"Having offered oblations verse by verse with the *sūkta*, and having fed the Brahmins with food or [the name of the deity], one should eat the *caru* oneself"— herein, the *lakṣahoma* (homa of one hundred thousand offerings) is to be performed,
as stated previously regarding "dreaming of a cow, seeing a marvel," and so forth.
And likewise, the recitation of the Caṇḍī is stated: "In all rites for pacification, as well as upon seeing a bad dream,
or when afflicted by the oppression of planets— listen to this most formidable majesty of mine."
"An evil dream seen by men turns into a good dream," and so forth, from the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa.
Parāśara:
O King, the worship of Brahmins and others, the recitation of mantras, fasting, and service to Brahmins;
the gift of sesame, food, cows, land, and gold—these destroy bad dreams, as does water from the Ganges and a cow.
Being composed, one should offer oblations there with sesame seeds.
One should give a cow as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) with the *tiloṣṭica* mantra;
there, one should satisfy the Brahmins with sacrificial fees, food, and other offerings.
Various kinds of gifts should be given for the cessation of inauspicious effects;
otherwise, after six full months have passed, death will occur.
In the Matsya Purāṇa, one should know the hymn to Vāsudeva, as well as his worship,
and the hearing of the story of Gajendra; this is known to be the destroyer of bad dreams.
For it is said: "The recitation of the Thousand Names of Viṣṇu is meritorious and destroys evil dreams."
In the *Prayogapārijāta*, Śaunaka states:
"In these cases of dreams and portents, Kālikā is the presiding deity;
one should diligently perform here as well the procedure for worship as previously described."
The best of the twice-born should diligently perform a fire sacrifice at night alone, offering one hundred and eight oblations with the mantra for the destruction of dreams and the like.
Having offered milk-rice with each verse, he should recite "The night has shone forth" in sequence.
Having diligently offered one hundred and eight oblations with this mantra—
that is to say, with the Kālarātri mantra—
one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor, as well as garments, gold, and even cattle.
If one is unable to give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) even when it is prescribed, [one is likewise unable] in the rite of fire-oblation (homa).
The wise man should give gold as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) at that very moment;
he should present all the items, such as garments and water-pots, to the officiating priest (hotṛ).
Regarding that very same [dream]:
if one should see an undesirable result in a dream, the following procedure is prescribed for it:
first, with the verse "Ā dyā no deva Savitar," [he should recite] once.
Thereafter, one should perform the supreme oblation with the five verses beginning with "dunvapna svapna," and following that, with the verse beginning with "rājanyujjya."
One should worship the Sun with all these Rigvedic verses.
When this is done, the vision of that bad dream will become fruitless;
thus, reciting "atha svapnasya" every morning, day after day.
One should recount the entire bad dream; therefore, one does not encounter fear from it.
In this regard, a *śrāddha* should also be performed when there is an abundance of materials suitable for a *śrāddha*, as well as upon the sight of a bad dream.

"One should perform a Śrāddha at will on one's birth-star (janmarkṣa) and during afflictions caused by planets," according to a statement from the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa in the Pṛthvīcandrodaya. This has been stated by us in the Nirṇayasindhu.

Thus ends the rite for the pacification of bad dreams (*duḥsvapna-śānti*) in the *Śāntiratna* composed by Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa. Now follows the rite for the pacification of the building site (*vāstu-śānti*). Regarding its timing, some details have been stated by us in the *Nirnayasindhu*; here they are briefly set forth.
Nārada:
O gentle one, the months of Phālguna, Vaiśākha, Māgha, Śrāvaṇa, and Kārtika are suitable for the construction of a house;
they bestow sons, health, and wealth.

Bādarāyaṇa states: The commencement of a house, the laying of the foundation stone, the installation of the wooden beam, and the erection of pillars are recommended in the months of Vaiśākha, Phālguna, Pauṣa, Śrāvaṇa, and Mārgaśīrṣa.
Grief, grain, the five elements, cattle, sleep, poverty, conflict, the loss of servants,
the attainment of one's own prosperity, fear of fire, and fortune— these are the effects produced by the months beginning with Caitra at the time of commencing a house.
In the Matsya Purāṇa it is said: In Āṣāḍha, there is the destruction of servants, jewels, and the class of cattle;
likewise in Mārgaśīrṣa, there is loss of grain; and in Pauṣa, there is fear from thieves.
The month of Āṣāḍha is said to be auspicious, while Pauṣa is declared to bestow inauspiciousness.
In the *Ratnamālā*:
"When the Sun is in Cancer, Leo, Aries, or Aquarius, houses should face east or west;
when it is in Libra, Aries, Taurus, or Scorpio, they say they should face south or north."
Garga says:

The commencement of a house is recommended under the three stars following Mṛgaśīrṣa (Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya), Rohiṇī, Puṣya, Anurādhā, Hasta, and Citrā, as well as under Dhaniṣṭhā, Uttara-phalgunī, and Uttara-bhādrapadā.
O Mātsya, let all days— Sunday, Tuesday, and Wednesday— be auspicious;
having obtained the strength of the Moon and Sun, and with the ascendant aspected by benefics.
One should perform the erection of pillars and so forth, while avoiding all other [such works].
Indeed, it should be performed in palaces, as well as in wells and ponds.
Regarding the examination of the ground, it is stated in that very same [text]:
"Having smeared a space measuring one *aratni* on all sides with cow-dung, and having placed a jar filled with water upon it, one should prepare four wicks."
One should kindle a full fire for the purpose of testing the ground in the direction of that mountain.
In the rite of illumination, one should take up the syllables in their proper sequence starting from the east;
having made a pit measuring one cubit, upon the filling of that excavation—
On the third, fifth, or seventh night, those [seeds] which sprout there are considered superior;
among them, the earth where the oldest sprouts is the best, while the others are considered inferior.
Or rather, having performed worship in the southeast corner (Va-rā-ha), one should lay down the first stone;
the remaining stones and the pillars should be erected by proceeding clockwise.
Lalla says: The site, the kitchen, the bedchamber, the elephant stable, the horse stable, and the treasury— these,
in order starting from the eastern direction of the deity, along with the center, are for the establishment of the king.
In the *Āśvalāyana Sūtra*:

"The waters used for the journey, having come together from all sides into the center, should leave the bedchamber by way of circumambulation; they should flow toward the east, for everything is fully auspicious when flowing in this manner."
Vasiṣṭha:
To the western part of his own house, his paternal uncle has a temple for Gaja.
Garga says:
A house constructed with another's corners, another's doorways, another's pillars, or even with another's wells, trees, and so forth, is useless.
Nārada says:
Entry [into the forest] should be known as mediocre during the months of Mārgaśīrṣa and Kārttika;
it is auspicious during the months of Māgha, Phālguna, Vaiśākha, and Jyeṣṭha.
Vasiṣṭha: Having prepared the auspicious site, having honored the Brahmins with water for the feet and placed a full water-pot before them,
he should enter the beautiful palace, which is adorned with arches, garlands, and canopies, accompanied by virtuous women and the sounds of song and instrumental music.
One should place two signs each in the directions starting from the east of the ascendant;
one should place one sign each on the left like a garland, and one should contemplate Indra there.
Nārada said:
A wise person should not enter a house that is without doors, covered with grass, where offerings have not been given, or which is devoid of food; such a place is a source of calamities.
One should place an earthen box containing gold, gems, grain,
and moss into a pit one cubit deep in the center of the house on the day of the planet.
In the Hemādri, according to the Mātsya Purāṇa:
"Having divided it into eighty-one squares with straight lines using gold,
and having smeared it with a paste, one should then stretch threads all around it."
Ten lines extending eastward and ten extending northward should be understood as the nine-by-nine division for the layout of all building sites.
One should worship forty-five deities established in their respective positions:
thirty-two are to be worshipped in the outer regions, and at the end, thirteen.
In the center, within the nine squares, Brahmā is recorded as occupying four squares;
there are twenty squares occupied by those with one square each, and an equal number recorded as having two squares each.
I shall describe them by name; listen to their locations as well.
One should worship the deities in sequence, beginning from the northeast corner.
Śibi, Parjanya, Jayanta, the wielder of the thunderbolt (Kuliśāyudha),
Sūrya, Nitya, Bhṛśa, Ākāśa, Vāyu,
Pūṣan, Cavitatha, Gṛhataka, and both Yamas.
Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, Mṛga, and likewise Pitṛgaṇa; Dauvārika, Godha, Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, and Jalādhipa.
Asura, Śoṣapāpa, Roga,
Hirbudhnya, Bhallāṭa, Soṣasarva, Aditi, and likewise Śati.
Outside, there are thirty-two deities;
listen now to those situated within the four corners, beginning with Īśāna, which the wise one should worship.
Āpaścaiva, Sāvitra, Jaya, and likewise Rudra—
Brahmā is situated in the center with these eight [deities] surrounding him.
Aryaman, Savitṛ, Vivasvat the lord of the gods,
Mitra, Dhara, Yakṣman, and likewise Pṛthvīdara are recorded.
Aṣṭama, Apavatsa, Apa, Apsat, Parjanya, and Aditi are recorded as being situated around Brahmā.
In the middle of that, on the outside, there are twenty two-footed [deities] on all sides:
Aryaman, Vivasvat, Mitra, and likewise Pṛthvidhara.
On all sides around Brahmā, let there be three steps everywhere;
Agni is established in his head, Viṣṇu in his arms, and the waters, the imperishable ones, in his mouth.
Pṛthvīdhara and Uryama are established in the position of the body;
likewise, Cāpavatsa should always be worshipped by the wise in the region of the chest.
Satyasoma and the others belong to that [deity]; from the word *bahu*, five and five [are assigned].
Rudra and Rājayakṣman are located at the wrist-joint of the hands. Sāvitra and Savitṛ likewise [belong] to the right hand in the act of protecting.
Vivasvān and Amitra were both situated within her womb.
Pūṣan and Pāpayakṣman are stationed at the wrists of the two hands;
likewise, Aśu and Raśmi are situated on the left side.
Likewise, on the right side, Vitatha, Saṃgraha, and Kṣata are to be known;
on the thighs, Yama and Ambupa; and on the knees, Gandharva and Puṣpaka.
In the two calves are Bhṛṅga and Sugrīva; in the buttocks and thighs are Dauvārika and Mṛga;
likewise, Jaya and Śakra are in the penis, and the Pitṛs are in the feet.
In the center, occupying nine squares, Brahmā resides in the heart and is worshipped there.
A temple site consisting of sixty-four squares has been prescribed by Brahmā for a palace.
There, in the four quarters of the Brahma-square, there is one square in each corner;
and in the eight outer compartments, both [the syllables] are situated together with their meanings.
Twenty are said to be two-footed, and four are remembered as four-footed.
Pūjāmahānārada:
One who knows the Vāstu-mantra [should worship] with *dūrvā* grass, curd, unbroken rice, and so forth, using the Vāstu-mantra.
Vasiṣṭha:
Or one may worship with the syllable Om, or else with their respective names.
The fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed on a threefold mortar or in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit;
it should be offered with barley, sesame seeds, and fuel-sticks (samidh) produced from milk-exuding trees.
With twigs of the palāśa, khadira, and udumbara trees, according to the ritual manual.
Or else, it should be performed with kuśa grass, dūrvā grass, and bhava plants combined with honey and clarified butter; or likewise with five bilva fruits, or even with bilva seeds.
At the conclusion of the *homa*, one should offer a *bali* in the site of the *vāstu* with various kinds of food, both solid and soft;
one should present food smeared with ghee to Śikhin in the northeast corner (*īśakoṇa*).
One should offer boiled rice mixed with blue lotuses and ghee to Parjanya; one should offer a yellow banner made of flour to Jayanta; and one should present an offering of flour to the Tortoise.
For Indra, one should offer five jewels and likewise a thunderbolt made of flour;
for Sūryā, a canopy, as well as a cake and parched grain flour.
One should offer ghee and wheat to Satya, and fish to Bhṛśa;
one should offer fried cakes to Antarikṣa, and flour-meal to Vāyu.
Parched grain (lājāḥ) should be given to Pūṣan, and boiled rice with sesamum to Vitatha.
One should offer honeyed food to Gṛhakṣata, meat-rice to Yama,
fragrant rice to the Gandharvas, and the tongue of a ram to Bhṛṅga.
One should give barley-gruel to the Mṛgas, and likewise kṛsara to the Pitṛs.
To the gatekeeper he gives a tooth-stick, and likewise to Gṛhakṣata an offering.
One should give cakes to Sugrīva, and milk-rice (pāyasa) to Puṣadanta.
Likewise, in the western quarter, there should be a lotus joined with a pillar of kusha grass.
One should give a golden image made of flour to an Asura who is considered a Surā;
to a Paippalada, ghee with rice and mustard; and to a Yātumāna, a monitor lizard.
A ghee-laddu should be given to Hiraṇyagarbha, a fruit of excellent quality to Hirbudhnya;
a cake should be offered to Mukhya, and thereafter, boiled rice with mung beans is prescribed.
At the location of Bhallāṭa, one should offer honeyed milk-rice (madhupāyasa) to Soma.
For Nāga, flour made from śāli rice; likewise, for Aditi, pośikā.
One should offer a *mārīkā* with the words "ditetu"; such is the external *bali*.
Milk should be given to Kṣīramāpa, curd to Māpavatsa,
and one should give a sweetmeat ball (laḍḍuka) with black pepper and rice cooked with kuśa grass to Sāvitra.
One should offer molasses cakes to Sāvitra, ghee and sandalwood to Jaya,
and again offer red sandalwood and milk-rice (pāyasa) to Vivasvat.
One should offer yellow orpiment with boiled rice mixed with ghee to Indra;
to Mitra, jaggery-rice; to Rudra, milk-porridge with ghee;
and to Rājayakṣman, raw grain as well as meat should be offered.
One should cause meat, earth, and kūṣmāṇḍa gourds to be given to Pṛthvīdhara;
one should give sugar, milk-rice (pāyasa), and a drink to Aryaman.

One should offer the five products of the cow, barley, sesame seeds, unbroken rice grains, sacrificial oblation (havis), cooked rice (caru), and various kinds of food, both solid and soft, to the Brahman priest.
Thus worshipped, may the gods always grant peace;
one should give gold to all [the priests] and a milch cow to the Brahmin.
An offering to the Rākṣasas should consist of meat and rice mixed with wine;
likewise, meat, curd, ghee, lotus filaments, and oblation (havis) combined together.
Taking recourse in the northeastern quarter,
one should offer the oblation consisting of meat, curd with blood, and turmeric with curd.
Taking recourse in the south-eastern direction, one should offer it after tearing [the victim];
one should give rice along with blood, combined with pieces of fish.
One should offer yellow and red oblations for the sake of subduing a human being;
for the Vāyavya and Pāparākṣasī spirits, one should offer fish, meat, wine, and spirituous liquor.
Milk-rice (pāyasa) should also be offered everywhere in due order under one's own name,
preceded by the syllable Om and accompanied by the word of salutation (namaskāra).
Then, one should cause the sacrificer to perform a bath with all medicinal herbs.
One should worship the twice-born with great devotion, as well as any other planets that have arrived;
having performed this pacification of the site (vāstūpaśamana), one should carry out the ritual action.
At the commencement of a palace, a mansion, or a garden; at their renovation; at the restoration of what is dilapidated; and likewise at the construction of a house or a garden.
Likewise, during the installation of the doors and other elements, as well as during the construction of the temple,
by entering the city and the residence, all defects are pacified;
having performed the pacification of the site (vāstu), one should then encircle it with a cord.
With the *rākṣasoghni* [mantra] and the *pāvamāna* hymn, one should perform the consecration of the dwelling and other such rites.

One should perform dancing, auspicious instrumental music, and the recitation by Brahmins. The wise person who performs this according to the prescribed rule every year, whether in his own home or in a temple, shall never encounter suffering.
One should perform the sequence of bali offerings according to the rules for oblation (homa) prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras.

The procedure for the pacification of the site (vāstu) of a palace that has been described is here prescribed in conjunction with the pacification of the site of a city-gate (paurāmavāstu), as taught in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra.

O King, he should satisfy the best of the twice-born with various kinds of food and drink; then, dressed in clean garments, he should enter his beautiful home. Having filled a water-pot with curds and unbroken grains of rice, adorned with soft flowers and fruits, and having given gold and clothing to the excellent brahmins, he should enter his own house, which is the abode of auspiciousness and peace.
Aśvalāyana says that one should enter while holding seeds;

likewise, the Vasiṣṭha-saṃhitā also prescribes this pacification (śānti), though a slight distinction is mentioned therein: "He who enters a new house without having performed the worship of Vāstu [will meet with misfortune]."
One does not experience various kinds of diseases, afflictions, or any manner of impurities.
Thus concludes the Vāstu-śānti.
Now follows the procedure for the Paramaśāyi-vāstu-śānti;
and now follows the procedure for the Vāstu-śānti performed by our father.

On an auspicious day prior to the day of entering the house, during the forenoon, the performer—accompanied by his wife, wearing a clean garment, and having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma)—having declared the place and time, shall say: "For the sake of accomplishing the auspiciousness of this dwelling at the commencement of the house-construction and so forth, I shall perform the Vāstu-śānti rite for the nine planets."

Having thus resolved, he should further resolve: "As an ancillary part of this, I shall perform the worship of Gaṇapati, the recitation of the auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana), the worship of the Mothers (mātṛkā-pūjana), the Nāndī-śrāddha, and the selection of the preceptor (ācārya) and others. Having made this resolution and selected the preceptor and the others, he should honor them with ornaments, garments, and other gifts. In that ceremony, there are four officiating priests (ṛtvij). Then the preceptor, having resolved, "I shall perform the ritual," should scatter cow-dung and white mustard seeds while reciting these mantras.
Whatever being is stationed here, having always occupied this place, let all of them leave this spot and go wherever they belong. Let no beings or piśācas wander about in any direction.
One should commence the rite of pacification (śāntikarma) without opposition from anyone:
"May the spirits, ghosts, piśācas, and other rākṣasas depart;
leave this place and go elsewhere; I shall take possession of this ground."

Then, having placed together in one place cow’s urine with the *gāyatrī* mantra, cow dung with the verse beginning "gaṃdhadvārām," milk with "apyāyasva," curd with "dadhikrāvṇo," clarified butter with "mimikṣire," and *kuśa*-water with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," he should stir them with *kuśa* grass while reciting the *praṇava*.
One should sprinkle all the houses and other structures with the three-verse hymn beginning with "śucī vo havyā."

Then, at the commencement of the planetary rite, having prepared for the sacrificer a square pit measuring one cubit with a sacrificial seat (*yoni*), a fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) with three circumferences, and a raised platform (*sthalam*) four finger-breadths high; and having fashioned two altars (*vedi*) to the east of that, each measuring one cubit and four finger-breadths in height out of clay; one should plant four stakes in the four corners starting from the northeast on the northern altar.
"Oṃ! May the twenty spirits of the earth and the world-protectors from all sides remain in this house forever, bestowing long life and strength"—with this mantra, one should install them.
In the case of re-consecration (pratiropaṇa), the repetition of the mantra alone [is required] even in the preceding [rites].
However, in the case of a temple (prāsāda) and so forth, if there is an obstacle from a planet, one should also substitute the respective names [of those deities].
Thus, at the end of all [mantras], the word "pīti" (protection) is applied to the locations.
Then, in the order of planting, one should offer oblations of *māṣa*-bean rice near the pegs with the formula:
"To the fires, to the serpents, and to whoever else has taken refuge here—I present this offering; may it be auspicious, pure, and well-prepared. Thus one should give.
Then, upon a fresh cloth on the altar, with saffron and other pigments using a needle made of gold, silver, or other metal, one should draw the ten [lines]:
Śāntā, Yaśovatī, Kāntā, Viśālā, Prāṇavāhinī, Satī, Sumatī, Sunandā, Subhadrā, and Suradhā.
Having first begun with the names ending in "namas," such as "it-oṃ-kāka" and so forth,
one proceeds from east to west in a straight line.
Having made ten furrows (khā) separated by two finger-breadths, they are oriented toward the north and are equal [in depth].
Furthermore, one should worship Hiraṇyā, Suvratā, Lakṣmī, Vibhūti, Vimalā, Priyā, Jayā, Balā, Viśokā, and Īḍā, in this sequence of ten.
By these names, the rites beginning with the south and ending in the north are thus completed.

Having prepared ten lines as before, whether in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should meditate upon Vāstu, install the sacred fire, and on the southern altar draw the mandala of the nine planets with colored powders. Having established the planets and other deities there, one should worship them with the sixteen types of offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra). Then, having placed a water-pot (kalaśa) in the northeast and proceeded to the Vāstu-mandala, one should invoke the deities beginning with Śikhin (Agni) into the images or onto heaps of unbroken rice (akṣata-puñja), starting from the square in the northeast corner, using their respective name-mantras preceded by the syllable Om and ending with "Namaḥ."
There, at the northeast corner of the site, on the head [of the Vāstu-purusha], one should say: "Salutation to Śikhin;
I invoke Śikhin," and thus install him.
Likewise, further on:
in its southern single square, in the right eye, [one places] Parjanya;
in its southern half, in the western region—that is, in the two squares of the right ear—one places Jayanta.
On his two right feet, on the right shoulder, is the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra).
On his two right feet, on the right arm, is Sūrya. On his two right feet, on the right arm itself, is Sūtya.
In the two feet on its right side, [one places] Fire intensely in the right elbow;
in the single foot situated to its right, [one places] Ether in the right forearm;
in the foot in the right corner, [one places] Wind in the right forearm.
In the single square immediately west of that, on the right wrist, is Pūṣan;
in the square west of that and the square north of that, on the right side, is Vitatha;
and in the two squares west of those, on the right side, is Gṛhakṣata.
To the west of that, at the two feet, [place] Yama on the right thigh;
to the west of that, at the two feet, [place] Gandharva on the right knee;
to the west of that, at the two feet, [place] Bhṛṅgarāja on the right calf.
In the square situated to the west of that, on the right side, [place] a deer; in the square situated to the west of that, on the right side, [place] a deer;
in the square in the south-western corner, [place] the ancestors at the feet.
In the first word following that, one places Dauvārika on the left buttock;
in the word following that, and in the preceding word, one places Sugrīva on the left thigh;
and in the two words following that, one places Puṣpadanta on the left knee.
Beyond that, in the next two squares, there is Maruṇa on the left thigh;
beyond that, in the next two squares, there is Asura on the left side;
and beyond that, situated above, there is Pāpa on the left wrist.
In the square of the northwest corner beyond that, there is disease in the left arm;
in the single square to the east of that, there is a horse in the left arm;
and in the single square to the east of that, in the right foot, there is a snake in the left elbow.
In the two squares preceding that, [he places] Ballāṭa on the left arm;
in the two squares preceding that, Soma on the left forearm;
in the two squares preceding that, Sarpa on the left shoulder.
In the two squares prior to that, place Aditi in the left ear;
in the two squares prior to those, in the single square, place Idā in the left eye; in the southern [square], in the corner square of the Śibi-foot, place Āpā in the mouth.
In the southeast, one places Āgneya in the square below the foot of Vāyu; in the southwest, Sāvitra in the square below the right hand;
in the northwest, Meḍhreya in the square below the penis;
and in the northeast, Rudra in the square below the left hand.
In the *madyapadas*, starting from the *īśāna* corner square, [one places] Aryaman in the three squares to the south, in the right breast;
Savitṛ in the square of the south-east corner, in the right hand;
and Vivasvat in the three squares to the west of that, in the right side of the abdomen.
In the square of the southwest corner behind that, one should place Viśvabudhādhipa on the two testicles;
in the square of the northwest corner to the north of that, Rājayakṣman on the left hand;
and in the three squares to the east of that, Pṛthivīdhara on the left hand.
One should place Āpavatsa in the nine-square space at the northeast corner of that [central area],
and Brahmā in the nine-square space in the center of the chest.

To the north of that is the site for the bull: "O Lord of the Dwelling, you are praised... (Vāstoṣpate prati tiṣṭha). This is in the Triṣṭubh meter. Its application is in the invocation of Vāstoṣpati. Om.

One should install [the deity] with the mantra: "O Lord of the Dwelling (Vāstoṣpati), recognize us. This should not be done with gold or silver. Then, outside the mandala, one should install Carakī, Vidārī, Pūtanā, and Pāparākṣasī respectively in the northeast, southeast, southwest, and northwest corners; and in the east, south, west, and north directions respectively, one should install Skanda, Mṛtyu, Jṛmbhaka, and Pilipiccha using their respective name-mantras as before. Furthermore, in the eight directions starting from the east, one should install Indra, Agni, Yama, and Nirṛti.

One should install Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kubera, and Īśāna, either with their respective mantras or by name, along with the rites of invocation, seating, and other offerings. Having established a water-pot (kalaśa) made of black clay and free from cracks—either individually or all together—and having placed therein sandalwood paste and other fragrant substances, barley, dūrvā grass, five types of sprouts, seven kinds of earth, and the five gems; having wrapped it with a cloth and placed a full vessel (pūrṇapātra) upon it, one should invoke Varuṇa and then invoke the holy waters (tīrthas) therein. Thereafter, the preceptor (ācārya) should perform the anvādhāna rite.

Therein, having recited up to "the two eyes with clarified butter (*ājya*)," one should offer oblations of fuel-sticks (*samit*), sesame, and clarified butter in such-and-such a number for the nine planets; likewise for the presiding deities (*adhidevatās*) and their respective subordinate deities (*pratyadhidevatās*), starting with Vināyaka and others, in such-and-such a number of fuel-sticks, sesame, and clarified butter oblations; for the forty-five deities beginning with Śikhin, in such-and-such a number of fuel-sticks, sesame, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and clarified butter oblations; and for Vāstoṣpati with the four verses [beginning] with "vāstoṣpate," in sequence with such-and-such a number of *bilva* fruits or their leaves, [and for] Carakī and others in such-and-such a number...

Having enumerated the principal deities with the four oblations beginning with the *samidh* (sacrificial fuel), one should offer the *samidh* and the other items as prescribed, starting with "with the remainder [one offers] to Sviṣṭakṛt. Then, the sacrificer, seated to the south of the fire, having enumerated all the deities and the materials, should relinquish them to them, performing the renunciation of ownership (*svatvatyāga*) with the formula "Obeisance to me," and so forth. Since it is impossible to perform the renunciation of ownership for every individual oblation when many priests are the performers of the *homa*, the preceptor (*ācārya*), after performing the gift of this [land] and so forth, should cause the principal *homa* to be performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

The specific substances for each [deity] are stated according to their respective order: for the nine planets, one should offer sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*) made of *arka*, *pālāśa*, *khadira*, *apāmārga*, *pippala*, *udumbara*, *śamī*, *dūrvā*, and *kuśa* wood—measuring a span (*pradeśa*) in length—either one hundred and eight, twenty-eight, or eight of each, as well as oblations of sesame seeds (*tila*) in the same number. When [the offering] is above these, the number of oblations remains the same; however, some say there should be one oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) for each.

Then, for the Adhidevatās and Pratyadhidevatās, as well as for Vināyaka and others, one offers fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of the same number but slightly fewer; likewise, for the respective deities of the house and so forth, one offers fuel-sticks of *palāśa* wood. According to the view that there are eight [deities] for the planets (*graha*), four [stanzas] are prescribed for these as well.

In this rite, one oblation is to be performed with three blades of *dūrvā* grass; thus the number is determined. Alternatively, one may use a single triple-bladed *kuśa* grass. Then, for Śikhin and the others, one should offer fuel sticks (*samit*), sesame, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and clarified butter (*ājya*) individually—eight thousand, eight hundred, twenty-eight, or eight times each—with their respective names preceded by the *praṇava* and ending in *svāhā*. Here, fuel sticks of *udumbara* are primary; if those are unavailable, those of *aśvattha* and other trees may be used. All the fuel sticks should be offered together with honey, clarified butter, curd, milk, or boiled rice.

The *tilas* (sesame seeds) should be black, and the *yavas* (barley) white; some say that among the sesame seeds, one should include as much barley as [prescribed]. With the four verses beginning with "vāstoṣpate," one should offer fuel-sticks (*samidh*), sesame, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and clarified butter (*ājya*) respectively, one hundred and eight times each. Then, with the two verses "vāstoṣpate" and "dhruvāstūṇām," one should offer five *bilva* fruits smeared with honey for each verse, or one fruit per verse. Regarding the four verses beginning with "vāstoṣpate": Viśiṣṭha is the deity, Vāstoṣpati is the seer, the first three are Triṣṭubh and the last is Gāyatrī; their application is in the fire-oblation (*homa*).
For the verse "vāstoṣpate dhruvāstūṇām," Bṛhatī is the meter and Vāstoṣpati is the deity; its application is in the fire-oblation.

Then, for Carakī and the others, one should offer four substances with a count less than the primary [eight]. According to the learned, when the primary count is eight, the number elsewhere is four. All these substances must be offered only with the *hasa* mantra. Then, having performed the rites from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering up to the end of the expiatory oblations (*prāyaścitta-homa*), one should present an offering (*bali*) of black gram (*māṣa*) and cooked rice (*bhakta*) along with a lamp to Indra and the other guardians of the quarters (*dikpālas*).

Having prepared twelve portions or four portions of clarified butter (ājya) in the *sruc* ladle and having placed a coconut or other fruit therein, one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the verse beginning "mūrdhānam. [The mantra is: "mūrdhānaṃ divo" by Bhāradvāja, addressed to Vaiśvānara, in the *triṣṭubh* meter; its application is in the fire-oblation (*homa*). Then, having completed the remainder of the ritual procedure, such as the removal of the *praṇītā* water and so forth, one should present the offering (*bali*) to Śikhin and the others in the western part of the *vāstu-maṇḍala*, saying: "This is your milk-rice offering (*pāyasa-bali*), obeisance! and so on.

The Brahmins, having cooked *pāyasa* mixed with ghee for those [deities] beginning with the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) as will be described hereafter, then—after the preceptor and others have consecrated the patron (*yajamāna*) together with his wife by sprinkling them with water from the *śānti-kalaśa* while reciting Vedic mantras such as "samudrajyeṣṭhāḥ" and Puranic mantras such as "surāstvā"—should meditate upon the Earth in the form of a woman adorned with all ornaments and worship her with the mantra "oṃ dharāyai namaḥ," [recalling that] the site (*vāstu*) consists of all the gods and the supreme deity of the site consists of all the gods.
Then, starting from the house, one should wrap it three times with a triple-thread cord using the *pāvamāna* hymn and the *rakṣoghnī* verses.

When the thread is severed, [the following] is auspicious: then, with one breast-vessel filled with milk and the other breast-vessel filled with water, he should perform the uninterrupted stream of oblations using those same two hymns (*sūkta*) beginning with the word *dhārā*.

Then the sacrificer, having dug a knee-deep pit in the southeast corner of the house within the space designated for the sky, having smeared it with cow-dung, having adorned it with white sandalwood, flowers, unbroken rice, and other offerings, and having placed therein the seven types of seeds such as śāli rice along with curd-rice, he should take a new water-pot filled with water, containing a single white flower and worshipped with perfumes and other articles, holding it with both hands; then, kneeling upon the ground, he should fill the pit with that water while reciting "Oṃ namo varuṇāya."

In that regard, it is auspicious when the water swirls clockwise and the flowers face upward. Then, having placed seven grains, curd-rice, śaivāla, fruits, and flowers into an earthen basket, one should bring the previously established bull-dwelling (*vṛṣavāstu*) with the sounding of musical instruments and auspicious chants, set it upon that basket, worship it with perfumes and other offerings, and pray to it with two verses.

I have worshipped you, O Lord of the Dwelling, with auspicious offerings such as oblations and other forms of adoration; be gracious, protect me, O Lord of the Universe, and grant me the happiness born of a home.
O Vāstupuruṣa, salutations to you, O Lord who delights in sleeping upon the earth;
grant prosperity in wealth, grain, and all else within my home at all times.
Then, having removed the chest from its place, one should gradually deposit it into that pit with this [mantra].
Just as you carry upon your head the earth together with its mountains and oceans.
"O auspicious one, carry me there together with my wife, sons, and others.

When the pit has been filled with that very same earth, the result shall be excellent if it is equal [to the original], middling if there is a slight deficiency, and inferior if there is a greater deficiency.
Having smeared the ground around the pit with cow dung,
one should adorn it with white flowers, perfumes, and unbroken grains of rice.
Then, having worshipped the preceptor (ācārya) adorned with ornaments to the west of the fire,
and having given a cow with its calf, a pair of garments, and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
and having given sacrificial fees to the Brahman and the other officiating priests (ṛtvij) according to one's capacity.
Having performed and completed the worship of the planets, beginning with Śikhin, as well as the deities of the site (vāstudevatās).

Having dismissed [the deities] with "O gods, arise," having handed over [the ritual items] into the hand of the preceptor (ācārya), having worshipped the fire, and having dismissed it with "Go, go," he should have the Brāhmaṇas recite the *Śānti* together. For the gratification of the planets and others, as well as Śikhī and others, he should feed one or two Brāhmaṇas for each according to his capacity. Having received the blessings (*āśiṣaḥ*), he should eat accompanied by his friends. Thus, having performed the *Vāstu-śānti* on the first day, he should perform the entry into the house on the second day.
And it is as follows:

Having taken a full vessel that is new, filled with water, provided with sprouts and *dūrvā* grass, smeared with lime, wrapped in cloth, and accompanied by fruit, the patron (*yajamāna*), together with the Brahmins, his wife, and his sons, should enter the house amidst the sounding of musical instruments. He should then place the jar upon a heap of grain in the middle of the principal room. Then, for the sake of the prosperity of the household, having caused the *puṇyāha-vācana* (declaration of an auspicious day) to be recited, having fed the Brahmins, and having received their blessings, he should eat together with his friends.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the pacification of the site (*vāstu-śānti*).

Some, however, maintain that in the laying out of the mandala, the worship, the fire-oblation (*homa*), and the offering of the sacrificial fee (*pālidāna*), one should begin with Brahmā and the others in the eastern direction.
Likewise—
in the nine central squares, Vāstu’s heart and navel are Brahmā; to his east,
in three contiguous squares, is Aryaman on the right hand.
Vivasvat is in the three squares attached to the southern side of the Brahma-square, in the right portion of the abdomen.
Mitra is in the three squares attached to the western side of the Brahma-square, in the left portion of the abdomen.
Pṛthvīdhara is in the three squares attached to the northern side of that same [Brahma-square], in the left breast.
The Brahmapada is joined to the Īśānapada, and the Apavatsa is in the chest.
Savitṛ is in the southeastern position on the right hand;
Vibudhādhipa is in the southwestern position on the testicles;
Rājayakṣmā is in the northwestern position on the left hand.
Water is present in the mouth at the tooth-mark where it is joined with the footprints of the childless one.
The Sāvitra mantra is recited over the right hand, which is placed upon the word "Agni" following the word "Savitṛ."
Jaya is at the genitals, attached to the square of the Lord of the Vibudhas (Indra) in the south-western square;
Rudra is in the left hand, attached to the square of the Vāyavya (Wind-god) in the north-western square;
and from the square of the Lord of the Maṇḍala (Īśāna), one should place [the deities] beginning with Śikhin and ending with Diti.
Having established Carakī and the others as before, one should not invoke them as previously;
one should perform worship, fire-oblations, and so forth in sequence, while other matters are as described before.
Thus ends the Vāstu-śānti as prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras. Now follows the Maṇḍūka-vāstu-śānti: for a temple, palace, and so forth, one should construct a mandala consisting of sixty-four squares.

There, O Lakṣmī, having drawn nine lines with their tips pointing eastward and extending toward the north— using these names ending in "namaḥ": Yaśovatī, Kāntā, Supriyā, Vimalā, Śivā, Subhagā, Sumati, and Īḍā— one makes [the diagram] auspicious.

With these names ending in "namaḥ"—Prāṇā, Viśālā, Sthirā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Niśā, Virajā, and Vibhavā—one should draw nine lines with their tips pointing north and extending eastward; having unified the four central squares and divided the squares outside the four corners by means of the lines, one should install Śikhin and the others.
There, on the southern half of the square of Īśāna, one should place Śikhī on the head;
on the southern half-square [of that], Parjanya on the right eye;
and on the two squares to the south of that, Jayanta on the right eye.
On his two right feet is Kuliśāyudha on the right shoulder; on his two right feet is Sūrya on the right arm;
on his two right feet is Satya on the right arm.
In the Sārthapada square to its south, on the right elbow, there is Bhṛśa;
in the Āgneyapada square to its south, on the right arm, there is Ākāśa.
To the west of that, on the right arm itself, is Vāyu;
to the west of that, at the right wrist in one and a half squares, is Pūṣan;
to the west of that, on the two squares of the right side, is Vitatha.
To the west of that, on the two feet, Yama alone is placed on the right side;
to the west of that, on the two feet, Yama is on the right thigh;
to the west of that, on the two feet, Gandharva is on the right knee.
To the west of that, on the southern shank in one and a half squares, is Bhṛṅgarāja;
to the west of that, in the south-western square, is the deer on the right buttock; and to the north of that, in the space of the feet, are the ancestors.
In the word following that, which refers to the object denoted by the latter member of the compound, one places Dauvārika on the left buttock;
in the two words following that, one places Sugrīva on the left shank;
and in the two words following that, one places Puṣpadanta on the left knee.
In the two squares following that, [place] Varuṇa on the left side;
in the two squares following that, [place] Asura on the left side;
and in the one and a half squares following that, [place] Śoṣa on the left side itself.
In the northwest sector beyond that, there is sin at the left wrist;
in the sector east of that, there is disease at the left forearm;
and in the sector east of that, there is wind at the left elbow.
In the space preceding that [corner], Bhallāṭa is the primary deity on the left elbow;
in the space preceding that, Bhallāṭa is on the left arm;
and in the space preceding that, Soma is likewise on the left arm.
In the object prior to that, on the left shoulder, [he places] Sarpa;
in the object prior to that, in the left ear, Aditi;
in the object prior to that, in the left eye, Diti.
In the intermediate quarters: at the mouth, in the northern part of the Īśāna square, [one places] the Āvam; at the southern part of the Āgneya square, on the right hand, the Sāvitra;
at the northern part of the Nairṛtya square, on the penis, the Jaya; and at the northern part of the Vāyavya square, on the left hand, the Rudra.
From the center, in the two eastern squares, [one places] Aryaman on the right breast;
in the southeastern square, Savitṛ on the right arm;
and in the two squares to its west, Vivasvat on the right shoulder.
In the eastern part of the southwest square, one should place the Lord of the Gods (Indra) on the two testicles;
in the two squares to its north, Mitra on the left abdomen;
and in the western part of the northwest square, Yakṣman on the left hand.
In the two preceding squares, one should place Pṛthvidhara in the left hand;
Īśāna in the right-hand square, and Apavatsa in the northern [square].
In the four middle squares, one should place Brahmā at the heart and the navel.
To the north of that, one should install Vāstu in a water-jar with the mantra "vāstoṣpate" (RV 7.54).
The installation of Carakī and the others is as before. In each respective case, the verses for the temple and so forth should be inferred according to the [rules for] the planets.
On the following day, there is no entry here;
everything else is without distinction.
Thus concludes the *Paurāṇavāstuśāntiprayoga*, composed by Rāmakṛṣṇa Bhaṭṭa, son of Śrī Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa Sūri, whose lotus feet are worshipped by hosts of learned scholars.

Now, the *vāstu-śānti* (propitiatory rite for the dwelling) as prescribed in the Sūtras is set forth; this is to be combined with that previously mentioned for the twice-born (*dvija*). If one is unable to perform the previously mentioned rite, then only that prescribed in one's own specific Sūtra should be performed, since it is equally effective. However, for those for whom there is no such rite in their Sūtra, as well as for Śūdras, only the previously mentioned rite is to be used, because it is ordained as being common to all. Therefore, it does not apply exclusively to Śūdras alone; thus, the rite prescribed in the Sūtra is to be combined with the former. Regarding this, the procedure according to the Āśvalāyana Sūtra is as follows:

Having entered a well-constructed house made of wood and other materials, provided with grains such as rice and joined with auspicious moments, accompanied by Brahmins and preceded by the sound of musical instruments, one should place four stones in a clean location, lay down *sudūrvā* grass upon them, and there install a clay vessel called a *maṇika* with this [mantra]: "Born from the earth... (RV 10.97.4), "O Araṅgara, come hither... (RV 10.97.5), "Bound in three ways by the triple cord... (RV 10.97.6), "He praises the refreshing food (*irā*)... (RV 10.97.7), or "The refreshing food, O you who are free from disease... (RV 10.97.8).

Then he should sprinkle the water-jar with this [verse]: "O King Varuṇa, may you remain rejoicing in this place with the waters; bringing refreshment and pouring out clarity, may they enter together with Mitra and the thousandfold people."

Then, having taken that water into another vessel and having placed therein fragrant *dūrvā* grass, *śamī* branches, *udumbara* branches, rice grains, sprouts, fruit, and gold, one should sprinkle the entire house three times, proceeding from the east and moving clockwise, while reciting this hymn: "śanna indrāgnī" (RV 7.35). For this hymn of fifteen verses, Vasiṣṭha is the seer, the Viśvedevas are the deities, the metre is *triṣṭubh*, and its application is for sprinkling. The hymn is to be recited once.

Then, starting from the east, one should offer an uninterrupted stream of water with this triplet of verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā. For this triplet, Ambarīṣa, Siṃdhudvīpa, and the Waters are the seers; Gāyatrī is the meter; its application is in the pouring of the stream. Here too, it is recited three times.

Then, having taken the central fire and established it, having proclaimed the principal deity Vāstoṣpati four times, and having performed the *anvādhāna* up to the placement of the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*), he offers to Vāstoṣpati four times. Having silently poured out [the oblation], he proclaims the principal deity Vāstoṣpati four times, performs the *anvādhāna*, and completes the rite up to the placement of the full vessel; then, having offered to Vāstoṣpati four times and silently poured out [the remainder], he sprinkles [the materials] on that very day and completes the rite up to the portioning, taking portions according to the rule for sacrificial cuttings (*avadāna*).

One should offer oblations with the four mantras beginning with "vāstoṣpate," ending with *svāhā*. Regarding these four verses beginning with "vāstoṣpate": the deity is Vāstoṣpati; the meters are Triṣṭubh for the first three and Gāyatrī for the last; their application (*viniyoga*) is in the fire-oblation (*homa*). In every instance, the ritual relinquishment (*tyāga*) is made with the formula: "To Vāstoṣpati, this [is offered]. Then, having completed the remainder of the sacrifice beginning with the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering, one should feed a hundred Brahmins, or half of that (fifty), or according to the general rule, ten, or if unable, three, using the remaining sacrificial porridge (*caru*) and other food.

There, another cooking of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) need not be performed. Then, he should say to the Brahmins, "May you say, 'Auspicious is the site! Auspicious is the site! When they have said, "Auspicious is the site! Auspicious is the site!", he should eat together with his friends. This same procedure is desired even for the restoration of a dilapidated house, as in the case of the common propitiatory rite (*sādhāraṇa-śānti*).
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the Vāstu-śānti as prescribed in the Āśvalāyana Gṛhya-sūtra, composed by Śrī Pāma Kṛṣṇa.
As for the Vāstu-śānti and Pratiṣṭhā of temples, royal consecrations, and so forth, these should be understood from my previous work, the *Pūrva-kamalākara*.
In the Baudhāyana-sūtra:

Now, one desiring the prosperity of the house should begin the *gṛhaśānti* (house-purification rite) every month, or without interruption, or once a year, during the bright fortnight under an auspicious lunar mansion. With *tāpamārga*, *palāśa*, *śimī*, *śirīṣa*, *udumbara*, *sadābhadrā*, *mustā*, *tṛṇa*, and *indravallī*, he should sweep the house. Then, having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) while reciting the two verses beginning with "mā no mahāntam" and "mā nas toke," and with a handful of *darbha* grass, he should perform the sprinkling while reciting the hymn beginning with "yata indra bhayāmahe" and "svasti-dā viśaspatiḥ. He should then proceed with the section beginning with "kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ."

Having scattered the prepared grains in the center of the site and having established the fire facing the east, he offers cooked oblations with the two verses beginning "O Lord of the Dwelling" (*vāstoṣpate*).
