He offers additional oblations of clarified butter with the two verses beginning "O Lord of the Dwelling, firm is the pillar. He offers additional oblations of clarified butter with the two verses beginning "O Lord of the Dwelling, firm is the pillar. Without pausing for breath, he should offer a thousand oblations with the *Sāvitrī* verse while reciting those six [verses] beginning "O Lord of the Dwelling, firm is the pillar."

The *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is established according to the original model, up to the granting of the boon and the cows. Having satisfied the Brahmins with food, one should cause them to recite: "An auspicious day! Prosperity! Success! By practicing in this manner, they attain great nourishment; many sons are born, and no children die young. Neither malevolent planets nor diseases seize them; they shall not be harmed by fanged creatures, nor shall thieves, serpents, *rākṣasas*, or *piśācas* cause them affliction. If cows should stray, one should offer oblations in the midst of the cows, and one should sacrifice a thousand [oblations] for the sake of the cows.
"This is what they call peace for bipeds and quadrupeds; this alone they declare to be the 'garment' as a sacrificial fee," so said the venerable Baudhāyana.
Thus ends the pacification of houses and so forth as taught by Bādāyana. Now follows the pacification of inauspicious menstruation; its fruit is stated:
On the new moon, the eighth, the sixth, the twelfth, and on the days of the sun's retrogression;
in the first half of the Parigha yoga, and during the Vyatīpāta and Vaidhṛti yogas.
If the *saṃdhyā* (twilight) occurs during an eclipse (*upaplava*), it is auspicious for conception at the first menses. An eclipse (*upaplava*) means a planetary seizure;
[the women born then become respectively] a sickly woman, a devoted wife, a woman who suffers, or a woman possessing enjoyments.
A devoted wife shall experience suffering on Sundays and the other days of the week in succession.
Poverty and the gain of a son; friendship and the destruction of enemies;
the acquisition of friends and the loss of foes; and mental distress and the ruin of kinsmen.
Death, increase of the lineage, lack of food, destruction of the family,
splendor, loss of sons, and decline of the family— these occur in sequence.
Garga says: [A woman may be] fortunate yet ill-behaved, barren yet endowed with sons,
devoted to dharma yet a destroyer of vows, or one who delights in the offspring of others.
O Citrakāriṇī, there are both good sons and bad sons who are always devoted to their father’s abode;
likewise, there are wretched wives and those blessed with many sons.
She was a virtuous wife, ever dear to her husband, possessed of excellent sons, and enduring hardships; devoted to her own duties, free from violence, and endowed with meritorious offspring.
Constantly attached to hoarding wealth, yet endowed with sons and grain,
and being a fool who disregards others— these are the results, in order, for one born under the asterisms beginning with Punarvasu.
Nārada: Cancer,
Taurus, Sagittarius, Pisces, Gemini,
Virgo, Libra, and Aquarius— these signs are to be known as auspicious for women during their first menses.
Garga says:
A woman who wears white garments is fortunate; one with firm clothing is devoted to her husband;
one wearing linen is a sovereign of the earth; and one with new clothes is endowed with happiness.
She who wears worn-out clothes is unfortunate; she who wears red garments is diseased.
Then, a woman wearing blue garments who has become widowed while her hair is in flower [blossom] shall wear unevenly stained red garments and give birth to a son.
If there is blood and the appearance of a crow, the result will be misfortune during the menstrual period.
Vasiṣṭha states that one should avoid sexual union with a woman: "If that flower (menstrual blood) is seen to have many defects, then a rite for averting calamity must be performed."
She should sleep on a single bed with her husband until the day she sees her menstrual flow.
Vasiṣṭha in the Jyotirnibandha states:

In the first period of menstruation, the months of Pauṣa, Śukra (Jyeṣṭha), Ūrja (Kārttika), Māgha, Caitra, and Nabhasya (Śrāvaṇa) are auspicious; however, the days of the week of the malefic planets, the Riktā tithis, the Parvan days, the eighth, sixth, and sixteenth lunar days, as well as the night, the two twilights, and the afternoon are inauspicious. Furthermore, [the house] of another and an ill-placed [husband] are unfavorable.

Mixed with the village-root and sharp-edged, the man is slightly more than a mere fragment; the ruler of the realm is thus afflicted by sin, and the rising sun, old and blue, is variegated and supreme.
If the first two stars of the *darbha* constellation are occupied by a woman in her menses during the *viṣkambha* yoga, [there will be misfortune].
In Atigaṇḍa, she is to be honored; in Śūla, she becomes afflicted by colic;
in Gaṇḍa, the woman is unchaste; and in Vyāghāta, she is a suicide.
In Vajra, she is said to be a wanton woman; in Pāta, she destroys her husband; in Parigha, she is a barren woman whose children die; and in Vaidhṛti, she is the slayer of her husband.
Regarding the remaining [yogas] that bring about auspiciousness, Śaunaka states in the *Pārijāta*:
"O Śaunaka, I shall describe the pacification (*śānti*) for women who have experienced [menstrual] flow; on the fourth or fifth day, preceded by the propitiation of the planets (*grahātidhyā*)."
Since three heaps of rice, measured by a *droṇa* each, are required,
one should place three jars upon each heap, wrapped with thread, cloth, and so forth;
each jar should be filled individually with water from sacred pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha*).
Then, with the hymn consisting of nine verses beginning with "prasuva āpaḥ," and then with the verse beginning with "pravataḥ," one should proceed in sequence with the Gāyatrī.
One should place grains, medicinal herbs, gold, udumbara wood, kuśa grass, dūrvā grass, lotuses, vaṭa wood, bilva fruit, and akā flowers into the central pitcher.
Viṣṇukrāntā, Tulasī, Barhiṣa, Śaṅkhapuṣpī,
Śatāvarī, Gandhā, Nirguṇḍī, the two types of mustard (Sarṣapa),
Apāmārga, Palāśa, Panasa, and likewise Jīvaka.
Priyaṅgu, vaṃśa, wheat, rice, and the aśvattha tree;
milk, curd, clarified butter, as well as a lotus leaf and a blue water-lily.
One should collect these thirty-two medicinal herbs as they are available: the three types of kuraṇṭaka, guñjā, vacā, bhadraka, and mustaka.
One should sequentially place earth and medicinal herbs there with that mantra;
then, one should set upon the pitcher a vessel made of bell-metal, clay, bamboo, or copper.
One should place Bhuvaneśvarī there, as well as Indrāṇī and Purandara.
Or another may worship the teachers with the Gāyatrī, the essence of all mantras.
One should worship the goddess Indrāṇī; among women, Indrāṇī is the foremost.
One should worship Indra as the Bull with offerings,
and in the center, one should touch the jar while reciting the mantra of Bhuveśvarī.
One should recite the Gāyatrī until the oblation is completed, and thereafter recite the Śrīsūkta;
while touching the southern pitcher, the officiating priests and the cowherds should likewise recite it.
Touching the northern pitcher, he should recite the four Rudra-sūktas along with the four mantras that follow them, as well as the Śrīrudra, each repeated eleven times.
There, touching [the vessel], he should mutter the *Śann Indra-Agni* hymn;
then, in the western part of the area of the water-pot (*kumbha*), he should perform the propitiatory oblation (*śānti-homa*).
With blades of dūrvā grass, rice, wheat, milk-rice (pāyasa), and ghee,
along with three blades of dūrvā each, there shall be one oblation for each.
One should offer the oblation here four times, reciting the Gāyatrī either one thousand and eight times or one hundred and eight times.
Then, having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, one should perform the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the *samudrād ūrmī* hymn, using a continuous stream of clarified butter until the ladle is full.
Then one should perform the consecration with water contained in each jar,
followed thereafter by the nine hymns beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
Indra indeed [is praised] with the Aṅgatrca and the Pāvamāna hymns in their proper order;
may he hear both of us, the giver of well-being, with his single [eye].
One should perform [the oblation] with the Tryambaka mantra, with one verse from the Jāgatavedas,
and with the three verses beginning with "samudra jyeṣṭhā" from the Trāyantī hymn, in due order.
With this triplet beginning with "devasya tvā," he placed these waters;
and with the mantra "tvam agne rudraḥ," he placed Īśāna below.
One should worship him with the mantra "tamuṣṭuhi," likewise as the father of the worlds;
and with the mantra "yā te rudra" and the Śivakalpa mantra.
One should consecrate him as Indra, the bull, with five mantras;
and one should give a milch cow along with ornaments to the preceptor.
He should give a draft ox to the one who recites the Rudra-mantra;
then, having performed a great propitiatory rite for the progeny, he should thereafter feed the Brahmins.
The ritual procedure performed by my ancestors is as follows:

having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*)—"I, the performer, for the sake of pacifying all misfortunes indicated by the appearance of the first menstrual blood of my wife, such as the inauspiciousness of the sixth month and so forth, shall perform the *rajo-darśana-śānti* rite together with the *graha-makha* (planetary sacrifice)," one should perform the worship of Gaṇeśa, the invocation of merit (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkā-pūjana*), and the *nāndī-śrāddha*, and then choose an officiating preceptor (*ācārya*) and sacrificial priests (*ṛtvij*).

The preceptor, having touched the ground with the mantra "mahī dyauḥ" (the great earth) in the center of the Īśāna direction and in the south and north, and having established three heaps of rice measuring one *droṇa* each with the mantra "oṣadhayaḥ sam" (O herbs, come together), and having placed three water-pots with the mantra "ā kalaśeṣu" (into the jars), repeating the mantras for each; then, with the two mantras "prasuva āpaḥ" (impel the waters)—of which the first is in the *navānāṃ* meter and the second in the *jagatī*—and "yāḥ pratyak vasiṣṭho nadyaḥ" (those rivers toward which Vasiṣṭha [look]), both in the *śakvarī* meter, he fills the eastern [heaps] with water. Then, having thrown into the three [heaps] sandalwood paste with "gaṃdhadvārām" (the door of fragrance), all medicinal herbs with "yā oṣadhīḥ" (which herbs), and barley with "oṣadhayaḥ sam" (O herbs, come together); [and having added] *audumbara*, *kuśa*, *dūrvā*, *arakta*, *utpala*, and *campaka* flowers...

One should cast into it, as available, thirty-two medicinal substances: Bilva, Vṛṣṇukrāntā, Tulasī, Barhiṣa, Śaṅkhapuṣpī, Śatāvarī, Aśvagandhā, Nirguṇḍī, red and yellow Naradhiṣā, Mārga, Palāśa, Panasa, Bandhūka, Priyaṅgu, Dodhūma, Vrihi, Aśvadha, curd, milk, ghee, lotus petals, blue lotus, and white, red, and yellow Kuraṇṭaka, Guñjā, Vacā, and those known as Bhadra and Mustaka.

Then, in the three jars, one should place five sprouts with the mantra "kāṇḍāt kāṇḍāt," seven types of earth with "syonā," fruit with "yāḥ phalinīḥ," five gems with "sahi ratnāni," and wrap them with cloth using "hiranyarūpa. Having placed a vessel full of barley and other grains with "pūrṇā darvī" along with cloths, and having fashioned eight doors there, one should invoke Bhavaneśvarī in the center with the Gāyatrī mantra.

In the southern pitcher, having invoked Indrāṇī with the mantra "vṛṣākapiḥ indrāṇīm" (Vṛṣākapi, Indrāṇī, Pajkti), "indramāvahā" (Indrāṇī, bring [Indra] hither); and in the northern pitcher, having invoked Indra with the mantra "indratvā viśvāmitra indro gāyatrī" (Indra, you, Viśvāmitra, Indra, Gāyatrī). Then, worship [them] with the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra) using their respective mantras. Then, touching the central pitcher, recite the Gāyatra-mantra eight thousand times. [The details are: "aśvaṃ ciklīta" (Aśvaṃ ciklīta)—Indirā is the seer; Śrī is the deity; the first three verses are in the Suṣṭubh meter; one is in the Prastārapajkti meter; two are in the Triṣṭubh meter; and the last is in the Prastārapajkti meter. This is the application for the recitation (japa).
Then, one officiating priest [recites] over the southern pitcher:
for the nine [verses] beginning with "kudrudrāya," Aghora is the seer, Kaṇva and Rudra are the deities, and Gāyatrī is the meter;
for the eleven [verses] beginning with "imā rudrāḥ," Kutsa is the seer, Rudra is the deity, Jagatī is the meter, and the last two are Triṣṭubh.
"Ā te pitar" (of the fifteen verses), Gṛtsamada is the seer, Rudra is the deity, and Triṣṭubh is the meter.

"Imā rudrāya sthiradhanvine" (of the four verses), Rudra is the deity, Triṣṭubh is the meter. "Tryambakam" (of the eleven verses), Vasiṣṭha is the seer, Rudra is the deity, and Viśvedevas are the deities; Triṣṭubh is the meter.
Thus one should mutter [the mantra].

Having established the fire and invoked the presiding deities (adhidevatās)—Rudra, Umā, Skanda, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Indra, Yama, Kāla, and Citragupta—along with the secondary presiding deities (pratyadhidevatās)—fire, water, earth, Viṣṇu, Indra, Indrāṇī, Prajāpati, and Sarva-Brahmā—and having invoked and worshipped Vināyaka and the other five world-protectors (lokapālas), one should worship Varuṇa in the pitcher located in the northeast and consign the oblation into the fire.

Having offered oblations to the nine planets beginning with Cakṣuṣmān using *samidh* wood, sesame seeds, or clarified butter according to the specified number, and having likewise offered one oblation each to Ādi-deva and the other deities; then, having offered to Bhuvaneśvarī twenty-eight or one hundred and eight oblations of either *durvā* grass mixed with sesame, wheat-porridge (*pāyasa*), or clarified butter; and having offered to Indrāṇī and Indra twenty-eight or eight oblations each of the aforementioned substances; and having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering with the remainder, and so forth—one should mentally offer to those deities mentioned previously while remaining silent.

Having examined the milk and prepared the sacrificial porridge (caru), when the sacrificer has performed the formal renunciation (tyāga) at the conclusion of the portion, the oblation (homa) is performed with that same number [of offerings]. In that rite, there is one oblation consisting of three blades of dūrvā grass smeared with curd, honey, or clarified butter.

In this manner, having anointed the fuel-sticks (*samidh*), then, after performing the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the subsequent expiatory oblations (*prāyaścitta-homa*), one should present offerings of *māṣa*-beans and cooked rice with lamps to the guardians of the quarters (*dikpālaka*s), the nine planets (*navagraha*s), Bhuvaneśvarī, Indrāṇī, and Indra. Then, having offered the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the three-verse hymn beginning "The wave of the ocean" (*samudrād ūrmiḥ*)—where Vāmadeva is the seer, Agni is the deity, and Triṣṭubh is the meter—and having completed the remainder of the ritual procedure including the release of the *praṇītā* water, one should sprinkle the bride and groom, or the bride alone, with the nine verses beginning "O Waters, you are most beneficent" (*āpo hi ṣṭhā*) and the verse "He who alone knows" (*ya eka id vidayate*) by Gautama, where Indra is the deity and Triṣṭubh is the meter.

In "tribhirdeva" and the following seven [verses], Vasiṣṭha is the seer of three; Agni and then the Viśvedevas are the deities; the first is Gāyatrī, then Anuṣṭubh; there are three Gāyatrīs, then two Anuṣṭubhs. In "samudra jyeṣṭhāḥ" and the following four, Vasiṣṭha is the seer; the Waters (Āpas) are the deity; they are Triṣṭubhs. In "devasya tve" and the following, Āpastamba Śākhīya is the seer; with three [verses], Gotama is the seer; Īśāna is the deity; it is Jagatī. In "tvamagne rudraḥ" and "tam u ṣṭuhi," Aṅgiras is the seer; Tiraścī Rudra is the deity; it is Triṣṭubh.

With the hymn "yajjāgata" consisting of six verses, Prajāpati is the seer, Manu is the deity, and Triṣṭubh is the metre. With the hymn "indrastvā vṛṣabham" consisting of five verses, Viśvāmitra is the seer, Indra is the deity, and Gāyatrī is the metre. Then, having consecrated [the king] with this very [hymn], he should worship Agni and give a milch cow to the preceptor (ācārya), an ox along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the reciter of the Rudra-hymns, and further sacrificial fees to others. Having performed the aforementioned worship of the deities, having dismissed them by placing [the offerings] in the hand of the preceptor, having worshipped Agni, and having dismissed him with the words "Go, go," he should recite the Mahāśānti, feed the Brahmins, and then eat himself.
Thus ends the rite for the pacification of the appearance of menses (*rajodarśana-śānti*) in the *Śāntiratna* composed by Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa.
In the Madanaratna, however, it is stated differently in the Ṛṣiputra-saṃhitā:
"Immediately thereafter, one should perform the pacification of the defects of the first menses."

One should prepare separate sacrificial altars (*sthaṇḍila*) there for the worship of the deities associated with the lunar days (*tithi*), asterisms (*nakṣatra*), weekdays (*vāra*), and so forth, using four *āḍhaka* measures of *śāli* rice. [The proportions are: one *āḍhaka* of rice grains, two *āḍhaka* of sesame and barley (*yāvaka*), as well as one *kuḍava*, one *prastha*, one *āḍhaka*, and one *droṇa*.
It is said that these four groups should be understood as being arranged sequentially within the measures of grain; one should place a lotus in the center of that which is strewn layer upon layer.
Having covered it with *darbha* grass, one should place the jar in the middle of that, upon a *karṇikā*;
[the herbs] are Puṇyodā, Devī, Ekapattrā, Viṣṇukrāntā, and Satradrikā.
Having ground together bilva leaves,
siṃhī, kuṣṭha, māṃsī, the two types of haridrā, murā, śaileya, and candana, one should place them in a jar.
The ten all-healing herbs (sarvauṣadhyaḥ) are known as vacā, kacchurā, and mustā. One should collect earth from elephants, horses, anthills, battlefields, lakes, cow-pens,
and the vicinity of a king’s gate, and cast it [into the vessel].
And the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), as well as white water-lilies and pearls.
One should place diamonds, lapis lazuli, rubies, and corals [into it];
having thus prepared the pitcher, one should worship it with auspicious perfumes and other offerings.
The twice-born man, touching the water-pot, should mutter the Sāvitrī mantra one hundred times.
Thus, at the time of twilight (pradoṣa), he should bathe those two with these [substances];
then, he should diligently perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the procedure prescribed in his own Gṛhya-sūtra.
Having offered oblations of dūrvā grass, clarified butter, and sesame seeds with the gātrya mantra one thousand and eight times,
or likewise one hundred and eight times.
Having offered oblations three times according to that number with dūrvā grass, clarified butter, and sesame seeds,
one should then feed the Brāhmaṇas and worship the deity.
Thus has been briefly described the first menses of women.
In that very context, Nārada says:
"There, one should perform a propitiatory rite (śānti) with ghee, dūrvā grass, sesame seeds, and unbroken rice;
then, one should offer oblations one hundred and eight times for each, reciting the Gāyatrī mantra."
"One should offer sesame seeds upon the golden ground to prevent the arising of all defects"—
thus it has been accepted by the learned, by the *Prayogapārijāta*, and by Śaunaka as well.
Thus ends the *Rajodarśana-śānti* (Auspicious Rite for the Appearance of Menstruation) composed by Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa.
Now follows the *Nāgabalividhi* according to Śaunaka:
Now I shall describe the supreme ritual procedure for a snake;
one should perform it on the day of Sinīvālī, on the full moon, or on the fifth lunar day.
A sinful Brāhmaṇa who has committed the killing of a snake in a previous birth must confess the murder;
he should perform fourteen *kṛcchra* penances and cause an iron staff or its monetary value to be given to another Brāhmaṇa.
Yājñavalkya also said: "In the case of killing a snake, a substitute [animal] should be given.
He states the price:
"Three niṣkas, or two niṣkas, or at least one kaṅkaṇīya niṣka."
This [text] serves to clarify the meaning for the performers of the Anumati and other rites, removing all doubt.
This should be understood as the proportion for gold and silver.
Then,
it may be made with a paste of *priyaṅgu*, rice, wheat, or sesame.
Having fashioned the form of a serpent and placed it upon the sacrificial pan, one should pray to the snake:
"Come, O serpent; you have died previously, so enter into this flour.
For the sake of the funeral rites, I entreat you with devotion in brief."
Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings brought by a cloth, he should take [the image] outside;
then, preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma), he should perform the consecration (saṃskāra) and the formal resolve (saṃkalpa).
In the rite of consecrating a serpent, it must be performed while wearing the sacred thread (yajñopavītin).
Having established the worldly fire and sprinkled it with water along with fuel-sticks, [one should proceed].
Having prepared the altar and strewn it with *kuśa* grass, with their tips pointing toward the fire,
one should sprinkle water around the fire, encircle it, pour water all around, and worship it.
Having performed the blowing and the two oblations according to the rule, he should likewise perform the two eye-rites.
Having carefully taken hold of the snake,
the wise man should place it upon the funeral pyre and offer oblations of clarified butter into the fire with the three *vyāhṛtis* using a sacrificial ladle.
One should offer clarified butter into the serpent’s mouth with the complete *vyāhṛti* mantra;
then, with the *sruva* ladle alone, one should sprinkle the remainder of the clarified butter over the entire body.
Having sprinkled water from the *camasa* vessels upon the serpent with the *vyāhṛtis*,
one should cause the fire to be offered to the serpents with the mantra "agne rakṣāṇaḥ," [reciting] "Whether intentionally or unintentionally, the killing of a serpent has been committed by me."
"You ought to forgive all that [transgression] arising from my dwelling in a previous birth.
Then, having sprinkled the fire with milk and clarified butter, and with water while reciting the *vyāhṛtis*.
There is no need for conduct or other such duties; three ablutions are prescribed for purification.
Whatever rite, such as the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), has been performed, purification is prescribed after three nights;
however, on the fourth day, one should bathe with one's clothes on and honor the Brahmins.

Likewise, one should worship the twice-born with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, incense, lamps, and other offerings, [honoring] those known by the names Sarpa, Ananta, Śeṣa, Kapila, Nāga, Kālika, Śaṅkhapāla, and Bhūdhara.
And with ghee, milk-rice, and various foods, one should feed the twice-born while reciting the Naṣṭa hymn.
When the ritual for the consecration of the snake has been performed according to this injunction, one is liberated from the sin of killing a snake; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the Nāgabali.

Regarding this, Mārkaṇḍeya says: "In the case of the conjunction of *lāla* and widowhood (*vaidhavya*), having performed a propitiatory rite (*śānti*) with water-pots, images, and so forth, thereafter the girl may be given away in marriage; so say others."
Furthermore, regarding the state of becoming [a deity] therein, it is stated in the Vithāna-khaṇḍa:
"One should fashion an image in the form of Viṣṇu out of gold, water, or pippala wood."
By marrying her, one does not become a paunarbhava (a son born of a remarried woman).
In the *Sūryāruṇa-saṃvāda*:
"And at a time prior to the wedding, when the moon and the stars possess strength."
One should carry it away together with the pitcher while reciting the mantra prescribed for marriage; thereafter, one should wrap it with a thread according to the rule of the ten strands.
Their bodies, adorned with saffron, should be placed together on Mount Mandara;
then, having brought forth the jar and broken it into the reservoir of water,
one should perform the consecration (abhiṣecana) with the waters of the five sprouts (pañcapallava).
The prayer to the water-pot (*kumbha*) is found in that very same place:
"O you who are the essential form of Varuṇa, the refuge of all living beings,
revive the husband of this maiden and grant her the long-lasting joy of having sons."
"O Lord Viṣṇu, grant me a boon; protect the maiden from suffering.
Then, she should present her, adorned with a veil and garments, to the groom.
The gift of an image is also mentioned in that very same place:
"Having invited a virtuous Brahmin and having honored him with various offerings,
one should give him an image of Viṣṇu with four arms according to the prescribed rule."
Or else, fashioned from pure gold according to one’s financial capacity,
it should be beautiful and marked with the conch, mace, and discus.
Wearing two yellow garments and garlanded with white and blue lotuses,
one should give her that gift while reciting this very mantra:
Whatever sin of killing a husband I may have committed in a previous birth—
whether by means of poison, potent herbs, weapons, or the like, or through my own aversion—
I have now encountered that most terrible consequence which destroys fame, happiness, and wealth.
For the destruction of the flood of intense suffering caused by widowhood, for the attainment of happiness,
and for the accomplishment of great good fortune, [I worship] this form of Mahāviṣṇu.
O twice-born one, he should present to you a spear fashioned of gold according to his ability, and he should recite three times: "I am now sinless."
Then he should perform the marriage rites for the fawn-eyed maiden according to the prescribed rule.
Such details are to be understood from the Nirṇayasindhu. Thus ends the rite for pacifying the conjunction leading to widowhood.
Now, regarding the *arka-vivāha*:
since the third type of human marriage (*mānuṣī-vivāha*) is prohibited, the *arka-vivāha* is prescribed for that purpose.
In the *Prayogapārijāta* and the *Mātsya-purāṇa*: "One should never marry a third wife for the sake of attaining sexual pleasure."
If one should approach a human woman out of delusion or even through ignorance,
he perishes without a doubt when Garga’s cooking takes place.
In the *Saṃgraha*:
"One should marry during the third lunar day after the four days of *adhivāsa*;
or on a Sunday, or under the asterism of Hasta, or on a Saturday."
On an auspicious day, during the forenoon, one should perform the marriage ceremony of the Sun.
In the Brahma [direction], to the east or north of the village, there is a dwelling-place endowed with flowers and fruits.
Standing before the sun, the best of the twice-born should pray:
"O Sun, dweller of the three worlds, possessor of seven horses, accompanied by your shadow!
O third eye of the day-maker, ward off the fault of the day and grant me happiness."
There, having placed the Lord of Gods, Ravi, together with Chāyā upon the two [seats].

One should worship with garments, garlands, and perfumes using that very mantra. When fourteen days have passed, having worshipped the previously mentioned [deity] and having dismissed the fire for the *homa*, one should marry a supreme human woman.
Vyāsa said:

One should take refuge in a place where there are fine flowers, fruits, and vegetables, and which has a single *arka* bush and a thicket of *marka* plants; for the sake of the success of the rite, one should first appoint an officiating priest (*ācārya*).
Having arrived at the presence of the sun, one should there invoke blessings with "svasti.
One should worship the Nāndī-śrāddha with gold and honor the assembly of Brahmins like a king. One should honor the bridegroom and the Brahmin from their hands with the madhuparka offering.
Wherever this ancient sacred thread was created by me for the sake of the hand;
While circumambulating the Arka plant, one should mutter [the mantra], "May he protect me at every step";
then, the knower of mantras should again perform a circumambulation with this mantra.
"Born from the sun and created by Brahmā, may she protect us.
Then, the knower of mantras should perform circumambulation again with this mantra:
"Salutations to you, O auspicious goddess; salutations to the daughter of the Sun."
O Goddess Kṛśayā, protect this man; you have come here to be his wife.
Created by Brahmā as the Arka plant for the welfare of all living beings,
you are the primordial source of trees and the increaser of the gods' delight.
The third [mantra] quickly destroys the defect born of the door and death;
thereafter, the selection of the bride shall uplift the lineage for three generations.
After observing the sun for a moment, one should recite the Svasti-sūkta.
O Brahmin, accept this daughter of Arka, adorned according to my ability, who has been given to you for the sake of the Śarman lineage. O Brahmin, take her as your wife.
Having first performed the añjali and the offering of unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and having first bound the bracelet, one should cause the thread—
consisting of five folds— to enter the Arka plant.
One should mutter the Gāyatrī mantra according to the tradition of one's own Vedic branch;
then, having made the thread fivefold, one binds it upon the shoulder with the mantra.
One should place the pitchers in front of the sun, behind it, and likewise to the south and north; thereafter, one should place them in the four directions beginning with the southeast (āgneya).
Having worshipped Mahāviṣṇu, the Supreme Lord, at each jar,
and having circumambulated them once more, one should utter this mantra:
This karma was committed by me among stationary beings while in the womb;
O Arka, take away my sins, for you ought to forgive all of that.
Having spoken thus and recited the Śānti-sūktas, he should dismiss her again;
at the conclusion, he should give a pair of cows as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and perform the Puṇyāha rite.
Śaunaka:
When the third marriage of a woman has arrived for a man,
he should perform the Nāndī-śrāddha and prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Having worshipped the Arka plant with offerings of scents, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth, dedicated to the Sun.
With a verse dedicated to Sūrya as its deity, namely "akṛṣṇena" (RV 1.50.10).
In the northern part of the hearth (arkasya), having performed the consecration with this [verse],
one should perform the rites beginning with the tracing (ullekhana) and ending with the two āghāra libations.
Then he should offer an oblation of clarified butter with the verse, "Bring him together with cattle," and thereafter with the verse, "For whomsoever you [O Agni], desiring his desire."
Then, with both the individual and the collective [mantras], the Sviṣṭakṛt offering should be performed.

The sequence beginning with the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*) and ending with the circumambulation (*paryanta*) should be understood from the *Nirṇayasindhu*, which provides the detailed ritual application (*prayoga*).
Thus ends the marriage ceremony of the Sun in the *Śāntiratna* composed by Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa, son of Rāmakṛṣṇa Bhaṭṭa.
Now, the ritual procedure for the Rudra-bath (*rudrasnānaprayoga*) performed by us is written: [The ritual procedure for the Rudra-bath is now set forth.]

This should be performed during the northern solstice and so forth, avoiding the setting of Jupiter or Venus and other such unfavorable times; specifically in a pure month, during the bright fortnight, in the fertile season, on the fourth day, or on the eighth or fourteenth lunar day, or on a Sunday, under an auspicious asterism, and when there is favorability regarding the strength of the moon and stars.
And this fourfold [reason] for being worthy of veneration applies specifically to one whose children have died.
At the confluence of these two great rivers, the Daurvāśī and the Vāśoṣī, the rite should be performed at the mere meeting of the waters;
or, if it cannot be done during the northern solstice (udagayana), it may be performed in all months, including the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana).
Therefore, O son, among all these gifts which are approved by the Brahmins, this must certainly be performed by one who desires the happiness of women.
Thus, according to the statements in the *Bhaviṣyottara* Purāṇa cited in the *Hemādri*:

first, the performer, together with his wife, should— being filled with remorse— perform a penance according to his capacity for the sake of removing the evil karma that obstructs the birth of long-lived sons and other such blessings.

The fruit of that [penance] corresponds to the degree of the evil committed, as determined by its relative intensity; it may take the form of a six-month, three-year, or one-and-a-half-year penance, or the forms of *cāndrāyaṇa*, *kṛcchra*, or *atikṛcchra*,
or else consist of recitation (*japa*), fire-oblations (*homa*), pilgrimage to sacred sites (*tīrthayātrā*), feeding of Brahmins, and so forth.
The duty toward the assembly has been taught according to the ancient tradition.
Then, for the sake of pleasing the illustrious Rudra, one should give a single black cow, accompanied by ritual accessories according to one's means.
If one is unable to do that,

one should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the *Gāyatrī* mantra one hundred thousand, fifty thousand, or ten thousand times, and offer oblations (*homa*) of sesame seeds with a tenth part of that number.
When this is done, one becomes a performer of the Rudra-bath and other rites.
Then, at the previously mentioned time and place, having performed his bath along with his wife,
being pure, having put on two clean garments, seated upon a seat, and having sipped water (ācamana),
he should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) after first purifying the ground, and then recollect the place and time.

May there be no obstacle to the long life and progeny of my sons and others, including myself and my wife; nor may there be any cause for such obstruction in this life or in future lives— whether due to ancestral rites such as the *aṣṭakā* festival,
through malice toward others, or by some other means such as the killing of a fawn.
Whether by the slaughter of a child, or by the abduction of a wife,
or by the separation from a calf, or by hatred toward one's father or mother.

By means of another ritual action, through the removal of the defects of sterility—whether of the fourfold kind or any one of them—and through the removal of all obstacles to progeny, such as the defects of the wife’s womb, the known or unknown impurity of her menses, the defect of touching the hem of a woman’s garment, and the defects arising from sharing food, bed, or seat with her, I shall perform the Rudrakalaśa-snāna rite according to the procedure taught by Bhāradvāja, for the sake of the pleasure of Śrī Rudra accompanied by Umā, and for the attainment of a long line of excellent sons and progeny.

Having thus made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one should perform the worship of Gaṇeśa, the recitation for the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the worship of the Mothers (*mātṛkāpūjana*), and the *nāndīśrāddha*, all preceded by the formal resolve. Having performed those, one should make the primary resolve (*pradhānasaṃkalpa*).
Then, having made the formal resolve: "I shall perform the selection of the Ācārya, Brahmā, and the officiating priests (Ṛtviks)," he should request the Brāhmaṇas to serve as the chosen priests.
These Brāhmaṇas are peaceful and tranquil; they are self-composed, yet possessed of a pure nature. They are indeed the givers of the gods and the protectors of all embodied beings.
Furthermore, priests are traditionally appointed for the purpose of satisfying the gods and the ancestors through recitations, sacrifices, burnt offerings, and various kinds of gifts.
The Vedas, residing within the body of this woman, purify the three worlds;
therefore, remain constantly engaged in the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) to protect her.
Then,

one should request a twice-born man who has maintained the sacred fires, who is tranquil, knows the Dharma, speaks the truth, is skilled in the rites of Rudra, and is a capable deity for the purpose of the ritual bath.
Thus, one should choose an ācārya endowed with these characteristics;
thereafter, one should choose eleven officiating priests (ṛtvij) for the Brāhma sacrifice.

Then, one should worship all our attendants with offerings such as garments and ornaments according to one's capacity. Thereafter, accompanied by the officiating priests and others, one should enter the inner sanctum.

Then, the officiating priest and preceptor, preceded by the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), shall construct either a *sarvatobhadra*, a *liṅgatobhadra*, or an eight-petaled lotus diagram in the northeast corner of the pavilion that possesses the prescribed characteristics.
Having placed the seven grains around it for the sake of the mandala,
and having abandoned all reliance on that constant abode, let everything go back to where it was originally situated.

"May the spirits and *piśācas* depart in all directions; without the opposition of anyone, I shall commence the rite of Brahmā. Having thus scattered grains of rice (*narṣapa*) and sprinkled [the area] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) while reciting the verse "śucī vo havyā," he should perform the worship of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), sit upon his seat, perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and other rites, protect himself, meditate upon the Śrī Rudra, and [recite]: "You are propitiated by humans, by the perfected ones (*siddhas*), and by gods, asuras, and others..."
"I propitiate you with devotion; accept me, O Maheśvara"—thus one should pray.

Then—having bowed to each of the world-protectors, beginning with Indra, with their respective name-mantras preceded by the *praṇava* (Om) and ending with *namaḥ*; having touched the earth with the mantra "mahī dyauḥ"; [he places] barley with "oṣadhayaḥ sumanasyamānāḥ"; all medicinal herbs with "yā oṣadhīḥ"; *dūrvā* grass with "kāṇḍāt kāṇḍāt"; fruit with "yāḥ phalinīḥ"; and the seven kinds of soil with "syonā pṛthivī."

Having cast in the sprouts of the *añjana* tree with the mantra "aśvad deva" (RV 10.87.20), the five gems with "sahiratnāni" (RV 10.87.21), gold with "hiraṇyarūpam" (RV 10.87.22), the two garments with "yuvaṃ vastrāṇi" (RV 10.85.29), and having wrapped them with a red thread, he places bamboo vessels with "pūrṇā darvī" (RV 10.87.24).

Having invoked the divine waters (*devatīrtha*) into the jars with the mantra beginning "Viṣṇu at the mouth of the jar," and having invoked the divine waters into the jars with the mantra beginning "In the conflict between the gods and the demons," [one should invoke] the jar with the mantra beginning "In the conflict between the gods and the demons."
Having made this prayer with the mantra "Tryambakam," one should invoke Rudra.
Then, with the mantra "tataḥ samudrād ūrmir," one should invoke the Ocean.
At the base of the jar, one should worship Brahmā with the mantra "brahmajijñāsam";
in the middle, Viṣṇu with "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ";
at the neck, Rudra with "namaḥ śambhave ca"; and at the mouth, Indra and Agni with "indrāgnī āgatam."
With "O Indra and Agni, what was given by Yama," he offers to Yama on all sides;
with "For the sake of food (iṣe tvā)," to the gods; and with "From the ancient... to Sūrya.
With "The all-seeing one," he worships Parameṣṭhin;
with "Homage be to the serpents on both sides," the serpents.
In the east, [he places] the Ṛgveda with the mantra "agnim īḷe";
in the south, the Yajurveda with "iṣe tvā."
In the west, [he recites] "O Agni, come hither" for the Sāmaveda;
in the north, "O divine waters" for the Atharvaveda.

In the center, one should place the Gāyatrī mantra beginning with "tatsavitur"; in the eight directions starting from the east, one should assign the eight deities, Indra and the others, using their respective mantras or names.

One should place *dūrvā* grass on the head while reciting "From joint to joint" (*kāṇḍāt kāṇḍāt*). Then, having placed cloths with eight petals upon bamboo vessels, one should place therein [an image] made of gold weighing one *niṣka* or half a *niṣka*, or, if unable [to afford that], two *vallās*.
Having installed an image of Rudra fashioned from gold, preceded by the consecration with the *vañcāmṛta* [mantra].

With the mantra "tāsvā tvāvahantu," one should invoke Rudra accompanied by Umā. Having thus invoked him, the seat is offered with "sadyojātaṃ prapadyāmi," and the water for the feet (pādya) with "sadyojātāya vai namaḥ."
"In existence after existence"—that is, "in every state of existence"—is the respectful offering (*arghya*).
"Bhavodbhavāya namaḥ"—with this, water for rinsing the mouth (ācamanīya) is offered. "Vāmadevāya namaḥ"—with this, water for rinsing the mouth is offered.
"Vāmadevāya sam" and with the verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," the ritual bathing (snāna) is performed.
Having given water for sipping (ācamana) and having offered it, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with eight [verses].

I satisfy the god Bhava; I satisfy the god Śarva; I satisfy the god Īśāna; I satisfy the god Paśupati; I satisfy the god Rudra; I satisfy the god Ugra; I satisfy the god Bhīma; I satisfy the god Mahant. Then, "Salutation to Vāmadeva"—with this [mantra] one performs the bath. "Salutation to Jyeṣṭha"—with this [mantra] the garment.

Silently, he should perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*). With "Salutation to Śreṣṭha," he offers the sacred thread (*upavīta*); with "Salutation to Rudra," the ornament (*alaṃkāra*); with "Salutation to Kāla," the fragrance (*gandha*); with "Salutation to Kalavikaraṇa," the flower (*puṣpa*); with "Salutation to Balavikaraṇa," the incense (*dhūpa*); with "Salutation to Bala," the food offering (*naivedya*); silently, the ritual rinsing of the mouth; with "Salutation to Balapramathana," the betel leaf (*tāmbūla*); with "Salutation to Sarvabhūtadamanā," the waving of lights (*nīrājana*); and with "Salutation to Manonmanā," he should give the priestly fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
One should offer eight handfuls of flowers with the words "To that Tatpuruṣa," while performing prostrations.

Oṃ, homage to the god Bhava. Oṃ, homage to the god Śarva. Oṃ, homage to the god Īśāna. Oṃ, homage to the god Paśupati. Oṃ, homage to the god Rudra. Oṃ, homage to the god Ugra. Oṃ, homage to the god Bhīma. Oṃ, homage to the god Mahat.
Then he should worship her with the verse, "O you of terrible form, from the terrible ones... (Raghorebhyas).
Then the salutation:
O Lord of the Universe, whose eyes are wide, whose form is the universe, Sadāśiva!
Be my refuge, O Lord of all beings, O Śaṅkara, the mine of compassion.
O Hara, O Śambhu, O Mahādeva, O Lord of the Universe, O Beloved of the Immortals!
O Śiva, O Śaṅkara, O Soul of All, O Blue-throated One, salutations be unto you!
"Salutation to the conqueror of death, to Rudra, to the blue-throated one, to Śambhu,
to the Lord of Immortality, to Śarva, and to Mahādeva."
Then follows the prayer:
"By the Rājasa mode, one is Brahmā himself; by the Sāttvika mode, one is Hari himself."
O Rudra, you yourself abide as the female principle within me through your tamasic nature;
I bow to you, O Virūpākṣa, O Nīlagrīva—salutations be unto you!
Salutations to you, the three-eyed one; salutations to you who bear half of Umā’s body;
salutations to you, the bearer of the trident and the Lord of all beings.
Salutations to you, the wielder of the Pināka bow; salutations to you who are sought by those desiring the foremost [boons]. I bow to you, O Mahādeva; I bow to you, the Lord.
You alone are the enjoyer and the object of enjoyment, the Lord who personally bestows happiness upon your devotees;
assuming the form of the sun, you are the sustainer of the bodies of embodied beings.
You are the giver of liberation to the sages and the giver of worldly enjoyment to your devotees yourself.
By your own will, all this comes to you and passes away;
no one else has the power to grant victory except for you.
Then—
[he was] propitiated by the Siddhas, and likewise by the gods, Asuras, and others.
"I worship you with devotion; accept me.
Thus he should offer himself as "Mahāśvara.
Then, on the eight lotus petals starting from the east, [he should worship] Indra and the other eight guardians of the directions.
Having worshipped and offered a bali-oblation of food and other items, one should pray:
"May Indra and the other gods, as well as all the world-protectors of the celestial realms," [be pleased].
May the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Viśvedevas, and the hosts of Maruts—
all these, being honored, grant whatever peace is desired.
Then, all [the participants], having restrained their breath and recollected the place and time,

[should perform] the recitation of the Rudraikādaśinī according to the common ritual procedure for attaining the longevity of the sacrificer, his sons, and so forth, as well as the uninterrupted continuity [of the lineage].
Having resolved, "At the end of the general nyāsa, we shall perform the special nyāsas," [one proceeds].
With the five [mantras] beginning with "sadyojātam," preceded by the *praṇava* and *vyāhṛtis* and ending with the *vyāhṛtis* and *praṇava*,
one should assign the heart, head, crest-lock, armor, eyes, and weapon.

Having thus deposited [the mantras] within oneself, one should likewise deposit them into the jars. Then, with the *rājasa* [mantra], preceded by the thought "I am Brahmā," the officiants, each touching their respective jars while meditating on the welfare of the patron, [should perform the rite] for each of the eleven Rudras.

Having performed the recitation with royal fervor and having praised [the deity] as "Brahmā himself," they should conclude it; even if deficient in accents, vowels, and all consonants, [they should say]:
"O Lord, may my recitation be forgiven; grant your grace to your servant."
Whatever deficiency or excess may occur in this recitation of the Mahārudra;
O Sadāśiva, may everyone attain perfection through your grace.
"Whatever syllable may have been mispronounced, and whatever may be deficient in its prosodic measure—all that may you forgive me, O God; be gracious, O Supreme Lord."
Then the preceptor, having established the fire in either the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or on the altar (sthaṇḍila) according to the procedure prescribed in his own Vedic branch, [proceeds].

Having prepared the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the offering of clarified butter and other ingredients to bring satisfaction, and having performed the rites up to the portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga),

one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) together with the officiating priests, using fuel-sticks, sesame seeds, the caru, and clarified butter— each substance being offered ten times the number of recitations of the mantra.

In this context, for all [the mantras], there are two hundred and thirty-one forms consisting of the eleven Rudras; ten percent of that is thirteen forms. Thus, there are forty-eight oblations (āhutis) from these, six hundred and twenty-four in the remaining forms, and for the two leftover forms, there are ten percent, which is thirteen oblations. There are fourteen Camaka oblations. Including all of these, there are six hundred and fifty oblations; this is the oblation for each substance.
If one is unable [to perform the full rite], the oblation should be performed according to the sixteen-fold and other alternative methods.
Thereafter, one hundred and eleven oblations of *arka* leaves should be offered with the root-mantra (*mūla-mantra*) and the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*).
Alternatively, the fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with the root mantra alone.

The Seer (Ṛṣi) of the Root Mantra is Parameśvara; the Deity (Devatā) is Rudra; the Metre (Chandas) is Paṅkti. Its application (viniyoga) is in the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites. Now, the placement of the limbs (nyāsa): *Namaḥ* to the Seer Parameṣṭhin on the head; *Namaḥ* to the Paṅkti metre on the mouth; *Namaḥ* to the Deity Rudra on the heart; *Namaḥ* at the tuft of hair (śikhā); *Śambhave* on the head; and *Lalāṭamaya* on the two eyes.
*Iva* is on the two ears;
*citi* is on the nose; *namaḥ* is on the mouth; and *śaṃkarāya* is on the neck.
"Me" in the heart; "Maya" in the stomach; "Karāya" in the navel;
"Ce" in the earth [of the feet]; and "Sama" in the hips.
With "śivāya" on the two thighs, with "śivatamāya" on the two knees, with "śive" on the two feet,
with "namaḥ śambhave" on the heart, and with "mayobhave" on the head.
"Salutation to Śaṅkara," [he says] over the crest-lock.
"Mayaskarāya" for the armor, *huṃ*;
"namaśśivāya" for the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*.
Śivatarāya-cetyastra-āyaphaṭ.

Having thus performed the *homa*, completed the *sviṣṭakṛt* and other offerings up to the *pūrṇāhuti*, and finished the remainder of the previous *homa*, the preceptor and others should worship [the deities] with offerings such as perfumes (*gandha*). Then, having performed the subsequent worship of Rudra and propitiated Rudra for the sake of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), one should prepare a square mandala marked with a *svastika* to the north of the fire. There, having placed two seats made of *udumbara* wood, the husband and wife—seated upon them, draped in pure white garments, and facing east—should be seated.

There are seven hundred and four names, each facing upward; with that single mantra, with each individual solar mantra, with the eleven Rudra mantras, and with the root mantra (mūlamantra), they should consecrate these.

In this regard, within the Mādhyandina recension, there are sixty-four mantras beginning with "Rudrādhyāya," and for the Ekādaśinī sacrifice, there is the designation of seven hundred and four; therefore, having consecrated [the disciple] with each mantra upon each leaf of the Arka plant, one should discard the leaves.
However, according to the tradition of Bodhāyana, for other branches, the consecration is performed in the same manner using only the root mantra (mūlamantra) repeated the same number of times.

Then, having quickly sprinkled [the image] with sprouts while reciting the hymn beginning with *śiśānaḥ*, the Soma hymn beginning with *āpyāyasva*, the verses beginning with *ā rohiṣṭha*, those beginning with *samudra jyeṣṭhāḥ*, the hymn beginning with *sahasraśīrṣā*, and the Puranic verses beginning with *sūrāstvām*, they should proceed saying "Śiva, Śiva. Or, some say that women here should take other Arka leaves.

The officiating priests (ṛtvij) shall sprinkle [the couple] with *arka* leaves during the eleven-fold ceremony (*ekādaśinī*), while the preceptor (*ācārya*) shall sprinkle them with the five sprouts (*pañcapallava*) as prescribed by the *Sūktīribhis*. Then, having been anointed on all their limbs with all medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadhi*), seven types of earth (*saptamṛd*), and fresh clay from both riverbanks (*ubhayatālamṛd*), the couple—specifically the woman, who has been especially anointed on the region of her womb—should have their bodies washed with the water from all the ritual jars (*kalaśa*) once the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering has been performed, and they should then be bathed with pure water. Thereafter, for those two...

"O twice-born ones, by this rite, may all those defects residing in the body, as well as those defects in the seed of the embryo, go to destruction. Having recited this mantra and discarded the two garments used during the consecration, [he should proceed].

Having put on two clean garments and being adorned with white sandalwood paste, garlands, and so forth, the preceptor, assisted by the sacrificer, should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the mantras beginning with "From the ocean, the wave," and then offer the *vasordhārā*.
Then,
one should cause [the disciple] to hear the hymns dedicated to Agni, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra;
and one should have him recite the Mahāvaiśvānara Sāman and the Jyeṣṭha Sāman.

Then the sacrificer, together with his wife, having performed the rite for the prolongation of life, shall offer a milch cow and gold to the preceptor as an honorarium according to his capacity, preceded by worship.

Having given a bull to the Brahman priest and gifts according to his capacity to the officiating priests (ṛtvij), and having asked for forgiveness (kṣamāpya), he should dismiss the deities invoked for the Śrīrudra rite. Then, for the sake of pleasing Śrī Rudra, he should feed one hundred or half that number of Brahmins. Finally, accompanied by the auspicious singing of songs and blessings performed by women whose husbands and sons are living, he should receive the benedictions (āśīrvāda) from the Brahmins.
"By this rite, Rudra, known as Kalaśa,
having enjoyed all pleasures through the grace of Caṇḍakara, [attains liberation];
thus said the venerable Bodhāyana."
The son of Bhaṭṭa Rāmeśvara, the grandson of Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa.
Rāmakṛṣṇa has composed this manual for the Rudra-bath, following the procedure for the Śrīrudrasnāna.
Thus ends the *Rudrasnānavidhi* composed by Rāmakṛṣṇabhaṭṭa, son of the venerable Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭasūri.
O Vandyā, the procedure for the Rudrasnāna is as follows;
now, regarding the Rudrasnāna described in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa within the Hemādri [compendium],
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
The army of the gods [honored] Skanda, the son of Rudra, the six-faced one, as their lord.
Agastya, the tiger among sages, seated comfortably, spoke: "O Kumāra, you are indeed omniscient; by your grace, please tell me how the bath according to the Rudra-vidhāna for women may come to pass."
Skanda said:
"A woman who has lost her children, one who is unfortunate, or one who is devoid of menstrual periods—"
For a woman who has given birth to a daughter or one who is barren, a ritual bath for the months [of pregnancy] is prescribed;
she should be devoted to fasting on either the eighth or the fourteenth lunar day.
When the fourth day of the pure period has arrived, or on a Sunday,
one should perform the union immediately— especially at the confluence of great rivers,
or in a temple of Śiva, a cow-pen, or a secluded place among the planets.
A twice-born man who maintains the sacred fire, who is tranquil, knows the Dharma, and speaks the truth.
O Rudra, I shall describe this skillful procedure for the bath;
thereafter, one should construct a square pavilion that is well-proportioned.
Having bound a garland of sandalwood and smeared [the ground] with cow dung,
one should draw a lotus in its center, filled with white powder.
One should install Mahādeva in the center upon the pericarp;
one should duly place Nandin and the others upon the four petals according to the prescribed ritual.

O King, one should properly place Indra and the other world-protectors (lokapālas), as well as the eight deities of the directions; and there, O Ruler of the Earth, one should install the Goddess and Vināyaka.
Having offered water for the feet, perfume, incense, flowers, a lamp, and rice mixed with jaggery;
Various kinds of edible foods and diverse fruits should be offered;
in the four corners, there should be a water-pot filled with leaves of the Aśvattha tree.
One should place each [portion] of Brahmā, accompanied by all medicinal herbs.
Likewise, one should offer the bali-offering to the spirits in the four directions of the pavilion.
In the south-eastern direction, near the pavilion,
the fire-rite should be performed in an auspicious sacrificial pit adorned with leaves and flowers.
One should offer salt combined with milk, ghee, and honey,
reciting the mantra prescribed for the mind, when the oblation for the nine planets has been performed.
The performer of the second fire-rite should be a Brāhmaṇa;
likewise, during the recitation of the Rudra-mantras, he should wear white sandalwood paste.
Clad in white garments and adorned with white garlands,
one should beautify [the deity] with bracelets, golden ornaments, earrings, and finger-rings.
The second auspicious maṇḍala should be prepared like the first;
in its center, the goddess should be placed, adorned with white flowers.
Clad in white garments and anointed with white sandalwood paste,
the preceptor, chanting the Rudra-mantra, sits facing east with a cheerful countenance.
Then one should consecrate her with water from arka leaves,
reciting the sixty-four [Vedic] verses and the eleven Rudra hymns;
there should be seven hundred and four leaves.
The word "of leaves" (*parṇānām*) ends in the suffix *vuñ*; this is the number for those sixty-four enumerations that have been recited one through ten times.
With the mantra beginning "accidreṇa," one should set down [the earth] for the purpose of bathing;
[earth] from a horse-stable, from an elephant-stable, from an anthill, from a confluence, and from a sacrificial ground.
Having brought from the Vaiśyāṅgaṇa, the Rājagṛha, and the cow-pen the Vaimṛdha,
the Rocana with all medicinal herbs, and the waters from river-tirthas;
Having condensed this into the water-pot, a virtuous woman should then bathe her with that pot over which the Rudra-mantra has been recited.
Thereafter, one should place water-pots filled with water and adorned with horse-tail feathers (aśvadalas) situated in all directions, along with pots containing unbroken grains (akṣatas).
Having bathed in this manner, one should give a cow and likewise gold to the one who performed the bathing; in this rite, a milch cow is prescribed as the sacrificial fee for the Hotṛ priest.
O bull among sages, having given garlands, garments, gold, and other gifts according to one's own capacity to the Brahmins and others, one should ask everyone for forgiveness.
O best of Brahmins, by performing this ritual bath with blood,
a woman becomes fortunate, endowed with beauty, and gives birth to many sons.
During all the months of winter, provided they have the approval of the Brahmins, a woman should certainly perform this rite; thus she attains happiness through her son.
She, having accepted that bath which is renowned as being for Rudra,
performed it with faith and with the approval of the best of the twice-born.
Having destroyed all the defects residing in the body,
O Bhārata, she becomes dear to her husband, bearing offspring like his very life.
Thus concludes the Rudra-bath as described in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa* within the *Hemādri*, which removes barrenness. Now, regarding the bath [described] in the *Hemādri*: Pārvatī said:
"A woman who has lost her children or is childless shall become one who possesses offspring."
Afflicted by planetary diseases or abandoned by her husband, she either leaves him or is abandoned by him.
Speak the story of that goddess; all of this shall perish.
And thus, both desired things arise; therefore, O Śaṅkarī, I ask you.
Īśvara said: Listen to how the faults of women that you have mentioned are overcome,
and how that which is desired by women is likewise brought about, as I shall now explain.
One should perform the purification of the ground with cow dung and cow urine in a secluded,
spacious place where no other person may enter.
In that same manner, he should bring eleven jars and likewise summon the twice-born;
having called them all, he should request them with the verse beginning "arcata" and with earth from a cow-dung heap.
Having washed them, one should set out the jars and fill them with water from a sacred ford;
then, having duly performed self-protection, as well as the svastika and the seat.
Restraining the breath and remaining silent, one should worship me, the Lord of all desires;
having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should place me within the water-pot (kumbha), saying: "Bring me alone hither."
One should arrange all the items, beginning with the seat, in that very place;
one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) in the outer region of the water-pot (kumbha),
according to the procedure taught by Bodhāyana, having brought them into the presence of Īśāna.
Having quickly bowed to Indra and the other deities with the root mantra, [one should proceed].
The Praṇava should be placed at the beginning, and likewise, the word "namaḥ" should be placed at the end.
The root mantra is proclaimed to be situated in the midst of the deity-word;
having touched one set of eleven Rudras, one should recite the mantra over the water in the pitcher.
Furthermore, having worshipped Māmi, Indra, and the others according to the prescribed rite,
all the best of the twice-born should perform this for every one of the water-pots.
Then, having taken up the jars, one should release them in sequence according to the Mārdhni rite;
this should be performed ten times by the best of the twice-born.
On the eleventh day, the honoring of the twice-born should be performed according to the rules;
having given sacrificial fees to them and offered salutations, one should dismiss them.
In this way, faults are destroyed and that which is desired arises. This rite should be performed for a man afflicted by planetary diseases,
as well as for a Kṣatriya who desires nourishment, long life, strength, and victory.
He who, endowed with faith, performs this every year on an auspicious day during the bright fortnight of Caitra, does so for the sake of liberation from manifold calamities.
Thus ends the Rudra-bath. Now begins the Caṇḍī-kalpa, concerning the Śatacaṇḍī and Sahasracaṇḍī rites.
O Goddess, listen as I describe the fruit obtained from the Cañjīpāṭha;
having first made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should worship it in its various parts in due order.
Through recitation or through the offering of oblations (*bali*), the practitioner attains accomplishment;
for the sake of pacifying calamities, one should always recite it three times.
O fair-faced one, when pacifying the planets, the rite should be performed five times;
when great danger has arisen, one should perform it seven times.
By reciting it nine times, there shall be peace, and one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
for the subjugation of kings and for prosperity, one should likewise recite it eleven times.
Through the reverse order of the planets, the fulfillment of desires and the destruction of enemies arise.
By repeating it twenty times, there is the destruction of enemies, and likewise, one comes under one's own control;
by fifteen repetitions, a person attains happiness and prosperity.
Through the Kalāvṛtti [yantra], they know the acquisition of sons, grandsons, wealth, and grain;
it serves for liberation from fear of kings and for the eradication of enmity.
One should perform this with twenty-five [recitations];
it shall bring liberation from bondage when one has encountered distress or an incurable disease.
When the destruction of one's lineage occurs, when the family line is severed, when the loss of life has arrived,
when enemies increase, when diseases multiply, and likewise when wealth is lost or exhausted.
Likewise, during the three kinds of portents and in times of great calamity, one should perform this with effort a hundred times; thereby, auspiciousness is attained.
Through a hundred repetitions, there is an increase in spiritual welfare, as well as an increase in royal power.
O Goddess, by reciting the *Siddhyaṣṭottara* mantra one thousand times as intended in the mind,
Lakṣmī herself becomes permanently established and bestows her grace.
Having enjoyed his heart's desires, a man may attain liberation;
by reciting the *Śatavṛtti* on the day of Caṇḍī, all supernatural powers (*siddhis*) are accomplished.
By means of a hundred-thousand-fold commentary, one shall become the sovereign of the circle of directions.

Then, having prostrated with: *oṃ nārāyaṇāya namaḥ*, *oṃ nārāyaṇāya namaḥ*, *oṃ narottamāya namaḥ*, *oṃ devyai namaḥ*, *oṃ sarasvatyai namaḥ*, *oṃ vyāsāya namaḥ*, one should recite [the following] for the sake of removing the errors of those who have fallen from the root through the recitation of ritual injunctions:
Having reached the end of an Adhyāya, one should cease, but never in the middle;
if one ceases in the middle of a Tṛca, one should recite from the beginning of that Adhyāya.
Likewise:
"Having placed it before the images of the gods, and especially before the Brāhmaṇas..."
Or the reciter, O descendant of Kuru, may loosen a knot.
Now follows the procedure for the Śatacaṇḍī and Sahasracaṇḍī rites.
Having bowed to Gaṇeśvara, the Goddess, the two Parents (Brahmā and Śiva), Rāghava, and Śiva,
[this work was composed] by Kamalākara Śarman, the son of Kāma and Kṛṣṇā.
The Ḍāmara, the Yāmala, and likewise the Yoginī Tantra.
Having diligently examined the Vārāhī Tantra and other texts,
as well as the Sahasra-caṇḍī and the Śata-caṇḍī, [I have composed this].

The ritual application according to the procedure for the placement of the nine syllables has been proclaimed. In that regard, the patron— desiring to construct a pavilion in an auspicious place— [should perform] the rites for Gaṇeśa, the remainder of the work, and the earth.
Having performed the worship for the Śatacaṇḍī rite, one should construct a sixteen-cubit pavilion; for the Sahasracaṇḍī rite, a twenty-cubit pavilion.
Then, having propitiated the deity at the base of the pillar in the southeast corner, one should proceed.

Having performed the worship of the aforementioned deities and taking the *argha* offering in a copper vessel, one should kneel upon the ground and recite: "Come, O Earth, auspicious in every way, sustainer of the worlds!
You were lifted up by the Boar with his supreme tusk, together with your mountains, forests, and groves."

"May the pavilion be established today; hereafter, may it possess auspicious characteristics. Accept this *arghya* offered by me; be gracious and bestow welfare. Having thus offered the *arghya* to the Earth and having constructed the pavilion, one should prepare in its center, toward the northeast (*īśānī*), a planetary altar (*grahavedi*) measuring one cubit (*hasta*) and four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in height. To the west of that, for the *Śatacaṇḍī* rite, one should construct a square lotus-altar or lotus-pit (*padmakuṇḍa*) measuring two cubits, and for the *Sahasracaṇḍī*, four or six cubits. In that case, for the four-cubit [pit], forty-eight finger-breadths must be made.

The eight, five, and eighteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas), as well as the two sets of seven and the two for the wind [sections], should be made on the six cubits [of the altar]. Having thus constructed the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should prepare an eight-cornered altar (vedi) in the middle of the pavilion (maṇḍapa). This is as follows: having made a regular square in the middle of the four central pillars within a sixteen-cubit pavilion, one should mark both sides at the corners with eighteen fingers and twenty fingers [respectively]—one cubit plus twenty fingers—and by laying down eight lines, an octagon is formed; this is the method stated by Rāghavabhaṭṭa.

Alternatively, having made a square measuring one cubit (hastamātra) with sixteen additional finger-breadths (aṅgula) in the center, and having made four squares of that same measurement attached to it in the four directions, one should draw eight diagonal lines from the corners of the outer squares toward the cardinal directions; thus, by joining the four squares in the four directions, an eight-sided figure is formed. Having thus constructed an altar (vedi) of one cubit in height with eight corners, one should prepare either a Varuṇa-maṇḍala or a Sarvatobhadra-maṇḍala upon it, and having tied a canopy above it equipped with small bells, chowries, and so forth—[one hundred...].

For the image of Caṇḍī, one should fashion a form with eighteen arms using five palas of gold—or half of that, or half of that again; for the thousand-fold Caṇḍī, using five palas—or half of that, or half of that again.
Now, the ritual procedure:

On an auspicious day, the performer, accompanied by his wife, having anointed his body with sesame oil and adorned himself, holding a full water-pot in his hand, shall circumambulate the pavilion while reciting the mantra "Bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ. Entering through the western door and recollecting the universal place and time, he should resolve: "In this birth of mine, for the sake of pleasing Durgā, I shall perform the Thousand Caṇḍīs, either myself or through a Brāhmaṇa. As part of that, having performed the worship of Gaṇeśa, the declaration of the auspicious day (Puṇyāhavācana), the worship of the Mothers (Mātṛkāpūjana), and the Nāndī-śrāddha, I shall choose an Ācārya and pray to him."
"Just as Bṛhaspati is the preceptor of Śakra and the other gods in heaven, so may you become my preceptor in this world, O observer of excellent vows."
Then one should choose the Brahman priest:
"Just as the four-faced Brahmā, the Grandfather in the heavenly world, so do I choose you as the Brahman priest in this sacrifice of mine."

Then, having chosen the Sadasya and the Gāṇapatya, and [chosen] half of the Japas, he should choose nine priests for this rite with the formula: "I choose you as the officiating priest (ṛtvij) in this ritual. In the case of a Śatacaṇḍī, he should choose one hundred; in the case of a Sahasracaṇḍī, one thousand. Then, having chosen eight door-keepers, and having performed the Madhuparka worship for all of them if possible, [the rite proceeds].

One should give a ring, ear-ornaments, two garments, a water-vessel, a seat, and vessels for the *arghya* offering—twice as much to the *ācārya*. Then, having scattered mustard seeds while reciting, "Whatever spirit resides here," and having sprinkled the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), with *kuśa* grass, and with the three verses beginning with "śucī vo havyā" and the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," one should recite the two mantras beginning with "asvastayana" and "tārkṣyam. Thereafter, one should perform the worship of the pavilion according to the procedure in my *Tulāpaddhati*, prior to the installation of the fire.

Then, in the east: "O Kādambarī, mounted upon an elephant, wielder of the thunderbolt, come, come! Approach, approach! Accept, accept this milk-soaked food offering (bali) accompanied by perfumes and flowers! Fulfill my desire, fulfill it! Svāhā! Having thus offered the bali, one should worship on the two doorposts with: "Salutation to Bāhmī, Māheśvarī, Cit-śakti, Māyā-śakti, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Śaṅkhanidhi, Padmanidhi, and Dvāraśrī. Then, one should worship Vāstupuruṣa and Asitāṅga Bhairava. Next, in the southeast, [one worships] Ulkā.

To the one mounted on a goat, with a spear in hand: "Come, come! and so forth; and Rurubhairava. To the one on the left door-post: to Karālī, mounted on a buffalo, with a staff in hand: "Come, come! and so forth. Having worshipped Kaumārī and Vaiṣṇavī on the two door-posts as before, along with Śakti and the others, one should worship Caṇḍabhairava. Then, in the southwest: to Raktākṣī, mounted on a corpse, with a sword in hand: "Come, come! and so forth; and Krodhabhairava. Then, in the west: to Kauberī, mounted on a horse, with a noose in hand: "Come, come! and so forth; and Vārāhī on the two door-posts.

Having worshipped Miṇḍarṇī, Ciñciñcchakti, and the others, one should worship Unmattabhairava—then, in the northwest, [worship] Kapālabhairava, who is mounted on a deer, holds kusha grass in his hand, and [is invoked with] "Come, come," and so forth. Then, in the north, [worship] Yakṣiṇī, who is mounted on a lion and holds a mace in her hand, [invoked with] "Come, come," and so forth. On the two door-frames, having worshipped Cāmuṇḍā and Lakṣmī, as well as Ciñciñcchakti and the others, one should worship Bhīṣaṇabhairava. In the northeast, [worship] Kālī, who is mounted on a bull and holds a trident in her hand, [invoked with] "Come, come," and so forth; and Saṃhārabhairava. [In the] northeast...

In the center of the eastern quarter of the entire kingdom, [one should worship] the one who rides upon a serpent and holds a discus in hand, with the mantra "Come, come," and so forth; this is the worship of the Earth. In the western quarter, in the middle of the direction of Nirṛti, [one should worship] the best of gods who rides upon a horse, holding a sword and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) in his hands, with the mantra "Come, come," and so forth; this is the worship of the Atmosphere. Then, on the altar: to Viṣṇu in the southeast, to Rudra in the east, to Brahmā in the northeast, to Gaṇeśa in the west, and in the center to Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahāsarasvatī. Having raised the banners and flags, one should perform their worship.

Then, the preceptor, having installed and worshipped the planetary deities (*graha*) upon the planetary altar (*grahavedī*), sits upon a seat on the central altar and performs obeisance as follows: "Guṃ, salutation to the Guru; Gaṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati; Dvāṃ, salutation to Dvāraśrī; Duṃ, salutation to Durgā; Kṣaṃ, salutation to Kṣetrapāla; Hraḥ, Phaṭ, salutation to the Astra-mantra; and salutation to Vāstupuruṣa and Mahālakṣmī. Having thus bowed, he prepares the earth-seat (*pṛthvyāsana*) and [offers salutations]: "Salutation to Anantāsana; salutation to Vimalāsana; salutation to Padmāsana."

Having struck the left foot three times with both hands while reciting *hraḥ astāya phaṭ*, and having performed the triple-clapping (*tālatraya*) while reciting *gaṇapati sarasvatī kṣetrapālān satvāraḥ phaṭ*, one should contemplate a wall of fire. Then, having offered a continuous stream of water from all [the vessels], sipped water for purification (*ācamana*) at the root [of the mantra], regulated the breath (*prāṇāyāma*), and recollected the place and time, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "In this rite of the Hundred Caṇḍīs, I shall perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), worship, and so forth, according to the procedure of the nine-fold ocean of Śrī Mahālakṣmī. Having thus resolved, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).

Having united one's own life-force with the Supreme Self situated in the head by means of the mantra "haṃsaḥ so 'ham," one should contemplate the earth from the feet up to the knees as "laṃ"; the phrase "the earth [is] in water" is to be applied everywhere.

From the knees up to the navel—*vaṃ*—I dissolve water into fire. From the navel up to the throat—*raṃ*—I dissolve fire into air. From the throat up to the space between the eyebrows—*yaṃ*—I dissolve air into ether. From the space between the eyebrows up to the *brahmarandhra*—*aṃ*—I dissolve ether into the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*).

O Mahālakṣmī, I dissolve the ego into the Great Nature (Mahat), the Great Nature into Primordial Matter (Prakṛti), Primordial Matter into the Spirit (Puruṣa), and the Spirit into the Supreme Self, the Brahman known as Mahālakṣmī—having first withdrawn all beings along with their attendants. Then, having burnt the sinful person, who is the size of a thumb, within your belly by means of inhalation (pūraka) sixteen times with the seed-syllable *yaṃ*; having burnt him again by means of retention (kuṃbhaka) sixty-four times with the seed-syllable *raṃ*; and having expelled him by means of exhalation (recaka) thirty-two times with the seed-syllable *vaṃ*; [I then] bathe him with the nectar-seed syllable *vāṃ*.

Having joined [the syllables] with *lam*, condensed them with *glaum*, and having established the limbs of the body with the seed-syllable of space (*ham*), one should unite the individual soul (*jīva*) there by reciting "haṃsaḥ so'haṃ haṃsaḥ."

Brahman is the primordial source (*prakṛti*). From the primordial source comes the Great One (*mahat*); from the Great One, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*); from the ego-sense, space (*ākāśa*); from space, air (*vāyu*); from air, fire (*agni*); from fire, water (*āpaḥ*); from water, earth (*pṛthivī*); from earth, plants; from plants, food; from food, semen; from semen, the person (*puruṣa*)—having thus detailed the origin of the body, one should perform the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*).
Of this great mantra for the consecration of life (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) of the venerable [Name], Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the seers (ṛṣis).

The *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas are the meters (*chandas*). The deity is the vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*), the creator of the universe, whose nature is consciousness. *Āṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); *hrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*); *kroṃ* is the peg (*kīlaka*). This is the application (*viniyoga*) for the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā*) of this Caṇḍī. *Oṃ aṃ hrīṃ kroṃ aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ | To the self consisting of earth, water, fire, air, and ether; *āṃ*, salutation to both thumbs. Salutation to the heart.*

The *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas are the meters (*chandas*). The deity is the Vital Energy (*prāṇa-śakti*), the creator of the universe, whose form is consciousness. *Aṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); *hrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*); *kro* is the pin (*kīlaka*). *Āṃ* is the seed-syllable; *hrīṃ* is the power; *kro* is the pin. This is the application (*viniyoga*) for the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇa-pratiṣṭhā*) of this Caṇḍī. *Oṃ aṃ hrīṃ kro aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ | To the self consisting of earth, water, fire, air, and ether; Āṃ, salutation to both thumbs. Salutation to the heart.*
Oṃ iṃ la caṃ chaṃ jaṃ ghaṃ ñaṃ, to the essence of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; īṃ, salutation to the two index fingers. Svāhā to the crest-lock (śikhā).
Oṃ-uṃ-ṭaṃ-ṭhaṃ-ḍaṃ-ḍhaṃ-ṇaṃ | To the self of hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell, ūṃ; to the two middle fingers, namaḥ. To the crest-lock (śikhā), vaṣaṭ.
Oṃ-eṃ-taṃ-thaṃ-daṃ-dhaṃ-naṃ; to the self of speech, hands, feet, anus, and generative organ, aiṃ; salutation to the two ring fingers—huṃ, for the armor.

Oṃ - Oṃ - Paṃ - Phaṃ - Baṃ - Bhaṃ - Maṃ. To the self whose nature is speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and pleasure: Oṃ, salutation to the two little fingers (kaniṣṭhikābhyāṃ namaḥ); Vauṣaṭ to the three eyes.

Oṃ - Āṃ - Yaṃ - Raṃ - Laṃ - Vaṃ - Śaṃ - Ṣaṃ - Saṃ - Haṃ - Kṣaṃ. To the self consisting of mind, intellect, ego, consciousness, and discernment; Aḥ, salutation with the palms and backs of the hands. Phaṭ, to the weapon. Thus is the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the six limbs, beginning with the heart.

Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ sohaṃ kroṃ hrīṃ āṃ. Oṃ, the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) of [Name] Caṇḍī are here as her vital breaths; once again my life-force (*jīva*) is established here;

once again speech, mind, eyes, ears, tongue, nose, breath, hands, feet, anus, and genitals—having come here, may they remain for a long time in happiness for the sake of well-being, *svāhā*. Having placed [the hand] on the head, heart, and navel, having recited [the mantra] three times or once, one should recite the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) fifteen times and contemplate the purificatory rites (*saṃskārān*).
Now, the Mātṛkā-nyāsa:
