For this venerable Mātṛkā-mantra, Brahmā is the Ṛṣi, Gāyatrī is the Chandas, and Mātṛkā-Sarasvatī is the Devatā; the consonants are the Bījas, the vowels are the Śaktis, and *kṣaṃ* is the Kīlaka; its application (*viniyoga*) is in the Mātṛkā-nyāsa.

Oṃ - aṃ - kaṃ - khaṃ - gaṃ - ghaṃ - ṅaṃ - āṃ, to the two thumbs, namaḥ. Oṃ - iṃ - caṃ - chaṃ - jaṃ - jhaṃ - ñaṃ - īṃ, to the two index fingers, namaḥ. Oṃ - uṃ - ṭaṃ - ṭhaṃ - ḍaṃ - ḍhaṃ - ṇaṃ - uṃ, to the two middle fingers, namaḥ.
Oṃ - eṃ - taṃ - thaṃ - daṃ - dhaṃ - naṃ - aiṃ - salutation to both ring fingers (anāmikābhyāṃ namaḥ).

Oṃ - oṃ - paṃ - phaṃ - baṃ - bhaṃ - maṃ - auṃ - salutation to both little fingers (kaniṣṭhikābhyāṃ namaḥ). Oṃ - āṃ - yaṃ - raṃ - laṃ - vaṃ - śaṃ - ṣaṃ - saṃ - haṃ - kṣaṃ - āḥ - salutation to the palms and backs of the hands (karatala-karapṛṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ). Likewise, āḥ - salutation to the palms and backs of the hands (karatala-karapṛṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ). In this manner, the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) beginning with the heart is performed.

Then, in the sixteen-petaled lotus at the throat, [place] the sixteen vowels beginning with *a* on the petals: *eṃ namaḥ*, *āṃ namaḥ*, *iṃ* (and so forth). In the twelve-petaled [lotus] at the heart, [place] the letters from *ka* to *ta*. In the ten-petaled [lotus] at the navel, [place] those from *tha* to *pha*. Below that, in the six-petaled [lotus], [place] those from *ba* to *la*. In the four-petaled [lotus] at the anus, [place] those from *va* to *sa*. In the two-petaled [lotus] at the forehead, [place] *haṃ* and *kṣaṃ*. These are the internal *mātṛkās*. Now follows the placement (*nyāsa*) of the Brahma-internal *mātṛkās*: the seer (*ṛṣi*) and the rest, as well as the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), are as before. *Aṃ namaḥ* on the head; *aṃ* on the face; *iṃ*...

To the right eye—*īṃ namaḥ*; to the left eye—*uṃ*; to the right ear—*ūṃ namaḥ*; to the left ear—*ṛṃ namaḥ*; to the right nostril—*ṛṃ namaḥ*; to the left nostril—*lūṃ namaḥ*; to the left nostril [again]—*lūṃ namaḥ*; to the right cheek—*lūṃ namaḥ*; to the left cheek—*eṃ namaḥ*; to the upper lip—*aiṃ namaḥ*; to the lower lip—*oṃ namaḥ*; to the upper row of teeth—*auṃ namaḥ*; to the lower row of teeth—*aṃ namaḥ*; to the tongue—*āṃ namaḥ*; to the throat—*kaṃ*.

*Namaḥ* at the base of the right arm—*khaṃ*; *namaḥ* at the right elbow—*gaṃ*; *namaḥ* at the right wrist—*ghaṃ*; *namaḥ* at the base of the right fingers—*ṅaṃ*; *namaḥ* at the tips of the right fingers—*caṃ*; *namaḥ* at the base of the left arm—*chaṃ*; *namaḥ* at the left elbow—*jaṃ*; *namaḥ* at the left wrist—*jhaṃ*; *namaḥ* at the base of the left fingers—*ñaṃ*; *namaḥ* at the tips of the left fingers—*ṭaṃ*; *namaḥ* at the base of the right foot—*ṭhaṃ*; *namaḥ* at the right knee—*ḍaṃ*; *namaḥ* at the right ankle.

— *Ḍhaṃ* namaḥ at the base of the right foot’s toes; — *Ṇaṃ* namaḥ at the tips of the right foot’s toes; — *Taṃ* namaḥ at the base of the left foot; — *Thaṃ* namaḥ at the left knee; — *Daṃ* namaḥ at the left ankle; — *Dhaṃ* namaḥ at the base of the right foot’s toes; — *Naṃ* namaḥ at the tips of the right foot’s toes; — *Paṃ* namaḥ on the right side; — *Ghaṃ* namaḥ on the left side; — *Baṃ* on the back; — *Bhaṃ* at the navel; — *Maṃ* on the abdomen; — *Yaṃ* namaḥ at the heart; — *Raṃ* namaḥ at the base of the arms; — *Laṃ* at the crown of the head.

— *vaṃ* on the two shoulders; *śaṃ* from the heart to the right hand; *ṣaṃ* from the heart to the left hand; *saṃ* *namaḥ* from the heart to the right foot; *haṃ* *namaḥ* from the heart to the left foot;
*laṃ* from the head to the feet; *kṣaṃ* *namaḥ* from the feet to the head; then the assignment of the *nivṛtti*-kalā and the others to the directions starting with the north-east (*īśāna*).

Aṃ *nivṛtti* (the power of cessation), salutation—on the head; Āṃ *pratiṣṭhā* (the power of foundation), salutation—on the mouth; Iṃ *vidyā* (the power of knowledge), salutation—on the forehead; Īṃ *śānti* (the power of peace), salutation—on the right and left eyes respectively; Uṃ *īdikā*, Ūṃ *dīpikā* (the powers of illumination)—on the right and left ears respectively; Ṛṃ *recakā*, Ṝṃ *mocikā* (the powers of liberation)—on the two nostrils; Laṃ *parā*, Lāṃ *sūkṣmā* (the subtle powers)—on the two cheeks; Eṃ *sūkṣmāmayā*, Aiṃ *jñānāmayā* (the powers consisting of the subtle and knowledge)—on the two rows of teeth; Oṃ *sāvitrī*, Auṃ *vyāpinī* (the pervasive powers)—on the two lips.

Aṃ, to Surūpā, on the tongue; Āḥ, to Anasūyā, on the throat; then on the right hand: Kaṃ, to Sṛṣṭi; Khaṃ, salutation to Budhi; Gaṃ, salutation to Samṛddhi; Ghaṃ, salutation to Medhā; Ṅaṃ, salutation to Kānti—thus one should place [these] on the base of the right hand, the elbow, the wrist, the roots of the fingers, and the tips of the fingers. Caṃ, to Lakṣmī; Chaṃ, to Dyuti; Jaṃ, to Sthirā; Jhaṃ, to Sthiti; Ñaṃ, to Siddhi—one should place these on the left hand as before.

One should assign [the syllables] as follows: *ṭaṃ* to Japā, *ṭhaṃ* to Pālinī, *ḍaṃ* to Kāntī, *ḍhaṃ* to Īśvarī, and *ṇaṃ* to Ratī at the root, knee, ankle, base of the toes, and tips of the toes of the right foot. Then, in order from the root to the knee of the left foot: *taṃ* to Kāmikā, *thaṃ* to Varadā, *daṃ* to Hladinī, *dhaṃ* to Prītī, and *naṃ* to Dīrghā. Then, in order from right to left on the belly: *paṃ* to Tīkṣṇā and *phaṃ* to Raudrī. Finally, *baṃ* to Ābhā on the back and *bhaṃ* to Nidrā at the navel.

— *maṃ* to *taṃdryai* (the goddess Taṃdrī), in the stomach; *yaṃ* to *kṣudāyai namaḥ* (salutation to Kṣudā), in the heart; *raṃ* to *krodinyai* (Krodinī), in the throat; *laṃ* to *kṛpāyai* (Kṛpā), on the hump of the neck; *vaṃ* to *ulkāyai namaḥ* (salutation to Ulkā), on the two shoulders; *śaṃ* to *mṛtyave namaḥ* (salutation to Mṛtyu), from the heart to the right hand; *ṣaṃ* to *pītāyai* (Pītā), from the heart to the left hand; *saṃ* to *śvetāyai* (Śvetā), from the heart to the right foot; *haṃ* to *aruṇāyai* (Aruṇā), from the heart to the left foot; *laṃ* to *asitāyai* (Asitā), from the head to the feet; *kṣaṃ* to *anantāyai namaḥ* (salutation to Anantā), from the feet to the head. Thus is the ritual placement of the Kalās (*kalānyāsa*).

Then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) three times with the root mantra: "Of this glorious nine-syllable mantra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the seers (ṛṣis); Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahāsarasvatī are the deities."

The meters are Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, and Anuṣṭubh; the powers are Naṃdā, Ākāmbaṛī, Bhūmā, and Śakti; the seed-syllables (bījas) are Raktadantikā, Durgā, and Bhrāmarī; the principles (tattvas) are Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya; the application (viniyoga) is in recitation, worship, and so forth. Now follows the eleventh nyāsa: one should place the letters from 'a' to 'kṣa', conjoined with the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, upon the external limbs and vital points (*marmasthānas*). For example: *hrīṃ aṃ namaḥ* on the head, and so on. This is the first [nyāsa].

Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ klīṃ—these seed-syllables (bījas) should be placed on both hands, starting from the little finger and the thumb, extending to the palms, the backs of the hands, and the wrists. Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ namaḥ to the two little fingers, namaḥ [to the other parts], and so forth—in this manner for the six limbs beginning with the heart, and likewise in the ten directions. This is the second [method].

Oṃ hrāṃ aiṃ—may Brāhmī protect me in the east. Oṃ hrīṃ hrauṃ—may Māheśvarī protect me in the southeast. Oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ—may Kaumārī protect me in the south. Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ—may Vaiṣṇavī protect me in the southwest. Oṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ—salutations to Vārāhī; may she protect me in the west.

Oṃ hrīṃ glau iṃdrāṇyai—may Indrāṇī protect me in the northwest. Oṃ hrīṃ bhryāṃ cāmuṇḍāyai—may Cāmuṇḍā protect me in the northeast. Oṃ hrīṃ vyomeśvaryai—may Vyomeśvarī protect me above. Oṃ hrīṃ saptadvīpeśvaryai—[may Saptadvīpeśvarī protect me below].
May Bhūmi protect me! Oṃ hrīṃ, may Nāgeśvarī protect me in the netherworld (pātāla)! Thus ends the third [section].

In all cases, the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) comes first: *oṃ ānandajāyai pūrvāṅge māṃ pātu* (Oṃ, may [the goddess] Ānandajā protect me on the eastern limb). *Kṣauṃ raktadaṃtikāyai dakṣiṇāṅge māṃ pātu* (Kṣauṃ, may Raktadaṃtikā protect me on the southern limb). *Kṣauṃ śāṅkambharyai paścimāṅge māṃ pātu* (Kṣauṃ, may Śāṅkambharī protect me on the western limb). *Kṣauṃ durgāyai vāmabhāge māṃ pātu* (Kṣauṃ, may Durgā protect me on the left side). *Hrūṃ pātrakarāyai śirasi māṃ pātu* (Hrūṃ, may Pātrakarā protect me on the head). *Mātaṅgakanyāyai mastakādi-pādāntaṃ māṃ pātu* (May Mātaṅgakanyā protect me from the top of the head down to the feet). *Śrīṃ citrakāntikṛdbhramaryai namaḥ*—may she protect me from the feet up to the head. Thus ends the fourth [section].

Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Brahmā; may he protect me from the feet up to the navel. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Vaiṣṇavī; may she protect me from the navel up to the *viśuddhi* [cakra]. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Rudra; may he protect me from the *viśuddhi* up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). Oṃ hrīṃ haṃ, salutation to Haṃsā; may she protect me in both feet. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Vainateya; may he protect me in both hands. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Vṛṣabha; may he protect me in both eyes. Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Gajānana; may he protect me in all limbs.
Oṃ hrīṃ! O Hare, who consists of bliss, may You protect me in all limbs within the two parts of the body—the front and the back—of the Supreme (Parā). Thus ends the fifth [section].

Oṃ hrīṃ, may Mahālakṣmī protect me in the middle of the body. Oṃ aiṃ, may Sarasvatī protect me in the upper body. Oṃ klīṃ, may Mahākālī protect me in the lower body. Oṃ hrīṃ kṣvoṃ, may [the goddess] with the lion’s hands protect me. Oṃ hrīṃ, may Haṃsa protect me in the eyes. Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Mahiṣa and the Preta; may Haṃsa protect me. Oṃ namaścaṇḍikāyai, may Caṇḍikā protect me in all limbs. Thus ends the sixth [section].

Oṃ Aiṃ, salutation to the head. Oṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to the right eye. Oṃ Klīṃ, salutation to the left eye. Oṃ Cāṃ, salutation to the right ear; may it protect me. Muṃ, salutation to the left ear; may it protect me. Ḍāṃ Cāṃ, salutation to the right nostril. Yaiṃ, salutation to the left nostril. Oṃ Namo Namaḥ, salutation to the mouth of the nose; may it protect me. Cai, salutation to the anus; may it protect me. Thus ends the seventh [chapter].

Ceṃ on the face; yaiṃ on the left nostril; ḍāṃ on the right nostril; māṃ; muṃ on the left ear; māṃ; cāṃ on the right ear; māṃ; kliṃ on the left eye; māṃ; hrīṃ on the right eye; māṃ; aiṃ on the head; māṃ. Thus ends the eighth [chapter].

With the root mantra *aiṃ hrīṃ klīṃ cāmuṇḍāyai vicce svāhā*, preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) at each syllable and ending with *namaḥ*, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) upon one's own front, right, back, and left limbs, by ascending and descending from the head to the feet and from the feet to the head. Thus ends the *namaḥ*-placement. With the aforementioned root mantra, preceded by *namaḥ*, one performs the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅga*) starting from the heart. Thus ends the tenth [section].

Then—having recited the single verse beginning with "khaḍginī śūlinī ghorā," and having meditated upon her as blue-colored, [one offers] "to the heart, namaḥ. Having recited the four verses beginning with "śūlena pāhi no devi," and having meditated upon her as red-colored, [one offers] "to the head, svāhā. Having recited the five verses beginning with "sarvasvarūpe sarveśī," and having meditated upon her as white-colored, [one offers] "to the tuft of hair, vaṣaṭ. This is the eleventh [section].

Then one should display the *yonimudrā*. It is as follows: having grasped the left ring finger with the right index finger, and the right ring finger with the left index finger, the two middle fingers are placed at the tips [of the index fingers], the two little fingers at the tips of those, and the two thumbs at the tips of those.
Now, as for the meditation:
she has a white face and blue arms, with very white breasts;
her waist and feet are red, and her shanks and thighs are blue and exceedingly intoxicated.
Her hips were most beautiful, adorned with variegated garlands, garments, and ornaments;
she was anointed with exquisite unguents and possessed a luster, beauty, and gracefulness that were truly magnificent.
She who possesses eighteen arms is to be worshipped, as is she who possesses a thousand arms;
here the weapons will be described in order, starting from the lower right hand.
A rosary, a lotus, arrows, a thunderbolt,
a mace, a discus, a trident, an axe, a conch, a bell, and a noose.
[He should place] the spear, the staff, the shield and bow, the drinking vessel, and the water-pot;
then, having fashioned a *sarvatobhadra* diagram upon the altar, he should install the deities therein.

In the center, [one places] Brahmā; to the north and other directions, Soma and the others. In the sequence starting from the middle between Vāyu and Soma, one places the Vasus with "janmayā atra," the Rudras with "ā rudrāsaḥ," and the twelve Ādityas with "tyān nu kṣatriyān. One places the Aśvins with "aśvināvartya," the seven Yakṣas with "abhityaṃ devam," the Sarpas with "āyaṃ gauḥ," and the Gandharvas and Apsarases with "apsarasāṃ gandharvāṇām. Between Brahmā and Soma, one places Kumāra with "kumāram mātā" and Ṛṣabha with "ṛṣabham me."

With the mantra "Aditir hy ajaniṣṭha," [one should worship] Dakṣa; with "Brahmeṃdramadhyetām agnivarṇām," Durgā; and with "Idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," Viṣṇu. With "Udīratām," [one should worship] Svadhā between Brahmā and Agni; with "Paraṃ mṛtyo," Mṛtyu and the diseases between Brahmā and Yama; with "Gaṇānāṃ tvā," Gaṇapati between Brahmā and Nirṛti; with "Śanno devīḥ," the Waters between Brahmā and Varuṇa; with "Maruto yasya," the Maruts between Brahmā and Vāyu; and with "Syonā," the Earth at the base of the foot of Brahmā.

In that very place, one should worship the rivers such as the Gaṅgā with the mantra *imaṃ me gaṅge*; and the seven oceans with the mantra *dhāmnodhāmnaḥ*. Outside, in the vicinity of Soma and the others, one should worship in sequence: the mace (*gadā*), trident (*triśūla*), thunderbolt (*vajra*), spear (*śakti*), staff (*daṇḍa*), sword (*khaḍga*), noose (*pāśa*), and goad (*aṅkuśa*). Again, starting from the north: Gautama, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, Kaśyapa, Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, Atri, and Arundhatī. Starting from the east: Aiṃdrī, Kaumārī, Brāhmī, Vārāhī, Cāmuṇḍā, Vaiṣṇavī, Māheśvarī, and Vaināyakī.

Then, having invoked with "Tat sad astu," worshipped, and offered oblations (*bali*), one should touch the ground in the center of that [site] with "Mahī dyauḥ. Having scattered the seven grains with "Oṣadhayaḥ saṃ vadante," one should place a pitcher made of gold, silver, or copper with "Ā kalaśeṣu. One should fill it with water using "Imaṃ me Gaṅge," with sandalwood paste using "Gandhadvārām," with all medicinal herbs using "Yā oṣadhīḥ," with *dūrvā* grass using "Kāṇḍāt kāṇḍāt," and with five types of sprouts using "Aśvatthe deva."

Having placed the seven types of earth beginning with "syonā," the fruit-bearing branches with the mantra "yāḥ phalinīḥ," and the full vessel with the mantra "pūrṇā darvi," one should draw the armor (astramantra) there upon a cloth.
For example:

having drawn three squares with four doors, one should draw a triangle in their center; then, having placed a southern corner on its western side, one should form another triangle connected to the corner situated at the eastern end of the western line. By that, six triangles are produced within the outer corners. Then, having drawn another triangle in the middle of that, one should form yet another triangle connected to it.
The method of drawing [the diagram]:
within a triangle, there is a hexagon; outside that, a circle; outside that, eight petals; and outside that, three squares with four doors each.

Having thus drawn the yantra, one should fashion an image of the Goddess—the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura—seated upon a lion, either with eighteen arms as described in the *Dhannā* [Tantra] or with eight arms as described in the *Rahasya*, made of gold weighing one pala for the Śatacaṇḍī rite, half of that for the Sahasracaṇḍī, or twenty, ten, or five suvarṇas for other rites; having established this image of the Goddess covered with a red silk cloth, one should worship it.
For example:

having washed it with "Svavāme astrāya phaṭ" and placed a water-filled jar upon it, one should first place those vessels to the south of the deity, filling them with flowers, unbroken rice, scents, and so forth, while reciting the root mantra.

Then, having drawn a triangle with fish-marks (*matsyamudrā*), outside of that a hexagon, outside of that a square, and outside of that a circle, using either cow-dung or water, and having stabilized it with the conch-gesture (*śaṅkhamudrā*), one should worship the fire with its ten digits (*kalā*): "Obeisance to Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī, Śuci, Surāpā, Kapilā, Havyavāhā, and Kavyavāhā. Having thus worshipped, one should place [the seed-syllable] *Hṛdayāya namaḥ* in the corners of the hexagon—namely, in the corners of Agni, Nirṛti, and Vāyu.

Having worshipped with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) while reciting: *Śirase svāhā*, *Śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *Kavacāya huṃ*, *Netratrayāya vauṣaṭ* (at the front), and *Sarvataḥ astrāya phaṭ*; and having placed the conch that has been washed with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), [one worships it] with: *Haṃ māṃ sūryamaṇḍalāya dvādaśakalātmane namaḥ*, followed by: *Tapanyai*, *Tāpinyai*, *Dhūmrāyai*, *Marīcyai*, *Jvālinyai*, *Rucyai*, *Suṣumnāyai*, *Bhogadāyai*, *Viśvāyai*, *Bodhinyai*, *Dāriṇyai*, and *Kṣayāyai*.

Having worshipped the conch with unbroken grains (*akṣata*), having cast perfumes and flowers into it with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, and having first offered water with the *śiras-mantra* using the reverse-order *mātṛkā* syllables—namely, *kṣaṃ namaḥ*, *laṃ namaḥ*, *haṃ namaḥ*, and so forth—one should offer [the following mantras]: "Oṃ, obeisance to the lunar orb consisting of sixteen digits; obeisance to Amṛtā, obeisance to Mānadā, obeisance to Puṣā, obeisance to Candrikā, obeisance to Kānti, obeisance to Jyotsnā, obeisance to Śrī, obeisance to Prīti, obeisance to Aṅganā."

"Salutation to Pūrṇā; salutation to Pūrṇāmṛtā; salutation to Kāmadāyinī. Having thus consecrated [the water] with the Kuśa-mudrā, having drawn the Tīrtha from the solar orb (sūryamaṇḍala), and having displayed the Āvāhinī and other mudrās, one should display the Śikhā-mantra, the Dhenu-mudrā, the Gālinī-mudrā, and the Garuḍa-mudrā. The Gālinī-mudrā is formed by joining the thumbs and index fingers of both hands. Joining the backs of both hands, one should press down the little and ring fingers, while the thumbs are positioned below and the two index fingers are extended forward.

Joining the tips of the middle and ring fingers together like wings, one should display the Garuḍa-mudrā; then, gazing with the Netra-mantra, forming the *saṅkalīkaraṇa* with the Kavaca-mantra, performing the Nyāsa of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) therein, providing protection with the Astra-mantra, worshipping with scents and flowers using the Mūla-mantra, sprinkling it over the hands seven times with the Mūla-mantra, and protecting it with the Cakra-mudrā—one should [use] that water.

Having placed a small amount [of water] in the pitcher, performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) upon oneself, worshipped with scents and flowers, and offered three handfuls of flowers to one's own head while reciting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), one should mentally present incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so forth. Then, assuming the form of the deity, one should mutter the root mantra, offer the recitation (*japa*) to the deity, and smell the flower. Saying "Salutation to the belly of the pitcher" (*kuṃbhodarāya namaḥ*), one should cast it into the left [hand], display the hand, and worship the pedestal (*pīṭha*). Just as for the Goddess, on the right: "Guṃ, salutation to the Gurus" (*guṃ gurubhyo namaḥ*); "Paṃ, salutation to the Supreme Gurus" (*paṃ paramagurubhyo namaḥ*). Having thus worshipped—

On the left: *Gaṃ* to Gaṇapati, *Namaḥ*; *Duṃ* to Durgā, *Namaḥ*; *Kṣaṃ* to Kṣetrapāla, *Namaḥ*. In the center: *Ādhāraśaktyai Namaḥ*, *Mūlaprakṛtyai Namaḥ*, *Varāhāya Namaḥ*, *Ananyāya Namaḥ*, *Bhūmyai Namaḥ*, *Amṛtārṇavāya Namaḥ*, *Ratnadvīpāya Namaḥ*, *Hemagiraye Namaḥ*, *Kalpatarave Namaḥ*, *Ratnavedikāyai Namaḥ*, *Śvetacchatrāya Namaḥ*, *Ratnasiṃhāsanāya Namaḥ*. Having thus worshipped—

In the corners starting from the southeast (Agnēya): *namaḥ* to Dharma; *namaḥ* to Jñāna; *namaḥ* to Vairāgya; *namaḥ* to Aiśvarya. In the directions starting from the east: *namaḥ* to Adharma; *namaḥ* to Ajñāna; *namaḥ* to Avairāgya; *namaḥ* to Anaiśvarya. Above: *namaḥ* to Brahmā; below: *namaḥ* to Ānandī. Having worshipped in the center with *namaḥ* to Vāstupuruṣa, [one worships] in the center with *namaḥ* to Sattvāgni-vidyā. On the pedestal in the eight directions starting from the east: *Oṃ Oṃkāra-giripīṭheśvarī*.

Together with [the consort], I worship the sandals of Oṃkāragiripīṭheśvarī Vambā. Oṃ, obeisance to Oḍḍiyāna—the sacred seat (pīṭha) situated in the eight directions beginning with the east: Oṃ, together with the mistress of the Oṃkāragiri sacred seat, I worship the sandals of Oṃkāragiripīṭheśvarī Vambā.

Oṃ, I worship the Śrīpādukā of Oḍḍiyāṇa Pīṭheśvarī Ambā, together with her consort Oḍḍiyāṇa Pīṭheśvara. Oṃ, I worship the Śrīpādukā of Mātṛkā Pīṭheśvarī Ambā, together with her consort Mātṛkā Pīṭheśvara, and together with Jālandhara Pīṭheśvarī Ambā. Oṃ, I worship the Śrīpādukā of Kolhāgiri Pīṭheśvarī Ambā, together with her consort Kolhāgiri Pīṭheśvara. Oṃ, I worship the Śrīpādukā of Pūrṇagiri Pīṭheśvarī Ambā, together with her consort Pūrṇagiri Pīṭheśvara.

Oṃ saṃ! I worship the Śrīpādukā of Saṃhāragiripīṭheśvarī together with Saṃhāragiripīṭheśvara—Oṃ kāṃ! I worship the Śrīpādukā of Kāmarūpapīṭheśvarī together with Kāmarūpapīṭheśvarī. Again, in all four directions starting from the east, [one worships] everywhere with their respective seed-syllables and names.

Gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇeśa; Kṣaṃ, obeisance to Śretrapāla; Pāṃ, obeisance to the sandals (pādukās); Vaṃ, obeisance to the young students (vaṭukas). In the corners starting from the southeast: Jaṃ, obeisance to Jayā; Vaṃ, obeisance to Vijayā; Jaṃ, obeisance to Jayinī; Aṃ, obeisance to Aparājitā. In that very place: Obeisance to Bhairava Agnimukha; obeisance to the Vetāla Pretavāhana; obeisance to the Vetāla Jhvalamukha; obeisance to the Vetāla Dumrākṣa. Kaṃ, obeisance to Kanda; Nāṃ, obeisance to Nāla.

Daṃ, salutation to the lobhas (desires). Keṃ, salutation to the kenaras (the eight guardians of the directions). Kaṃ, salutation to the karṇikā (pericarp). Aṃ, salutation to the solar orb (sūryamaṇḍala). Uṃ, salutation to the lunar orb (somamaṇḍala). Maṃ, salutation to the fire orb (vahni-maṇḍala). Aṃ, salutation to the Self (ātman). Āṃ, salutation to the inner Self (antarātman). Paṃ, salutation to the Supreme Self (paramātman). Ññaṃ, salutation to the Self of Knowledge (jñānātman). Then, in the east: Viṃ, salutation to Viśva. Māṃ, salutation to Māyā. Ceṃ, salutation to Cetanā. Buṃ, salutation to Buddhi. Niṃ, salutation to Nidrā.

— *Kṣūṃ*, obeisance to Hunger; — *Caṃ*, obeisance to Shadow, in the east; — *Śaṃ*, obeisance to Ability; — *Tṛṃ*, obeisance to Thirst; — *Kṣāṃ*, obeisance to Wretchedness; — *Jāṃ*, obeisance to Birth; — *Laṃ*, obeisance to Modesty; — thus, in the east: *Caṃ*, obeisance to Shadow; — *Śaṃ*, obeisance to Ability; — *Tṛṃ*, obeisance to Thirst; — *Kṣāṃ*, obeisance to Wretchedness; — *Jāṃ*, obeisance to Birth; — *Laṃ*, obeisance to Modesty.

*Namaḥ*—thus on the southeast. *Śāṃ* to Śānti, *namaḥ*; *śaṃ* to Śraddhā, *namaḥ*; *kāṃ* to Kānti, *namaḥ*; *laṃ* to Lakṣmī, *namaḥ*; *dhṛṃ* to Dhṛti, *namaḥ*; *vṛṃ* to Vṛddhi, *namaḥ*—thus on the west.

*Smṛṃ*, salutation to Smṛti (Mindfulness); *daṃ*, salutation to Dayā (Compassion); *tuṃ*, salutation to Tuṣṭi (Contentment); *puṃ*, salutation to Puṣṭi (Nourishment); *māṃ*, salutation to Mātṛkā (the Mother); *bhrāṃ*, salutation to Bhrānti (Delusion)—thus [at] the North. *Oṃ hrīṃ*, salutation to the Lotus Throne of all powers (*sarvaśakti-kamalāsana*), the self of the Yoga-throne which is the union with the Universal Self (*sarvātma-saṃyoga-yogapīṭhātmane*)—thus is the worship of the pedestal (*piṭhapūjā*).

Having meditated upon Mahālakṣmī, who is composed of light and accompanied by her retinue, seated within the expanse of one’s heart, one should recite the mantra: "Come, O boon-granting Goddess, destroyer of the Daityas and Tarpaṇa! Accept this worship, O fair-faced one; salutations to you, the beloved of Śaṅkara! O Goddess Durgā, come here and manifest your presence! Accept this offering and worship along with your eight Śaktis. Thus, having recited the mantra, [one should proceed].

Having drawn in the breath through the right nostril and having invoked the form [of the deity] with the root mantra, one should display the mudrās beginning with the invocation (āvāhana). After displaying the yoni-mudrā and performing the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) upon the form, one should offer the seat, water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamana), and the honey-mixture (madhuparka) with the root mantra and the verse beginning "jayantī maṅgalā kālī. Therein, having washed four vessels with the mantra, one should place sandalwood paste and other offerings within them. Among these, in the vessel for the water for the feet (pādya), one should place dūrvā grass, viṣṇukrāntā, śyāmaka, and lotuses; in the vessel for the respectful offering (arghya), sandalwood paste, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (akṣata).

Having offered *kuśa* grass tips, mustard seeds, barley, and *darbha* grass for the ritual sipping (*ācamanīya*), followed by *jātī* fruit, *kaṅkola*, and cloves for the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) consisting of curds and honey; then, having consecrated [the deity] with fragrant oil, the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), warm water, and waters from sacred bathing sites (*tīrtha*), while reciting the Śrīsūkta, Devīsūkta, and Sarasvatīsūkta; and having again offered water for sipping (*ācamana*), one should present a pair of fine silk garments (*paṭṭadukūla*), a bodice (*kañcuka*), ornaments, the eight fragrances, *bilva* leaves, various flowers, turmeric, saffron, vermilion, lac, and perfumed substances.
One should offer twenty-five thousand, twelve thousand, three thousand, or one thousand flowers.
Now, the worship of the secondary deities (avarṇapūjā):

at the right, *aiṃ mahākālyai vicce namaḥ*; at the left, *klīṃ mahāsarasvatyai vicce namaḥ*; on the left [of the main deity], *huṃ mahiṣāya namaḥ*; at the right, *kṣauṃ siṃhāya namaḥ*; in front, *gaṇapataye namaḥ*; behind, *huṃ kālāya namaḥ*; and behind, *huṃ mṛtyave namaḥ*. On the six petals: *hlaiṃ rudrāya namaḥ*, *hlaiṃ gaurī namaḥ*, *śrīṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*, *śrīṃ lakṣmyai namaḥ*, *aiṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*, *aiṃ sarasvatyai namaḥ*.

In that very place: *hrāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *hrīṃ* to the head, *svāhā*; *hruṃ* to the crest-lock, *vaṣaṭ*; *haiṃ* to the armor, *huṃ*; *hrauṃ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ*; *hruḥ* to the weapon, *phaṭ*. In that very place: *guṃ* to the gurus, *namaḥ*; *paṃ* to the supreme gurus, *namaḥ*; *paṃ* to the parameṣṭhi gurus, *namaḥ*; *haṃ* to Hari, *namaḥ*; *haṃ* to Hara, *namaḥ*; *gaṃ* to Gaṇeśa, *namaḥ*. In the directions: *na* to Nandajā, *namaḥ*; *raṃ* to Raktadaṃtikā, *namaḥ*.

— Śāṃ, salutation to Śākambharī — Duṃ, salutation to Durgā — Bhīṃ, salutation to Bhīmā — Bhrāṃ, salutation to Bhrāmarī — In the triangle: Tāṃ, salutation to Indrāṇī — Kṣāṃ, salutation to Nārasiṃhī — Preṃ, salutation to Cāmuṇḍā — In the directions: Aṃ, salutation to Asitāṅga Bhairava — Ruṃ, salutation to Rurubhairava — Caṃ, salutation to Caṇḍabhairava — Kro, salutation to Krodhanabhairava — Uṃ, salutation to Unnatabhairava — Kaṃ, salutation to Kapālabhairava.

*Namaḥ*—to the east and so forth: *laṃ indrāya namaḥ*, *raṃ agnaye namaḥ*, *yaṃ yamāya namaḥ*, *kṣaṃ nirṛtaye namaḥ*, *vaṃ varuṇāya namaḥ*, *yaṃ vāyave namaḥ*, *laṃ somāya namaḥ*, *haṃ īśānāya namaḥ*. On the outside, joined with their respective initial-syllable seeds: to the thunderbolt (*vajra*), to the spear (*śakti*), to the staff (*daṇḍa*), to the sword (*khaḍga*), to the noose (*pāśa*).

To Aṅkuśāya, Gādayai, and Triśūlāya; then, having offered incense and a lamp with the root mantra, having consecrated the food offering (naivedya) with the root mantra, having sprinkled it, having shielded it with the Kavaca mantra, and having offered a flower, one should transform it into nectar using the Dhenu-mudrā. Having offered it with the root mantra, having displayed the Ghrā-samudrā, and having given water for sipping (āpośana) at each interval, one should offer hand-paste, fruit, betel leaf, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), the waving of lights (nīrājana), an umbrella, a fly-whisk, a mirror, songs, instrumental music, and so forth.
Having offered the oblation (*bali*) consisting of cooked food, *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourds, and so forth, according to the procedure described in our own *Navarātra-nirṇaya*, one should perform the worship.

Now follows the worship of the sixty-four Yoginīs. There, in front of the Goddess, one should draw eight equilateral triangles with red cloth; having thus formed the circle of eight triangles, one should invoke them with the names to be mentioned below, worship them, and offer the water for drinking (*pāyana*) and the sacrificial offerings (*bali*). [To the first Yoginī: "O you of white complexion, holding a trident, a *ḍamaru* drum, a noose, and a sword, adorned with all ornaments, O Sanaisnī-Jayā! Come, come! Arrive, arrive! Accept this milk-rice offering (*pāyasa-bali*) and grant me my desires, svāhā! In this manner: "O you of white complexion, O Sanaisnī, O Vijayā! Come, come! [The sequence continues] ending with Jayā, and then Aparājitā.

Divyayoginī, Mahāyoginī, Siddhiyoginī, Gaṇeśvarī—then, O fair-complexioned one, holding a rosary, a goad, a book, and a lute, devouring the dead, come, come! [and so forth as before]—Ḍākinī, Kālī, Kārātri, Niśācarī, Ṭaṅkāriṇī, Rudrabhettāli, Huṃkāriṇī, O red-complexioned one, with a flaming spear, granting protection and boons in your hands, with hair standing erect, come, come! [and so forth]—Virūpākṣī, Śuṣkāṅgī, Narabhojanī, Phaṭkārī, Vīrabhadre, Dhūmrāṅgī.

O you who delight in strife; then, O you who resemble lightning, who possess a banner, arrows, a bow, and a noose, O Rākṣasī, come, come! And so forth—thus: O red-eyed one, O you of universal form, O terrifying one, O Vīrakauṃārī, O Caṇḍikā, O Vārāhī, O bearer of skulls; then, O you of solar hue, who hold a lotus, a rosary, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons, O Bhairavī, come, come! And so forth—thus: O you with eyes like a crow, O smoke-bodied one, O you whose vehicle is a corpse, O wielder of the sword, O you with a long hanging crest, O garlanded one, O you who are united with the mantra.

To her who has a blue lotus, a conch, a discus, a mace, and hands displaying the gestures of protection and granting boons; "Come, come! and so forth—likewise to Cakriṇī, Kaṅkāli, Bhuvaneśvarī, Troṭaki, Mahāmārī, Yamadūtī, Karāli; then to Dhūmravarṇā, Kuntakī, Bhaṇḍipālā, Mālākārī, Muṇḍāgradhāriṇī; "Come, come! and so forth—likewise to Vyāgrī, Kāṅkṣiṇī, Pretarūpiṇī, Dhūrjaṭinī, Ghorī, Karālī, Viṣalaṃbhinī. This is the worship of the Yoginīs. Then: "Gaṃ, O Gaṇapati..."

"Vaṃ! O Vaṭuka, glowing with a tawny eye, accept this offering (bali)! Protect me! Kadana hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ svāhā! Having thus offered the bali to Vaṭuka and the Kṣetrapāla, one should present an abundant bali. Therein is the mantra: "All the primary and secondary seats (pīṭhas), as well as the doors and thresholds; the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), situated in every direction and region; where all the Yoginīs and lords of Yoga have assembled—in the forest, at the edge of the woods, in the village, at the source of the river, and on its banks."

To those who dwell in ponds, wells, trees, cremation grounds, and at crossroads; to those who assume various forms and those who assume many forms—may you always be satisfied by this offering and accept this oblation. I have come to you for refuge, O all you of virtuous vows. Satisfied by the gift of this oblation, grant me my desires; perform all my tasks and destroy all obstacles forever.

Now, regarding the worship of the maidens (kumāris): they should be worshipped every day, either one hundred or nine in number— specifically, a girl born of a royal lineage for the sake of victory in matters concerning the king, and a girl of the Brāhmaṇa caste for all ritual duties.
For the sake of profit, she was born from a Vaiśya lineage, while her daughter was born from half of a Śūdra lineage.
"A man should worship those born in the final [period] of the *dāruṇa* [nakṣatra] according to the prescribed rite.
Having said this, Surūpa continued:
"By means of nine [offerings], one attains the earth; by double that number, however, one attains sovereignty (*aiśvarya*)."
By increasing by one, he obtains the Kṣatriya status; by each single [increase], he obtains prosperity.
One should avoid for the purpose of worship a maiden who is one year old,
as well as one whose limbs are knotted, cracked, or withered, and one marked by wounds of blood and pus.

One should avoid among all women those who are born of a low caste, those with deformed hands, those who are one-eyed, those who are ugly, those whose bodies are excessively hairy, and those born from the womb of a female slave.
For the specific details, consult my *Nirṇayasindhu*:

Having performed an oil massage with fragrant oil, seated the adorned girl upon a pedestal, and having recollected the place and time, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "For the sake of attaining [the fruit] such-and-such, I shall perform the worship of the maiden (*kumārī-pūjana*) for the rite of such-and-such. Then, having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the root mantra and having uttered the root mantra: "I invoke the maiden herself, who is composed of the syllables of the mantra, who bears the letters of the Mother-phonemes (*mātṛkā*), and who is the very essence of the Nine Durgās."

Having invoked [the deity] and offered a seat, one should wash the feet with warm water for the *pādya* offering; then, having honored [the deity] with *arghya* consisting of turmeric, saffron, vermilion, lac, gold, and flower garlands, and having presented incense and lamps, one should feed [the deity] with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and various edibles.
At the time of eating, one should recite the root mantra or the Saptaśatī;
thereafter, one should offer various fruits, betel leaves, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), the waving of lights (nīrājana), flowers, and handfuls of water.

In this manner, one should worship the others; the knower of mantras should perform the invocation with the mantra-syllables, having first invoked [the deity] everywhere as being composed of the syllables of the mantra.
"O you who are worshiped by the world, O you who are revered by the world, O you whose very nature is all-powerful!
Accept this worship, O Kaumārī; salutations to you, O Mother of the World. Thus is the second [verse].

"I worship here the goddess Tripurā, who is the support of the three qualities (guṇas), whose form is the path of knowledge, and who is saluted by the three worlds"— with these words, he performs the second [offering].
"I worship Kālī, who is beyond all parts (kalās), who is solely devoted to compassion, the auspicious Śivā, the eternal mother of well-being, the auspicious one. Thus ends the third [verse].

From this [source], the reading is as follows: "I worship Kāmākṣī, who is Kapilā, who has transcended the parts [of phonemes], whose nature consists of the letters beginning with 'A', and who is endowed with infinite power"— this is the fourth [verse].
"I invoke Kālī, who acts according to her will, who is the Night of Doom, whose very form is the Staff of Time, the bestower of desires, and who is noble in compassion"— this is the fifth [verse].
"I worship Caṇḍikā, who possesses fierce valor, who is composed of fury, who destroys Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, and who is not bowed down even by Brahmā, Īśa, and Viṣṇu"— this is the sixth [verse].
"I worship today the seventh [day], the goddess Śāmbhavī, who bestows happiness and bliss, who is peaceful, who is saluted by all the gods, and whose self is the essence of all beings."
"I worship the goddess Subhadrā— the beautiful one with limbs the color of gold, the bestower of happiness and good fortune, and the mother of contentment"— thus [is the hymn for] the eighth day.

I always worship with devotion Durgā, the remover of fear and sorrow, who is difficult to reach, who overcomes difficult tasks, and who takes away the suffering of those in distress—like a doe. Thus ends the ninth [chapter].

Then, O Brāhmaṇa, follows the worship of the married women (*suvāsinī*), as well as the worship of the Goddess, the maidens (*kumārī*), and so forth; this should be performed during the *navarātra* on the day of the vow (*vratyaha*). Furthermore, for the four days beginning with the *Śatacaṇḍī*, there is an increase by doubling and so on, up to the *Sahasracaṇḍī*, where the increase is tenfold. Then, having offered the worship to the Goddess, all the Brāhmaṇas, having performed the ritual placement of mantras upon their limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), should recite the nine-syllable mantra (*navārṇava*) one hundred times. Having recited the *Kavaca*, *Argala*, and *Kīlaka* once, and having recited the *Saptaśatī*, they should finally recite the secret nine-syllable mantra one hundred times.

The procedure for the recitation of the *kavaca* and other [protective mantras] is as follows: they should perform the recitation (*japa*) such that there is one form on the first day, two on the second, three on the third, and four on the fourth. For the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and the performer, the daily diet should consist of milk alone; in case of inability, sacrificial food (*haviṣya-anna*) may be taken. Every day, one should feed either a thousand or a hundred Brahmins. On the fifth day, the fire-oblation (*homa*) is performed. However, during the nine-night rite, the complete oblation is performed on the ninth day.
Now, regarding the fire-offering (*homa*):
in this matter, there is a combination of what is prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra* and the *tantra* taught in the *Āgama*.
Having performed that which is prescribed in the *Gṛhya*, one should perform that which is prescribed in the *Āgama*. For example:

Having remembered the place and time, for the sake of achieving the completion of this recitation of the *Navacaṇḍī*, *Śatacaṇḍī*, or *Sahasracaṇḍī* performed through a Brāhmaṇa, I shall perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) with an offering of milk-rice mixed with sesame seeds, using a tenth part [of the total count]. As a preliminary to that, I shall perform the consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa-saṃskāra*), the installation of the fire (*agni-sthāpana*), and so forth.

Having thus resolved, one should gaze at the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the root mantra, sprinkle it with water using the Astra-mantra, strike it with Darbha grass using the Astra-mantra, and sprinkle it again with the Kavaca-mantra. Then, having drawn three lines with fuel-sticks of Aśvattha wood using the root mantra—one pointing eastward and two pointing northward—one should worship Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Śakra upon the eastward-pointing lines, and Brahmā, Yama, and Candra upon the northward-pointing lines. Having fashioned a triangle, a hexagon, an eight-petaled lotus, and a square in the center, one should consecrate it with the root mantra, display the Dhenu and Yoni mudrās, protect it with the Astra-mantra, and encircle it with the Kavaca-mantra.

Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings using the root mantra, and having displayed the *jvālāvinī* mudrā while reciting: "Oṃ, hana hana, paca paca, daha daha, sarvajña jñāpaya svāhā," one should kindle the fire with fuel sticks using the *astra* mantra. Having bound the *kaṅkaṇa* (sacred thread) upon the substances, one should perform the purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) of the fire, beginning with the *garbhādhāna*. For each purificatory rite, one should offer oblations three times with clarified butter using the root mantra. In the rite of naming (*nāmakaraṇa*), having given the name "Hutāśanetvaṃ" (O Fire, you are the self), one should offer oblations. Now follows the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the sweat.

Oṃ *sarayāṃ* to Padmarāgā, Agnijihvā—*namaḥ* at the *liṅga*. Oṃ *ṣarayāṃ* to Suvarṇā at the heart. Oṃ *śarayāṃ* to Bhadralohitā at the head. Oṃ *varayāṃ* to Lohitā at the mouth. Oṃ *larayūṃ* to Śvetā, Karālī—at the eyes. Oṃ *yarayāṃ* to Karālī at all the limbs. To Sahasrārcis—*hṛdayāya*. To Svastipūrṇa—*śirase*. To Uttiṣṭhapuruṣa—*śikhāyai*. To Dhūmavyāpin—*kavacāya huṃ*. To Saptajihva—at the three eyes.

— *phaṭ* to the bow-wielder, the weapon. *Namaḥ* to Agni Jātavedas; [place] on the head: *namaḥ* to Agni Saptajihva; in the right hand: *namaḥ* to Agni Jātavedas; on the head: [again] *namaḥ* to Agni Saptajihva; in the right hand: [to] Agni Havyavāhana on the right hip; [to] Agni Viśvodara on the *liṅga*; [to] Agni Vaiśvānara on the left hip; [to] Agni Kaumāratejas on the left side; [to] Agni Viśvamukha on the right side; [to] Agni Devamukha.

At the *śikhā* [crown]: Then, having meditated upon the Fire-god, having swept around and strewn [the altar], and having placed the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) according to the sequence of the girdle (*mekhalā*), one should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Gaurī in the womb [of the fire-pit]. Having projected the yantra into the fire, one should worship the seven tongues of flame—beginning with "To Padmarāgā" and so forth—as previously described, in the six directions, in the corners starting from the southeast, in front, behind, and in the center. Then, in the corners starting from the southeast, in front and behind, one should worship the six limbs beginning with "To Sahasrārcis" and so forth, and [finally] on the eight petals.

Having worshipped the eight forms beginning with "To Agni Jātavedas" in the directions starting from the east, and having worshipped Indra and the other deities along with their weapons within the square, one should encircle the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with nine lines. Having performed the placement of vessels (*prātrasādana*) and other rites as prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, one should cook the milk-rice (*pāyasa*) previously prepared by means of pouring the oblation (*nirvāpa*) and so forth. Having consecrated the clarified butter (*ājya*) and the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the mantra "vaṃ hrīṃ," and having displayed the *dhenu-mudrā*, one should perform the rites up to the portioning of the butter as prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. Then, standing silently, one should place three fuel-sticks (*samidh*) into the fire on the left and right sides.

Having meditated upon the *riḍā* and *piṅgalā* within the *suṣumnā*, and having offered oblations into the two eyes for Agni and Soma; having offered in the center for Agni and for the principal deities, and having offered in the northeast for Sviṣṭakṛt; having offered one oblation of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*) for each of the previously mentioned forms beginning with the seven tongues using their respective mantras; having offered for the mortals, the ancestors, the gandharvas, the nāgas, and the yakṣas; and having taken four portions in the *juhū* ladle, [one should pray]: "O Vaiśvānara, Jātavedas! Bring [the gods] here, O red-eyed one; accomplish all rites."

Having offered oblations with "Sādhaya svāhā" and "Vauṣaṭ," one should then perform the sacrifice with the Gaṇeśa mantra. Then, having performed the previously mentioned *sarva-nyāsa*s and performed the worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha-pūjā*) in the fire, one should invoke the Goddess, display the *āvāhanādi* mudrās, perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and worship her with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*). Having offered one hundred and eleven oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the root mantra, and having offered sacrificial wood (*samidh*), clarified butter, and *caru* to the nine planets and the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) with their respective mantras, [one should offer] milk-rice (*pāyasa*), sesame, fruits, *āśa*, flowers, mustard seeds, betel nuts, and sugarcane.
Daṇḍa, dates, plantain fruit, parched grain, dūrvā grass, kuśa grass, barley, bilva fruit, pomegranate, red sandalwood, guggulu, jaggery, and bilva.

Having offered oblations for each verse with *dāḍima* flowers, lotuses, jasmine, *vakula*, and *pāṭalī* flowers, or with substances such as sesame-mixed milk-rice (*pāyasa*), along with the *kavaca*, *argala*, *kīlaka*, and *rahasya* sections, one should offer those aforementioned substances or sesame-mixed milk-rice at one-tenth the number of recitations of the *Saptaśatī* mantra performed for each verse. Furthermore, one should offer milk-rice mixed with clarified butter (*ghṛta*) for each verse, according to the injunction: "One should offer milk-rice together with clarified butter. At the conclusion of each chapter, at the place where the word *uvāca* (said) occurs, there is an offering of leaves, flowers, and fruits.

Alternatively, one may perform the recitation with the *Savarṇava* mantra ending with "namo davvyai," followed by a *homa* consisting of a tenth part [of that recitation]. Having thus performed the *pradāna-homa*, one should offer clarified butter and milk-rice (*pāyasa*) with the ladle (*sruva*), using the [deity's] names.

Just as everywhere: *kādabavaiṃ svāhā*—to Ulkā, svāhā; to Karāśī, svāhā; to Raktākṣī, svāhā; to Śvetakaubharī, svāhā; to Haritā, svāhā; to Yakṣiṇī, svāhā; to Kaṅkālī, svāhā; to Yakṣiṇī, svāhā; to Kaṅkālī, svāhā; to Suraśreṣṭhā, svāhā; to Sarparājñī, svāhā; to Brahmi, svāhā; to Māheśvarī, svāhā; to Kaumārī, svāhā; to Vaiṣṇavī, svāhā; to Vārāhī, svāhā; to Aindrī, svāhā; to Hiraṇyā, svāhā; to Vaiṣṇavī, svāhā; to Vārāhī, svāhā; to Aindrī, svāhā; to Nārasiṃhī, svāhā; to Yāmuṇḍā, svāhā; to Dhātṛ, svāhā.

To Vidhātṛ; to Śaṅkhanidhi; to Airāvatī; to Nārasiṃhī; to Cūmuṇḍā; to Dhātṛ; to Vidhātṛ; to Śaṅkhanidhi; to Padmanidhi; to Dvāraśrī; to Vāstupuṛuṣa; to Airāvata; to Puṇḍarīka; to Vāmana; to Kumuda; to Añjana; to Puṣpadanta; to Sārvabhauma; to Supratīka; to Dāmana; to Guggula; to Kuraṇṭaka; to Puṇḍarīka; to Ṛgveda; to Yajurveda; to Sāmaveda.

To Adarvaṇavedāya; with the names of the nine planets and the guardians of the directions: to Asitāṅgabhairava, Rurubhairava, Caṇḍabhairava, Krodhabhairava, Unmattabhairava, Kapālabhairava, Bīṣaṇabhairava, and Saṃhārabhairava. Then, having offered oblations to the previously mentioned deities of the seats (pīṭhas), such as Dhārāśakti and others, and to the deities of the enclosures (āvaraṇadevatās), and having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, [one offers] to Dīṃ Brāhmī, Maheśvarī, Vaiṣṇavī—*vauṣaṭ*.

Having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation with the mantra: "To Nārasiṃhī, to Aiṃdrī, to Cāmuṇḍā, to Sviṣṭakṛt, Svāhā! one should offer clarified butter (*ājya*). Then, having offered oblations with: "Oṃ hrīṃ, to Nandajā, Vicce! Oṃ hrīṃ, to Raktadaṃtikā, Vicce! Oṃ hrīṃ, to Śākambharī, Vicce! Oṃ hrīṃ, to Durgā, Vicce! Oṃ hrīṃ, to Bhīmā, Vicce! Oṃ hrīṃ, to Brāmarī, Vicce! Oṃ hrīṃ, to Prajāpati, Svāhā!", and at the conclusion of the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścitta-homa*), [one should offer] black gram (*māṣa*) to the guardians of the quarters (*dikpāla*), the nine planets (*navagraha*), Vināyaka, the local deities (*kṣetrapāla*), and others.

Having offered oblations of cooked rice (*bhakta-bali*), one should offer the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the three verses beginning with "The ocean with its waves" (*samudra ūrmiḥ*), ending with "Punastvādityāḥ," "Pūrṇā darvī," "Saptate," and "Dāmante," as well as with the root mantra. One should then dedicate the offering with the formula: "This salutation (*namaḥ*) be to Agni Vaiśvānara, to the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas, to Śatakratu, to Agni Saptavān, to the Waters, and to Mahālakṣmī. Then, having offered the *vasordhārā* and consumed the remnants of the oblations (*saṃsrava*), one should perform the remainder of the ritual, beginning with the release of the *praṇītā* water.

Having completed [the rite] with the root mantra, having offered libations with milk or water amounting to one-tenth of the number of oblations (*homa*), one should perform the purification (*mārjana*) with one-tenth of that amount.

Thereafter, having completed the ritual, one should honor the preceptor and others with garments and other gifts. To the preceptor, one should give one hundred [gold coins], or half of that, or half of that again, or eight pairs of cows, along with four parts of gold. To the *brahmā* priest, two *viṣkas* and two cows; to each of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), three *niṣkas* and a pair of cows. This is for a *sahasra-caṇḍī*; for a *śata-caṇḍī*, half of that; for a *navacaṇḍī*, half of that; and for half of a *navacaṇḍī*, half of that again. In case of inability, one should give gold to all of them.

Then one should give gifts to the preceptor and others, or to other reciters. Having honored a Brahmin, one should give a Kapila cow with golden horns, silver hooves, a copper back, a bronze milking vessel, and accompanied by her calf, while honoring her with the mantra: "O Kapila, you are the crown jewel to be worshipped by all beings; since you embody the deities of the sacred fords, therefore grant me peace. One should give it thus. As all the gods reside within all jewels, so may the gods grant me peace through this gift of jewels.
Thus [ends] the Nīlamaṇi [gift].

Now follows the gift of a white horse (śvetāśvadāna). Having honored a Brahmin, one should present a horse equipped with a golden saddle, silver trappings, ivory bits, diamond-studded eyes, copper hooves, a linen cloth, a parasol, a golden forehead-plate, a beautiful girth, weapons, a neck-bell, and garments; having placed it amidst grain and jewels, one should offer it to the Sun (Mārtaṇḍa), who possesses the speed of ten thousand [horses] and is the protector of Kāśī.

Having recited, "Salutations again and again to the Sun, the lamp of the world, the knower of the Vedas," and having said, "I give this white horse to you, O [Name] Śarman, student of the [Name] Śākhā, with the desire for residence in the solar realm or with the desire for the pleasure of the Goddess," and having spoken thus while placing his ear into the hand of the Brahmin, he should recite the mantra.
O great horse, born from the Vedas, together with your son Ucchaiḥśravas; since you have been given by me to this foremost of Brahmins, therefore, O horse, be happy.
"O best of Brahmins, accept this most beautiful horse presented to you by me; it has been offered to you by Vipramanyu."
Then one should give gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). Then [one should pray]: "O Lord Kevala, grant me protection from suffering in this world and the next."

"The umbrella, which resembles the rays of the moon and is as white as snow and sea-foam, was given by me along with you to the brahmin for the sake of your protection. Thus [he spoke regarding] the umbrella.
He said, "O beloved of the gods, drive away the impurity," and thus he gave the chowrie.
The earth, the support of all, was lifted up by the Boar.
May these [deities], who grant the fruit of grain, bestow peace upon us.
Thus [he saw] the earth—
just as the black bed of the ocean-born goddess was empty,
so may my beds be non-empty in birth after birth.
Thus, by providing a bed,
one brings satisfaction to all beings both in this world and in the next;
therefore, grain is given, so grant peace accordingly.
Thus are the seven grains; then one should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the door-reciters and others.
Then, with water from all the jars, [one sprinkles] the patron (*yajamāna*) together with his ministers.
They should consecrate [the deity] with the Puranic mantras beginning with "samudrajyeṣṭhā" and so forth, as well as those beginning with "surāstvām".
Then the sacrificer, having performed the subsequent worship of the nine planets,
having dismissed them and placed [the offerings] in the hand of the preceptor, and having fully worshipped the Goddess, should present the bali offering.
In that regard, a Kṣatriya and others should give one of the following: a ram, a goat, or a buffalo;
a Brāhmaṇa should give a kūṣmāṇḍa gourd, a bilva fruit, and sugarcane. As it is said: "One should worship the Goddess with droṇa flowers, bilva, mango, lotus, jasmine, and campaka."
Having worshipped [the deity], the performer, facing north, should worship the face of the goddess facing east with offerings such as fragrance and so forth, [saying]:
"O sacrificial victim, you have appeared before me in the form of a *bali* through my good fortune."
Then, having reflected upon him, I bow down to the one who possesses form and who possesses the form of Bali.
Caṇḍikā grants satisfaction through offerings; she is the destroyer of the calamities of her devotees.
O Cāmuṇḍā, who exists in the form of a sacrificial offering, salutations to you, O Bala!
"Offerings were created by the Self-born One himself for half of the sacrifice;
therefore, I cause you to be slain for the sake of the sacrifice. Having consecrated [the victim] with this mantra, he says, "The sacrifice is non-violence."
Having cast a flower there with *aiṃ hrīṃ śrīmati*, [one says:
"By the tongue of Caṇḍikā, you are the one who adorns the world of the gods."
Having worshipped the sword with *hrāṃ hrīṃ khaḍga āṃ hrūṃ phaṭ*, or some other weapon, one should strike [the victim] with the mantra: *oṃ kāli kaliyajñeśvari lohadaṇḍāyai namaḥ*.

Having offered the remainder of what was presented to the Goddess with the mantra: *Oṃ hrīṃ āṃ hrīṃ Kauśiki, may you be satiated with blood*, one should offer it to Pūtanā, Carakī, Vidārī, and Pāparākṣasī. Then, having fashioned an enemy out of black-gram flour (*māṣapiṣṭa*) and struck it with a sword, one should give it to Skanda and Viśākha; finally, one should cast the remnants of the offering (*baliśeṣa*) to the Rākṣasas.

The mantra is: *hrīṃ sphura sphara kaṃbha kuṃbha sunu sunu gulu gulu dhanu dhanu māraya māraya vidrāvaya vidrāvaya kaṃpaya kaṃpaya pātaya pātaya kṛntaya kṛntaya pūraya pūraya oṃ hrīṃ oṃ hruṃ phaṭ phaṭ huṃ mardaya mardaya huṃ*.
Then, with what remains, one should offer it outside:

"May these deities accept the offering here—the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Maruts, the two Aśvins, the Rudras, the Suparṇas, the Pannagas, and the Grahas; the Asuras, the Yātudhānas, the Piśācas, the Uragas, and the Rākṣasas."

The ḍākinīs, yakṣas, bhairavas, yoginīs, pūtanas, jackals, jṛmbhakas, siddhas, gandharvas, mālādharas, vidyādharas, and mountain-dwellers; the guardians of the directions, the protectors of the worlds, and whoever are the obstructors and Vināyakas— [all these are summoned].
May Brahmā and the other great ṛṣis, who bring peace to the worlds,
[grant that] there be no obstacle, no sin, and no adversaries;
may they be gentle, satisfied, and bringers of happiness to the bhūtas and pretas.
Then, having bathed and applied the *tilaka*,
one should pray with the four verses beginning with "khaḍginī śūlinī" and the five verses beginning with "namo devyā," using the mantra "O Goddess, protect me with your sword and trident."
Grant me beauty, grant me fame; O Blessed One, grant me fortune.
Grant me sons, grant me wealth, and grant me all my desires.
O slayer of Mahiṣa, O Great Illusion, O Cāmuṇḍā, wearer of a garland of severed heads!
O Goddess, grant me long life, health, and sovereignty; salutations be unto you.
Then:
"O most secret one, O protector of secrets, accept this recitation performed by us;
may accomplishment be ours, O beautiful goddess, through your grace."

Having thus informed the Goddess with the root mantra and with a flower, and having bid farewell to the Goddess from the nose to the heart, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga), saying: "O most auspicious one, remain as the bestower of boons," while reciting the mantra of installation (pratiṣṭhā).
The specific detail for the night of the conclusion is as follows:
on the tenth day, one should dismiss the Goddess.
The mantra is:
"Arise, O Goddess Caṇḍeśī; having accepted this auspicious worship, bring about my welfare along with the eight Śuktis. Having thus raised her up:
"Go, go to the supreme place, your own abode, O Goddess Caṇḍikā!"
O Vajrasrotas, stay here in these waters for their increase;
O Goddess Durgā, Mother of the World, being honored, go to your own abode.
When a year has passed, O Goddess, come again for the sake of my arrival, to this worship which has been prepared by me according to my ability.

Taking up the *vajra* for the sake of protection, one should cause it to flow back to its own supreme place within the water. Then, having worshipped the fire, scattered sacred ashes (*vibhūti*), and dismissed it with "Go, go," one should offer a thousand oblations (*caru*) into the fire and a thousand elsewhere. Having fed as many Brahmins as possible according to one's capacity, and having made the offering while reciting "By whose remembrance [this is done]," one should recite "Whatever has been done through negligence" and declare the rite complete. Having dedicated the work to the Lord of Action (*karmeśvara*), one should eat together with friends.
The plantain tree (kadalī) brings peace;
by whomsoever this tree is planted, they enjoy its fruit in truth. To the east of the measurer stands the Rambhā, which increases happiness.
In the south, it causes distress and brings about grief and torment;
in the west, there is a transition of fortune; in the north, however, it brings auspiciousness.
In the intermediate directions, beginning with the southeast, a middling result is said to occur.
For the sake of pacifying that fault, one should perform the supreme rite of propitiation.
One should wrap the garment that began with an evil birth-sign in a yellow cloth,
as well as the bodice, the neck-thread, and various ornaments.
Having offered [the oblation] at the root of a plantain tree, one should then worship her;
one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of sesame seeds with clarified butter and *dūrvā* grass.
Therefore, the postnatal rite for the mother is desired to be performed with the hymn beginning with "ato devī";
and one should give the ten gifts to the preceptor who maintains a family.
Therefore, the performance for the woman who has recently given birth is desired with the hymn beginning "ato devī";
and one should give the ten gifts to the preceptor who maintains a family.
Having dispelled all misfortunes and being free from stinginess regarding wealth,
she then gave half of that plantain grove to the wise and excellent brahmin.
The mantra for the gift is as follows:
"Born of the lineage of Anuras, endowed with strength and the fruits of your arms,
may my infinite prosperity be attained through this gift of yours."
Having gazed at one's own reflection in a vessel made of bell-metal filled with clarified butter, or in one filled with sesame oil, one should offer it together with silver.
Having respectfully gratified the Brahmins and others with sacrificial fees and other gifts,
when this procedure is thus performed, the pacification of obstacles occurs.
One obtains sons, grandsons, and indeed what is dear; there is no doubt in this matter.
Thus ends the ritual for the pacification of the evil birth of a plantain tree (*kadalī*) in the *Vidhānamālā*.
The illustrious one known as Nārāyaṇa became a learned man among his peers, and his son, named Rāmakṛṣṇa,
was an ocean for all-knowing scholars;
having seen the various compositions of Agastya, he, whose name begins with "Abja" (A), composed this incomparable work.
Bhṛṅga took his parents' feet and brought them to the feet of the Lord of the Raghus, causing them to attain their own refuge.
He is the helmsman of the deep ocean of the Yājñika-Bhaṭṭa system,
and the one who pierces the vital secrets of all other philosophical systems as well.
A refuge has been established here by Kamalākara;
may the virtuous Budharāmakṛṣṇa be pleased with this.

Thus ends the Śāntiratna, composed by Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa— the son of Rāmakṛṣṇa Bhaṭṭa, a Mīmāṃsaka and the grandson of Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa, who was the son of Rāmeśvara Bhaṭṭa Sūri, himself a master of the authoritative scriptures of words and sentences (Padavākya-pramāṇa).
Salutations to the illustrious Mṛtyuñjaya. Now, the propitiatory rite for Ugraratha as spoken by Śaunaka is written here in the Uttarapīṭhikā of the work *Śāntikamalākara*.
Now, O Śaunaka, I shall briefly proclaim the pacification of planetary afflictions for the twice-born, for the sake of removing all misfortunes.
For those with the *ugraratha* yoga, death occurs sixty years after birth;
for those with the *bhīmaratha* yoga, death occurs ten years after that [sixtieth year].
In the seventy-sixth year, there shall be death from passion known as Vijaya;
one meets death within six months, and loss of wealth occurs.
The loss of sons, the loss of wife, and likewise the loss of wealth—
on account of these, a wise person should perform a propitiatory rite (śānti) for the purpose of pacifying those evils.
In the year of one's birth, in the month of one's birth, likewise on the day of one's birth, and under the constellation of one's birth,
the propitiatory rite known as Ugraratha should be performed.
In a temple, on a riverbank, in one's own home, or at an auspicious spot—
in the northwestern direction of the house— one should have an auspicious pavilion constructed.
Having poured out a heap of rice, one should place half that amount of rice grains;
then, having placed half that amount of sesame seeds, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus.
Having written the syllable *hrīṃ* in the center, the wise one should install it upon a *maṅkhu*;
he should fashion the fierce god Mṛtyuñjaya out of gold.
Prajāpati and Yama are indeed the presiding and counter-presiding deities (ādhipratyadhidevate),
as well as the nine planets, the guardians of the directions, the rivers, and those who have attained long life.
One should worship Durgā, Gaṇeśa, Varuṇa, and Viṣṇu;
first, one should choose the preceptor (ācārya), and after that, the officiating priests (ṛtvij).
Having invoked and worshipped the deity with the verse "stuhi śrutaṃ" (RV 8.61.7),
one should then invoke other deities with their respective mantras.
One should perform the peace-offering (śānti-homa) according to the path taught in one's own sūtra,
using sacrificial cakes (caru), clarified butter (ājya), milk-rice (pāyasa), arka wood fuel-sticks, and likewise sesame seeds.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations for oneself, and ten or five for others,
one should afterwards perform the sacrifice to the planets and then carry out the consecration.
With the mantras of the planets, those of the world-protectors, and those from the Vedic and Puranic traditions; with the Āyuḥ-sūktas, the Mṛtyu-sūktas, the Śrī-sūkta, and others as well.
One should perform the consecration with the hymns beginning with "akṣībhyām" and other male (puṃsūkta) hymns;
then, one should present the cloth moistened by the consecration water to the noble-born woman.
One should worship the preceptor with devotion using garments, ornaments, and decorations;
one should offer a sacrificial fee consisting of an image accompanied by a garment and a water-pot.
One should give according to one's wealth, and also give a milch cow;
one should give sacrificial fees to the officiating priests and satisfy the poor and the helpless.
A garment, clarified butter, a viewing [of the recipient], a woolen blanket, a cow, as well as cotton and silk— one should give these ten gifts according to one's ability.
One should give grains for the nine planets according to one's financial means.
One should feed the Brahmins with devotion and satisfy them with sacrificial fees;
one should always remember Harihaya during ritual festivals and in the hereafter as well.
Thus, whoever performs this rite of pacification with faith and devotion shall be liberated from all calamities and live happily for a hundred years.
Endowed with sons, grandsons, and others, he shall obtain all his desires.
Thus ends the *Gṛhaśāntikalpa* as spoken by the venerable Śaunaka.
Now follows the *Gṛhaśāntikalpa* as spoken by Bodhāyana.

O Ugraratha, we shall now explain the ritual for pacification (*śāntividhi*). Beginning from the day of birth, in the sixtieth year for Brāhmaṇas, Rājanyas, and Vaiśyas, on the lunar month and the asterism (*nakṣatra*) of birth, one should prepare a square area the size of a cow-hide smeared with cow-dung. In the south-eastern quarter of that space, having placed a water-pot (*kalaśa*) upon a heap of grain, and having fashioned an image of Death (*mṛtyu-pratimā*) out of two *niṣkas* of gold and established it upon the pot, one should worship it with the sixteen services (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*). [Then recite: "May death depart; immortality is supreme, O Death! (*apaitu mṛtyur amṛtaṃ paraṃ mṛtyo*).

Having recited "manomahām," "mā nastoke," and "tryambaka" one hundred and eight times, and having performed the rites from the drawing of lines for the deity's worship up to the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha), he offers the cooked oblation. Having recited the *puronuvākyā* "mā no mahāntam," he offers it with the *yajyā* "mā nastoke. Having offered each verse of the *ghṛtasūkta*, and having performed the rites from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering up to the gift of a cow, he places the remnants of the oblation upon clumps of *dūrvā* grass to the east of the fire, while [the priest] stands to the west of the fire facing east.

Having sat down, one should perform an ablution with the *Mṛtyusūkta*, the *Āyuṣyasūkta*, and Purāṇic mantras; then, having given the cloth, the image, and the water-pot to the preceptor (*ācārya*), and having given sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) according to one's means, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas—thus said the venerable Bodhāyana.
Thus ends the *Gṛharathaśānti* as taught by Baudhāyana.
Now follows the *Ugraratha-śānti* as taught in the Śaiva Āgamas:
On the beautiful peak of Kailāsa, Guha, having bowed with reverence to the god Śaṅkara who was surrounded by all the deities, questioned him respectfully.
O Lord, the one named Ugraratha is terrifying to all living beings;
he causes the destruction of sons and grandsons, and the ruin of wealth and grain.
"I have heard many times that this is a demon who causes the loss of a kingdom;
who is he? He is not properly known—let him be fully described."
Īśvara said:
O Ugraratha, I shall tell that to you, my virtuous one, with respect.
He is declared to be equal to great death, the destroyer of all living beings;
he has a massive body, large fangs, a terrifying face, and is fearsome.
O son, when he is active, there is the destruction of one's sons, wealth, grain, and so forth.
There would be great suffering for kings and the destruction of their kingdoms;
likewise, there would be a severe drought and great distress among the people.
The destruction of elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as the loss of one's own kingdom—
these misfortunes indeed occur for one of fierce prowess when [the deity] manifests.
Sixty years after the year of his birth, the fierce Ratha is proclaimed;
by his mere manifestation, the transmigrating being incurs fear.
Guha said:
O Śaṅkara, tell me how living beings may be delivered from that [suffering].
Śaṅkara said:
O Guha, I shall tell you the pacification of the formidable chariot;
listen, so that by merely practicing it, the transmigrating soul is liberated from fear.
[He grants] sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, as well as wealth, grain, and so forth;
likewise, the king [obtains] his kingdom, elephants, horses, the increase of the treasury, and the destruction of enemies.
One obtains great devotion and ascends to the feet of Viṣṇu;
therefore, O Six-faced One, peace should be practiced with diligent effort.
Guha said:
"Of what nature is this peace proclaimed by the gods? What is its knowledge, what is its practice, and what is its fruit? Please describe it."
At what time is it taught, and by whom is it established?
O Lord, tell this truly to me who asks.
Īśvara:
This [teaching] is well-known in the Śaiva Āgamas and has been proclaimed by the sages.
O Guha, listen with an attentive mind to how there is peace from the fierce [state].
When the sixtieth year has arrived, a Brāhmaṇa should perform it himself;
so too a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or anyone else.
One should have this pacification performed diligently by Brahmins;
a wise person should perform the pacification rite on the day of one's birth-star (janmarkṣa).
The presiding deity there is proclaimed to be Death itself;
Ugra is said to be the presiding deity of the [subordinate] deities, and Ajaya is the counter-presiding deity.
Whether in a temple of Viṣṇu, in a temple of Śiva, or again on the bank of a river;
or in a cow-pen, in a fire-sanctuary, or even in one's own birth-village.
Accompanied by Brahmins, being pure, one should perform this rite for peace.
Having prepared the sacrificial ground and smeared it with cow dung, one should proceed.
Having adorned [the site] with colored lines and other decorations, and having performed the auspicious day ceremony (puṇyāha) preceded by the Nāndīmukha rite,
one should deposit a load of rice (vrīhi) as well as an equal amount of husked grain (taṇḍula).
Having strewn half of that area with sesame seeds, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus;
having drawn it, one should then place the syllable *hrīṃ* there and subsequently set down the water-pot (*kalaśa*).
Above that, one should make [the vessel] out of gold, silver, or copper,
or else of clay, according to one's means.
Then, having wrapped it with threads and covered it with cloths according to the mantra,
[one should place] a hundred auspicious roots and nine gems.
Ten measures of clay, five sprouts,
the astringent decoctions of five trees, and likewise the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
The five products of the cow, as well as merit, the three metals,
all kinds of grain, and likewise kuśa and dūrvā grass.
One should pour all the waters of sacred fords (tīrtha) into all the jars, as well as those from the Tāpī river, wells, ponds, streams, and springs.
Having diligently approached all sacred bathing places and all waters,
one should first fill the sacrificial grass mats and then fill all the water-pots in their proper sequence.
Having fashioned a golden image endowed with eight palas of weight,
one should make it half of that or even half of that again, according to one's means.
One should also fashion the presiding deity (ādhideva) and the secondary deity (pratyadhideva), corresponding in size to the intended fruit [of the rite],
as well as other images made of clay for that purpose.
One should place these [vessels] upon jars that have been established in their respective positions;
first, one should choose a preceptor who is virtuous and a householder.
One who worships the gods, is well-composed, has mastered the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras,
knows the procedures for rites of pacification, and is an expert in mantras and tantras.
Having adorned [the site] with silk cloths and the like, and with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, and so forth,
one should appoint Brahmā and the other officiating priests (ṛtvij), well-adorned according to one's capacity.
They should worship those images preceded by the recitation of their respective mantras; I shall describe those deities, who grant long life in seven ways.
Then [he worships] the Vatsaradevas, and then the deities of the two solstices.

Then [he taught] the seasons, then the months, then the fortnights, then the days, then the weekdays, then the lunar mansions, then the yogas according to the rules, then the karaṇas, then the zodiac signs, and after that the five Brahmans.
Seven are the Nīlas, nine the Naṣṭavasus, nine the Diśas, ten the Rudras, eleven the Ādityas, and twelve indeed [the Vasus], according to the rule.
One who is self-restrained should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Vighneśa, and Kṣetrapāla; [then] the gods Bhayaṅkara,
Nāsti, Varuṇa, Śatru, Mṛtyuñjaya, and Adhograha in the west.
Then one should fashion a large pitcher provided with four holes.

One should worship each of these individually according to the prescribed ritual with their respective mantras, for one year or more, or for a single year, or as much as possible according to one's capacity and wealth;
then, one should perform the primary recitation (*japa*) with the mantra "paraṃ mṛtyo."
One should worship Chādindeva with the mantra "sthihi śṛtam," and worship Pratyadhiśāṃśa with the mantra "triyaṃbhakam. Then, one should perform the Catirvid-japa and likewise the Dvāra-japa.
Having offered salutations to Bhānu, he performed a circumambulation of Pracaṇḍarāja.
The wise man should perform the ritual with devotion; thereafter, the consecration by Rudra, as well as the Śrīsūkta, the Bhūmisūkta, the Namaka, and the Camaka.
The hymn beginning with "āpohiṣṭhā," the Ābḷiga, and the hymn beginning with "muñcāmi tvā" constitute the collection of sūktas.
The hymn beginning with "yevā hitra" has been proclaimed, as well as the Pāvamānī verses.
The Śaṃvatī, the Svastimatī, and likewise the Āyusūkta.
One should recite these hymns dedicated to Indra, Agni, Yama, Nairṛta, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Kubera, and Īśāna;
then, one should construct a pit (guṇḍa) according to the prescribed rule in the western part of the pavilion.
Having established the sacrificial fire according to the method of one's own sūtra,
and having performed the rites up to the oblation to the mouth (mukhānta) according to the rules, one should then perform the ritual action.
Then one should offer the principal oblations with sacrificial fuel, cooked rice, sesame seeds, and clarified butter;
and with sprouts of dūrvā grass sprinkled with honey and speckled butter (pṛṣadājya).
One should perform one thousand and eight recitations of the previously mentioned principal mantras.
Then the preceptor should perform one hundred and eight oblations; furthermore, one who desires prosperity must certainly perform ten thousand oblations of sesame seeds.
One should perform one thousand and eight, or one hundred and eight,
oblations of ghee according to one's means.
For the other deities, however, one should offer oblations with sesame seeds, rice, and clarified butter,
using their respective names, along with fruits and gold.
One should perform the oblation to the planets according to the prescribed rite for the *grahayajña*;
having offered the oblations for *jaya* and *sviṣṭakṛt*, one should complete the remainder of the *homa*.
The preceptor, together with the Brahmins, should bathe the patron with water purified by mantras contained in a hundred-holed jar;
having performed the purification with auspicious hymns, he should offer the bali-oblation at the four cardinal points.
The sacrificer, having adorned himself, should perform the inspection of the clarified butter (ājyāvekṣaṇa);
thereafter, he should give the five items, beginning with the iron ball (ayaḥpiṇḍa), to the Brāhmaṇas.
Then, having adorned the preceptor with garments, garlands, and ornaments,
one should give a golden image along with its cloth to the preceptor.
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for these [images] is equal in number to their respective proportions;
for all of them, the fee is traditionally held to be one-third of the primary [image].
Then one should perform the tenfold gift (daśadāna), especially the gift of land;
as well as gifts of elephants, horses, chariots, grain, jewels, and lotuses.

One should give gifts of clothing, maidens, and so forth, as well as the installation of a Brahman and the Madhuparka; these should be bestowed upon the Brahmins according to the extent of one's wealth.
Then, on specially distinguished days, one should provide abundant gifts.
Whether one feeds twenty thousand, a thousand, or even a hundred Brahmins,
he who recites this peace-chant attains all his desires.
[He grants] sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, as well as long life and prosperity.
One attains an increase in elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as an abundant increase in the treasury,
and likewise acquires devotion to Viṣṇu and devotion to Śiva.
O Six-faced One, he who performs this difficult rite for the pacification of the chariot,
his enemies perish and he prospers happily through the attainment of wealth.
Thus ends the Ugraratha Śāntikalpa in the dialogue between the Supreme Lord and Ṣaṇmukha within the venerable Śaivāgama.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the pacification of the fierce chariot in the Śaiva Āgama;
this procedure is prescribed here according to the Śaiva Āgamas.
For the sake of the welfare of all the world, this easily accessible sequence is being described.

The method of composition: At the commencement of the sixtieth year from birth, on an auspicious day, under a favorable constellation or one's own birth constellation, the author, having performed an auspicious bath together with his wife and having adorned himself with garments, ornaments, and the like, [should proceed] to a temple, a riverbank, or a sacred place.

In one's own house, in the northeastern quarter, having constructed a pavilion adorned with plantain pillars and the like, decorated with various cloths and a canopy, and embellished with flower garlands; having smeared it with cow-dung and adorned it with colored powders, garlands, and so forth; having entered the pavilion amidst the chanting of auspicious recitations (*svastivācana*) and the sounds of various divine musical instruments; and having had the Brahmins proclaim the "Auspicious Day" (*puṇyāha-vācana*) and performed the *ānanda* rite, one should make the Great Resolve (*mahā-saṃkalpa*).

On this auspicious lunar day, distinguished by such specific qualities as the venerable [name of the deity] and others, for the purpose of removing whatever defects have arisen through my entry into the sixtieth year since birth, and for the sake of attaining all desired goals by warding off all calamities through the grace of the deities to be worshipped hereafter—whether arising from the influence of the zodiacal sign at birth, the asterism of one’s name, the zodiacal sign of one’s name, the birth asterism, the triple-birth asterism, the planets occupying the limbs of the body, or the planets in their transit (gocara)—[I perform this rite].

For the purpose of averting all calamities obtained through the influence of the southern Vedas, the six lunar mansions (*ṣaṇnakṣatra*), the planetary positions, the six-fold divisions (*ṣaḍvarga*) such as the birth ascendant (*janmalagna*), and by virtue of the Mahā-daśā, Antardaśā, Antarāntardaśā, Sūkṣma-daśā, Prāṇa-daśā, and the Kālacakra; and for the sake of attaining the fruits of auspicious positions by means of the removal of the evil calamities that will arise from whichever planets among the nine—beginning with the Sun—are situated in places of misfortune, [I shall perform] this rite... [the spiritual, etc. (ādhyātmikādhi...).
