For the sake of increasing longevity by warding off divine and elemental portents—whether terrestrial, atmospheric, celestial, or great calamities—as well as bad dreams, ill omens, and other extraordinary signs of impending evil and misfortune; for the purpose of destroying the power of others' mantras, yantras, and weapons and causing the enemy's strength to flee; and by virtue of the power of the *mukhala* facing [the enemy], the power of the month, the power of the fortnight, the power of the lunar day, the power of the solar transits (*saṅkrānti*), the power of eclipses and falling meteors, the constant power of the planets, the immediate power of the planets, and the power of the various astrological wheels (*cakras*).

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "And by the power of the manifestation of the various wheels, for the sake of the cessation of all defects, for the sake of attaining mastery over all people, and for the sake of the attainment of prosperity, I shall perform the rite of pacification (*śānti-karma*) of the planets, beginning with the Sun, according to the method taught in the Śaiva Āgamas," [one should proceed].
The officiant and others should perform the selection of the priests (*ṛtvigvaraṇa*):
"O son of a twice-born, choose you as the teacher (*ācārya*), the bestower of fruits, who is known as Śāntāya, Ugra, and Radha, and who is highly skilled in all rites."
In this foremost ratha-śānti rite, I choose you as my preceptor.
Thus is the selection of the teacher;
he, being chosen, should reply, "I am chosen; I shall do so."
When Brahmā, the four-faced Lord of Creatures, along with Śakra and the others,
are well-pleased, may they perform the ritual application according to the prescribed rules.

"In this rite for the pacification of obstacles (*ugra-rādhā-śānti*), in the chanting of mantras, the ritual of worship, and the ritual of fire-offerings (*homa*), I choose you as officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). They, being thus chosen, should reply, "We have been chosen; we shall perform [the rites].

Then the Preceptor (*ācārya*), having prayed to the Earth with the mantra "Syonā pṛthivi" ("O auspicious Earth"), should scatter a heap of grain—measuring one *bhāra*, or five *bhāras*, or as much as is available—with the mantra "Yato kāya" ("From where..."). Having made it square, he should scatter on top of that a heap of rice measuring half of that amount, and on top of that, half of that again.

Having cast a heap of sesame seeds and drawn an eight-petaled lotus upon it, one should place the syllable *hrīṃ* in its center. Then, with the mantra "ā kalaśeṣu," one should place the water-pots (kalaśas) in their respective positions; having encircled them with threads using the mantra "tantuṃ tanvan," and having mixed the hundred medicinal herbs (*śatauṣadhāni*), one should divide them according to the number of pots and place the herbs within them with the mantra "yā oṣadhīḥ. Then, with the mantra "oṣadhayaḥ saṃvadante," one should place the five barks and five sprouts.

Having cast grains—namely barley, wheat, black gram, green gram, priyaṅgu, chickpeas, king-bean, sesame, *kusumbha*, and *śyāmāka*—with the mantra "dhānyam asi"; having cast earth from an elephant's footprint, a horse's footprint, an anthill, a lake, a cow-pen, a royal gate, a crossroads, an *aśvattha* tree, and *tulasī*, with the mantra "uddhṛtāsi"; having cast the bark of the *udumbara*, *vaṭa*, *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, and mango trees, with the mantras "ruvatī" and "bīma"; having cast their sprouts with the mantra "pravo yajñeṣu"; and having placed the nine gems, gold, silver, and fragments of copper, with the mantra "sahi ratnāni" and "hiraṇyarūpa."
The sequence for the ritual placement of the jars (kalaśanyāsa) according to the Śaiva Āgamas is now described:
all the consonants from the *pra*-group [ka-ṭa-pa-ya-śa] are placed in the eastern direction, while those from the *pa*-group [ca-ṭa-ta-va-la-sa] are in the northern direction.
In the center is the principal deity; to its right is the presiding deity (adhidevatā);
and in the region to the north of the principal deity, the counter-presiding deity (pratyadhidevatā) is traditionally taught.
The deity Cirañjīvin should be installed facing all directions for these [deities].
To the east of that, one should arrange twelve [units] in each of the five rows in successive order.
The eight deities beginning with Janma should be placed in the east, ending toward the west; the deity of the southern solstice (Dakṣiṇāyana) should be placed in the south;
and to the south of that should be the deities of the triad of seasons beginning with the rainy season (Varṣā).
To the south, however, are the six Māna deities at Kaṭakamukha.
To the north of Pradhāna reside the deities of the northern solstice;
further to the north of that dwell the deities of the moon, spring, and summer.
Beyond that, however, one should place the deities of the six months at the mouths of the crocodiles;
in the southeast quarter, one should install the deities of the lunar days (tithis).
One should place the two wings in the north-eastern direction, and the days of the week (vāra) behind those wings;
the Vasus behind the days of the week, and the Rudras behind the Vasus.
The wise one should place Tārā to the west of Rudra, the constellations to the west of the Yogas,
and the deities of the Karaṇas to the west of the Yogas.
One should worship Pradhāna in the southwest direction (Nairṛti), as well as the nine Durgās,
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Vighneśa, and the Kṣetrapālas.
One should place Pradhāna and Dhanada in the west;
from the seven eastern deities, one should place those whose conclusion is in the northern direction.
O Pradhāna, you are situated in the wind; O Vāstunī, you are the bringer of fearlessness.
From the seven [deities] in the eastern direction, [worship those] ending in the northern direction.
In the northern direction from the principal [shrine], one should worship the nine grahas along with their presiding deities;
in the north-eastern direction from the principal [shrine], the twelve Ādityas as deities.
The illustrious Mṛtyuñjaya is established in the east, preceded by the twelve Ādityas;
then, in order, the guardians of the eight directions beginning with the East, headed by Indra.
One should place Ākāśa to the east of Indra, Varuṇa to the west, and Mahī in the four corners; one should install these four [deities] there.
One should place a large jar with many small holes in front of all [the deities];
then, one should perform the three sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) on the western side of the pavilion.
To the south, half of the oblation for the planets should have a pit one cubit in measure;
in the middle, half of the oblation for peace is traditionally said to have a pit one cubit in measure.
In the case of ten thousand *tila* oblations in a two-cubit sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), they may be released;
however, if all [the offerings] are performed together in a single location according to the ritual manual (*tantra*), there should be only one sacrificial pit.
One should construct an auspicious altar behind that spot where half of the sacrificer's seat is located;
and one should build a pavilion for the purpose of consecration in the north or the northeast.
Thus, the sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa) has been shown here, having been sealed upon the petals;
[it belongs to] the illustrious Cakravartin Yajñāryadīpaka, the sovereign of the earth.

Having poured the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) with the respective mantras beginning with "apyāyasva," having poured the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) with the respective mantras beginning with the Gāyatrī, having poured water from kuśa grass with the mantra "devasya tvā," having poured sprouts of dūrvā grass with the mantra "kāṇḍāt kāṇḍāt," and having placed a knot of kuśa grass with the mantra "punantu mā devajanāḥ."

Having filled the jars with water while reciting "imaṃ me gaṅge," "ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca," "āpo vā idaṃ," and "yāḥ pravata it"; having placed fruits and flowers while reciting "yāḥ phalinīḥ"; having covered the jars with cloths while reciting "yuvaṃ vastrāṇi"; having adorned the jars with perfumes, unbroken rice, and other offerings; and having performed the purification by heat over the jars while reciting "mūrdhānaṃ divo" and "viṣṇur yoniṃ kalpayatu," he should perform the purification with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and pure water, using their respective mantras, while reciting the hymn beginning with "agniḥ saptiḥ."

Having caused the images to be brought forward with the mantra "O Bṛhaspati, [the image] that resembles [thee]," and having placed those images upon the cloth atop the water-pot (kalaśa), one should perform the installation of life (prāṇapratiṣṭhāpana) with the mantra "anunīte," and then perform the worship consisting of the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra), beginning with the invocation (āvāhana).
He describes the sequence of worship:

one should meditate upon the image of Mṛtyu (Death) installed upon the principal *kalaśa* situated in the center of the syllable *hrīṃ*. Śrī! One should meditate on Yama, whose hand is radiant with a staff, well-established upon a buffalo, causing terror to all—[one should meditate on] Death, the sovereign of the world. [One should meditate on] Death, the sovereign of the world, whose lotus-like hands shine with a noose, a sword, a goad, and a mace. O Gīrvāṇa...

To Gaṇavandyā, Grīṃ, and Mṛtyu, who has a buffalo as his vehicle: "Oṃ bhūḥ, I invoke Mṛtyu; Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I invoke Mṛtyu; Oṃ suvaḥ, I invoke Mṛtyu; Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ, I invoke Mṛtyu. With the mantra "Paraṃ mṛtyo," one should perform the sixteen-fold worship (ṣoḍaśopacāra-pūjā) and the recitation (japa). One should recite the root mantra one thousand and eight times, or one hundred and eight times.

One should meditate upon the presiding deity (adhidevatā) situated upon the jar placed at its southern side as being "Mugra" (the Fierce). With the mantra "O Virūpākṣa, fierce in appearance, seated upon the best of tigers; O Mṛtyu, I invoke the presiding deity Mugra," [one should perform the invocation]. Reciting "Oṃ Bhuvaḥ," and so forth, one should perform the worship and the recitation (*japa*) with the mantra "Stuhi Śrutam. In this manner, one may also worship the deity Yama with the mantra "Imaṃ Yamam. To the north of that, one should meditate upon the image of Mṛtyuñjaya.

O Mṛtyuñjaya, obeisance to you; O Śaṅkara, whose vehicle is the bull! O Phālalocana (the Eyebrow-Eyed One), grant me victory arising from fierce battle. *Bhūḥ*: O Mṛtyuñjaya, I invoke the presiding deity over death. *Oṃ Bhuvaḥ*, etc. The worship and recitation are performed with the mantra "Tryambakaṃ". Thereafter, one should worship the seven long-lived ones, beginning with Atthāma.

First, the worship of the Seven Long-Lived Ones (*saptacirajīvins*): May the long-lived Aśvaddāmā, whose arms are radiant with the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), who sits upon a shining black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājināsana*), and who possesses a brilliant luster, grant me long life. *Oṃ bhūḥ, I invoke Aśvaddāmā,* and so forth.
May Bali, whose abode is the netherworld, who bears a bow and arrows, whose head is marked with the footprint of Viṣṇu, and who is long-lived, be gracious. *Oṃ bhūḥ bali* and so forth.
Vyāsa, the speaker of all dharmas, praised by the best of sages, the long-lived one—may he who wears matted hair grant me long life. *Oṃ bhūḥ Vyāsa*, and so forth.
May Hanumān, the excellent one whose form was praised by Rāma’s feet, who brings about restoration to life, grant me peace from disease. *Oṃ bhūḥ Hanumantaṃ*, and so forth.
May Vibhūṣaṇa, who is devoted to righteousness and dedicated to the worship of Rāma, and may Cirajīvī, who has conquered his senses, grant long life. Oṃ bhūḥ, "Vibhūṣaṇa," and so forth.
May Kṛpa—the ocean of compassion, an ascetic clad in bark garments—being well-pleased in spirit, grant freedom from disease for as long as life lasts. *Oṃ bhūḥ kṛpaṃ*, and so forth.
May the descendant of Bhṛgu, whose lotus-like hand holds a blazing axe, who is adorned with a circle of matted locks, and whose soul is gracious, grant long life. *Oṃ bhūḥ paraśūramam*, and so forth.

The worship and recitation for these [deities] are performed with the mantra "Oṃ namo 'śvatthāmne" and so forth. In another ritual manual (kalpa), it is stated that there are nine long-lived ones; according to that system, Mārkaṇḍeya and Prahlāda are also to be worshipped.
Then, in the eastern portion, one should invoke the deities of the sixty-year cycle— consisting of five groups of twelve, ending toward the east— in the order beginning with the year of one's birth.
The respective meditations:

[I meditate upon] the four-faced one, whose lotus-hands are marked with the [Svastika] and other signs, who holds the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and the *cin-mudrā* in his hands, who stands upon a fully blossomed lotus seat, whose chest-region shines with the brilliant and pure sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), and who bestows the increase of auspiciousness. I bow to this lotus-born Brahmā, the source of manifestation. *Oṃ bhūḥ; I invoke the deity of the syllable *pra-bha-va*, the lotus-born.*

One should meditate upon the Lord of Dharma, the bestower of prosperity, who wears a radiant crown, holds the excellent discus, the Śārṅga bow, and the mace—beautified by these four in his hands—and is seated upon the seat of Ananta. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the omnipresent deity, the Lord of Ramā.

I bow to the Lord of the Mountain, who has matted hair, whose limbs are adorned with serpent ornaments, who possesses three eyes, who wears the moon, whose chest is firm, who is draped in a tiger skin as an upper garment, who is mounted upon the excellent bull, who is known by the name Śukla, who is the lord of the gods to whom the lords of the immortals bow, and who holds a trident in his hand. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity of the Śukla year, the wielder of the trident.

One should constantly meditate upon Gaṇeśa, who has the face of a lordly elephant, who is radiant with a single tusk, who is named the Messenger of Joy, who resides upon a mouse, and who bestows the pacification of obstacles—thus, O firm one, [one should meditate]. *Oṃ bhūḥ*, I invoke Gaṇeśa, the god of the year, the Messenger of Joy.

I bow to the one whose face is marked by the lord of elephants, who possesses four arms, who is adorned with the crescent moon, who is the ocean of the fulfillment of the desires of her devotees, who is the full moon, and who bestows the power of procreation—Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the Śakti, the deity of the year, the source of progeny.

I praise the six-faced one, named Aṅgīrasa, who has a single arm adorned with a spear, wears a crown of the moon, is mounted upon a peacock, and is served by the lords of the immortals. *Oṃ Bhūḥ*, I invoke the six-faced deity Aṅgīrasa, the lord of the waters, and so forth.

I worship the creeper named Śrīmukhā, who has a moon-like face and beautiful eyes, who is mounted upon a cock, who is honored by Guha, and who bestows the increase of prosperity. *Oṃ bhūḥ*, I invoke the deity of the Śrīmukha year, the creeper.

I praise Gaurī, the daughter of the Lord of Mountains, who abides in the form of the year, who possesses the digits of the moon, and who is known as Bhāva—the full moon for the ocean of the curiosity of Śiva. *Oṃ bhūḥ*, I invoke Gaurī, the deity of the year Bhāva, and so forth.

I worship the Great Brahminī, whose pair of feet is saluted by Brahmā and the gods; she who is mounted upon the noble swan, and whose beauty and grace captivate the mind of Śambhu. "Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the Brahminī, the deity of the Yava-saṃvatsara," and so forth.

May Maheśvarī, the deity of the heart, reside eternally within me; may she who is known as Dhātṛ, accompanied by Candrāvataṃsa, always bestow the increase of auspiciousness upon Śambhu. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke Maheśvarī, the deity of the year Dhātu.

I invoke Kaumārī, the bestower of great success in the *miḍa*, who is eternally mounted upon a parrot, who is known by the name Īśvarā, and who by her very nature grants satisfaction to Śaṅkara. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the goddess Kaumārī, the deity of the year, as Īśvara.

I shall constantly meditate with my heart upon the Vaiṣṇavī goddess named Bahudhānyā, who dwells on the left lap of Śaṅkara and incessantly bestows half of her sweetness upon those who bow to her. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the Vaiṣṇavī deity of the Bahudhānya year.

We bow to Vārāhī, who is the full moon within the ocean of joy for Dhūrjaṭi, the nourisher of the increase of fame, and who has assumed her own name as "Pramādhī. Oṃ Bhūḥ Bhūḥ! I invoke Vārāhī, the deity of the Pramādhī year.

We invoke Māheṃdrī, who is known as Vikramā, seated upon a bull, possessing a form worthy of worship, and the constant destroyer of the race of Daityas. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke Cāmuṇḍā, the Viṣṇu-year [deity].

[One should visualize] the one called Erogāhvaya, the one who emits seed, Citrabhānu, who is ever-joyful, mounted upon a horse, with a crown and radiant hands. Oṃ Bhūḥ! O Citrabhānu, deity of the year, I invoke you for freedom from disease. || ||

I bow to Svabhānu, known as Bhrāja, who bestows health and success upon men, mounted upon an elephant, with a shining sword and shield in his hands. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke Bhrāja, the deity of the year Svabhānu.

I constantly meditate upon the one named Paṭara, who is youthful, who moves like the sun, and whose hand shines with a trident within the lotus of the inner heart, O Daughter of the Mountain. Om Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity of the Saṃvatsara year, Paṭara.

I take refuge in the one called Pārthiva, who is mounted upon a bird; I worship the great one who holds the conch and the discus and wears divine yellow garments. *Oṃ bhūḥ*, I invoke the deity Pataṅga, the presiding deity of the Pārthiva year, and so forth.

I invoke the deity of the Vyaya year, who is golden-hued, mounted upon a cuckoo, known by the name Vyaya, possessing matted hair, having three eyes, and resplendent with a trident: Oṃ Bhūḥ, I invoke the deity of the Vyaya Saṃvatsara, Svarṇara.

I bow to the one named Sarvajit, who possesses light and grants desired boons; he has Bhruśuṇḍī in his hand, is mounted upon a tiger, and is three-eyed. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity of the Sarvajit year, Jyotiṣimat.

I always salute the Sun, named Vibhāsa, who is called Sarvadhārin, who is seated upon his chariot with Pāśvin, for the attainment of desired objects. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity of the year, Vibhāsa, the Sustainer of All.
I bow to Kaśyapa, who is seated upon the peak of Mount Meru, named Virodhi, possessing five faces and ten arms. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke Kaśyapa, the deity of the Virodhi year.
I worship Ravi, named Vikṛti, who has three heads and six arms, mounted upon the lord of serpents, and clothed in beautiful yellow garments. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke Ravi, the deity of the Vikṛti year.

I salute the Sun, named Sūrya, who has four faces and eight arms, mounted upon the best of birds, and clothed in blue garments. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity Sūrya, the presiding god of the Kharasaṃvatsara year.
I worship Bhānu, named Nandana, who is beautifully adorned with radiance, who has the lion as his vehicle, five faces, and ten arms.
Oṃ bhūḥ! I invoke the deity of the Nandana year, Bhūnu, and so forth.
I salute the six-faced, twelve-armed Vijaya, who is mounted upon a tiger, clad in a tiger-skin garment, and possesses wings. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity Vijayā, the goddess of victory, from the sky.

I take refuge in my heart in Pūṣan, named Jaya, the bestower of victory upon the lineage of devotees, whose two hands are marked with the conch and the discus. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity Jaya, who is the year, Pūṣan.

I invoke Hiraṇyagarbha, who is mounted upon a noble swan, whose hands are adorned with a lute, who is named Manmatha, and who is the bestower of desired boons. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke Hiraṇyagarbha, the deity of the year, named Manmatha.

For the sake of joy, we take refuge in Marīci, who is known as Durmukha, who dwells within the monkey Manyu, whose mouth is wide open, and who brings fear to the world. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity Marīci, the subduer of Durmukha. ||| [Note: The text provided appears to be a liturgical invocation (āvāhana) for the deity Marīci, identifying him with the wrathful form of Hanuman (Manyu) and the demon Durmukha.]

I take refuge in Āditya, the abode of splendors, known as Hevilambi, who is mounted upon the seven-horsed chariot and is the eye of the worlds. Oṃ Bhūḥ! O Hevilambin, deity of the year, I invoke Āditya.

With my mind, I meditate upon Savitṛ, who is known as Vilambi, holding a bow and arrows in his two arms, and having the excellent sun as his vehicle. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity Savitṛ, the presiding deity of the Vilambi year.
I invoke Arka, whose name is Vikārin, who wields a saw as a weapon, who is mounted upon a cruel tiger, and who possesses a single eye. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity of the year named Vikārin, Arka.

I bow to Bāskara, known as Śārvarī, who fills the quarters and directions with his speech, whose hands shine with the discus, and who rests upon a radiant chariot. *Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity Śārvarī, Bāskara.* I perpetually salute Agni, who is garlanded with flames, free from injury, mounted upon a goat, holding a sacrificial oblation in his hand, two-headed, and known as Plava. *Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity of the Plava year, Agni,* and so forth.
O Jātavedas, I always worship the auspicious deity named Śubhakṛt, who is mounted upon a palanquin and holds a sword and a shield. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the year-deity Śubhakṛt, O Jātavedas. |||

I take refuge in Sahojasa, the creator of splendor for men, the bestower of desired objects, who is mounted upon a palanquin, whose hands are like those of gods, and who possesses beautiful eyes. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke Sahojana, the cause of splendor for those who possess it.

I invoke the Lord Ajirāprabhūmi, whose name is Krodhīkṛta, who is eternally mounted upon Goradhā, and whose lotus-like face is radiant with a trident. "Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity Krodī... and so forth.

I constantly worship Vaiśvānara, known by the name Viśvāvasu, the illustrious one who is mounted upon a man-borne vehicle (Puruṣavāhana) and holds a sword and a shield. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the supreme deity Vaiśvānara, who is like Viśvāvasu. || ||

I salute Parābhava, who is called by that name, whose splendor is equal to the sun, who is mounted upon a lofty horse, and who holds a blazing axe in his hand. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity of the Parābhava year, Naryāpas.

One should invoke Agni Plavaṅga, renowned as Paṅkirādha, who is eternally mounted upon his vehicle, the white horse, and always bearing the Śārṅga bow and arrows: "Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity Plavaṅga, known as Paṅkirādha."
I take refuge in the deity named Kīlaka, who is spreading fire, mounted upon a lofty elephant, with a hand moving a blazing trident.
Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity of the year, Kīlaka, the spreading one.

I bow my head in reverence to Lord Hari in the form of the Fish, known as Saumya, whose hands shine with the conch and discus, and who, through devotion, bestows all desired boons. "Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity of the Saumya year, in the form of the Fish," and so forth.

I bow to the great Tortoise, who bears Mount Mandara, who holds the Kaumodakī club and the Śārṅga bow in his hands, and who is known by the name Sādhāraṇa. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity Sādhāraṇa, the Tortoise.

I bow to the one renowned as Virodhikṛt, who bears the form of a boar, who has taken up a portion of the earth upon his tusks, and who bestows boons and fearlessness. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity Virodhikṛt, Varāha.

I worship Hari, the slayer of Sṛka-sarīsṛpa, the shatterer of the pillar, the bestower of joy upon Prahlāda, the deceiver of Bali, the one who assumed the form of a dwarf (Māyāmaya), and the one called Pramādīca. *Oṃ Bhūḥ*, I invoke Vāmana, the deity of the year, and so forth.

I take refuge in Rāma, the beloved of Sītā, who generates joy for the world, whose name is Ānanda, and who holds the bow and arrows. *Oṃ Bhūḥ*, I invoke the deity of the year Ānanda, O Rāma, and so forth.

One should quickly invoke Bhārgava Rāma, who wields a blazing axe, adorned with a circle of matted locks, and who slays those called Rākṣasas, in the northeast: *Oṃ bhūḥ! I invoke Bhārgava Rāma, the deity of the Rākṣasa year.*
I bow day and night to Balarāma, who is called Nīla, the illuminator of the head of Bhoja, who is clothed in blue garments. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke Balarāma, the deity of men.

I take refuge in my heart upon Kṛṣṇa, named Piṅgala, whose form is radiant like the plumage of a peacock, whose hands shine with fresh butter, and who is dancing. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity Piṅgala Kṛṣṇa.

I take refuge in Kalki, who is mounted upon a donkey, who always holds a bow and arrows, who has made enmity against the line of barbarians (mlecchāvali), and whose name is invoked according to the requirements of the time. "Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity Kalki, the embodiment of the requirements of the time," and so forth.

I worship the one named Siddhārthakṛta, who has the form of a Buddha, naked, a person with a body free from sin, for the purpose of revealing women. "Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the Buddha, the deity who bestows the perfection of success," and so forth.

I meditate upon that Durgā, who is designated as Raudrī for the destruction of calamities, the slayer of Daityas, and intent on consuming blood. "Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke Raudrī, the deity of the year, Durgā," and so forth.

"Let the gift go to the one with a crooked face, one-eyed, and of terrible form, whom I meditate upon for the sake of pacifying misfortune—the one named Durmati (Evil Mind). Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity Durmati, the Yātudhāna," and so forth.

I take refuge in the one who practices the *dundubhi* [drum] sound, who causes terror to all enemies, who possesses a loud roar, who is mounted upon a dog and a boar, and who is naked. *Oṃ bhūḥ*, I invoke the deity Dundubhi Bhairava. Thus it is said.

I take refuge in Hanumān, the son of Vāyu, who vomits blood, who is known by the name Rudhirodgārin, who is intent on leaping across the ocean, who is as formidable as a dark cloud, and whose tail is long. *Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke Hanumān, the deity of the year, who vomits blood,* and so forth.

I take refuge in the goddess Raktākṣī, known as Sarasvatī, who shines with a lute in her radiant lotus-hand and bestows the power of speech. *Oṃ bhūḥ*, I invoke Sarasvatī, the deity of the year, known as Raktākṣī, and so forth.

I worship Dākṣāyaṇī, who is mounted upon a parrot, who holds a trident, and who is fond of the fierce, for the sake of attaining my desired object—[specifically] for the two wrathful ones. *Oṃ bhūḥ*, I invoke Dākṣāyaṇī, the deity of the Krodhana year, and so forth.

Having approached Lakṣmī, the daughter of the Ocean of Milk, who is mounted upon a swan, moon-faced, and holding two lotuses in her hands—[I worship] Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke Lakṣmī, the deity of the Kṣaya year.
For these, worship and recitation are performed with the mantra beginning "Oṃ bhūḥ prabhavā ye" and so forth.

In the southern direction, one should invoke the deities of the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*), the deities of the three seasons beginning with the rainy season (*varṣā*), and the deities of the six months beginning with Cancer (*karkaṭaka*). In the northern direction, one should invoke the deity of the northern solstice (*udagayana*), the deities of the three seasons beginning with the month of Śrāvaṇa, and the deities of the six months beginning with Capricorn (*makara*).

Those various meditations—for the sake of ever-increasing welfare—should always take recourse in the Southern Solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*). [One should meditate on] the Sun seated upon his radiant chariot, surrounded by the moon and the stars. "Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the Southern Solstice," and so forth.

For the constant removal of afflictions, I take refuge in the Northern Solstice (Uttarāyaṇa), which is divine, mounted upon the celestial chariot, and joined by the sun and other planets. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the Northern Solstice.
I bow my head today to those who bestow rain and joy, who are constantly seated upon their seats facing the south. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the season of the rains.
The autumn season shall indeed be the bestower of our desires, seated facing westward and wearing a crystal bracelet. Om Bhūḥ! I invoke the autumn season.
May the auspicious Hemanta season, who rests upon the northern face of our Lord, who possesses a crest and wears the sacred thread, be gracious to us. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the Hemanta season.

I bow my head to the cool season (Śiśira), who stands with his face turned toward the goal, whose eyes are fixed upon the solar disc, and who is intent on the recitation of the five-syllabled mantra: *Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the cool season!*
The Spring season, the bull Mīḍha, seated upon a tiger skin, with hands radiant with a rosary of beads and adorned with the sacred thread (brahmasūtra). Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the Spring season.
I bow my head daily to Grīṣma, who sits facing the east upon a seat honored by sages, his hand radiant with a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu). Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the Grīṣma season.
The deities of the month of Śuci:
We worship the pure one of two heads and four hands, whose vehicle is the lord of serpents, who bestows the desired objects of his devotees during the month of Śuci. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke Śuci.
I bow today with my hair standing on end to Nabhomāsa, who has four faces, eight arms, and the excellent boar as his vehicle, for the removal of sins. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke Nabhomāsa.

I bow to the one known as Nabhasya, who has five faces and ten arms, and who stands upon a preeminent deer, for the sake of attaining my desired goal during the month of Nabhasya. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the month of Nabhasya; I invoke the month. |||
We worship the six-faced, twelve-armed [deity] seated upon a bear, who eternally grants the desires of his devotees, during the month of Īṣa. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the month of Īṣa.

We worship the month of Ūrja, who has three eyes, beautiful matted hair, and a lovely crescent moon as his crest-jewel, and who is seated upon the peak of Mount Kailāsa. *Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the month of Ūrja,* and so forth.
I bow my head every day for the month of Sahas to the god named Sahas, who is mounted upon a bull, holds a trident in his hand, and is served by a multitude of Pramathas.
I meditate with my mind, with constant devotion, upon the Lord who is mounted on a parrot vehicle, his hands radiant with a sword and a shield, throughout the month of Māgha.

With my mind focused on no other, I meditated daily for a month upon Indra—the one whose hand is radiant with the thunderbolt and who has the preeminent bird as his vehicle—for the sake of attaining my desired goal.
O excellent cuckoo, remain here for a month performing penance, with your head adorned by a crown and radiant with the sacred thread.
We worship the month of Madhu, whose hands shine with the conch and discus, whose head is radiant with a crown, and who generates bliss for the entire world.
I bow to the one known as Mādhava, who holds the Śārṅga bow, whose vehicle is Garuḍa, for the sake of attaining my desired goal. || ||

We worship Śukra, who has three heads and six arms, whose space between the arms is radiant with the sacred thread, and who is mounted upon his vehicle, the goat. We worship him for the month of Śukra.
Furthermore, their worship and recitation [are performed] with the mantra "oṃ namaḥ śucimāsāya" and so forth.

One should invoke the deity of the bright fortnight (Śuklapakṣadevatā) on the eastern side of the principal [altar]. Day by day, with the gods beginning with Agni, Indra, and Yama, one should worship and recite the mantra: "Obeisance to the one of white body, who fills the bright fortnight! Om Bhūḥ! I invoke the Moon-god, the deity of the bright fortnight! The worship and recitation may also be performed with the mantras "The Moon is the lord of the gods" (*induḥ devānām*) or "For great fortune" (*mahate saubhagāya*), or with the hymn "Whatever the gods" (*yad devāḥ*).

Salutations to you, O Asita (the Dark One), who nourishes the hosts of gods day after day with a stream of nectar and who indeed brings delight to the ancestors. *Oṃ Bhūḥ*, I invoke the deity of the dark fortnight, Sūrya. With the mantra "kṛṣṇāya dgoṣu ruṇīṣu... āsmṛtadru" or "imaṃ yama," one should perform worship and recitation (*japa*).

One should invoke the lunar-day deities (*tithi-devatā*) in the southern direction, beginning with the visualization of the first lunar day and so forth, along with the fortnight deities (*pakṣa-devatā*). "Come here directly, O Agni, you who carry the oblations of the gods; for the sake of worship in this rite of pacification (*śāntika*), enter this image. "Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke Agni, the deity of the first lunar day (*pratipad*). [Then follows] the worship and recitation (*japa*) with the mantra "āgneyanaya... (RV 1.189.1).

O Tvaṣṭṛ, creator of the three worlds, come here with great compassion; O Four-faced One, do thou take up thy residence within this image. *Oṃ Bhūḥ*, I invoke Brahmā, the deity of the second lunar day (*tithi*). With the mantra "brahmadevānām," perform the worship and the recitation (*japa*).

O Daughter of the Mountain, come to this golden image! I bow to your lotus feet for the attainment of supreme perfection. *Oṃ Bhūḥ!* I invoke Gaurī, the deity of the third lunar day (*tithi*). [Recite] the Ṛgveda mantra: "Gaurī mimāya... and the Yajurveda mantra: "Gaurī mimāya... for the worship and the recitation (*japa*).

O dispeller of the darkness of obstacles, O young sun born from the stainless Pārvatī, accept this worship of the elephant-faced one; O Lord, please take your seat upon the image. *Oṃ bhūḥ*, I invoke the fourth deity, Gaṇeśa. With the mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā," [perform] the worship and the recitation (*japa*).

Having offered oblations to the serpents and having shown reverence to their image, I worship their lotus feet; through this, may all prosperity be attained. *Oṃ bhūḥ*, I invoke the serpents, the deities of the fifth lunar day (*pañcamī-tithi*). "Salutations be to the serpents"—thus is the worship and the recitation (*japa*).

O Six-faced One, at the conclusion of my salutation, I shall perform worship at your two lotus feet. O beloved of the *Ihivallī* creeper, I invoke the six-faced one, the deity of the sixth lunar day (*ṣaṣṭhī-tithi*), into this golden image. [The ritual consists of] the worship and the recitation (of mantras) with the words "Kumāra" and "Mātā yuvati."

O Thousand-rayed One, O Fierce-beamed One, come here with reverence; at the conclusion of my salutation to the Embodiment of the Three Vedas, I perform this again and again. [The deity is] Āditya, the Lord of the seventh lunar day (tithi). The worship and recitation (japa) are performed with the mantra "Ā kṛṣṇena" or "Ā satyena."

O Savyojāta, salutations to you, O Lord of Gaurī, O Lord of the World! Grant me grace, O Śambhu; accept this image, O Sky-dweller! Rudra is the deity of the eighth lunar day (tithi). Thus is the worship and the recitation (japa) for Sadyojāta. ||4||
O three-eyed one, O Maheśvarī, whose tresses are adorned with the crescent moon, come here quickly and bestow your grace upon me.
For the deity of the ninth lunar day, Durgā, there is worship and recitation with the mantra "jātavedase."

"Obeisance, obeisance to the serpent whose head is bowed by the weight of the earth and whose crown bears the footprint of Viṣṇu; may he quickly grant me my desire. This is the mantra for worship and recitation dedicated to the deity of the tenth lunar day (Daśamī), beginning with "Ādiśeṣa, yā iṣapa."

Salutations to Dharma, whose essential nature is known through the Vedas, who takes the form of sacrifices and other rites, and who is the means for attaining abundant supreme welfare. On the lunar day (tithi) sacred to Dharma, the Ekādaśī: "Oṃ, salutations to Dharma"—thus is the worship and the recitation (japa).

O Lord of the three worlds, O Beloved of Lakṣmī, O Mādhava! Having approached Your image with all my heart, O Master, grant me Your grace. On the twelfth lunar day (Dvādaśī), one should perform worship and recitation (japa) of Viṣṇu—the deity of that day—who dwells within Hari and removes all suffering.

O beloved of Rati, whose weapon is the flower, born from the body of Nārāyaṇa! Come quickly to this image; be gracious, O Manmatha! [Salutation to] Kāma, the deity of the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī)—*oṃ namaḥ kāmāya*. Thus is the worship and the recitation (*japa*).

I bow to the King of the Kali Age, who strikes down all dharmas, who promotes all sins, who has five faces and four arms, and who is the source of worldly existence. On the fourteenth lunar day, I invoke Kali, the deity of the Kali Age. "Oṃ, salutations to Kali"—thus is the worship and the recitation.
Salutations to that supreme moon of the mind, who is served by all the gods, whose eyes are like the full moon, who is the beloved son of Lakṣmī, and who is dear to the Ocean of Milk.
I invoke the lunar deity of the full moon day (pūrṇimā-tithi). One should likewise perform the worship and the recitation of mantras.

Salutations again and again to the Lord of the Fathers who dwells in the world of the Pitṛs; having obtained this golden image, may they be forever gracious toward me. I invoke the deities of the New Moon day and the ancestors. "Punarmanaḥ pitaraḥ" is the mantra for worship and recitation.

One should invoke the deities of the weekday in the western quarter of the *pakṣadevatās*. Āditya, Indu, Aṅgāra, Budha, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, and Śani—these are declared to be the deities of the weekdays in their respective order.
Fire, Water, Earth, Viṣṇu, Indra, Indrāṇī, and Prajāpati are the presiding deities (adhidevatās) of the days beginning with Monday, as stated in their respective order.
Śiva, Durgā, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Indra, Indrāṇī, and Prajāpati are declared to be the presiding deities (adhidevatās) of the days of the week, beginning with the Sun, in their respective order.
The sequence of meditation on the presiding deities of the days beginning with Sunday:
"Mounted upon a bull, holding a trident in hand, and surrounded by his attendants—to the deity Śiva, the lord of the day of the Sun, I bow my head today;
I invoke him," and so forth.

I meditate upon that Durgā, the destroyer of demons, who is adorned with eight arms for the sake of dispelling calamities and misfortunes, and who is intent on consuming blood. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity Durgā, who presides over the syllable *idu*.
I invoke the six-faced Lord of Aṅgāraka, who has ten arms blazing with power, who wears the moon upon his crown, and who is mounted upon a peacock.

I invoke Viṣṇu, the lord of the earth, who wears a radiant crown, who holds a sword in his hand, who bears the moon upon his diadem, who is mounted upon a peacock, who is the protector of the home, the six-faced one, and the one who dwells in the heart of the Lord of the Maruts. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity Viṣṇu, the presiding divinity of the Earth.

Four-faced and four-armed, holding a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) and a rosary (akṣasūtra), with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, he is pure; he is considered the presiding deity of Thursday. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity Brahmā, who presides over Thursday.
I take refuge in Indra, the lord of Śukra, who is mounted upon a preeminent elephant and holds the thunderbolt, the goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness with his four hands.
Oṃ bhūḥ! I invoke the deity presiding over Friday, Indra.

I worship Yama, the lord of Saturday, who has a dark-blue body and is formidable; he possesses two arms resplendent with a noose and a staff, and he rides upon a buffalo. Oṃ Bhūḥ! I invoke the deity Yama, the presiding divinity of Saturday.
Following the meditation on the eight Vasus and the eleven Rudras and so forth, one should invoke the eight Vasu deities in that western portion with the mantra: "The eight gods are the Vasus."
The sequence for that meditation:

Holding a rosary, with the chest radiant with the sacred thread (brahmasūtra), I shall always joyfully water the tree of Dhruva’s fame. "Oṃ, obeisance to Dhruva"—this is the mantra for worship and recitation.

I meditate in my heart upon the pure Lord who holds the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) and spoon (*sruva*) in His two hands, who is clothed in a tiger skin, who is devoted to tending the sacred fire, and who delights in the sacrifice. "Oṃ, salutation to the Sacrifice" (*oṃ namo 'dhvarāya*); this is the mantra for worship and recitation.

I meditate upon Soma seated upon a jeweled throne in my heart—He who generates bliss for the world and whose eyes stream with nectar. *Oṃ namassomāya* (Om, salutation to Soma); this is the worship and the recitation.

May all waters, which destroy every evil, which are full of love for the ocean, and which grant auspiciousness when united with the one who has the fish as his vehicle, be propitious. *Oṃ nama udakāya*. This is the mantra for worship and recitation.

May the Wind-god, the purifier of the world, whose lotus feet are ever being honored by the entire host of gods, be forever auspicious to me. "Oṃ, salutations to Anila"—with this mantra, perform worship and recitation.

I meditate upon the one who has ascended [his chariot], the bestower of auspiciousness, accompanied by the goddess Svāhā, his head radiant with a crown, and glowing with fire. *Oṃ namo 'nalāya*—this is the worship and the recitation (*japa*).

One should meditate at dawn upon the one who wears white garments, whose body is anointed with white sandalwood paste, and who is the cause of uprooting all obstacles. "Oṃ, obeisance to Pratyuṣāya"—this is the mantra for worship and recitation.
On the southern side, one should invoke the eleven Rudras with the mantra "Kudrudrāya," [identifying them] as Vasudeva.

Regarding those various meditations: May Vīrabhadra—the destroyer of the lower [deities] by his mere glance, whose lotus-face is wrathful in form, and who holds a trident in his hand—be for my constant happiness. *Oṃ namo vīrabhadrāya* (Om, salutations to Vīrabhadra); this is the mantra for worship and recitation.
I bow down to that Śambhu, from whom Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Giriśāna, the gods, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas were born. "Oṃ namo 'śśaṃbhavāya"—this is for worship and recitation.

May Girīśa, the beloved life-breath of Girijā, who dwells within the jeweled temple shining upon the peak of Kailāsa, grant me joy. *Oṃ namo girīśāya*—this is for the worship and the recitation of mantras.

May Bhairava—the slayer of the three cities, the crusher of the pride of Kṛtānta (Yama), sword in hand, and possessing sharp fangs—be for my joy. *Oṃ namo bhairavāya*. [This is] the worship and the recitation.

I worship Pinākin, who is mounted upon Kṣamā (the Earth), endowed with the Brahmasūtra, accompanied by the four Vedas as his horses, and bearing the Pināka bow. *Oṃ namaḥ pinākine*—thus is the worship and the recitation (*japa*).

One should perform worship and recitation with the mantra: "Oṃ, salutations to Him who lies upon the left thigh of the Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī), who is the source of auspiciousness, the motionless Sthāṇu, who is equal to all, and who is saluted by all the gods. "Om, salutations to this water" (oṃ namostvam apaḥ). Thus ends the worship and recitation.

May the Lord Bharga—who wears the moon as an ornament, who possesses matted locks, who is white like the eye of a woman, and who dwells eternally within the heart—be present, for he is the destroyer of fear. *Oṃ namo bhargāya* (Om, salutations to Bharga) is the mantra for worship and recitation.

"Having become Brahmā, may He create the world; having become Viṣṇu, may He protect it; and having become Rudra at the end, may He withdraw it—may Sadāśiva be my refuge. Oṃ, obeisance to Sadāśiva. Thus is the worship and the recitation.

I take refuge in the enemy of Smara (Śiva), who possesses beautiful feet, who transcends the support of the world, and whose movement is established in the Vedānta. *Oṃ, salutations to the enemy of Smara*—thus is the worship and the recitation (*japa*).

I offer my salutation to Śiva, who is worthy of being sought after, who is the goal to be attained, whose abode is the syllable Om, and who is the repository of auspicious qualities. With the mantra "Oṃ namo 'śivāya," one should perform worship and recitation.

To Hara, whose feet are bowed to by the gods even when struck by venomous serpents, let there be salutation to the one who seizes the hand of the unexpecting (Vinākāṃkita-hastāya). "Oṃ, obeisance to Hara"—with this, let there be worship and recitation.
One should invoke Rudra as the deity in the western part, and the deities of the lunar mansions, yogas, and karaṇas.
Regarding the meditation on the Kṣatriya deities beginning with Kṛttikā and so forth—in the sequence starting with Kṛttikā:

"I bow to Agni, the deity of the Kṛttikās, who is stationed upon a ram-vehicle, holding a *sruc* ladle, a *sruva* spoon, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and the boon-granting gesture (*varada*) in his four hands. I invoke Agni, the deity of the Kṛttikā constellation. The worship and recitation are performed with the mantra: "May Agni protect us... (agnir naḥ pātu).

Prajāpati has four arms, holds a water-pot and a sacred thread, displays the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and is white in color; may these be my deities. I invoke Prajāpati, the deity of the Rohiṇī constellation. "O Prajāpati, may Rohiṇī partake [of this offering]"; thus is the worship and the recitation.

May Soma, white in color and form, possessing two arms and holding a water-pot and the gesture of granting boons, mounted upon his vehicle drawn by ten horses, and having Mṛgaśīrṣa as his asterism, be for my delight! "Soma is the King"—thus is the worship and the recitation.

May Rudra, who is mounted upon a white bull, adorned with white garlands, and four-armed, holding a trident, a sword, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons—may he be gracious to me. I invoke Rudra, the deity of the Ārdrā constellation. "Ārdrayo rudra" is the mantra for worship and recitation.

Aditi, who is of a yellowish-white complexion and holds a *sruk* and *sruva* ladle along with *darbha* grass, bestows auspiciousness when she is invoked under the asterism Punarvasu; her worship and recitation are performed with the mantra "punar no devī."

I reverently salute Bṛhaspati, the deity of the Puṣya constellation, the divine counselor endowed with all ornaments and possessing human-like form. I invoke Bṛhaspati, the deity of the Puṣya asterism. "Bṛhaspati was first..."—with these words, one should perform the worship and the recitation (japa).

The deity of Āśleṣā is yellowish-green, three-eyed, holding a mass of fruits in his two hands, clad in yellow garments, and bearing the boon-granting gesture; may he protect me. "idaṃ sarvebhyaḥ" [is the mantra for] worship and recitation.

"May the Pitṛs, holding funeral cakes (piṇḍas), emaciated, smoke-colored, and pure, grant us well-being—O deities of the Maghā constellation! O Pitṛs, you are summoned! Thus is the worship and the recitation (japa).

I worship the noble deity Phalgunī, the presiding divinity of the constellation Phalgunī, mounted upon a chariot, holding a spear in her hand, and accompanied by Dhūmravarman. I invoke the deity of Pūrvāphalgunī, Sūrya. The mantra for worship and recitation is "gavāṃ vatiḥ."

One should meditate upon Bhagavara, mounted on a chariot, two-armed, bearing the conch and the discus, the deity of Phalgunī, who bestows the desired boons upon his devotees. "I invoke Bhaga, the deity of the Uttarā-phalgunī constellation. The worship and recitation are performed with the mantra beginning, "Śreṣṭho devānām... (The most excellent among the gods...).

I worship the great Savitṛ, whose vehicle is a chariot drawn by seven horses; who is seated upon the lotus-faced one (the Sun), the Lord of Shade, and the deity of the Hasta constellation. "May the divine Savitṛ come for our life"—this is the mantra for worship and recitation.

I worship Tvaṣṭṛ, who has ascended his chariot, the deity of the constellation Citrā, wearing a crown and holding a conch and a discus in his hands. "Tvaṣṭṛ approaches the constellation"—thus is the worship.
I bow to Vāyu, mounted upon his excellent deer, the deity of the Svātī constellation, who holds a shield and a sword and possesses a pair of elephants. This is the worship of the constellation Vāyu.

May Indra and Agni, the bestowers of auspiciousness, both of whom are the presiding deities of Viśākhā, be present. I bow to those mounted upon a single chariot, whose lotus-hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. O presiding deities of the Viśākhā constellation, Indra and Agni, I invoke you. "dura masmacchatravah" is the mantra for worship.

I worship Mitra, the Lord of Manu’s lineage, seated upon the lotus throne, the deity of blood-red hue holding a trident and a goad in his two arms. "May we prosper through our offerings"—thus is the worship.

I take refuge in Indra, the Lord of Jyeṣṭhā, who is mounted upon an excellent elephant, holding a thunderbolt, a noose, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness with his four hands. Thus is the worship of Indra as Jyeṣṭhā.

I worship the deity presiding over the Mūla [constellation], who has a formidable face, is black, rides upon a man, has hair standing on end, and possesses deformed eyes. "Mūlam prajām" is the mantra for the worship.

May the deities of Āṣāḍhā always be present, bestowing auspiciousness; may the rivers flowing to the ocean purify all embodied beings. I invoke the waters, the deities of the Pūrvāṣāḍhā constellation. The worship is performed with the mantra beginning "yā divyāḥ."

I worship all the gods, the deities of the Aṣāḍhā constellation—Śrī, Puṣṭi, Kīrti, Dhī, and Dhātrī—for the removal of all sins. I invoke the Viśvedevas, the deities of the Uttarāṣāḍhā constellation. "Tanno Viśve" is the mantra for their worship.

May the Nirguṇa Brahman, which eternally bestows knowledge and sovereignty, be present before me—He who is superior to Abhijit, the Lord of the hair (Keśin), and the refuge established by the Vedānta. I invoke the deity of the Abhijit constellation, the very Brahman. "In whom is Brahman"—with these words, the worship is performed.

I meditate upon Viṣṇu, whose form is peaceful, who laughs with fourfold laughter, who is the beloved of the Śroṇā constellation, whose eyes are like lotus petals, and whose vehicle is Garuḍa. I invoke Viṣṇu, the deity of the Śravaṇā constellation. This is the worship of the one who hears.

I bow to the Vasu deities, who are seated upon excellent chariots, whose hands are marked with the conch and discus, and whose heads are adorned with crowns. I invoke the Vasus, the deities of the Dhaniṣṭhā constellation. "The eight gods are the Vasus"—thus is the worship performed.

I bow to Varuṇa, who is bent low, the bearer of the water-jar, holding a noose in his hand, the deity of the Śatabhiṣaj constellation, and the one saluted by the gods. I invoke Varuṇa, the deity of the Śatabhiṣaj constellation. The worship is performed with the mantra: "kṣatrasya rājā."

With my head, I salute the younger brother of Śiva, the one-footed dispeller of darkness; for the joy of Proṣṭhapadā, I bow to the peaceful one who is honored by all the gods. O deity of the constellation Pūrvābhādrapadā, I invoke Ekapāda. "O Ekapād, you have come hither"—with these words, the worship is performed.

May Ahirbudhnya, the lord of the Proṣṭhapadas, whose hands are marked with the conch and discus, who is radiant and wears a flaming crown, be for my joy. I invoke Mahirbudhnya, the deity of Uttarabhādrapadā. "O Ahirbudhnya!"—thus [is the invocation]. According to the Pājas.

I bow to Pūṣan, the lord of Revatī, who arises with two feet, whose hand is radiant with the granting of boons, and who is seated upon a jeweled lion-throne. I invoke Pūṣan, the deity of the Revatī constellation. Pūṣan follows after Revatī; this is the worship.

The two Aśvins are the deities; we praise those two who are white in color, four-armed, holding full jars of nectar in their hands, and having horses as their vehicles. I invoke the two Aśvins belonging to the Aśvinī constellation. Recite the verse beginning with "daśaśvinā" and perform the *japa*.

I worship Yama, the deity of the lunar mansion Bharaṇī, who has two arms blazing with a noose and a staff, who rides upon a buffalo, and whose dark-blue body is formidable. I invoke Yama, the deity of the Bharaṇī nakṣatra. "Tadyathorāja" is the mantra for worship and recitation.

I bow my head in salutation to Viṣkambha, who originates from the lineage of Viṣṇu, beginning with Yoga and Devatā; he stands facing east upon a triangle with his hands joined in *añjali*. "Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣkambha"—with these words, perform the worship beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*).

One should constantly meditate upon Prīti, born of the Brahmin lineage, facing east, seated upon a lotus, bearing an auspicious rosary. With "Oṃ namaḥ prītaye," perform the worship beginning with invocation (āvāhana) and so forth.
I pay homage to the Venerable Āyuṣman, who is praised by yogins, facing east, seated within a five-cornered [mandala], and born of the Atri lineage. *Oṃ namo āyuṣmate*—thus is the worship.

I bow to Saubhāgya, who rests upon the four corners of the head, born of the Kauṇḍinya lineage, facing east, and supreme for those engaged in recitation. Oṃ, salutations to Saubhāgya; here begins the worship.

Facing east, residing in a five-cornered [mandala], born of the lineage of Śāṇḍilya—O auspicious one, the bringer of auspiciousness, together with my mother, I always take refuge in you. *Oṃ namaḥ śśobhanāya*—thus is the worship.

I bow to the one born of the Vādhūla lineage, seated within a five-cornered [mandala], known by the name Atigaṇḍa, who always performs his recitation facing the east. "Oṃ namaḥ" and "Oṃ namaḥ gaṇḍāya"—this is the worship.
I take refuge in Sukarman, the great yogi facing the south, born of the Kauśika lineage, who recites [mantras] and is honored by the world. *Oṃ, obeisance to Sukarman*—thus is the worship.

May there always be steadfastness in yoga for the donor, who is born of a noble lineage and is intent upon the constant repetition of the Vedas while seated facing the south. *Oṃ namo dhṛtaye*—thus is the worship.
May there be well-being for the one named Gaṇḍa, born of the lineage of Āṇḍilya in this region; he dwells facing south, reciting the *Brahma-pārāyaṇa*. "Oṃ, obeisance to Gaṇḍa"—thus is the worship.

During the rites for prosperity (*vṛddhi*) and the offerings for prosperity, Kauśika, facing south, should meditate upon the Supreme Brahman while seated upon a seat of *bṛsī* grass. "Oṃ, salutations! Salutations to Prosperity!"—with this, the worship is performed.

For the sake of steadfastness, this yoga, facing south, is eternally fixed for me; holding a rosary in his hand and reciting the Gāyatrī with devotion, [he worships] with "Oṃ, obeisance to Dhruva"—this is the worship.
I bow with my head to Vyāghāta, born of the lineage of Vyāsa, who is seated facing west and resembles the rising sun. *Oṃ, obeisance to Vyāghāta*—this is the worship.

I salute Harṣaṇa, the one who gladdens, whose face is turned toward every direction, who possesses beautiful fangs, who constantly recites the *Dedam*, and who is born of the lineage of Kaśyapa. Oṃ, salutation to Harṣaṇa—thus is the worship.

Facing westward, O descendant of the lineage of Brahmā, may you grant me success, success! Seated upon a grass mat, intent on the recitation of the Vedānta, [one performs] worship with the mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to the True Faith."
I remember Vyatīpāta, born in the lineage of Vītahavya, who taught the Vedas day and night to his disciples while facing westward. *Oṃ namaḥ vyatīpātāya*—this is the mantra for worship.

"May this yoga of mine be most excellent; may you always be the bestower of boons upon me. Facing westward with palms joined in reverence, born of the lineage of the Sāmaveda—Om, salutations to the Most Excellent One. Thus is the worship.

Facing north, belonging to the Brahman lineage, the Yoga named Parigha, seated upon the peak of Mount Kailāsa and chanting the Sāman hymns, [is present] for your delight. "Oṃ, salutations to the Most Excellent One"—thus is the worship.
May Śiva be for my welfare—he who is intent on the worship of Śiva, born of the lineage of Niṣṇu, and devoted to the teaching of the Ṛgveda. *Oṃ namaḥ varadhāya*—thus is the worship.

May he who was born in the Kaṇḍu lineage, who constantly recited the Yajus formulas facing north for his own disciples, be the bestower of success upon success. *Oṃ namaḥ namassidhāya*—thus is the worship.

The yoga for the removal of sorrows should have the name of the person to be accomplished as its designation; facing north and recollecting the great Atharvan mantra, one should offer oblations with the formula: "Oṃ, obeisance to the one to be accomplished."

May he who is born of the lineage of Vasiṣṭha become auspicious and endowed with auspiciousness; facing north and reciting the auspicious five-syllabled Śaiva mantra, "Oṃ namaḥ śivāya," [this is] the worship.
May the great yogi named Śukla, born of the Kauśika lineage, who faces north himself yet gazes inward, be for our joy. *Oṃ, salutations to Śukla*—thus is the worship.

The Brāhma [deity], born of the Brahmin lineage, great, standing with face upward, having fixed his desire upon the Brahmins—may he, shining, grant us happiness. *Oṃ namo brāhmāya* (Salutation to Brāhma). This is the worship.

Salutation to the one who bestows boons upon the virtuous, born of the Vādhūla lineage, whose intellect is ever alert, and whose vision is directed toward the supreme; *Oṃ nama aiṃ drāya*—thus is the worship.

May that which is named Vaidhṛti, seen above the *gosāpa*, be auspicious for me. May he, born of the Kauṇḍinya lineage, remember Brahmā with his mind day by day. "Oṃ, obeisance to Vaidhṛti"—thus is the worship and the recitation (*japa*).
Now, for the meditation on the deities of the Karaṇas and so forth:

Sadyojāta, known as Bava, who has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel and is served by hosts of ascetics—to that Karaṇa I bow. "Oṃ, salutation to Bava"—thus [performs] the invocation and other rites of worship.

I bow to Bālavākhyāna Vāmadeva, the instrument; I bow to him whose face is radiant with three eyes, who bestows the increase of water. *Oṃ namaḥ bālavāya*, thus [is performed] the worship and the recitation (*japa*).

I bow to the Non-Terrible One (Aghora), the essence of the Kaula teachings, who wears a garment of skin, who is pure, the bestower of liberation, and established in the Vedanta. "Oṃ, salutation to the Kaula-Vāyu"—thus is the worship and the recitation.

I bow to the Tatpuruṣa named Taitula, whose head is illuminated by the Gaṅgā, who is praised by all the gods, and who bestows the increase of sons and other blessings. *Oṃ namas taitulāya*—this is for worship and recitation.

I perpetually bow my head to the Lord named Gaurīśa, who is eternally seated upon his left side and resplendent with the daughter of Mount Hemādri. *Oṃ namaḥ gaurajāya*—thus [is performed] worship and recitation.

I bow my head to that auspicious one in the form of a merchant, whose perimeter is surrounded by his attendants (pramathas) and whose fingertips shine with tridents. "Oṃ, salutations to the merchant"—with these words, perform the worship and other rites.
I pay homage to Virūpākṣa, who is known by the name Śakuni; he bestows health upon those who bow to him and is adorned with a circle of matted locks. "Oṃ, obeisance to Śakuni"—thus is the worship.

May the Lord of Pārvatī, whose neck is radiant with a garland of Rudrākṣa beads and who possesses an auspicious countenance, grant great prosperity to the one known as Bhadra. "Oṃ namo bhadrāya" is the mantra for worship and recitation.

Salutations again and again to Śambhu, who is known as Catuṣpāt, the blue-throated one, whose pair of lotus feet are praised by the immortals. "Oṃ, salutations to the four-footed one"—thus is the worship.

One should meditate upon the Lord of Umā, who is clothed in elephant-hide, known as Nāgavākya, and seated upon a lofty bull, for the sake of attaining all perfections. *Oṃ namaḥ nāgavāyāya*—this is the mantra for worship.

I shall offer perpetual salutation to the trident-bearer named Kiṃstughna, whose body is smeared with ashes and who has made his abode in the Vedānta. "Oṃ, obeisance to Kiṃstughna"—thus is the worship.
One should worship the nine Durgās in the northwestern direction (nirṛti-dig-bhāga) of the principal deity, beginning with the invocation: "Oṃ, obeisance to the daughter of Śiva! [and so forth].

I bow to the illustrious Śailaputrī, who is mounted upon a bull, who holds a trident, and who has the crescent moon as her crest-jewel, for the sake of attaining one's desires. Oṃ, obeisance to the daughter of Śiva! [Thus, perform the invocation and other rites.]
Holding in her lotus-like hands a rosary and a sacred circle, may the Goddess, the unsurpassed Brahmachāriṇī, be gracious to me. *Oṃ namo brahmacāriṇyai*. Thus is the worship.
Mounted upon a preeminent vehicle, accompanied by Caṇḍaropā and Arbhaṭī, may she who is renowned as Caṇḍakhaṇḍā extend her grace to me. "Oṃ, obeisance to Caṇḍakhaṇḍā"—thus is the worship.

Always seated upon a lotus-throne, with her two hands adorned with lotuses, may the illustrious goddess, the mother of Skanda, who bestows auspiciousness forever, grant us blessings. *Oṃ, salutations to Skandamātṛ*—thus is the worship.

May the auspicious Kūṣmāṇḍās—who hold in their lotus-like hands a jar filled with wine and one drenched in blood—grant me well-being. "Oṃ, obeisance to Kūṣmāṇḍā": thus is the worship and the recitation.

May Kātyāyanī, who possesses hands as radiant as the moon and a tiger as her excellent vehicle, and who is the slayer of Dānavas and Daityas, bestow auspiciousness. "Obeisance to Kātyāyanī"—thus is the worship.

The goddess Kālarātri, whose form is terrifying, whose body resembles a dark cloud, and who laughs with fierce, loud laughter—may she grant auspiciousness. *Oṃ, obeisance to Kālarātri*: thus is the worship.
Mounted upon a white elephant, wearing white garments, and pure, may Mahāgaurī, the bestower of joy to Mahādeva, grant auspiciousness. *Oṃ namo mahāgauryai*—thus is the worship.

May she, who is always served by Siddhas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and others, as well as by gods and Asuras, be the bestower of true prosperity and the grantor of spiritual perfections. "Oṃ, obeisance to the Grantor of Perfections"—with this, the worship is performed. One should perform the sixteen-fold ritual service (ṣoḍaśopacāra) with the mantra beginning "Jātavedase."

Then, to the west of the area primarily occupied by the meditations and other rites for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Gaṇapati, and the others, one should invoke Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Gaṇapati, Kṣetrapāla, Bhayaṃkara, Vāstupuruṣa, and the deities of the zodiac signs.

One should meditate upon [Brahmā] seated in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), four-faced, with two or four hands, radiant with the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*). After that, there is the repetition of the mantra "brahmā devānām" and so forth, beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*).

For the attainment of all desired objects, one should meditate upon Hari in the heart—mounted upon his vehicle Garuḍa, bearing the conch and the discus, and clad in yellow garments. The worship is performed with the mantra "Viṣṇornukaṃ".

I meditate upon Śiva, the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain, who has three eyes, matted hair, holds a shield and a garment in his hand, carries a trident, and is mounted upon a bull. The worship and recitation are performed with the mantra "Kadrudrāya... [RV 1.114.1].

I bow my head in salutation to the one with a single tusk, the elephant-faced one, the trunked one, the lover of sweetmeats (modaka), the one with ears like winnowing baskets, who dwells upon the mouse. The worship [is performed] with the mantra "gaṇānāṃ tvā."
I bow to Kṣetrapāla, who is mounted upon a lofty bull and has eyes as large as lotus petals, for the pacification of all misfortunes. The worship is performed with the mantra "kṣetrasya patiḥ".

I praise here Him who is the destroyer of the multitude of fears, the bestower of fearlessness, and the constant giver of happiness; [He] from whom [the mantra] "yata indra" [proceeds]. This is the worship.
I bow to Vāstupuruṣa, who purifies the earth while holding the measuring-staff and lotus in his hands,
and who lies upon an auspicious bed.
The worship of Vāstoṣpati: Now, the meditation and other rites for the deities of the zodiac signs.

I meditate upon the Ram in my heart—one possessing sharp horns, resplendent with a long mane and a lofty crest, red-eyed, and with curled feet. "Oṃ, salutation to the Ram. Thus is the worship beginning with the invocation of the vehicle (vāhana).

I meditate in my heart upon the bull, who moves with a shimmering gait, endowed with two sharp horns, and possessing shoulders like the king of mountains. *Oṃ namo vṛṣabhāya*—this is for worship and recitation.

I meditate upon [the couple] who are rich in mutual passion, whose forms are identical to one another, and whose lotus-hands are joined together at the heart. *Oṃ namo miḍunāya*. This is the worship and the recitation (*japa*).

I bow in my heart to Karkaṭa, who moves within the waters at the end of the rainy season, who has six legs, red eyes, and whose face is nestled in his belly. "Oṃ, obeisance to Karkaṭa"—thus is the worship performed.
One should visualize a lion in the heart—fierce with a loud roar, terrifying, the crusher of elephant heads, and endowed with a long tail. "Oṃ namaḥ siṃhāya" is the mantra for worship.

I meditate in my heart upon the beloved daughter, whose face is like the full moon, who is emaciated by penance performed for the sake of her husband and who subsists on a mere handful of food. "Oṃ, obeisance to the maiden"—thus is the worship.

We worship that which was fashioned by Brahmā in ancient times for the purpose of weighing, which is called *tulā* (the balance), and which exists in the form of number. *Oṃ, obeisance to the balance.* Thus is the worship.
I meditate upon a scorpion in my heart, resembling a dark blue cloud, smeared with *hālāhala* poison, and with its tail being raised up. *Oṃ namo vṛścikāya*—this is the worship.
I visualize in my heart a bow that is slightly bent at its tip, joined with a firm string, and upon which a fierce arrow-head has been placed. *Oṃ namaḥ dhanuṣe*—thus is the worship.
I meditate upon the lotus in my heart, which sports extensively within the terrible belly of the ocean and is terrifying to aquatic creatures. *Oṃ namo makarāya*—this is the worship.

One should meditate upon the heart a golden pitcher, studded with jewels and filled to the brim with nectar, brought by the son of Vinatā; [the mantra for this] is: *Oṃ namaḥ kumbhāya*. Thus is the worship.

I meditate upon the Fish [incarnation] in my heart, with eyes devoid of blinking, shimmering in the waters of the ocean, for the sake of accomplishing my desired goal. *Oṃ namo mīnāya*—thus is the worship.

I meditate upon the ram in my heart—seven-faced, with five Brahma-vehicles and the like, endowed with sharp horns, resplendent with a long, shaggy crest, red-eyed, and with curled feet. *Oṃ namo meṣāya* (Om, salutation to the Ram); thus is the worship beginning with the vehicle.

I meditate in my heart upon the bull, who appears to be in motion, endowed with two sharp horns, and whose shoulders shine with a prominent hump. "Oṃ, salutations to the Bull"—with this, one performs worship and recitation.

I meditate upon the couple in my heart, rich with mutual passion, each possessing a form identical to the other, their lotus-hands entwined. *Oṃ namo muddunāya*—this is the mantra for worship and recitation.

I meditate upon Karkaṭa, who moves within the waters at the end of the full moon, who has six limbs, red eyes, a face resting upon his belly, and dwells in the heart. *Oṃ, obeisance to Karkaṭa*—thus is the worship.
One should visualize in the heart a lion endowed with a long tail, possessing a fierce, loud laugh, terrifying, and tearing open the head of an elephant. *Oṃ namo karkaṭāya*—thus is the worship.

I meditate in my heart upon the beloved maiden, whose face is like the full moon, who is performing appropriate austerities for the sake of her husband and who observes moderation in food. *Oṃ namo kanyāyai*—thus is the worship.

We worship that which was fashioned by Brahmā in ancient times for the purpose of establishing the measurement of weights, which is called the "Balance" (Tulā), and whose nature is number. *Oṃ, salutations to the Balance!*—thus is the worship.
I meditate upon a scorpion in my heart, resembling a dark blue rain cloud, smeared with *hālāhala* poison, and with its tip of the tail being raised up. *Oṃ namo vṛścikāya*—this is the worship.
I visualize in my heart a bow with its tip slightly bent, joined by a firm binding of the string, and with the tip of a fierce arrow fixed upon it. "Oṃ, salutation to the bow"—thus is the worship.
I meditate upon the lotus in my heart, which sports extensively within the terrible belly of the ocean and is terrifying to aquatic creatures. *Oṃ namo makarāya*—thus is the worship.

One should visualize in the heart a golden pitcher, studded with jewels and filled to the brim with nectar, brought by Vainateya; [the mantra is] "Oṃ, salutation to the pitcher"—this is the seed-syllable.

With eyes devoid of blinking, gazing upon the waters of the ocean, for the sake of accomplishing my desired goal, [I meditate on] the Fish-form within the region of the heart. *Oṃ namo mīnāya*—thus is the worship.
Regarding the invocation of the seven Maruts and the five Brahmās:

in the northwestern direction (vāyavya) of the principal deity, one should invoke the seven Marut deities and the five Brahmā deities with the words, "Invoke [them]! [The mantra: "O Avaha, the best of the Maruts, who moves everywhere, seated upon a fierce Garuḍa—may you always be for my happiness! Om, salutation to Āvaha! Thus is the worship and the recitation (japa).

Causing the destruction of the worlds with contrary winds, the Vivaha wind, situated in the midst of the sky, bestows prosperity upon us. *Oṃ, salutations to Vivaha*—thus is the worship and the recitation.

I bow my head in salutation to Pravaha, the best of forests, who has caused the mountain to flee away like a messenger with a fierce gait. *Oṃ namo pravahāya*—this is the mantra for worship and recitation.
"Constantly tossing up the oceans, uprooting mountains, and agitating the world, he is served by me with the thought: 'Oṃ, obeisance to the One who tosses up (Udvaha). This is the worship.
May the breezes that produce joy for the world, which carry fragrances, which are gentle, and which waft cool droplets of water, bring me happiness. "Oṃ, obeisance to the Breeze"—thus is the worship.

Pervading the world in the form of inhalation, exhalation, and so forth, and sustaining all living beings, may the Wind, who is distinct from the vital breaths, be served by the multitudes of creatures. "Oṃ, obeisance to Parivāha"—thus is the prayer.
I eternally take refuge in the foremost of the Maruts, named Pravaha, who flows against the current and causes the three worlds to revolve. "Oṃ, obeisance to Pravaha"—thus is the worship.

With the mantra *mārutam asi*, one performs the worship of all the Maruts with all ritual services (*upacāra*) and the recitation (*japa*). With the five mantras beginning with *sadyojāta*, one performs the worship of the five Brahmas. For instance: "I salute Sadyojāta, who has three eyes and four faces, whose hands hold a rosary, the gesture of granting boons (*vara*), and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and who is as white as a kunda flower, the moon, or a conch shell. One should perform the rites beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) with the mantra *sadyojātaṃ prapadyāmi*.

I worship Vāmadeva, who holds a rosary, the gesture of fearlessness, and a battle-axe in his hands; he has three eyes, the luster of a jasmine flower, and four faces. Salutation to Vāmadeva, to Jyeṣṭha, and to the one whose vehicle is the goat (Aja). [The remaining mantras beginning with "vāhanādi" follow.]

Holding an axe, a hook, a noose, a rosary, a drum, and a skull-cup; three-eyed, four-faced, blue-bodied Aghora—may he protect me. Having invoked him with the mantra "Aghorebhyo 'tha Ghorebhyaḥ... [and so forth].

I worship Tatpuruṣa, who is visualized as having the color of lightning-gold, three eyes, and four faces, with hands holding the Vidyāvara, the *kūṭāra*, and other implements. "We know Tatpuruṣa..."—with these words, one performs the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the subsequent rites.

May Īśāna, who possesses a hammer, noose, goad, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a Veda, a drum (*ḍhakkā*), an eye, and a trident, and who is white in luster and five-faced, protect us always. [The ritual from] the invocation (*āvāhana*) onwards is performed with the mantra "Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām" (Īśāna is the Lord of all sciences).

Pervading the world in the form of inhalation, exhalation, and so forth, and enlivening it, may you be led by the multitudes of living beings as the wind known as Parivaha. "Oṃ, obeisance to Parivaha"—thus is the worship.
I eternally take refuge in this Pravaha, the foremost of the Maruts, who runs counter-current and perpetually whirls the three worlds.
Oṃ, homage to Pravaha; thus is the worship.

With the mantra "Mārutamasī," one performs the worship of all the Maruts with all the ritual services (*upacāra*) and recitation (*japa*). The worship of the Five Brahmans (*pañcabrahma-pūjā*) is performed with the five mantras beginning with Sadyojāta. Thus: "I take refuge in Sadyojāta, who has three eyes and four faces, whose hands hold a rosary, the gesture of granting boons (*vara*), and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), and who is as white as a kunda flower, the moon, or a conch shell"—with this, one performs the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the other rites.

I worship Vāmadeva, who has four faces, three eyes, and hands holding a rosary, the gesture of fearlessness, and a small axe; he is the color of saffron filaments. [The mantra is: *Oṃ namo vāmadevāya*. [Perform] the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites for Jyeṣṭhā.

Holding a battle-axe, a goad, a noose, a rosary, a drum, and a skull-cup; three-eyed, four-faced, non-terrible (Aghora), with a blue body—may he protect me. Having invoked him with the mantra "aghorebhyo'tha ghorebhyaḥ" and so forth...

One should perform the invocation and other rites with the mantra "tatpuruṣāya vidmahe," [visualizing] the protector who has four faces, the color of blazing lightning and gold, and who holds in his hands the Vidyāvara, the battle-axe, and other implements.

May Īśāna, who possesses a hammer, noose, goad, the gesture of fearlessness, a Veda, a drum, an eye, and a trident, and who is white in luster and five-faced, protect us always. [The mantra] "Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām" [is used for] the mounting of the vehicle and so forth.

To the north of the principal deity, one should worship the deities of the nine planets (navagraha) according to the method prescribed for the *grahayajña*. That procedure is now demonstrated: wheat (*godhūma*) and rice (*taṇḍula*)—these are the nine grains.

In the center, upon a circular maṇḍala made of wheat grain, I invoke the Blessed Sun, together with his limbs, weapons, vehicle, power, sons, friends, wife, retinue, tutelary deity, and counter-deity. Likewise, in the southeast, upon a square maṇḍala made of rice, [I invoke] the planet Mars. In the south, upon a triangular maṇḍala made of *aḍhaka* grain, [I invoke] the planet Mars.
In the northeast, upon green gram, is the planet Mercury in a bow-shaped mandala; in the north, upon chickpeas, is the planet Jupiter in a long quadrangular mandala;

in the east, upon flat beans, is the planet Venus in a five-cornered mandala; in the west, upon sesame seeds, is the planet Saturn in a bow-shaped mandala; in the southwest, upon black gram, is the planet Rahu in a winnowing-basket-shaped mandala; and in the northwest, upon lentils, is the planet Ketu in a cross-shaped mandala.

And so forth—in all instances, the phrase "with [his] limbs and weapons," and so on, should be recited; thus, in this *grahayajña* (sacrifice to the planets), their meditations (*dhyāna*) and other details are to be adopted here. "May the Lord of the Day, the Sun—the teacher of the world, wearing a crown, possessing the splendor of a lotus, with two arms, holding a lotus, seated upon a lotus-throne, and drawn by seven horses—be gracious unto us. With the mantra "Ā kṛṣṇena" or "Asatyena," one says "Oṃ Maḥ Ādityāya" for the mounting of the Sun's vehicle and so forth. This is the meditation on the Fire-god who is the presiding deity (*adhidevatā*) of the Sun.

One should meditate upon Agni, who holds a spear, stands upon a goat, possesses a red body, and has three tawny eyebrows, beard, hair, and eyes, with a subtle thread-like form. [The mantra is] "Agniṃ dūtam" (RV 1.12.1). The worship is performed with "Oṃ nama ādityādi-devatāyai agnaye. The presiding deity for Sūrya is Rudra; one should meditate upon Rudra as holding a *pināka* bow, a *khaṭvāṅga* staff, a skull, and a trident, having three eyes, a white-bodied luster, mounted upon a bull, granting boons, gracious, and marked by the moon. [The mantra is] "Kadrudrāya" (RV 1.43.1).
Oṃ, salutation to Āditya, the presiding deity, and to Rudra; [thus] the worship and so forth.

May the god Candra—the wearer of white garments, richly adorned with white ornaments, wielder of the mace, possessing white luster, two-armed, the essence of nectar, the bestower of boons, and crowned—grant me the highest welfare. With the mantra "Āpyāyasva" and "Oṃ namaścandramase," [one performs] the invocation of the vehicle of Candra and so forth. The meditation on the presiding deity of Candra, Revatī, is as follows: "I worship her who assumes a female form, who is white, whose vehicle is the water-monster (makara), and who, adorned with pearls, grants a noose and a jar. [The mantra is: "Somo 'psu."

*Oṃ, salutations to the presiding deities of the Moon and the Waters.* Thus one performs the worship and other rites. The meditation on Gaurī, the presiding deity of the Moon: I meditate upon Gaurī, who holds in her hands a mirror, a rosary, a water-pot, and a lotus; she is golden-hued and worshipped by the immortals. "Gaurī has measured out; Gaurī has measured out. *Oṃ, salutations to Gaurī, the presiding deity of the Moon.* Thus one performs the worship and other rites.

Clad in red garments, with a red body, wearing a crown, four-armed, mounted upon a ram, bearing a mace, the son of the Earth (Māheya) holds a spear and a trident; he is ever-granting boons, peaceful, and has fire as his head. "Oṃ, salutation to Aṅgāraka"—thus [performs] the invocation of the deity and so forth.
