The meditation on the Earth, the presiding deity of Aṅgāraka: I meditate upon the White Goddess, resplendent like the fierce-rayed sun, adorned with a garment of the sky, seated upon the backs of the elephants of the quarters, holding in her hands a lotus, a vessel of medicinal herbs, a vessel of grain, and a vessel of excellent jewels.

"O Earth, be pleasant—*oṃ namo 'ṅgārakāya devatāyai pṛthivyai*. Thus is the worship. The meditation (*dhyāna*) on the deity Skanda, who is the presiding deity (*pratyadhidevatā*) of Aṅgāraka: "I meditate upon the six-faced Kumāra, the son of Mātṛkā, who rides a peacock, wears red garments, holds a banner, a spear, a bell, and a cock, and is adorned with a peacock-feather plume. "*Oṃ namo 'ṅgāraka-pratyadhidevatāyai kumārāya*. Thus is the worship.
Clad in yellow garments, with a golden body, wearing a crown, four-armed, pure-minded, bearing a mace, holding a shield and a sword, he is the moon-like son.

One should worship Mercury (Budha), who is seated upon a lion, bestowing boons, and appearing radiant. [Recite] "Awake! O Agni! or "O Agni, awaken! [And] "Oṃ, salutations to Budha. For the gentle [deity], the vehicle and other attributes [are as follows]: one should meditate on the deity Budha and Viṣṇu. Performing circumambulation starting from the lower right hand, one should worship the white Viṣṇu, who holds in sequence the mace, lotus, conch, and discus. [Recite] "This Viṣṇu strode forth" (*idaṃ viṣṇurvicakrame*) and "Oṃ, salutations to the deity Viṣṇu, the presiding deity of the planet Budha"—this is the procedure for worship.

The meditation on the Supreme Person (Puruṣa), the presiding deity of Mercury: I meditate upon the form of the Supreme Person within my heart, with lotus-hands resplendent with a conch, a parasol, a mace, and a lotus, and possessing a golden complexion. [Recite] "The Thousand-Headed One" (Sahasraśīrṣā). "Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme Person, the presiding deity of the planet Mercury. Thus is the worship.

Clad in yellow garments, with a golden body, wearing a crown, four-armed, the preceptor of the gods, serene, and holding a staff, a water-pot, and likewise a rosary—may he, the bestower of boons, be gracious to me.

*Bṛhaspate ati*—*Oṃ namo bṛhaspataye*—thus [performs] the invocation of Bṛhaspati and so forth. The meditation on Indra, the presiding deity (*adhidevatā*) of Bṛhaspati: "I meditate upon Indra, the lord of the gods, the master of the East, golden-hued, mounted upon a four-tusked elephant, with hands skillfully holding the thunderbolt and the goad. *Indraśreṣṭhāni*, or *Indraṃ vo viśvataḥ*. *Oṃ namo bṛhaspatyadhidevatāyai indrāya*—thus [performs] the worship and so forth. The meditation on Brahmā, the counter-presiding deity (*pratyadhidevatā*) of Bṛhaspati: [as follows].

I bow to the pale-red one who holds a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), a book, a rosary, and a staff; who has matted hair, four faces, sits upon a lotus throne, wears a deer-skin garment, and has a swan standing beside him. Or [one may recite]: "O Brahmā, the desire to know Brahman. The worship is performed with: *Oṃ namo bṛhaspataye pratyadhidevatāyai brahmaṇe*.

May Śukra—clad in white garments, possessing a white body, wearing a crown, four-armed, holding a staff, as well as a rosary, a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), and matted locks, and bestowing boons—be for me. [The mantra for Śukra is: "Oṃ namaḥ śukrāya. [The vehicle and other attributes belong to] Bhārgava. [The meditation on the presiding deity Indrāṇī is as follows: "I meditate upon Śacī, who is golden-hued, holding a cluster of *saṃtāna* flowers in her left hand and displaying the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) with her right; she is the foremost among women. [The mantra for Indrāṇī is: "Indrāṇī māsu nārīṣu."

*Oṃ, salutations to Śukra’s presiding deity, Indrāṇī.* Thus [performs] the worship and so forth. Meditation on Indra, the counter-presiding deity of Śukra: I meditate upon Indra within my heart—mounted upon a white elephant, holding a thunderbolt and a goad in his hands, possessing a thousand eyes, and having a golden luster. *Indraṃ vo viśvatas...* *Oṃ, salutations to Śukra’s counter-presiding deity, Indra.* Thus [performs] the worship and so forth.

The son of the Sun, dark-bodied, wearing a crown, with bow and sword in hand, seated upon a vulture, cruel-natured yet possessing a compassionate form—may the Lord Saroruhi be gracious to us. May Agni be pacified by fires. *Oṃ namaḥ śanaye*. This is the meditation on the presiding deity of Saturn, Prajāpati: holding in his lotus-hands a *sruva* ladle, a book, a large rosary, and a water-pot, with a broad chest shining with a white sacrificial thread.

I meditate upon the Lord of the World, Prajāpati, who has a single face, possesses the luster of a great jewel, shines with the radiance of a lotus, and is accompanied by Sāvitrī. Having bowed to Prajāpati—*oṃ namaśśanaiścarādhidevatāyai*. I worship Yama, who holds a noose in his hand, whose vehicle is a buffalo, who is Time itself, with a formidable countenance, dark-limbed, and terrifying. *yamāya somam*. *oṃ namaśśanaiścara-pratyadhidevatāyai*. [The rites of] worship and so forth are performed for Yama.

May Rāhu—clad in black garments, possessing a black body, wearing a crown, with a formidable face, adorned with a garland of swords, four-armed, holding a shield, mounted upon a blue lion, and granting boons—be present. [Recite] *kayā naścitra-* || *Oṃ, salutations to the planet Rāhu*; this is for the invocation and other rites. The presiding deity of Rāhu is the serpent; the meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows: [One should meditate on] the Lord of Beings (*Bhavāya*), red in color, holding a rosary and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in his two lotus-like hands, possessing three eyes, adorned with serpents, and having limbs like those of a serpent. [Recite] *ayaṃ gauḥ pṛśniḥ*.

Oṃ, salutations to the presiding deity of Rāhu, who is the serpent; [this is for] the worship and so forth. I worship Death (Mṛtyu), the counter-presiding deity of Rāhu—terrible with a gaping mouth, dark-limbed and fearsome, holding a noose and a staff, and possessing serpents, scorpions, and crocodiles as his ornaments. [This is] the supreme hymn to Death. Oṃ, salutations to the counter-presiding deity of Rāhu, who is Death; [this is for] the worship.

May the banner Ketu—smoky-colored, two-armed, the bestower of boons, bearing a mace, seated upon a goat, with a distorted face, his limbs adorned with a crown and armlets, and being peaceful—protect me. "Making the banner... (Rig Veda 10.85.1). *Oṃ*, obeisance to the deity of the banner, Ketu; [perform] the invocation and other rites. The meditation on the presiding deity of the banner, Brahmā: I meditate upon Viriñci, the Lord of Speech, seated upon a white lotus, resembling a lotus in hue, holding a rosary, a water-pot, and displaying the gestures of protection and charity in his hands. [The mantra for] the desire to know Brahman (*brahma-jijñāsā*).

"Oṃ, salutation to the presiding deity of Ketu, Brahmā"—thus [performs] the worship and other rites. The meditation on Citragupta, the counter-presiding deity (pratyadhidevatā) of Ketu: "I worship Citragupta, who has tawny beard and eyes, who is golden-hued, and who holds a leaf in his left hand and a pen in his right. [This is] the *sacitra* mantra. "Oṃ, salutation to Citragupta, the counter-presiding deity of Ketu"—thus [performs] the worship and the recitation (*japa*).
In the northeastern quarter, one should perform the primary worship of the twelve Ādityas and invoke the deities of the twelve Ādityas as well as the deity Mṛtyuñjaya.
That meditation:

"May Dhātṛ be the bestower of auspiciousness, more and more, even for the most abundant; he who is enveloped by a web of rays and is the destroyer of the mass of darkness. *Oṃ namo dhātre*—thus is the worship and the recitation (*japa*).

May Aryaman, who moves among the peaks of Mount Meru and is the kinsman of the lotus-beds, always grant abundant prosperity to me who am bowed before him. *Oṃ, salutations to Aryaman*—thus is the worship.

May Mitra—who is skilled in warding off the night, who has taken refuge on the mountain of Rudra, and who destroys the mass of darkness—be for my great joy. *Oṃ, salutations to Mitra.* Thus is the worship.
Mounted upon his chariot, garlanded with flames, majestic, having become Time itself, and assuming forms at will—Aruṇa is indeed served by me. *Oṃ namo 'ruṇāya*—this is the worship.

May the ray of light that dispels the night, which delights in the forest, which is the pillar for the pavilion of the world, which is praised by the assembly of the lords of sages, and which bestows prosperity, be mine. *Oṃ namo 'śave*—thus is the worship.
May Bhaga, the creator of the fortnights, the seasons, the years, and even the collection of ghaṭikās, grant me good fortune. *Oṃ namo bhagāya*. [Thus] perform the worship.
I bow my head today to Indra, the granter of boons to the mortals, who is enveloped by a thousand rays and who bestows the increase of prosperity. *Oṃ nama indrāya*, etc.—thus is the worship.
I bow to Vivasvat, the creator of the universe, whose splendor pervades all directions, the great lamp within the house of the sky. *Oṃ namo vivasvate*—thus is the worship.
May Pūṣan, who is enveloped by a thousand rays and whose inner nature is entirely peaceful, be for my satisfaction and for the removal of all sins. "Oṃ, salutation to Pūṣan"—thus is the worship.
Scorching the world with his heat and again gladdening it with showers, Parjanya, the producer of joy for the universe, is worshipped by me. "Oṃ, obeisance to Parjanya"—thus is the worship.
May Tvaṣṭṛ, who is served by the most excellent Apsarases, who possesses various forms as the maker of diverse crafts, and who is the maker of light—Oṃ, salutations to Tvaṣṭṛ. Thus is the worship.

I bow with devotion to Viṣṇu, who stands in the center of the sacrificial altar, who is served by the three Vedas, and who is the one to be propitiated through the Gāyatrī mantra. "Oṃ, salutations to Viṣṇu"—thus is the worship.
The worship and recitation [of the mantra] "udyannadya" are for the twelve Ādityas.
Now, the meditation on Mṛtyuñjaya: One should always meditate upon Mṛtyuñjaya, who strikes down Yama and is intent on protecting his devotees,
for the sake of turning back all calamities.
Triyambakaṃ—Oṃ, salutation to Mṛtyuñjaya; thus is the worship.
One should invoke the guardians of the directions in these respective locations surrounding the fire.
That specific meditation:
one should contemplate Indra in the heart, mounted upon a white elephant, holding a vajra in his hand, the sustainer of the city, possessing a thousand eyes, and radiant with a yellow luster.
"Indraṃ vo viśvataḥ"—*Oṃ, salutations to Indra*; thus [is performed] the worship and the recitation.
I take refuge in Agni, whose body is golden, who is mounted upon his goat-drawn chariot, who possesses seven flames, who nourishes the world, and who is served by the goddess Svāhā.
"Agniṃ dūtam"—
"Oṃ, obeisance to Agni"— thus is the worship and the recitation.
I bow down again to Kṛtānta, who is of dark complexion, mounted upon a formidable buffalo, bearing the staff of death, and holding a noose in his hand.
For Yama: "Oṃ, salutation to Yama"—thus [is performed] the worship and the recitation.
We praise Nirṛti, who has taken refuge in a horse,
whose form is dark, who holds a trident in his hand, whose eyes are round, and who is terrifying.
Regarding "yaddeveti": *oṃ namo virūtaye* is for worship and recitation (*japa*).
I bow my head to Varuṇa, who is mounted upon his vehicle, the crocodile, who holds a water-pot and a noose in his hands, and who has a smoky-grey luster.
The worship and recitation are: "imaṃ me varuṇa" and "oṃ namo varuṇāya."
I worship the great smoke-colored wind-god, who is to be served by the Maruts, whose vehicle is the best of antelopes, and who resides within the vital breaths of all living beings.
For Vāyu: *oṃ namo vāyave*. Thus [is performed] the worship and the recitation.
I meditate in my mind upon Kubera, who is seated on the Puṣpaka chariot, surrounded by nine treasures, golden-hued, and red-eyed.
Some [offer] a cow—
*oṃ namaḥ kuberāya*— thus is the worship.
I bow to Śambhu, who has the moon as his crest-jewel, three eyes, a lofty bull for his vehicle,
wears a garment of skin, and possesses a red form.
To that Īśāna: "Oṃ, obeisance to Īśāna"—thus [is performed] worship and recitation.
In some places, on the eastern side of the world-protectors, the invocation of the protectors of the lower worlds and the protectors of the upper worlds is seen.
For instance:

one should meditate upon the Lord of Bhāratī, who sits in the lotus posture (padmāsana), has four faces and four arms, and is radiant with the sacred thread (brahmasūtra); thereafter, one should be intent on the repetition of the [sacred] syllables twice.
Behold that cattle!
Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā, the guardian of the lower world; thus is the worship.
In the eastern part of these, one should invoke the deity of space.
I bow my head eternally to the all-pervading space, which consists solely of sound and is imperishable, for the sake of constant health and pervasion.
Asmairudhrā Mohanā—Oṃ, obeisance to Ākāśa; thus is the worship and the recitation.
To the western side of these, one should invoke the deity Mahī.
I praise again and again this Earth, the support of the entire universe, who took refuge in a mere lotus-stalk, and whom the Lotus-born Lord touched at the beginning of time.
For the goddess Mahī: "Oṃ, salutation to Mahī"—thus is the worship and the recitation.

Having meditated thus: "In the four corners of those [lotuses], I worship the four Varuṇas— mounted upon crocodiles, possessing a pale-grey luster, holding nectar-jars, and with nooses in their hands."
One should invoke the deity Varuṇa with these four [verses]: "imaṃ me varuṇa," "tat tvā yāmi," "tvaṃ no agne," and "sa tvaṃ no agne."
The ritual service and the recitation are performed with those very same mantras.

In front of all [the vessels], one should worship the great pitcher (*bṛhatkalaśa*), which is provided with a cloth and a lid. Here, some say that one should worship Brahmā with the mantra beginning "brahma jñānam" and Varuṇa with the mantra beginning "ā vo rājānam".

Having performed the invocation and other rites for the grains placed within each respective pitcher, one should offer incense, lamps, and food offerings consisting of various kinds of eatables—namely, those to be chewed, swallowed, licked, sucked, drunk, and masticated—along with betel-leaf accompanied by diverse fruits; then, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and other rites, one should perform the offering of mantra-flowers, circumambulation, prostrations, and so forth.
He should cause three Brahmins to perform the recitation of those respective mantras either one thousand and eight times or one hundred and eight times.

Then, for the purpose of reciting the Veda in its entirety (vedapārāyaṇa), as well as the *japa* of the *Sūryanamaskāra*, the circumambulation of the *Aśvattha* tree, the *Rudrābhiṣeka*, the *Namaka*, *Camarapuruṣasūkta*, *Śrīsūkta*, *Bhūsūkta*, *Āyuṣyasūkta*, *Mahāśānti*, *Ghoṣaśānti*, *Mahāsaura*, *Apohiṣṭhā*, *Muñcāmi*, *Evāpitre*, the *Pāvamānī*, the *Śaṃvatī*, the *Svastimatī*, the hymns (*sūkta*) from Indra to Īśāna, the *Navagrahasūkta*, the *Viṣṇukavaca*, the *Śivakavaca*, and the *Nāmatraya* and so forth, one should invite Brāhmaṇas.

To the west of the pavilion (maṇḍapa), one should construct three sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) for the purpose of the peace-offering (śānti-homa), the offering to the nine planets (navagraha-homa), and half of the ten-thousand sesame seed offerings (ayuta-tila-homa). Alternatively, one may construct a single pit for all three using a common procedure. However, in the case of the ten-thousand sesame seed offering, one should construct a separate pit.

The measurement of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa): For fifty oblations, it should be the size of a fist; for one hundred, the size of an elbow (aratni); for one thousand to be offered, one should make the pit the size of a cubit (hasta). For ten thousand oblations, it should be two cubits; for a hundred thousand oblations, four cubits; and for ten million oblations, the pit should be eight cubits in size.

Based on the statement "more than that," one should construct a square sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) according to the prescribed proportions in accordance with the gradations of the *homa*. Having performed the rites from the digging (*ullikhana*) up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings according to the method prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*, one should perform the *navagraha-homa*, the *śānti-homa*, and the *tila-homa*. In a single *kuṇḍa* or on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), having performed the *grahaya-jña* (sacrifice to the planets) in the manner described for the planetary sacrifice, one should offer oblations of fuel-sticks (*samidh*), parched grain (*caru*), and clarified butter (*ājya*) one thousand and eight or one hundred and eight times, using the mantra of the principal deity.

One should offer oblations for that purpose with those substances and those mantras belonging to the primary deity and the secondary deity. One should perform a sesame (*tila*) homa according to one's capacity with the mantra "mā cṛtho mṛtyo. One should perform a homa of *dūrvā* grass sprinkled with honey and a homa of *pṛṣadājya* (clotted butter) according to one's capacity with the Gāyatrī mantra.

One should perform a *gulūcī* oblation according to one's capacity with the mantra "ete sahasram. Preceded by that, one should perform ten thousand (*ayuta*) sesame oblations with the *tryambaka* mantra—separately if there are multiple sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*), or according to one's capacity if there is only a single pit.

An oblation of twenty-eight or eight offerings of *samit*, *caru*, and clarified butter (*ājya*) is performed for the deities of birth, year, solstice, season, month, fortnight, lunar day (*tithi*), day of the week (*vāra*), asterism (*nakṣatra*), conjunction (*yoga*), lunar phase (*karana*), zodiac sign (*rāśi*), and [the deity of] the [birth] constellation. For the others, there is one offering each.

After the rites beginning with *ullekhana* (scratching) and the installation of the fire (*agni-pratiṣṭhāpana*), the sequence for the *anvādhāna* (replenishing the fuel) is as follows for one who performs the *anvādhāna*.

In this rite involving the *anvāhita* fire, having recited from "O Agni" (*asminnanvāhite agnau*) up to "the two eyes with clarified butter" (*cakṣuṣī ājyena*), one should offer oblations to all the deities of the auspicious mandala (*sarvato-bhadra-maṇḍala*) individually, using sacrificial fuel sticks (*samidh*), parched grain (*caru*), and clarified butter (*ājya*). One should likewise offer to the principal deities—the nine planets beginning with Āditya—using the intended number of *samidh*, *caru*, and *ājya* as available. One should also offer to the presiding deities (*adhidevatās*) beginning with Agni, and the secondary presiding deities (*pratyadhidevatās*) beginning with Rudra, using the intended number of *samidh*, *caru*, and *ājya*. Finally, one should offer to Mṛtyu, the principal deity of the *ugraratha*.

With the mantra *varaṃ mṛtyo*, one should offer oblations of *śamī* wood, parched grain (*caru*), and clarified butter (*ājya*) in the desired number, such as one thousand and eight; this is for the presiding deity of the Ugraratha [chariot], Mṛtyu. With the mantra *ugraṃ tu hi śrutam*, one should offer oblations of *śamī* wood, parched grain, and clarified butter in the desired number, such as one hundred and eight; this is for the counter-deity (pratyadhidevatā) of the Ugraratha, Mṛtyuñjaya. With the mantra *tryambakam*, one should offer oblations of *śamī* wood, parched grain, and clarified butter in the desired number, such as one hundred and eight.

Again, one should offer oblations to the principal deity, Mṛtyu, with *śamī* wood, *samidh* fuel, rice-oblations (*caru*), and clarified butter (*ājya*), according to the intended number. Again, one should offer to the principal deity, Mṛtyu, with sesame seeds as the substance, using the mantra "mā cchido mṛtyo" according to the intended number. Again, one should offer to the principal deity, Mṛtyu, with *durvā* grass sprinkled with honey, rice-porridge (*caru*), and *pṛṣadājya*, using its specific *gāyatrī* mantra according to the intended number.

Again, one should offer to the principal deity Mṛtyu with *guḍūcī* fuel-sticks, parched grain, and clarified butter, using the mantra "ete sahasram... according to the intended number; again, to the principal deity Tryambaka with sesame seeds as the substance, using the mantra "tryambakam... according to the intended number; and to Aśvatthāman and others who have long lived, with fuel-sticks, parched grain, and clarified butter, each eight times, using their respective mantras.

With the respective mantras for each of the sixty-year cycle, the two solstices, the six seasons, the twelve months, the twenty-four fortnights, the sixteen lunar days (tithis), and the seven-day week, one should offer oblations of sacrificial wood (samidh), parched grain (caru), and clarified butter (ājya) eight times each. With the respective mantras for the names of the eight Vasus and the eleven Rudras, one should offer oblations of sacrificial wood, parched grain, and clarified butter eight times each. With the Taittirīya mantras for the deities of the birth asterism and the other lunar mansions (nakṣatras), one should offer oblations of sacrificial wood, parched grain, and clarified butter eight times each.

One should offer oblations of sacrificial wood (*samidh*), parched grain (*caru*), and clarified butter (*ājya*) eight times for each of the deities associated with birth and other life-stages, using their respective names as mantras; [this applies to] the nine Durgā deities.

With the respective mantras of those names, one should offer eight oblations each of sacrificial wood (*samit*), parched grain (*caru*), and clarified butter (*ājya*): Brahmā with the mantra "Brahmaṇe brahma jñānam"; Viṣṇu with the mantra "Idaṃ viṣṇuḥ"; Rudra with the mantra "Kadrudrāya"; Gaṇapati with the mantra "Gaṇānāṃ tvā"; Kṣetrapāla with the mantra "Kṣetrasya"; Vāstupuruṣa with the mantra "Vāstoṣpate"; and Abhayakara with the mantra "Yata indra bhayāmahe. For each deity, there are eight oblations of sacrificial wood, parched grain, and clarified butter.

One should offer oblations of *samit*, *caru*, and clarified butter (*ājya*) eight times each with the respective mantras for the deities of the twelve zodiac signs (*rāśi*) and the seven classes of winds (*marut*). One should offer oblations of *samit*, *caru*, and clarified butter eight times each with the respective mantras for the five Brahmans known as Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna. One should offer oblations of *samit*, *caru*, and clarified butter eight times each with the respective mantras for the nine planets beginning with Āditya and their respective presiding deities (*pratyadhidevatā*).

One should offer oblations of sacrificial wood (*samidh*), parched grain (*caru*), and clarified butter (*ājya*) eight times each for the twelve Ādityas with their respective name-mantras; for Mṛtyuñjaya with the mantra "Tryambaka" eight times with *samidh*, *caru*, and *ājya*; and for Indra and the other world-protectors (*lokapāla*), the deity of space, the deity of the earth, and the four Varuṇas, each with their respective mantras eight times with *samidh*, *caru*, and *ājya*.

The presiding deities of the hundred apertures (*śatacchidrābhimāninī devatā*), namely Brahmā and Varuṇa, are each worshipped eight times with *samidh*, *caru*, and clarified butter (*ājya*) using their respective mantras. The deities of the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla-sādguṇya-devatās*) and Śrī are worshipped with clarified butter alone in the intended number of oblations. With the remainder, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is made, and so forth, concluding with "I shall sacrifice today" (*sadyo yakṣye*). This applies to the case of a single sacrificial pit (*ekakuṇḍapakṣa*). In the case of separate pits (*pṛthakkuṇḍapakṣa*), however, after the formula "with clarified butter" (*ājyenetyante*) in the pit for the planetary oblations (*grahahoma-kuṇḍe*), the principal deities—the nine planets beginning with Āditya—are worshipped in the intended number.

For the purpose of offering to the presiding deities (*adhidevatās*) and their subordinates (*pratyadhidevatās*), one should offer oblations with *samidh*, parched grain (*caru*), and clarified butter (*ājya*) in numbers such as ten or twenty, whichever is appropriate. For the directional guardians (*dikpālas*), the secondary deities (*sādguṇya-devatās*), and others, one should sacrifice with the remaining materials, using clarified butter alone, saying, "I shall sacrifice immediately. In the *śānti-homa* fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should perform the ritual intention (*saṃkalpa*) for all the deities, from those of the *sarvatobhadra* diagram up to the hundred-pored deity (*śatacchidra-devatā*). In the sesame-oblation fire-pit (*tila-homa-kuṇḍa*), [the same applies].

One should resolve upon [the performance of] ten thousand, one thousand, or one hundred offerings to the deities, ending with the deity-portion (devatānta), in the sesame-homa pit (*tilahoma-kuṇḍa*). One should resolve upon sesame-homas numbering ten thousand, one thousand, or one hundred as appropriate. In all three pits, one should resolve upon the sesame-homas numbering from the *idhmādhāna* (placing of fuel) up to the *cakṣuṣya* (eye-offering). In all three pits, the preliminary rites (*pūrvāṅga*) such as the *homa* from the *idhmādhāna* up to the *cakṣuṣya*, the subsequent rites (*uttarāṅga*) such as the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, and the ritual procedure (*tantra*) beginning from the placement of vessels (*pātrāsādana*) up to the dismissal of the Brahman and the Vināyaka, are all identical.
The Homa for the Seven Names of Cirañjīvin:
Oṃ namaś cirañjīvine aśvatthāmne svāhā;
Oṃ namaś cirañjīvine balaye svāhā.
Oṃ, salutation to the long-lived Vyāsa; svāhā!
Oṃ, salutation to the long-lived Hanumān; svāhā!
Oṃ, salutation to the long-lived Vibhīṣaṇa; svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to the long-lived one, to the compassionate one, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the long-lived one, to Paraśurāma, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the source of all power, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the all-pervading; svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Rudra, the pure; svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to Gaṇeśa, the ever-awakened; svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Śakti, the source of progeny, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to Kumāra, the son of Aṅgiras, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Vallī, the auspicious-faced one, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Gaurī, to Bhāva, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Brāhmī, to Yuvan, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to Māheśvarī, to Dhātṛ, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Kaumārī, to the one who is the supreme lord; svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Vaiṣṇavī, to the one of many forms; Oṃ, obeisance to Vārāhī, to the destroyer; svāhā!
Oṃ, salutation to the one who strides like Mahendra;
Oṃ, salutation to Cāmuṇḍā, svāhā to the poison;
Oṃ, salutation to the healthy one, to the one of variegated radiance, svāhā.
Oṃ, homage to Bhrāja, the self-luminous, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Paṭara, the deliverer, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Pataṅga, the terrestrial, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to the one who is golden, inexhaustible, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to the one possessed of light, the all-conqueror, svāhā! Oṃ, homage to the one of radiant splendor, the sustainer of all, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Kaśyapa, the adversary, svāhā! Oṃ, homage to Ravi, the deformed one, svāhā! Oṃ, homage to Sūrya, the harsh one, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Bhānu, to Nandanā; svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to Khaga, to Vijayā; svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to Pūṣan, to Jayā; svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Hiraṇyagarbha, O Manmathā!
Oṃ, homage to Marīci, to Durmukha, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Āditya, to Hevilambin, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Savitṛ, the one who hangs down; svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Arka, the transformer; svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Bhāskara, the dispeller of darkness; svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Agni Plava; svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to Jātavedas, the performer of auspicious deeds; svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Sahojas, the performer of beauty; svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to the one who is swift in power and wrathful, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Vaiśvānara, the lord of all;
oṃ, homage to the one who is beneficial to men and brings about supreme victory, svāhā!
Oṃ, salutation to Paṅkirādhas, the monkey; svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to Visarpiṇ, the stake; svāhā!
Oṃ, salutation to Matsya, the gentle one; svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Kūrma, the universal support; svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Varāha, the creator of obstacles; svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to Nṛsiṃha, who runs everywhere; svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Vāmana, the one who removes negligence; Oṃ, obeisance to Rāma, the embodiment of bliss, svāhā;
Oṃ, obeisance to Paraśurāma, the destroyer of the Rākṣasas.
Oṃ, obeisance to Balarāma, to Nala, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Kṛṣṇa, to Piṅgala, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Kalki, who is joined with the single time, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to the Buddha, the one who has accomplished his purpose, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Durgā, the fierce one, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to the Yātudhāna of evil intent!
Oṃ, obeisance to Bhairava, the one who strikes fear into the fearful;
Oṃ, obeisance to Hanumān, the vomiter of blood;
Oṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī, the red-eyed one; svāhā!
Oṃ, salutation to Dākṣāyaṇī, the wrathful one; svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to Lakṣmī, the imperishable one; svāhā!
Oṃ, salutation to Sūrya, the southern course.
Oṃ, obeisance to the Moon, to the northern course;
Oṃ, obeisance to the rainy season, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to the autumn season, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to the winter season, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the cool season, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to the spring season, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to the summer season, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to the month of Śuci, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to the month of Nabhas, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to the month of Nabhasya, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to the month of Īṣa, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to the month of Ūrja, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Sahāya-māsa, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Sahasya-māsa, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to Tapas-māsa, svāhā!

Oṃ, obeisance to the month of Śrāvaṇa, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the month of Bhādrapada, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the month of Āśvina, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the month of Kārttika, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the month of Pauṣa, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the month of Māgha, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the month of Phālguna, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the month of Caitra, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the month of Vaiśākha, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the month of Jyeṣṭha, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the month of Āṣāḍha, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the month of Madhu, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the month of Mādhava, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the month of Mādhava, svāhā!

Oṃ, obeisance to Śukra, the month; svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the waxing fortnight; svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the dark fortnight; svāhā! With the mantra "yad devā" or "yame ma," one offers oblations to both in sequence.
Oṃ, salutation to Agni, the first lunar day; svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā, the second lunar day; svāhā!
Oṃ, salutation to Gaurī, the third lunar day; svāhā!
Oṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati; to the fourth [tithi], svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the serpents; to the fifth [tithi], svāhā!
Oṃ, salutation to Skanda; to the sixth [tithi], svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Ravayenaptamī, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to Sadyojātā, the eighth [tithi], svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to Durgā, the ninth [tithi], svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Ādiśeṣa; svāhā to the tenth day! Oṃ, obeisance to Dharma; svāhā to the eleventh day!
Oṃ, obeisance to Hari; svāhā to the twelfth day!
Oṃ, obeisance to Kāma, the thirteenth lunar day; svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to Kali, the fourteenth lunar day; svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Candra, the full moon day; svāhā!

Oṃ, salutations to the ancestors; [salutations] to the lunar day (amāvāsyā) and the deities of the lunar days with their respective mantras—some say "vauṣaṭ"; Oṃ, salutations to Śiva, to the day of the Sun, svāhā;
Oṃ, salutations to Durgā, to the day of the Moon, svāhā.
Oṃ, obeisance to the six-faced one, to the day of Kuja (Mars), svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, to the day of Budha (Mercury), svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, to the day of Guru (Jupiter), svāhā!

Oṃ, obeisance to Indra, the deity of Friday; svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to Yama, the deity of Saturday; svāhā! Or, one may perform the fire-oblation (homa) for each of these presiding deities with their respective mantras:
Oṃ, obeisance to Dṛva, the forest-dweller; svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Adhvara, svāhā to the forest! Oṃ, obeisance to Soma, svāhā to the forest!
Oṃ, obeisance to the waters, svāhā to the Vasus!
Oṃ, obeisance to Anīla, the forest-dweller, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to Anala, the forest-dweller, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to Pratyūṣa, the forest-dweller, svāhā!

Oṃ, obeisance to Prabhāsa, svāhā to Vanave; or one may perform the oblation with the mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to the eight gods, svāhā to the Vasus. Oṃ, obeisance to Vīrabhadra, the Rudra, svāhā. Oṃ, obeisance to Śambhu, the Rudra, svāhā.
Oṃ, obeisance to Girīśa, to Rudra, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Bhairava, to Rudra, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Pinākin, to Rudra, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Sthāṇu, the Rudra; svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Bharga, the Rudra; svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Sadāśiva, the Rudra; svāhā!
"Oṃ namaḥ sarāraye rudrāya svāhā;
oṃ namaḥ śivāya rudrāya svāhā; oṃ namo harāya rudrāya svāhā; oṃ namo rudrāya rudrāya svāhā"—some say that the fire-oblation (homa) is performed with this mantra. Then follows the Nakṣatreṣṭi.
In this manner, one should perform the *sīvo-homa* for the deities of the twenty-eight lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*).
Oṃ, homage to Viṣkambha, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Prīta, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Āyuṣmat, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Saubhāgya, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Śobhana, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to Atigaṇḍa, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to the one of auspicious deeds, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the one who upholds, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the one with the trident, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Gaṇḍa, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Vṛddhi, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Dhruva, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to the Obstructer, svāhā! Oṃ, homage to the Gladdener, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to the Vajra, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Siddhi, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Vayatīpāta, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Varīyasa, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Parigha, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Śiva, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Siddha, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Sādhyāya, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to Śubhāya, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Śuklāya, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Brāhmaya, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Aiṃdrāya, svāhā! Oṃ, homage to Vaidhṛti, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta, to Bava, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva, to Bālava!
Oṃ, obeisance to Aghora, to Kaulava!
Oṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa, the one who is the weighing scale;
Oṃ, obeisance to Īśāna, the one born from the cow, svāhā;
Oṃ, obeisance to Bhava, the merchant, svāhā.
Oṃ, obeisance to the Lord of Pārvatī, to Bhadra;
Oṃ, obeisance to Virūpākṣa, to Śakuni;
Oṃ, obeisance to Nīlakaṇṭha, to the four-footed ones, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Umāpati, the serpent-bearer;
Oṃ, homage to Śulin, Kiṃstughna, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Śailaputrī, Durgā, svāhā!
Oṃ, salutations to Durgā, the practitioner of celibacy;
Oṃ, salutations to Durgā, the slayer of Caṇḍa;
Oṃ, salutations to Durgā, the mother of Skanda.
Oṃ, homage to Durgā, the daughter of Kuśmāya;
Oṃ, homage to Durgā, the daughter of Kātyāyana; Oṃ, homage to Durgā, the daughter of Kālarātri.
"Oṃ, salutation to the Great Gaurī Durgā;

Oṃ, salutation to Durgā, the bestower of success, svāhā. Some say that one should perform the oblation to the Nine Durgās with these seven verses beginning with *jātavedase*, and with the two verses beginning with *yaścaṃdasām*.
Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā, svāhā!
Oṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu! Oṃ, salutation to Rudra!
Oṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati; Oṃ, salutation to Kṣetrapāla;
Oṃ, salutation to Abhayaṃkara.

Some say that the oblation should be performed in sequence with the following mantras: "Oṃ, salutation to Vāstupuruṣa, svāhā"; "The limit of the Brahman-deities"; "Viṣṇu is indeed our protector"; "To Rudra"; "Of the hosts, thee"; "Of the field, the protector"; and "From where Indra. Regarding the mantra "O Lord of the Dwelling" (*vāstoṣpate*), some maintain it should be used accordingly.
Oṃ, homage to the zodiac sign Aries; Oṃ, homage to the zodiac sign Taurus;
Oṃ, homage to the zodiac sign Gemini.
Oṃ, homage to the zodiac sign of Cancer; Oṃ, homage to the zodiac sign of Leo;
Oṃ, homage to the zodiac sign of Virgo.
Oṃ, homage to the zodiac sign of Libra;
Oṃ, homage to the zodiac sign of Scorpio;
Oṃ, homage to the zodiac sign of Sagittarius.
Oṃ, homage to the zodiac sign of Capricorn;
Oṃ, homage to the zodiac sign of Aquarius;
Oṃ, homage to the zodiac sign of Pisces.
Oṃ, homage to Apahāyamaruta; Oṃ, homage to Vipahāyamaruta;
Oṃ, homage to Udvahāyamaruta.
Oṃ, obeisance to the wind that blows together; Oṃ, obeisance to the wind that blows away;
Oṃ, obeisance to the wind that blows around.
Oṃ, salutations to Prapahāyamaruta;
some say that the oblation with the seven [mantras] beginning with "Vurāvāto varṣan" is for the seventh [deity];
Oṃ, salutations to Sadyojāta, the Brahman, svāhā.
Oṃ, salutation to Vāmadeva, the Brahman; svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to Aghora, the Brahman; svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to Tatpuruṣa, the Brahman; svāhā!
Some say that the oblation (*homa*) is performed with the five *Brahma-mantras*, beginning with "Oṃ nama īśānāya brahmaṇe svāhā" and "sadyojātam".

Then, as a subsidiary part of the Śānti rite, one should perform the oblation to the nine planets (navagraha-homa) together with their presiding deities (adhidevatās) and counter-deities (pratyadhidevatās), according to the procedure prescribed for the Grahayajña.
Oṃ, salutation to Dhātṛ Āditya, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to Aryaman Āditya, svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to Mitra Āditya, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to the Sun, the ruddy one; svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Sun, Aṃśumat; svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to the Sun, Bhaga; svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Indra, the Āditya; svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Viṣṇu, the Āditya; svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Pūṣan, the Āditya; svāhā!
"Oṃ, obeisance to Tvaṣṭṛ, the Āditya; svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, the Āditya; svāhā!
Some maintain that the twelve Ādityas are worshipped with the three Ṛgvedic verses beginning with "udyan śaśvat mitramahaḥ."
With the mantra "Tryambakam," one should perform the *mṛtyuñjaya* oblation.
Oṃ, obeisance to Indra, the guardian of the quarter, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to Agni, the guardian of the quarter, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Yama, the guardian of the quarter, svāhā!
Oṃ, homage to Nirṛti, the guardian of the quarter, svāhā! Oṃ, homage to Varuṇa, the guardian of the quarter, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Vāyu, the guardian of the direction, svāhā!
Oṃ, obeisance to Kubera, the guardian of the direction, svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to Īśāna, the guardian of the direction, svāhā!

Others maintain that the oblation should be performed with these eight mantras: *indravo viśvataḥ*, *agnindūtam*, *yamāya somaṃ*, *yutedevāḥ*, *imaṃ me varuṇa*, *tavāye*, *sāmodhenuṃ*, and *tamīśānam*. Regarding this, some say that one should offer to Brahmā, the guardian of the nether world, with the mantra *adhaḥ paśyasva*, and to Viṣṇu, the guardian of the upper world, with the mantra *tadviṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam*.
*Oṃ namaḥ ākāśāya svāhā;
oṃ namo mahyai svāhā; asmerudrāmohānāḥ*—this is the oblation to Ākāśa (Space). Some say that *mahīṃ devīm ita* is the oblation to Mahī (Earth).

One should perform the four Varuṇa oblations with the four mantras: "imaṃ me varuṇa," "tat tvā yāmi," "tvaṃ no agne," and "sa tvaṃ no agne. Some say that one should offer oblations to the deity of the hundred-holed jar (*śatacchidra-kalaśa*) with the mantra "brahma jajñānam" for Brahmā, and to Varuṇa with "avate heḍo varuṇa"; however, others maintain that, as in the case of the *darvī* ladle and other implements, this is merely an injunction for the placement [of the vessel] for the sake of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), and there is no invocation of deities therein.

In some manuscripts, the invocation, worship, and fire-offering (homa) of the Aśvinī deities, the Viśvedevas, the seven oceans, the seven rivers, the four Vedas, the three junctions of the day (saṃdhyās), and so forth, are observed; however, because these are not universal and because they are not mentioned in the ritual manuals (kalpas), they have not been presented here.

Then, one should complete the remainder of the *homa*, beginning with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and ending with the *pūrṇāhuti* and the dismissal of the *brahmā*. In the case of the previously mentioned three fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*), having performed the *navagraha-homa* in one, the *śānti-homa* in another, and the ten-thousand-fold sesame *homa* (*ayuta-tila-homa*) in the other, one should complete the remainder of the *jayādi-homa*. Then, having performed the worship of the images once again, one should dismiss the deities.

Then, in the northeastern portion of the fire-altar, within the pavilion prepared for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the officiating priest (*ācārya*), together with the Brahmins, shall seat the patron (*yajamāna*)—accompanied by his sons, grandsons, and others, and adorned with all ornaments—upon an auspicious throne (*bhadrapīṭha*). Having poured the water from each of the ritual jars into a large jar with a hundred holes (*śatacchidra-bṛhatkumbha*), he shall purify him with the verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā* as they are about to be recited, and then bathe him. The consecration mantras are: *Āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ* (O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss), *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ* (Golden-hued ones), *pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ* (The purifying one, born of light).

The Vedic mantras beginning with "samudra jyeṣṭhāḥ," "āpa idvāsu," and "indraṃ vo viśvataspari" are the mantras for the guardians of the directions (dikpālas). The mantras for Varuṇa are: "paraṃ mṛtyo," "havig harantamanu," "depasyatyā," "muñcāmi tvā," "sarveṣu vā eṣu lokeṣu," "hiraṇyavarṇām," "trimūryambakam," "ṛtaṃ ca," and "taccayorāḥ. These and others are the Vedic mantras.
May the gods consecrate you—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara;
likewise Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, and the all-pervading Saṃkarṣaṇa.
May Pradyumna and Aniruddha bring about victory;
may the Lord Akhaṇḍalogni and Yamala-nirṛti likewise [grant it].
Varuṇa, Pavana, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera),
and Śiva, together with Brahmā— these gods shall always protect you.
Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Medhā, Tuṣṭi, Śraddhā, Kṣamā, and Gati [shall likewise protect you].
Buddhi, Lajjā, Vapus, Śānti, Puṣṭi, and Kānti are the Mothers.
May these wives of Dharma, assembled together, consecrate you:
Āditya, Candramas, Bhauma, Budha, Jīva, Śita, and Arkaja.
May the planets, accompanied by Rāhu, Ketu, and the others—
the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas— consecrate you.
The sages, the ascetics, the cows, and likewise the mothers of the gods; the wives of the gods, the trees, the nāgas, the daityas, and the hosts of the celestial nymphs.
All missiles, all weapons, kings, vehicles,
medicinal herbs, and gems— these are likewise portions of Time.
May the rivers, oceans, mountains, sacred fords, and those who bestow the fruits of recitation and charity consecrate you for the attainment of virtue, desire, and wealth.
May Vighneśa, Kṣetrapa, Durgā, the world-protectors, and the nine planets grant you constant auspiciousness and fulfill all your desires.
Such are the Puranic mantras.

After this, some say that one should perform the *nīrājana* (waving of lights) with lamps placed in vessels of bell-metal and other materials, moving clockwise around [the deity]. "Whatever beings dwell here, having taken this offering given according to the prescribed rite, may they prepare their residence elsewhere. Salutations to all those planetary spirits (*graha*)."

Thus, one should place offerings of various foods (citrānna-bali) in the four directions of the pavilion. Then, the patron (yajamāna), having put on sacred threads and marks (puṇḍra), having adorned himself with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and having given garments to the preceptor (ācārya) after bathing for the consecration, shall don protective amulets with the *Bṛhat-sāman*. Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "I shall perform the offering of ghee after inspection (*nirīkṣita-ājya-dāna*) for the purpose of warding off misfortune (*alakṣmī*)," he should look at his own face in the ghee contained within a bronze vessel (*kāṃsya-pātra*), reciting: "Form by form, he became the counter-form."

Having prayed with the mantra: "Whatever misfortune (alakṣmī) and whatever dullness of intellect resides in all my limbs, may that be pacified; grant me prosperity, nourishment, and strength," he should offer the clarified butter (ājya). Then, with the mantra: "Born from the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), auspicious and beneficial to Viṣṇu, clarified butter is the food of the gods; therefore, grant me peace," he should give the butter, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), betel leaf, and a bell-metal vessel to this Brāhmaṇa, saying: "I have given it; salutations to you, salutations."

In this manner, one should offer "difficult gifts" (durdāna) such as an iron ball, cotton, salt, sesame seeds, woolen blankets, and so forth. Since all actions without exception depend upon these, one should give forty fruits and other items, along with an iron fragment and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), to a Brāhmaṇa while reciting: "O iron ball, salutations to you; ward off evil portents. Thus ends the fortieth [section] concerning the iron fragment and other items.
Cotton, sacred to the deity Cañcu, is beneficial to human beings;
since you alone are its presiding deity, therefore grant me peace.
Thus, one should give cotton cloth together with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
"Since all tastes of food are not superior without salt,
and since it is eternally dear to Śiva and Śivā, therefore grant me peace.
[Thus he spoke, seeking] salt, the first-born and most excellent of tastes, which increases strength.
Therefore, for the sake of bestowing divine favor, perform the propitiatory rite from that point.
Thus, one should give one *droṇa* measure of salt.
Since these [fires] have arisen from the sweat of the body of Viṣṇu, the enemy of Madhu,
and are praised among the sacrificial fires (havyakavya), may they therefore bring us peace here.
Having thus honored the sesame seeds— “O Kāśyapa, sesame seeds are born as eternally auspicious destroyers of evil;
O Keśava, through this gift of sesame, destroy my unbearable sin.”
With this mantra, one should perform the gift of a *droṇa* measure of sesame seeds.
The plucking out of the wool of the ram wards off the fear of cold winds;
since it removes the fear of frost, may it therefore bestow peace upon me.
Thus, with this mantra, the gift of a blanket is performed.
Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "I shall perform the gift of a water-pot (ghaṭa) for the sake of averting inauspiciousness," one should then look at one's own face therein.
"Whatever inauspiciousness has befallen me, and whatever affliction is in my body—may you pacify all that today, and increase my nourishment. Thus one should pray.
Oil is always nourishing, life-prolonging, and a destroyer of sin;
it removes inauspiciousness and is meritorious; therefore, grant me peace.
With this mantra, one should offer a jar of oil.
Since among all tastes this sweet taste is the most excellent and is disliked by you, therefore I shall offer you jaggery; through that, grant me peace.
Thus, one should give the guṇḍa together with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and betel.

After the difficult gift (durdāna), having bathed, changed one's clothes, and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should become pure. Then, having seated the preceptor upon an auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha) and adorned him with perfumes, flowers, garments, and so forth,
[one should present] a bull together with ornaments and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
O Bull, O Lord, grant me the nature of Dharma, happiness, and peace.
Having worshipped with this mantra, some say one should offer [the oblation] with the following:
"May the Lord, who is the means for accomplishing sacrifice, who destroys the sins of the universe,
and who reveals His universal form, be pleased by this sacrifice."
The fourteen worlds abide within the limbs of the cow;
therefore, I shall give her away—grant me peace from this.
With this mantra, one should give a cow that is adorned, accompanied by her calf, provided with a milking vessel of bell-metal, and accompanied by a gift of gold.
Now, the gift of the water-pot (*kalaśa-dāna*): therein, first, the gift of the principal image.
[One should worship] her who holds a blazing staff in her hand and stands upon a preeminent buffalo.
I give this image of Death for the cessation of all defects.
Thus—
[I offer] her who holds a noose in her hand, whose eyes are red, who is terrible, and who is mounted upon a buffalo;
she who resembles Death itself, for the sake of turning back all calamities.
With this mantra, one should give a new cloth, a water-pot, a sacrificial fee, and an image of Death.
The gift of the image of the primordial deity Ādidevatogrā:
"I give this fierce image of Karālāsyā, who has deformed eyes and is seated upon an excellent tiger, for the cessation of all death."
Thus:
"I give this image of Ugrā, the bestower of fear, whose vehicle is a preeminent lion, to you for the sake of averting all calamities."
Or, with the mere recitation of "iti," one should offer as before.
The presiding deity is Pratyadhidevatā; the gift is the victory over death.
O Conqueror of Death, O Śaṅkara whose vehicle is the bull, salutations to you! Grant me peace of mind as I offer this image of your form.
Thus—
holding a jar filled with nectar in her hand,
I offer this image named Jayā to you for the increase of all prosperity.
With this mantra, one should offer [the oblation] as before.
"O best of Brahmins, I shall give to you this image accompanied by cloth for the cessation of impending misfortune, according to the prescribed procedure.
With this mantra, he should give all the pitchers along with the cloth, the image, and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).

Then—cows, land, sesame seeds, gold, clarified butter, grain, molasses, cooked rice, silver, and salt; these, they say, are the ten gifts of wealth (*daladāna*). One should perform them according to the Sun-god’s instruction. Among them, the gift of a cow is as previously described. "Land is the support of all crops and was raised up by the Boar; therefore, may Hari, the Soul of the Universe, be pleased by the gift of this [land]. Thus is the gift of land. "Sesame seeds, O Kāśyapa, were born of Kaśyapa; they are auspicious and eternally destroy sin. O Keśava, through the gift of sesame seeds, may my insurmountable sin be destroyed. Thus is the gift of sesame seeds.
O Hiraṇyagarbha, you who reside within the womb, the golden seed of the sun;
O bestower of infinite meritorious fruits, grant me peace from this moment forth.
Thus:
"Whatever evil has been committed by me throughout thousands of other births—
may there always be peace for me through this gift of gold."
Thus concludes the gift of gold.

"Born from the wish-fulfilling cow, present in all sacrifices, the great food of the gods—grant me peace through this clarified butter. (The ellipsis here is "I shall give [this]"; thus ends the offering of clarified butter.)
The supreme characteristic of modesty is protection from cold, wind, and heat;
O gods, grant us peace through clothing as an ornament.
Thus concludes the gift of clothing.
It makes the donor fortunate both in this world and the next;
therefore, I shall bestow this upon you, and may you grant me peace.
Thus concludes the gift of grain.
Secret giving is as previously described.

"The horse is indeed the vehicle of the Sun, the piercer of the hundred-fold willed one (Indra). Through this act of giving, may there always be peace of consciousness for me."
Now, the mantra for the gift of a chariot:
Obeisance to the chariot, to the master of the chariot; obeisance to you, the one whose actions are effortless. Obeisance to the master of all beings, and obeisance to the benefactor of the world.

To the north of the fire,

With the mantras prescribed for the nine planets, as well as the individual mantras of the guardians of the directions; with the hymn beginning "akṣībhyām," with the mantra "devasya tvā," with the mantra "trātāram indram," and with the mantra "tat tvā yāmi."

A Brahmin who is skilled in the application of yantras, endowed with good conduct, truthful in speech, a master of his senses, and a worshiper of the Supreme Lord, should—having bathed well and adorned himself with fine garments, sandalwood paste, and so forth—draw the yantra in a pure location using the prescribed materials. First, he should write the word "sādhaka" in the genitive case in the center, and beneath that, the seed-syllable *vi* joined with the vowel *i* (viḥ), which is the seed of creation;
this is the Gāyatrī of the yantra.
We know the King of Yantras; we meditate upon the Great Yantra.

"May that weapon of Him impel [me]. With this *yantra-gāyatrī* and with the syllables of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā-mantra*, one should encircle the *yantra* on all sides. Having thus drawn the *yantra* and carefully wrapped it in gold or other materials, one should perform the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the *yantra*. As for the procedure: having established a water-pot (*kalaśa*) in the center of a *sarvatobhadra-maṇḍala* or upon an eight-petaled lotus, according to the rite for placing the pot, one should place the *yantra* upon it. Regarding the material for writing, birch bark (*bhūrjapatra*) is used; as for materials not specifically mentioned for writing, saffron (*kesara*), *gorocanā*, *karpūra*, musk (*kastūrī*), elephant ichor, sandalwood (*candana*), and agallochum (*agaru*) are to be used. Regarding the pen not specifically mentioned, a golden stylus (*suvarṇa-śalākā*) is used; regarding the vessel not specifically mentioned, gold is used; regarding the limb for wearing [the yantra] not specifically mentioned, the right arm is used.
Thus, the general procedure for the construction of the yantra has been stated in the *Yantracintāmaṇi* treatise, which consists of a dialogue between Pārvatī and the Supreme Lord (Śiva).
Once, having beheld the Lord of the Gods, the goddess Śucismitā,

The castes, the stages of life, the duties, and the doubts—this is a great inquiry.

At that very moment, he becomes a perfected one (siddha), and the perfected woman (siddhā) grants all desires;
[she effects] killing, driving away, summoning, creating enmity, and likewise paralyzing.
In all rites of sorcery (*abhicāra*), for all purposes of desire,
at all times, in disputes, in marriage, in battle, and likewise for victory over enemies.
All this is indeed accomplished for the practitioner exactly as intended by the God; O Lord of the Gods, having investigated this, [reveal] the supreme secret state.
The illustrious Supreme Lord said:
"The Vedic conduct has been proclaimed by me for the high-souled sages;
the Śiva-dharma is for the liberated ones, and the Vaiṣṇava-dharma is for the Vaiṣṇavas."
This Sāṃkhya system dedicated to the Sun has been proclaimed by me for the sake of many who desire spiritual perfection.
The Śākta [tantra] has been declared in many ways, O beloved, and the Bhairava [tantra] in many ways.
O auspicious lady, the knowledge of dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa has indeed been revealed; yet the secret has been concealed everywhere—of this there is no doubt.
O lady of excellent limbs, a mantra devoid of its secret essence does not attain perfection even through meditation, let alone through hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
"O Lord of Gods, show me favor; tell me an easy means that is a profound secret, easily understood, and which produces immediate conviction."
Without fire-offerings, recitation, preparatory rites, or service, O Lord, one attains perfection in the Kali age;
therefore, please tell me the means for that.
The illustrious Supreme Lord said: "Excellent, excellent, O highly wise one who acts for the welfare of the worlds!
O lotus-eyed lady, I have never been questioned by anyone else in this manner."
Listen with one-pointed mind to this secret that grants success in an instant;
it is the great couch named Cintāmaṇi, more hidden than the most hidden.
It is the essence of all scriptures, the supreme essence of mantras,
and even further beyond the essence of the Atharvaṇa Veda.
At this time, O Goddess, there will be many kinds of auspicious yantras made of cintāmaṇi gems that accomplish all desired rites.
Listen now to the power of him in whose house this Kalpa is always kept written down and is worshipped every day.
There is no fear of untimely death, nor is there any fear of thieves;
the power of bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas does not arise at all.
The deceit of another never succeeds;
O fair-faced one, the practitioner must not place his trust in anyone else.
In this ritual manual, black magic (*abhicāra*) will indeed occur due to a lack of faith; of this there is no doubt.
A yantra performed with doubt results in the opposite effect.
Having bathed and become pure, one should worship the family deity;
the supreme yantra should be diligently drawn in a secluded place.
For whichever ritual application this procedure has been proclaimed, one should perform worship for three days according to the prescribed rules for enjoyments.
For three nights he should sleep on the ground, remaining celibate and pure; O fair-faced one, after three days, a dream arises for the practitioner.

The deity presiding over the mantra, through the power of the dream, certainly declares whether the goal is already accomplished, yet to be accomplished, an enemy, or else perfectly achieved and eternal.

otherwise, one should predict exactly as it was heard in the dream.
Having heard from the mouth of the god regarding the attainment of results through the ritual procedure in a dream,
when one is unimpeded in that dream, then this supreme yantra [should be employed].
Success is proclaimed for whoever acts after having drawn [the diagram] in this manner;

nor is there but one practitioner in the world, for people possess diverse natures.

The *siddha*, the *sādhya*, the *ari*, and likewise the *susiddha* and the other;
the *siddha* achieves success in time, while the *sādhya* may or may not achieve success.
The enemy cuts the root; when well-mastered, it grants its fruit in an instant.
Therefore, by the power of destiny, the zodiac sign, time, and dreams bring great prosperity.
Having correctly understood the mental disposition of the practitioner, one should act accordingly;
this is declared to be the supreme secret, the defining characteristic of the yantra. Thus it is said.
The Great Delusion Yantra:
Listen, O Goddess, to this great yantra for subjugating kings, which is adorned with the names of the sons;
having brought a pure bell-metal vessel prepared with ashes and other substances.
One should scratch [the surface] with *jātī* wood, as well as with *rocanā* and sandalwood;
one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in the center and then encircle it.
Above that, one should arrange eight petals and place the letters of the word *vāk* upon them.
Then, having wrapped it properly, one should make it perfectly circular as before, O Dear One.
Above that, one should fashion a sixteen-petaled lotus;
on each petal, the vowels beginning with 'a' should be written in successive order.
Then, one should encircle it perfectly with three lines and worship it with jasmine, *jātī* flowers, and white lotuses.
Having worshipped that king of yantras, known by the name Mahāmeghanasa, with other fragrant white flowers and white cloths;
Having performed this for seven days, one should then encase it with the three metals;
whoever wears it on the head, at the root of the arm, or on the neck, [shall attain success].
Whether it be a woman or a man, provided they are endowed with firm resolve,
all these [attendants] shall indeed always remain under their control like servants.
The Yantra for Victory in Dispute:
Now, therefore, I shall proclaim this yantra for the victory of men in dispute;
one should fashion it with great effort, for it is enchanting to all the world.
Having written the name "Madhu," one should then encircle it with a circle;
thereafter, a person should fashion four petals provided with seed-syllables.
Having inscribed "hrīṃ yaṃ hrīṃ yaṃ" on each petal with yellow pigment (rocanā) and saffron upon a birch bark leaf, the devoted and pure person should worship it.
Then, having worshipped with incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, and various kinds of auspicious flowers,
one should place the yantra encased in the three metals into the midst of milk.
Then one should go for the sake of resolving disputes; there is no doubt that victory will be attained.
This yantra, named "Victory in Dispute," is worshipped by the gods.
The Yantra for compelling the creditor:
When the destruction of wealth occurs due to the thread of the Rākṣasas,
the creditor demands his wealth from the debtor with persistence.
If that donor lacks the capacity and there is no wealth whatsoever,
then, for the purpose of deluding him, a great machine consisting of illusion (māyā) should be employed.
If he lacks the power to give it, and there is no substance whatsoever by which to explain it,
then, for the sake of deluding him, one should employ a great illusory machine.
On a very wide birch bark leaf, one should carefully draw a hexagon using yellow pigment and saffron, incorporating the name of the person to be accomplished.
In the corners of the interior, one should write the syllable *klīṃ* twelve times;
then, one should properly encircle that with a circle, which is said to be the *yaṃtra*.
One should surround it with twenty-five *hrīṃ* syllables and encircle it with the *kavaca* mantra;
then, one should properly enclose that with a circle as before.
Thus, for seven days, one should worship the yantra according to the prescribed rite;
thereafter, the wise practitioner should worship the goddess Mahāmāyā every day.
One should recite the supreme *Devīmāhātmya* as declared in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* for seven days, and thereafter, one should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*).
At the conclusion, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* oblation, one should feed three young girls;
furthermore, for each verse, one should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with honey and clarified butter.
One should properly wrap this excellent, circular yantra with three metals.
One should surround it with twenty-five *hrīṃ* syllables and encircle it with the *kavaca* mantra;
then, one should properly draw its enclosure in a perfect circle, just as before.
Thus, for seven days, one should worship the yantra according to the prescribed rite;
thereafter, the wise practitioner should worship the Goddess Mahāmāyā every day.
One should recite the supreme Devīmāhātmya as declared in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa for seven days, and thereafter perform the fire oblation (homa).
At the end, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should feed three virgins;
for each verse, one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) with honey and clarified butter.
Having encased it with the three metals and worn it on the upper arm, the forearm, or the neck,
merely by wearing it, one shall bring even a creditor under one's control.
He does not beg for the four kinds of wealth, yet he gives them away for the sake of trade.
The Mṛtyuñjaya Yantra that Compels the Evil One:
When a master, being enraged, desires to inflict death upon his servant,
then, for the sake of protecting one's own life, one should write the Mṛtyuñjaya Yantra.
Having brought birch-bark leaves, one should write upon two of them;
having written "ā" in the center, one should then draw a four-cornered square with a line.
Thus, one should draw a figure with seven corners and four triangles using an iron stylus;
and having drawn petals and spokes upon it in the four directions.
One should write *ī* and *śā* in the northeast; *la*, *li*, *lī*, *lu*, and *lū* in the south;
*le*, *lai*, *lo*, and *lau* in the west; and *laṃ* and *laḥ* in the north.
In this manner, a person should draw one seed-syllable on each of the twelve petals, and a trident with a bindu in each of the four corners.
In this manner, two yantras should be drawn;
thereafter, one should form a casket (*saṃpuṭa*) and place that yantra upon the ground, while the practitioner faces north.
One should certainly cast a large and firm stone upon him;
thereafter, one should go directly toward him, and his anger will be pacified.
This great Mṛtyuñjaya yantra is the supreme protector of life.
Even when time itself, which is otherwise difficult to overcome, becomes enraged against someone, this king of machines protects him then as well; of this there is no doubt.
The Machine for Victory in Legal Disputes:
Now, therefore, I shall proclaim this means of attaining victory in litigation;
this machine is praised as the remover of fear in legal proceedings.
One should write "namā" in the front row, and likewise "hrīṃ māṃ hrīṃ";
below that, one should encircle the name of the deity with the syllable "saḥ" at its end within a four-cornered figure.
One should place a petal in each corner and likewise in the center;
the seed-syllable *rodha* (ra) is in the south, and likewise *ikṣa* (i) in the northwest.
The seed-syllable of delusion (moha-bīja) is in the east, and likewise the syllable kṣaṃ is in the southeast;
having thus assigned these twelve seed-syllables to the eight petals.
Having worshipped you, the King of Yantras who brings victory, with a pair of shallow bowls (śarāva-sampuṭa) filled with water, using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, as well as eight lamps;
Having honored and fed the world-protectors and the young maiden,
one should then worship with offerings and lamps in the eight directions in due order.
One should strive to worship them in that manner, proceeding in sequence through the eight directions.
One should worship with diligence for as long as the task is not accomplished—
namely, victory in worldly affairs and likewise victory in legal disputes.
In disputes among kings and within royal families, one shall be victorious; there is no doubt in this matter.
Through the grace of the King of Yantras, his honor and status shall increase.
O Goddess, hereafter I shall describe to you the great yantra named Lalitā, which bestows conjugal fortune upon women and destroys their misfortune;
these yantras are the generators of good fortune and the fulfillers of the desires of those who love their beloveds.
One should draw a single-peaked hut, auspicious and adorned with three *hrīṃ* syllables;
beneath that, one should inscribe the name of the Vajramaṇi.

thereafter, one should properly enclose that with a four-cornered line.
Then, having adorned that eight-petalled [lotus], one should perform the placement of the seed-syllables (bījanyāsa);
O fair-faced one, the triad of the syllable *hrīṃ* should be written in the four directions.
The wise one should place the syllable *hrīṃ* in each corner with yellow pigment (*rocanā*),
saffron (*kuṅkuma*), musk (*mṛganābhi*), and sandalwood (*candana*).
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight, the practitioner, facing north, should draw the yantra upon a very large birch-bark leaf, having first unified [the ritual elements].
O fair-faced one, one should worship that yantra constantly, night after night,
with various kinds of enjoyments, flowers, garments, ornaments, and decorations.
Having performed this for seven days, at its conclusion,

O Goddess, beloved of Śaṅkara, O Lalitā, may you be pleased;
grant me beauty, grant me fame, grant me good fortune, and grant me prosperity.
"O Blessed One, may that which is desired by the gods be dear and increase my lifespan.

Having encased this great yantra, known as Lalitā, which bestows good fortune upon women, with the [respective] element, one should always wear it around the neck; thus she shall become endowed with beauty, auspiciousness, and most beloved by her husband.

then, having bathed on the fourth day, one should worship the three Subhagas.
"O Goddess, beloved of Anaṅga, may you be pleased with me;

O Goddess, listen as I describe the most beautiful *yoṣiddṛśya* (the "woman-to-be-seen") yantra, known as the *kāmarāja*, which brings about the sight of women;

Having engraved the yantra upon birch bark with *jātī* wood, one should write:

Then, one should carefully place five seed-syllables above the forehead:
Aiṃ, Hrīṃ, Klīṃ, Kṣīṃ, and Aiṃ; and likewise again at the end.
One should place the seed-syllables *aiṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and *klīṃ* in the corners;
likewise, lotus-shaped figures should be made above the seed-syllables in sequence.
Having thus fashioned a beautiful four-petalled [lotus] endowed with the seed-syllables, [one should proceed].
Having fashioned a silver image of Madana out of wood,
one should then install the Padma Yantra within its heart and worship it.
Every night, at the beginning and end of the day, one should perform [the worship] daily with auspicious enjoyments, various perfumes, incenses, lamps, and fruits.
When this is performed, that woman will certainly become a servant;
this supreme yantra, known as Śrīrāmarāja, brings women under one's control.
And here, Madana is to be worshipped within the belly of the image made of rājikā seeds:
Kāma, Anaṅga, Puṣpaśara, Kandarpa, and Mīnaketana.
O Lord, O Master, may the divine son of Śrī Viṣṇu be gracious toward us.
In this manner, it should be performed constantly until one reaches the state of being free from all constraints.
The Jāmadagnya Yantra for the pacification of anger: O wise one, if a friend, a member of one's kin, or even an enemy should become angry,
then one should construct this yantra for the purpose of quelling that wrath.
Having first drawn a circle in the center,
one should then encircle it above, below, to the north, and likewise to the south.
Having surrounded the excellent *bindu* in the four directions with a fence,
one should then write the syllable *huṃ* within the womb, above and below the middle of the *bindu*.
In the south and likewise in the north, the name of the one to be accomplished (sādhya) is written as before;
at the end, it is joined with the syllable *huṃ*, and below, [the word] "purify the mud" (*paṅka-prasādaya*) is placed.

Having placed this mechanism within the clay of a potter and having fashioned a small ball, one should perform worship; by this means, his anger is pacified.
The son of Jamadagni is a great instrument for immediately removing anger;
Jamadagni himself was free from anger, truthful in speech, and firm in his vows.
"O Janaka, the direct embodiment of pure being, salutations to you!
Having thus recited this mantra and having worshipped with diligence, [he should proceed].
