on the ninth day, a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas should be worshipped.
If not, boiled rice filled with human food should be given;
for anger departs from the heart in an instant, and one becomes serene.
The Lotus-named Yantra that Produces Good Fortune:
Therefore, I shall describe this yantra which bestows good fortune;
this yantra known as the Lotus is specifically intended for women.
O Goddess, by retaining that [fluid], a barren woman shall become pregnant;
and a woman whose children have died shall obtain an excellent son.
O Goddess, by wearing it, one is born with sons living, of this there is no doubt;
a man should write it on birch bark with yellow pigment (rocanā) and saffron (kuṅkuma).
One should first write the Praṇava (Oṃ), followed by the syllable Hrīṃ;
thereafter, the name of the Beloved (Ramaṇa) is established, ending with the syllable Hrīṃ.
Above that, one should draw three *oṃ* syllables in a row;
then, one should encircle all of that with a single circular line.
Upon that [lotus], one should place eight petals provided with seed-syllables; one should then assign the syllable *jūṃ* to the middle of each petal in the four directions.
The syllable *oṃ*, likewise *hrīṃ*, *juṃ*,
and similarly *hrīṃ* again— thus one should write these four seed-syllables (*bīja*).
One should worship the drawing located in a corner for three days.
With the *bhūṇaya* mantra, one should offer a single pair [of garments], saying, "May Lokeśa be pleased.
Afterwards, having wound it with thread, especially for the sake of the three worlds.
Having fashioned it into a circle like a jewel, one should wear it in the middle of a necklace;
by wearing it, O Goddess, incomparable and great good fortune is produced.
One will certainly obtain a son, and barrenness shall be pacified;
for this great yantra named Kamala was indeed created by Brahmā in the beginning.
O fair-faced one, this must not be given to just anyone by the practitioner.
The Yantra for Destroying All Fear of Tigers and Thieves: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim this yantra that wards off enemies;
when this yantra is held in the palm of one's hand, there is no fear of tigers whatsoever.
The procedure for writing and the materials previously mentioned are exactly as stated before;
O Goddess, in all rites of pacification, no other procedure exists.
The worship is as previously described, and the observances are likewise;
furthermore, this second, most excellent yantra should be inscribed upon birch bark.
A person should write the name of the target within the center of the syllable *hrīṃ*;
thereafter, the letter *ma* should be joined to each of its respective feet.
The letter *la*, the letter *va*, and the letter *ya* established at the end, joined with the vowel *ū*:
this is the captivating seed-syllable of Śāṭī.
Then, having properly wrapped it with two lines to form four corners,
and having encased it in the three metals, one should place it at the root of the arm or on the neck.
It destroys the fear of snakes and tigers, and likewise destroys the danger of thieves;
it destroys various calamities—there is no need for further deliberation.
The Child Protection Yantra:
Now I shall fully explain this most excellent yantra, which brings peace to children, provides protection, and destroys all calamities.
O Goddess, it should be drawn according to the previously stated procedure with the materials mentioned before in their proper order;
and upon a birch-bark leaf, worship is performed according to the previously stated procedure.
Having first drawn a circle in the center, one should then encircle it;
thereafter, one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus, beautiful and endowed with seed-syllables.
One should place each letter, ending with the *sakāra* and the *visarga*, upon every petal;
having subsequently performed the invocation according to the rules, one should [place them] at the root of the arm or on the throat.
One should wear the King of Yantras, encased in three layers of metal;
for by this, Śākinīs, Ḍākinīs, Bālagrahas, and others [will be subdued].
They go forth, leaving the fool behind, by means of the mastery of the King of Machines.
The Yantra for Destroying Fever Caused by Spirits—
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme destroyer of fever,
which exists as taught by physicians and destroys fever born of spirits and living beings.
A medicinal preparation of the *balās* (liquorice) should always be administered as a mechanical treatment for the pacification of fever.
It should indeed be obtained from the juices of a madman on a cloth from a cremation ground.
Having worshipped on the eighth and fourteenth days of the dark fortnight,
a person should then bury [the image] in a cremation ground during the day while remaining without food.
Having drawn a square with four corners, above it a four-petaled lotus, and likewise an eight-petaled lotus,
one should write the name in the center within the enclosure of the letter *ra*.
In the middle, within the interval, one should establish the letter *ra*;
thus there shall be twenty *repha*s (the letter *r*) everywhere in due order.
Having completely filled the ground and honored it with charming offerings of food and flowers,
at that very moment, the terrible fever-demon indeed blows away.
The Yantra for Stilling All:
Now, therefore, I shall proclaim the supreme protection against all things,
[which is effective] especially for those such as infants, spirits (pretas), and so forth.
O Goddess, just as fires are extinguished through negligence,
so too [the obstacles] are pacified by drawing [the deity] according to the previously mentioned rule and worshipping it according to the prescribed rite.
Having written the name in the center, one should encircle it with two circular lines and then draw eight petals, placing the seed-syllables of the swan (haṃsa) individually upon each.
Having encased it with three metals, one should wear it on the upper arm;
by the mere sight of it, venomous serpents will flee in the four directions.

When the foot has fallen due to negligence, it certainly remains paralyzed; likewise, when bitten through negligence, the poison does not ascend at all. This is the *yantra* spoken by Garuḍa for the purpose of paralyzing serpents.
The Bhūtatrāpaṇa Yantra: Now I shall explain that supreme yantra which terrifies the ḍākinīs,
as well as the bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and others, including the ḍākinīs and brahmarākṣasas.
When a man, a woman, or even a child is seized,
then one should employ a ritual device (yantra), whether for a woman, a man, or a child;
then one should employ that device to ward off the fear of spirits and demons.
Having written with a stylus upon a new and auspicious earthen plate,
one should draw four horizontal lines and five vertical lines;
thus, O fair-faced one, there will be exactly twelve squares.
Having written the syllable *hrīṃ* in each compartment, one should then worship it.
Then, having filled [the vessel] with cow dung, flowers,
and *harītakī*, one should place it upon a *dūlī* mat and kindle it with fires of *khadira* wood and *agaru*.
Seeing a great being weeping and trembling, he would flee;
abandoning the child at that very moment, he would depart by leaving the country.
The Yantra for Protecting the Fetus:
Now I shall proclaim that supreme yantra which protects the fetus; it should be inscribed with elephant-ichor upon a beautiful birch-bark scroll.
Having written the name in the center,
one should enclose it with two lines in a four-cornered [square];
having thus enclosed it, one should form a pericarp (karṇikā) that is circular in all four directions.

The syllable *ya*, the syllable *ra*, and [the syllable *la*] ending with the *visarga*, should each be written separately in the center of the pericarp; one should worship them in sequence as before.
Having wrapped it with iron wire, one should place it around the neck of a pregnant woman; delivery occurs easily, and miscarriage or abortion is averted.
Now I shall fully describe the instrument for the protection of the pregnant woman and for ensuring an easy delivery—
a device that brings relief to the pain of the birth canal and destroys malevolent spirits.

The wise one should write [the mantra] on birch bark according to the previously stated procedure and with the aforementioned materials in due order, following the prescribed rite in the central region.
One should write the Praṇava (Oṃ) and likewise the syllable Hrīṃ at the beginning and end of the name.
Then, one should enclose a long rectangular cloth with lines forming four corners,
and on each corner, both above and below, one should place three petals.
One should write "hrīṃ kṣaṃ" and likewise "hrīṃ" located in the corners and petals;
and one should write "kroṃ krīṃ raṃ" and likewise "hrīṃ" on the remaining petals.
Having thus drawn [the diagram] and worshipped it, it should be encased in three layers of metal.
For pregnant women, one should diligently apply this to the region of the throat; of this there is no doubt.
By this, colic, headache, and afflictions caused by malevolent spirits (bhūta-doṣa) are destroyed.
Thereafter, there will be an easy delivery; of this there is no doubt. This most wonderful king of yantras has been declared as a secret.

Now I shall explain that supreme *yantra* called Sarvatobhadra, which increases all good fortune, provides complete protection, and is known as the destroyer of deceit and flaws. It is auspicious in every respect.
One should draw five vertical lines and five horizontal lines;
when this is done, these sixteen squares are formed.
Having written the syllables beginning with 'a' in sequence in every square on a night during the day of Bhūtaja,
one should write them in order on a birch-bark leaf, encasing them with musk and sandalwood paste.
Having worshipped with various flowers, fragrances, and pleasing incenses,
and having honored the Brahmins with garments and wealth, one should worship that yantra while endowed with devotion to Him.

Thereafter, a man of composed mind should, according to the prescribed rite, diligently wear this excellent yantra at the root of his right arm, while a woman should wear it around her neck, using the three metals— copper, iron, and gold.
Through that retention, one quickly attains the supreme grace, becomes endowed with all beloved fortunes,
is freed from all fear, and obtains the great eightfold supernatural powers as they arise in this world.
The Yantra for Liberation from Bondage— Now, therefore, I shall proclaim this captivating yantra for liberation from bondage,
by the grace of which one who is bound or imprisoned is released in an instant.
When one does not find liberation for oneself despite being restrained by anyone,
then one should employ this yantra, which bestows liberation at that very moment.
On a very wide birch bark leaf, using camphor and saffron,
one should carefully write this most excellent yantra with a pen in a secluded place.
Having written the name in the center, and immediately after that the *hṛllekhā* mantra,
one should then properly encircle it with two circular lines.
One should cause [the mantra] "māṃ mocaya" to enter everywhere in the four directions;
having encircled the four corners with two lines.
It should be worshipped with effort by means of fragrant flowers and auspicious fruits.
Having encased it with the three metals and worn it as an amulet on the root of the arm or at the throat,
one is liberated from worldly existence in that very instant, becoming free from the sense of "mine."
The maintenance of one's natural state and constant restraint never fail to arise;
of this there is no doubt, even in dreams at any time.
The Machine for Achieving Victory in Gambling:
Now I shall describe that machine which brings victory in gambling;
by wearing this machine, one shall achieve supreme victory over all gamblers.
The "Vājina" (Horse) step is declared to consist of four squares;
by its retention, O Goddess, victory in gambling is certain in every case.
Having prepared ink from lampblack with a pen made of *kākapiccha* (crow-feather) on a birch-bark leaf (*bhūrja-patra*),

Nine lines should be drawn horizontally and vertically, extending across;
thus, O fair-faced one, there shall be sixty-four squares.
Having first inscribed them with the seed-syllables in the center, one should write them in direct order (anuloma) and then in reverse order (pratiloma);
indeed, those same syllables should be written again in the remaining squares according to the sequence of the wheel.
The low-born one, desiring to eat the flesh of a dog, was filled with longing for it.
The mantra for the *chadāvī* is "heṣṭivā mokṣiṇapātraṃ.
These very same [mantras] are the thirty-two *vājāni*, each consisting of three lines.
By which [treatise] the sixty-four arts are mastered by people according to their own desire,
and by whom this wonderful, enchanting, and pleasing yantra was proclaimed.
O Dear One, it is said that victory over all splendors arises from this meditative concentration (dhāraṇā).
The Yantra for Releasing One Bound in Shackles:
Now, therefore, I shall explain the yantra that releases one from fetters; by the power of this yantra, one bound by the soles of the hands and feet is liberated.
One should inscribe upon a bell-metal plate with yellow pigment (rocanā) and sandalwood paste,
as well as camphor, saffron, and musk.
Then, one should encircle the syllable *hrīḥ* located in the center with a circle;
thereafter, [one should draw] a sixteen-petaled lotus endowed with the vowels beginning with *a*.
Above that, one should construct [the mandala] endowed with thirty-two spokes;
one should write the consonants from *ka* to *sa* in their respective order.
Having performed the great worship with auspicious perfumes, flowers, and parched grain, as well as with food offerings, oblations, burnt sacrifices, and delightful gifts of land;
One should offer oblations one hundred and eight times with the mantra "Oṃ namaścaṇḍikāyai svāhā," using milk-rice, honey, sugar, and especially guggulu resin.
This should be performed every day, beginning on the seventh day;
first, having risen and bowed down, one should partake of food that is fragrant and pleasing to the palate.
One should provide wealth for the purpose of drinking [the nectar] and arrange it for half a ghaṭikā;
by holding that, even a man long bound shall be said to be liberated.
The yantra that pacifies artificial afflictions such as fever, stiffness, and dental diseases in children—
now, therefore, I shall fully explain the protection for children at all times,
the supreme yantra known as Jvalanarakṣā (Fire-Protection), which increases longevity.
The substance should be written according to the previously mentioned procedure using the auspicious materials described before;
it should be inscribed upon a birch-bark leaf with the name of the person to be accomplished placed in the center.
Then, one should properly enclose that with a line forming four corners;
above that, one should draw a trident with four corners starting from each corner.
In the corners, one should write the seed-syllable *ca*, adorned with a crescent moon;
the wise practitioner should then write the syllable *hrīṃ* above, below, and in between.
Having thus drawn that yantra and worshipped it according to the prescribed rite,
one should enclose it with the three metals and bind it around the middle of the neck.
Certain diseases, both physical and mental, arise from the presence of *upasargas*;
furthermore, there occurs envy, anger, as well as the affliction of the teeth.
The defect of breast milk never afflicts a young girl.
The Yantra for Paralyzing the Mouth of the Opponent—
Now, O beautiful one, I shall proclaim that paralyzer of speech,
the yantra known on earth as the "Paralyzer of the Opponent's Mouth."
One should draw [the design] with yellow pigment in the middle of a stone casket,
using yellow orpiment, green vitriol, turmeric, and realgar.
One should describe a yellow substance combined with saffron;
having written the name in the center, one should then encircle it with a triangle.
Then, one should properly encircle it with a single line to form a perfect circle;
thereafter, one should fashion eight petals upon that.
One should write the seed-syllable *la*, adorned with a bindu, in the center;
likewise, it should be written upon the eight petals, and one should worship it with auspicious flowers.
Likewise, with yellow-colored incense, clearly manifest and auspicious lamps,
and offerings of milk-rice (pāyasa) and jaggery, one should feed a single Brāhmaṇa.
Then, one should bury it in the ground and establish it as before;
[this applies] in disputes, legal proceedings, and in the pleasant deliberations of the scriptures.
The opponent's mouth becomes paralyzed; of this there is no doubt. O Great Goddess, this great yantra has been told to you as something to be strictly concealed.
The Yantra named Śāntika-pauṣṭika—
listen, O Goddess, to this supreme secret yantra which provides ultimate protection;
it is known as the great protector for children, women, and men.
On an auspicious lunar day and a beautiful day, one should inscribe [the mantra] upon a bell-metal vessel using yellow orpiment,
saffron, and especially camphor.
One should prepare a board smeared with musk and engraved with a piece of *jātī* wood,
featuring eight lines drawn vertically and likewise eight lines drawn horizontally.
In this way, forty-nine squares indeed come into being;
one should draw all of them in sequence starting from the northeast (īśāna) within each square.
In that very same sequence, the remaining consonants should be written in the remaining squares. Having thus written the seed-syllables (bījas), one should then draw three tridents;
one should certainly write them in succession above each line in the four directions.
Seven *kroṃ* syllables are to be inscribed in the western part of the eastern row;
having thus inscribed that yantra, one should worship it with a spirit of devotion.
With white lotuses, *puṇḍarīkas*, charming *śatapatras*,
as well as with *mālatīs*, *yūdhikās*, *ketakas*, and *mallikas*.
One should offer *vakula* flowers and whatever auspicious fruits are available according to the season;
however, one should carefully avoid flowers that are odorless or red in color.
With betel leaves mixed with camphor, incense, lamps, and white garments;
O Dear One, having worshipped for three days with various food offerings (naivedya),
one should daily recite the Saptashati and feed Brahmins for three days.
Having worshipped [the deity] with milk-rice and whatever ghee is desired,
one who sleeps on the ground for three days [should partake of] food and the fragrance of *rocanā*.
Having extracted the pill, one should make it and then encase it with the three metals;
that essence should be drunk with water, O fair-faced one.
When employed by means of the Vidyā, O Goddess, agitation arises in another;
one should wear the pill on the upper arm or on the neck.
By the retention of that yantra, misfortune is pacified,
as are strife and, in particular, ill fortune.
Whatever has been performed by another, all of that is rendered ineffective;
such rites for pacification (śāntika) or nourishment (pauṣṭika) are difficult to obtain even from the gods themselves.
First is that which is called the King of Yantras, which produces immediate results.
In this very manner, all yantras are to be accomplished; such is the direction for practitioners.
Thus ends [the section] on specific topics in the Uttarapīṭhikā of the Śāntikamalākara treatise.
The incomparable compendium on the ritual of the yantra is completed. Homage to Śrī Kāśī Viśveśvara!
The Vedic Āgama Sūtra spoken by Śrī Parāśara, from the Uttarapīṭhikā of the work of Śānti Kamalākara.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the installation of the Śiva-liṅga image. Having divided [the tradition] into five parts—namely, Pāñcarātra, Pañcaśaiva, Kevala-tāntrika, Paramahaṃsa, and [the fifth]—the Brāhmaṇa belongs to the Pāñcarātra; his ritual is Pāñcarātra. His practice regarding the liṅgas and images consists of mudrās, bandhas, and well-known rites such as showing [the deity], service, and so forth, excluding Vedic mantras. For all Brāhmaṇas, the Pañcaśaiva is the Brāhmaṇa; his ritual is Pañcaśaiva, and he lives by that, as does one who is self-perfected (svayaṃbhūta).

Among those that have become active, there is the self-manifested Narmada, as well as the self-manifested yantra, mudrā, ritual action (kriyā), and mantra, which are renowned in the Āgamas; these are called the "Fivefold Śaiva" (Pañcaśaiva) when their rites are accomplished. All agree that this pertains to the vision (darśana), service (sevā), and grace (prasāda). Whatever is offered therein must not be taken; it is the *nirmālya* of Śiva. Starting from the verse "except for the water of the triple-pathed river," it concludes with "one should place [it] upon all lingas."

The Vedic practitioners declare that this very [image] made of *vijjāyata* wood is the one to be used everywhere; however, there is a distinction regarding those from the Narmadā region and in the case of physical forms (*vigraha*). What is offered there should indeed be accepted because it is established by Vedic custom. As for the purely Tantric system, which abounds in mantras and rituals and is well-known among the Śūdra caste using wooden, earthen, or stone [images], some Brāhmaṇas desire it; yet in that regard, devotion is more important. Those fallen from their duties who perform acts involving the killing of living beings are merely called "Tantrikas."

When devotion arises toward the Supreme Swan (Paramahaṃsa), who is established in meditation within the divine fields of Kailāsa, then they establish Him as the worshipful Mānasa [Liṅga] within the forms of ritual emblems (kriyā-liṅga) and physical images (vigraha)—whether made of gem, yantra, or wood—as He is accessible through meditation. By the power of His attraction, the state of being "Bahulakī" (the one of many manifestations) exists there; everything is acceptable here, for there is no distinction regarding the scriptures (āgama). For Brahmins and others, devotion is voluntary; whatever is well-known according to one's own caste, that is how it should be performed.

When one is about to perform the meritorious rite of the installation of a Śiva-liṅga made of stone (aṃru), one should observe the Vedic initiation (dīkṣā) according to the Āgama; then, abstaining from women, avoiding salt and alkaline substances, becoming a lake for the meditation on Śiva, always speaking gently, truthful, virtuous, and having conquered the senses, one should practice for the sake of union with Śiva. Having prepared a Narmada-liṅga or a Kriyā-liṅga along with its retinue, as well as a bull and the Yakṣas beginning with Gaṇeśa—if it be a Vedic rite—then [the procedure follows].

Alternatively, it is taught that the installation of a Śiva-liṅga image should be performed upon a *bali-pīṭha*, under a *dhava* tree, during the asterisms sacred to Śambhu (*śāmbhavī*), on auspicious days, at the solstices, and in divine sacred fields (*divyakṣetra*) or pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha*). Regarding this, first, having performed the "attainment of the abode" (*ālayasiddhi*) as prescribed—starting from the verse beginning with "nirmite yadbhūmeḥ" and ending with "śivam"—one should prepare the following: the five roots, the five barks, the five fruits, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), and likewise five cloths and threads.

The five impurities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), the five fragrances, the five minerals, the five types of incense oils, and the five seed grains—these constitute fourteen. Likewise, the linga, the yantra, the cloth, the eye-salve, gold, collyrium, the cow, the trident, and the coconut—these likewise constitute [the set]. The linga, the yantra, the cloth, the eye-salve, and gold.

Having procured collyrium, a cow, a trident, coconuts, pumpkins, the five gems, yantras, offerings, lamps, mirrors, sacrificial fuel (samit), clarified butter, kuśa grass, ladles (sruk-sruva), sandalwood, and so forth; having procured five earthen bowls, full jars, and Brahmins learned in the mantras of the four Vedas and the Āgamas; and having procured tiger skins, rudrākṣa beads, mustard seeds, cooked rice, milk, bilva leaves, and balls of ash; and having procured the eight bindings, the eight pedestals, the sacrificial post, the banner, and the pitcher for the deities mentioned therein.

Having procured garments, images, and other auspicious items, musical instruments, vehicles, palanquins, umbrellas, fly-whisks, divine silk cloths, and ornaments, and having given the prescribed sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one who possesses the materials for worship should sit down and request the Brahmins.

Then, when the next day had dawned, having bathed in the waters of the great river and performed the *puṇyāha-vācana* rite together with mantra-perfected Brahmins in his own temple of Śiva, he should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), saying: "For the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord Śrī Parameśvara, I shall install [the deity] along with his retinue. Having chosen the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and honored the *brahmā* priest and the *ācārya*, and having fastened the *kaṅkaṇa* bracelet while reciting the *Bṛhatsāman* during the prayers (*japa-karma*), he should proceed at a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) four cubits square and two cubits deep.

Having established the fire according to the rules, and having performed the rites up to the *paristaraṇa* (spreading of grass), he should worship the fire and the water with ornaments. Then, having sown fourteen seeds into five shallow bowls (*pañcaśarāva*), he should invoke and constantly worship these five deities—Brahmā, Indra, Dharma, Varuṇa, and Soma—until the conclusion of the *yāga* rite. Having recited the *anuvāka* beginning with "triśūlam āśu śūśāna," he should place [the image] at the base of the banner, sprinkle it with the milk of the *arka* plant and water while reciting the Rudra-mantras, worship it as a sentient being, and place it within a *kūṣmāṇḍa* vessel.

Having established the two door-keepers with the mantra "cakratuṇḍāya" as far as the limit of the ritual action, one should render them insentient and equal; having summoned the guardians of the quarters, one should perform the binding of the directions, and having driven stakes all around the site of the temple, one should encircle it with five-colored threads.

Thereafter, having prepared a heap of grain and installed the Liṅga-yantra, one should invoke Brahmā into the Brahma-kalaśa in its center with the mantra "Iśānaḥ" (Iśānaḥ, namaḥ śambhavāya, namo hiraṇyabāhave, tatpuruṣāya); one should invoke Umā and the Vasus with the five mantras beginning with "Sadyojāta"; one should invoke the eleven Rudras with the twenty mantras beginning with "Nidhanapataye namaḥ"; and one should invoke Virūpākṣa with "Ṛtas tavyam" and Rudra with "Nama se rudramanyave."

One should worship the host of three hundred Rudras with the verse beginning "tvā"; Nārāyaṇa with the verse "sahasraśīrṣam"; Durgā with the two verses beginning "jātavedase"; Skanda with "mātāmahāsenāya"; the golden Sun with "ādityo vaḥ"; Virāja with "sahasraśīrṣā"; Caṇḍī with "brahma śivo me astu"; the Great Bull with "vṛṣabhaṃ mā cakratuṇḍāya"; Nandin with "cakratuṇḍāya"; likewise Bhṛṅgin; the twice-born [Brahmin] with "namaste rudramanyave"; the trident with "namostu sarpebhyaḥ"; and Śeṣa with the same.

One should offer gold for the nine planets and the guardians of the quarters with their respective mantras, [visualizing them] as having golden wings and shining eyes. One should offer [gold] for the rivers and oceans with "I measure thee, O Gaṅgā; from the ocean..."; for the earth with "The earth is a cow"; for water with "All this is indeed water"; for fire with "I praise Agni, the Lord"; for wind with "The wind is the breath of life"; for space with "Earth is the first"; for time with "The moments, the hours..."; for Soma with "Soma is the cow"; for the stars with "May Agni protect us"; for the sages with "In whom..."; for the meters with "By the meter..."; and for Dhruva, the king.

Thus, having invoked these groups of Śākinīs, Ḍākinīs, and the aforementioned deities into their respective jars, and having adorned them with garments and so forth and worshipped them with perfumes and other offerings, one should pray to them properly.
Now, one should perform the preliminary consecration in water (*jalādhivāsa*) for the forms of the venerable Śiva-liṅgas in order to eliminate defects such as cruelty and the like.

One should perform the *saṃmukhīkaraṇa* (making present), the consecration with those mantras, and the statement by the Brāhmaṇas, "May that be so. In every case, one should touch the water while reciting the *anuvāka* beginning with "In the waters... (*ambhasyapāre*). Having touched the water, one should mutter [the mantra] beginning with "The gods made the night... (*devakṛtasyainaso 'vayajanam asi*) for one night, or three nights, or two months; this is what has been declared. One should always touch the water while reciting the *anuvāka* beginning with "In the waters... (*ambhasyapāre*). After worshipping the water as the "Womb of the Gods" (*devagarbha*), it should then be raised up. Likewise, the perfection of the seed (*bījasiddhi*) is well-known from the Vedic tradition, such as through the consecration of grains (*dhānyādhivāsa*) for seven nights and so forth.

One should place fourteen types of grain within [the vessel] with the mantra *yājāce*. Having touched the heap of grain, one should mutter [the mantra]; this is the consecration (*abhimantreṇa*) of the grain-heap by that mantra. Having worshipped the grain-heap and then lifted it up, one should touch the ghee with the two mantras beginning with *vīryatejo balavṛddhi*; this is the consecration of that ghee by those mantras. Having worshipped that ghee and then lifted it up, one bathes [the deity] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*); this is the external purification of the body, the removal of the defects such as the heat of the heated metal.

One should sprinkle [the disciple] with pure fire-mantras using both stated and unstated words; through this, the attainment of divinity is achieved. Having bound [him] with *darbha* grass, the attainment of the twenty-five principles (*tattvas*) is accomplished in due order by performing the sprinkling while reciting: "The earth is vastness, the earth is the cow, the earth is the upholder"—thus the attainment of the earth-principle is achieved. By consecrating him with those respective mantras, the attainment of the element earth is secured. With the three verses beginning "O Waters, you are most beneficent" (*āpo hi ṣṭhā*) and the hymn "The golden-horned one" (*hiraṇyaśṛṅgam*), he is sprinkled with the five waters; by consecrating him with those respective mantras, the attainment of the element water is secured. "O Agni, you are... [and so forth].

Having sprinkled [the disciple] with ashes while reciting the mantra "Agneryatte" and consecrating it with the respective mantra, there is the accomplishment of the element fire (tejobhūtasiddhi). Having sprinkled [him] with ashes while reciting the mantra "Vāyor-yatte" and consecrating it with the respective mantra, there is the accomplishment of the element air (vāyubhūtasiddhi). Next, having bathed [him] with the five incenses while reciting the respective mantras, there is the accomplishment of the element air; thereafter, having sprinkled [him] with the five flowers while reciting the mantras, there is the accomplishment of the great elements (mahābhūtasiddhi) through the consecration with the respective mantras. One should act in this manner, and thus the accomplishment of the five great elements occurs—accomplishment occurs, accomplishment occurs, accomplishment occurs.

Thus, for those who have mastered the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*) and possess bodies that are Śiva-liṅgas, one should effect the accomplishment of the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*). One should perform a bath with earth using water from the earth-element with the two verses beginning "The earth is the support of all" (*bhūmir bhūmnāsyonā pṛthivī*), accompanied by the consecration of those respective mantras. A bath with the five types of bark-water is performed with the consecration of those respective mantras, using the five verses beginning "O Waters, you are most healing" (*āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*) and "The golden-colored ones" (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*). A bath with the water of five sprouts is performed with the consecration of those respective mantras, using the two verses beginning "O Agni, you of vast radiance" (*agne yatte bṛhadbhāno*). [Then follows] the wind... [tavavāyu].

One should perform the bath with the five decoctions (*pañcakāṣāya-snāna*) using the two verses beginning with *vṛddhaṃ ha spate* and *aśvatthe vo*, followed by consecration (*abhimarśana*) with their respective mantras. Thereafter, one should perform the bath with the five honeys (*pañcamadhu-snāna*) using the two verses beginning with *madhu vātā*, followed by consecration with their respective mantras. By doing so, one achieves mastery over those five subtle elements (*tanmātras*). Then, one should effect the mastery over the five organs of action (*karmendriyas*) and the five organs of perception (*jñānendriyas*). One should bathe [the deity] with the waters of the five jewels (*pañcaratnodaka*) using the *Aṇoraṇīyān* anuvāka, the *Saharaṇā* mantra, and the *Nīti* mantra, each with its respective mantra.

From the consecration with mantras, there is the perfection of the five organs of action; one should show five lamps while consecrating them with the five mantras beginning with "Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ," "Yaḥ prāṇataḥ," "Āpo hi ṣṭhā," "Mānastoke," and "Iṣe tvā. From that consecration with those respective mantras, there is the perfection of the five organs of knowledge. Then, one should effect the perfection of the five objects of sense through the three mantras beginning with "Madhu vātā" [and the following two]: "Āpyāyasva," "Adhikrāṇoḥ," and "Ghṛtaṃ mimikṣire"; and with the eight mantras beginning with "Madhu vātā," "Svāduḥ pavasva," "Svāduḥ pavasvāyāḥ," "Phalinīḥ," and "Āpo hi ṣṭhā."

One should bathe [the deity] with the five honeys (*pañcamadhu*), the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and the waters of the five rivers, consecrated by their respective mantras; thereby, success in the five daily rites (*pañcādyavasthā*) is attained, as well as success regarding the seed-body (*bījaśarīra*). Then, for the sake of attaining the gross, subtle, and causal bodies—which are the form of the power of the Cosmic Egg (*brahmāṇḍa-śakti*), the consciousness of the entire moving and unmoving phenomenal world—one should properly bathe [the deity] with cow’s ghee, reciting from "Obeisance to Nidhanapati" up to "All this indeed is He. This is the bathing of the Śiva-liṅga with cow’s ghee, reciting from "Sadyojāta" up to "Truth is the Real."

One should bathe the images with clarified butter using these respective mantras: for Śivā with "tām agnivarṇām" (RV 10.184.3) and "gaurīm imām kātyāyanāyai" (RV 10.86.13); for the Goddess with the three verses beginning "gaṇānāṃ tvā" (TS 4.1.11.1); for Gaṇapati with "vakratuṇḍāya" (Ganapatistotra); for Kumāra with "kumāraṃ mātā mahāsenāya" (RV 2.33.1); for the Bull with "mā caṅkramuṇḍāya"; and for Cañcikā with "śivo me astu". Having thus bathed them with ghee and water consecrated by those respective mantras, one should perform the *pañcīkaraṇa* (fivefold refinement), whereby the accomplishment of the seed-body (*bīja-śarīra*) occurs. One should then offer milk to the sentient [deities] as a sacrificial oblation.

Then one should perform the purification of impurities (*malasiddhi*) for those who have accomplished the *pañcīkaraṇa* and whose forms are the *śivaliṅgas*. For the Brahmins, there is the sprinkling of nectar with the mantra "Śukramasi" and so forth; the consecration with the five oils (*pañcataila*); bathing with powders and ointments; bathing with warm water; and the consecration with their respective mantras beginning with "Hiraṇyavarṇā" and ending with "Brahmavarcasāya. One should bathe [the deity] with the five perfumes (*parimala*), turmeric, saffron, sandalwood, and water, using the hymn (*sūkta*) "Hiraṇyavarṇā," followed by the consecration with mantras from the *Mahārudra*.

One should bathe [the deity] with the waters of five jars consecrated by five Brahmins using mantras such as the *Puruṣasūkta*, *Śrīsūkta*, *Gāyatrī*, and the *Pañcākṣarī*. By means of the mantras beginning with "May the heroes consecrate you" (*sūrāstvābhiṣiñcantu*) and "From the field of the God" (*devasya kṣetrāt*), there is the attainment of sovereignty through such consecrations. Having wiped the form of the Śiva-liṅga with a cloth, one should worship these: the *Liṅgayantra* of Śiva, the *Śrīyantra* of the Goddess, the *Bhadrayantra* of Gaṇapati, and the respective *yantras* of the other deities.

In the four directions, adorned with divine ornaments and a bed of swan-feather cushions, and further beautified by eight auspicious vessels such as *śātibhāṇḍas* and *kalaśas*, along with banners, flags, and pennants; in divine places such as swinging couches and gate-towers (*gopuras*), decorated with various wonderful five-colored creepers; and within the jeweled pavilions of the assembly halls, having installed the respective yantras upon the center of washed white couches and worshipped them with fragrant flowers such as jasmine (*mallikā*), *kunda*, *bakula*, *campaka*, *āsphota*, *ketakī*, and *pāṭalī*.

Having scattered [flowers] everywhere and having turned all people toward delight, and having taken hold of the deities established in the Vedic Āgamas with auspicious musical instruments, the sounds of *bhāṃkāra*, dance, song, and ritual services, one should have the brother’s insignia fashioned in gold using auspicious mantras such as "Bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ," "Mamāgne," and "Dhruvastesthām. At that time, while some remain within the range of vision, others, standing at the side, should perform all the ritual services for the King during the night watch until the end of the service on the couch.

In front of Ciṣya, one should place a trident, a kūṣmāṇḍa fruit, a coconut, a full water-pot, an offering (bali), a lamp, and a mirror; for the others, a coconut, a full jar, an offering, incense, and a lamp. Some [place these] within the inner curtain. One should meditate upon all the officiating priests (adhvaryus) and the patron (yajamāna) as the deity, because of the recollection [of the mantra] beginning with "The Rudra who is the slayer... and so forth.

Then, having seated the deities invoked within the sacrificial ladle (*yāgalālā*) and worshipped them, one should adorn the Lord of Sacrifice (*yajñeśvara*), spread the sacred grass (*paristīrya*), and sprinkle water around the altar (*pariṣicya*). One should prepare the vessels and provide fourteen thousand measures of sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*), parched grain (*caru*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and *kuśa* grass. Then, in due order, one should perform the principal oblation (*pradhāna-homa*) for the invoked deities of the jars using the substances of fuel-sticks, *caru*, and *ājya*. For the specific deity intended, one should perform twelve thousand oblations with its respective mantra, as well as for the auxiliary deities (*aṅga-devatāḥ*) and the principal deities (*pradhāna-devatāḥ*).

Having performed the expiatory oblations (*prāyaścitta-homa*) and completed the remainder of the rite by offering the *pūrṇāhuti*, he should then pay homage to the deities of the couch (*paryaṅka-deva*), who are established through Vedic scriptures and mantras. Having touched water for purification (*upaspṛśya*), he should mutter the *asuvāka* hymn beginning with "divaspari" and the Yajus mantra "asminn aham. He should offer wealth to the deities with the eight mantras beginning with "ayaṃ kaliḥ. Having offered the husks and grain-particles (*phalīkaraṇa*) into the fire, and having addressed the deities of the couch with the mantra "mām agne varcaḥ," he should go with the Brahmins to the northern side of the four-fold path (*uttara-catuṣpatha*). Returning quickly, he should remain there for a *muhūrta*.

O Lord, one should accomplish [the rite] while remaining within the body; having placed the knots of *darbha* grass into their respective jars, performing the placement of mantras (*nyāsa*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and recitation (*japa*), and having taken up the deities, one should then come to the pedestal. There, at an auspicious moment, having prostrated in the *vīrabandha* posture, having uttered the *vyāhṛtis* along with the *praṇava* and the *sarvaliṅga* mantra, and having meditated upon the Supreme Lord situated in the center of the heart-lotus, one should invoke Him here with the mantra "Bring [Him] here" (*āvaha*). Thus, the *liṅga* established through the Vedas and Āgamas is the *brahmamāyā*.

One should place the *bāṇa* (the linga) upon the pedestal of Viṣṇu’s form for a *muhūrta*; one must remain in seclusion, display the *sthāpana-mudrā*, and perform the laying of the stone while reciting the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣara*). One should properly endow the various forms with consciousness using their respective mantras, sound the bell, and perform the binding of the nine directions. Without touching water, one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of life-force) with the appropriate mantras, restrain the vital breaths (*prāṇāyāma*), and again apply the knot of *darbha* grass. Then, the principal consecration jar (*mukhya-kalaśa*) of the respective deity should be used, along with gold.

When the accomplishment of the *kalā* through the *spaśanā* has occurred, one should then offer milk to the Lord. At an auspicious moment, the Brahmins should recite the *svasti* mantras; there should be the ringing of bells, the sound of *ghaṇṭā*, and the blare of trumpets. Facing north, one should sit and kindle oneself as the Lord Īśāna, reciting the threefold mantra: "Obeisance to Īśāna, obeisance to Śambhu. Having honored the deities of the directions and scattered mustard seeds, one should perform the binding of the quarters (*digbandhana*) and recite the mantras for the hands.

Then, having written the name of the patient and the names of the [relevant] times in a copper vessel containing cow’s ghee, and having consecrated it with the respective mantras—specifically with the five mantras beginning with "agnirāyuṣmān"—the preceptor, together with the Brahmins, should perform the rite of tying [the vessel] around the neck of the disciple and declare him free from affliction. He should invoke Śrīyam, Brahmā, the eleven Rudras, and all the purifying waters of the jars; he should perform the sprinkling of the stream of water one hundred times for the sake of the senses. He should mutter the Madhu-mantras and cause [the disciple] to consume honey. [He should apply] the lotus-mark on the eyes and the tiger-skin mark.

Having worn a leather Rudrākṣa and sacred ash on his body, and having adorned [the image] with silk garments and ornaments of gold, one should perform a great worship (mahā-pūjā) with twenty-five offerings and satisfy the Supreme Lord; thus one attains union with Śiva. With the eight mantras beginning with "hiraṇyagarbha," one should offer eight lamps, as well as offerings of food (bali), incense, and light. Having touched the deities while reciting "satyaṃ prapadye," one then causes a firebrand of Darbha grass to be carried around [the image]. One should hold great festivals at the four quarters, feed the Brāhmaṇas, and fully honor the officiating priest (ṛtvij).

After the consecrated deities have been purified with the *praṇītā* water, one should complete the concluding oblation (*homa-śeṣa*). Then, the Brāhmaṇa should give everything to the Kṣatriya and others according to the prescribed rule, saying: "This field, this wealth, and this temple of Śiva have been prepared by me; I bestow them upon you. O Wielder of the Trident, please perform the final consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*)."

Having spoken thus, one who is firm-minded and free from desire should perform the rites according to the sequence of his birth; he should offer a cow to the preceptor as a definitive gift, and he should purchase the fruit [of the rite]. He enjoys the fruit in this world and is glorified in the world of Śiva. "He is glorified in the world of Śiva," so said the Blessed Parāśara.

Next, they declare the following regarding what occurs within the five-thread boundary (pañcasūtra) in a temple of Śiva: if there is the intentional or unintentional entry or touch by heretics (pāṣaṇḍa), the most sinful, those afflicted with leprosy, outcasts (vrātya), Vaiśyas, Śūdras, Caṇḍālas, those of mixed castes (saṃkarajāti), or those of low birth; or by dogs, cocks, donkeys, vultures, crows, and other wicked creatures; or by kings, thieves, or due to the adversity of time—[in such cases] one must perform expiation (prāyaścitta). Regarding the breach of the sequence of the five threads, the first and second [rules apply]; this is the sequence therein.

The bull, the leader of the Gaṇas (Gaṇeśa), the Liṅga, the sacrificial altar (Vedi), the seat for offerings (Bali-pīṭha), the king of banners (Dhvajarāja), and the Śāmbhavī [mudrā]—these are the eight ancillaries (Upāṅgas); among them, there is no fault in the first.

The sprinkling with the five *sūktas* is the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for that very [incident]. We shall describe its procedure: if there is loosening, shaking, or burning by fire, the re-installation (*saṃsthāpana*) must be performed according to the previously stated method. Having become pure and having invited excellent Brāhmaṇas who know the four Vedas under an auspicious constellation, and having caused them to pronounce the *puṇyāha* (day of merit), one should create Śiva through an uninterrupted consecration (*abhiṣecana*) beginning with "In the water" (*ambhasi*) and ending with "All beings" (*viśvaṃ bhūtam*). Then, one should mutter the mantra: "Tāmagnivarṇām," "Gaurīmimāya."

Having touched Umā, one should perform an uninterrupted consecration while reciting the mantra beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇām" and mutter that mantra; for other deities, one should likewise follow the sequence of their respective mantras. In this manner, [one should worship] Vakratuṇḍa, Cakratuṇḍa, Kumāra, Caṇḍikeśvara, Bhṛṅgīśa, Nandikeśa, Balipīṭha, and Dvaja in succession. Whatever deities are present, as well as the trident and the aforementioned deities, [should be worshipped].

Having thus consecrated [the vessel] with these mantras, one should perform the installation of the pitcher (*kalaśa*). The procedure there is as follows: having first honored the Brahman, Īśāna with his retinue, and as previously mentioned, the guardians of the directions, the nine planets, Nārāyaṇa, Āditya, the Earth, the rivers and oceans, the hosts of Rudras, and Agni—the impurity—having performed this according to the rules in due order, one should satisfy Maheśvara by offering four times each of sesame, milk-rice, *rudrākṣa* fruits, fuel-sticks, and clarified butter with their respective mantras, accompanied by the *vyāhṛtis*, according to the characteristics of each deity.

Having performed the purification with water from the ritual pitcher (kalaśa) using the respective mantras for each deity and having established the foundation of the temple, and having worshipped those respective deities amidst the sounding of auspicious musical instruments, one should offer an oblation at the site of the offering with a trident on a four-footed base while reciting the mantra "Hiraṇyanābha. Then, one should conduct a great festival that brings supreme joy to Maheśāna and the other forms [of the deity], complete the remainder of the fire sacrifice (homa), and thoroughly purify the deities with the water from the full-vessel (pūrṇapātra). Taking cow's ghee and the ashes of the sacrifice in a copper vessel—

Having consecrated the deities with the five mantras beginning with "Devanāmāni saṃlekhyāgamanirāyamuṣmān," one should recite those respective mantras. Having performed the placement of the stone (śilānyāsa), that secret [rite] shall be the binding of the directions (digbandhana). Then, having worshipped the tortoise (kūrma) and adorned it with garments and other offerings, that secret [rite] shall be the binding of the directions. Then all the Brāhmaṇas should offer a handful of flowers with mantras, as well as the bali-offering, lamps, incense, and a firebrand of *darbha* grass.

Having performed that, he should say, "I take refuge in Truth," touch the gods, and mutter [the mantra]; having offered the bali-oblation to the Kṣetrapāla and touched water, he should perform the ācamana three times; having adorned the preceptor, he should give him a cow with its calf; having honored the officiating priests (ṛtvij) and fed the Brāhmaṇas, he attains union with Śiva.

Now, one should likewise perform a great festival for the sake of the welfare and the pleasure of men—a festival for the limbs of the ritual—for those forms of Mahādeva that are well-known in the Vedic scriptures, yet have been neglected by those deceived by the Pāñcarātra and whose worship has been interrupted. We shall proclaim the procedure for that: one should perform the *soma-aryaman* rite for three nights, reciting the mantra three thousand times during the three junctions of the day; with the *triśūla* mantra, one should offer oblations (*bali*) on the path three times over the three days; and having summoned the gods with great festivals, [one should lead them] to the temple of Śiva, the triple-heaven.

Upon the great king of trident banners of those who have taken their stand, one should raise up the exceedingly radiant great cloth [painting] and the great bull in the upper portion—[depicting] Mahāviṣṇu, Māyādevī, Maheśāna, Maheśvarī, Vidhi, Sarvasvatī, Skanda, Gaṇanātha, and Cañcikā.

Having invoked Deva-senā, Suvarṇa, Soma, Aryaman, Paramahaṃsa, Mahendra, and the other guardians of the directions (dikpālakas) according to their respective tantras, and having worshipped them while the Udgātṛs sing, one should present the bali offering on the bali-pīṭha with the trident. On the altar (vedikā), having invoked the aforementioned deities upon the *kalisa* [pedestal], and having duly worshipped the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) during the three days in due order. Every day, at the two twilights, one should conduct the protective initiation (*rakṣādīkṣā*) according to the sequence of the Śaiva branch (*śākhā*), accompanied by the *nāndī* and *puṇyāha* rites, using the seeds of the *aṅkura*, *āra*, and *paṇa*.

Having duly honored the Brahmins with great musical instruments, one should prepare a water-pot for Kātyāyanī and Kapardin. One should offer *madhuparka* and boiled rice with ghee as a sacrificial gift (*nivedana*), along with new garments and a palanquin. On the head and forehead, one should mark auspicious signs of the head; and one should meditate upon the auspicious maiden who is the daughter of the Great Mountain, the Root Mountain, and the Himavat Mountain. Then one should say: "I give [this] to the Auspicious Excellent One, Sadāśiva, the remover of obstacles, belonging to the lineage of Paraśiva, Parameṣṭhiśiva, and Parāparaśiva. Thus he should speak.

Then, with auspicious words, she should place into the joined palms of the bridegroom—held by the bride as an offering—unhusked grains, bark-cloth, unbroken rice, milk, honey, ghee, and unmixed curd, along with the nine gems. Śiva should then fasten auspicious protective amulets upon the couple and bind the auspicious marriage-thread around the neck of the bride; he should certainly meditate upon the Seven Sages and recite the auspicious mantra.

Having thus performed the extensive installation of a Liṅga with all its ancillaries in the mortal world, a mortal who possesses all his goals and desires fulfilled attains union with Ambā at the end of his life in that world of meritorious deeds.
Thus ends the *Vaidikāgamasūtra* spoken by the venerable Parāśara.
May there be the attainment of the grace of the venerable Sāmbasadāśiva.
[Now follows] the deliberation on the consecration of village deities and other matters.

*Śrīgaṇeśāya namaḥ*. The *Parāśara Sūtra*: Now, for the prosperity of their own sacrificial rites (*samiṣṭi*), villagers should install and worship the village goddess (*grāma-śakti*) in a place within the village or outside the village. Vaiṣṇavas should worship her in the middle of the village; Śāktas on the outskirts; Kāpālikas in a cremation ground; Gāṇapatyas at the gateway or at the base of a pillar; others, such as merchants, in the marketplace; and all others in a forest near water. They should worship her in shrines made of stone, wood, or clay.

Therein are the deities: the Brāhmaṇa, the Skull (Kapāla), Viṣṇu’s Head, Reṇukā’s Head, Draupadī’s Form, Sītā’s Body, the Pramathas, the Śaivas, the Vaiṣṇavas, the attendants (pāriṣada), the planets (graha), the Yoginīs, and various kinds of Śaktis born of wood, stone, and clay; those who have fallen from grace and those who have not attained perfection; Śunaḥśepha, Triśaṅku, Ghaṭotkaca, and others; Durgā, who is multiformed and born from the womb of Devakī; the Śakti Pūtanā and others who devour children; and the Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, Śākinīs, and Ḍākinīs.

Betālādyākṣa, Kirātadevī, Śabara, Rudra, and those of hundreds of millions of fierce forms; Mātaṅgī, Śyāmalā, Ucchiṣṭa-Gaṇapati, Ucchiṣṭa-Cāṇḍālī, Surabhāṇḍeśvara, Mohinī, Rākṣasī, Tripurālaṅkhiṇī, Saubhadevī, Sāmudrikā, Vanagurgā, Durgā, and the self-sacrificing ones who have been instructed; the village deities such as the Dravyadevis, Guṇadevis, and Kriyādevīs are worshipped collectively with offerings of liquor, meat, oblations, lamps, and festivals.

There, the heroes who follow Ghaṭotkaca and those who follow Bhairava—namely Bhairava, Mahākāla, Vīrabhadra, Vṛṣabha, Gaṇapati, and Hanumān—are present; among them, the Teacher (Śiva) is especially worshipped as Bhairava, along with Śūlinī, Pratyaṅgirā, and Rāśmaśānavāsinī, and Kṛtyā.

Having worshipped these [deities] with the leaves, flowers, perfumes, milk, and other offerings of *kapivīra*, *raktakaravīra*, *śvetārka*, *nīla*, *unmatta*, *japā*, *picumanda*, *snuhī*, and so forth, as described in various Purāṇas, one should fasten a black goat, a kid, or a *ṣahiṣa* animal to the flagstaff of the house in the eastern direction by circumambulating the fire-pit. Having cut off its leg with a sword, one should insert it into its mouth and place a bowl of oil upon its head, facing the deity.

Having lit a lamp with new cloth, while accompanied by the sound of musical instruments and great dancing, the villagers praise the goddesses with joined palms; if they behold her, they carry even a mere glance upon their heads as a favor. If the village deity is pleased, diseases such as pestilence, cattle plagues, famine, and epidemics are pacified in that village; fire does not excessively burn the houses, river water does not flood them, and untimely death perishes. Furthermore, serpents, scorpions, and the like do not afflict them with the power of poison, nor do wild fanged beasts cause them harm.
For when there are no gadflies, bears, tigers, lions, and other such creatures, security and prosperity prevail in the kingdom, and the welfare of the subjects is ensured; thus it is understood.
At the consecration, he has been initiated; [he drinks] from the *parisrut* with honey, liquor, ghee, milk, or water for the sake of manly vigor.

In that pavilion, which is adorned with coconuts placed as offerings upon the heads [of the deities] and decorated with live cocks and other items, and where the images have been consecrated with the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* rites, certain worshippers, having honored them with offerings of red rice and the like, sever their own limbs and offer them. In this regard, there is neither binding nor any doing of harm; rather, it is a feat of daring. Lord Parāśara has declared that in the Kali age, this very fruit—which becomes manifest for those who are heroes of poison—is the appropriate practice for Śūdras.

In the *Smṛti-purāṇa-samuccaya*: "The villages of Palli, Pakkaṇa, and Kheṭa; the camp of the Ābhīras; the village of the Kirātas; the guilds of merchants; the cities of Śūdras and farmers; the towns and the suburbs; the dwellings of Tvaṣṭṛ and the pathways; the villages of Caṇḍālas and the dwellings of those who live in opposition; likewise the villages of Pulindas and the dwellings of weavers—those goddesses who are objects of pride are called the deities of the village."

In the *Āgamasmarisāragrantha*: "For Brāhmaṇas, Śiva is the deity; for Kṣatriyas, however, Mādhava; for Vaiśyas, it shall be Brahmā; and for Śūdras, the village deities. This is its explanation: Śiva is Agni and the Veda; Mādhava is Dharma and Sacrifice; Brahmā refers specifically to the Brāhmaṇas; and the village deities are those mentioned by Parāśara for the four varṇas, who are to be worshipped in their respective order.

In the *Devīyāmala*, the village deities (*grāmadevatā*) are described as follows: "The village deities, known through the power of time and action, are conceptualized through the application of the intellect; they are worshipped by means of their own local names and dialects. Regarding their worship, some maintain that even Brahmins perform it. This is faultless, for according to Vedic statements such as "One should meditate on the Blessed One, who is the Self of all, as 'That, from which [all things] arise, into which they enter, and in which they breathe'" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1), everything becomes composed of Brahman for the Brahmin. This has been stated with reference to those who desire worldly fruits: "For one who desires nothing, there is nothing at all. A villager should worship the village deities for the sake of protecting the village."
"The goddesses headed by Indrākṣī, all of whom are born from portions of you, are worshipped there in various forms during the Kali age."
Thereupon the village deity said:
"Bappa-deva, Śiva-śakti, Suvarṇāmbā, Reṇuka, and Cāṇimā; likewise Vīrāmabā, Mārikā, Gaṅgā, Phasagairī, and Nagnikā."
Arkika, Vīrabhadra, and Vīraśvapati;
Bhillas, Kirātas, and Laddas; likewise the elder brother of Draupadī; Garvāmbā, Ācārya-nādha, and Bhavānī-saddhapūruṣa.
Raidrī, Rudrā, Mahārāṣṭrī, Mānikārudrā, and Saṃdhikā; Mūkāmbā and all the Vallas, as well as the Yādavas who are devotees of Kṛṣṇa;
Lakṣmī, Tārā, Brahmarakṣas, Tṛṇāmbā, and Pullalocanā.
Pharmaīśa, O Great Goddess, Rudrāṇī, Caṇḍikeśvara,
Vināyaka, Okamātā, Ciṃtyeśī, Varaṇā, Valmīki,
Nīcabheruṇḍā, Durgā, Āndā, Argalā, and Ambikā.
Jyotirmaheśī, Yegīnī, Bakalā, Śukahastā, Śṛṅkhalākā, Māyūrī, Siṃhāvāhinī, Vāruṇī, Īśā, Kulīkṛtyā, Rākṣasī, and Candraśekharā.
Virguṇḍikā is situated on the Arka tree; Prasthā resides in the Paryaṅka; Añjanābhū is the resin; Oṣadhīśvarī is in the lake;
Vyāghreśa is at Dhanuṣkoṭi; and Indirā is likewise at Tulākoṭi.
Upala, Nāgarūpa, Jaṭīśāsta, and Bhairava; Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Jāmadagnya, Pārṣata, Śakuna, and Śamī;
Dṛṣadvān, Kīṭanātha, Nahādaṇḍa, and Kuṇḍika.
Śreṇika, Cāṇakheḷa, Kūṣṭāṇḍa, Vināyaka,
Masūrikā, Hipeṇa, Tulasī, Paśurat, and Sapa;
Retasśiras Mahāviṣṇu was worshipped by Siddhas in Kāñcī.
Prātītika, Stamāla, Gaṅgābhṛt, Śaṭhakūlika, Nīla, Mihirasvāmī, Spoṭāmbā, Munīśvara,
Cālinī, Śūrpikā, and the leaders of the herds of elephants (Ugravaiṣṇavayūthapa).

Malinī is in the form of a yakṣa, Mārkaṭī is the essence of the mortar, Haimavatī is the pestle, and Kumārī has the form of a ladle. Jalamūrti and Agnimūrti are the leaders of the cakravāka birds and others.
"Laṃbhinī, Pūjanā, and so forth—these village deities are worshipped. || ||
Thus concludes the deliberation on the installation and other rites for the village deity.
May there be prosperity!
Hrīṃ! Salutations to Śiva!
The Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī Kacchapuṭī Tantra: Homage to the Illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.
Having paid homage to the Great God, the cause of creation, preservation, and dissolution;
The mechanical device known as the *kacchapuṭī*, along with its secret instructions, is now described.

The commencement of the *Kaccha* yantra of Bhuvaneśvarī: In ancient times, for the benefit of the world, Śiva described the wheel that bestows all desired fruits when its numerical values are calculated.
One should draw five vertical lines and likewise draw five horizontal lines;
thus the sixteen-square wheel is known by means of the *kaṭapaya* system.
A hero, Bali, Rajju, Yegī, Gāvo, Vaya, and Ruru—one, eight, and ten; one should write these in those respective positions.
By the first [number] the ritual procedure (vidhi) is indicated, and likewise by the latter, the house.
This wheel of the eight fixed [verses] is equal in all ritual actions.
Having moistened it, one should gradually write down that which is most desired.
[The syllables] are *bhogī*, *raghu*, *paṭu*, *rgairī*, *laṃkā*, *putraḥ*, *khago*, and *bhuḥ*;
they are either expressed by their numerical values or by conventional designations.
Zero, zero, seven, six, seasons (six), and two;
sky, sky, sky, sky, elephants (eight), moon (one), Vedas (four), arrows (five), and sky, sky.
Herein is the fixed configuration in calculation,
the completion of numbers through the arrangement of numerals beginning with one and ending with sixteen.
By whatever method, in a square of forty-four [squares], there would be thirty-four [units]; that sixty-eight is indeed not diminished.
Therefore, it should be understood that the transcription of what has already been written occurs when there is a deficiency in the instruction;
however, in the case of an excess, there is no repetition of the enumerations therein.
Thus is the placement of the collective [deities] in a symmetrical wheel;
however, if an asymmetrical collective is desired, they are placed in the odd-numbered spokes.
Furthermore, there is the recurrence of one [number], or the reduction of one by one;
the definition of the interruption of numbers consists of the various options according to one's desire.
Daṃja, pārśva, koṇa, cakra, and vyasta—these are, in order, the names of the five piercing methods (vedhas); the nirvedha is called the cakra.
O Pārvatī, tell me of that number which is the fruit of yoga, the wheel, free from the five piercings, and indeed the seed of all siddhis.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Yoga of Numerical Counting of Bhavaneśvarī," in the *Tantra* concerning the practice of *kakṣaluṭī* within the *Mayāsura-upadeśa*, from the *Śrī Umāmaheśvara-saṃvāda*.
Oṃ: In that [maṇḍala] of Bhuvaneśvarī, one should write the two goddesses in the middle of the Māyā-bīja and in the three [triangles], as well as the Vāgbīja and the Kāmabīja on both sides.
In that very place, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished and the ritual action characterized by the joining [of mantras],
together with all the seed-syllables (*bījas*) according to the paths proclaimed for the fixed [mantras].
And there, upon those very non-leaking [vessels], he should draw all the long [syllables];
he should also inscribe the mantras impelled by the ritual action together with the Māyā.

Having written the letters from *ka* to *gha* on the first line, one should write those from *ḍha* to *dh* on the subsequent line; having written those from *kṣa* to *la* on the first line, one should write those from *na* to *ra* on the subsequent line.

One should draw the *cūḍās* at the tips of the lines using the letters ṅa, ña, ṇa, ai, ru, jha, gha, and i, in both reverse and direct order; and one should write the syllable *prīṃ* in the central spike.
On its two sides, one should draw the seed-syllables known as the noose (pāśa) and the goad (aṅkuśa);
likewise, the syllables of the world-protectors (dikpāla) in their respective directions and the syllables of the Mothers (mātṛ).
One should draw the eight [planets] beginning with Kṣatra, as well as the eight elephants of the quarters,
the eight great serpents, and likewise the eight Vainateyas.
Then one should place the ninefold group of planets and the twelvefold group of zodiac signs;
likewise, one should draw the sevenfold group of winds and the five arrows.
Having arranged five groups of birds and four groups of attendants one above the other, one should encircle them with the syllable *hrīṃ*.
One should place the *raṅgha*, *jhaṃ*, and *yaṃtra* instruments in each compartment;
this is done according to the number of the odd-numbered *yugas* that have passed from the initial portion.
In the calculation of the *parāṃśa* and so forth, one should write the remainder as before;
[this applies] to the penultimate, the eighth, the first, the tenth, and the ninth—these two pairs.
On the seventh and the last [day], one should employ the diagram known as Kacchapuṭī; one should draw it with a single half-moon at the top, endowed with numerical seed-syllables (saṃkhyā-bīja).
Through the grace of Bhuvaneśvarī, this [mantra] shall become the bestower of all siddhis;
herein, for the sake of discerning the seed-syllables (bījas), they are extracted separately and explained.
The seed-syllable of Māyā—*hrīṃ*; the seed-syllable of the noose—*āṃ*; the seed-syllable of the goad.
Kroṃ; these are the seed-syllables of the eight guardians of the directions, beginning with Indra.
Laṃ, Raṃ, Haṃ, Ṣaṃ, Vaṃ, Yaṃ, Saṃ, Śaṃ. These are the seed-syllables (bīja) of the seven Mothers.
Aṃ, iṃ, uṃ, ṛṃ, luṃ, eṃ, oṃ are the seed-syllables (bīja) of the guardians of the ear.
Āṃ, Kaṃ, Caṃ, Ṭaṃ, Taṃ, Vaṃ, Yaṃ, Śaṃ. These are the seed-syllables of the eight elephants of the directions.
Aṃ kṣaṃ saṃ vaṃ haṃ yaṃ paṃ kaṃ. This is the eight-syllable mantra of Mahānāga.
Gaṃ, caṃ, kṣaṃ, saṃ, jaṃ, bhaṃ, kaṃ, baṃ. These are the eight seed-syllables of Vainateya.
Vaṃ, saṃ, gaṃ, kaṃ, caṃ, jaṃ, paṃ, ṭaṃ. These are the seed-syllables (bīja) of the nine planets.
Laṃ, vaṃ, raṃ, yaṃ, kaṃ, iṃ, eṃ, taṃ, naṃ. These are the twelve zodiac signs.
Āṃ - Āṃ - Iṃ - Īṃ - Uṃ - Ūṃ - Eṃ - Aiṃ - Oṃ - Auṃ - Aṃ - Aḥ || This is the group of seven Maruts.
Aiṃ Raṃ Traṃ Ghaṃ Yaṃ Saṃ Haṃ. These are the seed-syllables (bījas) of the five arrows.
Śaṃ, Caṃ, Bhaṃ, Śāṃ, Āṃ. This is the group of five birds.
Aṃ, iṃ, uṃ, eṃ, oṃ: these are the four [syllables] of Gaṇanātha.
Gaṃ Oṃ Suṃ Kṣaṃ || These are the seeds of the celestial tree.
Saṃ Kaṃ Kṣaṃ. The Śrī-bīja.

Śrīṃ. Thus ends the placement of the seed-syllables (bīja-vinyāsa). "Aṃ" is the anusvāra; "Āḥ" is the visarga. Together with the anusvāra and visarga, they become fourteen; all eighteen are to be known along with the vowels beginning with 'A' and their respective mātrās. Thus concludes the second chapter, titled "The Method for the Placement of Seed-Syllables," in the *Kaccapūṭī Tantra* as spoken by Umā and Maheśvara.

Oṃ. I shall now declare the knowledge of the application of yantras together with their mantras, including [the rites of] subjugation (vaśya), enchantment (mohana), inciting enmity (vidveṣa), eradication (uccāṭana), and attraction (ākarṣaṇa).

Stambhana (paralysis), māraṇa (killing), and veda (piercing)— these eight types of applications are considered to be performed according to one's will through the yoga of the self, demonstrating a variety of results.
HŪṂ is for causing enmity; GHAṬA and UṬṬĀṬE are for driving away; KHEKHE is indeed for killing;
NAMASTAMBEVA is for subjugation; VOṢAḌĀ is likewise for summoning.
*Klīṃ* for delusion (*mohana*) and *kaḍ* for piercing (*bhedana*); these are proclaimed as the sprouts (*pallava*).
Each pair of vowels, beginning with *a*, is likewise employed in each of the eight rites.
Now, the mantra for subjugation: *laṃ hrīṃ paṃ khaṃ vaṣaṭ sarvajanaṃ me vaśamānaya svāhā*.
Now, the mantra for enchantment (*mohana-mantra*): *laṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ laṃ līṃ klīṃ klīṃ klūṃ klaiṃ kṣlauṃ klaḥ haṃ sakala mohaya sarvendriyāṇi preraya prasīda mahāmāye sarvamohinyai namaḥ*.
The mantra for causing enmity:
Oṃ hrīṃ raṃ hrīṃ huṃ, obeisance to Bhuvaneśvarī.
Now, the mantra for eradication (uccāṭana):
Oṃ hrīṃ raṃ raṃ laṃ, O Goddess Hariharā, drive away the adversary, phaṭ! Go, go quickly, svāhā!
Now, the mantra for attraction:
Oṃ hrīṃ oṃ vauṣaṭ! Homage to you, O Blessed One! Attract all the sense faculties; attract them, svāhā!
Now, the mantra for immobilization (staṃbhanam):
Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ haṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ jhāṃ namassvāhā namonamaḥ.
Now, the mantra for killing:
Hrīṃ raṃ raṃ raṃ kheṃ kheṃ Bhairavi, Bhūvaneśvari, Mahāmārike, kill, kill the enemy! Svāhā.

Now, the mantra for causing division: Oṃ hrīṃ ṅīṃ klīṃ kaṭ! Salutations, salutations to the Lord of the Abode! O destroyer of all evils, destroy the evil! Cut through the mutual affection between those two; cause a breach of friendship, cause it! Oṃ hrīṃ huṃ! Separate them! Hrāṃ hrīṃ klīṃ! Salutations to the Progenitor of the World!
Thus are the mantras for the eight applications.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Ritual Procedure for the Mantras of Application," in the *Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī Kakṣapuṭī Tantra*, within the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara. Oṃ.
Oṃ. Now I shall describe the procedure for the worship of Bhavaneśvarī.
One should place Gaṇeśa, Durgā, Senānī, and Kṣetrapāla in the cardinal directions.
O Bhuvaneśvarī, O Mother of the Earth, come, come, O Sovereign of the World!
O Great Goddess of mantras and yantras, you who possess the power of all knowledge and action!
Having thus invoked [the deity] and worshipped according to one's means, one should apply the respective mantras in accordance with the ritual procedure; this is the summary.
The sixteen vowels are to be known by their connection with the beginning and end of the consonants;
they are [repeated] both in direct and reverse order, excluding the three letters *jña*, *ṇa*, and *ña*.
These three syllables are to be known as being applied individually in each ritual service;
"tadrūpiṇyai namaḥ svāhā" is the same everywhere.
Subjugation and enchantment are proclaimed to be effective during the spring;
expulsion is recommended in summer, and the killing of enemies specifically in the rainy season.

Stambhana (paralysis) is performed during the time of Śata; dveṣa and bhedana during the winter; ākarṣaṇa (attraction) during the cool season; and for the sake of vaśīkaraṇa (subjugation), the sequence is likewise applied.
Subjugation, delusion, attraction, and immobilization are accomplished during the bright fortnight;
other rites are to be performed during the dark fortnight, as are the days classified as gentle or cruel.
Gradually, through the gateway of the path of practice, one chews the karmas in succession,
following the sequence of cold, heat, thorns, milky sap, fruit, and the binding tree.
White, blue, smoky-grey, yellow, green, red, brownish-red, and variegated— these are used in the applications for the eight types of ritual acts.
The sacrificial offerings, such as unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) and flowers, should be prepared in this manner.
For the rites of subjugation (*vaśya*), attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), and immobilization (*stambha*), the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be square.

For the piercing of delusion (mohoccāṭana) and for subjugation (vaśya), a circular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is prescribed; for inciting enmity (vidveṣa) or for killing (māraṇa), a triangular one is proclaimed.
One, two, or three spans [of the hand] should be used for the destruction [of obstacles], as in the case of Viśāla;
likewise, Koraṇṭa, Tulasī, Guñjā, and Mallikā are for the rite of subjugation.
Kuṭaja, dundubhī, śigru, śikhī, and soma are used for bewitching;
likewise, dhattūra, khadira, śṛṅgī, vera, and vṛścikapuccha.
Veśyā, jaṭājaṭā, māṃsī, markaṭī, gāravallikī, babhrupāda, dhūmā, muṣaka, and śruti.
Now, in the treatise on hatred (dveṣatantra), there are these twelve root-herbs:
*saumya-snuhī*, *brahmadaṇḍī*, *śamyā*, *aśvattha*, *kuśa*, and *amṛtā*.
Gāndhārī, Sahadevī, Bhūtalī, Balarākṣasī, garlic (laśuna), sulphur (gaṃdhaka), loman, lac (lākṣā), sarjarasa, and uśīra.
Salt, kaṭphala, vahnī, durgandhā, and durālabhā— these, along with other alkaline substances (kṣāra), are used in all rites for eradication (uccāṭana).
White arka, red dhattūra, blue unmatta, and kuśa grass;
as well as pāribhadraka, camphor, excellent incense, and ashes.
Red cotton, *nepālī*, turmeric, *abhayā*, *punarnavā*,
*kadamba*, saffron (*kuṅkuma*), and so forth are used in all rites of attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*).
White arka, white guñjā, jasmine,
white palāśa, suvarṇavallī, vārāhī, vajravallī, and mercury.
Raktonmatta, Pītamallī, Gairika, Manasśilā,
and Ketakī— these should be known as [the substances] for all rites of immobilization (staṃbhanakarma).
Abhraka, tālaka, lead, the bristles of a boar,
the sinews of a corpse, a tiger’s whiskers, and the tila-tree.
Castor oil, vyāvarta, droṇa, maricavallarī,
linseed (atasī), lotus, rudrākṣa, and nīlikā are also used for killing.

The head of a human being born under a hostile sign, the skull of a crow, the eye of a jackal, the ear of a rabbit, the head of a mongoose, the egg of a crow, the egg of a cock, and the head of a peacock.
Jyotiṣmatī, Bheruṇḍī, Muṇḍī, and Drurapibhedanī are used for collyrium; likewise Nīlakārpāsa, Matsyākṣī, and Bhṛṅgarāja.
The root of the boar and the root of the īśvarī plant are especially excellent for the rites of wearing protective amulets and for the employment of medicinal herbs.
One should employ the tilaka, collyrium, and ointment as appropriate;
furthermore, in certain instances, a snake’s slough is used here in incense and other such preparations.
In rites of inciting enmity, eradication, subjugation, and killing, one should offer blood-sacrifices outside the city; however, in rites other than killing, one should never give a blood-bali.
The fourfold [practices] of inciting hatred, deluding, creating dissension,
and killing must not be performed by those desiring their own welfare, even toward enemies, if they are righteous.
Having bathed in water reaching up to the neck, he should remain there intent upon his practice,
either in a forest, in a mountain fastness, or in the vicinity of a peerless *aśvattha* tree.
In the Kali age, by touching a cow's tail, a Śiva-liṅga, or a coconut while reciting a mantra,
one shall attain mastery over a hundred thousand syllables of that mantra.
There is no instruction here, no restriction, and no ritual assignment of limbs;
it is clear that accomplishments will be attained here within a month.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, on the accomplishment of ritual applications, in the Kaccapuṭī Tantra.
Oṃ! In all applications of yantras, hear this supplement:
in the absence of recitation, mantras, and so forth, mere visualization alone is most important.
For the all-pervading consciousness of the Self, though unmanifest as it were through Māyā,
[appears as such] due to its identification with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and with all objects superimposed upon it.
The One shines as everything, omniscient and omnipotent;
it is the seed of all, utterly distinct from all else, yet eternally non-different from the Self.
Having understood that power, the yogi shall attain the perfection of the yantra through the straightness and symmetry of the lines and the syllables within the compartments of the yantra.
The power that produces results arises [from the ritual] and never otherwise;
in matters concerning the unseen (adṛṣṭa), a yantra serves only for fruitlessness.
Observe that the coexistence of cause and effect is for the sake of self-preservation;
let the relationship between the probandum and the probans be somehow conceptualized.
Even toward an object of one's own enjoyment that is pleasant, or a means of happiness,
or even toward that which is just and righteous, this restraint must indeed be maintained within the body.
For the purpose of facilitating entry into the enclosure of the house and so forth,
and for the removal of obstruction, there [should be] a door and such at the top of that [enclosure].

One should bind it with deluding [mantras], but at that time, one should occasionally show it; in that very context, the wise should write down [the methods for] counteracting [obstacles] and so forth.
For inciting enmity or for causing division, digging in the earth is prescribed;
for attraction, it is the scattering [of substances], and likewise for that, spreading them upon the ground.
One should shatter the machine at the left [side] during the non-combative state, or burn it from the root of the other;
this proclaims the two fruits: happiness and the cessation of suffering.
Having meditated upon the internal *mātṛkā* with a mind focused on that supreme reality,
one who knows many things and is very generous should draw the *yantra* using the external *mātṛkā*.
O Pārvatī, tell me of the one who is capable [of this], through the power of number, syllables, ritual action, mantra, yoga, and substances.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Supplementary Ritual," in the *Kacchapuṭa-bhuvaneśvarī-tantra*. Oṃ.
Oṃ. Through the penetration of the intentional meaning (abhisaṃdhi), the cause of the ultimate result is enumerated;
because of the attainment of the summary teaching, the division of the wheels (cakrabheda) is here explained.
In the water-chambers of the wheel, with the number of Sahās being divided, the total sum is obtained by multiplying by four through detachment; such is Samavartanī.
Due to differences such as the tantra, the deity, and so forth, it results in a difference of fruit;
from the mere circularity [of the fire], the fruit arises from the irregularity of the two lines.
The entire *puruṣārtha* is said to consist of half-*puruṣārtha* units;
likewise, the attainment of the lineage (*saṃtāna*) is characterized by qualities (*guṇa*) that increase successively by two.
May there be health, victory, the cessation of affliction, and peace;
may there be the subduing of poison, the destruction of enemies, and self-protection.
The protection of one's family, the silencing of an opponent's speech, the destruction of a craft,
the immobilization of weapons, and the binding of the mouths of small wild animals.

The attainment of desired objects, the subjugation of women, the enchantment of others, the sowing of dissension among friends, contraction, expansion, and the taking of refuge with the host of enemies.
One should know [the results of] the increase of grain, the increase of cattle, the construction of tanks and the like,
the establishment of gate-towers and other structures, the restoration of ruins, and agricultural activities.
The establishment of treasures, the untying of knots, the breaking of undertakings,
the accomplishment of tasks, reconciliation, and concealment— these are the eight powers of the earth.
In rites such as those involving yantras and the like, through the power of the *māyā-bīja*,
men who are highly skilled in ritual action should diligently perform what is to be joined and what is to be removed.
This accomplishment (siddhi) of Bhuvaneśvarī, the Mistress of the Tantras, is thus proclaimed;
she possesses the power of the diversity of yoga and the assembly of people born of pure substance.
This secret of the science of mantras, proclaimed in the *Kaccapūṭī-tantrasāroddhāra*, shall indeed be realized as truth in the Kali age.
