Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Wealth of the Fruit," in the Kaccapuṭī Tantra.
Thus ends the compendium, the *Kaccapuṭītantrasāroddhārasaṃgraha*.

All these applications of numerical arrangements and the *kacchapuṭī* instrument should be constructed according to the rules prescribed in the Tantra; only a mere indication of the directions has been provided here. May there be auspiciousness!
Salutations to the venerable Gurus.
Now begins the *Bhīmaratha-śānti* as taught in the Śaiva Āgamas.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the propitiatory rite known as the *Bhīmaratha-śānti*.
At seventy, death arises for men—terrible, crushing, and piercing.
There will be the loss of wife, loss of sons, loss of wealth, and likewise illness;
within six months one meets death, and there shall be great misfortune.
To pacify those defects, one should perform a propitiatory rite according to the rules when the seventy-first year has arrived, during the birth asterism and the birth month.

On the day of one's birth, on the lunar day of birth, when the Moon and stars are endowed with strength, or even on the anniversary of the completion of the year, the wise man should perform the propitiatory rite (śānti).
To the northeast of the house, one should have a beautiful pavilion constructed,
provided with a canopy and garlands, and adorned with banners and other ornaments.
There, one should construct an altar that is square and level on all sides;
there, one should pour thirty *droṇas* of rice.
Having placed half of that amount of rice, one should place sesame seeds upon it;
having installed there a very firm, unblemished, new pitcher.
Having installed there a golden image of Mṛtyuñjaya weighing thirty niṣkas, he worships Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
Adhi, pratyadhi, deva, and autu—these four are equal to one svarṇa in weight.
Indra and the other eight lords of the directions, likewise the deities of longevity,
all the deities of the six qualities (ṣāḍguṇya), and the nine planets beginning with Āditya.
Having prepared four *maruṇa* fruits, each measuring exactly one *pala*, the wise man should place them in the jars according to the correct ritual procedure.
Having performed the Puṇyāhavācana, one should then perform the worship of the Mātṛkās;
having then performed the Nāndī-śrāddha, one should carry out the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the rite.
According to the ritual procedure for Mṛtyuñjaya, one should first worship Mṛtyuñjaya,
and then one should certainly worship Brahmā with the mantra *brahma jijñāse*.
One should worship Viṣṇu with devotion using the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ," and all other deities individually with their respective mantras.
The Karudra, the Puruṣa-sūkta, the Saura, and likewise the Gāma-pata.
And they should recite the Mahāśānti, as prescribed by the sequence.
One should perform the ritual sprinkling of Rudra and offer salutations to Mārtāṇḍa.
Likewise, one should perform circumambulations of the Aśvattha tree.
Thereafter, one should perform the fire-oblation preceded by the sacrifice to the planets;
one should carry out the ritual up to its conclusion according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Sūtra.
One thousand oblations of honey and nectar-creeper (huneda-mṛtavallī) smeared with ghee should be offered,
preceded by the ritual placement (nyāsa), while reciting the mantra taught for the conqueror of death (mṛtyuñjaya-vidāna).
One should offer oblations with palāśa fuel-sticks while reciting the Ṛitam mantra;
then, one should offer oblations with palāśa sticks while reciting the "Brahma jijñāsā" mantra.
For the other deities, however, one should perform the oblation with their respective mantras;
for Tryambaka, it is performed with his mantra, preceded by the ritual placement (nyāsa) and meditation (dhyāna).
One should perform the sesame oblation (tilahoma) a thousand or even ten thousand times;
then, having offered the Sviṣṭakṛt oblation, one should complete the remainder of the sacrifice.
One should offer a handful of flowers to the invited deities with the Abhilaṅga hymns,
the Pāvamānī verses, and the Sūkta beginning with "akṣibhyām."
O Lord, the deities shall consecrate the patron, who is well-seated upon an auspicious throne, with the mantras prescribed for the nine planets; thereafter,
they shall cause the rites of gazing at the clarified butter, the giving of gifts, and the offering of cruel oblations to be performed.
One should offer the cloth used for the ritual bath to the preceptor.
Having first honored the preceptor with garments, ornaments, and other offerings.
One should present an image of Mṛtyuñjaya, together with its cloth, as a gift;
and all other images should be bestowed upon the officiating priests.
And one should give a milch cow with her calf to the preceptor.
One should perform these fifteen gifts: the gift of a Śrīmūrti image, the gift of land, the gift of a daughter, as well as the gift of a Brahmin, and the installation of a deity.
One should bestow abundant gifts upon the poor, the helpless, and the distinguished;
thereafter, one should feed three thousand or a thousand Brāhmaṇas.
Thus, whoever performs this rite of pacification with faith, like a hidden treasure,
shall be liberated from all diseases and freed from all suffering.
Having enjoyed manifold pleasures for a full hundred years,
he finally attains the state of Śiva and rejoices there forevermore.
Thus ends the *Mārkaṇḍeya-bhīmaratha-śānti* as declared in the Śaivāgama.
Now follows the procedure for the *Bhīmaratha-śānti* as spoken by Śaunaka:
"I, Śaunaka, shall proclaim the peace rite known as Bhīmaratha."
In the year following birth, there will be death; O Bhīma, it shall occur in the subsequent year.

Within six months, one shall encounter death as well as the loss of wealth; furthermore, there will be the destruction of sons, wife, and so forth, along with the depletion of money, grain, and livestock.

To pacify those defects, one should perform a propitiatory rite (*śānti*) according to the prescribed rules on the birth-month, the birth-day, or under a birth-asterism when it is endowed with strength.
In a temple, on a riverbank, in one’s own home, or at an auspicious place,
one should first cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) to be made, and thereafter perform the *nāndīmukha* rite;
having first chosen the preceptor (*ācārya*), one should then appoint the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Then, one should have a pavilion constructed in the northeast corner of the house.

Having deposited a load of rice, half of that amount of *taṃjula* (a type of grain), and half of that again as a load of sesame seeds, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus. Upon that, one should place water-pots wrapped in threads, cloth, and other materials.
Having inscribed the syllable *hrīṃ* all around, one should worship Bhīma Mṛtyuñjaya with gold weighing at least one *vala*, or even half of that amount.
One should likewise fashion the two deities Ādhipratyadhi for that purpose,
as well as the world-protectors beginning with Indra, Durgā, and the planets beginning with the Sun.
One should perform worship according to one's ability with the respective mantras;
one should adore the principal deity with the sixteen types of offerings.
Praise with the *śṛta* mantra,
and [worship] the presiding deities with the *brahma jijñāsa* mantra and the mantra beginning with "tad viṣṇoḥ."
Having performed the worship as previously described, one should then recite the respective mantras in their proper sequence;
one should perform the complete recitation of the Vedas (vedapārāyaṇa) and likewise carry out the door-recitation (dvārajapa).
The Namaka, the Maka, the Śrīsūkta, and the Bhūmisūkta.
To the western side of the pavilion, there should be a square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa);
one should perform the rites according to the procedure stated in one's own ritual manual, up to the portioning of the clarified butter (ājyabhāga).
One should perform the respective oblations with the mantras prescribed for the nine planets;
one should perform the oblation of sacrificial wood (samit), parched grain (caru), and clarified butter (ājya) with the principal mantras.

The primary oblation (pradhāna-homa) should be performed one thousand and eight times, or one hundred and eight times; likewise, an oblation of sesame seeds (tila-homa) should be performed in the same manner.
One should also perform oblations for the two presiding deities with the same number [of offerings],
and one should cause the *dūrvā* oblation to be performed with the *traiyaṃbaka* mantra.
Having offered oblations to Indra and the other world-protectors, as well as to the deities of the [nine] qualities,
he should then offer the *sviṣṭakṛt* and complete the remainder of the *homa*.
The preceptor and others should perform the consecration of the patron;
however, the patron himself, having performed the ritual duties, should carry out the inspection of the clarified butter.
Then one should perform the rites for the Kumbhaḍas and cause the ten types of gifts to be bestowed;
furthermore, one should cause abundant gifts to be given to the poor, the blind, and the destitute.
One should feed the Brahmins and afterwards cause them to pronounce blessings;
thus there shall be the cessation of all suffering, and one shall enjoy happiness at all times.
Even enemies perish, and sons, grandsons, and so forth increase;
one should constantly remember Hari alone, especially at the beginning and end of ritual actions.
Thus ends the Bhīmaratha-śānti in the venerable Bṛhat-śaunakīya;
now follows the procedure for the hundredfold consecration (śatābhiṣeka) as taught by Śaunaka.
I, Śaunaka, shall describe the hundredfold consecration (śatābhiṣeka) for the twice-born;
it should take place in the month of Āśvina, when one hundred and eighty-one years have elapsed, including intercalary months.
A twice-born man who has performed meritorious deeds should see the thousand-fold moon after he has risen;
this should be done during the auspicious northern course of the sun, in the bright fortnight, on a favorable day.
When Venus is in its exaltation, in a favorable *lagna*, and shining in the sky, one should perform [the rite] in a temple,
on a riverbank, in one's own courtyard, or in an auspicious place.
Having obtained the permission of the Brāhmaṇas, one should perform the expiation;
one should practice the Kṛcchra penance for a number of years equal to one's own age.
One should subsequently offer oblations of *kūṣmāṇḍa* and the *gaṇa* at the three daily libations;
furthermore, there should first be the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, as well as the auspicious thread ceremony (*kautuka*) and the sowing of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*).
One should first choose an Ācārya who is devoted to the service of the deities;
afterwards, one should choose the officiating priests (Ṛtviks) and honor them with the Madhuparka offering.
Thereafter, one should have a pavilion constructed, provided with a threshold and arches;
having adorned it with fruits and flowers, one should prepare the site for the fire sacrifice.
One should smear an area measuring one cubit with cow dung;
having arranged two bhāras of rice, one should place half of that amount of rice,
then half of that amount of sesame seeds, and draw an eight-petaled lotus.
One should fill his unemptied jar with water from a sacred bathing place (tīrtha),
and cast into it various seeds, the five gems, and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should fashion the form of Viṣṇu with one *niṣka* of gold;
the form of Dhātṛ with half of that, and the forms of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) with half of those [respective amounts].
Having invoked [the deities] individually into the center of the water-pots (kumbhas) with their respective mantras— namely,
"idaṃ viṣṇurvicakrame," "brahmaṇā te," "idaṃ te pratimucyate," as well as "agnimīḷe," "dūtam," "agna āyāhi," and "yoṣā"— [one should proceed].
"O Lord of the Ṛta, for the sake of your own power, [I offer] the great [oblation] to the one who is well-disposed."
Having worshipped that Lord Saumēdhu with these Ṛg-verses,
and having honored him individually with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, as well as various food offerings (naivedya), he proceeded.
One should designate the place for the fire sacrifice (homa) in the western part of the pitcher;
having performed the plastering and other preliminary rites according to the procedure prescribed in one's own ritual manual (sūtra).
Having established the fire according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the ritual up to the portioning of the clarified butter (ājyabhāga);
one should offer oblations with sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh), clarified butter, and cooked rice (caru) one hundred and eight times.
Excellent rice, rice with curd, rice with ghee, kṛsara, jaggery,
barley meal, honey, madhuka, milk, wheat, and sugar.
One should offer fuel-sticks in sequence from the Aśvattha, Palāśa, Khadira, Śamī, Vaṭa,
Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Bīja trees.
The Ghṛtasūkta, the Puruṣasūkta, the Āyussūkta, and the Vihavya hymn.

Having offered the *ṅīsūkta* and the *bhūmisūkta* with curd, parched grain, clarified butter, and flour-meal, and having performed the *iṣṭakṛt* oblation, one should complete the remainder of the fire-sacrifice; then,
after giving the inspection of the clarified butter as a gift to a learned *śrotriya*, [the rite is concluded].
Having carefully prepared a vessel made of copper or even of clay,

shaped like a lotus and provided with a hundred perforations, one should perform the consecration with the Puruṣa-sūkta; thereafter, one should perform the sprinkling with [mantras] originating from the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
Having bathed, put on unwashed garments, and being well-adorned,
he should perform the worship of the quarters with the hymn "ud u tyaṃ jātavedasam."
"Citraṃ devānām udagādanīkam" and "Om ity ekākṣaram" are the two hymns.
The hymn beginning with "sūryo na," the "vibrāḍ bṛhatī" hymn, the hymn beginning with "yamāya dharmarāja," and the "varuṇaṃ vo riśādanam."
The twice-born should touch the ground and recite the hymn beginning with "tvaṃ somapracikite," as well as the "ityāmuṣyam" hymn, the Śrīsūkta, and the Bhūmisūkta; thereafter,
they should recite the Mahāśānti and have the Puṇyāha declaration proclaimed.
Thereafter, one should honor the preceptor with garments, cows, land, and gold;
one should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests (ṛtvij), and after that, ten gifts.
Thereafter, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas and then cause them to pronounce blessings.
Having mounted either an elephant, a chariot, a palanquin, or even a horse,
and having performed a circumambulation of the city and other sites along with the twice-born,
he should proceed accompanied by the sounds of auspicious drums, as well as dancing and singing.
And afterwards, one should enter the house and offer words of blessing.
Whether it lasts for one day or two days, one should perform the rite in this manner;
it purifies twenty-one generations— ten preceding, ten following, and oneself—
and [purifies] sons, friends, and others for sixty thousand years.
Having transcended the enjoyments of heaven, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the procedure for the hundredfold consecration (*śatābhiṣeka*) from the *Bṛhaccāunakīya*,
as well as the rite for pacifying the birth of a great-grandson through the sight of a thousand moons.
O Blessed One, Lord of all worlds, you who bestow grace upon your devotees!
By what means may a living being in this world be liberated from bondage?
Please explain some ritual procedure for the welfare of mortals who are unable to perform [the great sacrifices] but desire the fruits of immense merit.
Mahādeva said:
Listen, O blessed lady, I shall declare a certain auspicious rite,
the most secret of secrets in the world, which increases the merit of mortals.
By beholding a thousand moons, a man on earth is liberated from all sins; even by beholding his great-grandson, he is likewise freed from all sins.
A man who beholds a thousand moons at Vāpī attains great merit that is difficult even for the gods to acquire.
In this world, one is liberated from the debt to the ancestors; of this there is no doubt.
Thereafter, the formal consecration (abhiṣecana) should be performed according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.
Through the hundredfold consecration, one is honored by all men in the world;
one attains abundant prosperity and reaches heaven.
Whatever merit is gained from bathing in the Gaṅgā, from beholding the Setubandha,
from bathing at sacred fords (tīrthas), and from performing penances such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa;
By this easy means, a person seeking existence attains all of that;
he should perform the golden consecration with the measure of one hundred niṣkas.

Or one may perform it with half of that, or even half of that again; one should not act out of stinginess regarding wealth. Indeed, according to one's capacity, one should have the consecration performed even with jewels.
Pūrvatī said:
"O Lord Mahādeva, by what ritual procedure should this sacrifice be performed? Please explain it in detail."
O Goddess, you have asked me out of a desire for the welfare of mortals;
I shall now proclaim that procedure, which bestows the fruits of all rites, out of a desire for the welfare of all actions. I shall proclaim that procedure which grants the fruit of every ritual act.
On an auspicious day, under a favorable constellation, and when the moon and stars were endowed with strength,
he was joined by his wife, as well as his sons, grandsons, and others.
Having performed the auspicious bath and completed the daily obligatory rites,
one should perform the declaration of the auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana), and after that, the Nāndī-śrāddha.
One should choose as an Ācārya one who is self-controlled, learned in the Vedas (śrotriya), a master of the Vedas,
skilled in the application of mantras and tantras, of noble birth, and a householder.
Having thus prepared the Brahmin and the officiating priests thereafter, [he should proceed].
One should have a pavilion constructed, adorned with cloth canopies and other ornaments.
Then, having prepared a heap of grain measuring five *droṇas*, which is covered with clusters of gold and adorned with jewel-holding ornaments,
one should install the Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa along with the offering-pitcher.
Then, having placed the sun and the moon on both sides,
one should wrap them with threads and cloths while reciting the prescribed mantras.
Having fashioned a golden image weighing eight *palas*,
one should likewise fashion the presiding deity (*adhideva*) and the counter-presiding deity (*pratyadhideva*), each measuring one *pala*.
The Brahmin should likewise place the images upon a mat woven from *darbha* grass;
then, once the jars have been mounted upon the platform, he should arrange these [images] within them.
One should worship each of these individually according to the procedure of their respective mantras.
Having thus worshipped them according to the ritual rules, one should construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in accordance with the prescribed injunctions.

One should perform the fire-sacrifice (homa) there in the western part of the pavilion; having performed the rites up to the final oblation of the mouth as prescribed for the [specific] deity, one should carry out each respective ritual action.
One should perform the oblation for the planets; thereafter, one should offer oblations to each respective deity one thousand and eight times using the previously mentioned principal mantras.
One should offer oblations to Viṣṇu with the Gāyatrī mantra using wood produced from the Brahma-tree;
thereafter, one should offer the sviṣṭakṛt oblation, and after that, the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having completed the remainder of the *homa*, one should then perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*);
O best of the twice-born, having seated the patron upon an auspicious throne.
And with the mantras prescribed for the nine planets, and from the Śatarudrīya mantra.
One should perform the consecration with one's own gold and recite the Lakṣmīsūkta.
The gods, having consecrated [the deity] with mantras as declared in the Purāṇas, should cast the bali offering;
the patron, having adorned himself, should worship the Ācārya and the others.
One should present a golden image and garments to the preceptor;
one should cause the remaining jars to be given to the officiating priests and to the Brahmins.
Then one should perform the tenfold gift, and especially the gift of land.
Then one should perform the gift of a cow and carry out the gift of food.
Then one should feed Brāhmaṇas who are poor, blind, and miserable;
O Maheśvarī, that mortal who acts in this manner attains a state like his own.
It is auspicious, conducive to fame and long life, the destroyer of great sins,
a source of merit that brings delight to the world, and the eradicator of debt and poverty.
In this way, one undoubtedly purifies twenty-one generations;
whatever merit is found in all gifts and whatever fruit is found in all sacred fords [is attained].
Then one attains everything—renown immediately, in an instant.
Having enjoyed happiness in the heavenly world, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Then, having reached my world, he attains union with me.
Thus ends the procedure for the hundredfold consecration and the golden consecration, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara, within the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Śrīśaivāgama.
Now follows the procedure for the hundredfold consecration of one who has lived for a hundred years and beheld a thousand moons.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the procedure for the hundredfold consecration (*śatābhiṣeka*). For one who intends to live for a hundred years and behold a thousand moons, during the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, having gratified the Brahmins with food and caused them to pronounce an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), and having performed the rites from the marking of the sacrificial ground for the gods up to the placement of the *praṇītā* vessel, he should rise and prepare a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with rice or barley. Having placed the principal water-jar (*kalaśa*) there and having strewn it with the primary substances—fragrances, flowers, and fruits—

Having placed the pitchers in order from Indra onwards, starting from the south and ending in the north; having placed a strainer across them; having filled them with pure water; having scattered gems into the central principal pitcher; having covered it with a new cloth; and having adorned it with perfumes and flowers—one should invoke Brahmā into the central principal pitcher, and Indra and the others in their proper order, saying: "I invoke Prajāpati."

"I invoke Parameṣṭhin; I invoke Caturmukha; I invoke Hiraṇyagarbha. Having thus invoked them, and having performed the rites from the *paridhāna* (laying of the enclosing sticks) up to the *agnimukha* (offering to Agni), and having worshipped the deities, he purifies himself with the three verses beginning with "pohiṣṭhā mayo bhuvaḥ," with the four verses beginning with "hiraṇyagarbhaḥ," and with the section beginning with "pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ. Then, having honored them with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food, saying "Obeisance to such-and-such" and "Obeisance to such-and-such," and then saying "Svāhā to such-and-such," he offers the cooked oblation with the verse beginning "āyuṣṭe."

Having recited the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*), "viśvatodadha viśvatodadha diti," he offers the oblation with the offering verse (*yājyā*), "āyūrdhā agne ha viṣa. With the *Brahmasūkta*, beginning with "brahmajijñānam," and with the five sections of the *Agnirāyiṣmān* hymn, he performs the rites starting from the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering up until the gift of the cow as a boon. Then, in front of the fire, he places the remnants of the oblation upon bundles of *darbha* grass with the two verses, "āmuṣṭa" and "āyurdhā agne. At this point, he performs the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with the four verses beginning, "yā sugandhārasauvarṇā."

For each image, he performs the consecration with the water remaining in the principal pitcher, using the four verses beginning with "yā prācī" (which flows eastward) and ending with "samabhiṣekaṃ karoti" (he performs the sprinkling), in the order starting from Indra. He then sprinkles [the images] with the remainder of the water from the principal pitcher while reciting "yā ūrdhvā" (those which flow upward). Having dressed them in new garments and performed the *ācamana* rite, he gazes at the sun while reciting "udvayaṃ tamasaspari," "udutyam," "citraṃ," and "taccakṣurdevahitam."

Saying, "The sun has risen for me," he does not return by that same path. Having spread out a skin of black antelope or a tiger skin, he sits upon it facing the east. Having poured clarified butter into a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or bell-metal, and having placed a piece of gold therein, he looks at it with eyes both closed and open, and then gives it to a Brāhmaṇa.

Having mounted a chariot, having circumambulated the village, and having given a boon to the preceptor with the sound of drums and the *svastisūkta*, he honors the Brahmins and causes the disciples to recite [the benediction]; he purifies twenty-one generations—ten preceding, ten following, and himself—and having dwelt for sixty thousand years in the heavenly world, that Brahmin, upon passing from there, attains both *sāyujya* and *sālokya*. Thus said the venerable Bodhāyana.
Thus ends the procedure for the hundredfold consecration of one who has beheld a thousand moons and lived for a hundred years, as declared by Bodhāyana.

Now follows the consideration of the mantra, friendliness (*maitrī*), vision (*darśana*), and so forth, according to the method of the *siddhāricakra*: *a*, *ka*, *tha*, *ha*; *u*, *ca*, *pa*; *ū*, *ja*, *pha*; *o*, *ja*, *ba*; *ai*, *gha*, *ma*; *au*, *ḍha*, *śa*; *au*, *ña*, *ya*.
ī ghana ṛ jabha i ga dakṣa ṛ cha bha aḥ tasa ai ṭha la am̐ ṇa ṣa e ṭa ra a i u ṛ la e ai o au aṃ aḥ.
ka kha ga gha ṅa ca cha ja jha ña ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa ta tha da dha na pa pha ba bha ma ya ra la va śa ṣa sa ha

Multiply the letters of the name to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by 14, 27, 12, 4, 3, 5, 6, and 8 respectively; and multiply the letters of the practitioner's name (*sādhaka*) by 10, 1, 7, 4, 8, 3, 7, and 3 respectively. Having determined the remainder of both after division by 8, 1, 7, and 3, the one with the greater remainder is the creditor (*dhanin*), and the other becomes the debtor (*ṛṇī*). One should add [the value of] the letters of the *sādhya* to those of the debtor. When divided by 8, the remainder is called "wealth" (*dhana*) by the wise.
One should also join the doubled letters of the *sādhaka* with the letters of the *sādhya*; the remainder when divided by twelve is called *ṛṇam* (debt) by the wise.
Thus [it is stated] in the work titled *Rāmārcanacandrikā* and also in the *Mantraratnamahodadhi*.

In all cases, the connection with the enemy (ari) is to be understood. The "middling" (madhyama) is that which is to be accomplished (sādhya). "Susiddhi" means it grants success when offered. "Siddha" grants results by the mere fact of its connection. "Miśra" means mixed.
One should not purify mantras beginning with the Praṇava using the Siddha-ari method;
likewise, for mantras consisting of sixty-three syllables, purification is done by means of the square (koṣṭha).
However, one should not perform such testing for those [mantras] that have come down through the lineage of the Kula.
One should practice that which is obtained in a dream or received from a guru without even examining it.
In certain cases of rites performed for desired ends (*kāmya*), even the recitation [of mantras] at that very time does not incur fault;
indeed, for all ritual acts, there may be purification through the repetition of mantras.
Otherwise, having seen the perfected enemies of all mantras, one should seek their destruction.
*Maṃtrasārāvali*:
Counting from the asterism of the mantra up to the asterism of the practitioner by way of reverse numbering,
three asterisms in each of the three divisions are praised for the sake of accomplishment.

The first section extends from the head to the navel; the middle is said to extend from there to the feet; one should contemplate this [mantra] throughout all three sections. Thus ends [the section on] the *Rahasyatilaka*.
The "Devaghaṭana" (Divine Union) should be understood as the divine maiden; the sacrificer is traditionally known as the suitor.
One should consider the house-friendliness, the planetary group, the cord, the caste, and the channel.
In the absence of the five peaks, the deity is indeed [attained] through the jar alone; thus it is said in the *Pūjādarpaṇa*.
Determination of Direction:
The direction at birth and the direction at the time of the sun's rising are auspicious for beneficial undertakings;
however, the direction at the time of death is sometimes inauspicious.
Alternatively, it is the view of some that the *abhimukhī* [stage] occurs previously for the practitioner.
The characteristics of the meaning, the ritual for receiving the karma, the procedure for nourishment according to the sequence of months,
the medicinal rites for preventing miscarriage, and the procedure for the protection of the pregnant woman have been declared in all the scriptures:
Alternatively, O Great Goddess, I shall describe to you in brief the physical [constitution],
by knowing which men in this world, along with their offspring, may become happy.
If the female and male blood and semen are pure,
they are always capable of producing offspring for one another.
The characteristics of pure semen and menstrual blood:
semen that is white, heavy, unctuous, sweet, thick, abundant, and resembling clarified butter, honey, or oil indicates a woman who possesses a fetus; as for the menstrual blood, it is likewise.
Lac-dye, which has the luster of a hare's blood, becomes free from impurities when washed.

The characteristics of vitiated semen and ovum: when vitiated by vāta, pitta, or śleṣman, they become like a corpse, fetid, or putrid; they may resemble pus, be diminished, or smell of urine and feces—such impurities are detrimental to conception.
When [the blood] is vitiated by blood alone, by the three humors individually, by two at a time, or by all together,
it becomes certainly seedless and likewise incapable of producing offspring.
Treatment for vitiated semen:
The physician should have the man whose semen is like that of a corpse drink ghee prepared with dhātakī flowers,
khadira, pomegranate, and arjuna.
Likewise, one should have him drink ghee prepared with *sālasāra* and other ingredients;
or, when a glandular swelling has formed, [ghee] prepared with *śaṭhī* or even in the ashes of the *pālāśa* tree.
One should prepare [a decoction] from *parūṣaka*, *vaṭa*, and so forth, resembling pus;
when it has been processed and resembles feces, one should administer it along with *citraka*, *uśīra*, and *hiṅgu*.
Treatment for malignant ulcers (duṣṭārśva):
Even when the ulcer is extensive, one should apply pāṭhā, trikaṭu (tryūṣaṇa), and vṛkṣaka;
likewise, when the ulcer is foul-smelling, resembling pus, or like marrow.
O auspicious one, one should drink a decoction of *śrī* and likewise a decoction of sandalwood.
When the semen and blood are pure, a being, impelled by its own karma and afflictions,
enters the womb by the power of causal necessity, like fire entering wood.
If the woman's *śukra* (vital essence) is greater than the man's, she becomes female; if the man's is greater, he becomes male.
If the two are equal, a neuter (*klība*) is born; furthermore, this applies when the *śukra* is intended for procreation.
When the semen is excessively depleted by the wind (vāyu), it becomes scanty according to its own nature;
therefore, for the sake of purifying the semen, one should consume aphrodisiacs and unctuous substances.
When a man and woman are in union, if the man emits his semen first,
then a heroic son is born— one who is powerful and firm.
If, however, one should first emit [the seed] mixed with blood,
then a daughter endowed with beauty and firm constitution is born.

The sequence for the man's engagement: A man who has bathed, adorned with garlands and perfumes, looking beautiful and joyful, neither over-satiated nor hungry, and full of desire and passion, should proceed to sexual union.
One should approach one's wife during her fertile period, avoiding the sacred festival days.
One should never, even in thought, go to another's wife;
for men, visiting another's wife brings prosperity in both worlds.
Thinking thus, a wise man should approach his own wife when she is in her fertile season;
for as long as he is not yet satiated with his wife, a man desires another woman.
"Likewise, a lustful woman who is unsatisfied with her husband desires another;

having made this comparison with oneself, one should refrain from one's own wife. A self-possessed man should protect himself from excessive sexual union with women, for [excessive indulgence] leads to consumption, cough, asthma, emaciation, jaundice, and wasting."
From excessive sexual indulgence, diseases such as consumption (kṣaya) and others arise;
however, those who practice it moderately become long-lived, slow to age, endowed with a beautiful complexion and strength, possessed of firm and well-developed muscles, and blessed with offspring.
For three days at a time, O giver of boons, the wise man should approach his wife during all seasons; however, he should do so every fortnight, O bestower of boons.
One who is menstruating, one who is unwilling, one who is soiled, as well as one who is unloved,
one who is advanced in years, and likewise one who is afflicted by disease.
One who has a missing limb, one who is pregnant, one who is detested, one afflicted by a disease of the female organs,
one of the same lineage, the wife of a guru, and likewise even one who has renounced the world— [these should not be approached].
At the junctions of day and night, on festival days, as well as at midday,
in a place that brings about the realization of the sacred knowledge, in an open space, and indeed in a pure place.
A person who is hungry, thirsty, or afflicted by disease, whose mind is agitated,
who feels the urge to pass wind, feces, or urine, who is parched with thirst, or who is extremely weak;
Even if one has attained the retention of semen through the practice of the animal posture (tiryagyoni),
even a strong person should avoid emission by means of that wicked path.
Excessive emission of semen,
or even its retention, is especially censured when one is lying on a bed;
a wise man seeking his own welfare should avoid it even during sexual play.
For a man who has approached a woman during her menses and lacks self-restraint,
there occurs a loss of luster and vitality, and from that, unrighteousness arises.
One who approaches a woman wearing sectarian marks, the wife of a guru, a woman of the same lineage during sacred festivals, or an elderly woman at twilight, shall suffer the destruction of his life.

If she is pregnant, there will be suffering for the fetus; if she is diseased, there will be a loss of strength. One should avoid a woman who is deficient in limbs, one who is filthy, one who is hateful, or one who is barren, especially in an uncovered place.
In the region of Śukra, there will be a decline of semen and of the mind;
one will be hungry with an agitated heart, thirsty at midday, yet possessing strength.
One who remains [in this state] experiences the decline of semen and incurs the provocation of the wind (vāyu).
From excessive indulgence, there arises consumption (śoṣa), which brings about the depletion of semen.
When [the disease] has opened wide, consumption, splenomegaly, and death arise from the head;
furthermore, at dawn and at midnight, the wind and bile become aggravated.
And likewise, by the birth among animals and by wicked speech.
Upon urinating, voiding feces, or suppressing the emission of semen, one should quickly adopt the supine posture; otherwise, there may be the occurrence of seminal discharge or urinary obstruction.
Therefore, one should avoid all such acts, for they are detrimental to both worlds.
She practices wicked deeds, does not delight in hearing his story,
aligns herself with his enemies, and carries herself with arrogant pride.
She does not highly value a kiss or a caress on the face that has been given;
she sleeps even when he is already asleep, and likewise wakes up after him.
She shakes her limbs when touched and repels limb after limb;
she hears words only faintly, even those that are pleasing, while turning her face away.
She loses her composure when he takes the lead, and she hides herself when he eats; upon seeing him, her face turns pale, and she then turns her back toward her friends.

He was observed to be indifferent toward women he desired and neutral toward those who were neutral; even at the time for adorning his kinsmen, he did not apply ornaments. He abandoned those women who were disaffected and became devoted to those who were full of affection.

The characteristics of a woman in her menses: one should recognize a woman as being in her fertile period when she has an emaciated yet serene face, throbbing hips and breasts, sunken eyes and belly, and a longing for a man.
Just as a lotus closes its petals when the day has passed, so too,
when the fertile period has elapsed, the womb does not receive the semen.
Accumulated over a month, the menstrual blood (ārta-vam) becomes slightly dark and foul-smelling; at the proper time, the wind (vāyu) expels it from the opening of the womb through the vessels.
Every month, for women who possess menses, the essence-born [fluid] flows for three days;
after twelve years, it reaches its cessation by the age of fifty.
The duty of a woman during her fertile period:
Then, O Lord, Puṣpekṣaṇā, meditating on auspiciousness for three days,
remained free from cleansing and ornaments, sleeping upon a bed of darbha grass.

A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacāriṇī) should eat a small amount of milk-rice or barley-gruel, which cleanses and emaciates the digestive tract, either at the time of the Varṇeśa or Rāu offerings.

From sleeping during the day, one becomes habitually sleepy; from [eating] human flesh, one becomes blind; from weeping, one becomes deformed of eye; and from bathing [with impure substances], one suffers misery; and from [using] ointment, [one suffers the same].

One suffering from leprosy [is affected] by anointing with oil; one with deformed nails [becomes so] from cutting the nails; one becomes fickle through running, and a dark complexion results from laughing.
One suffers from inflammation of the teeth, lips, palate, and tongue through excessive talking;
one becomes deaf by listening to excessively loud sounds, and likewise from scratching [the ears].
Through association with a woman in her menses, a fool may become intoxicated;
therefore, one should avoid these [acts] during the three days of her menstrual period.
Having bathed on the fourth day, wearing white garlands and garments and remaining pure,
she who desires a son resembling her husband should look upon her husband before her.
A woman who has bathed after her menses should look upon whatever kind of man she sees;
she will give birth to a son resembling him. Therefore, she should show her husband [to herself].
The twelve nights of the Ṛtu period are [divided such that] the first three are censured;
on the eleventh and the even-numbered nights, a son is born, while on the others, a daughter.
Then the preceptor should perform the rite for the son according to the prescribed rule;
however, for a Śūdra woman who is devoted to prostration, it should be performed without mantras.
The determination of what is improper for pregnant women: excessive sexual intercourse, heavy loads, heavy clothing,
waking at improper times, sleeping during the day, and sitting on high seats.
The suppression of grief, anger, fear, agitation, and the force of faith [is harmful],
as is fasting, travel, pungent, hot, heavy, and constipating food.
One should abandon the wearing of red garments, looking into pits and wells, intoxicants and meat, sleeping on one's back, and desiring the womb of a woman.
Likewise, from the eighth month onwards, there may occur discharge of blood or purification through the bladder;
by these [complications], the fetus may be discharged prematurely, the womb may dry up, or the woman may die.
A pregnant woman who desires to eat those sensory objects that she finds pleasing should be given them by the physician after they have been brought forth, for fear of injury to the fetus.
A woman who has experienced pregnancy-longings (dauhṛda) shall give birth to a son endowed with splendor;
one who has not experienced such longings shall obtain safety for herself within the womb.
If one who possesses yoga should harbor a longing for the objects of the senses or even a sense of pride,
he will be reborn with a desire for that very object and for that very sense-faculty.
That woman who feels a longing for the sight of a king gives birth to a son who is wealthy and highly fortunate.
From her longing for fine cotton cloths, silk garments, ornaments, and other such things,
she gave birth to a graceful son who desired decorations.
Upon a worthy recipient, one gives birth to a self-restrained person of virtuous character;
but upon an image of a deity, one gives birth to one who is like a servant.

From the sight of species of serpents, one gives birth to a son of a violent nature; from eating the flesh of a monitor lizard, one gives birth to a son who is desirous of offspring and possesses a retentive memory.

From seeing species of serpents, one gives birth to a son of a violent nature; from eating the flesh of a monitor lizard, one gives birth to a son who desires to procreate and possesses a retentive memory.
From the flesh of cows, one obtains a horse that is dirty and capable of enduring all hardships;
from the longing of a buffalo, one obtains a horse that is brave, red-eyed, and covered in hair.
From the meat of a boar, one quickly gives birth to a son who is a dream-attainer and a hero; from the meat of a deer, a son who is courageous, with powerful shanks, and always moving about.

From a *sṛmara* she will give birth to one of agitated mind and constantly fearful; from a *taittira*, one who is not fond of food; and whatever longing (*dauhṛda*) a woman conceives for those [beasts] when she is unwell, she will give birth to a child equal to them in bodily conduct and character.
The procedure for the conduct of a pregnant woman:
She should be pure, dressed in clean garments, always contented, adorned with ornaments,
devoted to auspicious activities, abstaining from meat, deeply attached to her teacher, and averse to all else.
Upon seeing something that causes fear, or likewise upon smelling a foul odor,
one should quickly eat a small amount of food while listening to this meritorious narrative.
She consumes food that is neither stale nor dry, and never that which has been kept overnight;
she moves about in sacred places, avoiding going outside.
She repeatedly performs oil massages and other such treatments,
consumes liquid that is sweet, unctuous, refined, and combined with digestive stimulants.
One who always remains seated on a couch with soft bedding and so forth while pregnant will surely suffer miscarriage; otherwise, there would be no affliction from labor pains.
In the first month, one should offer food that is sweet;
likewise, in the second, it should be cool; and in the third, it should be mixed with liquids.
On the sixth day, sixty-day rice with ghee; on the fourth, combined with curd;
on the fifth, joined with milk; and on the sixth, indeed, accompanied by clarified butter.
In the seventh [month], one should drink ghee prepared with *pṛthakparṇī* and other herbs;
in the eighth, *kola* and the two types of *balā* are recommended as a decoction.
One should administer a Nirūha enema consisting of Śatapushpī juice, meat broth, curd, oil,
ghee, salt, and Madana fruit, mixed with honey.
In the ninth month, it is recommended that he eat unctuous meat with savory rice,
or very unctuous barley gruel (yavāgū), and perform the aforementioned ritual service.
Then, one should always place cotton wool in the womb;
when the woman is pregnant in the ninth month, she should enter the maternity chamber.
Treatment for miscarriage:
Madhuka, Śākabīja, Payasyā, Suradāru,
Āśmantaka, black sesame seeds, Tāmravallī, and Śatāvarī.
Vṛkṣādanī, payasyā, acalatā, utpalaśāribā,
anaṃtā, śārivā, rāsnā, padmā, and likewise madhuka.
The two types of *bṛhatī*, *kāśmarya*, milky *śuṅgā* sprouts, bark, ghee, *pṛśniparṇī*, *balā*, *āśigru*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, and *madhuparṇikā*.
Śṛṅgāṭaka, kaṇṭakārikā, kharjūra, kaśeru, madhuka, and sugar;
One who conquers these seven yogas with milk, reciting them along with the *Ṛgveda* verses,
shall cause the fetus to flow away in the course of seven months.
In the eighth month, one should administer milk boiled with the roots of *kapittha*, *bṛhatī*, *bilva*, *paṭola*, sugarcane, and *nidigdhikā*.
In the ninth month, one should administer honey and liquorice to alleviate the heat caused by the enemy of the lord of the house;
in the tenth month, one should provide milk from a milch cow for success,
or alternatively, liquorice, ginger, and catechu.
Regarding the treatment for the head of the newborn:
Having thoroughly cleansed the mouth of the newborn infant with rock salt (saindhava) mixed with clarified butter,
one should apply a cotton swab soaked in ghee to the crown of the head.
Having drawn out the navel-string to the measure of eight finger-breadths,
and having bound it with a thread, one should cut it and tie [the thread] around the child's neck; then, having thoroughly purified the remainder of the thread with water, [one should dispose of it].
Then, with the thumb and ring finger, one should lick gold, honey, and ghee, along with the *anantā* and *brāhmī* juices, using the tip of the little finger.

Having bathed the patient at the appropriate time with lukewarm water mixed with a decoction of milk-yielding trees prepared with *vātyālaka* and *kapittha* leaves, one should lay him upon a soft bed.
Due to the scolding of children, due to sudden awakening,
due to the obstruction of wind and other humors, and likewise due to swift striking;
Indeed, from sprinkling [the head] a child becomes bald, and from seating him on a humpbacked seat he becomes a hunchback;
therefore, one who desires the welfare of the child should always avoid these things before the deities.
Thus, and so forth, this should be properly reflected upon with the assistance of a wise teacher.
Consideration of the Root-Plants for Subjugation: Or rather, O Great Goddess, I shall now describe the root-plants for subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*):
*subhagā*, realgar (*manaḥśilā*), and yellow orpiment (*tāla*), combined with the juice of lac (*lākṣārasa*).
A tilaka-mark on the forehead made from the milk of a young woman brings subjugation;
likewise, viṣṇukrāntā, sarpākṣī, sahādeva, and gorocanā [achieve the same].
A tilaka made from these ground together with goat’s milk brings about subjugation:
priyaṅgu, kuṅkuma, kuṣṭha, mohinī, tagara, and ghee.
A sectarian mark (tilaka) must certainly be made with red lead, yellow orpiment, realgar, sandalwood,
antimony, yellow myrobalan, and likewise with priyaṅgu and mustard seeds.
Yohinī, hirītākrāntā, sahadevī, and śikhā,
ground with the juice of mātuluṅga, form a tilaka on the forehead that brings others under one's control.
Even the gods and asuras fall under its sway, how much more so the lowly Niṣādas;
it is like madder, red sandalwood, and a passionate, flirtatious woman.
This ointment, combined with punarnavā, is like the sun in its power to bring others under one's control; it consists of candana, nāgapuṣpa, mañjiṣṭhā, tagara, and vacā.
Oil prepared with lodhra, priyaṅgu, gura, jananī, and māṃsī is a means for subjugation;
such applications exist, yet a practitioner capable of them is rare.
Thus ends the procedure for the root-mantra of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).
Now follows the consideration of the merits and defects of the luminaries, *muhūrta*s, and so forth.
For it has been stated in the *Vidyāmādhavīya* regarding the determination of defects:

Now, having extracted from the original scriptures certain points sung by the great seers for the benefit of astrologers, I shall here declare the defects of auspicious moments (*muhūrta*); for it is impossible to describe them in their entirety.

One should avoid inauspicious lunar days, asterisms, and weekdays, as well as the *viṣaghaṭikās*, the dark fortnights, and the afternoon. One should avoid the five [periods] beginning with *dūma*, the *saurāgula*, the *agulika*, the daily disease (*dinagada*), the *sagraha* and *ardhaprahara*, the *viṣṭi*, the six evil conjunctions (*duṣṭayoga*), the hollows of the asterisms and lunar days (*tithikuhara*), the *kālacakra* and *arthapāta*, the *sthūṇā* and other three types of death (*mṛtyu*), the *vidṛk*, the *himasikha*, the two *kaṇṭakas*, and the *gaṇḍa*.

One should avoid an inauspicious lunar mansion and the house of the architect, as well as the Vaināśika, Ekārgala, and Śūnya yoga; a lunar mansion occupied by or conjoined with malefic planets, those that are to be traversed or already passed over, and the six yogas beginning with Jvala. One should also avoid odd-numbered months, years, and days, the heliacal setting of Venus and Jupiter, their conjunction, and their aspect; as well as the Vedha and Śūla yogas, the months of Adimāsa and so forth, and the appearance of Ketu and Uḍuda.

One should especially avoid marriage during the *vedha* known as *śalākā*, as well as the highly censured planetary movements associated with various rites, and the [inauspicious] months, seasons, zodiac signs, and so forth. Discerning minds, having avoided all these and other remaining defects that destroy the efficacy of the rite—including those concerning the father and the brother—should perform all such ceremonies.

The Agnyaṃtaka, Dvirasana, Tridaśeśa, and Rudra yogas; the first three of the Pūrva-trayam; the Bahula, Pitṛ, Mūla, and Śūrpam; the Chidras; the days of the malefic planets; and the Kālahorās—this entire group must be avoided in all auspicious undertakings.

The Agnyantaka, Dvirasana, Tridaśeśa, and Rudra yogas; the first three of the Pūrva-nakṣatras; the Bahula (Kṛttikā); Pitṛmūla (Mūla); Śūrpā; the Chidra-yogas; days with malefic planets; and the Kālahorās—all these groups must be avoided in all auspicious rites.
