Ten *dyānas* for the king, thirty-five *janāsas* for the people of Sibi; beyond that, for four *ghaṭīs*, it should be known as the period designated as "poison" (*viṣa*) in the *kṛkā* and other [divisions].

When the Sun is joined with the Moon in the sign of Aries (the house of fire) at ten degrees, there occurs the Vyatīpāta yoga; when it has moved further, at sixteen degrees, there is Pariveṣa; at eighteen degrees, Indradhanus (a rainbow); at twenty-eight degrees, Ketu appears from the orb; and when the Sun is conjoined with that same asterism, it is called Tārauka.

An earthquake accompanied by lightning and thunder, the falling of all the stars at night, and an eclipse occurring during the day—these are known as the Brahma-daṇḍa and Dhvaja. Furthermore, when these occur in the forenoon, they are known as the Vidya; if they occur in the afternoon, they are known as the Upavidya. These [periods] last for sixty-four nāḍīs, measured by the sun, the mountain (seven), the lion (eight), and logic (six).

The lords of the planets and days are, in order, increased by one-eighth of the measure of the day; likewise, for the watches (yāma), the first part of the fifth [of the day] is the same as the eighth part below the initial portion.

According to the stated sequence, they say that the portion of the son of the Earth (Mars) is Kulika, while the portion of Jupiter is Yamakaṇṭaka. On days such as those of death and others, [the periods] are four, seven, two, five, eight, three, and six degrees for each half-prahara.

In the first [navāṃśa], Budha (Mercury) is present; in the second, there is a dual-taste (sweet and sour); in the third part of Maghā, Viṣṇu (Jupiter) is present; in the fourth part of Bhaga (Pūrvaphalgunī), the Moon is present; and in the final [part], the Sun is present, which opposes auspicious results. Therefore, in this third part, death is powerful for one day.

When the Moon occupies a single sign along with one planet among those beginning with Śukra (Venus), it causes fear of the king, fear of enemies, calamity, exile, loss of wealth, and lack of refuge for the performer during auspicious rites.

In the bright fortnight of the month of Śukla-vāridhi (Jyeṣṭha), the Viṣṭi-karaṇa arises on the lunar days numbered by the Nāgas (eight), Rudras (eleven), and likewise [the others], starting from the first day of that bright fortnight during the day. It occurs sequentially in the watches (yāmas) numbered by the directions (ten), the eyes of the arrows (two), the mountains (seven), the pair (two), the six, the three, the eight, and the moon (one). Within these watches, it occurs in the nāḍīs numbered by the Āryas (three), the world (four), the chariot (seven), the end (zero), the fire (three), the end (zero), the Āryas (three), and the fire (three).

One should always examine the non-defilement (*avipamka*) of the days, lunar mansions, weekdays, stars, and lunar days; for the combinations of stars and lunar days, and of lunar mansions and lunar days, there are six types of yogas—both auspicious and inauspicious—that must be considered.

In this context, regarding constant conjunctions, the *navaparigha*, *vyatīpāta*, *vajra*, *vyāghāta*, and *vaidhṛti* are censured; likewise, the first set of *parivṛtas*—namely *śūla*, *gaṇḍa*, and *atigaṇḍa*—are condemned. Furthermore, the *nāḍīs* (periods) numbered as thirty-one, nine, six, four, three, five, seven, and six are also certainly to be avoided by people at their respective ends, according to the fixed rule.
For the Sun: 12, 3, 2, 12, 4; for the Moon: 1, 11, 8, 7, 60; for Mars: 5, 24, 7, 10, 2; for Mercury: 1, 8, 7, 10, 8.

The lords of speech (the planets) are associated with the days of the week as follows: for the Sun, the second and sixth; for Venus, the eighth and ninth; for Mercury, the third and seventh; for Saturn, the first, tenth, eleventh, and ninth; and for Jupiter, the twelfth—these are the lunar days perpetually joined with their respective weekdays.

In the asterisms of Rohiṇī, Kṛttikā, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mṛgaśiras, Pūrvā-phalgunī, Uttarā-phalgunī, Svāti, Śravaṇa, Punarvasu, Āśleṣā, Maghā, and Bharaṇī; and when the Sun, Jupiter, Venus, and the Moon are situated in the signs of Aries, Taurus, Virgo, Gemini, Sagittarius, Leo, Capricorn, Libra, Pisces, Scorpio, Aquarius, and Cancer respectively—these are the prohibited planetary configurations (vārayogas) for auspicious undertakings.

The *tithis* (lunar days) in sequence are: three, eight, thirteen, thirteen, eight, four, eight, eight, nine, eight, and eleven; these are the names of the asterisms (*ṛkṣas*) that are excluded [from the *yoga* calculations].

One should avoid, in sequence, the Citrā, the three Uttaras, Maitra (Anurādhā), Makhā (Pūrvaphalgunī), Vaidhasa (Śatabhiṣaj), Arka (Puṣya), and Nairṛta (Mūla) among the auspicious asterisms; as well as the thirteenth, the ninth, the second, the fifth, and the eighth lunar days.

The crocodile, monkey, lion, horse, crab, deer, tiger, bull, goat, and snake are the odd-numbered signs; likewise, these same signs become even when joined with the tenth house. Furthermore, in order, the fish, bull, rabbit (Aries), woman (Virgo), and crocodile (Capricorn) are the signs associated with the Moon.

The square of the number of men multiplied by two, plus the square of the number of horses; twice the number of men, plus the square of the number of elephants; twice the number of chariots, plus the square of the number of foot soldiers.
Atyaṣṭi, Giri, Haritsvara-giri, Tathaya, Manu, Yugendra, Yuga, and Bāṇa—these are the numbers for the [periods] beginning with Svāti, Nāḍī, and Uda, which are designated as "low."

The group of seven consists of two, six, seven, five, seven, seven, and eight; these are the *nāḍikās* for the final [tithis] known as *kūpa*, which are to be censured among the lunar days (*tithis*).

One should avoid two ghaṭikās on either side of the junction of the lunar day (tithi) and the stars (tāraka), as well as the low-flowing channel (nimnanāḍī). By disregarding this, a man wandering in the interval between them might fall like one into a well.

The wise say that the seventh lunar mansion from Śanaiścara is Time; others, however, calculate it as follows: on the days of the Sun and the other planets, [the time] consists of degrees numbered by the sun, fire, moon, eyes, water, and ocean.

They say that when half a circle has passed, the remaining portion of the asterism is what remains in the sky; twenty-three [degrees] are left when the half-circle is joined with the half of the *śaka* (the sign). Others know it to be such until the asterism of Aditi (Pūrvaphalgunī) arises; when their own time arrives, they all determine it at that very moment.

Where there is the conjunction of the upper wheel (cakrordha), that day becomes mine, fit for giving; one should perform auspicious rites during it. Some, however, declare that the three days following that [conjunction], as well as those preceding it, are inauspicious.

By calculation from the Sun and the Earth up to the Nairṛta [asterism], there are two stars here, known respectively as Kaṇṭaka and Sthūṇa. From those two, including the root-count, the number is two; thus the Kaṇṭaka and Sthūṇa named ones are reckoned. Raktasthūṇa is Vasiṣṭha; when deprived of the Earth, it would be Saṃhṛti in Kaka.

If the Sun or Rāhu is in the eighth house from the expenditure (Vyaya), or the Moon or Jupiter is in the ninth house, or Mars and Saturn are in the tenth house; or if Venus, Mercury, or Saturn reside in the seventh house—that house is designated as "Death" (Mṛtyu) and one should avoid it in all undertakings that cause distress.
Citra, Śūrpa, Śakra, Ambu, Viṣṇu, Kṣīra, Ādheśa, Budhnya, Aśvin, Antaka, Dhātṛ, Rudra, Deva, Sūra, and Ajādyā—these [months], joined with half a year, bring death.

One should subtract Jupiter, Rāhu, the Sun, and so forth, multiplied by three, from their respective revolutions; [the resulting] stars are nine, nine, eight, and two, with one eye and two eyes respectively.

The number of nāḍīs for the nakṣatras mounted on the Sun (arka) is, from both sides, three, three, six, and six; then one, two, two, and two. These are joined with the "one-eyed" (kāṇa) stars, which are praised as the supreme garland of hymns. Having subtracted the days and lunar mansions from the end of that day, the remainder is divided by seven;
the resulting "one-eyed" values, when multiplied by four, are declared by others to be the number of stars equal to the delight of the world.

In the asterisms beginning with Aśvinī, the portions of Capricorn (Makara) reaching from the tenth degree onwards are unfavorable for stinging [by insects] in sequence; those of the twelfth degree in Viśākhā and the following are likewise. For the portions of Aries (Meṣa), the first ten degrees are auspicious for the Kaurpi [insect], while the remaining degrees are unfavorable; one should avoid these in all undertakings, as they are known as the "Hot-rayed" (Uṣṇa-śikhā). The portions of Leo (Siṃha) in Mṛgaśirā and the following are also unfavorable at their ends. One should abandon all such times in every activity.

When the Moon is afflicted by a harsh planet in the Pūrṇātmajā yoga, they declare it to be the Gaṇḍa yoga occurring at the twenty-second degree; having thus described the forty-second [degree], these defects must be avoided in auspicious rites.

The asterisms beginning with Kṛttikā are proclaimed as the "doers" (kartṛ) of birth and so forth; they produce birth, prosperity, adversity, and security, and are respectively retrograde, favorable, friendly, and otherwise friendly, according to the sequence of the cycle.

The birth asterism, the eighth house from the birth asterism, the eighth house from the moon, and the eighth house from the ascendant are to be avoided; likewise, the sixth and twelfth houses from these, as well as other [inauspicious] positions, are abandoned for auspicious rites.
That star in which the group of factors beginning with birth does not exist as the eighty-eighth part is a nihilistic one; they abandon that very part, which is the mind itself.

When the nine-fold conjunction beginning with Parigha has arrived, and when the host of stars is calculated sequentially before and after the asterisms of Maitra (Anurādhā), Puṣya, Aditi (Punarvasu), Tvaṣṭṛ (Citrā), Śibi (Śatabhiṣaj), Suṣāri (Viśākhā), Kiraṇa (Kṛttikā), Mūla, and again from Maitra; and if the number of stars is equal to that of the Moon and Sun [twenty-seven], then the single Arghaśa is for my fault.
Aquarius, Taurus, Virgo, Scorpio, Cancer, Capricorn, Sagittarius, and Leo are the empty signs in the months beginning with Caitra.

One should abandon the limited [periods] in the months beginning with Caitra according to the sequence of zero, nine, six, twenty-six, zero, five, and eight: [the periods] of Viśvārya (Jyeṣṭhā), Citrā, Anila (Svātī), Bhama (Aśleṣā), Rasau (Punarvasu), Bhāgya (Pūrvaphalgunī), Viśva (Uttaraphalgunī), Arkaka (Hasta), Viśvarṣaka (Citrā), Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), Antya (Revatī), Śara (Ārdrā), Kṛti (Kṛttikā), Mitabha (Anurādhā), Soma (Mṛgaśiras), Citrā, Agni (Kṛttikā), Pūṣan (Puṣya), Ṣaḍ (Viśākhā), Viṃśa (Jyeṣṭhā), Drā (Bharaṇī), Agni (Kṛttikā), Mitra (Anurādhā), Asra (Aśleṣā), Vitu (Punarvasu), Aśva (Aśvinī), Śiva (Ārdrā), Viṣṇu (Śravaṇa), Mūla, Yama (Bharaṇī), and Indra (Jyeṣṭhā).

In the months numbered six, five, twelve, seven, four, ten, ten, one, seven, eight, nine, and nine, the days known as "voids" (śūnya) are proclaimed for the bright fortnight; these are to be avoided in the sequence of fifteen. In the dark fortnight, however, they begin from the second day.
In certain regions, the month of Pauṣa is considered empty by some; it is avoided for auspicious undertakings, especially for marriages.

A constellation that is released from, joined with, or conjoined by the planets Mercury, the Moon, and Venus—whether it be successively burnt, blazing, or smoking—one should abandon it even among auspicious [planets].

From Mars (Bhauma), [the yogas] are Bhauma, Bhūpa, Naga, Abdhi, Tatva, Manu, Jvālā, and Aṅgabhanga; from Jupiter (Guru), Vyādhi and Soma; from Mercury (Somaja), Aṣṭa and Saṃkṛti; from Venus (Śukra), Dhṛti and Kīlaka; from Saturn (Rāhu), Duhkha and Kaṇṭaka; from Rāhu (Pāta), Pañcama and Īśvara; and from Venus (Śukra), Parigha and Tithi—these are the two [sets] known by the wise as Khaṇḍa-khaṇḍa, [occurring] from the Sun's son (Saturn) at ten, six, four, and zero [degrees].

The solar month is known to be the transition of the sun through the zodiacal signs; the lunar month is to be understood as ending with the new moon (darśānta); the pitṛ-month consists of thirty days beginning from the first day of the fortnight (pakṣati); and the sidereal month is that which lasts until the moon returns to its original position in the lunar mansion (nakṣatra). These are the four types of months in order.
At the end of the first two, one should discard three nāḍīs (twenty-four minutes), and at the end of the last two, five nāḍīs.

The solar year consists of twelve months; the lunar year is likewise [twelve]; and another, known as the *prākṛta* (natural) year, begins from the heliacal rising of Jupiter from the Sun—it is thus that the year has been conceived by the wise in these three ways.

The six transits known as Viṣṇupada enter the fixed signs; beyond these are the four [transits] called Ṣaḍaśītimukha. O goat-faced one, the transits occurring in Aries, Capricorn, Libra, and Cancer should be known in order as the northern, southern, equinoctial, and solstitial.

One should abandon both the preceding and the following day due to the transition; likewise, for the sake of auspicious rites, one should avoid the day following the equinox (viṣuva) and half a day from each successive [junction].

One should avoid five days at the end of the seven-day period of the solar year, and five days at the beginning of the two subsequent periods; for all three of these, the wise know that one should avoid a fortnight at the end of the triad of years. Furthermore, ten days are to be avoided following a lunar eclipse or the death of a king.

At the end of seven days of the solar year, five days each at the beginning of the two following [years] are to be avoided; for all three of those, the wise know that the first fortnight at the end of the triad of years is inauspicious, as is the seventh day after an eclipse or the tenth day after the death of a king.

In the bright fortnight, starting from the first day of the lunar phase (pakṣati), the lunar days (tithis) are joined with the eyes (two); having subtracted the immovable (nine) from the others, that which remains is this group of seven, beginning with the auspicious day (Śrī).

For seven days, O son of Śrī Kālī, they are liberated from the Ear-of-Death (Kālakarṇī). Among those [days] called Jaya, Vardhana, and Arṇava, the odd ones are auspicious; the even ones are auspicious.

O Noble One, when Venus and Jupiter are visible to the people of Hanu, when they are setting, or when they have entered into a state of mutual conjunction, one should not perform auspicious rites during that time; nor should one undertake learning when they are eclipsed by Rahu.

If the son of Bhrigu (Saturn) speaks out of order—before or after the Sun—the days of the island of Bāṇa (the Kali Yuga) pass away; for these two, through the reversal of their sequence, the days are diminished. In marriage, this same sequence applies to the woman and the man; thus the Guru (Jupiter) is the elder of all, while for those two, the state of childhood and old age is mutually hostile to their undertakings.

Of the ten [periods] of Śakra, who has the face of a deer, one should abandon all those that are clearly manifest during the waxing moon, as well as the remaining [periods] in this auspicious rite, because they are afflicted by the planetary conjunction (vedha) of that [Śakra] period.

Dhātṛ, Śrīnātha, Rudra, Nila, Ravi, Varuṇa, Kāla, Mitra, Aryaman, Ambubhūdhnya, Aryamā, Śukra, Pūṣan, Aśvin, Nirṛti, Makha, Tvaṣṭṛ, Vasu, Indu, Bhadra, Indra, Agni, Arka, Viśvedevas, Aditi, Dahana, and Bhaga—these are the five groups (pañcavarga). O Sage, avoid the end of these groups as it is defective; in the performance of rites involving planets, one should avoid those stars that belong to the same group as the planet.

One should draw seven straight lines facing forward and that same number of lines across them; at the ends of those lines, one should mark the constellations beginning with Agni in their proper order. Where one planet stands facing another, they are together in a *śūla* (triple-pointed) configuration; if it is with benefics, it is called *mudita*, but if with malefics, it is a great *mahāśūla*.

If there is a pair of new-moon days (darśa) or a pair of full-moon days (pūrṇā) in the month of Āśvina, and if a pair of asterisms belonging to the constellation Puṣya (the Puṣṇayuga) should occur therein, some know that to be Jupiter (Bṛhaspati). If there is a conjunction of the sun and moon (arkenduyoga), or a pair [of such conjunctions], or if the sun is in the middle of two transits (saṃkrānti)—this is an intercalary month (adhimāsa). These three types of months are censured.

One should avoid three days on that day when the planets begin their retrograde motion (*vakra-gamana*), on which divine festivals and royal celebrations occur, and on which various portents and calamities happen; likewise, one should avoid three days following the departure of a messenger, at the birth of a son, during a meteor shower, when the quarters of the sky are aflame, during an earthquake, and during a planetary strike.

One should first draw two lines each for the pairs [of asterisms], and five horizontal lines below them; then, starting from the northeast corner (Īśa), one should mark the various directions such as the east. In whichever [asterism] the Moon and the planet are situated face-to-face, that single stick [of the diagram] is afflicted by the piercing of the asterism (*nakṣatrabheda*); it brings about calamity in the rite of marriage.
The fourteenth quarter of Viśvabhuk and the first four channels of Viṣṇu constitute what is called "eating through openings. A planet situated in this [period] pierces the donor star.

O Brahmin, one desiring auspiciousness should avoid the following: the commencement of the study of the Vedas (*adhyāya*), the first feeding (*prāśana*), the tonsure (*caula*), the binding of the topknot (*mauli-bandhana*), and the commencement of Vedic recitation (*graha-prāraṃbhaṇa*)—in these rites performed in sequence, malefics situated in the ascendant (*lagna*) or the seventh house (*saptama*) invariably destroy the fruits of all actions. This applies to all malefics, including Jupiter, the Moon, Venus, and Mars, when they are so positioned.

Vasiṣṭha declared that for all undertakings, the months of Āṣāḍha and Kārttika are the most excellent and supreme; he stated that for noble persons, these are auspicious for rites such as the *caula*, while other annual auspicious rites are performed during the remaining months. He further declared that the months of Mārgaśīrṣa, Phālguna, Jyeṣṭha, and Caitra—along with the four months joined with the asterism Puṣya and the month of Āṣāḍha—are also conducive to prosperity.

The wise do not perform these seven rites on the night of the new moon: agriculture, sowing seed, the consecration of a king, the commencement of a school of learning, the installation of a deity, the tonsure ceremony, and the naming rite.

Thus, fourteen rites such as plowing and others not explicitly mentioned here are to be performed at night; regarding these, including the drawing of the furrow, piercing [the ground], and entering a house, I shall now state the purification required for the eighth house.

In the three houses beginning with Cancer, when the Sun has entered them in succession—namely those numbered by the mountains (seven), the arrows (five), and the digits (nine)—they declare the fault known as *duṣpradharṣaṇa*, which has sixty-four aspects.

The *gaṇḍānta* of the zodiac signs, lunar days (*tithis*), and stars (*nakṣatras*) occurs at the ends of the fourth, sixth, and ninth divisions respectively; in those cases, one *nāḍī* on either side should be avoided. In the case of a sign, five *nāḍīs* are to be abandoned.

One should abandon the defects of the ascendant, the aspect of malefic planets, the rising of malefics, fear of thieves, and the state of being malefic; as well as the state of being joined with malefics in the eleventh, sixth, or third houses, and the state of being occupied by malefics in the angles (kendras).

One should avoid a residence with a foul odor, entry into a group of evildoers, and the inauspiciousness of the timing and state of actions; furthermore, one should abandon any unknown adverse omen of the moon in all undertakings, such as the occurrence of sneezing and the like.

The digits of the moon multiplied by thirty-six, having subtracted the elapsed tithis, are multiplied by three and divided by twenty-seven; the result should be understood as the state of the karma based on its manifestation.

A man fallen from his position; an ascetic devoted to another’s young wife; a thief; one who has mounted an elephant; a king seated upon the lion-throne; a leader of the army; a virtuous man; one breathless; one whose head is severed; one whose hands and feet are cut off; one bound in fetters; one whose wealth is destroyed; one who recites the Vedas; and one who remembers his past good conduct while performing righteous deeds—[these are the ones who do not fall].

One born under Saturn is a repository of good lineage, associated with the virtuous, comparable to a refuge, devoted to exposition, a lord of enemies yet conquered by them, and one who has departed from his own country. He is a servant, a destroyer of half his dwelling, and possesses a court along with his ministers. He is a supreme plunderer of the earth, accompanied by his wife, terrified of elephants, fearful of battle, cowering in dread, and a giver of water and fire.

Wandering here, afflicted by hunger, he eats coarse food; wounded, he dwells with his wife, filled with anxiety; the king, though possessed of splendor, wanders about distressed. One lies upon a bed attended by servants and meditates on friends along with his wife; another, having performed good deeds, remains at ease, drinking milk and eating delicacies.
Having thus determined these fivefold lunar actions within the signs beginning with Aries, one should declare their results in all undertakings according to those results.

O Moon, these states—dwelling in one's own home, lack of contentment, devotion to the honored rank of kings, the destruction of life, sovereignty, addiction to virtues suited to one's own lineage, freedom from disease, attendance at court, being tormented by fear and hunger, lying on beds of straw, and eating with clenched fists—are sung of by the wise as occurring even in the abode of Indra due to the power of destiny.

The disease of the head is joyfulness; the disease of the eyes is the state of happiness; the disease of the tongue is the absence of pride; the fierce fever is the shedding of tears; the consumption of vomit is the shaking of the head; and the disease of the belly is the wearing of golden ornaments.
Playing, licking, laughing, crying, setting out on a journey, madness, immersion in water, entering a forest, and conflict.

Abiding according to one's own will, fear of hunger, acquisition of sacred scriptures, spontaneous gatherings, battle, meritorious deeds, sinful conduct, cruel acts, and great joy—these are declared by the wise to be the lunar periods (candravelā).

Now follows the examination of the refutation of defects (*doṣāpavāda*). In this Kali age, alas, unfortunate people cannot find even a single moment free from all these defects. Since they meet their destruction through the multitude of such accusations, I shall here describe them in their proper order, beginning with the first.

In the case of auspicious rites, the defective lunar days (chidra-tithis) for the first four [lunar days] are, in order: nine, nine, eleven, and ten; beyond these ghaṭikās, they should be known as auspicious.

Gārgya declared the day of the Sun’s appearance to be auspicious for the propitiation of the gods, the administration of mantras and medicines, mounting horses, the consecration of kings, the performance of vows, and the commencement of learning and agriculture; others, however, held it to be auspicious for all these matters except for tearing the sky and supporting the celestial nymph Rambhā.

Salutations to you! Regarding undertakings during the bright fortnight, the rising of Venus, the days of the week, and the divisions of time are declared auspicious; however, when Mercury is weak, the Viṣṭi yoga is always inauspicious, as is the rising of the moon at a wedding.

Even on the day of an inauspicious planet, if a task must necessarily be performed there, one should select a time-period (horā) of an auspicious portion; however, it should not be taken from a planet that is in its sign of debilitation.

When the self has been attained through the intellect regarding all days of planetary influence (graha-vāsara), which are by nature auspicious, they should be known as having middling results; therefore, among those that are auspicious, they are to be accepted, with the exception of the two—the Earth (Saturday) and the Son of the Earth (Tuesday).

Starting from the first day of the bright fortnight (pratipad), there are thirty days here for those possessing intelligence. These are to be known, in sequence, by the numbers of earth (1), fire (3), arrows (5), Smara’s shafts (5), arrows (5), Brahmā (4), and again Brahmā (4). They are classified as difficult, middling, excellent, most honored, best, middling, and very difficult. It is said by some that even in the dark fortnight, these three types of strengths are to be applied according to the planets.

The morning period (prātaḥkāla) lasts for six nāḍikās from sunrise, and the junction (saṃgava) likewise for six; similarly, the period known as midday (mādhyāhnaka), the afternoon (aparāhṇa), and the evening (sāyaṃkāla) [each last for six]; one should know that the two remaining periods here are the same.

Even when combined with an inauspicious weekday, or lacking the conjunction of an auspicious day, the Sun situated in its period of accumulation (upacaya) removes defects such as the five-fold obstacles (pañcadūṣaṇa).

Bharadvāja said: When the Moon is in Puṣya, Śaśin (Mṛgaśiras), or Śukra (Śravaṇa) conjoined with Mars, Saturn, or Jupiter respectively, there is destruction of the king and others; then again, in all the lunar days [beginning] from the seventh, eighth, and fourteenth, when the Sun is in its own or exaltation sign and is aspected by benefics, Jupiter is the bringer of victory.
During the first watch of the night, when Kaṇṭha is in the middle and Gulika is at the end, two nāḍīs must invariably be avoided.

If the lord of the week (vāreśa) is strong and situated in the Gulika’s form, or if a benefic planet is in the ascendant; if the Sun is in the seventh house and is auspiciously placed in a quadrant or a trine; if the Moon is in the third house and is aspected by benefics while situated in its own Navāṃśa; and if the lord of the ascendant is conjoined with benefics—then there shall be no fear from the blow of the husband.

In the night, the Moon is easily subdued when it is in its sign of death or afflicted by malefic planets; however, during the day, even such a Moon may be rendered capable of remedying the defects of the Lagna if it is endowed with strength.

When the Viṣṭi-karaṇa occurs during the latter half of the lunar day, it is auspicious; when it occurs during the first half, it is inauspicious. Furthermore, the earth at that time should be taken as being outside the rising period (udaya-yāma) of its own sign, provided the lord of the ascendant is strong and situated in its own division (navāṃśa).

Some say that at the time of dawn, during the conjunction (yoga), the instruction on the Barīyāna [is given]; others, however, state that the conjunction lasts until midday, while the other three conjunctions end with their respective separations.
The Moon, situated in Taurus, Virgo, Capricorn, or Pisces, aspected by benefics and occupying a benefic Navāṃśa, is powerful enough to remove the defect of Udvartanā and Dāhadoṣa.

The powerful Moon, even when not full, if situated in its own exaltation degree, its own exaltation sign, or in a *vargottama* division, certainly carries one across the low-flowing channels of the *nimna-nāḍīs*.

The third *kāla* division, known as *gaṇḍa*, is censured; it destroys the fault called "the time of the auspicious" (*śubhakāla*) that arises at the time of death. The first [division] is [also] condemned.

If the Sun and Mars are situated in their own signs or their own vargas and are aspected by benefics, they are called *kaṇṭaka* and *sthūla*; when these two are joined with one [benefic], they remove the affliction arising from the Moon.

If the lords of the third and twelfth houses are situated in the seventh house, they are declared to be "death-signs"; however, if they are aspected by their own lord or by Jupiter, they are auspicious. Even if they are conjoined with or aspected by Jupiter, they are irreproachable in all undertakings.

A strong, auspicious planet situated in a quadrant during the *śiśu* period destroys the defect of being born blind caused by the aspect of those two [the Sun and Moon]; likewise, a malefic planet occupying a benefic *navāṃśaka* there bestows happiness, or one that has risen with the light of a beautiful eye [the Moon].

In the first birth, one should avoid all auspicious and inauspicious rites except for those involving clothing and ornaments; one should not perform the *bhukti* (enjoyment) or *nāvābhojī* (boat-eating) rites. Having excluded the procedure for oil massage along with the *nikṣepa* (depositing), and the alkaline substances, the remaining auspicious acts should be performed; so say the sages regarding the other two births.

One should avoid all these misfortunes in the first five *vadhya* (mortal) yogas; in the middle ones, one should avoid those measured by four and three [planets]; and in the last ones, one should avoid those measured by fire (three). However, a strong benefic planet situated in its own division (*aṃśaka*) and aspected by gentle planets dispels the misfortunes arising from birth and the faults of the year, provided it is not afflicted by malefics.

The eighth house from one's birth is not considered unfavorable simply because of its friendship with the lord of that eighth house; rather, the state of being a friend between the lord of the birth sign (Janmeśa) and the lord of the tenth house (Karmeśvara) truly destroys even the most fierce malefic defect.

If, in a pair of lunar mansions, the second and third are occupied by the Moon and Jupiter respectively, and the first and last are occupied by Saturn and Mars in order, then it is called *Rekārgala* (the bolt of obstruction), which is weak according to the wise; otherwise, some declare this defect to exist only in the Avanti region.
If two strong planets are situated in auspicious vargas, or in their own vargas, and are aspected by benefic planets, they remove the defect of Ekārgala; thus others say, like Ravi and Śaśin.

If the Ascendant is conjoined with or aspected by its own lord, Jupiter, or Mercury, it removes the defects of emptiness, sorrow, and the like. Furthermore, a benefic planet situated in a quadrant (kendram), a trine (trikoṇam), or endowed with strength, removes the fear of emptiness regarding the month, the lunar mansion (nakṣatra), the zodiac sign (rāśi), and the lunar day (tithi).

When the planet Mars is scorched by the Sun, it returns to its natural state after one month; after one year, it is afflicted by portents such as eclipses, meteors, and conflagrations. After half a year, it is likewise corrupted by such calamities.

Just as water that has been heated by the summer sun is increased again at the end of the heat through contact with falling rain, so too does that which was burnt by the movement of Rahu increase further through conjunction with the bright lunar digits at the conclusion of the solar heat.
Like the moon moving through the midst of the scorched bear and the burning planet, this powerful one dispels the affliction and protects this weak army besieged by the strong.
If a planet situated in its exaltation causes this defect while in the celestial realm, that very planet, when aspected by a benefic planet, removes that defect.

On the eighth day of either fortnight, or on the days of the two teachers of poetry (the full moon and new moon), one should avoid looking at the sun during the day; likewise, they avoid the *saṃsarpa*, the *mahaḥ*, the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*), and the month of *nabhas* when performing the rites prescribed for those months. They also avoid the six [specific lunar days].

Gārgya and others declare that all rites prescribed for the night—beginning from the dawn of the sixth lunar day until sunrise, or likewise from sunset until three ghaṭīs later—should be performed at the time of dawn, whether it be tonsure, the sacred thread ceremony, or any other.

If the lords of the Moon sign and the ascendant are strong and the ascendant is a head-rising (mūrdhodaya), then the malefic planets, provided they are not situated in the seventh house, do not cause defects through their aspect on the ascendant.
When Saturn is in its own exaltation or its own sign, and Jupiter is weak in the ascendant, then the aspect of Saturn or Rahu situated in the seventh house does not cause harm.
When the moon is eclipsed, when half a year has passed, or when it is auspicious, strong, and rising, the conjunction of two planets should be taken as auspicious for both good and evil undertakings.

The defect of two malefics being situated between the ascendant and the [relevant] planet is destroyed by Jupiter when he is strong and occupies a quadrant; likewise, a benefic occupying a quadrant, a trine, the eleventh house, or the first house (mūrti) and possessing strength destroys that defect.
When malefic and inauspicious planets have entered unfavorable positions, they become givers of auspicious results if they are strong in their own houses or situated in their own signs.

If the Moon is situated in a malefic sign or Navamsha, is not aspected by benefics, and occupies a benefic house, it produces auspicious results even while waxing; likewise, even when situated in the sixth or eighth house, it brings about welfare.

The Moon, when situated in a gentle sign, occupying a benefic portion, aspected by benefics, and joined by auspicious planets; or when placed in the angles (kendras) of its own sign, its own navāṃśa, or its own decanate; or even when located in the angles of Jupiter during its waxing fortnight—such a powerful Moon, though performing fourfold actions, destroys its own defects arising from an evil navāṃśa as well as those produced by its own [evil] portion.

O Lord, the Moon, when situated in a benefic sign and being strong, destroys the defects arising from the influence of inauspicious divisions (asaumyavarga) and those produced by evil deeds, unfavorable times, and the like, provided it is not aspected by malefics.
When Jupiter is situated in its own varga, in a quadrant, or in a benefic division, and is aspected by benefics, then at that time the fault of the Moon's conjunction with malefics is neutralized.

The preceptor Jupiter, being well-illuminated and situated in an angle (kendram), is exceedingly powerful, especially when placed in the ascendant; likewise, Venus or Mercury, situated in their own division (varga), destroys all defects in that same manner.

Situated in the trines from its own sign, in the angles, or in the Navāṃśas of the Sun, Moon, Jupiter, or the Sun, the ever-increasing Sun-rayed One constantly destroys all defects and brings about auspicious actions.

If the odd-numbered degrees of the ascendant are occupied by benefics, or if Jupiter, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Mars, Mercury, and Venus are situated in mutual kendras; or if there are many benefics for the lord of the ascendant with numerous unimpaired points in their ṛṣṭavargas; or if benefics occupy the degrees of the *samāśrita* (concordant) divisions and the *grahalābha* (planetary gain) divisions—then [the yoga is auspicious].

Benefic planets situated in the ninth-parts (navāṃśas) of the ascendant, its trines, or its domicile; Jupiter in a quadrant and in the ninth-part of the Sun; Venus, Mercury, and the Moon in the quadrant of the Sun; Jupiter in the quadrant of the Moon; benefics occupying the fifth or ninth houses from the sign and ninth-part reached by the Moon and situated in quadrants; and benefics possessing strength when placed in the signs, navāṃśas, or quadrants of the Moon, the lord of the self (the ascendant), or the lords of the ascendant and the upacaya houses—these are auspicious.

The lord of the year, along with the minister, occupies the excellent elephant or the throne; the Moon is in the tenth house in a favorable sign, and Jupiter is situated in the ascendant. The lord of the hour, the year, and the day is strong in the ascendant as a benefic planet; from the ascendant, the sixth and third houses are occupied by malefic planets of intense strength.

These yogas, which have been described here primarily, all destroy defects without exception. There are thousands of others not mentioned here; they have not been stated for fear of excessive bulk in the book.

Even those who are energetic in this regard become weak due to the defects of their local customs; for those defects established by the customs of other regions constitute an exception to that very place.
In the absence of an emergency, this is the highest time; in a moderate emergency, it is moderate. Even if he is wicked, he may be accepted during a great emergency on account of his own reputation.
Now follows the description of the six qualities (*ṣadguṇa*).

Since it is extremely difficult to find a time that is entirely free from defects, one should undertake an auspicious action even when there are many qualities and only a few defects. I shall here describe some of those excellent moments (*sumuhūrta*) regarding the qualities mentioned by the sages in the statement: "One should begin a virtuous deed."
The first great quality of time is that its defects are few and difficult to find; the second very great quality is the absence of all defects.
The speech of a distinguished Brahmin, the heliacal rising of a benefic planet, and the placement of the ascendant in the divisions of a benefic—these three are recorded as great virtues.

The five-limbed yoga (*pañcāṅgayoga*), which consists of unimpeded performance of prescribed duties and is the word of the Lord of Qualities (*guṇanāyaka*), is called the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), the king of qualities (*guṇarāja*). The seven-limbed yoga (*saptāṅgayoga*) is the king of the kings of hosts (*gaṇarājarāja*).

That kingdom of the auspicious moment—bestowed by a clear-sighted astrologer according to the rules, granting happiness, difficult for those of little merit to attain, and equal to the perfection of the seven constituents of sovereignty—is obtained through well-performed deeds.

Benefic planets situated in the angles (kendras), trines, or the fifth house cause injury to siblings; however, when all these same planets are situated in the eleventh house, they bestow auspicious results in virtuous undertakings.
The moon, the stars, and the increase of water; the jar being non-empty and the pots being full—this yoga, called Pañcapūrṇa, is the king of virtues and is desired for auspicious rites.

Among the lords of the directions, there are three known as Madhyama-stambha, Saṃjñapti, and Srasti; and three known as Pārśva, Ghaṭa, and Anya-stambha. Wherever the Sun stands empty, that is called Kuṃbha; likewise, wherever it is full, that is called Anya-stambha.
A fifteenth part of the day is a *muhūrta* known by the name *tāraka*; fifteen such parts are said to constitute the day, and they are likewise remembered for the night.

Ārdrā, Uraga (Aśleṣā), Mitra (Anurādhā), Makhā (Pūrvaphalgunī), Asujala (Śatabhiṣaj), Viśva (Uttarāṣāḍhā), Abhijit, Viriñci (Rohiṇī), Indra (Jyeṣṭhā), Aindrāgni (Viśākhā), Mūla, Varuṇa (Śravaṇa), Aryaman (Hasta), Bhaga (Pūrvaphalgunī), and Tārā (Revatī) are the muhūrtas of the day.
The *niśas*, *muhūrtas*, Rudra, Bhadrā, and the eight stars are said to follow in succession; Aditi, Guru, Viṣṇu, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Samīra are likewise proclaimed by the sages.

The muhūrtas of the day and night that have been described as having the form of stars should be avoided; those consisting of eleven [units] are auspicious, while others are highly esteemed for virtuous rites.

The Muhūrta called Abhijit destroys the defects of portents, inauspicious lunar mansions, and Vyatīpāta; it causes success even when one travels toward the southern direction or toward intermediate quarters.
The Bānara, Aryama, and Daivata muhūrtas belong to the Sun; the Brāhmya to the Moon; the Nairṛta to Mars; the Pitrya and Vahnidaivata to Mercury;
Abhijit to Jupiter; the Pitrya and Brāhmya to Venus; and the Brahma and Budha-daivata to Saturn. These muhūrtas, along with Sārpa, are to be avoided by the wise during the day according to the rules.
The designations previously mentioned are Raudra, Śveta, Maitra, Ārabhaṭa, Sāvitra, Vairāja, and Gāndharva.
Ābhijit, Rauhiṇa, Bala, the one called Vijaya, Nairṛta, Śakra, Vāruṇa, Bhaga, and Daivata—these are to be known as the muhūrtas of the day.
Ajijit, vairāja, śveta, sāvitra, maitra, balivijaya, and śubhakarmasiddhijanaka—these seven have been proclaimed by those who know the Purāṇas.

When the lunar day is excellent, the asterism is Tārā, the tithi is auspicious, the muhūrta is good, and the occasion is favorable, this yoga named Pañcakalyāṇa is declared by Gārgya to bestow all prosperity.

The days of the week beginning with Sunday, the asterisms Guru (Jupiter), Mūla, Hasta, and Citrā, and the half-day periods of Śravaṇa, Indu (Moon), and Tārā; the asterisms Bhadrapadā, Aśvinī, Viśvā (Uttarāṣāḍhā), Bhaga (Pūrvāphalgunī), and Prajeśa (Rohiṇī); and the tithis of Niśvāgni (Agnitithi) and Citrā (Citrā-tithi)—these are the [auspicious] times for the two [types of] rites.

The thirteenth lunar day, the asterisms Mūla and the last three of the Maghā group (Pūrva-phalgunī, Uttara-phalgunī, and Hastā), Bhaga, Pracetas, the Maruts, and Saṃnanda; these, together with Bhadrā and the Vasu-giving Tārā, are in order the conjunctions known as Amṛta.
Uttarāsāḍhā, Śaila, Puṣya, Viṣṇu, Maitra, Māruta, Vasu, Pracetas, Mitra, Daṇḍadhara, Pauṣṇatāraka, Saumitra, Bhaga, and Viśvavedhana.

Maitra, Āśvinī, Māruta, Mātrikṣya, the triad of Bhaga, Nairṛta, Pauṣṇa, and Dasra; Dhātṛ, Agni, the triad of Vāyu, Vārinātha, along with Sārkādi, the days of the week, and the auspicious Siddhi-yogas.

Citrā, Agnīśvara (Pūrvābhādrapadā), Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), Dinapati (Pūrvāphalgunī), Vāreśa (Śravaṇa), Nandā (Revatī), Tathā (Anurādhā), Ambu (Pūrvāṣāḍhā), Bhujaṅga (Āśleṣā), Pauṣṇa (Revatī), and Marut (Svātī) are known as the Yogaparā and are auspicious for Mars. Nandā is auspicious for Venus, Mars, and the Moon; Bhadrā for Mercury and Venus; Jayā for the Moon and Mars; Cāndrī (Mūla) for Mercury and Venus; Varā (Pūrvāphalgunī) for Saturn; and Pūrṇā (Uttarāphalgunī) for Jupiter bestow success.

The lunar days (tithis), weekdays (vāras), asterisms (nakṣatras), and planetary conjunctions (yogas) that have been prescribed for auspicious rites grant success especially when performed during those specific combinations of weekday, asterism, and yoga.

The *nāḍī* (one-thirtieth part of a day) is composed of the following numbers of *kalās* (minutes) respectively: 32, 31, 30, 29, 28, 27, 26, 25, 24, 23, 22, 21, 20, 19, 18, 17, 16, 15, 14, 13, 12, 11, 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, and 1. Beyond these thirty divisions in the zodiacal signs (*bha*), there are further *nāḍīs* which are immortal.

All the Amṛta-ghaṭikās should be taken like the Amṛta-yoga for auspicious rites; it need not be said that they grant auspicious results when known by one skilled in the medical treatment of poison, disease, and so forth.

When the Moon, the lord of the sign occupied by it, the lord of the ascendant, and the lord of the [relevant] house are endowed with strength and the aspect or conjunction of benefic planets, they declare that time to be one of superior merit.

Having performed the calculation of the planetary *aṣṭavarga* from the time of birth according to the method taught by the Sun (Āditya), one should determine the auspiciousness of the planets situated in the signs, months, houses, and positions through the influence of many asterisms (*nakṣatra*) and their conjunctions, after having analyzed the results for the various actions.

These alone are the qualities here, as well as the established faults and censures; others have declared that their various divisions are exceedingly subtle and have been proclaimed in detail by the lords of sages.

Vyāsa [taught] delight of mind; Manu, great virtue; Pradhāna, the rising of the vital breath; Kapila, the vital soul (jīva); Śukra, the dawn; Mṛṣi, Gārgya, and Trirūpa, the sacred revelation (śruti); and Viṣṇu, the word of the Brahmins in all auspicious rites.

Just as an official propitiates a king with devotion, so did Sumantra propitiate his guru; having honored the astrologer, he was granted an auspicious moment by him, for otherwise it would not have been favorable.

The astrologer who is devoted to the worship of the gods, who has mastered the mantras, who knows the seven constituents [of the state], and who understands the strength and weakness of virtues and defects—whatever result he declares regarding a moment is true; it is like the word of the Ṛṣis, not false.

In the Drekkāṇa, the Navāṃśa, the Kālahorā, the Ascendant, the planets, the rising signs, and the aspects—whichever among these possesses strength, one should describe the characteristics of that time during the Muhūrta, such as the narration of objects corresponding to it, its arrival, and so forth.

Thus ends the collection of verses defining the merits, defects, and exceptions regarding auspicious moments (*muhūrta*) in the *Viśvasahitā*, within the *Śāntikamalākara*, in the northern section (*uttarapiṭhikā*).

The venerable Mādhavācārya—who is a personification of omniscience, having reached the further shore of the ocean of all systems of thought (*sarvatantra-svatantra*) through his mastery of words, sentences, and means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); who is preeminent in his skill in composing great works such as the *Vedabhāṣya*; and who composed this *Vidyāmādhavīya* out of compassion for the world to provide a source of guidance for those seeking astrological knowledge—has produced this invaluable treatise along with its Telugu commentary, the *Tātparyavivaraṇa*, so that it may be accessible to all people. (Madras)

O Brahmaśrī, who has performed the *pajitu* (worship) during the Christian era! May you, Rāmasvāmi Śāstrulavāru, graciously reveal and manifest this science. For one born under the influence of the *muhūrta*, this is indispensable; it is the root of all matters, the time, and the giver of results. By examining the auspicious and inauspicious consequences, one may achieve victory in all undertakings. Having sought this complete and unobstructed science, and having mastered its essence, one shall indeed rejoice in the objects of the senses. May you be filled with bliss.

The Śuddha-Ratha-saptamī vow in the month of Māgha;
the Daṇḍirāja-nakta-vrata.
Śu || Vasantapañcamī Śu || Bhīṣmāṣṭamī Śu || Tiladvādaśī
Kṛ. Regarding the Śivarātri vow, it should be observed on the night when [the moonrise] extends through the night;
in the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna, on the fourth lunar day known as Śāntā.
Śu || The Holikā-vrata; the Madanapūrṇimā; the Vasantotsava; the beginnings of the Kalpas.
The third day of Vaiśākha, the third of Phālguna,
the third of Caitra, as well as the fifth of the bright fortnight;
the thirteenth of the bright fortnight in Māgha, and the seventh of Kārttika.
The ninth day of Mārgaśīrṣa, the third day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna—
these seven days are of great merit and auspiciousness.
This is the summary determination of the Sāma-vrata.
The *Sarvatra Kṛṣṇa Saṃkaṣṭa Gaṇeśa Vrata* is to be observed at the time of moonrise;
the *Śivarātri* throughout the month of Kṛṣṇa is to be taken when it extends through the *pradoṣa* period;
and on Tuesdays in the month of Śrāvaṇa, the *Maṅgalagaurī Vrata* is observed.
On Saturdays in the month of Śrāvaṇa—the Vekaṭeśvara Vrata;
on Mondays in the month of Śrāvaṇa—the Śiva-nakta Vrata.
This is the determination of specific Yoga-vratas.
The conjunction of the eighth lunar day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra with the asterism Punarvasu and the weekday Wednesday is known as the Caitra-śuklāṣṭamī.
Having bathed according to the rules at dawn, one shall obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
The tenth lunar day, known as Daśahārā, is a conjunction occurring in the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha on the tenth tithi, when the weekday is Wednesday and the nakṣatra is Hasta;
it is further characterized by the Vyatīpāta yoga, the Garānanda karaṇa, the Moon in Virgo, and the Sun in Taurus.
The Gaṅgā-vrata bestows merit everywhere; the Bhānu-saptamī-vrata occurs on every conjunction of a Sunday with the seventh lunar day of the bright fortnight;
and the Bhauma-caturthī-vrata occurs on every conjunction of a Tuesday with the fourth lunar day.
Everywhere, on the conjunction of the white fortnight with Wednesday, there is the Budhāṣṭamī vow;
everywhere, on the conjunction of the white fortnight with Thursday, there is the Jīvavāraikādaśī vow;
and everywhere, on the conjunction of the white fortnight with Friday, there is the Bārgavarākā vow.

Everywhere, when there is a conjunction with Saturday on the dark fortnight, it is the Śanipradoṣavrata; everywhere, when there is a conjunction with Monday on the new moon day, it is the Amāsomavāravratam;
[these are] the Ārdodaya and Mahodaya yogas.
If the new moon (amā) is conjoined with Arka-pāta (Rāhu), Śravaṇa, Puṣya, or Māgha, it should be known as Ārchi-udaya; Mahā-udaya is slightly less than that.
In this yoga, bathing in the ocean, giving gold, performing śrāddha, and other such acts yield excellent results.
O Brahman, when the conjunction of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa occurs during the bright fortnight under the Viṣṇu asterism (Śravaṇā),
or on the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) in the month of Nabhas (Bhādrapada) joined with the Moon or Mars;
In the *atigaṇḍa* yoga, one should perform auspicious rites;
in that *lakṣmīnārāyaṇa* yoga, one should worship the Deliverer (*uddhara*).
When the six-fold yoga occurs, whether by day or by night.
The Hari-Śaṅkara yoga occurs on the ninth lunar day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada when it is conjoined with the tenth;
it is established through the Śiva yoga when Punarvasu is joined with Puṣya.
In the month of Kārttika, when the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) coincides with the Garaja yoga, it is a great festival.
Whether by day or by night, this Hari-Śaṅkara yoga lasts for eight ghaṭikās; one who performs a vow during this time gains the merit of all the gods.
The determination of Jayantī:
on the bright [fortnight] of Caitra, in the afternoon, is Kūrmajayantī;
on the bright [fortnight] of Vaiśākha, in the evening, is Varāhajayantī.
Bhādrapada Śukla: Tṛsiṃhajayantī at midday.
Vaiśākha Śukla: Vāmanajayantī in the evening.
Bhādrapada Śukla: Paraśurāmajayantī at midday.
Vaiśākha, bright fortnight: at midday—[or] at dusk (this is the majority view)—Caitra, bright fortnight: at midday. Śrī Rāma-jayantī.
Śrāvaṇa, dark fortnight: at midnight, the incarnation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

On the bright fortnight of Āśvina, in the evening, is the *Buddhāvatāra*; on the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, in the evening, is the *Kalkijayantī*. These [festivals] are to be observed when they extend through their respective times. Here, regarding the incarnations of Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Buddha, and Kalki, other months such as Āṣāḍha, other lunar days (*tithis*) such as Ekādaśī, and other times such as the morning have been mentioned according to other scriptural statements; these are to be settled according to the specific Kalpa. Devotees should observe the fasts according to the specific positions accepted by themselves. However, the *Jayaṃtīs* of Śrī Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and Nṛsiṃha alone are obligatory and must be observed by all cultured people (*śiṣṭas*).
The determination of the beginnings of the Manvantaras and Yugas:
the beginning of the Uttama-manvantara is on the bright fortnight of Caitra;
the beginning of the Raucya-manvantara is on the bright fortnight of Caitra.

Jyeṣṭha, bright fortnight, Tuesday: the beginning of the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara. Āṣāḍha, bright fortnight: the beginning of the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara. Āṣāḍha, bright fortnight: the beginning of the Rudrasāvarṇika Manvantara.
The beginning of the Sūryasāvarṇika Manvantara is on the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa;
the beginning of the Tāmasa Manvantara is on the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada;
the beginning of the Svārociṣa Manvantara is on the bright fortnight of Āśvina.
The beginning of the Svāyambhuva Manvantara is on the bright fortnight of Kārttika;
the beginning of the Indrasāvarṇika Manvantara is on the bright fortnight of Puṣya;
the beginning of the Raivata Manvantara is on the bright fortnight of Aśvina.

The beginning of the Vaivasvata Manvantara is on the bright fortnight of Māgha; the beginning of the Brahma-sāvarṇika Manvantara is on the dark fortnight of Phālguna; the beginning of the Agni-sāvarṇika Manvantara is on the dark fortnight of Phālguna.

"Indeed, that day is like Agni; it is like a guest; O friend, on the dark [fortnight] there is the eclipse of the sun; it is like the sun and the moon; it is the night of the new moon; these are the Manvādi days of the month of Madhu"—thus it is stated in the Nirṇayasindhu.
The afternoon is the primary time for these.

The beginning of the Yuga (Yugādi) occurs on the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha; the beginning of the Tretā Yuga occurs on the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada; and the beginning of the Kali Yuga [occurs on the same].

The beginning of the Kṛta Yuga occurs on the bright fortnight of Kārttika; the beginning of the Tretā Yuga occurs on the dark fortnight of Māgha. When it falls on the bright fortnight, it is observed in the forenoon; when on the dark fortnight, it is observed in the afternoon.
The determination of the meritorious time (*puṇyakāla*) for the transits (*saṃkrānti*):
some say that for Aries, it is [six] *ghaṭikās* before and after;
for Taurus, the former [six] *ghaṭikās*.
Midday: 18 ghaṭikās;
in Cancer: the first part—6 ghaṭikās; in Leo: the first part—6 ghaṭikās.
In Virgo, the subsequent *ghaṭikās*;
in Libra, the preceding and subsequent *ghaṭikās*.
In Scorpio, the first [period] consists of *ghaṭikās*; in Sagittarius, the latter [period] consists of *ghaṭikās*;
in Capricorn, the latter [period] consists of *ghaṭikās*.

In Aquarius (*Kumbha*), the first two *ghaṭikās* [of the day] are meritorious; in Pisces (*Mīna*), the latter two *ghaṭikās* are meritorious. On days with less than two *ghaṭikās* remaining [at sunrise], the [first] two *ghaṭikās* are meritorious even in Virgo, Pisces, Dhanus, and Capricorn. In the morning, during a very short period of less than two *ghaṭikās*, the latter two *ghaṭikās* alone are meritorious even in Taurus, Leo, Libra, Scorpio, and Aquarius. Regarding the transit (*saṃkrānti*) into Cancer at dawn, some say the previous day is meritorious. When the transit occurs at night, if it is before midnight, the latter half of the previous day is meritorious; if the transit occurs exactly at midnight, the [latter half of the] previous day is meritorious. If the transit occurs precisely at midnight, both days are meritorious.

Generally, merit accrues on both the preceding and the following days; however, at the time of the Sun’s transit (ayana-saṃkrānti), merit belongs to the preceding day alone. Three ghaṭikās after sunset constitute the evening twilight (saṃdhyā); during a Capricorn transit (makara-saṃkrānti) occurring therein, the preceding day is meritorious. Three ghaṭikās before sunrise constitute the morning twilight; during a Capricorn transit occurring therein, the preceding day is meritorious. Three ghaṭikās before sunrise constitute the morning twilight; during a Cancer transit (karka-saṃkrānti) occurring therein, the following day is meritorious.
Thus concludes the index of the determination of all lunar days (*tithi*) and times, compiled from authoritative treatises such as the *Nirṇayakaumudī* and the *Dharmasindhu*.
In each particular case, matters such as specific determinations should be understood by the eminent Brāhmaṇas residing there, in accordance with the traditional conduct of the ancient learned.
Salutation to the great sages, such as Jaimini, Āpastamba, and others, who are the determiners of Dharma.
The completion of the work:
[I bow to] the Lord of Gods, whose form is peaceful, who reclines upon the serpent, whose navel is a lotus,
who takes the form of the universe, who resembles the sky, who is cloud-colored, and whose limbs are auspicious.

I bow to Viṣṇu, the beloved of Lakṣmī, the lotus-eyed one, who is accessible through the meditation of yogis in their hearts, the remover of the fear of worldly existence, and the sole protector of all the worlds.
The illustrious Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa, having thoroughly churned the entire essence of the multitude of scriptures of the Vedas and Āgamas, composed this treatise named Śānti-kamalākara.
Having gathered many objects that support it found in various places, he associated with them; indeed, this was a perfect sealing.
By this, may the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, the Great Lord, be pleased; may they who uphold the Śruti and Smṛti scriptures grant their grace.
Śambhu is the one to be honored by the learned, the bestower of boons, the wise, the beautiful, and the author of the scriptures;
he assumes both female and male forms, the barren, the impeller, and the follower who approves.
May there be peace; may this work named *Kamalākara* reach its completion; may there be victory for Dharma and the destruction of Adharma;
may there be virtuous intentions among living beings, and may there be well-being for all in the world.
May the regional protectors attain victory over all directions;
may there be well-being for all, and may every auspiciousness prevail— Śrī Śrī Śrī Śrī Śrī.
